Mideast escalation risks an oil shock ahead of the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
21:09:44 UTC
06:09:44 KST

Mideast escalation risks an oil shock ahead of the midterms
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A drone attack on Saudi Arabia’s most crucial pipeline has led to its closure, potentially taking 4% of the world’s supply off the market.
- Signs are emerging that the latest attacks could trigger an acute market panic.
WASHINGTON — A bold military push by Iran and its proxies to create a choke hold on global oil supplies has once again caught the Trump administration off guard, threatening a market shock and a steep political backlash in the U.S. midterm elections.
A drone attack on Saudi Arabia’s most crucial pipeline, which siphons crude oil from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, has led to the line’s closure, potentially taking 4% of the world’s supply off the market.
And a lightning advance by Iran-backed Houthi rebels along Yemen’s Red Sea coast threatens commercial traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, second only to Hormuz in its importance to regional shipping.
The strikes put the Trump administration in a newly precarious position less than two months until the November midterms. President Trump’s military advisors have warned him that any retaliation could lead to a further depletion of critically low U.S. munition stockpiles, endanger American personnel in the field and risk escalation that could spiral out of Washington’s control.
On Tuesday, the global price of oil topped $107 a barrel — the first time in U.S. campaign history that an incumbent president has faced rising pump prices at this stage of an election.
The Iranian strikes come as Europe and the United States are facing increased energy needs entering the fall and winter months, and as Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure have surged, pushing diesel prices up to record highs.
Signs are emerging that the latest attacks could trigger an acute market panic, with Brent crude buyers paying a steep premium for early delivery — an indication that the industry fears an impending supply crisis.
“I fear there is a considerable risk of much higher gas and diesel prices in the weeks to come,” said Michael O’Hanlon, director of research of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution.
“No one is quite sure how to predict the fuel markets,” he added, “but the military dynamics are seriously worrisome.”
Last week, Trump told reporters that the Iranian government is “desperate to try and affect the election” and could be trying to keep oil prices elevated to hurt Republican prospects.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”
Polls have found that likely voters are prioritizing the economy far beyond any other policy matter going into the fall election season, with a New York Times poll published Tuesday showing voters trusting Democrats to handle the economy more than Republicans.
“There’s no quick fix,” said Simon Henderson, the director of the Washington Institute’s Gulf and Energy Policy program. “The main question is whether it is a big shock to the oil market or just another more minor shock. The answer depends on whether the damage to the East-West pipeline cable is repaired quickly.”
Region on edge
The latest Iranian campaign threatens Saudi Arabia’s economic core, straining a long-standing alliance built on robust U.S. defense of Riyadh’s vital interests.
The attack on the East-West oil pipeline originated in Iraq, where Iran continues to operate proxy militias, according to government officials in Riyadh and Baghdad. Saudi Arabia agreed not to retaliate militarily against targets on Iraqi soil, temporarily staving off a regional conflagration.
While the Iraqi militia group denied involvement, it also praised the Houthi advance in Yemen and the militants’ “ongoing battlefield victories against Saudi forces.”
Israel has been providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence to help thwart further attacks, using American military intermediaries, according to Israeli media reports.
Active combat in the war between Iran and the United States eased after a ceasefire was brokered in June. While that truce collapsed in July, the two sides have opted for asymmetric tactics over the resumption of direct attacks, with the United States maintaining a full naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The Trump administration has since focused instead on targeting Iran’s economic partners with aggressive secondary sanctions, seeking to further pressure Tehran into a meaningful peace agreement. But negotiations have failed for months to get back off the ground.
When he first launched the war in February, Trump projected the mission would last roughly six weeks. He said the goal of the U.S. operation was to incapacitate Iran’s ballistic missile program, its navy and its nuclear program.
Trump was warned ahead of the war by his joint chiefs of staff that Iran could attempt to close the Strait of Hormuz in response. But he dismissed the threat, anticipating Tehran would quickly back down from a direct confrontation with the United States.
More than six months on, Iran’s ballistic missiles continue to pressure U.S. defense systems across the Middle East. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted and discussions on Iran’s future nuclear work have broken down. In private, Trump administration officials fear the war could drag through the remainder of the president’s term.

US to divert $52 million in military aid from Europe and Middle East to Trump-friendly nations in Americas

It comes after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made a trip to South America last week, where he met with the conservative leaders of Peru, Colombia and Ecuador to pledge further support and cooperation.
The Trump administration is redirecting $52 million in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to help back US-aligned governments in the Americas.
The US State Department notified Congress on Tuesday that it would divert the funds from Iraq, Tunisia and NATO members Slovakia and North Macedonia to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Panama.
The US State Department said the funding would go towards combatting "narcoterrorism in our backyard" and helping "continue to secure the Panama Canal," adding that it would "prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere."
The impacted countries are still expected to receive some assistance despite the change, although the exact amount is unclear.
Trump has increasingly turned his attention to the Americas since his return to the White House in January 2025, carrying out strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats coming from the region and launching an operation to capture former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. He has also sought to gain access to Venezuela's oil industry - striking a major oil deal with Caracas in August.
But Trump has also worked to deepen relations with governments he considers aligned to his goals as he looks to build the US' presence in the region.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made a trip to South America last week as part of this push, meeting with the conservative leaders of Peru, Colombia and Ecuador to pledge further support and cooperation.
In Europe, however, Trump has made no secret of his wish to reduce the US' role, repeatedly hitting out at European NATO allies over their defence spending and threatening to withdraw American forces from the continent.
In August, the State Department said it also planned to announce a $1 billion security package for new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella's right-wing administration.
The office of the spokesperson for the department said the package aimed to help Washington and Bogotá achieve "our shared goals."
Trump has long been complimentary of de la Espriella, calling him a "smart, strong, and tough leader" and promising the "total support and strength of the United States behind him."

We are allocating UAH 328.5 billion for education and UAH 292.5 billion for healthcare. This is more than this year. Funding for social programs, support for veterans and internally displaced persons, and housing is also increasing. More resources are to be allocated to regions and municipalities for reconstruction, development, and improving people's quality of life.
All these parameters are reflected in the draft budget.

We are allocating UAH 96 billion for business support programs — almost twice as much as this year. This includes affordable lending, grants, and support for defense innovations. We are also providing separate funding for war-risk insurance,” the Prime Minister emphasized.

After drone attacks, half of Russia's key oil refineries cut diesel production, with some operating at only 25% capacity
Kyiv • UNN
Half of Russia's six largest oil refineries have reduced or halted diesel production following drone attacks. Moscow has restricted fuel exports.
Half of the six largest Russian oil refineries by diesel fuel production volumes in September significantly reduced or completely halted output after drone attacks. Reuters reports this, citing its own calculations and data from fuel market participants, UNN writes.
Details
The enterprises in question together account for about half of all diesel fuel production in Russia. They include the Omsk Refinery, Kirishi Refinery, TANECO, Volgograd Refinery, NORSI and Perm Refinery.
According to Reuters sources, the Kirishi Refinery has completely shut down, while the Volgograd Refinery and NORSI are operating at approximately 25% of their nominal capacity. As a result, diesel output at these facilities has fallen severalfold compared with normal levels.
Russia is already forced to restrict fuel exports
Strikes on the oil refining industry have led to reduced production and forced Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel. According to traders' estimates, before the restrictions were introduced in June, Russian diesel exports amounted to less than 1 million tonnes per month.

The consequences have already extended beyond the Russian market. U.S. President Donald Trump called on Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure, saying that the resulting fuel shortage "harms the whole world."

Russia Faces Looming Potato Deficit as Harvest Drops by 1 Million Tons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
21:03:50 UTC
06:03:50 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Faces Looming Potato Deficit as Harvest Drops by 1 Million Tons
Russia is confronting the prospect of a renewed agricultural shortage as projections indicate the domestic potato harvest will fall from 8.5 million tons last year to 7.5 million tons this year, creating a gap of 0.5 to 1 million tons against an annual domestic demand of 8 to 8.5 million tons, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 15.
Industrial potato planting areas have shrunk to an 18-year low of 277,800 hectares, accompanied by a drop in yield per acre.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Wholesale market trends now echo the 2024–2025 agricultural season, during which harvest volumes dropped to 7.3 million tons, domestic retail prices increased by up to 173%, and foreign imports—including supplies from China and Mongolia—were required to cover domestic shortfalls.
By late August, retail potato prices rose 35% year-over-year to 59.1 rubles ($0.65) per kilogram, while wholesale prices recorded a matching 33% increase.
Russian agricultural supply chains traditionally increase foreign potato purchases around February as domestic reserves run low, but analysts predict foreign imports will need to begin a month earlier this year.
Other key staple vegetables are experiencing similar price surges far above official headline inflation of 6%. Cabbage prices are up 35.2% year-over-year, onions have increased by 27.2%, beets are up 20.4%, and carrots have risen 17.7%, according to The Moscow Times.
Retail trade representatives attribute the rising produce prices to systemic cost pressures across the agricultural sector. Farmers are facing higher expenses for fuel, lubricants, seeds, fertilizers, and storage facilities.
Transportation costs have also increased significantly, particularly for long-distance deliveries from southern agricultural regions to major metropolitan centers. Fuel price increases, which have exceeded 20% since the start of the year, are contributing directly to rising transport and operational expenses across the sector.
In the first quarter of 2026, the share of profitable Russian agricultural enterprises dropped to 68.6% from 77.9% a year earlier, while loss-making farms expanded to 31.4%. During that same period, profits across crop and livestock farming fell by 22.5%, and overall losses surged 1.6 times, pushing average profitability for agricultural producers in the Rostov region into negative territory.

Moscow Deploys 300,000 CCTV Cameras to Trap Draft Evaders and Dissidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
21:03:21 UTC
06:03:21 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Moscow Deploys 300,000 CCTV Cameras to Trap Draft Evaders and Dissidents
Moscow’s integration of cutting-edge digital amenities has transformed the Russian capital into one of the world’s most heavily monitored cities, weaponizing urban convenience to enforce an expanding surveillance state, The New York Times reported on September 15.
While residents utilize facial recognition for daily transactions and subway access, the city’s network of roughly 300,000 CCTV cameras is increasingly deployed by the Kremlin to track political dissidents and enforce military conscription.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The technological dragnet has fundamentally altered how the Russian state manages military recruitment. Following the mass exodus of draft-eligible men in 2022, authorities introduced electronic summonses via the centralized State Services app. These digital notices carry full legal weight and automatically bar recipients from leaving the country.
With biometric tracking deeply embedded in Moscow’s public transit and urban infrastructure, draft evaders are effectively trapped, forced to abandon the subway system and navigate the city in fear of triggering facial recognition alerts.
Despite the system’s efficiency, severe internal friction has emerged between Russian technocrats and the Federal Security Service (FSB). According to an anonymous official involved in developing the digital infrastructure who spoke to The New York Times, the FSB’s political-policing department favors analog control methods and views artificial intelligence as a threat to its sprawling apparatus of human agents.
This conflict routinely spills into public view; in March, security services abruptly shut down mobile internet access across central Moscow for over two weeks following a security scare, paralyzing the billions of dollars invested in the city’s digital services, according to the publication.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has framed the development of artificial intelligence as an existential necessity for Russian sovereignty, demanding domestic innovation insulated from Western influence. However, the reality of Russia’s technological sector contradicts these ambitions.
Crippled by Western sanctions that restrict access to advanced microchips and hollowed out by the mass exodus of top technical talent since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia remains highly dependent on foreign architecture. The New York Times writes that the country’s flagship AI models, developed by state-aligned banks and tech monopolies, rely heavily on Chinese open-source blueprints as Moscow attempts to build an isolated digital perimeter.
Moscow’s efforts to build an isolated digital perimeter also extend to web infrastructure, with the recent development of a state-approved browser designed to enforce domestic encryption algorithms. Following Google’s removal of Russian electronic signature plugins from its platforms, a sanctioned cryptographic firm is creating a domestic alternative to Western browsers.
The new software, which integrates encryption protocols explicitly approved by the Federal Security Service (FSB), is expected to become mandatory for all Russian government institutions within two years of receiving necessary security certifications.

Rubio announces US visa curbs for some foreign nationals from South Africa
- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions for South African nationals linked to policies on uncompensated land seizures and race-based discrimination.
- The Trump administration criticises South Africa over land reforms, racial policies, and a genocide case against Israel, claiming these harm the white minority.
- South Africa denies discrimination against whites, condemns white superiority ideas, and President Ramaphosa urges debunking false claims of white persecution.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sept 15 the US was announcing a new visa restriction policy targeting some foreign nationals from South Africa as President Donald Trump’s administration continues to cool ties with the country.
The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over a range of issues including actions aimed at addressing racial inequality that Trump claims hurt the African nation’s white population.
Washington has also criticised land reform policies and South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, over the US ally’s assault on Gaza.
The visa curb policy targets “foreign nationals who are responsible for, or complicit in, the enactment or implementation of laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of minority ethnic or racial groups in South Africa,” Rubio said in a statement.
“The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid out concerns,” Rubio said.
The South African embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Pretoria says there is no evidence of discrimination or persecution against white people and that ideas of white racial superiority are a threat to South Africa’s post-apartheid unity, its sovereignty and its diplomatic relations.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has called for global efforts to debunk false stories about white persecution.
Trump has previously cut aid to South Africa, offered refuge to white minority Afrikaners, expelled the country’s ambassador and made false claims of white genocide in the African nation.
Trump’s portrayal of South Africa as dangerous and oppressive for white people also aligns with some of his domestic policies that have targeted diversity initiatives aimed at addressing historic inequities for marginalised groups.
Trump casts them as discriminatory against white people and men.
Rubio’s statement on Sept 15 did not identify any person by name.
Three decades after the end of apartheid in South Africa, some fringe groups lament the loss of white power that democracy brought.
While South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world, most victims are Black. REUTERS

The Mexican Senate has unanimously authorized the entry of 139 US military personnel for joint training exercises in the northern state of Chihuahua, according to authorities.
The troops will take part in activities at the Santa Gertrudis military base from Sept. 20 to 30.
The Senate said the exercises will strengthen military capabilities and improve cooperation between the two countries.
The US personnel from the Army's 101st Airborne Division will enter Mexico carrying weapons aboard a US Air Force aircraft.
The authorization was requested by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum under an urgent procedure and approved with 75 votes in favor.
It is the fourth authorization this year for US military personnel to enter Mexico for training and the largest contingent approved in 2026.
The exercises come as Mexico and the US have increased security cooperation, particularly on drug trafficking and organized crime.
Authorities have repeatedly stressed that security cooperation with Washington must respect the country's sovereignty. US forces cannot conduct unilateral operations on Mexican territory and require authorization from Mexico.
Sheinbaum has maintained that Mexico is willing to cooperate with the US on security issues while rejecting any form of unilateral intervention. Her government has sought to strengthen coordination on organized crime and drug trafficking through agreements between Mexican and US security agencies.
The exercises will take place 520 kilometers (323 miles) south of the US-Mexico border.
The deployment also follows tensions earlier this year about the presence of US intelligence personnel in Chihuahua, highlighting the sensitivity surrounding foreign security operations in Mexico.
Mexico and the US have continued to expand cooperation in areas including military training, intelligence sharing and border security.

The war with Iran has already cost the US $38 billion and could push up inflation – Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
23:47:39 EEST

The war with Iran has already cost the US $38 billion and could push up inflation – Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
The first five months of the war cost the US $38 billion, and each subsequent month could add $2–3 billion. Inflation could rise in 2027.
The war with Iran cost American taxpayers $38 billion in just the first five months of hostilities, and each subsequent month could add at least $2–3 billion in expenses. Bloomberg reports this, citing a new estimate by the U.S. Congressional Budget Office (CBO), writes UNN.
Details
The $38 billion includes the costs of replacing used munitions and lost equipment, additional aircraft flight hours, and fuel. At the same time, the CBO was unable to estimate the cost of repairing or restoring damaged U.S. military bases, so the actual expenses could be higher.
The war will also affect prices in the United States. Due to disruptions in oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, the CBO expects the key inflation measure to be approximately 0.5 percentage points higher at the beginning of 2027 than forecast before the conflict began. Core inflation could be 0.3 percentage points higher.
Munitions stockpiles could take more than 5 years to replenish
The CBO describes the depletion of U.S. munitions stockpiles as one of the most serious consequences of the hostilities. According to the office's estimate, replenishing them could take 5 years or more.
Such a shortage could become particularly dangerous in the event of another major conflict with an adversary that has significant stockpiles of ballistic and cruise missiles. The report mentions a conflict over Taiwan as one possible scenario.
At the same time, U.S. President Donald Trump previously stated that the country had a "practically unlimited quantity" of munitions. Estimates by the CBO and the Pentagon inspector general point to problems replenishing certain types of weapons.
In July, Republicans in the House of Representatives proposed allocating another $73 billion to the military and intelligence services for direct expenses related to the war in Iran. Consideration of this funding has currently stalled in the Senate.

Rush to put Zverev in Alcaraz-Sinner tier premature despite twin titles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:40:22 UTC
05:40:22 KST

analysis
Alexander Zverev remains below Alcaraz-Sinner tier despite grand slam breakthroughs
When the latest edition of the ATP singles rankings dropped earlier this week, a 24-year streak came to an end.
After being bounced in the first round of the US Open, Novak Djokovic dropped out of the top-10 for the first time since 2018.
Djokovic's exit marks the first time since October 2002 that neither he nor Rafael Nadal nor Roger Federer is inside the top-10.
For tennis fans who wondered when the 'Big 3' era in the men's game would end, the end is now.
With the Djokovic-Federer-Nadal triumvirate dominating the men's game for so long, the question of who their successors would be has been a popular one around tennis.
Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz have emulated Federer and Nadal's rivalry from the mid-2000s, exchanging grand slam titles while playing some spellbinding epics along the way, but would any other men's players on tour join them as Djokovic joined Federer and Nadal?
Alexander Zverev appears to be the third member of the party, having claimed two of the four available grand slam titles this year.
But questions remain as to whether Zverev's candidacy to join the very top tier of men's tennis is legitimate.
Since first achieving a top-10 ranking in May 2017 as a 20-year-old, Zverev has been one of the most consistent performers on the men's tour.
Zverev has spent 414 weeks as a top-10 ranked player throughout his career, currently 15th all-time. He ranks second among active players in this metric, behind only Djokovic, with 959 weeks, just behind Federer's 968.
At the time of writing, Zverev has spent 102 consecutive weeks ranked inside the top 10 since his most recent streak began in September 2023.
Those numbers are not the problem when it comes to Zverev's bid to be considered the best player in the world.
It is this one.
Despite being a constant presence in the top-10 rankings over the best part of the last decade, Zverev has consistently struggled to beat the other players ranked in the same vicinity.
The German owns an unenviable 5-18 (21.7 per cent) win-loss record against fellow top-10 opponents in grand slam matches. He has won 59 of his 146 matches against top-10 opponents overall, roughly a 40 per cent conversion rate.
Zverev's record pales in comparison to Alcaraz and Sinner, as well as Djokovic, Federer and Nadal.
Alcaraz has an astounding 16-7 record against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with his 69.6 per cent conversion rate by far the best among the elite cohort, while Sinner has gone 14-14 in such matches.
Nadal, Djokovic and Federer all won over 60 per cent of their matches against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with Djokovic's 69 wins leading the way.
This record against the very best players helped make Zverev a perennial grand slam semifinalist and finalist before he broke through with his first title at Roland-Garros earlier this year.
While Zverev now has two grand slam titles to his name, the calibre of opponents he has overcome suggests he hasn't really gone up a tier.
The German claimed the French Open title without facing a single top-10-ranked opponent, with the runner-up Flavio Cobolli the top-ranked player at No.14.
Overall, the average ranking of the players Zverev beat en-route to his first grand slam title is 57.7, with his fourth-round opponent, world No.106, Jesper de Jong the lowest-ranked.
Zverev had a slightly tougher run to the US Open title, but still faced just one top-10-ranked opponent in finalist Ben Shelton (eighth).
On average, Zverev's US Open opponents ranked 45th overall, with his first-round opponent, Lorenzo Sonego, the lowest-ranked at No.89.
Zverev's victories offer hope for the rest of the non-Alcaraz and Sinner division on the men's tour, including players such as Australia's Alex de Minaur.
De Minaur, like Zverev, has struggled against top-10 opponents at grand slams, winning just two of 14 matches.
Despite reaching a career-high ranking of No.5 this year, de Minaur has yet to win a grand slam quarterfinal.
The Australian has a 0-7 record in quarters, with six of those losses coming over the last three seasons.
De Minaur has looked downtrodden after his recent grand slam exits, but will hope that like Zverev, he too can capitalise on the bracket breaking just right for him at some point down the line.
For now, Zverev looks to have graduated above the class featuring the likes of Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Felix Auger-Aliassime, de Minaur and others.
But for him to truly climb into the upper echelon of men's tennis, it is time he starts taking down the big names when it matters most.

Romanian farmers clash with police over livestock export ban
Dozens injured as 2,000 farmers – backed by far-right groups – protest the extension of a livestock export ban.
Riot police have clashed with Romanian shepherds and farmers as they rioted during a protest against a ban on livestock exports due to disease.
About 2,000 people gathered to demonstrate in the capital, Bucharest, on Tuesday against the extension of a live sheep export ban, imposed by the European Union due to the highly contagious small ruminant plague. As in other protests by farmers across Europe in recent years, the rally was encouraged and supported by far-right forces.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
Violence broke out in front of the Romanian government building in Bucharest when some protesters demanding the reversal of the ban began throwing rocks, metal barriers and other objects at law enforcement.
Police responded with tear gas in a bid to disperse them. Twenty-six people were detained, riot police said in a press release.
Twenty-four demonstrators and police officers required medical attention – some for broken bones, others for the effects of the tear gas. Four were hospitalised.
The government and the opposition called on the demonstrators to refrain from violence.
The demonstration was called by farmers and shepherd groups. Protesters held banners calling on the country’s president and prime minister to resign.
Some chanted the name of far-right politician Calin Georgescu, a former presidential candidate who is standing trial for acts against the constitutional order following the annulment of the presidential elections in 2024.
Supporters of Georgescu had shared messages on social media ahead of the protest, asking people to join.
George Simion, the leader of the main far-right group in the country, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), wrote on Facebook that “AUR stands with the farmers and all working Romanians”, but called on protesters to demonstrate peacefully.
‘Legitimate protest to street fighting’
The Romanian government said in a press release that the protest had “degenerated into regrettable acts of violence” and called for “calm”.
President Nicusor Dan condemned the “extremely serious” violence and “any attempt to turn a legitimate protest into street fighting” in a social media post.
Romanian shepherds had protested outside the government building at the end of July over the EU ban on live sheep exports, which expires at the end of 2026.
The country of 19 million people has been struggling for months with the highest inflation in the EU and a political crisis with no end in sight.
The pro-European government, which adopted austerity measures to rein in a high budget deficit, was brought down in a no-confidence motion in May, and a divided parliament has failed to confirm a successor.

UN warns Yemen escalation threatens Red Sea navigation, global trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:37:33 UTC
05:37:33 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The UN warned on Tuesday that escalating fighting in Yemen and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait risks further destabilizing a critical international maritime route, while Yemen's government urged the Security Council to take stronger measures against the Houthi group.
Addressing an emergency Security Council meeting, UN Assistant Secretary-General Khaled Khiari said fighting had intensified along Yemen's western coast as the Houthis advanced toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and claimed capturing several islands in the southern Red Sea.
Although commercial shipping through the Red Sea appeared largely unaffected so far, Khiari said the developments were adding to market concerns amid continuing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
He said Yemen's government had launched a counteroffensive following the Houthi advances, with clashes reported across several frontlines.
The escalation has also exacted a heavy toll on civilians. UN humanitarian officials estimate that at least 125,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since the beginning of September, while the UN human rights office has recorded 40 civilian casualties, including eight deaths. Women and children account for half of those killed and more than half of those injured, Khiari said.
He highlighted growing regional repercussions, including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and strikes said to have damaged Saudi energy infrastructure. He called on all parties to protect civilians, comply with international humanitarian law and facilitate humanitarian access.
Yemen's representative, Abdullah Ali Fadhel Al-Saadi, said the Houthi escalation had become a threat extending beyond Yemen's borders, affecting regional security, energy supplies and global trade.
Al-Saadi urged the Council to condemn Houthi attacks, enforce existing arms embargo measures and support Yemen's government in restoring control over its territory, coastline, ports and territorial waters.
He also warned that instability around Bab el-Mandeb Strait could create an environment conducive to arms, drug and human trafficking and cooperation between militant and organized criminal networks.
Khiari stressed the need for restraint and renewed UN-led political engagement, saying freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb must be restored and respected under international law.
He warned that prolonged disruption of maritime trade could raise global costs and threaten energy markets, food security and vulnerable economies, underscoring the urgent need to prevent Yemen's conflict from further spilling into regional and international security.

Iran war costs $38 billion so far, could rise by up to $3 billion per month: US budget office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:34:54 UTC
05:34:54 KST

Merve Aydogan
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The US Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated on Tuesday that America's war against Iran has cost the Department of Defense approximately $38.1 billion as of Aug. 1, with further months of conflict likely to add $2 billion to $3 billion each, depending on the intensity of hostilities.
In a letter to House Budget Committee Ranking Member Brendan Boyle, CBO Director Phillip Swagel said the figure covers the replacement of expended munitions and lost equipment, increased flying hours, fuel costs, and other operations tied to Operation Epic Fury, which began Feb. 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
Replacing munitions accounted for the largest share, $21.7 billion, including $13.1 billion for missile defense interceptors, the letter said. If hostilities stayed as low as in May and June, an extra month would cost $2 billion, but that figure would rise to $3 billion at July's intensity levels, it added.
The conflict has pushed up global oil and fuel prices due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, contributing to higher inflation and interest rate projections through 2027.
The CBO's estimate is roughly 10% below the Administration's supplemental funding request of $42.3 billion for directly related costs and below Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July estimate of $37.5 billion through September, the letter said, citing differing methods and a lack of complete data from the Pentagon.
The US and Israel launched large-scale attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, targeting government buildings, military sites, missile infrastructure, and air defenses. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks against Israel and US bases across the region.
The war has since expanded in the region, while diplomatic efforts have sought to end the hostilities.

“Only the first season” – Ukraine unveils secret counteroffensive in Donetsk after 12 years of Russian attempts to seize the region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:34:28 UTC
05:34:28 KST

Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has revealed details of an offensive operation in northern Donetsk Oblast, saying its forces cleared Russian infiltrators from several settlements and liberated the village of Serednie.
Russia has made seizing the entirety of Donetsk Oblast both a battlefield and diplomatic priority of its invasion of Ukraine, repeatedly trying to break through heavily fortified Ukrainian defensive lines while demanding that Kyiv withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in negotiations. Despite years of fighting and sustained Russian assaults, Moscow has failed to capture the entire oblast, and Ukraine is now conducting an offensive of its own.
The operation, dubbed “Vivaldi,” was conducted under a period of information silence and involved Ukrainian drone, reconnaissance, special operations, infantry, and other units working under a unified tactical command. The corps said the first phase cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and liberated another 10 square kilometers of territory.
The announcement was made by Third Army Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi on 15 September.
Ukraine targets Russian infiltration
According to the corps, the operation focused initially on Russian troops that had infiltrated Ukrainian positions and settlements in the area.
Ukrainian forces cleared Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, the outskirts of Korovyi Yar, and liberated Serednie, the corps said. It described the total area cleared or retaken as 85 square kilometers.
The operation brought together units from the 60th and 125th Mechanized Brigades, the Third Assault Brigade, the KRAKEN special unit, and other formations of the Third Army Corps, alongside attached units from the 66th Mechanized Brigade, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces, the military intelligence unit Artan, and the State Border Guard Service.
The corps said the operation was coordinated by a joint headquarters that brought special operations and reconnaissance units under a single tactical plan specifically to counter Russian infiltrators, whom it referred to as “flagovtyky.”
Russian logistics pushed back across the border
The Ukrainian operation also targeted Russian logistics supporting the front.
The corps said its drone units cut Russian supply routes and struck fuel infrastructure and storage facilities that had been supporting Russian forces.
According to the Ukrainian military, Russian forces subsequently moved the supply of fuel and lubricants out of Ukraine and into Russia’s Voronezh Oblast after a pipeline and fuel depots were destroyed.
The corps claimed Russian forces lost around 1,500 personnel during this phase of the operation, as well as more than 12,000 drones and hundreds of armored vehicles, artillery systems, and other vehicles.
‘This is only the first season’
Biletskyi said the operation’s ultimate objective has been the subject of speculation in open sources, with some reports suggesting Ukrainian forces could be seeking to reach the Chornyi Zherebets River.
He declined to confirm that objective, instead emphasizing the name of the operation.
“Our operation is called Vivaldi. And Vivaldi, as is known, has four seasons. And this is only the first one,” Biletskyi said.
The remarks suggest Ukraine does not consider the actions revealed on 15 September to be a standalone tactical operation, although the corps did not disclose what its next phase will involve.
The Third Army Corps said further details would be released in subsequent official statements.
Donetsk remains Russia’s main territorial objective
Donetsk Oblast is central to Russia’s territorial demands in Ukraine. Moscow claims the entire oblast as Russian territory despite not controlling all of it, and has demanded that Ukraine withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donetsk as part of peace talks.
The Donbas region – consisting of Donetsk and neighboring Luhansk oblasts – has been a battleground since Russia’s 2014 invasion, and capturing the remaining Ukrainian-held territory has remained the Kremlin’s core objective throughout the full-scale invasion since 2022.

Most Americans value free press but back some limits: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:34:00 UTC
05:34:00 KST

Most Americans consider press freedom vital to society but many are willing to accept government restrictions on news coverage under certain circumstances, revealing a divide between broad support for a free press and views on how far that freedom should extend, a new Pew Research Center study showed.
About three-quarters of U.S. adults said press freedom was "extremely" or "very" important to society's well-being, according to the study. Yet at least half supported government intervention in some cases, including when reporting could threaten national security or contain false information.
The findings come amid heightened tensions between U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and major news organizations, with about 7 in 10 Americans describing their relationship as "very" or "somewhat" bad.
Americans were also divided over whether press freedom has deteriorated since Trump returned to the White House. About 44% said the media had become less free during his second term, while 26% saw no change and 12% believed the press had gained greater freedom.
The survey also exposed a sharp partisan divide. About 8 in 10 Democrats considered a free press extremely or very important, compared with roughly two-thirds of Republicans, while Republicans were more likely to support restrictions on reporting involving national security or inaccurate information.
"People are not all or nothing,” says Katerina Eva Matsa, director of news and information at Pew Research Center, when asked what was striking about the findings. "When you give them options and scenarios ... they are negotiating. That was a very interesting perspective that the data gave us.”
The study, which was based on two surveys conducted earlier this year, also found that Americans were divided about whether the media is completely free to report the news, with Democrats and Republicans expressing very different levels of worry about restrictions on the press.
The analysis comes as the relationship between the U.S. media and Donald Trump's second administration becomes ever more fraught as the president, in his second term, seeks to restrict press coverage not to his liking. He or his administration has attacked, sued or taken administrative action against media outlets that have drawn his ire.
Matsa said that tension was one impetus for doing the report now. Other reasons: the changing media environment and the evolution of what "the press” is now, as well as the emergence of tech companies as gatekeepers of the news.
"Overall, there’s a lot of public conversation - and it’s the 250th anniversary of our nation,” she said. "So, it kind of felt like a good moment to look at how Americans think about this.”
Most Americans, about 7 in 10, said the Trump administration and the U.S. news media have a "very” or "somewhat” bad relationship. That's a slight increase from 2025, when 64% of U.S. adults said this.
They're more divided on whether the press faces additional restrictions under Trump's second term, although few think the press is freer than it was before. About 44% of U.S. adults said the press has become less free under the second Trump administration, while about 26% said there has been no change. Only 12% said the press is more free, and 17% said they're not sure.
Despite U.S. adults' broad belief in the ideal of press freedom, the survey found they're willing to contemplate restrictions in specific circumstances.
Most U.S. adults said the government should not be able to require a news organization to take down a story if it is critical of the government or clearly favors one political side. But about half say it should be able to force a retraction if a story contains false information, and about 6 in 10 said this about a story that poses a risk to national security.
The findings indicate most Americans are open to some form of government restriction on the media, despite their broad embrace of press freedom as a concept. At the same time, there is unlikely to be uniform agreement about what constitutes a national security risk, for example, or who gets to determine that - and the poll did not probe those distinctions further.
When asked whether it was more important for the press to be free to report news even if some reporting is inaccurate, or if preventing inaccurate reporting should be prioritized even if it limits press freedom, about half, 53%, of U.S. adults said it was more important to prevent inaccurate reporting, and 45% said press freedom was more important.
But they see limits for government too. Just over half of Americans say it is "rarely” or "never” acceptable for the U.S. government to force journalists to reveal the identities of unnamed government sources or take away a news organization's license to broadcast. About 2 in 10 say these actions are "sometimes” acceptable, and only about 1 in 10 say they are "usually” or "always” acceptable.
Perhaps not surprisingly in a highly politicized environment, views on press freedom differed sharply according to political leaning.
Democrats were more likely than Republicans to prioritize a free press to begin with, the study found. About 8 in 10 Democrats said a free press is "extremely” or "very” important for society's well-being, compared to about two-thirds of Republicans.
Republicans were also more likely than Democrats to say the government should be able to require a news story be taken down in cases of national security. About 7 in 10 Republicans said this should be allowed, compared to about half of Democrats. A similar gap emerged on the publication of false information.
The share of Americans who said the media was "completely” free to report the news fell slightly from 33% last year to 28% in the latest survey. About half - 48% - said the press was "somewhat” free and about 2 in 10 said it was "not very” or "not at all” free.
There were differences between the parties there, too.
In the new study, only about 2 in 10 Democrats saw the media as "completely” free to report the news.
Meanwhile, most Democrats, 64%, said they were "extremely” or "very” concerned about potential restrictions on press freedom, while only about 3 in 10 Republicans held similar worries. The reverse was true during the Biden era.
The report is accompanied by a knowledge quiz based on the surveys that users can take to test how much they know about the First Amendment. It has eight questions, all of which were included in the survey. Matsa noted that while many Americans understand the basics of the First Amendment, many don’t know the mechanics of who it protects - and from whom.
For example, the study found that while 58% of U.S. adults know the Constitution protects the press from interference by the U.S. government, only 33% know that it does not protect the press from interference by private companies, such as a social media company or a web-hosting service.

U.S. 10-year treasury yield hits highest level since 2007 amid inflation fears, Fed hike bets

2026-09-16
04:31:38 CST
05:31:38 KST

NEW YORK, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note rose to 5.04 percent in early trading on Tuesday, the highest level since July 2007, signaling higher borrowing costs across the broader U.S. economy.
Higher oil prices, prospects of persistent inflation and expectations of further interest rate hikes have been seen as factors driving up yields on U.S. Treasury bonds in recent days.
The relentless upward march in bond yields this year translates directly into heavier financial burdens for consumers seeking to buy homes, finance vehicles or take out personal loans. It simultaneously drives up the cost of capital for businesses and increases debt-servicing costs for the U.S. government itself.
The global bond market, anchored by the nearly 32-trillion-U.S.-dollar Treasury market, has experienced a significant sell-off. Investors are grappling with a complex array of macroeconomic headwinds, including surging energy prices, mounting uncertainty surrounding the ongoing war against Iran, unchecked U.S. government spending, and expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve.
The surge in yields has come despite concerted efforts by the U.S. Treasury Department to stabilize the market. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has orchestrated various interventions in recent weeks to contain the rise in longer-dated yields. So far, those efforts have yielded little success.
The latest spike in bond yields comes just ahead of the Federal Reserve's highly anticipated monetary policy decision on Wednesday. Traders have priced in a 92 percent probability that the central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points at the conclusion of the Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
The Fed has "little choice but to hike rates" this week, as the bond market has been "signaling for weeks that higher rates are warranted," said Carol Schleif, chief market strategist at BMO Wealth Management, on Tuesday. Citing hot inflation data, strong corporate earnings, a resilient labor market and severe geopolitical disruptions, Schleif cautioned that elevated yields "could be here to stay for some time."
Wall Street analysts are closely monitoring the fallout in the stock market, though opinions remain divided on the severity of the threat.
In a note to clients on Tuesday morning, Barclays strategists warned that higher rates have already pressured valuations and are increasingly putting equity portfolios at risk.
"While earnings have so far offset the drag, the approaching 5 percent threshold in 10Y yields marks a historically important inflection point, beyond which rates have typically become a more persistent headwind for equities," the Barclays strategists wrote. They added that the risk of a "sharper repricing" would grow if yields move materially above current levels.
Conversely, the BlackRock Investment Institute maintained a more optimistic outlook in its own Tuesday note, saying that the rising global interest rates "have not knocked us off our pro-risk stance."
U.S. stocks posted significant losses in Tuesday morning trading. ■

Roundup: Award-winning Gaza documentary "NAZA" sparks backlash in Israel
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:31:35 CST
05:31:35 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The award-winning documentary "NAZA," named after the Hebrew military acronym for "collateral damage" and accusing the Israeli army of mass civilian killing in Gaza, has triggered a fierce backlash in Israel in recent days.
Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir called its allegations "blood libels" and ordered legal officials to examine possible action and investigate whether classified information had been leaked.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the film "outrageous" and accused it of contributing to what he described as global "antisemitic incitement."
Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar accused the filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of "treason against the state" and called for examining whether their citizenship could be revoked, while threatening sanctions against institutions that screen the film.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir circulated an artificial intelligence (AI) -generated video depicting them behind bars.
The rage spilled onto social media, where the filmmakers faced a torrent of anger and abuse, including death threats.
Analysts say the heated political climate ahead of Israel's October election has stoked the backlash. By contrast, when Abraham and Szor premiered the film at the Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 10, it received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation and later won the Special Jury Prize.
Abraham told Israel's Channel 13 he feared he might not be able to return home, but said it was "critical" for Israelis to see the film and learn about the military's actions in Gaza. He said efforts were underway to distribute it in Israel.
The 80-minute film, produced by The Guardian and directed by Abraham and Szor, is based on interviews with 24 Israeli soldiers and military intelligence whistleblowers involved in Israel's operations in Gaza. They were filmed at night on rooftops overlooking Tel Aviv, speaking anonymously to protect their identities.
"NAZA," a Hebrew shorthand, refers to the number of civilians expected to be killed or injured in a strike. The documentary examines the systems used to select and approve targets in Gaza, including AI-assisted tools, and alleges that expected civilian deaths were routinely calculated before attacks were authorized.
In one testimony from the trailer, an intelligence officer describes how a detailed map of Gaza can be opened at the click of a button, showing the estimated number of people who would be harmed if a particular building were bombed.
"I can literally click on any house and see how many people will be harmed when you bomb it," he says.
"This is a film about a system," the filmmakers wrote in +972 Magazine, an online Israeli-Palestinian magazine.
They said that the film examines "orders, policies, and patterns of operation, not deviations from them," and shows that mass civilian killing was not merely a "tragic byproduct" of the campaign against Hamas but was knowingly incorporated into military decision-making.
An Israel Defense Forces spokesperson told Xinhua on Tuesday that the military "categorically rejects these allegations," saying the film relies on anonymous testimonies whose identities and roles cannot be verified and includes claims beyond the interviewees' likely knowledge. The spokesperson said strike decisions are made "by human personnel only," not AI, and that the military operates under international law, seeks to minimize civilian harm, and investigates suspected violations by soldiers.
The controversy has exposed the gulf between perceptions of the Gaza war inside Israel and abroad. In Israel, the war continues to be viewed widely through the trauma of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed about 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostages. Internationally, Israel's conduct has generated mounting allegations of war crimes.
On Tuesday, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said the recovery of the "remains of what appears to be entire families" from sites pulverized by Israeli attacks raised new concerns about war crimes. More than 8,000 people are believed to remain buried beneath Gaza's rubble, he said.
Gaza-based health authorities said Tuesday that at least 73,789 Palestinians have been killed and 174,798 injured in Israeli attacks since Oct. 7, 2023. ■

Feature: Between school and survival -- Lebanese parents caught in education squeeze
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:31:25 CST
05:31:25 KST

BEIRUT, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- For Rana Aido, a Lebanese mother, deciding where to educate her children has become less a question of public versus private school than of whether to pay tuition or put food on the table.
Aido, mother of two, was paying about 4,000 U.S. dollars a year for each child at a private school, while her family earned about 9,600 dollars annually.
"We've had to cut back on food and other basic necessities just to make ends meet," Aido said, noting that the 8,000-dollar tuition bill consumed about 83 percent of the family's annual income, leaving just 1,600 to cover transportation, books, uniforms, extracurricular activities and food.
In Lebanon, many parents choose private schools for their children, citing higher educational standards and other advantages. By the 2022-23 academic year, private schools accounted for about 72 percent of students, according to Lebanon's Center for Educational Research and Development.
However, in recent years, soaring private-school fees have put parents under growing financial strain.
Lama Tawil, head of the Union of Parents' Committees in Private Schools, said tuition fees increased by 15 to 30 percent this year, with average annual tuition reaching about 4,000 dollars per student.
For a family with three children, annual tuition can reach 12,000 dollars, she said. Before the economic crisis, education accounted for roughly one quarter of a family's salary, whereas it can now consume more than three quarters of household income.
"We have a social disaster," Tawil said.
Education costs rose by 130 percent in 2024 and another 36 percent in 2025, following a nearly 600 percent increase in 2023, said Nassib Ghobril, chief economist at Lebanese Byblos Bank, adding that education had consequently become a leading driver of inflation.
Private schools, meanwhile, say they are also struggling with rising costs of their own. Khaldoun Farhat, director general of Al-Maanieh School, said his school raised tuition by about 10 to 12 percent this year, citing higher costs for teachers, fuel, electricity, insurance, maintenance and transportation.
Whatever the reasons for the increases, Lebanese parents are feeling the financial pressure in very real terms. According to Ministry of Education data compiled by UNESCO, more than 31,000 students moved from private to public schools during the 2024-25 academic year.
But the harsher reality is that Lebanon's public education system has also been severely weakened by years of conflict.
A June 2026 assessment by the Lebanese Education Ministry with UNICEF support found that 340 educational institutions had been damaged during conflict, including 17 completely destroyed, putting at least 100,000 children at risk of being left without classrooms.
Nearly 80 public schools were still being used as shelters as the new academic year approached, according to the education ministry, with some expected to partially reopen while continuing to accommodate displaced families.
The education ministry says it is seeking to regulate private-school budgets while strengthening public education.
Imad Achkar, the ministry's director general, said private schools are now required to submit their budgets, while a new electronic system allows the ministry to compare expenses and assess proposed tuition increases. He stressed that the state has a duty to provide every student with access to a free public-school place.
These government measures have done little to ease Aido's immediate predicament.
Believing that private schools offer their children a better future, Aido and her husband, Fadi Zakkour, decided to keep them enrolled. Zakkour sold his car last year to help pay the tuition. This year, he borrowed 4,000 dollars to help cover the tuition bill.
"Our children's education is the most important thing to us," Aido said. "We want to keep going for as long as we can, but we don't know how much longer we can afford it." ■

Feature: From ambulance to cinema -- Gaza kids find brief respite beside "Dream Bus"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:31:10 CST
05:31:10 KST

GAZA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- In the heart of Al-Nakheel Camp in the town of Al-Zawaida, central Gaza, an ambulance-like vehicle from the Palestine Red Crescent Society arrived, carrying not doctors and stretchers, but chairs and a projection screen.
Team members spent about an hour unloading the equipment and setting up a temporary cinema under a canopy.
Chairs were arranged in rows facing the screen mounted on the vehicle's door. Children gathered, some watching the preparations curiously, others waiting quietly for the screening to begin.
Then the cartoon started. Tired, distressed faces gradually brightened into smiles. Nearby, in the activity area beside the bus, other children drew, colored, played games and joined in recreational activities.
The activity is part of an initiative called "Dream Bus," a mobile cinema and recreational space designed to provide children with psychosocial support.
The bus travels to displacement sites where safe, dedicated spaces for children's activities are often unavailable, bringing moments of entertainment, connection, and relief directly to them.
"We responded to an invitation from camps in the area, coming to help ease the psychological pain the children are enduring," said Niveen Abdel-Hadi, director of the mental health department at the Palestine Red Crescent Society.
The initiative aims to ease distress caused by bombardment, displacement, and the loss of family members, as well as children's deprivation of education, play and a normal life, Abdel-Hadi explained.
Ghaleb Abu Khater, who coordinates the "Dream Bus" team, said the vehicle had originally been a damaged ambulance taken out of service during the war before being refurbished.
His team also sought to change children's perception of ambulances, which had become associated with injuries, bombardment and fear.
"We wanted to transform the vehicle into a place associated with play and joy," Abu Khater said.
The initiative offers a range of activities, including cartoon screenings, drawing and coloring, storytelling, games, competitions and physical exercises.
According to Abu Khater, the films are carefully chosen to suit different age groups, combining entertainment with educational elements. Art activities such as drawing and coloring give children an alternative way to express feelings that may be difficult for them to put into words. Meanwhile, games and physical exercises help ease stress and release pent-up energy, while storytelling encourages children to interact, communicate, and share their experiences.
Mobility and security challenges, along with shortages of fuel and activity materials, limit operations. But after each event, the team packs up and moves on, touring the enclave from north to south.
The need is overwhelming. Data from the nongovernmental Gaza Community Mental Health Programme, cited in an October 2025 report, indicate that 67.8 percent of Gaza residents suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder, while 96 percent of children feel that death is imminent.
Psychologist Samah Al-Qassas told Xinhua that group recreational activities can help children express emotions and reduce tension and fear, though they cannot replace specialized treatment.
At Al-Nakheel Camp, 12-year-old Saja Hammad, displaced from Jabalia, said she had lost more than 45 family members during the war.
"It was extremely difficult. We didn't draw; we were afraid and in hiding, and we never played," Hammad said, sitting in front of the screen. "But now, we play, go outside, the 'Dream Bus' visits us, we watch TV, and we draw and color. We really enjoy ourselves." ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:31:03 CST
05:31:03 KST

DAR ES SALAAM, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania has made significant progress in cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment and is seeking to position itself as a regional center of excellence for cancer care and training, according to a statement issued on Tuesday by the communication unit of the Vice President's Office.
Tanzanian Vice President Deogratius Ndejembi said the government investment had expanded cancer services from primary to specialized healthcare levels while addressing the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Scientific Forum in Vienna on behalf of President Samia Suluhu Hassan.
He said coverage of the single-dose human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine for girls aged 9 to 14 increased from 58 percent in 2018 to 98 percent in 2026.
The number of radiotherapy centers also increased from three in 2020 to six in 2026, raising access to radiotherapy services from 14 percent to 26 percent and benefiting about 6,500 patients, he said.
Tanzania plans to establish nine comprehensive cancer centers across six strategic zones in mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar by 2030, the statement said.
Ndejembi added that Tanzania had begun using a PET-CT scanner linked to a cyclotron for advanced cancer diagnosis, becoming one of the first 10 African countries to offer the technology. ■

NOUAKCHOTT, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Mauritania on Tuesday for a seven-day friendly visit, during which it would provide medical services.
The hospital ship, which is carrying out the Mission Harmony-2026, docked at the Friendship Port in Nouakchott, the capital of Mauritania, at around 10:00 a.m. local time.
Mauritanian military and government officials, military personnel, the Chinese ambassador to Mauritania, staff of the Chinese embassy, representatives of the Chinese community and Chinese enterprises, as well as local residents attended a welcoming ceremony at the port.
The crowd waved the national flags of China and Mauritania, while local residents held flowers and colorful flags and a Mauritanian military band played music during the ceremony.
Following the ceremony, the commander of the Mauritanian navy boarded the hospital ship, where he inspected the guard of honor and toured the vessel. He later held talks with representatives of the mission personnel.
During the visit, the hospital ship will provide medical services aboard the vessel, while medical teams will visit local medical facilities and Mauritanian military units to offer consultations, conduct medical training and carry out professional exchanges.
The mission will also organize a deck reception, as well as cultural and exchange activities between personnel from the two countries.
The Islamic Republic of Mauritania is located in western Africa. China and Mauritania established diplomatic relations in 1965. Mauritania is the first stop of Mission Harmony-2026. This marks the second visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. ■

UNESCO's AI ethics forum opens in Riyadh, calls for practical governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:30:56 CST
05:30:56 KST

Asa Regner, deputy director-general of UNESCO speaks at the opening ceremony of the 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Sept. 15, 2026. The 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) opened in Riyadh on Tuesday, where delegates discussed aligning AI development with safety and responsibility requirements. (Xinhua/Luo Chen)
RIYADH, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) opened in Riyadh on Tuesday, where delegates discussed aligning AI development with safety and responsibility requirements.
Co-hosted by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and Saudi Arabia, the forum runs until Thursday, bringing together government officials, representatives of technology firms as well as experts and researchers.
"AI is advancing at unprecedented speed, while governance struggles to keep pace," Asa Regner, deputy director-general of UNESCO, said at the opening ceremony.
Regner stressed the need for stronger global cooperation and equitable participation in AI governance, adding that the forum will explore how to turn AI ethical principles into practical implementation.
Abdullah bin Sharaf Alghamdi, president of the Saudi Data and AI Authority, said at the ceremony that countries should pursue AI governance based on common principles while tailoring policies to their own national priorities and cultural contexts.
"We need to work together, turn shared principles into action and make AI governance inclusive, accountable and people centered," he said.
Since its inception in 2022, the forum has convened global stakeholders from government, academia, civil society, and the private sector to advance dialogue and cooperation on the ethical governance of AI. ■

Canada launches new tax incentives to boost competitiveness
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:30:49 CST
05:30:49 KST

TORONTO, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday announced a package of tax incentives at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, aiming to sharpen the country's competitive edge among Group of Seven (G7) nations and attract a fresh wave of business investment.
Carney highlighted Canada's strong fiscal foundation, noting that the country maintains the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. Leveraging free trade agreements covering 1.5 billion consumers globally, Canada has become one of the world's most connected economies with the fiscal capacity to catalyze 1 trillion Canadian dollars (about 718.45 billion U.S. dollars) in new investment, he said.
Under the new "Productivity Mega Deduction" tax incentive, the proportion of eligible capital assets will expand significantly from roughly 15 percent to over 65 percent. Covered assets include fibre-optic cable, mining property, oil and gas pipelines, software, research and development, computer equipment, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges and roads.
The federal government is also making immediate expensing permanent, allowing businesses to recover investment costs faster and reduce post-tax investment burdens.
With these measures, Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new business investment will fall from about 13 percent to 6.4 percent, less than half that of the United States and the lowest among major economies worldwide, according to Carney.
To further optimize key infrastructure, Carney also announced plans to open Canada's four largest airports to private investment through long-term concessions, seeking to enhance the efficiency and capacity of the national transportation network. ■

Profits in Australia's property market still 'exceptionally high' despite recent downturn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:29:20 UTC
05:29:20 KST

IN BRIEF
- New data from Cotality shows that 95.4 per cent of dwelling sales made a gain in the June quarter.
- While dwelling values declined over the quarter, prices remained significantly higher than six years earlier.
Australia is undergoing one of the steepest housing downturns in decades, but years of strong growth mean most homes are still being sold for a hefty profit.
In the June quarter, 95.4 per cent of dwelling sales made a gain, down from the 21-year high of 96.1 per cent recorded in the three months to March, research from data provider Cotality showed on Wednesday.
While national dwelling values declined 1.5 per cent over the June quarter, prices were still more than 67 per cent higher than six years earlier.
Several years of very strong growth had left many home owners with a substantial equity buffer, helping vendors rake in a combined $35.9 billion in profit in the quarter, Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.
"Profitability is still exceptionally high by historical standards, but we are starting to see the impact of weaker housing market conditions flow through to resale outcomes," Burg said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Most sellers are still benefiting from the significant value growth accumulated over the past five years, which is providing considerable protection against the early stages of the downturn.
"With home values falling across more markets, that buffer will become increasingly important in determining resale outcomes."
Australia's housing downturn continued to deepen in July and August, as the outlook for interest rates worsened and investors continued to count the cost of the federal government's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains discount.
Nationwide prices are only down 3.6 per cent from their March peak, but several economists, including at HSBC and Morgan Stanley, expect the total fall in values to hit 10 per cent or more, which would be the deepest downturn in more than 40 years.
The pace of the decline has also rattled sentiment, with the 2022/23 downturn the only time prices have fallen faster for longer since the 1980s.
Buyers who held onto their property for a longer period of time were better able to ride out the cyclical ebbs and flows.
"Owners who have held their property for nine or 10 years have generally experienced several periods of value growth, giving them a much larger equity buffer when market conditions weaken," Burg said.
Houses that sold for a profit were held for a median 9.3 years, compared with the typical holding time of 4.4 years for loss-making house resales.
Overall, 97.8 per cent of houses were sold for a profit, underscoring the growth advantage of freestanding homes over units. Only 90.5 per cent of unit sales made a profit.
Sydney was still the top money spinner in dollar terms, with a total profit of $6.6 billion.
But the proportion of sales that made a profit eased to 92.7 per cent, well below Brisbane, which recorded a profit in 99.8 per cent of sales.
Nationally, the median gain eased from a record $378,000 to $371,000, while the median loss increased from $44,000 to $45,000.

Argentina submits 2027 budget bill to Congress, foresees 4% GDP growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:27:02 UTC
05:27:02 KST

Argentina submits 2027 budget bill to Congress, foresees 4% GDP growth
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 15 - Argentina's government presented its 2027 budget proposal to Congress on Tuesday, laying out President Javier Milei's economic projections and spending priorities ahead of a presidential election next year.
According to the bill, the government forecasts GDP growth of 4% in 2027 from an expected 3% this year, and expects Argentina to record a trade surplus of over $15 billion next year.
Annual inflation is projected at 18%, compared with 29% this year.
Argentina will hold presidential elections in October 2027, and Milei is widely expected to seek re-election. The budget is expected to serve as the administration's final full-year fiscal plan before the vote, and is likely to operate as a roadmap for economic and political priorities heading into the campaign.
The bill now moves to the budget committee, then to Congress. Argentina has operated for extended periods without an approved budget, with the previous year’s rolled over, which is the fallback if the process fails to secure approval.
Milei has previously said that Argentina should increase defense spending as part of a broader effort to strengthen its sovereignty claims over the Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.
Milei has adopted a harder line on Argentina's claim to the Falkland Islands, that Argentina calls the Malvinas after signals from U.S. President Donald Trump that Washington's longstanding neutrality on the dispute could soften.
Since taking office in late 2023, Milei has centered his economic program on spending cuts and eliminating the fiscal deficit through austerity measures that have sharply reduced public expenditure, making any proposed increase in areas such as defense particularly notable, analysts said. REUTERS

Canada to emerge from US trade war more independent: PM Carney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
20:27:00 UTC
05:27:00 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada intends to emerge from its trade war with the United States with a stronger, more resilient and independent economy, signaling Ottawa will not rush into an agreement with Washington simply to end the dispute.
"And to our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbors,” Carney told hundreds of global investors gathered in Toronto for his Canada Investment Summit. But he said the relationship works when the two countries engage as "true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”
"When those opportunities return, Canada will be an even better partner - stronger, more resilient, more independent,” he said.
Carney also announced that Ottawa will seek private investment through long-term concessions to operate Canada’s four largest airports, while retaining public ownership of the land and assets. He said the plan could raise tens of billions of dollars to reinvest in transportation and other infrastructure.
Without naming U.S. President Donald Trump, Carney then took aim at the increasingly transactional and zero-sum approach to international economic relationships that has characterized Trump’s trade policies.
"Our reputation - as a reliable, predictable partner - has rarely been more valuable in a world where transactions are replacing relationships, and zero-sum is favored over win-win,” Carney said.
Carney said economic integration and national sovereignty are increasingly in tension, arguing that countries seeking to preserve their independence need to work more closely with like-minded partners. He heads to Europe later Tuesday, where he is scheduled to address the European Parliament.
Trump has repeatedly used tariffs to pressure trading partners and pressed manufacturers to shift production and investment south of the Canadian border. He has also repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st U.S. state, comments that have further strained relations between the longtime allies.
But Carney noted that about 80% of the trade with the U.S. remains tariff-free.
"There is a mutually beneficial arrangement that can be had,” Carney said in a fireside chat after his speech. "When it is the right time to strike that deal, we’ll be ready to do that.”
Trade talks between Canada and the United States collapsed last month before Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa. The United States has since announced additional restrictions on Canadian products.
Carney also joked about the uneasy state of the U.S.-Canada relationship, contrasting a ceremonial key he once received from his hometown of Fort Smith, Northwest Territories, with a box of gold keys to the White House that Trump later gave him.
Carney said Trump told him that if he brought the key, "They’ll let you in,” before adding: "Maybe they’ll shoot you.”
"And that sort of sums up the relationship,” Carney said. "In Canada, you get the key. In the U.S., they might shoot you.”

NATO jets down drone over Lithuania as Russian ship fires flares at Danish helicopter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
