NATO jet shoots down suspected Russian drone over Lithuania
EU chief warns of wider conflict as border incursions stoke fears that Ukraine war is spilling into neighbouring states.
An Italian fighter jet flying for NATO has brought down what officials said was a suspected Russian drone in Lithuanian airspace.

Wider conflict
The drone was intercepted over Lithuania after Russia fired flares at a Danish military helicopter monitoring a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea on Monday.
In a post on X on Tuesday, Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said, that “recent days show that Russia’s actions threaten the security of the entire Europe”.
The escalations followed a series of Russian drone strikes on Sunday, prompting NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to pledge more support for Ukraine. Russian drones hit a train close to the Polish border, minutes after a delegation of current and former officials from the United Kingdom, the United States and Europe passed through the station.
At a press conference, Kaunas warned that the Russia-Ukraine war has spread and that incidents would continue unless there was a negotiated settlement, but maintained that “Putin does not want” a peaceful settlement.

What Is the Status of the U.S.-Iran Peace Talks? Here's What Both Sides Are Saying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:58:15 UTC
04:58:15 KST

President Donald Trump at the start of the Iran war predicted it would last four-to-five weeks, but the conflict is now in its seventh month, with no clear timeline for when the fighting will end.
Active hostilities between Washington and Tehran resumed earlier this month, with oil tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz coming under fire. Iran is vying to maintain a chokehold over the vital trade route amid the U.S. blockade against its ports. The Strait effectively remains in a military stalemate, bringing renewed regional instability and gravely impacting transit via the waterway, through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed before the war began on Feb. 28. Oil prices last week soared to over $100 a barrel for the first time since July, as the disruption sends energy markets spiraling once more.
The balance of power in the Gulf has come under further strain as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have made significant advances following weeks of fighting with the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthis last week captured the strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another vital trade route situated between Yemen and Djibouti and Eritrea in the Horn of Africa, that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. This came as they traveled along the Red Sea coastline, aiming to tighten their grip on the critical maritime chokepoint. The disruption has placed further pressure on the global oil market.
The Houthis’ expanding presence in the Red Sea and the potential it has to severely disrupt trade via the Bab el-Mandeb arguably gives Iran leverage in its war with the U.S., experts say.
“This has the effect of turning up the pressure on the U.S. and its allies who have been relying on alternate routes,” Daniel Benaim, a former U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for the Arabian Peninsula, tells TIME. “In a contest of economic wills, the alternate Red Sea has been a very important release valve for the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Diplomatic efforts in the Middle East have faltered. The Gulf states, many of which house U.S. bases that have been targeted by Iranian strikes, on Monday postponed a critical meeting with Tehran on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Despite pressure mounting for a clear way out of the war, meaningful negotiations between the U.S. and Iran also remain stalled. Here’s what each side has said regarding the status of peace talks, and how experts predict Iranian officials could use the Houthis’ disruption in the Red Sea to their benefit.
Trump says U.S. is 'open' to restarting negotiations
Trump on Monday said the U.S. is “open” to the concept of restarting negotiations between Washington and Tehran. High-level officials from both sides last convened for official peace talks in Switzerland in June.
“The failing nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly,” he claimed. “I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage—the concept of which we are open to.”
Trump’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the position he laid out on Sept. 2, when he said he was “not trying to force” Iran to the bargaining table. “I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable,” he insisted.
On Sept. 9, Trump assured the American public that the war will likely end “immediately after” the November midterms and said Iran’s government is holding out in hopes of hurting Republican political prospects.
Trump has expressed full confidence in the U.S.’ two-pronged military and economic campaign against Iran, with the latter aiming to choke Tehran off from the global economy through various sanctions.
Ali Vaez, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, tells TIME that Trump’s diplomatic approach will dictate how successful future negotiations may be.
“President Trump might be interested in getting a deal with Iran, but that's not necessarily a guarantee that he will get a deal. It all depends on what approach he would adopt to diplomacy. If it's maximalist, then it doesn't stand a chance of succeeding,” he says, adding that dealing with Iran requires “a multi-dimensional diplomacy” in order to achieve a “sustainable de-escalation between Iran and the United States.”
Trump has repeatedly insisted that the U.S. has near total control of the vital waterway and that “oil is flowing,” but traffic via the Strait remains disrupted.
Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, shared data with TIME that shows that only 10 ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Monday—a significantly lower count than the 138 vessels that typically passed through the waterway during a 24-hour period before the war.
“The United States has shown over time that it has capabilities to move significant amounts of shipping through the Strait, but Iran has innovated,” says Benaim. “Iran and its allies are innovating in their ability to disrupt. So it's a bit of a foot race between U.S. attempts to bypass Iran's restraints and Iran's attempts to enforce its own de facto blockade.”
The Iran war, and its economic impact, has been deeply unpopular with Americans who are facing increasingly high energy costs. Diesel prices last week reached a record $6 per gallon. The war with Iran has cost the U.S. government around $38 billion and contributed to growing inflation, according to newly-published analysis by the Congressional Budget Office. A national UMass Amherst/YouGov poll, conducted from Aug. 21 to 26, found that 68% of Americans view Trump’s handling of the war negatively.
Iran says 'no talks until conditions met'
Iran has responded to Trump’s openness to negotiations by doubling down on its demands.
“Don’t get distracted by the U.S. President’s mixed signals—from ‘no negotiations’ to ‘we’re ready to talk,’" said Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's recently-installed secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, on Monday. “No talks until Iran’s conditions are met. Period!”
While Rezaei did not directly name any conditions, Iran previously put forward a list of six demands for the U.S. to meet before the Strait of Hormuz would be fully reopened. Rezaei also seemingly pointed to the recent developments in the wider region, arguing that the “stakes around oil and the straits have changed” and warning that “damage control won’t stop what’s coming.”
The remarks from the hard-line national security adviser took an elevated position from that of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who in early September said Tehran was prepared to “reciprocate,” if the U.S. returned to the cease-fire conditions both countries negotiated in June. He was referencing the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed on June 17, but the pact fell apart, with Washington and Tehran seemingly adopting different interpretations of the language used in the interim agreement.
Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa program, says the Iranians are now “negotiating for the sake of negotiating,” arguing that their demands are intended to draw out talks while energy prices continue to rise.
“They can wait. They can afford it. They have no [democratic] parliaments. They don't care about public opinion, as you imagine, and they are not allergic to pain,” he tells TIME.
Has Iran gained leverage as the Houthis close in on the Bab El-Mandeb Strait?
With the Houthis tightening its grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Iran has gained another potential source of leverage, experts say.
Amid the ongoing disruption to the Strait of Hormuz since the war started, there has been an uptick in the volume of crude oil and petroleum liquids that transit via the Bab el-Mandeb, increasing from 5.6 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Despite the Houthis having claimed that they will not disrupt maritime traffic—except for Saudi Arabian oil tankers—experts tell TIME that the group’s ability to threaten shipping is enough to give Tehran greater leverage in any future round of negotiations.
“The Houthis march to the beat of their own drummer, but these actions certainly help Iran gain leverage by complicating alternative routes out of the Strait of Hormuz,” says Benaim.
In agreement, Al-Muslimi adds “the Iranians now have a new card they can use, and they haven't totally used [it] yet, but they will. It's a matter of time.”
“The Houthis are primarily concerned about advancing their own position within Yemen and globally. In this case, it happens to coincide with the pressure that Iran would like to apply on the United States and the international community,” Benaim adds.
Alternatives to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait present fresh challenges
The Bab el-Mandeb, which is Arabic for "Gate of Tears," serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal— ships must pass through it to access the canal from the south. If the Houthis were to close the Bab el-Mandeb, it would increase the pressure on the global flow of oil.
Experts say shipping companies, if forced to find an alternative route, could be left to transit around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope.
The Cape of Good Hope “could be a temporary solution, but it adds to insurance and travel costs, and timelines,” says Vaez. The EIA has estimated that the Cape route adds approximately 15 days to an oil voyage from the Arabian Sea to Europe.
Disturbances in the Bab el-Mandeb are particularly significant for Asian countries, experts say.
Asia has traditionally been Saudi Arabia’s primary export market for crude oil, receiving 75% of Saudi Arabia’s total annual crude oil exports in 2023, according to data from the EIA. China, Japan, South Korea, and India were its top crude oil importers.
The EIA on Sept. 9 acknowledged the concessions required when using alternative routes, noting that although “Saudi Arabia has increased oil shipments through the Suez Canal at the north end of the Red Sea,” it is “a longer and costlier route for customers in Asia.”
The Suez Canal also has constraints. As detailed by the International Energy Agency (IEA), “large crude carriers (VLCC) can only transit the canal when loaded below their 250,000 tonnes capacity.” As such, tankers following the route must first unload part of their cargo into a pipeline south of the canal and then reload the crude at a port before continuing their voyage, according to Reuters.

The U.S. Just Admitted it Has Weapons in Space. Why That's a Big Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:56:00 UTC
04:56:00 KST

On Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the quiet part out loud. Speaking at the Air, Space, and Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Md., Meink openly conceded something U.S. policymakers have been avoiding acknowledging for years—that the American military intends to weaponize space, and indeed, that it already has hostile hardware in Earth orbit.
“We are increasing readiness against existing threats,” Meink said. “[T]he United States has on orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”
The announcement was headline-making both for what it said about the escalation of weapons development to off-planet domains, and for Meink’s surprising candor. Weaponization of space has been officially forbidden under international law since Jan. 27, 1967, when the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies—better known simply as the Outer Space Treaty—was signed and ratified by the U.S., the U.K., and the old U.S.S.R. Since then, 112 other countries have joined the pact. China, which was not remotely a global power at the time the treaty was adopted, signed on to it in 1983.
But the agreement has been honored as much in the breach as in the observance—at least by the U.S., China, and modern-day Russia. As long ago as 1985, the U.S. Air Force shot down a defunct American weather satellite with a missile launched by a military jet flying at 31,500 ft., a first test of a technology that could just as easily be used against the space assets of enemy nations. The Soviet Union experimented with similar R&D beginning in 1983, but did not succeed at it until 2021, when it famously destroyed a Soviet-era satellite with a ground-based missile. Beijing beat Moscow to the punch 14 years earlier, skeet-shooting a Feng Yun-1C weather satellite out of the sky with a projectile fired by a ground-launched ballistic missile, scoring a hit more than 500 miles up.
The U.S. has—officially at least—disavowed and condemned this kind of cosmic escalation. At the time of the Chinese action, senior members of the George W. Bush administration criticized the move as “very troubling,” “very worrisome,” “destabilizing,” and “quite unpleasant.” A senior Air Force spokesperson told the media flatly, “We don’t want to do that.” But what America ostensibly wants to do and what it has actually been doing are two different things.
In 1983, then-President Ronald Reagan announced plans for a tactical umbrella known as the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), which aimed to use missiles that could reach orbital and suborbital space to knock down nuclear and conventional ordnance launched by the Soviet Union and other foes. The program did not quite run afoul of the Outer Space Treaty since it was nominally defensive rather than offensive, though the Kremlin decidedly did not see things that way. The SDI ran for a decade—until the presidency of Bill Clinton—and produced no technology of note, while burning through an inflation-adjusted $70 billion. Presidents since then have continued to invest in space-based missile defense—though at lower funding levels—with President George W. Bush going so far as to withdraw from the 1972 U.S.-U.S.S.R Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) treaty, to pursue the technology without officially breaking America’s diplomatic word.
In his two terms in the Oval Office, President Donald Trump has escalated the Pentagon’s push into space. During his first term, in 2019 Trump created the Space Force, a sixth branch of the armed services, with particular focus on the orbital domain. The new branch is small compared to the rest of the military, with just 10,000 uniformed service members (compared to 450,000 for the Army), and a $71 billion budget for fiscal year 2027 (against the Army’s $253 billion). What’s more, most of the work the Space Force has been doing was already being performed by the U.S. Air Force’s Space Command, meaning that the establishment of the new branch represented less an increase in the Pentagon’s off-Earth activities than a mere shift in the shingle under which the jobs were getting done.
But upon his return to the White House in 2025, Trump stepped up the militarization of space—and did so fast. On Jan. 27—the 58th birthday of the Outer Space Treaty and just a week after his inauguration—Trump issued Executive Order 14186, establishing the so-called Iron Dome (later renamed Golden Dome), a space-defense system that the Congressional Budget Office has estimated could cost $1.2 trillion over 20 years, with a down payment of $25 billion, or about the same as NASA’s annual budget, spent in its first fiscal year alone. Among other things, Golden Dome calls for space-based missile interceptors and a global constellation of satellites to monitor hostile nations’ space activities—both pillars of Reagan’s SDI.
Golden Dome has been moving at a sprint since the Executive Order was signed. In the past 18 months, the program has advanced from the contract phase to actual flight-ready hardware. Beta-tests of both interceptors and surveillance systems are set for launch before the end of the year. Indeed, said Meink in his remarks, “We start launching our Air Moving Target Indicator constellation this month,” referring to the monitoring satellites.
It’s not just defensive weapons that are in play as the arms race in space accelerates. And it’s not just missiles that will be the agents of that combat. Lasers and microwave technology—flashed and pulsed by armed satellites—are widely believed to be in development, and could be used to fry the brains and blind the optical systems of opposing countries’ satellites. Meantime, Foreign Policy magazine reports that China is developing military satellites with robotic arms that could literally yank opposing satellites out of their intended orbits. In the wake of Meink’s announcement, Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at England’s Durham University, told the BBC that the U.S. could be developing similar technology as well. “[S]ome sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be [a] possibility,” he said.
The biggest danger, however, comes from missiles and orbital projectiles that would effectively blow satellites up, since that kind of kinetic attack produces a swirling cloud of orbital debris that would fan out from the site of the strike, threatening other satellites with unplanned destruction. Accidental collisions with space junk already worry both the commercial and military sectors. There are currently nearly 15,000 operational satellites in Earth orbit, and up to 10,000 defunct ones, making for a lot of celestial traffic. Just as troubling, according to NASA’s Orbital Debris Program Office, there are an additional 500,000 objects measuring 1 to 10 cm (.39 in. and 3.9 in.), and 100 million in the 1-mm range. Such tiny bits of mass matter. Traveling at 4.85 miles per second, even a fleck of paint could do significant damage to a satellite, or, worse, a crewed spacecraft.
What truly keeps space planners up at night is something known as the Kessler Effect—a slow-motion chain reaction in which the flotsam produced by a collision with even a single piece of space debris could strike other satellites, producing more debris still, and more collisions still, ultimately leading to the loss of all spacecraft in that orbital band. A runaway Kessler effect was the premise of the 2013 film Gravity, and while the screenwriters took liberties with the science (the collisions all played out within hours when in fact they could take months or even years), the eventual results would be the same. China’s 2007 satellite-destruction exercise was estimated to have produced more than 3,000 pieces of debris—which could have taken out the country’s own spacecraft as readily as those of rivals. Russia’s similar duck-hunting in 2021 is estimated by the Pentagon to have produced 1,500 fragments. It was luck more than anything else that prevented either move from setting a Kessler cascade in motion.
For now, Meink is not saying anything about just what kind of assets the Pentagon has recently placed in space—only that they’re up there, they’re operating, and they’ll be followed by more. “Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” he said. “We face a mix of rapidly changing technologies [and] adversaries moving aggressively to employ them. We must…innovate faster than anyone else.”

Promo-LEX says Transnistria’s military schools prepare children for service in the separatist administration’s security forces and paramilitary units. At the same time, Russian “patriotic education” programs expose them to indoctrination and security risks. Those programs connect Transnistria’s school system to Russia’s wider militarization and re-education of children in occupied Ukraine.
Beyond the classroom, dozens of Transnistrian children attended “patriotic education” programs in Russia and occupied Crimea this summer, the Association for the Reintegration of Crimea (ARC) said, citing Promo-LEX.
ARC said one group attended events at Artek, a Russian-run children’s camp, in June 2026. From 23 June to 13 July, another group participated in the “Circle of Friends” program at Russia’s Orlyonok children’s center.
The Artek camp is under EU, UK, and US sanctions over its role in deporting and re-educating Ukrainian children. Promo-LEX has documented Transnistrian children attending Artek-run camps for nearly a decade.
Transnistria is internationally recognized as part of Moldova but has remained under Russia-backed separatist control since a war in 1992, with Russian troops still stationed there.
A Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) video showed students raising Transnistria’s flag and singing its anthem at the start of the school week. Tiraspol authorities described the ceremonies as promoting patriotism and discipline.
Of the 127 children who enrolled in the two military schools (up from 120 the previous year), 65 entered the Tiraspol Suvorov Military School, and 62 entered a cadet school in Bender, according to Promo-LEX. About half of this year’s new students in Bender are girls.
Students from the age of 11 wear camouflage, live under a barracks regime, and receive training in handling weapons and drones, Promo-LEX says. The intake includes children from vulnerable families and boarding schools. The group has also warned that graduates may face pressure to sign contracts with Tiraspol’s paramilitary structures.
How Russia militarizes children in occupied Ukraine
Russia uses the same education-to-service pipeline across occupied Ukraine. More than 582,000 children at nearly 2,000 occupation schools study under an imposed Russian curriculum, while schools are adding military-training tracks and ideology classes, according to the Almenda Center.
In December 2025, UN monitors documented Russia imposing weekly “patriotic” lessons in occupied Ukraine on children as young as three and putting older children through combat training—including instructions on how to handle drones.
At “Zarnitsa 2.0,” a Russian military-training competition for children held in May 2026, a Kremlin-backed youth movement taught children to handle weapons and explosives and operate drones, Ukraine's military intelligence said.
Earlier, 24 teenagers from occupied Kherson Oblast received drone, combat, and cyber training at Russia's Avangard camp, according to Ukraine's Center for National Resistance.

Space Force Accepting Applications for Interservice Transfers Until Oct. 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:50:09 UTC
04:50:09 KST

For the next 17 days, the Space Force is accepting applications from Airmen, Soldiers, Sailors, and Marines to transfer into the Space Force and become Guardians.
The first interservice transfer window in three years opened Sept. 15 and closes Oct. 2. The Space Force is looking for “several hundred” new mid-grade officers and enlisted members during this period, a Department of the Air Force spokesperson said. Only Active-Duty members are eligible; members of the various Reserve and National Guard components, as well as the Coast Guard and Merchant Marine are not.
Any service member can apply, even those with no experience in space operations. But priority will be given to those not requiring retraining into one of the Space Force’s three main operator career fields—space, cyber, and intelligence. Also of interest: acquisition and engineering officers.
The Space Force provided a cross-service map detailing how Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps specialties align with Space Force job codes.
Individuals with “derogatory information” in their file or are on any sort of administrative or medical hold will also be disqualified.
To transfer, service members must submit a service career brief, their last five performance reports, their most recent physical fitness and body composition assessment, and an endorsement for transfer from their unit commander. Interested members must also submit documentation of any approved religious or medical accommodations they have received, and whether they have been selected for promotion.
The price of a transfer: a four-year service commitment upon joining the Space Force.
The Space Force was formed by transferring members, with most transferring from the Air Force. Then it held interservice transfer windows in each of three fiscal years, 2022, 2023, and 2024. USSF accepted 720 transfers in 2022, 511 in 2023, and 148 in 2024.
In 2025, the Space Force took in transfers from the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve, and at the same time created a new hybrid full-time/part-time system under the Space Force Personnel Management Act. Around 300 Guardsmen and Reservists transferred to the Space Force on a full-time basis, and nearly 250 joined as part-timers.
Now, as the Space Force embarks on doubling the force from about 10,000 to 20,000 uniformed Guardians in the next five years, interservice transfers are back on the table.
USSF continues to benefit from extremely high interest from the public and has consistently met or exceeded its recruiting goals every year since its start in 2019. Interservice transfers of mid-grade enlisted and officer personnel are essential, however, to ensuring the Space Force maintains an appropriate mix of junior, mid-grade, and senior personnel.
The department spokesperson said the focus on mid-grade transfers is necessary “to meet our … requirements and account for the service’s steep growth as projected.”

Viral Putin, Modi and Xi selfie at BRICS summit is AI-generated
Unknown

2026-09-15

Viral Putin, Modi and Xi selfie at BRICS summit is AI-generated
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
A viral selfie allegedly showing Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, Narendra Modi and other leaders together at the BRICS summit in New Delhi is AI-generated. A SynthID watermark shows it was created using OpenAI tools, while several leaders pictured, including Brazil’s Lula and Turkey’s Erdogan, did not attend. Another AI selfie features former Iranian president Ebrahim Raisi, who died in 2024. Both images were widely shared online, including by official embassy accounts. Vedika Bahl fact-checks.
The BRICS 2026 summit in New Delhi brought together leaders from some of the world’s major emerging economies, as the bloc pushes for a greater role in global affairs. But amid the official summit images, two unofficial selfies have gone viral, falsely portraying world leaders together and fuelling claims of BRICS unity.
Russia’s embassy in South Africa shared the photo with the message “BRICS is a superpower”, with the post receiving millions of views. Official Iranian embassy accounts in India and Armenia also shared the image.
One of the selfies appears to show Russian President Vladimir Putin taking a selfie alongside the BRICS world leaders: Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also present in the "selfie", alongside alongside leaders from Egypt, Ethiopia and Indonesia, as well as Abu Dhabi’s President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed.
The image, however, is AI-generated.
The picture contains an invisible digital watermark known as SynthID, which indicates that it was created using OpenAI tools.
There are also several clues in the image itself.
Lula did not attend the BRICS summit. Brazil was instead represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, who was pictured with Modi at the event. And while Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed is shown in the selfie, Abu Dhabi was represented at the summit by Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
A second AI selfie
A second AI-generated selfie claiming to show BRICS leaders together has also circulated online.
This version again appears to have been taken by Putin, but includes former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The image was shared by several Indian social media accounts, including one belonging to Shazia Ilmi, a spokesperson for India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. Ilmi posted the image with the caption “this pic says all” and tagged opposition politicians, including opposition leader Rahul Gandhi.
But the image contains even more obvious inconsistencies.
Whilst it's been established Lula was not was present, while Erdogan was also absent, andTurkey is not a BRICS member or partner country. A more glaring error is that the selfie includes Ebrahim Raisi, who died in a helicopter crash in May 2024.
Ilmi later deleted the post and described sharing the image as a “mistake”.

Staunch Israel supporter Coons expected to win Delaware Democratic Senate primary handily
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:48:55 UTC
04:48:55 KST

Delaware incumbent Sen. Chris Coons, a longtime supporter of Israel, secured a landslide victory in Delaware’s US Senate primary on Tuesday, despite criticism from party progressives.
The Associated Press called the race just minutes after polls closed, at 8:16pm, when Coons had accrued 84.6% of the votes, with 26% of ballots tallied. At that point, his opponents, Jeff Appelhans, Mary Louve and E. No-Trump Hansen, had earned 7%, 5.5% and 2.9%, respectively.
In the November general election, Coons will be up against Republican Mike Katz, a physician and former state senator. The AP declared Katz’s win against military veteran John Shulli on Tuesday just two minutes after calling the Democratic race. Coons is expected to easily defeat Katz, with the Cook Political Report deeming Delaware “solid” Democratic territory.
Coons, a mainstay of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has repeatedly backed measures to bolster Israel’s capacity for self-defense. He also joined a bipartisan delegation to visit Israel immediately after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks.
But the senator has faced pushback in recent months for his refusal to back measures that would cut military aid to Israel.
This past spring, he was one of just seven Democrats to join Republicans in voting against a resolution authored by independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, which sought to stop the sale of military bulldozers to Israel. Coons was among just 11 Democrats who opposed a second Sanders resolution that proposed similar sales bans on massive bombs and other defense equipment.
Coons has served nearly three terms in the Senate. He won a special election in 2010, about a year after Joe Biden resigned to become the US vice president, and then went on to secure two full terms in 2014 and 2020.
In Tuesday’s primary, Coons faced off against Appelhans, an artificial intelligence systems builder and historian, as well as Louve, a naval architect and marine engineer, and Hansen, a former business executive who changed his legal first name from Eric to E. No-Trump.
While Coons has earned endorsements from establishment Democrats, such as Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester and Gov. Matt Meyer, he has drawn criticism from party progressives for both his support for Israel and the financial backing he gets from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel lobbying group.
Who are Coon's opponents?
Of Coons’s opponents, the most vocal critic on Israel-related policy has been Appelhans, whose campaign priorities included ending US support for Israel’s war in Gaza. Appelhans slammed Coons for voting against the Sanders bills, writing on his campaign site that “the liberal consensus moved to block the sales.”
Appelhans condemned Coons’s voting record on “moving armaments to Israel,” noting in a recent interview that “there’s never been a vote that he’s stopped” on this issue. He was speaking with Delaware Public Media last week as part of a series of candidate interviews.
Regarding the conflict in Iran, Appelhans slammed “Congress’ unwillingness” to challenge the president, noting that “there was very much a sense that Israel would be a staunch ally and they could sort of get this done really easily.”
In the same radio series, another candidate, Louve, expressed uncertainty as to “why we’re still backing Israel,” while acknowledging the country’s history as a US ally.
“Is it worth us continuing to step up for a bully?” she asked. “It’s aggression that is unnecessary that’s continuing to escalate because we’re helping it.”
Hansen did not participate in these conversations, Delaware Public Media stated.
This summer Coons pledged to stop taking donations from the data company Palantir, which has come under scrutiny for its work with the Israel’s Defense Ministry, the US military, and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to the nonprofit news site Spotlight Delaware.
Coons has significantly criticized Trump administration
Despite his more centrist reputation, Coons has had significant criticism for the Trump administration’s strategies in Iran. In his own Delaware Public Media interview, Coons accused the president of selling the conflict “as a cheap, quick war.”

04:44:28 KST

It comes as a Ukrainian unit launched a counteroffensive against Russian forces near the city of Lyman in eastern Ukraine, according to the unit's commander.
At least five people have been killed and more than a dozen have been injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the last 24 hours.
The mayor of Kyiv, Vitali Klitschko, said on Tuesday afternoon that at least 12 people had been injured in strikes on the Ukrainian capital since the morning, with one critically injured person dying in hospital.
Kyiv police said warehouses, a business center and a fast-food restaurant were damaged in attacks on the city, with Ukrainian media reporting that the restaurant was a McDonald's.
In the southern city of Kherson, a 74-year-old woman was killed by a Russian drone strike, Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Region Military Administration, announced on Telegram.
Two men, aged 38 and 60, were also wounded in a drone attack on the Kherson region on Tuesday morning, per local authorities.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, the acting head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration, Mykhailo Semkin, said early on Tuesday that another man was killed and a woman was injured after an attack that reportedly targeted the power grid.
Two others were killed and one person was injured in strikes on Sloviansk in the eastern Donetsk Oblast, authorities said.
Moscow launched 200 drones overnight at Ukraine as it continued its attacks on the country, with 187 intercepted, Ukraine's armed forces said.
Russian oil refinery struck
For its part, the Ukrainian military reported attacks on Russia's Syzran oil refinery, as well as on the Atlant Aero facility in the city of Taganrog, which reportedly specialises in the making of unmanned aerial vehicles and components.
In an operation carried out by Ukraine's Special Operations Forces, including its deep strike units, the Syzran refinery's primary crude oil distillation unit and tank farm were hit, the Ukrainian General Staff said.
Ukraine launches counteroffensive
It comes as a Ukrainian unit's commander announced that it had launched counteroffensive against Russian forces near the eastern Ukrainian city of Lyman.
The city of Lyman remains one of the few in the region of Donetsk not to have been occupied by Russian forces since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but Russian forces have been making efforts to encircle it for months.
Military analysts say that its occupation could facilitate Russia's advance towards taking the Ukrainian strongholds of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
But the commander of Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, Andrii Biletskyi, said in a video on Telegram that the unit had launched an "offensive operation" and that Ukrainian forces had cleared an area of around 75 sq km.

The 2027 draft budget allocates UAH 4.8 trillion for defense, nearly 44% of GDP — Koretskyi
Kyiv • UNN
The government submitted the 2027 draft budget to parliament with UAH 4.885 trillion allocated for defense. More funds were also earmarked for education, healthcare, and business support.
Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhii Koretskyi stated that, in the 2027 Budget draft, UAH 4 trillion 885 billion is allocated to defense alone, which is nearly 44% of GDP, reports UNN.
Today, the Government approved and, within the timeframe established by law, submitted to the Verkhovna Rada the draft State Budget for 2027. This is the budget of a country at war. Our key task is to ensure security and defense needs while preserving financial stability. UAH 4 trillion 885 billion is allocated to defense alone in this budget draft. This is nearly 44% of GDP
According to him, partners additionally provide us with material and technical assistance. This includes missiles, weapons, equipment, shells, means of destruction, and more.
We expect this to amount to no less than UAH 1 trillion, which is even more than this year. However, I want to emphasize that the needs of the defense forces for 2027 are significantly higher. The cost of the war is increasing. We are working to finalize the precise calculations
The prime minister stressed that "we clearly understand that Ukraine can cover only part of its expenditures with its own revenues. Therefore, responsible and coordinated work with partners is the foundation for replenishing the state budget and covering all necessary expenditures and needs. Military and social ones."
In addition, according to Koretskyi, UAH 328.5 billion is allocated for education in the draft Budget, and UAH 292.5 billion for healthcare. This is more than this year. Funding for social programs, support for veterans and internally displaced persons, and housing is increasing. Regions and communities are to receive more resources for recovery, development, and improving people's quality of life.
Another important priority is to help the economy withstand the conditions of the radical intensification of Russian attacks. We are allocating UAH 96 billion for business support programs—almost twice as much as this year. This includes affordable lending, grants, and support for defense innovations. We are also providing separate funding for insurance against war risks. The document is already in the Verkhovna Rada today. All ministers and I personally are ready for a productive dialogue with Parliament and count on the support of the members of parliament

British bosses to be forced to meet with employees who request flexible working
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:33:25 UTC
04:33:25 KST

Company bosses will have to sit down with workers who request flexible working and justify their reasons for any refusals under new rights announced by Louise Haigh on Tuesday.
The first secretary of state told the TUC conference that employers would have to “properly consider” requests for flexibility and offer a face-to-face meeting under new rights for workers.
Speaking to trade union representatives in Brighton, she said: “Life isn’t always as neat as we’d like it to be or as employers would like it to be. There’s kids to pick up, parents to look after, families who rely on us at short notice.
“And sometimes a little bit of flexibility can make all the difference. Now I know that businesses have to make things work too. Not every job can be done from home and not every request can be agreed.
“But every request can be taken seriously. So today I can announce that we will strengthen the right to flexible working. If an employer wants to turn down a request they will have to sit down with their employee, properly consider it and explain why.”
Under current rules all employees have a legal right to request flexible working which employers must consider in a “reasonable manner”, but the new rules would entail bosses sitting down with employees and explaining the reason behind their decision.
Haigh also praised unions for their work campaigning for the Employment Rights Act, which introduced significant new rights for workers on sick pay, parental leave and zero-hours contracts.
She said: “Because of you, working people have had the biggest uplift in their rights in a generation. Changes that won’t just transform lives today … but the lives of our children and our grandchildren.”
In a speech that was pointedly warm towards unions, some of whom were openly critical of the former prime minister Keir Starmer, she said that Andy Burnham understood that “the strength of our movement is drawn from our roots in the trade unions”.
She added: “We need to go further and faster to deliver the scale of change the country expect. But never be in any doubt whose side we are on. Whether it was standing up for workers illegally sacked by P&O Ferries … Or changing public procurement to create more good jobs here in Britain. We are proudly on the side of working people.”

I survived a massacre. Before that night, I didn’t believe evil existed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:31:46 UTC
04:31:46 KST

Are some of us born bad, or is harmful behaviour shaped by experience? How do nature and nurture influence our choices and morals? Watch Insight episode Born Bad? on SBS On Demand.
I was 20 years old when I learned an individual's actions could forever change the lives of many.
I grew up on farms in NSW and had lived a very sheltered life. I believed people were generally good, the world was generally safe, and I had never really been exposed to violence.
But that would soon change when I grew tired of farm life and decided to move interstate.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
On the night of 18 August 1983, I arrived at the Inland Motel at Uluru/Ayers Rock for a friends' farewell around 11pm — after finishing my shift at the nearby Uluru Hotel.
I remember the Inland's bar being very busy.
There were locals, workers from the other motels and people from the now-resort town Yulara, which was then under construction.
It was a small, remote community where most of us knew each other.
Travelling along the winding dirt road that night, I remember seeing Douglas Crabbe's road train parked in the middle of the road on a bend. Several of us in the pub had commented that somebody could easily hit it and be killed.
Crabbe was not a stranger to me. He was a delivery driver and made weekly deliveries to my work, where I had spoken and eaten lunch with him on numerous occasions.
I had seen different sides to him. He could be charming, but he also had a very quick temper and could suddenly snap.
And that night at the Inland, Crabbe was combative and behaved badly towards several people.
He approached me at the bar and groped me inappropriately. At one point, he jumped over the bar, and a scuffle ensued.
Eventually, he left — about half an hour past midnight.
I remember the glare he gave us as he walked away. But I didn't think anything more of it.
'It was like a bomb exploding'
Approximately 40 minutes later, I heard a truck engine roar.
I saw the hotel lights reflect off Crabbe's truck and a split second later it came crashing through the bar.
The only way I can describe what followed is that it was like a bomb exploding: Besser blocks and sections of the ceiling collapsed, and I was struck to the floor.
I remember seeing the enormous wheels only millimetres from me.
When the truck finally stopped, its engine was still running. And there were five dead and 16 seriously injured people among the rubble.
I watched Crabbe get out of the truck. To leave, he had to climb over people who had been killed or injured.
I remember him smiling and laughing as he left.
That image has never left me.
Life divided into 'before' and 'after'
My life changed forever in those few minutes, and I no longer recognised the world I thought I knew.
Before that night, I had never seriously considered whether evil existed.
Afterwards, I had to reconcile the person I knew as our delivery driver with someone capable of deliberately driving a huge road train into a crowded bar.
My life became divided into "before" and "after".
The cuts, bruises, broken ribs, sprained ankle, internal bruising and back injury may have occurred in a matter of seconds, but their consequences have followed me throughout my adult life.
Even now, 43 years later, I continue to require psychological support and pain-management procedures because of what happened.
My internal alarm system also seemed to change.
A loud noise, a crowded room, a sudden movement or seeing a truck on the road can make my body react to danger even when logically I know I am safe.
When I enter a crowded room, I automatically notice the exits and the people around me.
It's exhausting to be constantly automatically assessing your surroundings.
Living with PTSD
Trauma was not understood or spoken about in 1983 the way it is today.
I moved back to my family in the Tweed Valley in northern NSW for two years to recover. My family heard my nightmares — my screams would wake them up during the night.
But none of them really understood what was happening to me or what to do about it.
I don't say that to blame my family; there just simply wasn't the understanding or support that exists now. So, I put it away and tried to get on with my life.
Thirty years later, I finally sought psychiatric help, received a post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) diagnosis and began dealing with what had happened.
'Mass murder is permanent'
Five people were killed that night; five people with lives, relationships, families and futures, just enjoying a night out. Those futures were stolen from them.
What I witnessed that night has shaped my opposition to Douglas Crabbe ever being released on parole. It is not about revenge.
For me, it is about protecting the community, respecting the enormity and permanence of what happened, and speaking for people who no longer have a voice.
More than four decades have now passed, but the passage of time does not undo what happened. Mass murder is permanent.
The people who died cannot walk out of a prison door after serving enough years. Their families don't get their loved ones back. The injured and traumatised don't suddenly return to the people they were before that night.
The justice system understandably looks at the imprisoned perpetrator and asks what has changed when their parole is considered.
I want it to also look backwards.
Look at the victims. Look at the lives that ended. Look at the families who were changed forever. Look at the survivors who are still carrying that night with them 43 years later.
In my view, Crabbe has never demonstrated any remorse or accountability that I would need to see to change my position.
I do not believe the risk is one society should ever be asked to take.
No excuses for evil
Despite everything I have witnessed, I don't believe people are born bad; I believe we are born with free will.
People experience terrible childhoods, trauma, disadvantage and unimaginable struggles.
Those things can profoundly shape a person, and they deserve understanding. But experiencing hardship cannot automatically excuse violence.
Children can grow up in the same family, exposed to the same circumstances and trauma, and make very different choices as adults.
What survival has given me
The effects of that night did not stop with me; trauma can travel through a family without anyone intending it to.
I became a mother to three children, and looking back, I recognise that some of my fear and hypervigilance affected the way I raised them.
I think the 20-year-old me would be sad to see that I sometimes have unwittingly projected the trauma I've carried onto our children. But I also think she would be proud of me.
Today I provide peer support to families affected by homicide through a victims' support group in Queensland.
I support them through court proceedings and trials, and I speak on the telephone when they need someone who understands — whether it is daytime or in the middle of the night.
I cannot take away their grief — nobody can. But I can make sure they don't have to walk through it completely alone.
Using evil for good
Surviving a massacre changed me completely, but it does not define me.
I will never leave that night entirely behind; it is part of me.
There are still difficult days, memories, reminders and ongoing physical and psychological treatments.
I don't think of myself as having "moved on". Instead, I have learned to walk beside what happened.
And I have learnt to use something unimaginably evil for good — helping others find their way through the darkest moments of their lives.
For crisis and mental health support, contact Lifeline (13 11 14), SANE Australia (1800 187 263) or 13Yarn (139 276), a 24/7 Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islanders crisis support line. For PTSD support, contact Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma (FASSTT).

Iran war has cost US military $48 billion: Congressional Budget Office
Unknown

Iran war has cost US military $48 billion: Congressional Budget Office
WASHINGTON - The war with Iran cost the US military around US$38 billion (S$48 billion) as of Aug 1, the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said on Sept 15, with billions more potentially added to the price tag each month the conflict wears on.
“As of August 1, 2026, the armed conflict with Iran has cost (the Department of Defense) approximately US$38 billion,” said the CBO in a report, referring to the war that started after US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran from late February.
It added that depending on the intensity of violence, costs per month could range between US$2 billion-US$3 billion or more if the conflict continued.
The overall figures reflect the cost of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle and increased fuel costs for the military, among other factors, the report said.
The price of replacing munitions used through Aug 1 was estimated at US$21.7 billion, with CBO noting that such replacements have been the largest single component of costs incurred by the Defense Department in the conflict.
The “main opportunity cost” for the department meanwhile has been the depletion of missile defence interceptors, leaving the United States with reduced inventory for several years.
Comparing the reported expenditures of missile defence interceptors with total numbers the department has bought suggests the United States “has probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025,” the CBO warned.
The analysis was prepared following a request by Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, along with other Democratic lawmakers.
In July, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth estimated the Iran war had cost US$37.5 billion.
The CBO estimated on Sept 15 that the main economic effect of the Iran conflict involves inflationary pressures due to oil and natural gas disruptions.
Iran had retaliated in the war by blocking off the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for energy transit, sending costs soaring.
The CBO now estimates that inflation in the first quarter 2027 would be 0.5 percentage points higher than what it projected in February – referring to the personal consumption expenditures price index.
“Core” inflation, stripping out the volatile food and energy segments, would also likely be 0.3 percentage points higher than earlier predicted, the CBO said.
The higher inflation rates will also boost interest rates on Treasury securities, the report added. AFP

Russian forces have stepped up their attempts to break through toward Dobropillia in recent weeks, staff sergeant Dmytro Davydenko of the Svoboda Battalion headquarters said on the Suspilne Studio broadcast on 14 September.
Dobropillia is an important transportation hub in northern Donetsk Oblast, with a key road connecting it to Kramatorsk. Russian forces are using every possible factor, including weather conditions, to seize Dobropillia as part of their efforts to capture the entire Donetsk Oblast.
He noted that Russian forces may be taking advantage of the “greenery” to move as many troops as possible closer to the settlement and then enter Dobropillia when the weather deteriorates, potentially leading to urban combat.
The actions may be part of a tactic Russia has used before, but Ukraine has taken it into account
“Right now, there is a huge increase in the number of mobile groups moving in this direction. Sometimes we simply cannot keep up with engaging those we detect because there is a very large number of movements advancing in all directions right now,” Dmytro said.
Russian forces may use poor weather conditions to attempt something similar to what they did in Pokrovsk, when they tried to bring in a large number of troops using mechanized columns, the staff sergeant said. He added that the Ukrainian military had “drawn certain conclusions” and created obstacles for Russian forces along the routes to Dobropillia: the roads have either been destroyed, mined, or blocked.
The number of assault troops has increased, but Russia faces limitations
Russia can increase the number of troops in the area, but its capabilities are limited, Davydenko said. He explained that one drone operator cannot simultaneously support 20–30 assault groups on different axes, so an increase in the number of Russian troops is unlikely to result in a “critical onslaught.”
“To bring in an even larger number of fighters, I don’t know how well they will manage that, because there is the factor of the physical ability to bring this number of people to the staging point and then lead this large number of people along the route,” Davydenko said.
The Kremlin revives its push toward Dobropillia
Russia prioritized offensive operations toward Pokrovsk and Dobropillia to encircle Ukraine’s fortress belt in Donetsk Oblast from the southwest, but the timeline for such an encirclement is “extremely unrealistic,” the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its 7 August report.
The fortress belt consists of four fortified cities that have formed the backbone of Ukraine’s defense in Donetsk Oblast since 2022: Kostiantynivka, Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk, and Sloviansk. Dobropillia sits at its southwestern corner.
The city initially became a target of Russian strikes as Russian forces advanced toward Pokrovsk, and later became a target for capture. On 11 August 2025, Russian forces managed to approach Dobropillia and cut the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk highway in the opening days of their offensive. Ukrainian forces later reported that they had encircled and eliminated these troops.
In spring and summer 2026, Russia would “almost certainly” attempt to repeat its success in Dobropillia, predicted Francis Farrell for the Kyiv Independent. That is what happened. On 26 July, reports emerged that Russia was once again massing around Dobropillia, using quad bikes and motorcycles, following the same infiltration pattern as in 2025.

Democrats accused the FBI of protecting President Donald Trump from fallout over Epstein while failing to provide survivors with adequate transparency and accountability.

Patel further defended a policy change removing certain incidents of bestiality or animal cruelty from before the age of 18 from the FBI’s list of automatic hiring disqualifiers. He said the change was designed to prevent victims of trafficking or coercion from being automatically excluded from consideration.
“We are not going to criminalize and prevent victims from serving the United States,” Patel said.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy questioned why the FBI had addressed the issue at all. Patel acknowledged that his initial reaction was similar but said officials had shown him cases involving people who had been forced into such acts.
Patel portrayed the bureau’s broader record as one of major public safety gains, citing 54,000 violent -criminal arrests, more than 5,000 arrests of child predators and human traffickers, and the seizure of more than 3,200 kilograms (7,055 pounds) of fentanyl.
Democrats disputed his claims and accused Patel of politicizing the FBI. Durbin called him “the least qualified and most partisan FBI director” in US history.

How this state's pothole problem exposes a national blind spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:30:14 UTC
04:30:14 KST

In brief
- Nearly half of Victoria's state road network is now rated poor or very poor.
- Experts say better funding and new technology are needed to identify damage before roads deteriorate.
The death of a motorcyclist on a country Victorian road has renewed scrutiny of the state's growing pothole problem and prompted fresh calls for urgent road repairs.
Peter Mason, 71, was killed after he struck a pothole and crashed on the Western Highway near Ballarat on Sunday.
Rob Salvatore, chair of the Victorian Motorcycle Council, said the tragedy highlighted the danger posed by poor road conditions, while Victorian Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said immediate repairs were needed to prevent more deaths.
The condition of Victorian roads has become a key issue ahead of the state election in November, with Premier Ben Carroll last month acknowledging the state's roads were "not good enough".
"We're putting lots and lots of money into fixing potholes. But let's be very clear, the system's not working. We need to do it better," he told ABC radio.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
On Tuesday, Carroll said the pothole believed to be responsible for Mason's death has been fixed.
According to a Victorian Auditor-General's report tabled in state parliament last week, nearly half of Victoria's more than 23,000km state road network was in poor or very poor condition in 2024 — up from 39 per cent in 2021.
A growing repair backlog, rising costs, under-investment, flooding and increased traffic and freight demand were among the key factors cited for the deterioration.
Defects are also outpacing maintenance, with the gap between identified and rectified problems more than doubling between January 2025 and June 2026.
According to the auditor-general, the transport department estimated it would cost more than $3 billion to maintain existing road pavements and replace age-expired roads, but only $1.04 billion was allocated for 2026-27.
What can be done?
Since becoming premier in July, Carroll has promised to return to the "basics", which includes fixing potholes.
He announced an extra $352 million to double the number of potholes fixed this year from 250,000 to 500,000 — bringing the total funding for road asset management to $1.39 billion.
The state Opposition's plan is to invest $5 billion — a 25 per cent increase on current funding — over four years to maintain and repair roads, including fixing one million potholes.
However, some experts say that is the wrong approach.
A 2023 Grattan Institute report found many councils — which manage more than 75 per cent of Australia's roads — operate under a "worst-first" scheme, meaning roads are only fixed when they become unusable.
The report says local government funding shortfalls have driven a reactive approach, despite major repairs costing five to 10 times more than preventive maintenance, referred to as a "stitch-in-time" approach.
Regional councils often lacked the funding and technical expertise to maintain their vast road networks, with the report recommending reforming grant distributions to prioritise areas of highest need and reducing local government red tape.
The report suggests a $600 million annual increase in financial assistance grants and $400 million for the Roads to Recovery program, both indexed to reflect cost changes and population growth.
An annual $200 million fund should also be established to assess and upgrade local roads identified as priority freight routes, in exchange for the council providing permit access to compliant heavy vehicles.
Ambarish Kulkarni, a road infrastructure expert at Swinburne University, says technology could play a growing role in helping authorities identify road damage before it becomes severe.
Potholes are often preceded by gradual deterioration, with "crocodile cracking", which resembles reptile scales, an early indicator.
Other warning signs include rutting, where wheel paths wear into the road surface, cracks running parallel to the pavement edge, and water pooling after rain.
Kulkarni's research has explored the use of drones or vehicle-mounted cameras to create digital models of roads. Machine learning models can then be trained to detect early signs of deterioration.
"Potholes are certainly becoming increasingly visible across Victoria, particularly in Melbourne, and they are a significant concern for commuters," he said.
"The research demonstrated the potential to nearly halve monitoring and associated costs. More importantly, it shows how we can move from reactive maintenance, fixing potholes once they become obvious, towards predictive and preventative maintenance."
Calls for a national approach
While the Grattan Institute reported targeted funding for local road repairs, identifying the areas most in need can be difficult.
A 2023 federal parliamentary committee report into the impact of severe weather events on Australia's roads found the condition of the network was poorly understood due to data gaps and a lack of standardised data sharing between federal, state and local governments.
"It is critical that governments have access to high-quality, consistent data to inform evidence-based strategic investment and preventive maintenance regimes for both state and locally owned road assets," the report said.
State and territory governments generally oversee major highways, while local councils are responsible for local roads.
The report found the largest data gaps were among councils, many of which lack the funding and specialised equipment needed to carry out regular road condition surveys.
It called for a national approach, with all levels of government working in collaboration on road assessments and the implementation of standardised recording methods.
While official data gaps remain, figures from Snap Send Solve, an app that allows people to report issues such as potholes to local authorities, show that Victoria recorded the highest number of damaged-road reports.
In the 12 months to March 2026, there were 33,115 reports in Victoria, compared with 22,291 in NSW and 19,441 in Queensland.

Finland Expands Military Support to Ukraine With New €290 Million Assistance
Finland will provide Ukraine with its 34th military aid package, valued at approximately €290 million ($335 million), according to the Finnish Ministry of Defense on September 15.
This decision brings the total value of defense assistance supplied by Finland to Ukraine to roughly €3.6 billion ($4.15 billion) since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This latest package marks the second-largest defense allocation from Helsinki to Kyiv since the full-scale invasion began.
The newly allocated support includes weapons and defense equipment, a portion of which was purchased directly from the Finnish defense industry.
Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen stated, “Finland continues to support Ukraine, which is defending itself against illegal aggression by Russia. Throughout the war, we have provided Ukraine with material assistance according to its needs.”
He added that sourcing equipment from domestic manufacturers concurrently supports the expansion of Finland's own defense production capacity.
Details regarding the contents of the package, delivery schedules, and transit methods are remaining confidential due to operational security.
On May 29, 2026, Finland provided Ukraine with its 33rd package of defense material following a decision made by President Alexander Stubb based on a proposal from the government.
The aid was valued at approximately €128 million ($138.5M), which brought the total value of defense material delivered by Helsinki to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine to €3.4 billion ($3.68B).

US Congress Democrats probe Russian oligarch financing of Trump Jr wedding parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:22:00 UTC
04:22:00 KST

US Congress Democrats probe Russian oligarch financing of Trump Jr wedding parties
WASHINGTON - Democrats in the US Congress launched an investigation this week into reports that a Russian oligarch paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding celebrations of President Donald Trump’s son earlier in 2026.
The Democrats’ move comes on the heels of an article by ProPublica that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association, paid for wedding festivities for Donald Trump Jr in the Bahamas in May.
The report said that Kremlev has close ties to the Russian government.
“Why is a Russian oligarch and friend of Vladimir Putin financially supporting the President’s son? What does Umar Kremlev expect in return for funding this three-day wedding in the Bahamas?” Representative Robert Garcia wrote on Sept 15 in a social media post.
Garcia is the senior Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and is expected to chair the panel if Democrats win a majority in the House of Representatives in November’s midterm elections.
A representative for Don Jr declined to comment.
His wife, Bettina Trump, said in an Instagram post on Sept 14 that Kremlev was a friend who had extended an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift,” stressing that Kremlev had paid for two after-parties, not the wedding itself.
Kremlev and the IBA did not respond to requests for comment on Sept 15.
The president, who did not attend his son’s wedding, said in a statement that he did not know Kremlev and that the wedding controversy was “not a big deal!”
Aides to Republican Representative James Comer of Kentucky, who chairs the committee, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Garcia and other leading House Democrats already have been gearing up for probes into Trump, his family and ethics questions that have arisen since the start of the president’s second term in January 2025.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York on Sept 15 called the wedding arrangement “so corrupt, so venal, so endangering our national security.”
In a speech to the Senate, Schumer added, “You’re dealing with a Russian oligarch, not just a cousin who’s giving you a gift...sometimes a wedding gift is a bribe from a foreign autocrat.” REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Warner Bros killed Coyote vs. Acme, but now it's back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:21:50 UTC
04:21:50 KST

Films can be left unfinished or unreleased for a variety of reasons, but it's rare for one to come back from the dead.
This week, Coyote vs. Acme will conclude its long journey to Aussie cinemas, having previously looked deader than a cartoon coyote trapped under a comically oversized boulder.
So how did this Looney Tunes spin-off finally make it to the big screen, and why is its resurrection such a big deal?
What is Coyote vs. Acme?
The film tells the story of the down-on-his-luck animated carnivore Wile E. Coyote and his legal battle with Acme, whose products have repeatedly failed him in his quest to catch his nemesis, the Road Runner.
The comedy combines its Looney Tunes stars with a flesh-and-blood cast, including Will Forte and John Cena, in a style reminiscent of the semi-animated film noir classic Who Framed Roger Rabbit?
The real-world spin on the failures of Wile E. Coyote stems from a spoof New Yorker article from 1990 by Ian Frazier, in which he imagines Mr Coyote launching a civil suit against Acme seeking just over $US38 million in damages and compensation for "personal injuries, loss of business income, and mental suffering caused as a direct result of the actions and/or gross negligence of said company".
So, what happened to the film?
Dave Green (Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Out of the Shadows) signed on as director in late 2019, and Coyote vs. Acme began filming the live-action scenes in early 2022.
British special effects house DNEG, which also worked on Denis Villeneuve's Dune trilogy, began work on the film's hybrid 2D and 3D animation effects, and the film was set for a July 21, 2023, release.
The film studio Warner Bros quietly handed that release date off to Barbie instead, and Coyote vs. Acme languished on the shelf.
Then on November 9, 2023, Warner Bros announced that even though the film was finished, it had no plans ever to release it.
Wait, what? Why?
According to a Deadline.com article from the time, Warner Bros. execs decided that rather than shell out another $US40 million ($55.7 million) to promote the $US70 million film, they'd cut their losses and ditch it as a $US30 million tax write-off.
What was most perplexing, aside from the fact the movie was scrapped despite already being finished, was that it had been shown at test screenings where audiences had responded positively to it.
It was the third time Warner Bros. had done this, having also shelved the DC superhero outing Batgirl and the animated Scooby-Doo prequel Scoob! Holiday Haunt in August 2022, although both those films were unfinished.
Perhaps most damningly, according to Hollywood industry website The Wrap, the four Warner executives responsible for axing Coyote vs. Acme "hadn't even seen the finished version of the movie", noting the film had been "greenlit by a previous regime".
Burying films made by a studio's former heads is a classic Hollywood move.
Back in 1988, Terry Gilliam's underrated The Adventures of Baron Munchausen scored glowing reviews and four Oscar nominations but became the biggest box office bomb of all time, purely because the new heads at Columbia Studios buried and under-promoted the film's release as revenge against their predecessors (and Gilliam).
But axing a completed film as a tax write-off was something totally new.
Cue the outrage
The cast and crew of Coyote vs. Acme were blindsided and outraged by the decision to ditch the film.
Composer Steven Price called the move "bizarre anti-art studio financial shenanigans I will never understand", while another crew member described it to Rolling Stone as "deflating and frustrating".
Other creatives suggested they would think twice about working with Warner Bros., with some reportedly cancelling meetings with the studio.
The internet, as usual, was angry — cue the obligatory hashtags (#ReleaseCoyoteVsAcme and #SaveCoyoteVsAcme).
The outrage was short and sharp, and within four days, Warner Bros had relented somewhat, instead agreeing to let the filmmakers shop the film around to find a new distributor.
A new hope
After several months of Warner Bros rejecting suitors (including Netflix, Paramount and Amazon), there were fears the studio's backflip was a ruse.
The Wrap reported Warner Bros had called the film's producers and suggested they better find a buyer soon (despite Warner being in charge of the price and the rejections).
The implication from The Wrap was that if they didn't make a deal, the studio would "unceremoniously delete (Coyote vs. Acme) … never to be seen again".
But somehow, the filmmakers persevered, and the film endured, spurred on by the continuous online burblings, public statements by the cast and crew, and a growing mystique around this "lost" movie.
Finally, on March 31, 2025, Deadline reported that indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment had bought Coyote vs. Acme, with the aim of a 2026 release.
That's all, folks
The saga has proven to be a monumental PR misfire for Warner Bros., and better publicity than money could buy.
While far from a runaway blockbuster, it's already made more money than Warner Bros intended to recoup from its tax write-off manoeuvre.
The film has grossed $US65 million worldwide, including close to $50 million in the US, and has yet to roll out in many countries.
Ahead of its US opening, critic aggregator Rotten Tomatoes has the film at a remarkable 96 per cent "Fresh" rating from 264 reviews (for comparison, Toy Story 5 is 93 per cent "Fresh" from about 320 reviews).
Australian audiences will get their opportunity to see what all the fuss is about this week.
But in the end, it seems Wile E. Coyote has finally achieved something he never could in the old Looney Tunes cartoons — a win.
And perhaps the film has extra resonance now, because of its struggles.
As the film's editor, Carsten Kurpanek, put it, maybe Warner Bros. weren't worried about the film bombing, but about its message.
"#CoyoteVsAcme is about a giant corporation choosing stock over empathy, doing nothing 'illegal' but morally shady stuff for profit," Kurpanek tweeted.
"It's a David vs Goliath story … about the cynical and casual cruelness of capitalism and corporate greed.
"No wonder Warner (didn't) want to #releasecoyoteVsACME."

Azerbaijan says coordinating with Türkiye on new projects for ‘coming decades’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:20:07 UTC
04:20:07 KST

Burc Eruygur
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov said on Tuesday that his country and Türkiye are coordinating on new projects for the “coming decades.”
At a joint news conference alongside his Turkish counterpart Hakan Fidan after talks Baku, Bayramov said sectors “traditionally distinguished by their strategic importance” were the subject of their discussions.
Putting special emphasis on the energy sector, Bayramov said the implementation and operation of the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline project and the Southern Gas Corridor represent a “massive” contribution to the energy security of Azerbaijan and Türkiye, as well as a “vast geographical region.”
“We believe that, at the current stage, there are projects with immense prospects and great potential geared towards the coming decades, and work on them is currently being carried out through close coordination between the two countries,” Bayramov said.
He also highlighted initiatives in the field of alternative energy, including projects involving the delivery of alternative green energy produced in Azerbaijan to Europe via the Black Sea, as well as the project to connect Azerbaijan’s autonomous Nakhchivan region with Türkiye via a new energy cable.
Describing these initiatives as holding “great strategic importance,” Bayramov said they view their implementation as opening up “new avenues with immense potential.”
“They facilitate the delivery of alternative energy – via Türkiye – not only to the markets of Azerbaijan and Türkiye but also to the European market,” he added.
Bayramov said he and Fidan held extensive talks regarding Azerbaijan's engagement in multilateral platforms, and that their bilateral cooperation within various platforms, such as the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), was specifically discussed.
Noting that the OTS will hold its upcoming summit in Türkiye next month, Bayramov said they had productive discussions regarding preparations for that meeting and that the organization holds "special significance" for both countries.
"As the COP29 presidency, our country expresses its full support for Türkiye — which will soon host COP31 — and our entire team, having participated in COP29 and remained active in climate diplomacy since then, will play a highly active role in the successful execution of COP31 ... both during the preparatory phase and the event itself," he said.
Bayramov said he and Fidan also exchanged views on the situation in the South Caucasus and the Middle East.
Speaking of measures taken by Baku and Ankara concerning regional connectivity, Bayramov said the establishment of new transport infrastructure in Azerbaijan is proceeding rapidly.
In this context, Bayramov said, approximately 95% of highways leading from mainland Azerbaijan to the border with neighboring Armenia is completed, while railway construction is about 75% complete.
Bayramov said reconstruction work on railway connections in Nakhchivan is essential, and operations have already commenced in this regard.
The foreign minister said direct talks are being conducted between Yerevan and Washington concerning the 42-kilometer section of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project passing through Armenian territory, and that the US regularly informs Azerbaijan about the issue.
He described this section as the "missing link," noting that a "significant new transport corridor," linking Europe to Central Asia via Türkiye and Azerbaijan, will emerge once the route is established.

'Revolutionary change in American foreign policy': Canada pivoting towards EU, India and China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:18:43 UTC
