'Revolutionary change in American foreign policy': Canada pivoting towards EU, India and China
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Anne Applebaum, staff writer at The Atlantic and author of Autocracy, Inc. According to Applebaum, the upheaval in American diplomacy and foreign policy transcends any one administration. She describes a full-fledged transformation in the way the United States exerts power, pivoting away from leadership of a democratic alliance and toward a transactional, mafia-style politics that fuses ideology, private economic interests, personal relationships and geopolitical leverage.
In Applebaum’s analysis, the consequences are already extending well beyond Washington. Canada, for example, has begun taking a far more proactive approach to strengthening its economic and political ties with the EU, India and China, as Carney actively seeks to reduce the country’s dependence on its once-cozy, decades-long relationship with the United States.
Nor is this shift limited to the American continent. European governments are now being forced to confront a far less predictable and increasingly adversarial ally. At the same time, far-right movements abroad are finding new opportunities for political alignment as the United States embraces a harder-line, populist and increasingly autocratic style of politics at home and abroad. The resulting uncertainty is pushing countries around the world to quietly explore alternative economic and security relationships that leave them less dependent on an increasingly combative and impulsive American partner.
What makes Applebaum’s argument particularly striking is that she presents these developments as both a revolution and the beginnings of a counter-revolution. Trump’s political model has imitators, she argues, but it is also provoking fierce resistance. As confidence in American reliability declines, governments are beginning to hedge their bets for the long term, diversify their partnerships and imagine a world in which Washington is no longer automatically at the center of the geopolitical universe.
This may not be the “America First” that Donald Trump envisioned. In Applebaum’s telling, we are no longer navigating only the uncharted waters of what America itself might be becoming, both at home and on the world stage. We may also be witnessing the emergence of a new world order in which the United States occupies a diminished role, brought about, paradoxically, by a fiercely isolationist policy intended to reassert American dominance.
The irony is difficult to miss: in seeking to make the world bend once again to American power and self-described exceptionalism, the United States may instead be accelerating the world’s search for ways to live without it.

Meta in Spanish lawsuit over mass content moderator layoffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15

04:18:13 KST

Meta in Spanish lawsuit over mass content moderator layoffs
BARCELONA - A Spanish union demanded on Sept 15 that a court cancel the redundancies of more than 2,000 staff who worked for a company tasked with moderating content for Meta.
Canadian tech firm Telus International, which operated locally as CCC Barcelona Digital Services, slashed the jobs in 2025, citing the end of its contract with the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
Some 2,062 workers were laid off in a package agreed with the main unions.
But minority union FIST launched a lawsuit against Telus and Meta, alleging before a Barcelona court that the layoffs were an “attack and a retaliation against the workers’ exercising of their basic rights”.
According to the lawsuit, more than half of the affected workers had started legal action for alleged “salary discrimination” based on language and origin, as the moderators’ wages varied according to their working language.
Some employees had also taken legal action complaining of the psychological toll caused by constant exposition to violent content, the lawsuit added.
FIST, which wants the redundancies declared null and the staff rehired, rejects the economic reasons for the layoffs, saying Telus continues to offer services elsewhere in Europe.
Lawyers representing Meta and Telus told the court the decision was taken on economic grounds after Meta terminated the contract covering the Barcelona-based staff.
“The relationship between Meta and CCC is purely commercial,” said Paula Talavera, lawyer for the US tech giant’s Irish subsidiary, rejecting FIST’s allegation that the companies formed a “corporate network”.
The court did not give a timeframe for announcing its decision.
Telus had provided content moderation for Meta in Barcelona since 2018. Its staff revised content in Spanish, Catalan, French, Dutch, Hebrew and Portuguese.
AFP is involved in a partnership with Meta providing fact-checking services in Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Latin America and Africa. AFP

After settlements sanctions, Israel is planning a war on Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:16:59 UTC
04:16:59 KST

Breadcrumb
After settlements sanctions, Israel is planning a war on Britain on the world stage
UK Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced a wide-ranging ban on the sale of products produced in Israeli settlements, and on financing and business activities there. He did so in concert with France and Canada, which strengthened the impact of the new policy. They acted in response to a government campaign to terrorise Palestinian inhabitants of the West Bank.
Over 60 villages with almost 5,000 inhabitants have been entirely depopulated. At least 1,100 have been killed by armed settlers and IDF soldiers who not only protect them, but participate directly in the attacks.
An import ban on goods from illegal settlements and a new ban on arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation” were among the measures announced. A comprehensive sanctions regime against services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK, as well as personal sanctions against the main individuals accused of promoting settler violence, were also included.
Israel lobby
Israel’s political leadership reacted with fury to the sanctions. In August, Netanyahu had declared bizarrely that “the first Islamic Republic to have nuclear weapons will be the Islamic Republic of Britain.” He further retaliated by closing the country’s East Jerusalem consulate and placing ten Labour MPs on a travel ban list. Curiously, the foreign secretary was omitted, as were other government ministers, including PM Andy Burnham, who publicly supported the new policy.
The Board of Deputies and chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis released statements accusing Labour of anti-Semitism. This is ironic considering Miliband is a child of Holocaust survivors, who came to Britain as displaced persons after WWII.
Among the lobby’s claims is that the new policy will “make Jews less safe.” This is a mantra repeated whenever Israel faces anti-genocide measures. Mirvis added they would embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews.”
In fact, defending Israeli crimes as the Lobby does actually endangers Jews, because it gives the impression that supporting such behaviour is intrinsic to Judaism itself.
The Israel Lobby demands condemnations over the settlement ban while saying nothing about Israel’s mass murder of nearly 75,000 Palestinians in Gaza and thousands more in attacks on Lebanon and Iran. Since 10/7, two British Jews have been killed in an attack on a synagogue.
The Board of Deputies linked the government’s measures to the High Holidays, claiming it would put Jews in jeopardy from anti-Semitic attacks against their synagogues on Rosh Hashanah. They even argued that the Labour government was putting the “party’s interests” above those of “the nation.”
This too is an attempt to dismiss the moral element of the new policy. Labour instituted it not because it offers a political advantage, but because it honours international humanitarian law and upholds rulings of courts of justice.
Zionists (and white supremacists) deliberately conflate Jews with Zionism. Thus they exploit the universal condemnation of anti-Semitism for the purpose of tainting efforts to hold Israel accountable for its crimes, including the Gaza genocide, and wars of aggression in Syria, Lebanon and Iran.
The Argentina distraction
In a search for anything that might damage the UK government, far-right ministers like Itamar Ben Gvir, dredged up Argentina’s long-dormant Falklands claim. They are encouraging Argentina to revive its right to sovereignty in the hopes of stirring up an international controversy that might embroil the UK.
The Israeli minister wrote in a Spanish-language post on X: “It's time for the State of Israel to publicly recognise that the Malvinas Islands are Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently stole from the Argentine people.”
Ben Gvir is also aware that, as the police minister responsible for the torture and murder of Palestinian prisoners, he has been banned by multiple countries. In response to the government’s recent action, Australia, New Zealand, and Canada announced new sanctions on Ben Gvir and Betzalel Smotrich.
It seems the Israeli far-right doesn’t recognise the irony of linking Argentina seeking the return of its territory from a colonial power to Israel’s colonising of Palestine.
It couldn’t be clearer that the Malvinas dispute is an apt metaphor for Israel’s occupation of Palestine and usurpation of Palestinian national rights. What is Israel doing if not occupying the Palestinian people and appropriating its natural resources?
Just as “it’s time to recognise that the Malvinas are Argentine,” it’s time for the world to recognise that Palestine is for Palestinians, and it has been “violently stolen” from them.
Unprecedented settlement ban and sanctions regime
While foreign governments have made gestures of protest, including scores of nations recognising Palestinian statehood, the new measures mark the first time Western governments have taken such a stance.
Recognising a Palestinian state was a symbolic political act with low cost; just as the suspension of arms shipments to Israel during the worst of the genocide was temporary and soon lifted. All of these had little economic or reputational impact.
The settlement ban imposes real (though limited) economic costs on Israel. It restricts global markets for settlement products and shuts off foreign financing for their projects. More importantly, Miliband’s new foreign policy legitimises such sanctions for other nations, which will undoubtedly follow suit.
Nevertheless, the settlement ban has limitations. In fact, British diplomats told the Trump administration that the measures were largely cosmetic. Bloomberg reported that British diplomats have privately told the US the sanctions are largely symbolic and will have no material impact on the UK’s wider relationship with Israel on trade or security, in a bid to soothe the Trump administration’s response.
In addition, these sanctions will have limited practical impact. The UK exports $8 billion in trade to Israel. It has not broken down that figure to isolate trade with settlements. Thus, it is difficult to know how it will enforce the ban. Britain imports only $6 million worth of Israeli goods. So any prohibition on these products would have minimal impact.
The Israeli state vs. Israeli people
The foreign secretary suggested that the government’s anti-settlement plan targets the Israeli government rather than the Israeli people. However, polls show this distinction should no longer hold.
The majority of Israelis serve in an occupation army responsible for these crimes, and most don’t raise their voice against the mass murder and expulsions by settler terrorists in the West Bank.
Israelis are also clearly voting for parties that not only support such an approach but also devise and enact it. This is the work of the entire state of Israel: its government and its people.
Another inadequacy of the new policy is that it targets a relatively small sector of the Israeli public and economy. It will not punish the country in any substantive way. Furthermore, the settlements are only one element in the regime of oppression which Israel has inflicted on the Palestinian people. It will not address the genocide in Gaza, apartheid or ethnic cleansing. It will not restrain Israel’s wars of aggression, which are riling the entire region.
There must be sanctions that impact Israel’s entire economy, including ending military aid, joint weapons development with Israeli arms makers, and severing diplomatic relations. Britain must campaign for fellow members of the UN Security Council and its European allies, in a united front. They, in turn, must enact real, punishing sanctions that will shock Israelis into the realisation that they are no longer welcome at the table of nations.
In what appears to be a diplomatic non sequitur, in order to make the settlement policy less controversial, Miliband has declared new sanctions on Iran and Hezbollah. These punishing measures impose actual harm on Iranians and Lebanese, unlike the settlement policy.
It’s interesting that the measures against Israel captured the world’s attention, while having limited impact, whereas those against Iran and Hezbollah will have real impact and are rarely, if at all, reported by the media.

Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:14:00 UTC
04:14:00 KST

Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.
The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.
During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”
“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.
Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.
“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”
The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pits Moraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.
Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.
Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.
With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.
The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.
Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.
Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.
Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealed an explosive police dossier relating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. In one text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”
Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.
The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.
The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.
“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.
Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.
Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.
In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.
“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.
Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.
“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.

 Colombian businessman Alex Saab, a close associate of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, pleaded guilty Tuesday to money laundering charges in a US federal court in Miami as part of a deal with prosecutors, according to court documents and authorities.
Saab agreed to cooperate with US investigations and forfeit $195 million in illicit proceeds under the plea agreement.
The 54-year-old admitted to a single count of money laundering linked to a scheme involving Venezuelan government contracts to import food.
US prosecutors accused Saab of using fictitious companies and falsified shipping records to divert funds from government contracts. The scheme was also linked to bribes paid to Venezuelan officials.
The case centers on the Venezuelan government's CLAP food program, which was created to provide subsidized food to millions of Venezuelans during the country's economic crisis.
Prosecutors alleged that Saab and his associates used shell companies and bank accounts in the US to move and conceal proceeds from the scheme.
Saab previously pleaded not guilty to the charges. His change of plea came after a federal judge in Miami scheduled a hearing Tuesday and canceled a planned trial.
The guilty plea marks a new development in the long-running US investigation into Saab, whom American authorities have described as a key financial intermediary for Maduro.
Saab was first charged by US authorities in 2019 and arrested in Cape Verde in 2020 while traveling to Iran. He was extradited to the US in 2021.
In 2023, former US President Joe Biden pardoned Saab as part of a prisoner exchange that secured the release of several Americans detained in Venezuela.
Saab was later returned to US custody after Venezuelan authorities deported him in May amid renewed American pressure.
His cooperation with US investigators could make him a potential witness in other cases involving Venezuelan officials, including the prosecution of Maduro, who is facing drug trafficking charges in the US.
The plea comes as Washington continues to reshape its relations with Venezuela following Maduro's removal from power earlier this year.

F-117, the Original Stealth Fighter, Will Join Smithsonian Collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:13:22 UTC
04:13:22 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force F-117A Nighthawk—America’s first stealth fighter—will soon go on display among other iconic aircraft at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Air and Space Museum’s Udvar-Hazy Center outside Washington, D.C.
Shrouded in extreme secrecy while under development in the late 1970s and early ’80s, the F-117 stunned the world when it flew unobserved into heavily defended Iraqi airspace on Jan. 17, 1991, in the opening salvo of Operation Desert Storm.
Now more than three decades later, an F-117A airframe—nicknamed the “Overachiever” for being the only Nighthawk to fly combat missions in all four major conflicts of its era—will become a permanent exhibit at the museum in late October, Jeremy Kinney, assistant director of the museum’s research, collections and curatorial affairs office, said Sept. 14 during AFA’s Air, Space, and Cyber conference.
The F-117 has “earned its place in the national collection,” Kinney said. “It revolutionized modern airspace and military technology.”
Aircraft maker Lockheed Martin, which developed the airplane, is restoring the aircraft to its final operational appearance, Kinney said.
In early October, an aircrew from the 512th Airlift Wing from Dover Air Force Base, Del., will transport the restored F-117 on an Air Force Reserve C-5M Super Galaxy transport to the museum’s Stephen F. Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Va.
Soon after, the aircraft will go on display joining other aircraft, including Lockheed’s SR-71 Blackbird, the Boeing B-29 Superfortress bomber nicknamed “Enola Gay,” which dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Japan in August 1945, and the Space Shuttle Discovery.
Kinney thanked the teamwork that went into saving the airplane, saying it “is only possible through the support and collaboration of partners” including the Air & Space Forces Association and Lockheed Martin, in addition to the U.S. Air Force.
The F-117 was developed in response to improved air defenses and offensive counter-air systems developed by the Soviet Union. Losses by U.S. Air Forces in December 1972 and by Israel in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, triggered U.S. weapons developers and the Air Force to collaborate on radar-evading technology. The F-117 proved the concept, paving the way for modern stealth aircraft including the B-2 bomber, F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, and future B-21 and F-47 aircraft.

Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:08:37 UTC
04:08:37 KST

Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”.
Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States.
Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation.
“The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies.
“Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”
While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country.
That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks.
Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels.
European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy.
Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence.
“Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.”
The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe.
But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force.
French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.”
Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain.
EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 when Ceta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn.
Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner.
“We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”
In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US.
Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.”
Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted.
Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed.
But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some.
Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for the Many vs the Money counter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects.
“Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.”
Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s office announced nearly C$500bn in new domestic investment.
“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”

Domestic violence cases 'disproportionately high' in regional areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:08:33 UTC
04:08:33 KST

Experts plead for more domestic and family violence support in regional and rural Australia
A particularly chilling detail emerged in the aftermath of Molly Ticehurst's murder: her killer and ex-partner Daniel Billings threatened to exploit her small country town's lack of an after-hours police presence.
"I will come in the middle of the night … The police won't stop me. I will get to you quicker than they will," he said in a phone call before her death.
Ms Ticehurst was murdered just before midnight in her Forbes home a few weeks later. On Friday, Billings was sentenced to 28 years' jail.
As Australia grapples with what the prime minister has called a domestic violence "crisis," experts are pleading for more to be done in regional and rural Australia.
"We know that regional Australia has a disproportionately high number of domestic and family violence cases," said Chris Lacey, general manager at No To Violence.
"The scale of the problem is massive, and we're just focusing way too late in the piece too often."
Distance and control
There is no shortage of intersecting factors that make domestic and family violence such a pronounced issue in regional and rural Australia.
For the University of Melbourne's Sarah Wendt, the concept of isolation is central.
"Geographical isolation always plays a factor in how women think about seeking help and coping with domestic and family violence," said Professor Wendt, a chief investigator in the Centre for Excellence for The Elimination of Violence Against Women.
"I have heard stories from women who talk about their partner's use of power and control by using distance to their advantage."
She cited examples where perpetrators have limited the use of the family car and where farm cameras have been set up to monitor a partner's movements on and off properties.
Then there is social isolation.
"Victim-survivors often describe the erosion of their social networks at the hands of a perpetrator, so women become socially isolated," she said.
"I've heard multiple stories about community not wanting to believe that about 'him.' The downplaying or the minimisation when it's a powerful figure in a rural community is quite common.
"It's just so complex and often rural communities will just want to stay away from it."
Who to trust
Women outside major cities in Australia are more likely to experience domestic and family violence, according to government data.
When they do, they are more likely to end up in hospital.
Kaara Ray Calma, an academic and registered nurse, was living in a regional town when she says she experienced violence from her partner.
She presented to a range of clinical settings but was not asked about her situation at home.
"I was never really asked explicitly about my experience at home or the dynamics of my relationships or whether or not I was experiencing violence," she said.
"On the one hand, I was wondering why wasn't I being asked, but at the same time, with my clinical hat on, I know that I didn't receive formal training whatsoever in how to initiate conversations about violence."
That set her on a path to understand how clinical and support services could better identify and assist in situations of domestic and family violence.
Now a researcher and lecturer in the School of Nursing at Griffith University, she is currently interviewing victim-survivors and clinicians as part of a new project centred around rural and remote Australia.
Common themes continue to emerge.
"There is a fear of disclosure," Dr Calma said.
"Particularly for rural and more remote areas where the communities are quite tight-knit, and people may know one another, they fear a lack of confidentiality, and therefore this dissuades them from disclosing because they're unsure how and who to trust.
"This obviously impacts not only identification, but also providing timely support."
'Postcode lottery'
Despite the billions spent and heightened national profile, there is alarm within the domestic and family violence sector about the direction Australia is heading.
"I am deeply worried about the trajectories that we're on," domestic, family and sexual violence commissioner Micaela Cronin told ABC Radio National last week.
A report this month from Australia's peak body for ending men's use of family violence found Australia's response was "highly fragmented," with uneven distribution of support services.
"One [domestic and family violence] practitioner talked about it being a postcode lottery — depending on where you live can drastically change the supports that are available to you," said Mr Lacey from No To Violence.
Those support services and programs, he argues, need to be better tailored toward specific communities, so that country town organisations can play a bigger role in identifying and preventing domestic and family violence.
The report also found just two per cent of men who commit physical and sexual violence to a partner undertake any form of behaviour change intervention.
For Mr Lacey, it reinforces why far more resources should be directed toward earlier preventative programs.
"We're really wanting to call on government and everyone to see where we can intervene much earlier in the piece," he said.
"Rather than waiting for the police to be involved and then the courts and the justice system, so these victim-survivors aren't being created in the first place."
Breaking the cycle
It is a sentiment that resonates in the regional Victoria town of Ballarat, where a community remains haunted by recent tragedy.
"We're in a crisis and just doing more of the same, running a program here and a program there, that's not going to be enough," the CEO of Child and Family Services (CAFS) in the Central Highlands, Wendy Sturgess, said.
Her organisation was one of several to receive state funding as part of Respect Ballarat, a "saturation model" initiative launched following the high-profile deaths of three women in 2024.
As concern grows around the impact of 'the manosphere' on young men's behaviour, the CAFS-administered programs will be geared toward earlier intervention and breaking cycles of violence.
One newly-launched program will work with 8- to 12-year-olds and their families, while a For Baby's Sake model involves supporting new fathers and parents.
"We've got to start younger if you want to get effective change,"
Amid a bleak national picture, Professor Wendt believed there was still an opportunity to better harness the connections, clubs and community bonds that make country towns special.
"Rural communities can often show us how to do things really well," she said.
"I've heard really good stories where the community rallies to support a victim of domestic and family violence, so that she can stay in her community.
"It kind of goes to the question: what are we willing to accept as a community?"

Dozens of lawyers and legal academics on Tuesday warned the British government that sanctions announced against illegal Israeli settlements fail to meet the UK’s obligations under international law.
In a letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, more than 130 legal experts said they welcomed the decision to act alongside its allies but noted that the action "falls far short" of Britain’s obligations to oppose Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory.
The letter called for measures including extending the sanctions to cover insurance, accountancy services, and digital infrastructure; confirming publicly that no UK public body, pension scheme, or sovereign fund holds investments in settlements; and imposing a full arms embargo on Israel.

"The consequences of this illegality (occupation) for the UK and other states – special legal duties to take comprehensive action to bring this and other illegal actions by Israel, including its genocide in Gaza, to an end – are far more wide-ranging than the important but limited actions against settlements and settlers announced," UCL professor of international law Ralph Wilde said in the statement.
"The elephant in the room is that the occupation is not a bug, it’s a feature," said SOAS professor of law Nimer Sultany.
Last week, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a series of measures, including a ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements, sanctions on companies and individuals facilitating settlement expansion, and additional sanctions on extremist Israeli occupiers accused of supporting or inciting violence against Palestinians.

He also said that Although Iran's sensitive nuclear facilities are located underground, they have always been under monitoring of the IAEA and its inspections.
The spokesman also noted that "Military attacks, sabotage, and assassinations cannot destroy Iran's nuclear knowledge and industry."
According to Press TV, the comments come following two rounds of US-Israeli aggression against Iran that have in part targeted Iran’s safeguarded nuclear facilities amid the silence and inaction of the IAEA.
Kamalvandi said Iran had developed its nuclear capabilities after decades of experience in dealing with unreliable international partners and external pressure.
He said Iran’s nuclear science and technology had an 80-year history, while the AEOI was 52 years old. Iran was also among the earliest members of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), he said, and had consistently maintained the peaceful nature of its nuclear activities.
He recalled that Iran had endured pressure and sanctions over its nuclear program for more than 25 years while continuing to pursue negotiations and honor its agreements, including the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA).
According to Kamalvandi, the United States was the only JCPOA party that withdrew from the agreement. Iran nevertheless continued implementing its commitments unilaterally for about 1.5 years after the US withdrawal.
He said 15 consecutive reports by the IAEA director general at the time had confirmed Iran’s implementation of its JCPOA commitments. He added that Iran’s approach was nevertheless followed by unilateral sanctions, including measures described by their proponents as “crippling.”

Turning to the IAEA, Kamalvandi questioned whether the agency’s repeated inspections of Iranian nuclear facilities had ever produced a finding of nuclear material diversion by Iran.
He also criticized the IAEA director general for politicized conduct and double standards, noting that recent statements and reports had provided pretexts for Iran’s adversaries to attack the country.
Kamalvandi called on the agency to condemn military attacks against Iran’s nuclear facilities and engage with Tehran. He also urged the IAEA to fulfill its responsibilities on the basis of its statutory mandate and treat Iran in the same manner as other member states.
He said Iran had a peaceful and transparent nuclear program and that its sensitive facilities had been located in secure, including underground, sites because of the country’s continuing exposure to military and security threats. Such measures, he said, should not be viewed as concealment.
He said Iran’s pursuit of indigenous nuclear capabilities stemmed from its experience with European countries that had failed to fully honor nuclear-related contractual commitments both before and after the Islamic Revolution.

'Australia first' senator Ralph Babet's new fashion line not made in Australia

Britons of all ethnicities feel racial equality is worsening, study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:04:55 UTC
04:04:55 KST

Many Britons feel inequality is worsening and that discrimination has become more common, according to a thinktank study.
The report by British Future has found that people across ethnic groups believe racial equality is worsening in Britain. One in six people are from minority ethnic backgrounds.
“Most ethnic minorities in Britain feel there was a positive change against racism in our lifetimes yet now fear that progress being reversed,” said the thinktank’s director, Sunder Katwala.
The research found nearly half of ethnic minority respondents had faced racial or nationality prejudice over the past year, with the problem notably higher among those aged 18 to 24. Prejudice was most often reported in public spaces, followed by on social media and in the workplace.
The research found that 62% of ethnic minority Britons saw racial inequality as a serious problem, a view supported by 57% of the white population.
White respondents were less likely to see structural barriers in education, work and public services and more likely to believe minority communities received equal or preferential treatment.
The report, part of a three-year study funded by the Nuffield Foundation, found a growing polarisation over perceptions that minorities received preferential treatment.
Among white respondents, 37% felt ethnic minorities were treated better than white British people, while 33% disagreed. Among ethnic minorities, 23% agreed and 48% disagreed.
The report found divisions by age and politics were deeper than those relating to ethnicity. “In both the white and ethnic minority surveys, gaps between rich and poor are seen as the most important divide impacting the UK,” the report said.
The research was driven by two online surveys of 2,009 white adults and 3,014 ethnic minority adults between 30 March and 29 April. It was supplemented by information from 12 focus groups.
The study noted a difference within ethnic minority attitudes, finding Black respondents were frequently more positive about the UK making progress on racial equality. By contrast, Bangladeshi and Pakistani heritage respondents were found to be more pessimistic, with heightened anxiety seemingly linked to the 2024 riots.
“Women, particularly ethnic minority women, are also more pessimistic than men throughout,” the report said.
The study found that ethnic minority Britons would like to see more effort to promote equal pay and tackle disparities in essential services and unequal treatment in media reporting.
This was brought into “sharp focus”, the report said, by the intense media scrutiny on Jason Arday, a Cambridge University professor who died at his London home after allegations of plagiarism.
The report, which criticised successive governments for having “rarely held” a sustained focus on race, laid out 10 recommendations for the government, including challenging zero-sum thinking, supporting grassroots activities and pushing the watchdog Ofcom on compliance against online racism.
Overall, it found low trust among political parties. While the Green party and Labour led narrowly in terms of treating people of different backgrounds fairly (+15 and +13 in net trust scores respectively), Reform UK had a net score of -31 (16% trust/47% distrust).
Katwala said leaders should “counter the sense of a zero-sum contest over race equality: that fairness for ethnic minorities comes at the expense of the white majority, or vice versa”.
He added: “The antidote to that is to pursue a broad and proactive fairness agenda – with the confidence and tools to tackle racism and discrimination where it is most needed.”

A Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish military helicopter during a routine photographic mission in international waters off Denmark, with one flare passing close to the aircraft, Denmark’s armed forces said.
The incident comes amid a growing series of confrontational incidents involving Russia and NATO countries, as Western officials warn that Moscow is becoming increasingly willing to test the alliance’s defenses and intimidate its members.
Flare passed close to Danish helicopter
The Danish Fennec helicopter was conducting routine photographic coverage of the Russian frigate when the ship fired two flares at it, according to Denmark’s Armed Forces. The incident occurred off Gedser, at the southern tip of Denmark, on 14 September.
One of the flares passed close to the helicopter. The Danish military did not report any injuries or damage and said it had no further comment on the incident.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the incident “completely unacceptable” and said Russia’s ambassador had been summoned for talks.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it “reckless action from Russia towards Danish military” during a routine overflight, saying Russian actions were intended to “intimidate and divide.”
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, disputed Copenhagen’s account, telling DR that Moscow would investigate and accusing the Danish helicopter of provocative actions near the Russian frigate.
Another incident in a growing pattern
The episode comes as Russia’s behavior toward NATO countries has become increasingly confrontational in recent months.
NATO fighters have repeatedly been scrambled over Russian military aircraft in the Baltic region, while European countries have dealt with airspace incidents, suspected Russian drones and other security threats linked to the war against Ukraine.
On 15 September, NATO aircraft also shot down a drone over Lithuania after it entered the country’s airspace from the direction of Belarus. The drone was believed to have been carrying an explosive device.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart described the Danish incident as “another irresponsible Russian action” intended to intimidate the alliance, adding that NATO would continue defending its territory and supporting Ukraine.
The incidents are unfolding as Russia continues its full-scale war against Ukraine and expands pressure beyond the battlefield. Western officials have increasingly warned that Moscow is using military intimidation and other forms of pressure against European countries while testing how far it can push NATO without triggering a direct confrontation.
The flare incident comes amid a broader deterioration in European security, with Russian military activity increasingly creating dangerous encounters with NATO forces.

The proposed package would exceed previous US transfers of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel under both the Biden and Trump administrations.

New global definition of heart attack to improve outcomes for women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

New global definition of heart attack to improve outcomes for women
In short:
Australian experts welcome a new global definition of heart attack, which they say will make it easier to diagnose women.
The updated guidelines group coronary events more common in women alongside the main type of heart attacks and recommend sex-specific diagnostic blood test thresholds.
What's next?
Although these new guidelines will help improve diagnosis, experts say there are some gender gaps relating to cardiac treatment that still need to be addressed.
Nadene Hall had never heard of a spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) heart attack until she had one.
It was 7:30am on March 25, 2023, and Ms Hall was finishing up a strength-based session at the gym when she felt a cramp across her chest.
"As I was walking downstairs to the car park, I started to feel a bit hot, like clammy, and my left hand started to feel a bit tingly," she said.
Ms Hall went home feeling nauseated, vomited and then called an ambulance.
"I was 47, fit and healthy," she said.
"I do everything I can to not have a heart attack, so it was the last thing on my mind."
Ms Hall was diagnosed with SCAD, a type of heart attack caused by a tear in a coronary artery that mainly affects women with few traditional risk factors.
An Australian study suggests that nearly one in four acute coronary syndrome events in women under the age of 60 were caused by SCAD.
But the condition can be easy to misdiagnose and is sometimes associated with menopause, extreme stress or childbirth.
Experts said a new global definition of heart attack, published recently in the European Heart Journal, would help improve the diagnosis of women like Ms Hall and lead to better outcomes.
New heart attack definition
The new definition separates heart attacks into three categories depending on how the patient presented clinically:
- primary and sudden, caused by reduced blood flow to the heart
- secondary due to an acute medical condition
- procedure-related, following a cardiac procedure.
Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute professorial research fellow Tom Marwick said the "good update" considered the underlying cause of a heart attack and made it easier to communicate to patients.
Heart Foundation head of clinical strategy Natalie Raffoul said the update would improve heart attack diagnosis in women for two key reasons.
Firstly, she said, the global guidelines included a recommendation for sex-specific troponin ranges.
When the heart is damaged or inflamed, it releases proteins called troponin into the bloodstream, which doctors can test for.
But troponin levels differ between men and women.
Ms Raffoul said sex-specific ranges would help doctors do a "better job at picking up heart attacks in women when they're presenting with symptoms".
The second key change Ms Raffoul said was that coronary events more common in women, such as SCAD, were now grouped with the main type of heart attacks.
"That's a great thing because that means when a woman comes to the emergency room, presenting with heart attack symptoms, clinicians can consider less common coronary events such as SCAD," she said.
Ms Raffoul said the global guidelines were closely aligned with the Heart Foundation's clinical guidelines for diagnosing and managing acute coronary syndromes in Australia.
'Significant treatment gap for women'
Cardiovascular disease is one of the leading causes of death for Australian women.
Ms Raffoul said although chest pain or pressure were the most common symptoms of a heart attack in men and women, there could be some differences between the sexes.
"Women are more likely than men to experience non-chest pain symptoms," Ms Raffoul said.
These may include:
- nausea or vomiting
- shortness of breath
- indigestion
- dizziness, or the feeling of faintness
- pain in the arm, jaw, neck, shoulder and back.
A 2025 study found Australian women having a heart attack were less likely to be promptly diagnosed and treated compared to men.
Ms Raffoul said although the new guidelines would help clinicians detect and diagnose heart attacks in women, there was still a "significant treatment gap for women".
"A woman is less likely to receive best practice treatment and care,"
"Less likely to receive that stent or ballooning within a certain time frame, less likely to receive preventive medicines after diagnosis and also less likely to be referred to, and attend, cardiac rehab.
Treatment not 'one-size-fits-all'
Ms Raffoul said many updates in the global guidelines, including sex-specific troponin blood test thresholds and an emphasis on cardiac events more common in women, such as SCAD, were already included in the Heart Foundation's guidelines, putting Australia on the "front foot".
But Julie Redfern, a Bond University professor of public health who contributed to Australia's guidelines, said some women were still "falling through the cracks" and not being diagnosed or treated in a timely fashion.
"We need better adherence [to the guidelines]," she said.
Professor Redfern, who specialises in heart attack survivorship, said this meant providing the best possible treatment for each patient based on factors like the type of heart attack they experienced, not offering a "one-size-fits-all" approach to cardiovascular disease.
Loading...
Ms Raffoul and Professor Redfern hoped the new global guidelines would encourage clinicians in Australia to learn more about heart attack causes and symptoms for women.
Ms Hall wants women — especially healthy, young women like herself — to know the warning signs and reach out for help.
"Listen to your body," she said.
"We always put everyone else first. Sometimes we have to put ourselves first and get checked out."

In a social media post, Trump said the renovation work would not start until an appeals court weighs in on the judge’s order.
“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the US Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The developments on Sept 15 were the latest twists in the saga of the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts since Trump regained the White House, named himself chairman of the centre’s board and announced plans to reshape its programming.
The centre, which is also a memorial to the assassinated Kennedy, opened in 1971 with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein’s requiem mass for Kennedy.
It has over the decades been home to the Washington National Opera and the National Symphony Orchestra and hosted such performers as Mikhail Baryshnikov and Wynton Marsalis.
It also hosts the annual Kennedy Center Honors, recognising the lifetime of achievement of leading artists.
In response to Trump’s takeover, artists have cancelled performances in protest, and the opera and the symphony were forced to find other venues, while revenue cratered.
The board has warned the centre’s finances are so shaky that it may soon not be able to honour payroll obligations or maintenance contracts.
Trump’s campaign to remake the centre is part of his broader effort to leave his cultural and aesthetic mark on the US capital, including a large new ballroom to replace the White House East Wing he ordered demolished, a troubled renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a planned “triumphal arch” near the nation’s main cemetery honouring its war dead.
The centre’s board has said the venue is in dire need of immediate repairs.
Trump spoke to the board during Sept 15’s meeting, according to a statement from US Representative Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who sits on the board due to her position in Congress.
Beatty has sued to prevent the centre from adding Trump’s name, arguing that only Congress has that authority.
“The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away. Now the Board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We’ll see the Defendants in court,” said Representative Beatty’s counsel, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group in a statement.
Judge blocks Trump name from building
As part of that litigation, US District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington issued an order earlier on Sept 15 temporarily halting the center’s latest proposal to put Trump’s name on the building.
The centre was named for Kennedy as a memorial under a law signed by former president Lyndon Johnson after his assassination.
In addition, Cooper said the board cannot proceed with plans to rename the campus where it sits the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
“Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’ blessing,” Cooper wrote.
Like Trump, the board has argued that adding his name in honour of his efforts is necessary to ensure his continued commitment to its survival.
“The Board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center,” the board wrote in a draft resolution ahead of the meeting.
Trump said on social media that the Justice Department, which represents the centre, will appeal the order.
Cooper had previously ordered the centre in May to remove Trump’s name from the building after the centre changed its marble facade in December to read “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts.”
At that time, Cooper also blocked the centre from closing down, finding that the board had not adequately considered the financial consequences.
Workers stripped Trump’s name from the centre in June and left the exterior masked by scaffolding and a white tarpaulin.
In a vote on Aug 13, the board signed off on the addition of an inscription honouring Trump and renaming the centre’s plaza after Trump.
The 10 options for how the president’s inscription could be rendered included: “A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump” and “Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump.” REUTERS

Next few decades will be 'very difficult', influential economist warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:56:43 UTC
03:56:43 KST

analysis
Next few decades will be 'very difficult', economist Charles Goodhart warns
"The next 30 to 40 years are going to be very difficult," the influential economist Charles Goodhart warned recently.
"Those who lived primarily in the years between 1950 and 2020 — those 70 years — those were probably the best years in terms of growth, living standards, [and] conditions that not only the UK but effectively the Western world has ever seen.
"We didn't know how lucky we were, and many of the conditions that gave us that magnificent period are over," he said.
Goodhart is an emeritus professor at the London School of Economics and a former senior official at the Bank of England.
He is famous for his adage, called Goodhart's Law, that an observed statistical relationship will tend to collapse once you try to target it for policy purposes.
He turns 90 next month, and to mark the occasion, The Financial Times published an article last week that discussed some of his contributions to economic thought.
But Goodhart's warning, at the top of this piece, was made in July and is worth exploring.
Long-term economic trends
He was appearing as a guest on the Peter McCormack podcast (a British podcast).
Peter McCormack is a bitcoin enthusiast who describes his personal politics as "small-c conservatism with a strong bent toward libertarianism", and he has had extremely controversial figures on his podcast, including Tommy Robinson and Curtis Yarvin.
But he has had some economists on his podcast too, such as Ann Pettifor and Steve Keen, and his conversation with Goodhart stuck to economics.
If you are unfamiliar with Goodhart's approach to life, he made this observation at the start of their conversation (while smiling wryly):
"I've always been a pessimist, partly on the grounds that if you're wrong, you're happy, because things are actually better than you feared.
"But if you're an optimist and you're wrong it's doubly awful, because not only were you wrong, but things are worse than you expected."
He then spent an hour talking about some macro-economic trends that were making life increasingly hard for British workers, which sounded very familiar to Australian ears.
And he said people ought to prepare for a future that would be increasingly difficult to navigate.
Inflation targeting and independent central banks
According to Goodhart, the early decades of the UK's inflation-targeting era, which began in the early 1990s (like Australia's), coincided with a period of globalisation in which Western countries increasingly pushed manufacturing industries offshore and shifted domestic production to services.
He said that period saw nominal and real interest rates falling in multiple countries simultaneously, which made it "very easy" for central banks for a while.
"Central banks were doing exactly what governments wanted [by] making life easier for them by lowering interest rates," he said.
"It was a temporary fortunate period, but people didn't realise how temporary and how fortunate it was, partly because they thought it was all due to the brilliance and expertise of the central banks in maintaining these inflation targets.
"But the central banks didn't have any difficulty.
"Indeed, if you take the period after the great financial crisis … the problem that central banks had was easing monetary policy sufficiently to bring inflation back up to target," he said.
And unfortunately, he said, that long-term decline in interest rates from the 1990s onwards contributed to the housing anguish younger people feel today, because asset values rose so quickly relative to incomes during those decades.
"As interest rates decline, asset values rise," he explained.
Tax systems will have to be overhauled
Jump forward to 2026, he said, and younger people are living in a very different world.
He said living standards were still rising, but much more slowly than society was used to.
He said the environment for younger people trying to enter the workforce today was incredibly tough.
"I think the conditions for young university leavers at the moment are considerably worse than they would otherwise have been because of AI," he said.
"And again, add the problem of [how] you can't afford housing, [and how] it's increasingly difficult to get a job, and the young potentially white-collar workers are certainly joining the blue-collar workers in feeling that … the conditions have moved against them."
In coming decades, he said, aging populations would also put younger workers under an increasing tax burden, and the UK government would have to overhaul its tax system to adjust to some serious demographic and fiscal realities.
"It ought to shift away from taxing incomes and profits to taxing assets, particularly land and property," he argued.
"We've got to shift taxation away from the producers — the workers and businessmen — and put it on those whose assets have increased dramatically in value."
But of course, he warned, any attempt to tax assets and land more heavily would upset some very wealthy people, who would fight the changes.
Growing political polarisation
McCormack asked Goodhart if he thought that was why more people were supporting socialist ideas today.
"I think there's a lot in that, yes," Goodhart replied.
"And one of the difficulties [for] somebody my age is that in the old days you always had effectively a two-party system where the difference between the 'left' of the Conservatives and the 'right' of Labour was pretty small.
"[But] now we've got increasing political polarisation with the parties both of the right and of the left … becoming more extreme, and for somebody who was brought up essentially to be a centrist like myself, [it] feels as though this polarisation makes things more difficult."
McCormack then wondered whether today's political polarisation reflected the fact that the "middle ground" had failed in a policy sense.
"Good question," Goodhart said.
"But when you say, 'The middle ground having failed,' it's not entirely clear to me what else could, or should, have been done.
"If you look at the economics, a combination of the decline in the birth rate everywhere [which has been] very sharp, the rise of China, and the end of the Soviet empire and the inclusion of eastern Europe into the world's trading system, it was inevitably going to reduce real wages in the advanced economies because it was a huge supply of additional cheaper labour elsewhere.
"So it was inevitably going to reduce equality [in the UK] to some extent," he said.
Look on the bright side
Altogether, he said he wished more people understood how much the world had changed.
He said we had to accept that we could not vote our way back to the "magnificent period" from 1950 to 2020.
Falling birth rates, aging populations, rising dependency ratios, the need for more expenditure on defence and climate change, and rising debt levels were creating a fiscal crisis that governments still could not face, he said.
"I've just written a book, called The Unanchored Central Banker, which is really saying that because the politicians have not dealt with the severely worsening fiscal position, it's going to be very difficult for central banks to maintain the inflation target and monetary control," he warned.
Can we become prosperous again?
"Oh yes, you never say never about anything," he said wryly.

Prosecutors charged Tel Aviv resident Udi Ayalon, 48, on Monday with threatening a media professional’s career, reputation, and privacy in an alleged campaign to force her to renew a business and personal relationship with him.
The indictment, filed in Tel Aviv Magistrate’s Court, charges Ayalon with multiple counts of extortion by threats, threats, violation of a court order, harassment through a communications device, and invasion of privacy, the prosecution said.
According to the indictment, Ayalon produced paid lectures for the woman as part of a business relationship that later developed into a friendship.
Prosecutors allege that about two years into the relationship, Ayalon became dissatisfied with the amount of attention he received from her and began sending WhatsApp messages threatening to damage her livelihood and reputation. Ayalon then allegedly sent further threatening messages, published posts on social media and repeatedly appeared at her workplace. 'I am going to be cruel at a level you never imagined'
“You have ended your career,” he allegedly wrote in one message. “I am going to be cruel at a level you never imagined.”
In another message cited by prosecutors, Ayalon allegedly wrote that his desire for revenge was driven by her refusal “to make a fresh start” with him.
The woman later obtained a restraining order prohibiting Ayalon from contacting or harassing her in any form. The court also issued a gag order covering the proceedings. The indictment alleges that Ayalon violated both orders.
Following the alleged violations, the woman filed a police complaint. Prosecutors said Ayalon continued to threaten her during a confrontation conducted as part of the investigation, despite the presence of a police investigator.
“You do not know how dangerous I am,” he allegedly told her, according to the indictment. “You have something to fear.”
He also allegedly said: “I will continue doing what I want. I am not afraid of anyone. No one will tell me what to do.”
The prosecution has asked the court to impose restrictions on Ayalon for the duration of the criminal proceedings, including a prohibition on contacting, harassing, or threatening the woman, either directly or through other people.
In the earlier investigation, Ayalon’s attorney had denied the allegations and argued that his client was the victim in the dispute.

PFLP-linked New Zealand party running on Palestine platform enters election, sparking concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:56:17 UTC
03:56:17 KST

Less than two months ahead of the New Zealand general elections, a PFLP-linked party running entirely on a pro-Palestine platform is raising questions about the normalization of Israel and Jew hate in the southwestern Pacific nation.
The Palestine Free from the River to the Sea Party was almost not allowed to register after over 200 submissions opposing it; however, the Electoral Commission ultimately decided to allow it to pass on August 5. This means it has at least 500 members, as that is the threshold needed to secure registration.
Not only will the party feature on the ballot paper, but it has also been allocated nearly NZ$79,000 in taxpayer-funded election broadcasting money.
According to its website, the Palestine Free from the River to the Sea Party has three main aims: Building a democratic party that unites supporters of Palestine from all traditions; pressuring the New Zealand government to support the prosecution of war crimes and genocide; and recognizing that Palestinian liberation is bound up with the broader struggle against imperialism.
It also calls for the return of Palestinian refugees to their homeland and the dismantling of the State of Israel.
The party was founded and is led by Paul Hopkinson, who also serves as the national spokesperson for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) campaign in New Zealand.
Hopkinson told the New Arab on June 23 that he plans to use his position as a registered political party to hold other parties to account on the issue of Palestine.
“Successive New Zealand governments have failed to take any steps to hold Israel accountable for its violations of international law or to support UN resolutions related to Palestine,” he said.
“As is clear from the party’s principles, we offer unconditional support for all forms of Palestinian resistance, including armed resistance.”
Therefore, he said, Hamas and other Palestinian groups (such as the PIJ) should not have been placed on the terrorism list in NZ. The PFLP itself is not designated.
Interestingly, this is the same Hopkinson who was at the center of a relatively well-known NZ court appeal in 2003.
On 10 March, 2003, between 500 and 1,000 people protested the Australian Government’s support for the United States-led invasion of Iraq. During the protest, Hopkinson – at the time a schoolteacher – held the New Zealand flag on a pole upside down and another activist lit it on fire, resulting in a column of flame.
Hopkinson became the first person to be prosecuted under the Flags, Emblems, and Names Protection Act 1981. He appealed, and a judge later ruled that “the prohibition of flag burning under the act was a breach of the right to freedom of expression, and such a limit was not justified under s5 of the Bill of Rights.”
In February this year, Hopkinson was arrested for attempting to burn an American flag, as well as for assaulting a police officer. He appears to have been arrested on several occasions in relation to his pro-Palestine protesting. He also ran as a Workers Party candidate for Christchurch East in 2008.
Zionism becomes an election issue
Israel Institute of New Zealand spokesperson Greg Bouwer told the Australia Israel and Jewish Affairs Council (AIJAC) that “If ‘From the River to the Sea’ becomes the formal identity of a registered political movement, we should expect the meaning of Zionism, Israel’s continued existence and Jewish national self-determination, to become election issues.”
“That makes it especially important that other parties do not respond by competing for the same constituency through increasingly inflammatory rhetoric.”
In a separate piece on the IINZ website, Bouwer raised the question of why any party should make a foreign policy position its only ethos.
“That raises a legitimate question for a party seeking representation in New Zealand’s Parliament. Why should determining the constitutional future of Israelis and Palestinians be the organizing purpose of a New Zealand political party?” he asked.
And it is not as if other parties in NZ don’t have Palestine on their list of campaign issues.
The Green Party, for example, is openly hostile toward Israel, as is Te Pati Maori. Labour has also moved toward a more anti-Israel position.
New Zealand Jewish Council (NZJC) President Juliet Moses told AIJAC that Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins “seems reasonable” but that Spokesperson for Foreign Affairs Vanushi Walters “has said a genocide is unfolding in Gaza, and that if Labour was in power it would have recognized Palestine, sanctioned Israel, and looked to join South Africa’s case against Israel at the ICJ.”
New Zealand sees ongoing rise in antisemitism
The anti-Israel messaging throughout the parties is significant due to the way in which it provokes a rise in antisemitism in the country.
According to the NZJC, 2025 saw the highest number of antisemitic incidents ever recorded in a single year in New Zealand.
The incidents included five assaults (the most in any year), two threats, and 15 incidents of desecration or damage to Jewish sites.
According to NZ Police, New Zealand Jews are disproportionately targeted compared with other ethnic and religious groups – and Jews are only 0.2% of the population.
Geopolitical incidents involving Israel are often associated with an increase in antisemitic incidents in New Zealand, particularly from far-left and Islamist-motivated individuals.
In the same report, NZJC warned that antisemitism has become “tolerated or even endorsed by persons of social and political importance and other leaders.”
“It is concerning that members of our parliament feel free to participate in online forums that routinely express vile antisemitism, or join rallies promoted by groups that have been widely condemned for their racism, let alone participate in the hateful chants of “From
the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” or endorse “intifada,” it said.
The fact that a party’s name is that very slogan is cause for concern.

The B’Yachad party will be committed to ensuring equal rights for the LGBTQ community and enabling civil marriage if it joins the next government, opposition leader Yair Lapid, who holds the second slot on former prime minister Naftali Bennett’s party slate, told The Jerusalem Post on Tuesday.
The B’Yachad party was formed from an alliance between Bennett and Lapid’s centrist Yesh Atid Party. It is one of the leading parties in the opposition bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the October elections.
Lapid said Tuesday that B’Yachad would seek to pass legislation within the first 100 days of the next government guaranteeing equal rights for every couple in Israel.
Civil marriage is not performed in Israel, as the religious status quo in the country dictates that Jews can only marry and divorce through the rabbinate.
This prevents same-sex couples from legally marrying in the country. As a result, many couples travel abroad to marry in civil ceremonies, which are later legally recognized upon their return and grant them marital rights.

“He is no less Jewish, he is no less married, and my granddaughter is no less Israeli than anyone else."
"In the State of Israel, there should be a parallel civil marriage option for anyone who wants it," he said.
“As a liberal party, we are committed to equal rights for everyone. Discrimination against the LGBTQ+ community must end, and we will make sure of it,” Lapid added.
Bennett shifting towards liberal stances, maintains right-wing view on security
Bennett has shifted from his stance in past campaigns, taking a more liberal position while maintaining a strong right-wing stance on security.
Bennett said that during his time away from the political scene after being prime minister in 2021, he consulted experts to prepare a comprehensive plan for the country’s future, which includes the establishment of a written constitution, raising competition in the market to lower the cost of living, improving transportation, cutting down the crime rates, and investing in AI to advance the country’s technology and defense.
