Concerns raised over 'problematic culture' at Suncorp's debt collector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:52:52 UTC
03:52:52 KST

Suncorp's debt collector engaging in 'worst kind' of bullying, former ACCC chair says
Debt collector ARMA Group spent months harassing and intimidating 81-year-old Diane Walker into paying an insurance claim she was not responsible for.
ARMA, acting on behalf of insurance giant Suncorp, ended the ordeal with an apology to Ms Walker and financial compensation for the distress caused, but only after months of legal threats and pressure to pay.
"They were rather bullying-type letters … it's in the back of your mind all the time," Ms Walker said.
ARMA's website says its workflows are "AI-driven", boasting it takes the company "less than two minutes to set up a smart payment plan and no manual intervention is required".
Ms Walker's case is just the tip of the iceberg as the consumer watchdog takes ARMA Group and Force Legal, both owned by Credit Clear Limited, to court, alleging that between them they sent 320,000 debt enforcement notices to individuals that were allegedly misleading.
Legal experts are appalled and say it is a clear breach of Australian consumer laws.
"This is Robodebt 2.0 of the worst form," said Allan Fels, former chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).
"I'm very concerned … this seems to be the worst kind of illegal, deceptive conduct applied to bully, intimidate, frighten.
"It's traumatic for the individual to be confronted in a Robodebt situation with no opportunity to respond or fight back, or talk to someone, or explain their personal circumstances.
"There needs to be a serious, substantial crackdown on this kind of approach."
'Bullying' and 'intimidation'
Just before Christmas, Ms Walker was involved in a minor two-vehicle car crash she was not responsible for, and that caused no damage.
The other driver's insurer, AAMI, a subsidiary of Suncorp, contacted Ms Walker looking to recover costs, despite having no evidence.
"I would have emailed them at least half a dozen times saying, 'Send me some photos, send me something that demonstrates that at least something happened,'" said Scott Walker, who stepped in as his mother's representative on the claim.
About two months after AAMI first contacted Ms Walker, it engaged its debt collector, ARMA Group, to recover the funds.
Without providing evidence, the debt collector concluded that Ms Walker was "liable".
Previously a freelance camera operator for the ABC, Mr Walker said he spent hundreds of hours trying to make sense of ARMA's communication.
"It was just this level of intimidation … the wording sounded very much like there's been some legal decision made, some type of independent, judicial system that has found an outcome," he said.
Threatening court action
Ms Walker and her son said ARMA's letters were relentless.
Despite initially telling Ms Walker she had been found "liable" for the car accident, ARMA began threatening court action, suggesting culpability remained unresolved.
One letter said: "If you choose to dispute the issue with arguments that are not relevant — such as claiming there is no dashcam footage or no photos of the vehicles at the moment of impact — we will have no choice but to escalate the matter further.
"You are welcome to present those arguments in court if you believe they support your case. If you are found liable, you would be liable for court fees as well."
ARMA Group was initially claiming $1,175.51 from Ms Walker.
But after three months, the company increased the amount to $1,395.51 without explanation.
Mr Walker was then sent a separate claim, arguing he was now responsible for the accident, even though he wasn't there at the time.
"The system's not designed to have a sensible conversation with someone at the other end; it's a system that is designed to make you pay," Mr Walker said.
"To try to get you to fold or give up."
ARMA Group did not respond to questions from ABC News.
Suncorp did not provide an on the record response to the ABC's questions.
Tip of the iceberg
The number of Australians with debt is rising sharply, with contact to the National Debt Help Line increasing by nearly 12 per cent in the year to August.
The chief executive of the Consumer Action Law Centre, Stephanie Tonkin, said Ms Walker's case represented a larger problem.
"Over many years, we've seen really poor conduct by debt collection companies and individual agents as well," she said.
"What Diane's case signals to me is that there is a very problematic culture at ARMA that runs deep into the organisation.
"What these proceedings [against ARMA and Force Legal] by the ACCC show is that at the heart of the problem are the lawyers at ARMA," Ms Tonkin said.
"They are preparing the documents, preparing the communications that are overly aggressive, factually inaccurate, and they are likely causing extreme stress."
She is concerned automation has been used with little or no oversight.
"I am really worried about the future of this industry, and the lack of consumer-centred design and the lack of safeguards that businesses are putting in to ensure that consumers aren't harmed."
An apology and compensation
After months of back and forth, Mr Walker contacted Suncorp executives, who in June dropped the claim due to a lack of evidence and admitted the company engaged its debt recovery partner "prematurely".
Suncorp apologised to Ms Walker and compensated her with a $1,500 goodwill fee.
It also told her that ARMA had acknowledged the matter was not handled appropriately.
In contrast, ARMA said it found Mr Walker's claims "unsubstantiated" and was "comfortable with how this matter was handled".
While Suncorp confirmed "formal disciplinary action" was taken with ARMA Group, it also said the relationship would continue "under our usual arrangements".
"I just find that extraordinary, and it's quite insulting," Mr Walker said.
Without her son's support, Ms Walker admitted the process would have looked very different.
"I probably would've just given them my insurance details or paid whatever they asked me to."

US Treasury’s Bessent will meet with China’s He Lifeng this weekend
WASHINGTON - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sept 15 said he would meet with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng this weekend ahead of a meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next week.
Bessent told a hearing of the House Financial Services Committee that Trump and Xi would continue discussions on Iran and China’s financial links to Tehran, which Washington has been seeking to shut out of Western financial systems.
The Treasury secretary said US officials had been in talks with China about a crackdown on countries supporting Iran.
“With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart, the Vice-Minister Lifeng, and I’m sure it will continue during President Xi’s state visit,” Bessent told lawmakers during the hearing.
A Treasury spokesman had no immediate comment on the venue or exact date of the planned meeting.
The Chinese and US presidents are expected to meet in the US on Sept 24, although China has yet to officially confirm the meeting will take place.
Trump on Sept 13 reiterated his view that he has a good relationship with Xi, and brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops.
Reuters reported last week that Iran had bypassed sanctions on its oil sales by using a barter-like arrangement to buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods, including military gear, from China.
Treasury in August launched a new push to isolate Tehran and crush its ability to fund the war in the Middle East. Dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” the US has imposed sanctions on three banks including Russia’s VTB, Iran’s proxy networks in several countries, and Iran’s entire aviation industry.
It also put sanctions on some Chinese independent refineries, but it has thus far refrained from going after larger Chinese financial institutions, despite Bessent’s repeated warning that Washington will not tolerate any support for Iran and will continue to hunt down its enablers.
Bessent and He held what China’s state news agency Xinhua called “candid, in-depth, and constructive” discussions by phone in July. The two sides agreed to use the China-US economic and trade consultation mechanism to strengthen communication, enhance mutual trust and expand cooperation, Xinhua said.
Beijing, however, also raised “serious concerns” over recent US trade and economic restrictions on China, after Washington announced new tariffs of 10 per cent and 12.5 per cent on goods from 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of forced labour bans. China was assigned a 12.5 per cent rate.
China-US trade relations have remained largely stable since a truce announced in 2025. The two countries agreed this year to set up the Board of Trade to explore areas where they could cut duties on goods worth some US$30 billion (S$38 billion). REUTERS

Russia has made Germany a priority espionage target, and the threat from cheap, deniable sabotage carried out by civilians paid for one-off jobs is rising, Germany's Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD) said in its 2025 annual report—the first published under a new law obliging annual disclosure. MAD blamed Germany's geostrategic position in Europe and NATO, the expansion of the Bundeswehr, and the introduction of new weapons systems. Repeated sabotage cases on German soil last year were "with high probability" Russian-run, MAD said.
For two years Berlin has publicly warned about a Kremlin campaign of arson, surveillance, and drone incursions run through cheap local proxies—mostly at press briefings and closed sessions. A January 2026 transparency law now forces that warning onto the statutory public record, sharpening the burden of an operational answer. Germany hosts NATO's logistics spine for arming Ukraine—the very hub Moscow's proxies keep aiming at.
Sabotage on the cheap
"Hybrid attacks have increased in Germany," MAD said.
The threat from "low-level agents"—residents paid small sums to plant fires or photograph military sites—has significantly increased. Recent incidents match the model: a bomb-laden drone found in August beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport was traced this month to a Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal, and two Bulgarian nationals were arrested over a September suspected arson near defense-electronics firm Rohde & Schwarz in Munich. Russia's Legalresidenturen — intelligence outposts inside embassies, semi-state bodies, and press agencies—remain a central instrument of Moscow's information-gathering.
A masked figure got into a Polish drone-parts plant—Poland now suspects a foreign spy service set the fire
Chinese drones over bases, blackmail risk for soldiers
Some drone overflights and unauthorized entries at Bundeswehr sites are attributable to Chinese intelligence, MAD said, which is also drawing on parts of the Chinese diaspora in Germany.
The service flagged travel by German soldiers to Russia and Belarus: personnel with family ties there kept visiting despite the security climate, drawing the attention of Russian and Belarusian intelligence services and creating particular exposure to blackmail and threats.

Kennedy Center board votes to close venue immediately as judge again blocks addition of Trump's name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:49:26 UTC
03:49:26 KST

Kennedy Center board votes to close venue immediately as judge again blocks addition of Trump’s name
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Kennedy Center trustees, dominated by Trump appointees, voted to immediately shutter the main building.
- Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty is seeking emergency relief to halt the closure, arguing that trustees exaggerated structural dangers and misrepresented consultants’ findings.
- The fight caps months of upheaval since Trump ousted the previous board and made himself chair, triggering a talent exodus, legal rebukes and plans to shift programming to the Reach and offsite.
The Kennedy Center Board of Trustees voted Tuesday to immediately close the performing arts venue, a few hours after a federal judge ruled that President Trump’s name could not be restored to its facade, according to sources familiar with the situation. It remains unclear when the venue might actually close since U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper would have to lift his preliminary injunction against the closure — an action that will almost certainly be fought in court.
Trump, however, threatened to block the renovation if his name isn’t restored to the building.
“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” he wrote on Truth Social.
The whipsaw turn of events came after a 57-page packet was distributed to the board over the weekend claiming the center was in egregious physical decline and nearly bankrupt — a prospect that could be avoided only with Trump’s help.
“The Kennedy Center is in such a precarious fiscal position that it will not be able to support its payroll obligations, nor routine maintenance contracts within a matter of weeks,” the draft resolution seeking the addition of Trump’s name reads. It continues, if Trump is not “legally and appropriately recognized and acknowledged on the facade of the Kennedy Center,” it is doubtful he will agree to “carry the burden of managing the renovation and [provide] the Center with a much required financial rescue.”
In a 22-page ruling Tuesday, Cooper wrote, “Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing.”
A federal judge has ruled that President Trump’s name was illegally added to the Kennedy Center and blocked the administration from closing the cultural and arts venue for major renovations.
The vote to shut down for a two-year, $250-million renovation comes after previous efforts by the Trump-appointed board to close the venue and add Trump’s name have been stymied in court — most recently in May when Cooper first ruled that only Congress could rename the venue. Cooper did not rule that the board could not shut down the center, only that it should take more time to consider the issue.
In mid-August the board again voted to move forward with Trump’s plan to shutter the building for renovations and to inscribe Trump’s name on the facade. Tuesday’s vote solidified those plans, tying the closure and the need for Trump’s name to imminent bankruptcy and building conditions that it alleges are dangerous to staff and the public.
Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex-officio member of the board, who sued late last year to block Trump’s name from being added to the facade, included the two new draft resolutions in a court filing Monday, hoping to get Cooper to consider them at a discovery hearing scheduled for Tuesday.
“For years, the Kennedy Center has planned to undergo phased renovations, in which we both renovate and maintain some performances. This is how major performing arts centers in the country operate. But donors, patrons, and artists all fled after the unlawful attempt to rename this sacred memorial after Donald Trump,” Beatty said in a statement to The Times. “Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity. That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution.”
In her most recent filing, Beatty’s lawyers argued that documents distributed to the board of trustees over the weekend, which contained the draft resolutions and made the case for closure, “incorrectly asserts that the Delta Consulting Group considers the main building ‘unsafe for continued occupancy,’ when Delta expressly disclaimed providing any such opinion.”
The filing also notes that the draft resolution “seeks to justify the closure by citing a recent leak in the building which caused a portion of the ceiling plaster to detach,” and notes that, “In the past, similar such defects appear to have been addressed without closing the Center.”
President Trump says he will move to close the Kennedy Center performing arts venue for two years starting in July for construction.
“The Board’s latest shutdown vote is more of the same failure and abuse that has characterized this administration’s treatment of the Kennedy Center,” said Beatty’s counsel, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group. “The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away. Now the Board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We’ll see the Defendants in court.”
The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the closure.
This latest chapter in the battle over the future of the Kennedy Center comes after more than a year and a half of turmoil arising from Trump’s February 2025 decision to fire the center’s board and appoint himself chairman. The move set off a chain reaction that included an exodus of high-profile talent and shows — a trend that ramped up again in December when the board voted to rebrand the venue after Trump, placing his name above that of former President Kennedy.
In February, Trump announced his plans to close the building for renovations beginning July 4, which was pushed back amid ongoing litigation.
The board notes that the center will continue to present educational and artistic programming at the venue’s new Reach expansion, and it will also still present the Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor offsite. The proposal cited the center’s continuing support for the National Symphony Orchestra, which has also been performing at alternate venues.

Labor pledged $5m for soccer precinct before it was planned or costed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:48:00 UTC
03:48:00 KST

Documents spark 'due diligence' question over Labor's $5m election pledge
In short:
Labor approached an Adelaide local council to submit a multi-million-dollar sports club upgrade proposal before the project had been formally costed, scoped or designed.
Documents reveal how the $5 million election promise in Health Minister Mark Butler's electorate developed at his office's urging.
What's next?
The Coalition has said the funding did not follow a "proper process", but Mr Butler said the grant followed Commonwealth rules.
Federal Labor asked an Adelaide council to put forward a multi-million-dollar sports precinct upgrade for federal funding before any detailed costings or formal planning had been done.
Documents released under Freedom of Information reveal Health Minister Mark Butler's office urged the City of Charles Sturt council to submit a proposal with a total price tag of "around $6m", with Labor then pledging $5 million for the project in the lead-up to the 2025 election.
The proposal to redevelop Jubilee Reserve in Mr Butler's electorate as a permanent home for the Adelaide Jaguars women's soccer club was awarded the funds under an invite-only grant scheme, which has been scrutinised for its focus on Labor-held or targeted seats.
The council had originally requested $1.2 million for lighting and development of a master plan for the reserve, but told the ABC the federal government had subsequently "approached" to seek support for the broader Jaguars proposal.
The funding was for the council as the owner of the sporting precinct and did not go to the soccer club directly.
The Coalition has criticised the process and argued developing an overall cost first and "manufacturing" the detail later was not "due diligence".
Mr Butler defended investing in a "terrific" women's soccer club and said the grant was both "consistent with past practice" and delivered in line with Commonwealth rules.
The Albanese government is facing questions about how it nominated projects during the 2025 election campaign for funding under a $560 million grant scheme, with a Senate inquiry to examine what role ministers and MPs may have had.
Upgrade proposal was 'gobsmacking'
The FOI documents obtained by the ABC reveal earlier City of Charles Sturt council discussions about a possible Jaguars move to the reserve had stalled as the soccer club's wish list was considered too ambitious.
One council official described the Jaguars' proposal as "gobsmacking" and warned of "exclusive access" issues, saying it looked "more like a takeover" of the space by the club.
Mayor Angela Evans was later contacted by Jaguars chair Bronny Brooks, revealing she had been "urged by Mark Butler's office to seek your support and facilitation of the process" to access federal funds for the upgrade.
"I have been given a very short turnaround time to present the project for their consideration," Ms Brooks said in an email from October 2024.
City of Charles Sturt chief executive Paul Sutton told the ABC that Labor then asked if the council would "consider an in-principle contribution" for the larger project.
"We agreed to explore the opportunity, subject to future council decisions and community consultation," he said.
Council told to estimate cost at 'make-or-break' point
Documents show Mr Butler's electorate office staffer emailed Ms Evans in January 2025 asking for a letter confirming the plan and including an approximate cost "which, as we discussed, would be around $6m, with council to provide an amount towards that".
Then in a February email, the staffer described the project as at a "make-or-break point" as he sought a "more rigorous" breakdown of the "$6m costing" and a timeline, suggesting the council base the estimates on past projects.
That same day the council produced a costing for the redevelopment that totalled exactly $6m.
The final proposal closely reflected the Jaguars' wish list, including a dedicated senior pitch, fencing, four change rooms and additional playing fields.
Mr Sutton, the council's CEO, said the $6 million figure reflected an "early indicative estimate associated with that broader proposal," noting further "planning, design and costing work would be required to confirm scope, feasibility and cost".
"The federal government then made a $5 million election commitment," he said.
Mr Sutton said the council then agreed to "further investigate the broader opportunity through community engagement and design phase before determining whether to proceed with a grant funding application".
The project was ultimately announced as a $6.5m package, including potentially $1.5m in council funding.
A formal master planning and consultation process was not scheduled to begin until July last year, months after the election commitment.
Labor scrutinised over grants process
Shadow Sport Minister and South Australian Liberal Senator Anne Ruston said Australians would be "rightly appalled" if government ministers were "coming up with numbers first and then manufacturing justifications afterwards".
"This is the opposite of the accountability and transparency Australians deserve," she said.
"That's not proper process, it's a press release looking for a business case."
Senator Ruston said it was not "due diligence" to set the dollar figure in January and "look for a costing to match it in February".
"Councils and communities deserve grants built on actual need, not a minister's office working backwards from a number that sounded good in a campaign speech,"
Senator Ruston said Mr Butler could not avoid "accountability" for the process behind the grant in his electorate and involving correspondence from his staff.
Last week, the ABC revealed a Centre for Public Integrity investigation of a $560 million grant program used to deliver Labor's election promises was overwhelmingly directed to seats either held or targeted by the party.
The invite-only Major and Local Community Infrastructure program was defended by the government as an appropriate way to ensure election commitments remained value for money.
But Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been criticised for not declaring an honorary membership to the Marrickville Golf Club in his electorate, which was promised $6m at the election under the program.
Mr Albanese said he was not aware of the membership — valued at $5 for two years — and he has subsequently relinquished it.
Labor defends funds for 'terrific' women's club
Mr Butler said his office had "multiple discussions" with the City of Charles Sturt Council about what a redevelopment of Jubilee Reserve would look like and what federal funding would be needed to deliver the project.
"The council outlined to us in a detailed budget proposal how much funding would be needed to develop Jubilee Reserve,"
"The election commitment is consistent with past practice and is delivered in line with Commonwealth Grants Rules and Practices."
Mr Butler said he was "proud" to invest in helping women overcome barriers to participating in sport, adding the Jaguars had campaigned for "years" to have their own facilities.
"This terrific club deserved its own home," he said.
Last year, when the funding was announced, the Adelaide Jaguars Women's Soccer Club said the commitment would give women and girls the chance to play the game they love at any level.
In a statement shared on Facebook, the club revealed it had already had to turn up to 100 players away in 2024 due to "capacity" constraints.

EU says glorification of war criminals has no place in candidate countries after Mladic funeral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:47:01 UTC

Melike Pala
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos on Tuesday said the glorification of war criminals, denial of genocide and historical revisionism are fundamentally incompatible with the European Union's values, stressing that such practices have no place in either the EU or countries seeking membership.
"Last year in Srebrenica, I witnessed the burial of seven more victims 30 years after the genocide. Many are still missing, and their families continue to suffer unimaginable pain. It is incomprehensible that anyone responsible for such crimes is honored as a hero," Kos said during a European Parliament plenary session in Strasbourg, France, referring to the funeral of former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic.
She condemned the public honoring of Mladic, who was convicted of genocide and other war crimes, saying images from his funeral were "profoundly disturbing" and reflected a failure to confront the region's past.
"They show a failure to confront the past and contradict the values at the heart of European integration," Kos said.
She also expressed particular concern over the attendance at the funeral of Serbian ministers, state officials and military representatives, as well as leaders and politicians from Republika Srpska.
The commissioner called on Serbian authorities and all regional actors to contribute to reconciliation and good-neighborly relations.
Kos stressed that the EU does not seek to force Serbia to abandon its identity or history but expects the country to confront its past honestly, including its darkest chapters.
"We can disagree about politics. We can have difficult conversations about reforms and about Serbia's European path, but we cannot negotiate about the dignity of the victims of genocide and war crimes," she added.
Mladic, a former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, died in The Hague on Aug. 27 at age 84 while serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
He was convicted of crimes committed during the 1992-95 Bosnian War, including genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
Mladic's body was flown from The Hague to Belgrade and received with a guard of honor, where a funeral ceremony was also held in a controversial move that has sparked widespread condemnation, especially across Europe.

John Healey is in talks with the Canadian government about joining a new global defence bank intended to help allies rearm to counter mounting security threats, just weeks after Rachel Reeves rejected the move.
The chancellor is understood to be actively considering a bid to join the proposed Canada-led defence, security and resilience bank (DSRB), which proponents say could help the UK fund defence projects at lower cost, before planned talks with his Canadian counterpart this week.
When he was defence secretary, Healey was understood to have been a strong advocate for keeping UK observers present at Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney’s, defence bank talks, despite resistance from the Treasury, which wanted to shut off those international discussions.
Reeves, his predecessor as chancellor, was concerned the bank would not address the UK’s defence procurement issues and was more focused on lending to smaller defence firms in nations with lower credit ratings. The UK has had a AA credit rating since 2016.
Healey, who has long been a proponent of multilateral funding mechanisms, met the Canadian finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, twice at a G20 summit in North Carolina two weeks ago.
They are due to meet again in the UK this week, when the two men are – according to sources – likely to discuss the defence bank, and both are expected to be at EU finance minister talks in Dublin later this week.
Canada is understood to have already formally invited the UK to become a founding member of the bank, along with eight other countries including Ukraine and Turkey.
Healey resigned as defence secretary in June, accusing Keir Starmer and his chancellor, Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk because the defence spending package fell £13bn short of what he argued was required.
As chancellor, he is expected to avoid setting a target date for reaching 3% defence spending in next month’s budget and instead is planning to set out a pathway to reaching the goal at the 2027 spending review.
The DSRB could play a role in this by using financial leverage, separate from the balance sheets of already indebted nations, to boost defence investment. But it would need additional sovereign backing beyond current commitments to become a major player.
Reeves announced at the Nato summit in Ankara in July that the UK would join the Netherlands, Finland and Poland to launch a new lender called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.
She said the MDM would help the UK with procurement – saving the UK as much as 20% – and stockpiling, which would give taxpayers better value for money while allowing government to borrow at a low rate to fund defence. The UK has committed an initial £600m to the new lender.
The former chancellor had called for the two rival international defence financing schemes to merge, arguing that it made sense for countries to only fund one institution that could work for all nations.
In addition to overlaps with existing initiatives, there were also understood to be concerns in the Treasury over the amount of capital that countries would need to commit while public finances are strained. The UK’s initial capital contribution would be between £1bn and £2bn over three years.
The DSRB has been seeking to raise around €100bn, which it would use to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It would also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers.
A government spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity.
“We are working closely with our Canadian allies on ensuring the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and Defence Security Resilience Bank are complementary.”

Iran War could cost $2 billion per month, Congressional Budget Office estimates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:42:14 UTC
03:42:14 KST

Iran war could cost $2 billion per month, Congressional Budget Office estimates
The war with Iran could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, according to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office on Tuesday. The report estimates those costs could rise when there are tit-for-tat exchanges of fire with Iran.
The office estimated the war between Feb. 28 and Aug. 1 has directly cost the U.S. about $38 billion, a figure that does not include repairing U.S. bases in the region damaged during the conflict. In addition, the office estimates inflation during the first quarter of 2027 could be 0.5% higher than what was projected before the war because of rising energy prices.
The CBO noted that replacing munitions accounts for the majority of the costs incurred during the war. In particular, the CBO said the large expenditure of interceptor missiles used to defend against incoming missiles leaves behind a "reduced inventory of interceptors for several years."
"The shortfall would become especially problematic if a conflict arose with an opponent whose arsenal included large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles," according to the report, which pointed out that China maintains such an arsenal and could employ it if there were a conflict over Taiwan.
The report said a comparison of the reported use of interceptors with the number the Pentagon has purchased indicates the U.S. has "probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025." Those munitions include Patriot and THAAD interceptors as well as the Navy's Standard Missiles 3 and 6.
The White House and the Pentagon have downplayed concerns about depleted weapons inventories. President Trump on Truth Social said, "We have virtually unlimited amounts of mid- to high-grade ammunition, far more than we can ever use." Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of forces in the Middle East, recently told "60 Minutes," "I'm not concerned at all. We're well-armed and ready for any contingency."
The CBO said the Defense Department did not respond to requests for information.
The CBO analysis was released a day after the Pentagon inspector general published a report that said the Pentagon's Office for Acquisition and Sustainment concluded the use of munitions in the conflict has led to "strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply."
The CBO estimates it will cost $21.7 billion to replace the munitions used in the conflict through Aug. 1: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile-defense interceptors and $1.2 billion for other munitions.
It will also cost about $1.9 billion to replace lost equipment, according to the report, including a THAAD air defense radar destroyed by Iran. The CBO noted the radar can cost roughly $500 million and is essential for the battery to take down missiles. If the Pentagon decides to request supplemental appropriations to replace lost aircraft with newer versions, the total cost could rise from $1.9 billion to $3.3 billion.
If the war continues at a relatively low intensity, it could cost roughly $2 billion to $3 billion each additional month, according to the report. Monthly costs could rise if there is an escalation similar to the one in July, which saw repeated tit-for-tat strikes. The CBO said the war in July cost about $3 billion.
In June, the Trump administration sent Congress an $87.6 billion supplemental funding request that included $67 billion for the Department of Defense for needs related to the Iran war.
Republicans are trying to provide up to $73 billion in new funding for the war through the party-line reconciliation process, but the House-adopted budget blueprint to initiate the process has been stalled in the Senate.
The CBO released its estimate in response to a request from Democratic Rep. Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania, who is the ranking member on the House Budget Committee.
"Donald Trump's disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded. Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs," Boyle said in a statement to CBS News.

How pizza can solve this unusual math puzzle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:41:31 UTC
03:41:31 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
How do you think the number sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... continues? Most people would guess 32 because all the listed values so far have been the previous number doubled. But this sequence, which was devised by number theorist Leo Moser in 1949, takes a surprising turn: 16 is followed by 31.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In fact, this sequence, designated as “A000127” in The On-line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), continues with the numbers 31, 57 and 99. So even though it begins innocently enough with doubling, it suddenly deviates from that obvious pattern at the sixth term. Moser used this example to warn against drawing hasty conclusions from supposed patterns.
But where did this sequence, now known as Moser’s circle area problem, come from? It’s not random; the underlying logic can be derived using the example of cutting a pizza.
Imagine two people want to cut a circular pizza into many small slices. One person marks points on the edge of the dough, while the other makes a straight cut between all the marked points. They use a pizza cutter to cut from point to point along the edge. The question Moser posed was, essentially: What is the maximum number of pizza slices that can be created in this way?
Strange Pizza Patterns
To think of this situation as a sequence, let’s assume the first person adds one point at a time to the outer edge. With only one point, the pizza cannot be divided according to the rules mentioned, so there is only one slice: the whole pie.
With two points, the surface can be cut in two by cutting through both of them. With three points, three cuts can be made, thus dividing the surface into four. With four points, there are six possible cuts, resulting in eight pizza slices. The pattern continues as expected until there are six points, whereupon the expected pattern breaks down, and the result is 31 slices. But why?
There’s a formula that will tell you how many slices, or areas, are created for n points on a boundary, such as a pizza’s edge. We’ll start by thinking about a simpler relationship: the intersecting lines that result from connecting any two of n points with cuts from a pizza cutter. If you ever studied combinatorics in school, you may know there’s a handy quantity for this: the binomial coefficient, written as B(n, 2) = n!/(2!(n – 2)!). This can be quickly verified using the example with n = 5 boundary points; in this case, there are B(5, 2) = 10 intersections.
A similar approach can be used to determine how often the cut lines intersect. If you consider the pizza with one, two or three points on the edge, the cuts do not intersect as they crisscross the pizza. When there are four or more cuts, however, there is at least one intersection point. Therefore, for every four points, there is one intersection point. The number of these intersections can be expressed using a binomial coefficient as well: B(n, 4), where n points are marked at the edge. For the example with n = 5 edge points, this results in B(5, 4) = 5 intersection points on the pizza.
To keep things simple, we can disregard certain slicing scenarios. Moser’s initial question was: What is the maximum number of separate pizza slices that can be created? To maximize the number of slices, we can disregard cases that involve the intersection of more than two cuts through the pizza.
If you look closely at one of the sliced pizzas, you might notice that it resembles a graph: it consists of a jumble of points connected by lines. It turns out we can use Euler’s polyhedron formula (which I wrote about in last week's newsletter about perfect shapes) to think about this problem.
According to this formula, for any graph where all points are connected, there is a relationship between the number of points, V, edges, E, and faces, F. Specifically: V – E + F = 1. Applying the formula to our pizza, F will correspond to the total number of pizza slices, so if we know how many points along the crust and edges of individual slices there are in the graph, we can calculate our total slices of pizza pie.
The only problem is that, in our example, the number of cuts doesn’t correspond to the number of edges in the formula because each segment of a cut made by intersecting cuts counts as an independent edge of the graph.
To determine the total number of edges, we should recognize that there are three basic types of edges. The first type connects two points on the boundary or crust without being interrupted by other cuts. For n boundary points, there are also n of this type of edge.
Then there is the second type of edge, which connects interior intersection points with boundary points. Each of the B(n, 2) intersections is bounded by two boundary points. This means that a total of 2B(n, 2) edges emanate from all boundary points. This also includes edges of the first type, however, meaning any edges that directly connect two boundary points to each other must, of course, be subtracted to avoid counting them twice. Thus, there are 2(B(n, 2) – n) edges of the second type, which connect outer boundary points with interior intersection points. For n = 5 boundary points, for example, this results in 2(10 – 5) = 10.
Finally, there is the third type of edge, which connects internal intersection points. Four edges terminate at each internal intersection point, of which there are B(n, 4). Therefore, each internal intersection point is connected by four edges, resulting in a total of 4 × B(n, 4) edges. To avoid including all edges connecting internal points and boundary points, we need to do some subtraction and division: 1/2 × 4 × B(n, 4) – 2 × (B(n, 2) – n) = 2 × B(n, 4) – (B(n, 2) – n). Again, the result can be tested for n = 5 points: 2 × 5 – (10 – 5) = 5 edges connecting interior points.
Now we only need to add up all three edge types to get the total number: n + 2 × (B(n, 2) – n) + 2 × B(n, 4) – (B(n, 2) – n) = 2 × B(n, 4) + B(n, 2). With that, we’re almost ready to calculate the number of pizza slices.
Only one small detail is missing: because we abstracted the pizza into a graph to use Euler’s formula, the pizza’s crust also represents edges. Therefore, the term n is added to the previously calculated total. This gives us the E from Euler’s formula: E = 2 × B(n, 4) + B(n, 2) + n.
We already know V, the number of intersection points, and the number of boundary points, n, so: V = B(n, 4) + n.
From Euler’s formula, we obtain the following formula for the number of pizza slices: F = 1 – V + E = 1 – B(n, 4) – n + 2 × B(n, 4) + B(n, 2) + n = 1 + B(n, 4) + B(n, 2). So if you have a pizza in front of you, and you mark n points and divide it by B(n, 2) slices, you get 1 + B(n, 4) + B(n, 2) pizza slices. And as it turns out, for n = 1, 2,..., 5, this always results in the power of 2n – 1, and deviates from this starting at n = 6.
So now you know the logic of Moser’s circle problem—and have learned how to divide a pizza into 31 slices, albeit not all the same size. Fortunately, mathematics can also help us find the fairest way of divvying up pizza pie—but that is a different story.
This article originally appeared in Spektrum der Wissenschaft and was reproduced with permission. It was translated from the original German version with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by our editors.

China Builds World’s First Mothership to Deploy Giant Submarine Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:40:46 UTC
03:40:46 KST

- Category
- World
China Builds World’s First Mothership to Deploy Giant Submarine Drones
China is accelerating its naval modernization with the construction of what appears to be the world’s first mothership designed to deploy full-sized uncrewed submarines, Naval News reported on September 15.
Spotted at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai, the specialized vessel marks a significant milestone in Beijing’s undeclared initiative to operationalize extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles (XXLUUVs).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to satellite imagery reviewed by Naval News, the new vessel resembles an amphibious landing ship equipped with a stern well-deck. Unlike standard well-decks, this design is open underneath and utilizes a large cradle on 12 vertical “jack-up” arms to deploy and recover the drones.
Forward of the well-deck, an internal hangar provides space to house the submersibles. Given the dimensions of the Chinese XXLUUVs, the mothership is estimated to be capable of carrying up to four of the massive drones simultaneously.
China is currently the only nation building full-size autonomous submarines. Two models, measuring between 35 and 45 meters (115–148 feet) in length, are undergoing testing in Hainan. These Chinese platforms are roughly six to eight times larger than the US Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV, according to Naval News.
Until now, the Chinese Navy has relied on specially designed floating docks for coastal testing, making the introduction of a mobile, deep-water mothership a critical upgrade for operational deployment.
While the new ship’s design shares similarities with a 2025 proposal for a civilian undersea research submersible, its sheer scale and the inclusion of a closed internal hangar strongly indicate a military application. Naval News assessed that the only plausible role for the vessel is as a drone submarine tender and combat launch platform.
The exact strategic doctrine for China’s XXLUUV fleet remains undisclosed. However, the drones are expected to fulfill long-range combat roles, which could include autonomous deployments off the west coast of the United States during periods of heightened tension. This dedicated infrastructure investment indicates that Beijing is pushing well ahead of global competitors in integrating uncrewed platforms into deep-water naval operations.
Meanwhile, the evolution of uncrewed naval capabilities is already transforming active combat zones. In the Black Sea, Ukrainian forces recently recorded what is considered the first naval battle in history between two uncrewed surface vessels. A Ukrainian Sargan-3000 maritime drone, equipped with a remote-controlled 12.7 mm machine gun turret, successfully intercepted a Russian surface drone.
After targeting the Russian vessel’s communication antennas from approximately one kilometer away to disrupt its remote control, the Ukrainian drone immobilized and sank the target.

Oil trading and shipping sources said on Sept 15 that Saudi Arabia had informed European customers that some September-loading crude cargoes will be cancelled and oil loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu had been suspended.
State oil company Saudi Aramco declined to comment.
The cut in Saudi flows through the Red Sea will prompt Saudi Arabia to try to export more oil via the Strait of Hormuz using so-called dark shipments similar to those already used by the United Arab Emirates and Iraq, trading sources said.
Such shipments have allowed Gulf oil producers to export 7 million to 9 million barrels per day, which is 30 per cent to 40 per cent of pre-war volumes.
The supply disruption supported oil prices, with Brent oil futures trading near US$108 a barrel and cargo prices in Europe’s physical market even higher, with key benchmark dated Brent at around US$122 per barrel, LSEG data showed.
Saudi Arabia loaded 22 million barrels of oil across 12 vessels at Ras Tanura/ Juaymah in the week of Sept 7 to 13, as opposed to 6 to 7 vessels per week for the prior three weeks, data from Vortexa showed.
Reuters could not immediately determine how many cargoes to Europe would be cancelled or for how long Yanbu loadings would be suspended.
Poland’s Orlen rushes to find alternatives, traders say
Polish integrated oil firm Orlen PKN.WA was rushing to find crude oil cargoes from the North Sea and further afield to replace disrupted Saudi imports, five industry sources said.
Aramco became Orlen’s top supplier in 2022 and now supplies around 40 per cent of its oil, helping wean it off Russian oil but making it reliant on the Saudi producer.
Orlen declined to comment on details of specific commercial transactions, but said it actively manages its supply portfolio to ensure the uninterrupted operation of its refining assets.
“Adjusting and optimising purchase volumes is a standard, ongoing part of the Orlen Group’s operations, driven by both current production needs and changing market conditions,” an Orlen spokesperson told Reuters.
Orlen purchased several cargoes of crude oil in spot tenders on Sept 11 and Sept 14, the sources said.
It picked up North Sea grades including Grane, Johan Sverdrup and Johan Castberg, two said. It also tendered for grades further afield including US WTI Midland and Kazakh CPC Blend, two sources added.
It issued another tender on Sept 15 to buy North Sea or Algerian crude for October delivery and Guyanese crude for November delivery, one trader said, but results were slow to surface.
Orlen and subsidiaries operate oil refineries in Poland, Lithuania, and the Czech Republic.
The Baltic port of Gdansk in Poland received around 160,000 bpd of Saudi crude this year to date, and Lithuania’s Butinge received 63,000 bpd, data from analytics firm Kpler showed.
No further details on the tenders were available and the results could not be directly confirmed with the counterparties.
Feedstock deliveries to Orlen refineries are proceeding without disruption, the company spokesperson said. REUTERS

Thirlwall inquiry has left biggest questions around the Letby case unanswered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:37:07 UTC
03:37:07 KST

Just two months before Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall opened her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital and the crimes of Lucy Letby, a report by Chris Henley KC was published into the “atrocious” wrongful conviction of Andrew Malkinson for rape.
Henley prefaced that report with a plea for the legal establishment to recognise that the criminal courts produce miscarriages of justice. Right up to top judges in the court of appeal, Henley wrote, the system has “a deep-seated … cultural reluctance” to accept it “will on occasion make mistakes” and that “entirely innocent defendants will sometimes be convicted”.
He said the system needed a culture that acknowledges mistakes can be made and ensures “in our various roles when making decisions we are all alive to this potential risk”.
The Thirlwall inquiry was set up in 2023 by the then health secretary, Steve Barclay, on the basis that Letby was guilty of murdering seven babies, and attempting to murder seven more, at the Countess of Chester hospital’s neonatal unit where she was a nurse. Thirlwall’s terms of reference were to spotlight the hospital’s management, and whether their actions and culture “contributed to the failure to protect babies from Lucy Letby”.
Many distinguished experts had already looked at the evidence and expressed very serious concerns that the system had made another of its mistakes and convicted an entirely innocent person. As the Guardian reported, 24 experts wrote to Wes Streeting, who took over as health secretary after Labour’s general election win in 2024, urging him to pause the inquiry or widen its terms of reference to examine the possibility of a miscarriage of justice. Streeting did not do so.
In her opening speech in September 2024, Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, referred to the criticisms of Letby’s convictions dismissively, referring to “a huge outpouring of comment” since the court of appeal refused Letby leave to appeal in May 2024, and to “all of this noise” that had caused distress to the bereaved parents.
“It’s not for me to set about reviewing the convictions,” she said. “The court of appeal has done that with a very clear result. The convictions stand.”
The core premise of the inquiry from the start was that the hospital’s managers had not acted on warnings about Letby from the consultants, and should have called in the police earlier. That was the central conclusion Thirlwall has reached in her 822-page report.
She criticised “a prolonged delay by senior managers in calling the police” after two of three triplets, babies O and P at the trial, died in June 2016. There was an assumption throughout that the police, the Cheshire constabulary, were uniquely equipped to find the forensic truth about how the babies died.
Thirlwall again emphasised in her final statement that her inquiry was “not an investigation into the criminal convictions or the guilt of Letby”. But the report is based on it being a fact that Letby is guilty and Thirlwall has delivered the devastating conclusion that babies would have been protected if the hospital had acted more quickly to safeguard them from the nurse.
There was almost no moment in any of the gruelling inquiry sessions in the long, glittering ballroom of Liverpool town hall that engaged with the question looming over the proceedings: whether Cheshire constabulary may have got the case catastrophically wrong.
A large group of British and international experts, led by the renowned Canadian neonatologist Dr Shoo Lee, who has argued relentlessly that his own research was misrepresented by the prosecution, concluded that there were no murders, only vulnerable newborn and premature babies, and poor care on the unit.
Thirlwall heard in exhaustive detail about the actions the medical director, Ian Harvey, his management colleagues and the consultants took when considering the deaths and collapses of the babies. Postmortems had been carried out by three very experienced consultant pathologists at Alder Hey, Liverpool’s renowned children’s teaching hospital. They found no deliberate harm or any suspicion of it.
Harvey had asked the Alder Hey pathologists to review their conclusions and they confirmed their original findings. He also had the babies’ deaths reviewed by a consultant neonatologist, Dr Jane Hawdon, of London’s Royal Free hospital. She also did not find any deliberate harm, but identified many areas of “sub-optimal care” on the unit.
Harvey invited a review by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, whose team came to a conclusion grimly familiar to maternity and children’s units in the NHS around the country. It had insufficient consultants and not enough consultant time was being spent on babies of such medical vulnerability, just two ward rounds each week. The management downgraded the unit so that it would no longer care for babies born so prematurely.
Thirlwall examined all those processes and has concluded that none were adequate. Her conclusions are that when the consultants had raised concerns about Letby, safeguarding should immediately have been introduced and the police should have been called in earlier.
So during two years and £18m spent on so much legal inquiry, the question has not been answered, nor was it allowed to be asked: how and why did Cheshire constabulary and the Crown Prosecution Service, and the doctors they recruited as expert witnesses, come to so wholly different a conclusion about the causes of death, from all the experts that had looked at the same medical evidence before?
And nor was there permitted to be any solid engagement with the new experts, led by Lee, as to why they so fundamentally disagree with the prosecution’s case and convictions.
In his call for more vigilance after the Malkinson catastrophe, Henley wrote: “Miscarriages of justice disfigure the lives of all connected to the case and make the public generally less safe.”
The Criminal Cases Review Commission, the strained body whose role is to refer potential miscarriages of justice back to the court of appeal, is still looking at Letby’s application, and the copious expert reports submitted with it. In the meantime, a public inquiry chaired by a senior judge was set from beginning to end not to consider the possibility that the police, CPS and courts might have made a mistake, and served up a terrible injustice.

Espionage or sabotage?

UK paying £56,000 for each person returned to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:34:04 UTC
03:34:04 KST

The government’s “one in, one out” deal is costing about £56,000 for every person sent back to France, Shabana Mahmood has told MPs.
The home secretary disclosed the figure as she was questioned by the home affairs select committee over whether the scheme was delivering value for taxpayers.
About 1,400 people have been removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some have subsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats.
Asked how much each return had cost, Mahmood said: “I’ll need to write to the committee on the most recent figures.
“I think it’s per person for the numbers that have been returned so far, it’s about £56,000.”
She later defended the cost, saying it was “still cheaper, or just about the same as supporting someone in a hotel for a year”.
Under the deal, the UK sends a person who arrives by small boats back to France in exchange for taking an asylum seeker applying through a legal route.
The pilot has already been extended once and is now due to run into October, with its long-term future still to be decided.
France wants the bilateral arrangement to be eventually replaced by a wider EU-UK returns deal.
An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders.
Mahmood dismissed suggestions an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis.
She said the deal had already returned more migrants than Britain ever managed under the EU’s old Dublin arrangements.
“It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away because I promise you, it would not,” she said.
She said the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns, adding that it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space.
“It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said.
Laurent Nuñez, the French interior minister, has told Mahmood that he wants to end the scheme, it emerged earlier this week.
In June, Nuñez told a French parliamentary inquiry: “For our part, we want to move away from this bilateral relationship with the UK. We consider that France should not have to carry it alone, and that it would be better to integrate it into an agreement between the EU and UK.
“So I have already clearly told my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be renewed beyond October 1, 2026.”
Mahmood told the committee only “relatively small numbers” of rejected asylum-seeking families had taken up a separate pilot offering them as much as £40,000 to voluntarily leave Britain.
She said: “If you’re a failed asylum-seeking family, what you’re trading off is an offer of £40,000, which will help you resettle back in your country of origin, versus, you know, access to free healthcare and education for your children.”

Poland can’t arrest its way out of Russia’s spy pipeline—107 espionage cases in 20 months, and the tempo is holding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:29:17 UTC
03:29:17 KST

Sabotage preparation, remote recruitment, and data collection on military sites account for a significant share of Poland's espionage docket, and public arrests have not dented the pace, RBC-Ukraine reported on 15 September. The published figures cover only the highest-complexity investigations, so with district prosecutors' cases counted in, the real scale of Russian activity is larger still.
Russia's covert campaign inside the EU has escalated from online disinformation into physical attacks since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine—arson at defense plants, assassination plots, and bomb-rigged drones found at European airports.
Recorded sabotage incidents across Europe tripled between 2023 and 2024 alone. Poland, as NATO's primary overland corridor for Western military aid to Ukraine, sits at the center of that pressure—its railway routes near the Rzeszów logistics hub have drawn particular attention.
What the prosecutors count as espionage
Poland's National Prosecutor's Office opened 67 criminal cases under Article 130 of the Criminal Code—espionage and activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service—during 2025, spokesperson Przemysław Nowak told RBC-Ukraine. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, prosecutors added at least 40 more.
At that pace, 2026 could yield roughly 60 new cases, RBC-Ukraine noted, concluding that the tempo of recruitment and sabotage preparation is not slowing but staying steadily high despite public detentions and strengthened counterintelligence.
Courier bombs and expendable operatives
Earlier, Polish law enforcement exposed two Russian citizens prosecutors say worked for Russian special services. One of them planned to send an explosive device through a delivery service—part of a wider Russian sabotage campaign that recruits low-cost, expendable operatives for arson and disruption across the EU.

Russia’s Leningrad region will limit fuel purchases to 30 liters (almost 8 gallons) per fill-up. About one in five independent and small gas stations have stopped operating.

Russia’s Leningrad region will limit fuel purchases to 30 liters (almost 8 gallons) per fill-up. About one in five independent and small gas stations have stopped operating.
The Leningrad region will introduce a uniform fuel-purchase limit of “30 liters per fill-up” in the coming days, the regional government’s press office told Fontanka. Officials did not explain what “30 liters per fill-up” means, but it most likely refers to a 30-liter limit per vehicle.
The regional government called it a “temporary measure” that will remain in place until October 1. Governor Alexander Drozdenko said earlier that oil companies proposed the limit.
“We decided against QR codes and ration coupons for residents — they would cause needless inconvenience. We’re keeping an odd-even system in reserve, but for now we’ll try to manage without it,” he said.
The governor described the region’s fuel situation as “difficult.” He said the top priority was “preventing panic,” which “fuels a surge in demand.” Drozdenko said about 20% of independent and small gas stations had stopped operating “because they were unable to buy the quantities they needed on the commodities exchange.”
Drozdenko said the supply of AI-92 gasoline “is stabilizing”: “Fuel is available, and the outlook is positive.” As for AI-95, he said, “Things remain difficult: it is available, but there is less of it on the market than usual.” The region has no diesel shortages, the governor said.
The second wave of Russia’s fuel crisis began in August, driven by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Gasoline prices rose, and lines formed again at gas stations, as they had in previous months.
According to Reuters, three of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries sharply reduced production or shut down entirely in September because of damage from the attacks.

US lawmaker calls for public execution of Lindsay Clancy
US Congresswoman Nancy Mace has called for the public execution of Lindsay Clancy, wading into an increasingly bitter national debate over the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children.
Clancy, a former nurse, admitted to strangling five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson, and eight-month-old Callan at the family home in 2023 before attempting suicide. However, her lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was therefore not criminally responsible. Her trial ended in a mistrial earlier this month after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
“Her children are dead, she should be dead too,” Mace told TMZ on Monday, adding that Clancy deserved the death penalty and that it should be carried out publicly.
“It could be by firearm, it could [be] electric chair, I don’t really care,” the Republican lawmaker said, arguing that the execution would serve as a “warning to women everywhere” not to kill their children.
The case has sharply divided public opinion. Prosecutors have argued that Clancy carefully planned the killings, deliberately sending her husband out on errands before strangling the children in the basement. Their experts have also disputed her psychosis defense, arguing her actions required a series of deliberate choices.
Her critics have also rejected the idea that postpartum illness can effectively excuse murder and argued that although mental illness may explain Clancy’s actions, it should not erase responsibility for deliberately killing three defenseless children.
On the other side, Clancy has attracted a large and highly mobilized following, particularly among women and advocates focused on postpartum mental illness, who view the killings as the catastrophic result of psychosis and failures in maternal mental healthcare. A fundraiser set up to support her parents, who have financed her legal defense, has raised over $1.2 million.
The mistrial has further intensified the dispute after jurors revealed they had split 11-1 in favor of finding Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, with the lone holdout preventing a verdict after seven days of deliberations.
The man has since been doxxed online and subjected to intense scrutiny over his personal history. Supporters have raised nearly $200,000 for him, while Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has offered him “asylum.”
Several fellow jurors have publicly criticized his reasoning, with one saying he “had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children.”
Clancy’s lawyers are now seeking to have the case dismissed to avoid a retrial. Prosecutors have yet to announce whether they will retry her, with the next hearing scheduled for September 29.

Kim Kardashian was awarded symbolic compensation of 1 euro for the robbery in Paris
Kyiv • UNN
Kim Kardashian received symbolic compensation for the robbery in Paris. Her $4 million engagement ring has still not been found.
On Tuesday, American reality TV star Kim Kardashian was awarded symbolic compensation of 1 euro (US$1.15) from the robbers who tied her up at gunpoint in a Paris hotel in 2016 and stole jewelry, including her $4 million engagement ring. Her lawyer reported this, UNN reports, citing Reuters.

Putin lost at some overseas polling stations in 2024. Here’s how Russians abroad can vote in this weekend’s State Duma elections.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:19:11 UTC
03:19:11 KST

Putin lost at some overseas polling stations in 2024. Here’s how Russians abroad can vote in this weekend’s State Duma elections.
Russia will hold elections for the ninth State Duma from September 18 to 20, 2026. The campaign’s biggest development has been the disqualification of Yabloko, the only anti-war party and one that had drawn enthusiastic support from young social media users. Even so, many Russians, including those who have left the country, still see the election as an opportunity to make their views heard. At some polling stations abroad, the Kremlin-backed party or candidate could lose. Vladimir Putin even lost at some polling stations in 2024. This guide explains how and where Russians can vote abroad.
Deciding where and when to vote
Voting will be available in 152 countries in 2026. Russia’s Central Election Commission plans to set up 319 polling stations, including at Russian Houses cultural centers. If your city or country has no polling station, you will probably need to travel. You will not be able to vote in Georgia, for example, but you could travel from there to Armenia or Turkey. To avoid problems, it is best to start planning now.
You can find all polling stations abroad on Kovcheg’s map or the Central Election Commission’s website.
Voting dates vary by country. Most polling stations abroad will be open for just one day, September 20. But several countries have different dates: September 17 in Israel, and September 19 in Bahrain, Kuwait, China, Iraq, and Yemen. The Central Election Commission said it changed the dates because September 20 is a workday in those countries.
You should also check whether early voting is available. Early voting is available in 45 countries, including Mexico, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, New Zealand, and Japan. These countries have polling stations, but some Russians live too far away to reach them. You can check whether early voting is available in your country at this link. Keep in mind that voting has already taken place in some locations, while it will run for several days in others.
Because mobile election teams and polling places operate on widely varying schedules, check official sources for the exact voting times in your area.
Preparing the necessary documents
More precisely, one document. At the polling station, you will need an original document proving your identity and Russian citizenship. This can be:
- A Russian passport valid for international travel, preferably an unexpired one;
- A diplomatic or service passport;
- A certificate of return to Russia if, for example, you have lost your passport.
What is a certificate of return to Russia?
You can obtain a certificate of return from any Russian diplomatic mission. This special document confirms the identity of a Russian citizen abroad whose documents have expired or who has no documents at all. It is valid for 15 days and, despite its name, does not require you to return to Russia. It takes one or two days to get one, so you may still have time before the election if necessary. To apply, bring two photographs, an application, and any documents confirming your identity to the consular section.
You will not need anything else, including advance registration at a polling station abroad. Russian citizens are added to overseas voter rolls on election day after asking in person to be added — an oral request is enough — and presenting identification. Russian law explicitly provides for this simplified procedure.
Plan for voting day
Because all you need to do to vote is show up at a polling station on the designated date, the preparations are mostly practical. Be prepared for a possible line and, if you can, avoid scheduling important meetings or errands for the same day.
It is best to arrive around the time the polling station opens. This will help you avoid the busiest period, meet like-minded people, and take part in the “Noon” campaign, which many organizations are urging people to join.
Russians who can’t get to a polling station can try voting remotely
Russians who still have a registered address in Russia can use remote electronic voting if that address is in a region where the system is available. You can check whether your region is on the list here; the same link provides detailed instructions for voting remotely.
There is one technical complication: Officially, you cannot vote while abroad. But if you use a VPN server located in Russia, the authorities will be unable to stop or punish you.
Assessing the personal risks
For the vast majority of Russians, visiting a Russian diplomatic mission is completely safe. Anastasia Burakova, a lawyer and founder of the human rights organization Kovcheg, told Meduza that many people mistakenly believe embassy grounds are part of the country the embassy represents. They are not. This means Russian authorities cannot detain visitors there, she said:
Russia cannot and does not conduct searches or other law-enforcement operations on embassy grounds or elsewhere in another country. No one has been dissolved in acid there, and no one has been kidnapped. They simply do not have the capacity for that. Even if you imagine someone being kidnapped, [that person] would then have to be taken somewhere — you wouldn’t keep them in the embassy; they couldn’t live there.
People designated as “foreign agents” in Russia and those subject to military conscription can currently vote at polling stations abroad. No laws restricting these groups’ voting rights have yet been adopted.
Article 32 of the Russian Constitution states: “Citizens who have been declared legally incompetent by a court, as well as those serving a prison sentence, do not have the right to vote or stand for election.” This restriction apparently does not apply to people convicted in absentia. Burakova believes that Russians facing political persecution can also vote at polling stations abroad.
The only Russians who should never visit diplomatic missions are asylum-seekers and people with refugee status. Any interaction with their home country’s authorities could result in the loss of that status, Burakova said: “If you are in contact with your country’s government agencies, that suggests the country is not so unsafe for you after all. That is why we strongly advise against it. [Visiting a polling station abroad] could have consequences. Such cases are very rare, but they do happen.”

US to send $2.8B arms package for Israel including controversial bombs: WaPo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:15:21 UTC
03:15:21 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
 The administration of US President Donald Trump is preparing a $2.8 billion arms package for Israel that would include 40,000 bombs weighing 2,000 pounds (907 kilograms) each, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday.
The proposed package includes 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads. The weapons would be purchased with US taxpayer funds.
The MK-84 is among the most destructive conventional munitions in Western military arsenals. Its blast can propel metal fragments thousands of feet, penetrate thick concrete and metal and create large craters.
Israel has used 2,000-pound bombs extensively in Gaza and Lebanon, where their use has been linked to significant civilian casualties. Israel has also faced criticism over the use of MK-84 bombs in areas it had designated as safe for civilians in Gaza.
The proposed package would exceed previous US transfers of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel under both the Biden and Trump administrations.
It would also be larger than a controversial $2.04 billion arms sale approved in 2025 that bypassed the standard congressional review process.
Trevor Ball, a former US Army explosive-ordnance-disposal technician, described Israel's use of the weapons, saying they are frequently employed when targeting buildings.
“If Hezbollah or whoever is in a building, an MK-84 will bring down the whole building,” Ball said.
The MK-84 was nicknamed the “hammer” by US pilots during the 1991 Gulf War. It was the only munition whose shipment to Israel was temporarily suspended by former President Joe Biden in 2024 over concerns about civilian casualties.
Trump reversed the policy in January 2025.
Brian Finucane, a senior adviser at the International Crisis Group, said there are “real concerns” over how such weapons could be used in densely populated areas, given Israel’s conduct of its air campaign in Gaza and, to some extent, in southern Lebanon.
