OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are working to create an AI standards body
NEW YORK – The world’s biggest AI companies are working on creating a standards body, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Sept 15, as fears rise about the dangers of AI and pressure is on to create a safer version of the technology.
OpenAI said it was working with Anthropic and Google on an idea that originated from a proposal by Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis for a self-regulatory body modelled after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority that oversees US brokers and investment firms.
In July, Hassabis called for the United States to create an organisation that would test the most powerful AI systems before they are released to the public.
“Funding would need to be substantial and likely mostly come from industry, in order to attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing,” Hassabis wrote.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman on Sept 15 voiced support for industry-wide collaboration and acknowledged the public’s fear that competition between companies and countries might sideline safety.
“I think it’s great for our industry to say we want to come together and we want to be able to coordinate and make sure we have enough time to do this safely,” Altman said at a conference hosted by Salesforce in San Francisco.
“When there’s any implication...” that some in the industry might “not do the right thing, I think that’s when people get very scared”, he added.
Some tech figures fear cooperation among the AI giants will push out smaller rivals.
The chief of Canadian AI company Cohere recently accused the dominant American AI labs of forming a “cartel” under the guise of safety.
“AI needs guardrails. That is not the dispute and never has been. The dispute is over who writes them, who gets to participate and whose interests the rules are protecting,” Cohere co-founder and CEO Aiden Gomez wrote in a blog post on Sept 13.
Concerns about AI safety have escalated in recent weeks, including warnings from two workers who resigned from major AI developers amid concerns about the industry’s risks.
Last week, researcher Jacob Coxon left Anthropic and warned that AI companies were “gambling with our lives”. He also previously worked at OpenAI.
On Sept 14, former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed the concerns raised by Coxon and others. “I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome,” Chughtai wrote on social media.
On Sept 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development, a sentiment that Altman, Elon Musk and Hassabis all supported.
US Senator Bernie Sanders, who fears catastrophic consequences of AI, said that tech leaders could not be trusted to honour pledges to slow down development or set safety standards.
“When the future of humanity is at stake, we need binding international safety rules, not voluntary standards from the industry,” Sanders said at an AI safety event in Washington.
Altman warned that AI accidents, small and large, might be inevitable.
“Accidents with any new technology are unavoidable, and we should have a great culture of transparent reporting about them,” Altman said.
“Learning from them quickly and adapting as they happen, I think, will serve our industry well, and maybe we can avoid” the bigger, potentially catastrophic incidents, he added.
US President Donald Trump on Sept 14 dismissed warnings about the risks of AI as “hoaxes”.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also pushed back, signalling a belief that the warnings on AI were part of a coordinated campaign.
“The confluence of these words and then the prediction is alarming and troubling and it shouldn’t be done. It’s irresponsible,” Huang said Sept 14 at a conference in Los Angeles where Trump called him while he was on stage.
Huang, in the call, thanked Trump for “seeing through” the warnings on AI.
Nvidia sits at the centre of the AI revolution, with its chips powering the vast majority of the systems, and Huang has become an informal adviser to Trump. AFP

Could AI really wipe out humanity and hijack the internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:54:48 UTC
02:54:48 KST

Experts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis. Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExperts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis. Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesExplainerCould AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksWe examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI developmentThere have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop.Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them.‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University.It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”.With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said.Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said.Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still.Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system.One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios.“These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.“If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work.Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet.Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”.'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime?The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”.Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals.View image in fullscreenElon Musk, CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have said AI firms should slow down AI development. Composite: Fabrice Coffrini; Julien de Rosa; Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said.“If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said. 'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026“Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.”But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035.The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems.AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making.'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology.The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”.Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going.“The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.”'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown.This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications.Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”.Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models.These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. Ukraine war latest: New interceptors for Russian jet-powered drones 'successfully tested,' Zelensky says
Key developments on Sept. 15:
- Ukraine has 'successfully tested' new interceptor against Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky says
- Russia launches drone attack on Kyiv, killing at least 1, injuring 12
- Russia suffers over 300,000 military losses in Ukraine since start of 2026, General Staff says
- Belarus holds 'defensive' military drills near borders with Poland, Lithuania
Ukraine has "successfully" trialed another interceptor drone designed to target Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sept. 15 following a briefing by Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
As Russia expands its arsenal of Shahed-type jet-powered drones, including the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5, and the cruise missile-like Banderol loitering munition, Ukraine is facing mounting difficulties intercepting the weapons during prolonged attacks, with Kyiv and the surrounding region frequently targeted.
"A 'shahed' was hit successfully, but some aspects of controlling the interceptor still need to be refined. The work continues – it will take some more time," Zelensky wrote on X.
The jet-powered drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (nearly 370 miles per hour), making them more difficult to intercept than earlier, piston-powered Shahed variants. Their use also increased sharply this summer, rising roughly fivefold in July compared with June, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Aug. 31.
Russia launched nearly 800 jet-powered drones toward Ukraine over four days in late August, according to Zelensky.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Aug. 29 that Ukraine had field-tested four potential interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, without specifying which companies were developing them or how far along the projects were.
Anatolii Hrapchynskyi, deputy director of an electronic warfare company and a reserve Air Force officer, told the Kyiv Independent that the use of jet-powered drones was to be expected as Russian forces had been seeking ways to overwhelm Ukraine's anti-aircraft defenses.

Russia launches drone attack on Kyiv, killing at least 1, injuring 12
Russian forces attacked Kyiv on the morning of Sept. 15, killing one person and injuring at least 12 others, local authorities said.
Kyiv City Military Administration reported at 8:39 a.m. local time that a Russian drone had crashed at a petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of the capital.
Another gas station in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district was hit at around 6 a.m. local time, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. One person was hospitalized in critical condition and later died in hospital, according to the mayor.
As of 10 a.m. local time, seven people had been injured in the morning attacks on Kyiv, while two of those wounded were hospitalized in serious condition, Klitschko said.
As of 5 p.m. local time, six of the injured remain hospitalized, Klitschko said.
Six of the injured were in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, where a non-residential building was damaged in the early hours of Sept. 15, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported.
Russia's attack also damaged the data center of BeMobile, according to Ukraine's National Paralympic Committee, whose website was temporarily unavailable following the morning strike.
The committee said emergency restoration work was underway and that it was awaiting the resumption of services by its partner company, UCloud.
The Kyiv Independent contacted UCloud, which confirmed that its Kyiv data center had been affected by the Russian attack.
The company did not specify the nature or extent of the damage, but said the affected websites were expected to resume operation within "several hours."
According to preliminary reports, there were also strikes on warehouses in the city's Obolonskyi district, Klitschko said.

Russia suffers over 300,000 military losses in Ukraine since start of 2026, General Staff says
Russian forces have lost 301,030 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15.
The statement comes after the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, with Russian losses exceeding 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
The General Staff said nearly 300,000 losses were roughly equivalent to the personnel strength of 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an estimated 2,000 troops per regiment.
"The enemy's significant losses are the result of effective combat operations by all components of the Ukrainian Defense Forces," the General Staff said.
Since the beginning of 2026, Russian forces have suffered around 30,000 casualties per month in Ukraine.
The largest losses were recorded during the three summer months, when Russia suffered 124,170 military casualties, the General Staff said. In July alone, the figure surged to a record 42,860 — the highest monthly toll since the start of the full-scale war. In August, the monthly figure again topped 40,000.
"Such high Russian casualties are primarily linked to their tactics. They continue to deploy infantry — often in waves — in an attempt to overwhelm our positions with sheer numbers. At the same time, manpower remains one of their primary tools for achieving results," electronic warfare operator 'Strada,' who asked to be identified by callsign only for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.
In September, Russia has already lost 20,360 troops as of the morning of Sept. 15, the General Staff said.

Belarus holds 'defensive' military drills near borders with Poland, Lithuania
Belarus is holding military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania from Sept. 15-18, the Belarusian Defense Ministry said on Sept. 15.
The Belarusian Defense Ministry described the drills as "defensive" and said they are aimed at improving the military's ability to "protect the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
The exercise is focused on preparing troops to conduct a "strategic military operation," including securing the border, countering alleged sabotage and reconnaissance groups, and combating drones and light aircraft.
Exercises are being held at the Gozhsky training ground in Grodno Oblast, around 6 kilometers (4 miles) from the Lithuanian border, as well as at the Brestsky and Ruzhansky training grounds, roughly 15 and 60 kilometers (9 and 37 miles) from the Polish border.
Belarus has a history of tensions with its NATO neighbors, including Poland and Lithuania. Minsk has previously been accused of using hybrid tactics against the two countries, including facilitating the arrival of migrants from the Middle East and Africa to its borders with the EU, which triggered a major migration crisis.
Belarus also allowed Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The exercises also come amid a buildup of military infrastructure along the Belarus-Ukraine border, leading Kyiv to warn that Moscow may be planning to draw its closest ally deeper into the full-scale war.

Erdogan to visit Syria soon, Turkey's Fidan says from Damascus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:51:09 UTC
02:51:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Fidan reiterates deep Turkey-Syria ties in Damascus ahead of Erdogan visit
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will visit Syria in the near future, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said, as Ankara and Damascus seek to further deepen political, economic and security cooperation following the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
Fidan made the comments late Monday after a two-day visit to Syria, during which he met Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, as well as Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Interior Minister Anas Khattab.
He said his talks in Damascus had included preparations for Erdogan’s upcoming visit, describing the current period in the region as "decisive".
Erdogan’s visit to Syria has not yet been confirmed.
"The common determination to preserve Syria’s unity and territorial integrity" was reaffirmed during the meetings, Fidan said in a post on X, adding that Turkey would continue to stand alongside Syria during the current phase.
Fidan also said he had seen during his visit how Damascus was "regaining its safe and vibrant character", expressing hope that Syrians would build a "safe, stable and prosperous state that embraces all segments of society".
The Turkish foreign minister visited several of Damascus' prominent religious and historical sites during his trip, including the mosque and shrine of Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi, the shrine of Khalid al-Baghdadi, the tomb of Saladin and the Sulaymaniyya Takiyya.
He also met a delegation from the Syrian Turkmen Council headed by Abdul Rahman Mustafa, according to Turkey’s Anadolu Agency, citing diplomatic sources.
Fidan first announced Erdogan’s planned visit on Sunday during a joint press conference with Shaibani in Damascus, saying the Turkish president wanted to make the trip and that preparations for it had been among the issues discussed by the two sides.
The visit would mark a further step in expanding ties between Ankara and Damascus, with the two countries seeking to strengthen cooperation across various sectors.
Shaibani said Syria and Turkey had held dozens of meetings at presidential and ministerial levels and had signed around 40 agreements and memoranda of understanding. The agreements form part of a growing institutional relationship between the two countries, with Syrian ministries and government bodies developing links with their Turkish counterparts.
The Syrian foreign minister said the two sides were also working on a "comprehensive strategic document" on energy and hoped to increase bilateral trade to around $10 billion annually.
He said an energy agreement signed in May 2025 had helped facilitate electricity supplies across the border into northern Syria, while praising Turkey’s role in rehabilitating infrastructure and public services and its support for lifting sanctions on Syria.
The two countries are also working towards a broader energy strategy covering gas, electricity and electricity-grid interconnection, according to officials.
Fidan said Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat had recently visited Damascus and Aleppo with a delegation of businesspeople, with talks focusing on increasing investment and expanding trade, particularly in the energy sector.
Syria could also play a key role in connecting Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Gulf countries and Iraq with Turkey and the Mediterranean, Fidan said.
The Turkish minister also said the two sides were working to activate a Joint Higher Committee that would oversee political, diplomatic, economic and security cooperation. The committee is expected to meet regularly and operate through specialised sectoral committees, with its agenda including energy, refugee returns, education and culture.
Fidan said Erdogan’s upcoming visit would provide an opportunity to review decisions and measures taken by the committee.
Turkey has emerged as a key player in Syria following the ouster of Assad and has maintained a troop presence in the north of the country.

The FBI Doubles Down on Easing ‘Bestiality’ Hiring Standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:50:40 UTC
02:50:40 KST

Kash Patel, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, told confused members of the Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday that new FBI hiring standards are aimed at protecting “victims of bestiality.”
Prior to the current administration, FBI policy was to bar applicants who had, among other things, hired sex workers, stolen from an employer, or engaged in bestiality. In August, CBS News reported that these standards had been relaxed and that multiple sources claimed “the FBI did so to facilitate hiring in some cases.”
According to a letter from Senate Democrats to Patel, new standards appear to have been quietly enacted as early as February 2025. They now allow for the hiring of someone who, for example, stole from an employer more than three years ago, or “paid for sex fewer than three times more than 10 years ago”—traditionally disqualifying because it carries blackmail risk—as long as they weren’t in a position of “public trust.”
But one change has captured more attention than the rest: A “history of bestiality or animal cruelty,” according to the letter, “is not automatically disqualifying under this new policy either, so long as the conduct occurred before the applicant turned 18.”
“You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality,” said Senator Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democrat, during an oversight hearing Tuesday. “Not victims of bestiality, applicants who have been engaged. Do you disagree with that?”
“Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so,” replied Patel. “At this FBI we are not going to criminalize and prevent victims from serving.”
In a further exchange, Patel explained to Senator John Kennedy, the Louisiana Republican, that previously, regulations had barred anyone who engaged in bestiality “on either side of it.”
“Either side of what, the bestiality?” asked Kennedy. “So you disqualified the animal?”
“We have great canines, but we’re not going to disqualify them,” said Patel.
Kennedy said that the change in standards had “really hurt the FBI.”
“Why would you even get into bestiality?” he asked.
“We’re not into bestiality,” said Patel.
In a response to a request for clarification from WIRED, the FBI sent a statement that suggests multiple individuals have been disqualified from applying for the agency because they were victims of human-trafficking-related bestiality.
“The FBI has and always will maintain the highest suitability standards for its applicants and employees in the US Government,” the FBI’s national press office said. “The changes you reference allow the FBI to consider applicants and consider the whole of a person in certain circumstances. For example, the FBI has had a number of applicants in previous years who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing questions about prostitution, bestiality, or other similar issues to affect their background check process through zero fault of their own. Previously, those applicants would be barred from consideration. Now they can be considered. It is false to suggest criminal behavior like this is no longer disqualifying at the FBI—any applicant who has engaged in criminal sexual acts like those referenced would of course not be eligible for employment, and it is ridiculous to suggest otherwise.”
Under President Donald Trump, the FBI has lost a huge number of experienced personnel. The letter from Senate Democrats asserted that since the beginning of Trump’s second term, a “purge” carried out by Patel has led to the departure of “over 5,000 nonpartisan career personnel, all six former Executive Assistant Directors, and at least 18 Special Agents in Charge,” as well as more than a thousand special agents.

Why US is pushing a halt to Russia-Ukraine energy strikes in the war's fifth year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:50:20 UTC
02:50:20 KST

Washington, DC — Immediately after US President Donald Trump announced on Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy targets — which he claimed were causing a global diesel squeeze — reactions from Moscow and Kiev were swift but measured.
Russia described the proposal as a "good idea", without confirming whether it would halt attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Kiev pledged "de-escalatory steps" provided that "our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia".
Both sides continued to exchange strikes following Trump's announcement, with Russia reportedly attacking petrol stations in Kiev and Ukraine claiming to have struck a Russian oil refinery.
With global oil prices climbing again amid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and growing risks in the Red Sea, analysts note the US president's announcement is driven more by the oil shock from the fighting in the Middle East than by anything else.
"Yes. This is Trump's motivation," Arkady Moshes, director of the EU's Eastern Neighbourhood and Russia programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affair, tells TRT World.
"But this will have little bearing on Moscow which gains financially from the high energy prices," Moshes argues.
Trump insists that the Russia-Ukraine war and not the US war on Iran, is driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November. Opinion polls indicate that the US war on Iran is unpopular. Meanwhile, inflation in the country remains elevated — and the Democratic Party is seeking to capitalise on politically.
Months of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have caused domestic fuel rationing and an export ban, further tightening global markets already strained by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, attacks by the Houthi group near the Bab al Mandab Strait have jeopardised commercial shipping in the southern Red Sea, further exacerbating global oil supply pressures.
However President Trump has claimed that Kiev was "hurting the world" with its strikes on Moscow's diesel facilities.
"The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran," Trump said on Monday as he announced an agreement between Ukraine and Russia to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.
When it comes to the Ukraine-Russia conflict, says Moshes, President Trump's statements "do not correspond to reality."
"But even if this were true, this would be one step down the escalation ladder," he says, but adds the situation would still be nowhere near a lasting truce, noting that since 2014 not a single ceasefire agreement has held even for several days.
Fuel supply crunch
Past US-brokered energy pauses have seen limited success: one in January 2026 lasted only a few days, while another 30-day proposal in 2025 never fully materialised. Reports indicate that Russia remains reluctant to ease winter pressure on Ukraine.
US average retail diesel prices rose above $6 a gallon for the first time last week. Russia has restricted diesel exports after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged its refineries, tightening an already strained global supply that has been squeezed by the war with Iran and recent attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure.
Experts cited by The New York Times say tensions involving Iran drove price rises, with US diesel up 65 per cent, while Russian and Middle Eastern exports fell by roughly 90 and 75 per cent.
An analysis by the Reuters news agency concluded that even a sustained halt to attacks on Russian oil refineries would not promptly reverse the ongoing fuel supply crunch.
According to the International Energy Agency, Ukrainian drones have struck a Russian refinery on average every three days, with repair efforts facing severe logistical obstacles.
Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a Washington-based think tank, told Bloomberg that "the thought here is that a stop in attacking refineries would give Russia time to repair and reduce risk of further outages."
"But if Gulf channels are still blocked it won't help much."
October talks
Trump has been pursuing an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, despite his pledge to halt the conflict on the first day of his term.
Recently, his special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Russian President Vladimir Putin and later Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, but the talks yielded no breakthrough.
The Kremlin described the talks positively, while US officials assessed potential next steps. However, fundamental territorial disputes remain unresolved.
Zelenskyy said US officials presented "decent ideas" for peace, emphasising that diplomatic efforts must deliver tangible results to end the war, now in its fifth year.
Mikhail Alexseev, a political science professor at San Diego State University, tells TRT World that Washington's failure to designate Russia as the "aggressor", expand support for Ukraine, and impose further sanctions on Moscow makes this diplomacy unlikely to succeed.
"Absent those conditions, no diplomacy would succeed, and only the battlefield would decide the war," argues Alexseev, adding, continuing the talks merely for the sake of it may be interpreted by Moscow as a sign of weakness from Washington and its allies.
Moscow insists that Kiev cede claimed territories, particularly in the Donbass, and abandon its ambition to join NATO.
Meanwhile, Kiev rejects formally surrendering territory to Russia and insists that any settlement must safeguard Ukraine's sovereignty and defensive capabilities.
Even as the war continues, both sides have signalled their readiness for US-mediated talks tentatively set for October 2026.
"We are preparing for October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine's Defence Intelligence, last week. "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov added.
However, a diplomatic breakthrough remains unlikely without a significant shift in strategic leverage.
Europe and US role
Then there is Europe.
In peace negotiations, Moscow does not regard Europe as an autonomous player, believing European involvement would only complicate the process.
Trump — for better or worse — appears to share that perspective, says Moshes of the Finnish Institute of International Affair.
"He [Trump] has achieved what was important for him — Europe paying for American weapons delivered to Ukraine. Europeans may not be happy, but they can hardly do anything about it," argues Moshes.
"The imminent risk is that no one will drive the process: Russia will veto European involvement, whereas Washington may withdraw once more."
Europe remains vital to Ukraine, and vice versa, but alignment between the US and Europe on the conflict is critical. Any strategic divergence between the Western allies ultimately benefits Moscow.
From a European vantage point, security guarantees and mutual trust are paramount to prevent any disadvantageous agreement from being imposed upon Ukraine.
"We already saw this kind of understanding most likely reached at the Alaska summit, and subsequent events demonstrated that Ukrainian resilience combined with European support provides Ukraine with significant safeguards," says Alexseev.
Another indirect safeguard lies in the White House's transactional approach to foreign policy, with the procurement of American armaments serving as an influential incentive, he adds.
Moshes emphasises that confidence in Washington as an impartial mediator has waned over time.
He says Kiev remains wary of potential US-Russia economic compromises, while Moscow expressed dissatisfaction following the Anchorage summit when Washington declined to endorse terms reflecting Russian priorities.
"That occurred prior to the US-Iranian conflict, which continues to consume significant military and diplomatic resources of the United States."

NCPCR summons Meta India chief (representative image)
NEW DELHI: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) has again summoned the managing director and head of Meta India in connection with its inquiry into alleged Child Sexual Exploitative and Abuse Material (CSEAM) advertisements on the platform.The Commission has fixed September 16 for the next hearing and is expected to seek the personal appearance of Meta's India MD and head after the company was represented by senior executives at the previous hearing on September 9.NCPCR had first issued a notice to Meta on July 3, 2026, seeking an explanation over CSEAM advertisements. Meta submitted its response a week later.The Commission subsequently decided to institute a formal inquiry to establish the facts of the case. As part of the inquiry, it summoned Meta's India MD and head to appear before the Commission.The Meta head did not appear at the September 9 hearing and the company was represented by senior executives. Meta officials cited urgent reasons for the senior executive's non-appearance, following which NCPCR directed that the company's India head be present at the next hearing.
The Commission's continued follow-up in the CSEAM matter has also led to a change in Meta's reporting practices concerning child sexual abuse cases.

'Flamingo Revolution' Mounts Direct Threat to Albania's Edi Rama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:49:00 UTC
02:49:00 KST

Reported by
What began as a localized environmental campaign against a luxury resort development backed by Jared Kushner has hardened into a 100-day siege of Albania’s political center, mounting the most formidable challenge in years to the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama.
Demonstrators marched along Tirana’s main thoroughfares, rallying near local high schools to mobilize students into the movement, dubbed by organizers as the “Flamingo Revolution” as flamingos inhabit the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland ecosystem where the resort was supposed to be built. Chanting “Rama, resign” and “Your time is up,” protesters confronted security forces in the latest escalation of a campaign that has repeatedly paralyzed parts of the capital.
The unrest originally erupted over government plans to allow Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, to construct high-end tourism facilities on the uninhabited Sazan Island and within the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland along the Adriatic coast. While Rama framed the investment as a key catalyst for tourism and European Union integration, environmentalists fiercely opposed the privatization of pristine reserves.
OCCRP revealed that Rama backed a 2023 law relaxing environmental restrictions on protected areas shortly before the project was advanced. Furthermore, OCCRP reported that the project’s ownership structure was concealed behind a cascade of offshore shell companies stretching to Amsterdam and Doha, and that Albania's anti-corruption agency had unfrozen $127 million in related assets after facing political pressure.
In recent weeks, those revelations have transformed the demonstrations into a wider revolt against systemic corruption and state capture. Tensions reached a boiling point after social media footage showed a police officer punching a handcuffed protester in Tirana. Although authorities suspended the officer and opened a disciplinary probe, police have initiated criminal proceedings against dozens of rally organizers. Roughly 160 citizens have been detained since the unrest began, with recent clashes outside Parliament drawing an deployment of 1,600 riot officers.
“The standard for the police is necessarily higher than the standard for the protester,” said Lutfi Dervishi, a local journalist and analyst, emphasizing that state security must exercise restraint.
Rama, however, has remained defiant. Addressing his party, he cast the unrest as a sign of a maturing society and introduced a governance reform plan, dubbed “Besa,” aimed at improving transparency. Rama declared that Albania is moving into an era where citizens rightly demand higher standards, even as he condemned the demonstrators' tactics and insisted his government would not be coerced into resigning.

Lithuanian Authorities Target Founders of Failed Cryptobank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:49:00 UTC
02:49:00 KST

Reported by
Lithuanian law enforcement authorities have formally named three co-founders of the cryptocurrency project Bankera as suspects in a criminal investigation, accusing them of siphoning off at least 45 million euro ($49 million) in investor funds following one of Europe’s largest digital token sales.
The move by Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service (FCIS) marks a major escalation in a yearlong probe stemming from investigative reporting by local news outlet 15min and OCCRP. Authorities confirmed that formal notices of suspicion were issued to the founders—Mantas Mockevičius, Vytautas Karalevičius and Justas Dobiliauskas—for the unlawful dissipation of high-value assets. All three have been requested to appear for questioning but they have reportedly left the country and apparently settled in Monaco. Their lawyer has not responded to reporter's request for comment.
Bankera’s initial coin offering (ICO) raised more than 100 million euro between 2017 and 2018 from over 100,000 retail investors, as claimed by project developers. Promised a European-licensed commercial bank tailored for the digital currency era, investors instead saw token values drop, regular dividend payouts cease, and the promised banking institution fail to materialize.
According to financial records detailed by investigators, the founders secretly routed over 45 million euro of the ICO proceeds into Pacific Private Bank, an offshore entity in Vanuatu that the trio acquired shortly before the token sale concluded. The Pacific institution subsequently extended millions of euros in personal loans back to the founders. Secured by accounts holding investor capital, these funds were used to acquire luxury real estate across Europe, including prime real estate on the French Riviera and in Lithuania.
In late August, prosecutors moved to freeze key assets tied to the operation. Authorities seized high-end real estate in Vilnius and Kaunas held by Eternity Ventures Foundation—a Liechtenstein-based entity controlled by the founders—as well as personal property owned by Dobiliauskas.
The intensifying legal crackdown has triggered widespread reshuffling across the group’s corporate network. Several executives have stepped down, and the primary domestic entity, UAB Bankera, was recently rebranded as BankingLab Technologies. Despite the executive turnover and corporate restructuring, public records show that Mockevičius, Karalevičius, and Dobiliauskas remain listed as the ultimate beneficial owners across several underlying entities.

It’s official: The U.S. has weapons in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:48:07 UTC
02:48:07 KST

In a first for the U.S. Space Force since its inception six years ago, the military branch has announced the deployment of weapons in space.
Speaking at the Air and Space Forces Association’s annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Monday, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink declared that the U.S. has placed offensive technology into orbit, though he did not disclose any details about the weapons.
“We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” he said.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Although this is the first such acknowledgement from any global power, experts have long suspected space weapons are already a reality. In recent years, Russia has allegedly jammed communications satellites across Europe, and U.S. intelligence agencies have accused Russia of planning to put nuclear weapons in space. China, too, has demonstrated advanced capabilities for tracking and targeting satellites; these capabilities include a reusable space plane, similar to the U.S.’s X-37B, that could rendezvous with and capture adversarial spacecraft. Both Russia and China—as well as the U.S.—have a history of antisatellite missile tests and “cat and mouse” orbital encounters in which spacecraft maneuver to shadow or threaten others.
The U.S. deployment is a matter of necessity, Meink said in a press conference on Monday.
“Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?” he said. “For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space. We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment.”
According to Victoria Samson, chief director for space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation (SWF), the militarization is escalating rapidly in Earth orbit as more nations develop robust space programs. According to an SWF report co-authored by Samson from earlier this year, 13 countries have developed counterspace capabilities of some kind, including co-orbital satellites, which can disable or destroy other spacecraft, and space situational awareness satellites, which can track other objects in orbit.
“A lot of countries are saying, ‘We depend upon very heavily our space capabilities for national security reasons. They’re at risk; it’s a threatening environment. Therefore we need to build offensive capabilities that can threaten others,’” Samson told Scientific American before the Space Force announcement.
Despite their own well-documented military activity in space, both Russia and China responded to Monday’s announcement with statements warning against space militarization, with China opposing an “arms race” in the final frontier and Russia calling for the “complete demilitarization of space.” The current international framework for preventing space warfare is threadbare and filled with loopholes; signatories of the United Nations’ Outer Space Treaty of 1967 are merely obliged not to place weapons of mass destruction in orbit and to build no military bases and conduct no weapons testing on the moon or other planets.
Regardless of who is most culpable in the ongoing push for more and better offensive off-world capabilities, experts fear this announcement will further escalate the situation, raising the chances of space warfare that could prove ruinous for the entire world. John Barentine, an astronomer and formerly a policy expert at the International Dark-Sky Association (now DarkSky International), believes the militarization of space will ultimately prove “unwinnable” and will require a stabilizing doctrine similar to the Cold War’s nuclear threat of mutually assured destruction.
“I wonder if that’s not where we will end up with space militarization generally,” Barentine says, “where everybody rushes to acquire the technology, and we quickly realize that if war breaks out in space, it’s probably ‘game over’ for everybody.”
Other experts aren’t necessarily convinced this announcement will change much inhe ta galactic game of chicken. Among them is Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“With this disclosure, the U.S. is hoping that the knowledge of weapons on orbit may change behaviors. But without knowing exactly what these weapons could do and having a general sense of when the U.S. would decide to use them, it is hard to see China or Russia significantly altering their behaviors,” Swope says. “Deterrence requires convincing an adversary you will use a weapon, not just that you have one.”

Ukraine largely absent from Republican midterm convention stage, but party members weigh in offstage
President Donald Trump takes the stage at the conclusion of Vice President JD Vance's speech at the 2026 Republican National Convention on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026 at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas (Joel Angel Juárez/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)
DALLAS U.S., Texas — As the U.S. Republican Party convened for its first-ever national midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9-10, neither U.S. President Donald Trump nor Vice President JD Vance made Russia's war against Ukraine a significant part of their convention appearances.
The convention was designed primarily to rally Republicans ahead of the November elections. The official program featured more than 100 speakers and focused on domestic issues and the president's agenda.
But Russia's war against Ukraine still mattered to many of the Republican lawmakers, activists, and voters who spoke to the Kyiv Independent in Dallas. Their views ranged from calls to send more U.S. weapons to demands that the U.S. end its support for Ukraine fully.
Louisiana state Senator Michael "Big Mike" Fesi told the Kyiv Independent that foreign policy becomes harder to address during an election cycle.
"That is so difficult about these midterm elections, because we never give it enough time to solve problems," Fesi said. "Midterm elections put a hindrance on completing certain problems, like we have in the world, by having to worry about the elections."
read also
Trump's peace push
Just days before Republicans gathered in Dallas, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, then continued to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on possible peace negotiations. It was their first visit to the Ukrainian capital. Trump spoke to Putin by phone on Sept. 8, the day before the convention.
"It's a complicated situation. I want there to be peace between the Ukrainian and the Russian people. I don't want to see people die. So we have to find a way to have peace," Greg Gandrud, a businessman from California, told the Kyiv Independent in Dallas.
On Sept. 5, Zelensky said that Russia deliberately targeted airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of the planned visit by the U.S. envoys.
A temporary agreement between Russia and Ukraine suggested that both countries would cease attacks on each other's capitals from midnight Sept. 5 to Sept. 8 during the visit by Witkoff and Kushner. The Kyiv City Military Administration issued a brief air raid alert on Sept. 7 as Russian drones flew toward the capital.
Far-right influencer Laura Loomer in an interview with the Kyiv Independent said Russia had violated the pause and pointed to the Russian strike on the airport where the U.S. delegation was expected to arrive.
"It just shows you that the Russians cannot be trusted, and Vladimir Putin is a pathological liar, and a leader of a terrorist state," Loomer said.
Loomer, who visited Ukraine at the end of July, told the Kyiv Independent the trip was a "remarkable, life-changing experience" and said it changed how she viewed the war and the prospects for peace.
"I'm confident that the president will be able to help negotiate an end to the war," she added.
read also
Patriots and the limits of U.S. support
Ukraine has repeatedly identified the U.S.-made Patriot systems as one of its most urgent military needs, as Russia continues to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure with massed drone and missile strikes.
Zelensky said the Sept. 6 talks with Witkoff and Kushner also covered Patriot systems and a broader "winter package" covering air defense and energy infrastructure.
Several Republicans interviewed in Dallas said they supported providing Ukraine with additional air defense capabilities. But they also said the U.S. does not have enough Patriot systems to satisfy every demand, including for its war with Iran.
Conrad Mazeika, president of the Baltic American Freedom League, was blunt when asked whether the U.S. should send more Patriots to Ukraine.
"Just send it over there," he said. "Just send the blueprint and you guys will make it out. Hey, bring it to the Baltic states. We'll build it and send it to Ukraine. Not a problem."
"Technology is transforming the West. Ukraine, you guys are transforming the West with drones and everything that's going on there. Very, very impressive," Mazeika added.
Loomer went further, saying that Ukraine's experience on the battlefield offered lessons for the U.S. and that Washington should consider developing a long-term strategic military partnership with Kyiv beyond the immediate question of weapons transfers.
Shaun, a U.S. combat veteran who asked to be identified by first name only, disagreed.
"We shouldn't be supporting Ukraine. We think he [Trump] is doing excellent, whatever he says. He has information that we don't have and we trust that he knows what he is doing and he has our best interest at heart," he said.
read also
Immigration and 'America First'
Most Republicans who spoke to the Kyiv Independent were unfamiliar with the challenges of the Ukrainian refugee community in the U.S. under the Trump administration.
Ukrainians already in the country face uncertainty over their immigration status and the expiration of temporary protections. The Trump administration has also halted new applications under the Uniting for Ukraine parole program. Some Ukrainians have faced immigration enforcement, including arrests and deportation proceedings.
One Republican participant said Ukrainians displaced by the war should be protected in the U.S. and Europe until conditions allow them to return and rebuild their country. Not everybody agreed.
"We need to be taking care of our American citizens and not so much abroad. It's America first," said April, Shaun's wife, who also declined to give her surname.
Pennsylvania state Senator Scott Martin highlighted the Ukrainian community in Lancaster County as an important part of the local area while stressing that refugees and asylum seekers should follow the legal process.
"I think where you lose most Americans, or where most people are [concerned], is when people … totally ignore the process, who don't go through a true refugee process," Martin said.
Martin's district includes Lancaster County, which a 2017 BBC report called the refugee capital of the U.S., finding it resettled refugees at a rate about 20 times higher per capita than the national average.
Mazeika told the Kyiv Independent, "It's just amazing that what we're learning from Ukraine with … the warmth here, it's starting to seep into the social culture."
As the convention closed, Ukraine remained largely absent from the party's public campaign messaging, but not from the minds of many Republican attendees who spoke to the Kyiv Independent.
"I think [Ukraine] is important for global security, the security of Europe. All people have to have peace. Why should we have people dying? Especially innocent civilian people," Gandrud said.

BRUSSELS — France has a week to reassure fellow EU countries that its push to remove a controversial Russian-Uzbek billionaire from the bloc’s sanctions list won’t start a free-for-all that fractures restrictions on Moscow.
Ambassadors failed to agree on Monday on whether to remove mining and metals tycoon Alisher Usmanov from the blacklist during a closed-door meeting, known as Coreper. Five diplomats and officials involved in the discussions told POLITICO it’s now up to Paris, which blindsided colleagues in backing the delisting of Usmanov, to explain how doing so wouldn’t set a dangerous precedent. The envoys will reconvene Sept. 22.
“If France goes ahead with this, others will come forward with their own oligarchs that should be delisted ... [then] the house of cards starts to fall,” said a senior EU official who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak frankly. “We have a week for them to come up with safe-guardings and negotiate, saying ‘if we do this, what’s the timeline, how do we stop it applying to everyone.’ But I don’t see how that’s possible.”
Advertisement
Foreign ministers are huddling with Paris on the issue Tuesday and Wednesday, said two EU diplomats, who expressed skepticism about the move at a time when Moscow is stepping up strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure and threatening neighboring countries. “Talks are ongoing to find a solution. Russia has given us no reason to allow any delistings,” one said.
Paris initially cast its advocacy for Usmanov, who has been sanctioned by the EU, the U.S., the U.K. and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as a concession to Slovakia — which had long advocated his removal from the list.
However, French officials and diplomats have since been given lines by the Élysée, acknowledging that Paris has “a specific national security issue and wish[es] to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.” That could include the release of French nationals jailed by Azerbaijan, a close ally of Uzbekistan, as reported by the FT.
“We don’t want to send the message that if you are a Russian oligarch wanting to get off the sanction list, [you should] hold some Europeans hostage,” Dutch MEP Thijs Reuten said.
Member states lobbying for vested interests in sanctions talks is nothing new, said another diplomat. “But the fact it’s France, which aspires to be a leader in the EU on the foreign affairs side, means they [are held to] a different standard.”
Ambassadors received no intel on a behind-the-scenes deal during Monday’s meeting. “Maybe there is a legitimate case to be made, but Coreper doesn’t know why the French are doing this,” they said.
Advertisement
Paris, however, insists it has been transparent with other EU countries about its plans. “Ambassadors were told that there are national security reasons. Coreper is not the right place to discuss those in detail,” said a senior French diplomat who was granted anonymity to speak frankly about the sensitive discussions. “Member states were told a week ago that if they needed more precision, they could get it through the appropriate channels.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday evening, he wrote on X, but shed no light on the situation, only saying that they "discussed the situation in the diplomatic process in detail."
Brussels imposed financial and travel restrictions on Usmanov in 2022 as part of sanctions on those “undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine,” citing his alleged material support for Russia’s war. Usmanov rejects those charges along with his depiction as an oligarch, and has campaigned to be removed from the list.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

According to the Ukrainian military, the Nebo-M was deployed near the Millerovo airfield, a facility regularly used by Russian forces to launch Shahed-type attack drones against Ukraine.

Russia’s Starlink Rival “Rassvet” Fails to Reach Target Orbit 6 Months After Launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:43:24 UTC
02:43:24 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Starlink Rival “Rassvet” Fails to Reach Target Orbit 6 Months After Launch
Russia’s Rassvet-3 satellite constellation, intended to form the basis of a domestic alternative to Starlink, has yet to reach its planned operational orbit six months after the first group of satellites was launched.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on September 15, none of the satellites from the initial Rassvet-3 deployment has reached the planned altitude of 800 kilometers, preventing the constellation from beginning full-scale operations as originally envisioned.
The system is being developed by Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440. The first group of Rassvet-3 satellites was launched on March 23, followed by a second deployment on July 19.
Most satellites from the first launch have remained at an altitude of about 507 kilometers for roughly three months.
Defense Express reported that 13 of the original 15 satellites have reached that altitude and appear to have established positions relative to one another. Two others remain at lower altitudes, while another satellite associated with the deployment has already left orbit.
The current configuration may explain why the first group has not yet climbed toward its planned 800-kilometer orbit. Satellites deployed from the same launch vehicle must first separate and establish their positions along the orbital plane. Carrying out those maneuvers at lower altitudes can reduce the amount of propellant required.
Orbital tracking cited by Defense Express indicates that the 13 satellites have spread across roughly half of their orbital path, although a gap remains in the formation. The two satellites operating below 500 kilometers may still be maneuvering into positions intended to close that gap.
Once the formation is established, the satellites could begin raising their orbits together toward 800 kilometers. However, Defense Express noted that available tracking data does not indicate that such a maneuver is imminent.
The second Rassvet-3 group, launched on July 19, is meanwhile continuing to increase its altitude. Those satellites may also pause at around 500 kilometers while they establish their positions before attempting to move higher.
The constellation has faced additional setbacks. Two satellites from the second deployment are currently at risk of reentering Earth’s atmosphere, according to earlier Defense Express reporting, while one satellite from the first group has already deorbited.
Future launches could also face complications following a Ukrainian strike on the Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, a major Russian facility involved in producing Soyuz launch vehicles.
Ukraine previously struck the Progress facility with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles. The plant produces Soyuz-2.1b rockets, the launch vehicle previously used to place Rassvet satellites into orbit.
Bureau 1440 is developing Rassvet as a low-Earth-orbit communications network designed to provide broadband connectivity through a constellation of satellites, placing it in the same general market as SpaceX’s Starlink. The latest orbital data, however, indicates that the first operational Rassvet-3 group has not yet reached its intended deployment altitude.

Russia says US acknowledgement of orbital arms ignores space conflict consequences

Russia says US acknowledgement of orbital arms ignores space conflict consequences
Sept 15 - Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday the U.S. acknowledgement that Washington had deployed orbital weapons ignored the possible consequences of a conflict and threatened long-term stability in space-based activity.
"In pursuit of its narrow self-interests, Washington is ready to completely ignore the catastrophic consequences for humanity of any armed conflict in orbit," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a commentary on the ministry website.
Zakharova said the presence of U.S. weapons in space risks the prospects for space exploration.
"Colossal risks are created for numerous socio-economic processes on Earth and people's well-being directly depends on them," she said.
U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told a conference near Washington, D.C., on Monday that the United States possessed "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action."
The statement was the strongest admission by a U.S. official of American weapons in space amid rising space tensions with Russia and China.
Zakharova described the acknowledgement as part of attempts to "distract world attention from the U.S.' own aggressive strivings in terms of space," including "absurd" accusations that Moscow was developing anti-satellite weapons.
"The moratorium on testing ... anti-satellite missiles promoted by the so-called 'collective West' is laden with hypocrisy, as in reality it does not affect the use of weapons that the U.S. already has and does not apply to other types of anti-satellite systems that Washington is seeking to develop," she said.
Zakharova said resolutions co-authored by Russia on barring deployment of space-based weapons and transparency in using space would be presented to the U.N. General Assembly next month. REUTERS

US Republican lawmaker seeks Hegseth’s impeachment over Iran
WASHINGTON - Republican US Representative Thomas Massie filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Sept 15, accusing him of abusing his office by executing an order for hostilities against Iran without approval by Congress.
The impeachment resolution is unlikely to pass, but the manoeuvre by the Kentucky Republican could force a vote in the chamber that could be difficult for some of his fellow Republicans as they prepare to leave Washington before November's midterm elections.
"The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first," Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in an emailed statement.
Massie filed his articles of impeachment against Hegseth as privileged, meaning the House must take them up within two legislative days.
Massie, an outspoken critic of the war on Iran and aid to Israel, is not up for reelection. He lost his primary in May to a candidate backed by Republican President Donald Trump after Massie angered the president by leading a push to release Justice Department files tied to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Massie was defeated by Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL backed by Trump and bolstered by heavy spending by pro-Israel groups.
Polls show the war that began with Feb 28 attacks on Iran by US and Israeli forces is unpopular with voters. Members of Congress, mostly Democrats, have voted repeatedly in favour of resolutions calling on Trump to end the conflict unless he obtains congressional support, but they have not led to a cessation of hostilities.
Opinion polls show that Trump's Republicans face an uphill struggle to keep their control of the House and Senate when voters go to the polls on Nov 3.
Reuters/Ipsos poll results released on Sept 14 showed Democrats lead Republicans 44 per cent to 37 per cent in congressional vote preference.
Trump’s popularity has declined since he launched the war, which has disrupted oil shipments and pushed fuel prices near record highs, hitting US household finances. REUTERS

More than 100,000 displaced as they flee violence in Yemen: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:39:58 UTC
02:39:58 KST

More than 100,000 displaced as they flee violence in Yemen: UN
Thousands making risky maritime journey to Djibouti as conflict between Yemen gov’t and Houthis intensifies.
More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee the conflict in Yemen between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, according to the United Nations.
The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) said in a statement issued on Tuesday that the rapidly escalating hostilities along Yemen’s western coast have displaced more than 100,000 people inside the country, and forced thousands more to risk the dangerous journey across the Bab al-Mandeb strait to reach Djibouti in search of safety.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands flee to Djibouti amid renewed Yemen fighting
- list 2 of 3Renewed fighting worsens Yemen’s humanitarian crisis
- list 3 of 3Inside the Houthis’ expanding war economy in Yemen
The UNHCR statement warned that the violence threatens to trigger a humanitarian crisis, as more people are displaced, pressuring communities with limited resources.
The agency said it requires an estimated $14m in new funding to meet the immediate needs of displaced families inside Yemen, with additional support needed for those arriving in Djibouti.
“Many families fled at short notice with few belongings. Shelter, food, clean water, health care and protection services are among the most urgent needs, as receiving communities and displacement sites become overstretched,” the statement reads.
More than 65,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers inside Yemen, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia, are also facing risks due to the fighting.
The displacement began when the Iran-aligned Houthis began a rapid advance, seizing control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast to cement their grip on Bab al-Mandeb.
The strategic waterway is a critical maritime corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has become an alternative shipping route as the United States’ war against Iran choked the Strait of Hormuz.
Aisha Muhammad, a displaced woman, had to leave her five children in their village near the port city of Mocha when it was overrun by the Houthis last week.
“They are being blocked and shot at, so they are trapped inside their homes. They are cooking only rice, no bread, nothing else. My daughters called me saying they want to join us, but it has become too difficult,” said Muhammad.
Hussein Haydara, a displaced man from Hodeidah, said he was forced to escape suddenly with his family.
“You could barely take your children and the fewest essentials with you,” he said. “We were terrified of the shelling and sniper fire, and you just flee as quickly as you can out of fear for your children and your family.”
UNHCR reports that more than 2,400 people made the journey across the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the past four days. Most arrivals are women, children and older people, it said.
“People are arriving after a difficult sea journey, many exhausted, distressed and carrying what little they could take with them,” Sandrine Desamours, UNHCR’s representative in Djibouti, said.

Over 500 locomotives destroyed or damaged by Russian attacks, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:38:47 UTC
02:38:47 KST

More than 500 locomotives have been either "completely destroyed" or damaged by Russian attacks throughout the full-scale war, more than half of which occurred since the start of this year, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 15.
The statement comes as Russia intensifies its drone attacks on trains running across the country, with one of the most recent strikes hitting the locomotive of the Kyiv-Warsaw train about two kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
Yet another Russian attack overnight on Sept. 15 hit unspecified railway infrastructure in western Volyn Oblast, according to Sybiha. The State Emergency Service reported that a diesel locomotive caught fire, but there were no casualties.
"Russia continues its systematic attacks to disrupt logistics across Ukraine," Sybiha said in his post on X.
Sybiha stressed that the country urgently needs replacements and called on Western allies to help find and finance the procurement of locomotives compatible with the 1520 mm gauge.
"Supporting Ukraine's railway resilience will help avert a humanitarian crisis and strengthen our resilience under the challenging conditions of full-scale war," Sybiha added.
The rising number of attacks prompted Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) to introduce an evacuation protocol in March in the event of a heightened aerial threat, which has helped minimize casualties. However, the increased number of evacuations has caused significant train delays.
Russian drone attacks have usually targeted locomotives and the railway infrastructure in front-line regions. But two Russian attacks in recent days on a train and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine have raised concerns about the growing threat to rail routes long considered relatively safe.

‘I feel more free’ reporting in Russia – Rick Sanchez (VIDEO)
RT’s Rick Sanchez has said that he feels more free to control his own narrative reporting from Russia compared to his time working in Western mainstream media.
Sanchez told aspiring journalists of his decades of professional experience in a wide-ranging lecture at the World Youth Festival (WYF) in Yekaterinburg, Russia on Tuesday. The talk touched on the freedom of the press, the psychology of a good journalist, and the art of conducting a good interview.
“The freedoms that I lacked working at CNN, the freedoms that I lacked working in NBC, working in Western media, I now find working in Russia. I feel more free. I feel like I have more control of my own narrative,” he said.
Messaging is all about empowerment, and that means you can’t be afraid to ask the question because the question is the power.
Sanchez stressed that journalism and the right to ask questions and gather ideas from different people serve as “a democratizing force in the world.”
“You have to empower yourself. You cannot be afraid,” he said, adding that aspiring journalists should be prepared to interview international leaders such as Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, or Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The lecture by the veteran news anchor was organized as part of RT’s educational outreach project, the RT Academy.
The week-long WYF opened in Yekaterinburg last Friday, bringing together thousands of participants from 191 countries. The festival is scheduled to run until September 17, hosting assorted international lectures, competitions, exhibitions, panel discussions, and other events.

Two U.S. government employees were injured in a shootout in southern Africa
Kyiv • UNN
Two U.S. government employees were accidentally injured during an Eswatini operation against smuggling. The army is investigating the incident.
The government of Eswatini — a monarchy in southern Africa — reported that last week, two U.S. government employees sustained accidental gunshot wounds during an operation by the country's armed forces to combat smuggling, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Acting government spokesperson Tabile Mdluli said late Monday evening that the incident occurred on Friday in a rural area near the village of Maphiveni, located approximately a two-hour drive from the country's capital, Mbabane.
It was initially unclear what exactly the American specialists were doing in the area, but Mdluli said the army had launched an investigation into the circumstances of what happened.
She added that Eswatini's authorities were maintaining contact with the U.S. government as the investigation progressed and remained committed to strengthening long-standing relations with Washington.
The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In addition
The publication notes that Eswatini maintained close ties with the United States during Donald Trump's presidency; in particular, the kingdom accepted more than 30 people deported from the United States (citizens of third countries).
Overall, the country agreed to accept 160 people under a deal worth $5.1 million. Lawyers are challenging the agreement, pointing out that the deportees are being held in custody despite having already served their sentences for crimes committed in the United States.

US task force aiding Saudis with intel, planning support: US official
WASHINGTON - A US military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces, a US official said on Sept 15, as the kingdom faces attacks from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi fighters.
US Central Command “has a task force in place for enhancing intelligence sharing and planning support with Saudi forces,” the official said on condition of anonymity, adding that the military command “maintains a strong security alliance with our Saudi partners in confronting regional challenges.”
The Houthis have renewed fighting against Saudi-backed government forces since Yemen’s civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
The Houthis seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait last week, which has become increasingly vital as the wider US-Iran war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz, another key Middle East shipping route.
The Houthis have also attacked oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world’s leading crude exporter, and the group says the kingdom has hit back with dozens of air strikes in Yemen.
The sudden revival of Yemen’s war, dormant since 2022, has left Riyadh rushing to respond. Last week, US media reported that the kingdom’s crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but was turned down.
On Sept 12, Trump said that the Houthis have asked Washington not to intervene.
The Yemen war dates back to the Houthi seizure of the capital Sanaa in 2014, with Saudi Arabia leading a coalition that intervened the following year on the government’s side.
Iran has long supported the Houthis, a member of its anti-Israel “axis of resistance,” including with weapons and technology, but has denied any role in the current war. AFP

Iranian journalists discuss ties between cinema, city in Tehran gathering
TEHRAN- A gathering marking Iran’s Cinema Day was held at the City Journalists' House in Tehran on Monday evening, bringing together journalists to share their experiences of covering cinema and discuss the relationship between film, the city and society.
