China finally acknowledges its massive missile silo fields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:07:17 UTC
02:07:17 KST

- A CCTV documentary marking the PLA's 99th anniversary gave China's first semi-official acknowledgment of its western missile silo fields, first discovered by satellite imagery in 2021.
- Analyst Robert Rust wrote that the documentary frames the rushed construction as driven by concerns over U.S. missile defense, not a shift from China's no-first-use policy.
Chinese state television has aired the first semi-official acknowledgment of the country’s massive intercontinental ballistic missile silo fields in a documentary marking the 99th anniversary of the People’s Liberation Army.
The program, produced by China’s national broadcaster CCTV, features an army engineer describing years of work building what he calls “houses for missiles” in the country’s western deserts.
The engineer, identified as First Master Sergeant Cui Daohu of an unspecified People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force brigade, says the project came under intense pressure from senior leadership in Beijing to finish on schedule. His account, first reported by the South China Morning Post, marks the first time a state-linked source in China has openly discussed the silo project since satellite images exposed it in 2021.
Those images, analyzed by open-source researchers, showed roughly 320 silos under construction across three fields in western China, plus a related training site at Jilantai. The discovery prompted years of speculation among Western governments and analysts about whether China was abandoning its long-standing “no first use” nuclear policy in favor of a more aggressive posture. Chinese officials have consistently avoided commenting on the silos directly, even as the government reissued a 2025 white paper insisting its arsenal remains sized at “the minimum level necessary for national security.”
The documentary’s framing suggests a different explanation for the rapid construction than a doctrinal shift. Cui describes the urgency as driven by a need to secure China’s ability to strike back after absorbing a nuclear attack, its so-called second-strike capability, rather than by any intent to use nuclear weapons more aggressively. Robert Rust, a China analyst with the Global Security Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, wrote in an analysis published by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists that the framing points to concern in Beijing over American missile defense programs, including the Trump administration’s Golden Dome initiative, as a driver of China’s nuclear expansion.
Cui says he was repeatedly pressed on the same question by colleagues at China’s National People’s Congress, where he has served as a military delegate since 2023.
“Will the project be finished on time?”
He describes developing a faster construction method to meet the deadline, including a change to how a core structural component is installed, and says the pressure came from an understanding that the silos needed to “ensure the country can play its strategic trump card,” a phrase commonly used in China to refer to its strategic nuclear missiles.
Rust noted that Cui had appeared in Chinese military media before, in a 2025 series honoring soldiers selected by the Central Military Commission, but that earlier appearance focused on his engineering inventions and made no mention of the silos or their role in national deterrence. The new documentary’s willingness to connect his work explicitly to strategic missiles, he wrote, suggests the silo project itself may now be complete.
The acknowledgment comes as outside researchers continue to debate how large China’s nuclear arsenal could eventually grow. The U.S. Department of War and some independent researchers have projected China could field 1,000 or more warheads by 2030, partly by diverting plutonium from civilian fast-breeder reactors. But those reactors have faced delays, and a 2025 Pentagon report on Chinese military power assessed that the first such unit likely still was not operating. Separate estimates cited by Rust suggest China may already possess enough plutonium to reach 800 to 1,000 warheads without relying on the delayed reactors, raising questions about how the reactor-based growth projections align with the documentary’s portrayal of a leadership in a hurry.
China has continued to display its newer missile systems publicly, including the DF-61 and DF-31BJ intercontinental ballistic missiles shown at a Victory Day parade in Beijing last year. Rust wrote that the shift from total silence to this kind of semi-official signaling could open space for more direct dialogue between Washington and Beijing on reducing nuclear risk, though no such talks have been announced.

Ukrainian monitoring project DeepState updated its map of the fighting in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk Region, marking the territory around the village of Serednie in Kramatorsk District as having been liberated by Ukrainian forces. According to analysts, Ukrainian troops also pushed Russian units back from positions near Shandryholove. Both villages are located on the approaches to the city of Lyman, which has been the site of static, positional fighting for several months.
On the afternoon of Sept. 15, the Ukrainian offensive in this sector was publicly confirmed for the first time. In a video address posted to Telegram, Andriy Biletsky, the commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, announced that operation was codenamed Vivaldi, adding that while it was operating under conditions of information silence, the corps’ units eliminated pockets of Russian infiltration across 75 square kilometers and deoccupied a further 10 square kilometers in the areas of Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, and Korovii Yar. In addition to clearing the territory, Biletsky noted that Ukrainian drone units had also cut the enemy’s logistics, forcing Russian troops to relocate their fuel and lubricant depots and dismantle a pipeline, shifting their supply lines into Russia’s Voronezh Region. Biletsky estimated the personnel losses of Russia’s 20th and 25th armies at roughly 1,500 soldiers, while equipment losses totaled more than 12,000 drones and hundreds of armored vehicles, along with artillery pieces and other vehicles.
At the same time, Biletsky cautioned against jumping to conclusions about the operation’s ultimate goal, saying rumors about Ukrainian troops aiming to reach the Chornyi Zherebets River were premature. “Our operation is called ‘Vivaldi.’ And Vivaldi, as everyone knows, has four seasons. This is only the first of them,” Biletsky said, promising further official updates on the corps’ progress.
The scale of the operation had previously been reported by independent OSINT analysts who had been following the situation near Lyman for several months. In particular, French analyst Clément Molin noted that Ukrainian units had launched a counteroffensive north of the city back in late May, but information about it was deliberately withheld until now. By Molin’s estimate, Ukrainian forces used that time to cut off the Russian salient north of Lyman and liberate more than 200 square kilometers of land, pushing the enemy back across the Zherebets River.
Molin called the operation one of Ukraine’s most significant victories of 2026, noting that its success could complicate further Russian advances on Lyman, Izium, and Sloviansk, thereby delaying the occupying forces’ progress in northern Donbas. Similar assessments came from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW). As its experts wrote, Russian military bloggers are already acknowledging Ukrainian counterattacks in the Lyman sector and are increasingly criticizing the Russian command for masking territorial losses with fabricated reports of success.

Forest fires in Indonesia threaten the main orangutan research center in Borneo
Kyiv • UNN
The fire has approached the station in Borneo, where more than 2,500 orangutans are being studied. Scientists warn: the flames could reach the camp in 20 days.
Forest fires in Indonesia are engulfing an important research area where Bornean orangutans are studied and are now threatening a renowned scientific camp — the site of one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild great apes, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Over the past few days, the fire has come within 200 meters of the “Rangkong” station — an auxiliary facility of the “Cabang Panti” research station, located approximately four miles to the north within Gunung Palung National Park.
Hundreds of Bornean orangutans (*Pongo pygmaeus*) — one of three orangutan species — live in the immediate vicinity of these stations; overall, the park, significant parts of which are currently engulfed in flames, is estimated to be home to more than 2,500 individuals. All three orangutan species are critically endangered.
“The orangutans are fleeing these forests. It’s just horrific,” said Professor Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has led scientific research on orangutans at the “Cabang Panti” station for 32 years.
In most cases, the fires are caused by deliberate burning to clear land — a practice carried out on the island every year. However, an extremely powerful El Niño event (a rise in sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific that disrupts global weather patterns) has caused abnormal heat and drought across the country, allowing the fire to easily spread out of control. In West Kalimantan province, there are areas that have received almost no rain for many months.
Scientists at the “Cabang Panti” station have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and the details of their lives; they have observed individual animals from birth until they themselves became grandmothers. Research conducted in this area helped determine the orangutans’ reproductive cycle: it was found that these apes give birth only once every eight years — the longest cycle of any mammal. “The uniqueness of this database lies in its long-term nature and extraordinary level of detail,” Knott emphasized.
However, the fires threaten to interrupt these continuous observations. According to scientists, if no action is taken or wide firebreaks are not created, the fire will reach the “Cabang Panti” station within 20 days at its current rate of spread. “[Cabang Panti] protects one of the few areas of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo that have remained truly ecologically intact,” said Professor Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who led the orangutan research project in the area from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuous field data, we will not be able to understand how tropical ecosystems adapt to or suffer from global climate change.”
In a desperate attempt to save the “Rangkong” research station, a team of more than 40 people — mostly field assistants, staff members, and local residents — is fighting around the clock against the steadily advancing fire. Recently, they established a firebreak and an improvised irrigation system, using a perforated hose around the station to saturate the surrounding peat with moisture.
When fire reaches peatland, it can smolder underground for months — even after the surface flames have been extinguished. Maintaining peat moisture is therefore a crucial protective measure.
“The scale of the problem exceeds the capabilities of any local organization,” said Caitlin O’Connell, deputy director of the Gunung Palung Orangutan Conservation Program. — “We need large-scale aerial water drops and professional firefighters.”
Even if the research station can be saved, it may prove futile if the orangutans lose their home.
"Orangutans need the forest," Nott said. "If all we have left is a building, what will we study when the orangutans themselves and their food are gone? They will not be able to survive without this forest."
Because orangutans lead solitary lives, they need large territories and live at low population densities. "You cannot simply herd them all together into a patch of remaining forest," Nott remarked.
Those directly managing the firefighting efforts on the ground have already seen how this is affecting the animals. "We spotted five orangutans from the population we have been studying for a long time; they were fleeing the fire, and some were just a few meters from the flames," said Wahyu Susanto, the scientific director of Yayasan Palung, an Indonesian non-governmental organization dedicated to protecting Bornean orangutans. "These are individuals we have observed and studied for years."
Indonesian meteorologists are forecasting an intense fire season lasting until October, as climate forecasts point to a strengthening El Niño phenomenon. "Fire hotspots are everywhere," O'Connell said. "It would not be an exaggeration to say that what we thought could not burn may in fact disappear completely if this drought continues for months."

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google in talks to create a standards body as AI fears rise
The world’s biggest AI companies are working to create a new industry standards body, OpenAI said on Tuesday, as rising concerns over the risks of artificial intelligence fuel pressure for greater oversight and safer development of the technology.
The world's biggest AI companies are working on creating a standards body, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Tuesday, as fears rise about the dangers of AI and pressure is on to create a safer version of the technology.

In July, Hassibis called for the United States to create an organization that would test the most powerful AI systems before they are released to the public.
"Funding would need to be substantial and likely mostly come from industry, in order to attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing," Hassabis wrote.
There is no consensus on how to move forward, though.

"AI needs guardrails. That is not the dispute and never has been. The dispute is over who writes them, who gets to participate and whose interests the rules are protecting," Cohere co-founder and CEO Aiden Gomez wrote in a blog post on Sunday.
Concerns about AI safety have escalated in recent weeks, including warnings from two workers who resigned from major AI developers amid concerns about the industry's risks.

On Monday, former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed the concerns raised by Coxon and others.
"I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome," Chughtai wrote on social media.

Roundup: Poland strengthens eastern defenses after Russian strikes near border
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
01:02:31 CST
02:02:31 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Poland is stepping up security along its eastern border following recent Russian attacks on western Ukraine, some of which occurred just a few kilometers from the Polish border.
"We are strengthening the protection of our border crossings with Ukraine," Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in a post on X on Tuesday.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said infrastructure used by Poland's Border Guard was being reinforced, while military engineers were carrying out work to strengthen posts and other facilities near the Polish-Ukrainian border.
Observation and guard posts are being built near the border in Dorohusk, Medyka and Korczowa, said Polish Armed Forces General Command in a separate post on X on Tuesday.
Military engineers are also constructing border fortifications using collapsible wire-mesh containers that can be filled with sand or gravel and used as blast barriers or retaining structures, according to the General Command.
Russian forces continued striking railway infrastructure in western Ukraine and logistics centers storing supplies for the Ukrainian forces, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday.
According to Ukrainian media reports, a petrol station in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn region near the Polish border was struck on Sunday. On the same day, a Russian attack struck the locomotive of a passenger train in the Volyn region, about 2 km from the Polish border, Ukrainian state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday Ukrainian forces have struck a naval base in Russia's southern Krasnodar Territory, hitting a terminal used to load oil, military port facilities, and warships carrying Kalibr missiles in the city of Novorossiysk.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland would strengthen coordination among customs officers, police, the Border Guard and the military at border crossings, with the aim of keeping traffic flowing and preventing concentrations of vehicles near the frontier.
Tusk also said he would consult other NATO members on preparations for a potential joint response.
The measures come as Poland continues to strengthen its military capabilities and defenses along NATO's eastern flank.
Airspace security has been tightened. A temporary restricted area over eastern Poland came into effect on Sept. 10, limiting air traffic up to an altitude of approximately 3 km. The restriction will remain in place until Dec. 9.
Poland is also expanding its "East Shield" defense program along its eastern frontier and developing an anti-drone defense system for the area at an estimated cost of around 2 billion euros (2.3 billion U.S. dollars). ■

Canada launches new tax incentives to boost competitiveness
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
01:02:07 CST
02:02:07 KST

TORONTO, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday announced a package of tax incentives at the first-ever Canada Investment Summit here, aiming to sharpen the country's competitive edge among Group of Seven (G7) nations and attract more business investment.
Carney highlighted Canada's strong fiscal foundation, noting that the country maintains the lowest net debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio in the G7.
Leveraging free trade agreements covering 1.5 billion consumers globally, Canada has become one of the world's most connected economies with the fiscal capacity to catalyze 1 trillion Canadian dollars (about 719 billion U.S. dollars) in new investment, he said.
Under the new "Productivity Mega Deduction" tax incentive, the proportion of eligible capital assets will expand significantly from roughly 15 percent to over 65 percent. Covered assets include optical fiber cables, mining properties, oil and gas pipelines, software, research and development, computer equipment, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail tracks, bridges, and roads.
The federal government is also making immediate expensing permanent, allowing businesses to recover investment costs faster and reduce post-tax investment burdens.
With these measures, Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new business investment will fall from about 13 percent to 6.4 percent, less than half of that of the United States and the lowest among major economies worldwide, Carney said.
To further optimize key infrastructure, Carney also announced plans to open Canada's four largest airports to private investment through long-term concessions, seeking to enhance the efficiency and capacity of the national transportation network. ■

AfDB urges key reforms to build resilient African food systems
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
01:02:03 CST
02:02:03 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Targeted policy and fiscal reforms are essential to protect Africa's food systems from growing global disruptions, a senior African Development Bank (AfDB) official said at a virtual forum on Tuesday.
Martin Fregene, officer in charge of the vice presidency for Agriculture, Human and Social Development at the AfDB, said that external shocks, including pandemics, conflicts and geopolitical tensions, have severely impacted the continent's food supply.
To build long-term resilience, Fregene urged African nations to prioritize domestic financing, rapid technology adoption, community-led climate initiatives and stronger market linkages.
"Our food systems are always on the receiving end of global shocks, including COVID-19 and conflicts that have disrupted supplies of fertilizer and other farm inputs," Fregene said.
Fregene noted that armed conflicts, climate shocks, market volatility and protectionist trade policies have disrupted global supply chains, pushing local African communities toward hunger, malnutrition and poverty.
To build resilient agri-food systems, he advocated for a decisive policy shift supported by domestic capital and political will.
Fregene also urged investment in modern post-harvest technologies, expanded extension services and stronger national and regional supply chains to connect local producers with markets better.
"We should also incentivize local fertilizer manufacturers to reduce dependence on imports. Strengthening institutions and expanding access to finance for smallholder farmers will also reduce the negative impact of external shocks on food systems," Fregene said.
He urged governments and industry partners to invest in continental-scale anticipatory action and high-quality data to better prepare for climate shocks threatening food production.
The webinar brought together senior policymakers, scholars, regional leaders, civil society advocates and representatives of donor agencies to chart new strategies for strengthening Africa's food system resilience against global disruptions.
Debisi Araba, managing director of AKADEMIYA2063, said the continent's quest for food and nutritional security is being jeopardized by high fuel and fertilizer costs and declining household incomes.
Araba called for the speedy implementation of continental treaties that seek to revitalize Africa's farming systems through policy harmonization, sustained funding and capacity building for smallholder farmers. ■

Kim Kardashian awarded symbolic €1 damages over Paris jewel heist
PARIS - US reality TV star Kim Kardashian was awarded a symbolic €1 (S$1.50) in damages on Sept 15 from the thieves who tied her up at gunpoint in a Paris hotel in 2016 and stole her jewels, including her US$4 million (S$5 million) engagement ring, a lawyer said.
Kardashian, who had testified that she thought she was going to die during the ordeal, had sought the symbolic amount from some of those convicted in May 2025 over the heist in a civil damages case, according to a lawyer for the hotel’s receptionist - another plaintiff.
The robbers, often referred to in France as the “Grandpa Robbers” because of their advanced ages, wore ski masks and were disguised as police officers. The robbery was, at the time it occurred, France’s largest in 20 years. Most of the jewels were never recovered, including the engagement ring given to her by then-husband, rapper Kanye West (now known as Ye).
The hotel receptionist had sought €500,000 in damages, and was awarded about €110,000, his lawyer said.
Kardashian’s Paris lawyers did not respond to a request for comment.
Kardashian in court in 2025 told Aomar Ait Khedache, the mastermind of the robbery and then aged 69, that she forgave him, but that doing so did not take away the trauma of the events. He was jailed for three years, and seven others were convicted for crimes linked to the heist. REUTERS

Army officers ‘let down’ soldier over sexual assault claim before she killed herself, court martial told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:01:56 UTC
02:01:56 KST

Two army officers “let down” a teenage soldier who went on to kill herself when they did not deal properly with a sexual assault allegation she made against a superior, a court martial has heard.
Jaysley Beck, 19, told Col Samantha Shepherd that she had been touched on the leg by a warrant officer during a social event at an adventure training exercise, the court was told.
But Shepherd allegedly misrepresented what Beck had told her when she reported the claim, falsely saying there had not been physical contact.
The second officer, Maj James Hook, failed to take the incident seriously and was sceptical of what Beck had reported, believing she wanted to leave the training package, the court heard.
Shepherd and Hook deny “conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline”. Shepherd is accused of misreporting what she had been told by Beck while Hook allegedly did not treat information passed to him in a manner “consistent with its seriousness”.
At the start of the trial, the assistant judge advocate general Edward Legard said he expected the board hearing the case – an RAF air commodore, navy captain and army colonel – almost certainly knew of the Beck case.
He told them she had taken her own life and there had been significant press interest but they should put anything they had heard about it to one side.
Legard also instructed them not to be influenced by anyone’s views – including their chain of command – on the subject of unacceptable sexual behaviour in the armed forces.
Cdr Paul Patterson, for the crown, said Beck was taking part in the training package in Hampshire in July 2021. Hook was running the exercise while Shepherd was the regimental colonel.
Following a social function, Beck was found distressed and sleeping in her car early in the morning by a colleague, L/Cpl Drew Tudor. She told him there had been an incident the night before with a warrant officer, Michael Webber, who was senior in rank to her.
Hook was alerted and Beck expressed concern over what would happen if she made a complaint. He gave her until noon to decide what she wanted to do.
The court was told he was sceptical as Beck was not enjoying the adventure package and he thought she may be wanting to leave.
Patterson said rather than empowering her, Hook could be seen as “leaning on her”. He said an issue for the board to consider was if Hook knew he was dealing with a potential sexual assault.
Shepherd was told of the incident later. She went for a walk with Beck, who told her Webber had touched her leg and tried to kiss her, the court heard.
Patterson said when she went to speak to an adjutant, whose role includes advising on discipline, about the incident, Shepherd was asked if there had been physical contact and allegedly replied that there had not been.
The prosecutor said that the colonel “edited the information” when she “should have told the truth”. He told the court it was the crown’s case that Shepherd deliberately tried to suppress the detail about touching, knowing that if she did report this it would go to service police.
Patterson said Beck told each of the officers enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted and she had been let down by them.
Tudor became emotional as he gave his evidence. He said when he found Beck in her car she was distressed and told him that Webber had “tried something on with her”. He said he could not now remember Beck’s exact words but added: “I was concerned enough to want to report it.”
The adjutant, Maj Mae King, told the court Shepherd had told her Webber had attempted to kiss Beck but Beck had leant away. She said: “My understanding was no physical contact had been made.”
King said incidents such as this were “relatively normal” and it was not the most serious she had dealt with.
King told the court that Webber’s wife worked in the same building as her and there was concern about her welfare. She said she did not know if the wife knew about what had allegedly happened during the adventure package. “It wasn’t our business to tell her,” King said.
Beck’s mother, Leighann McCready, from Cumbria, sat in the front row of the public gallery, holding her daughter’s army cap.
The trial at Catterick in North Yorkshire continues.

Kroller-Muller Museum displays all its Van Gogh paintings for 1st time since 1984
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
01:01:47 CST
02:01:47 KST

A visitor views a piece of work by Van Gogh at the exhibition "Van Gogh, All Our Paintings" at the Kroller-Muller Museum in Ede, the Netherlands, on Sept. 15, 2026. The exhibition takes place here from Sept. 15, 2026 to Jan. 3, 2027. (Xinhua/Shao Haijun)
EDE, the Netherlands, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Dutch Kroller-Muller Museum in the Netherlands has this week displayed all paintings in its collection by Vincent Van Gogh for the first time since 1984.
The museum is home to 88 paintings by the 19th-century Dutch artist. It is one of the world's largest collections of his work.
"The exhibition presents all the paintings in relation to the three divine virtues: faith, hope and love," the museum said.
The exhibition, called "Van Gogh, All Our Paintings," opened on Tuesday. It features some of the artist's best-known works, including The Potato Eaters, The Sower, Cafe Terrace at Night, Sorrowing Old Man (At Eternity's Gate), L'Arlesienne and The Old Tower at Nuenen.
"Even before he became an artist, he wanted to help and comfort people through his work. That remained important to him throughout his artistic career," said the museum's curator Renske Cohen Tervaert.
Helene Kroller-Muller, the museum's founder, began collecting Van Gogh's works in 1908. Between then and 1930, she and her husband, Anton Kroller, acquired 88 paintings and more than 170 works on paper by Van Gogh.
Born in 1853, Van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose life and artistic career have had a lasting influence on art around the world. He died in 1890 at the age of 37. ■

CHANGSHA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing said on Tuesday that China will further enhance technological innovation of the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) so that it can better serve global users.
Zhang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks in a speech delivered at the 5th International Summit on BDS Applications held in Zhuzhou in central China's Hunan Province.
He said China is willing to work with all parties to uphold the principles of openness and integration, coordination and cooperation, as well as mutual complementarity for shared benefits.
He said China will strengthen the integration of BeiDou with artificial intelligence, satellite internet and other technologies, continue to advance system iteration and upgrading, and promote the healthy and orderly development of the BeiDou industry.
China will seek to enhance the system's applications in terms of service coverage and quality and contribute to global governance in satellite navigation, Zhang noted.
The BeiDou system benefits not only the Chinese people but also people around the world. The BDS has been providing stable and reliable positioning, navigation and timing services to users worldwide with its continuously improving performances and service quality, as well as its steadily expanding application scenarios and scale, according to Zhang.
The BDS has been used in a wide range of fields, including transportation, agriculture, forestry, fisheries, hydrological monitoring, meteorological forecasting and disaster relief.
About 900 people, including Chinese and foreign experts and scholars, business leaders, government officials and representatives of international organizations, attended the summit's opening ceremony. ■

How much do universal lunch programs affect academic performance?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:01:36 UTC
02:01:36 KST

After months of back-and-forth about how the program would be paid for, late this summer, Seattle’s public school system joined the thousands of districts nationwide that cover meals for every student, regardless of income, while they are in class.
As school is back in session throughout much of the U.S., a growing number of children are eating at school through universal meal programs. According to federal data, the number of students enrolled in schools that offer such programs has more than tripled since the 2016–2017 school year.
The funding comes from many sources. Some cities, such as Seattle, and states, such as New York, fund their own universal school meals programs, but many schools pay for free-for-students breakfasts and lunch with federal dollars. The government’s National School Lunch Program is the second largest food and nutrition assistance program in the U.S., spending roughly $17.2 billion from October 1, 2024, to September 30, 2025. The program provided funding for more than 4.87 billion lunches according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers the program.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Experts who spoke to Scientific American said these programs can have broad benefits, including on student test scores, absenteeism and food insecurity.
“To me, it’s the best thing since free sliced bread,” says Amy Ellen Schwartz, a professor of public policy at the University of Delaware. “In terms of an intervention, it’s cheap compared to almost any of the other things that you might be thinking of to improve your school.”
In a working paper looking at New York City middle schools, Schwartz and a colleague found the implementation of universal free meals programs raised math scores by as much as 0.083 standard deviation and English scores by 0.059 for students who were not poor—roughly three and two percentile points for a student in the middle of the pack—with smaller but significant gains of 0.032 and 0.027, respectively, for poor students.
Orgul Ozturk, a professor of economics at the University of South Carolina, said she was inspired to write a paper on universal meal programs after her child’s school implemented one. Ozturk and her co-authors used student-level data to show that elementary schools in South Carolina that implemented free meals programs saw math state standardized test scores rise by about 0.06 standard deviation.
“I think you see variation on who benefits, and definitely the effects are heterogeneous—it doesn’t impact everyone in the same way,” Ozturk says. “And benefits are positive, even when they are small, considering it’s not a very costly program in some ways.”
But a recent working paper analyzing the results of 42 different studies concluded that school meal programs in high-income economies had minimal effects on students’ behavioral, health or educational outcomes.
Despite limited academic literature describing its benefits, some have called for federal meals programs to be defunded.
“Subsidizing school food is an outdated use of federal dollars,” said Chris Edwards, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, in a report last year. “Congress should repeal school food programs to reduce budget deficits and hand power back to the states.”
To better understand the effect of free meals on school performance, Scientific American analyzed two datasets to examine the relationship between universal free meals programs and districts’ test scores. We used publicly available standardized test score estimates from the Stanford Education Data Archive and federal data that show which schools participate in programs that provide funding for free meals under the federal Community Eligibility Provision, as well as Provisions 2 and 3 of the National School Lunch Program.
The analysis, which covered three school years before the COVID pandemic (2016–2017, 2017–2018 and 2018–2019) and two after (2022–2023 and 2023–2024), found that free meals programs were associated with reading test scores that were 1.6 grade levels lower and math test scores that were roughly 1.66 grade levels lower, though the gap shrunk to about two-thirds of a grade level lower when accounting for demographic factors such as poverty, race, district size and the question of whether the school district lay in an urban or rural area. We excluded states that had their own universal free meals programs in the relevant school year and, to avoid skew, those whose data for that school year appeared to be an outlier when compared with other sources. We also excluded schools who did not report their universal meals status.
When comparing 1,452 pairs of school districts that fed every student for free with districts in the same state that had a similar size, poverty level, and community type and did not provide free meals during the 2023–2024 school year, the districts with federal meal programs scored, on average, 1.14 grade levels lower in math and 1.08 grade levels lower in reading.
We also compared each district’s test scores with its own scores in other years, accounting for changes in poverty and yearly shifts shared across districts. We found no clear link between changes in the share of students covered by universal free meals and changes in math or reading scores. None of the analyses we conducted could definitively show, one way or another, whether universal free lunch programs caused scores to change; they only showed the associations between scores and the existence of meal programs.
Experts who discussed our analysis with us said the Stanford data may have gaps in reporting that may skew the results and that more granular data at the student level may be needed to show the true effects of these programs. Differences in how and why schools implement a program, such as the nutritional quality of the meals provided, the amount of time that students have to eat lunch and the students’ backgrounds, also play a role, the experts said.
“The reason why you sometimes get mixed findings [in published scientific studies] is for a couple different reasons,” says Juliana Cohen, a professor of nutrition and public health at Merrimack College and an adjunct professor of nutrition at Harvard University’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health. “Some studies, what they’ve really found, is that you see improvements in test scores among kids who are food insecure.”
Experts suggested that the greatest direct benefit would likely be to children just above the cutoff for other subsidized meal programs and for those who were eligible for means-tested free meal programs but did not take advantage of them.
“This actually has a really profound impact on children’s diets, especially those that are at greatest risk for food insecurity and adverse health outcomes,” Cohen says.
“There are a large number of students in these schools who are maybe just above those thresholds that likely are ... maybe not food-insecure but still struggling to make ends meet,” says Michelle Marcus, an associate professor of economics at Vanderbilt University.
Marcus and some of the other researchers say that it is likely too early to determine the long-term impacts of universal free school meal programs on students in the U.S. but that the economic effects of even small benefits on things like test scores could compound over time.
Universal free school meal programs may have benefits beyond just helping students; they may also benefit their family's finances. A 2021 working paper estimated that the indirect effects of these programs reduced grocery shopping costs by about 4.5 percent for the median household by 2016. The researchers also found that after local schools adopted the program, grocery spending by households with school-aged children fell by about 7 percent relative to households without children.
Even households outside of areas with universal meal programs may reap the benefits. The researchers found that many grocery chains charge the same prices across their stores, so price cuts driven by one area’s free meals reach the chain’s shoppers elsewhere.
Perhaps the most robust finding in all the scientific literature: schools that have universal free lunch programs get more students lunch in the first place.
“I want to shed light on something I heard from many students: food security is safety,” said Sabi Yoon, a recent graduate of the Seattle school system and a member of the School Meals & Food Education Working Group, in a statement. “After speaking with students from diverse communities and backgrounds, we learned that being safe can also mean knowing if they will have access to a healthy meal at school, or even a meal at all.”

Which million-dollar math problem could AI solve next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:01:32 UTC
02:01:32 KST

The mathematics community is still in shock. On September 8, 2026, OpenAI announced that an artificial intelligence model may have solved one of the most significant problems in the field, the infamous Navier-Stokes problem, which had baffled countless mathematicians for decades.
Just a year ago, AI programs were only barely capable of solving some problems in the Mathematics Olympiad. Many researchers laughed at the programs’ sometimes embarrassing errors and doubted the models’ utility. But with recent breakthroughs, no one can deny that AI large language models (LLMs) have fully arrived in mathematical research and could dramatically change the field.
Solving the Navier-Stokes problem was a particularly prestigious achievement because it is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, mathematical puzzles that, in 2000, were selected by the Clay Institute of Mathematics as challenges that would shape the coming century of mathematics. Solving any of the problems—by, for instance, finding a counterexample that refutes a core conjecture—comes with a $1-million prize. To date, two have been solved: in addition to the recent Navier-Stokes solution, mathematician Grigori Perelman succeeded in proving the so-called Poincaré conjecture in 2003.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Now only five Millennium Prize Problems remain, and major AI companies are racing to solve them. OpenAI told the New York Times that it has already made significant progress on another one of the problems—but didn’t specify which one. In forums, at conferences and workshops and, of course, on social media, people are speculating about which of these remaining problems AI will tackle next. Here’s an introduction to all five, in order of how likely it is that each will be resolved by the technology, according to most experts.
The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture
In the early 1960s mathematicians Bryan John Birch and Peter Swinnerton-Dyer developed a conjecture involving algebraic equations called elliptic curves. Contrary to what their name might suggest, these objects do not describe ellipses but are related to “elliptic integrals,” which, among other things, specify the arc lengths of ellipses.
In general, elliptic curves are generated by the following type of equation: y2 = x3 + ax + b, where a and b can take any value. These curves play a central role in cryptography and were the key to solving Fermat’s last theorem.
These deceptively simple equations contain numerous puzzles. One involves rational elliptic curves, where a and b must correspond only to rational numbers (meaning numbers that can be expressed as fractions). For centuries, experts have been trying to determine how many points on the corresponding curve have purely rational values in this case. Some curves, for example, contain infinitely many fractional points, while others contain only a finite number.
These rational points are partially interrelated: If you know one point, other rational points on the curve can be calculated using simple arithmetic. But this method may not find all the points. Many independent rational points can be constructed from a different rational starting point. The complexity, or “rank,” of an elliptic curve can be expressed by the number of independent rational starting points. Determining the rank of such a curve, however, proves to be an extremely difficult task.
Through a computer-aided search, Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer found evidence of a criterion that could quickly answer the question of rank. But it remains unclear whether this criterion can truly determine the correct rank for all elliptic curves. One way to resolve this puzzle would be for an AI model to construct a counterexample: an elliptic curve that does not meet Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer’s criterion.
Past experience has shown that language models are particularly good at finding such examples. That’s partly beca
use people often invest more resources in proving a hypothesis they believe to be true than in a possible refutation.
The Hodge Conjecture
A second strong candidate for an AI solution is the Hodge conjecture, which is arguably the most abstract of the seven Millennium Prize puzzles. In 1950 mathematician William Vallance Douglas Hodge put it forward at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Cambridge, Mass. It has since become one of the most important open questions in topology.
It deals with the categorization of geometric figures—specifically, the question of whether an object has holes and, if so, how many it has. To calculate the number of holes even in large dimensions—when people can no longer visualize these figures—mathematicians use special tricks. For example, they can cover the surface of a figure with a net of triangles: as it turns out, the number of vertices and edges of the triangles that are required to cover the surface can reveal the number of holes. That technique works regardless of how fine the net is or how precise the triangles are.
Unfortunately, even that method is insufficient in high dimensions because the resulting nets are very difficult to examine. Instead of triangles, however, you could work with smooth curves generated by polynomial equations. These can be investigated using an algebraic equation. You might remember this from school: if you want to find the intersection point of two lines, you can do so graphically, but it is usually easier to equate the two corresponding equations and solve for x and y.
Hodge addressed the question of when it is possible to replace the triangular mesh used to cover a geometric object with smooth curves. He found a supposed criterion for this: a definite integral must equal zero. If this was the case, Hodge realized, experts could continue their calculations using familiar algebraic structures instead of struggling with the triangles. The Hodge conjecture has been proven for certain special cases in low dimensions. It remains unclear, however, whether it holds true for more complex situations.
This is precisely where AI programs could come into play. They could construct situations in which a vanishing integral is not sufficient to guarantee an algebraic structure for determining the holes.
The Riemann Hypothesis
The Riemann hypothesis is arguably the most prestigious of the Millennium Prize Problems. For more than 160 years, it has occupied mathematicians worldwide. In 1900 mathematician David Hilbert included it in his list of 23 major mathematical questions of the coming century—yet it remains unsolved (despite both human and AI efforts).
This puzzle was named after mathematician Bernhard Riemann, who worked primarily in the field of analysis, which revolves around functions and their derivatives. He published a single six-page paper on number theory, and it contained the famous conjecture. This work later proved that prime numbers, while randomly scattered in small sections of the number line, appear to be regularly arranged over sufficiently large intervals.
This order is reflected in the prime counting function π(n), which Riemann discovered. The function gives an estimate of how many prime numbers there are up to a given number n. The prime counting function is not exact, however. The actual number of prime numbers deviates from the prediction. And these fluctuations are related to the so-called Riemann zeta function.
Riemann observed that the zeros of this function appear to follow a pattern. Within a certain interval, the zeros appear to all lie on a straight line. If this observation can be proven mathematically, it will have far-reaching consequences, indicating that fluctuation in the number of prime numbers is limited and that people can therefore deduce the distribution of prime numbers very precisely.
Most mathematicians assume the Riemann hypothesis to be correct. But so far, no one has proven that all relevant zeros of the zeta function actually lie on this line.
Should an AI model find a counterexample, such as a zero off the straight line, the achievement would be sensational. This is because there are numerous results in mathematics that were proven under the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is correct. Such a finding would at least strongly call its validity into question.
Yang-Mills Theory and the Mass Gap Problem
This two-part Millennium Prize Problem originates in particle physics. The theories that describe the interactions of elementary particles are based on certain symmetries, meaning properties of a system that remain unchanged despite transformation. For example, in physicists’ electromagnetic equations, all positively charged particles can be replaced by their negatively charged antiparticles without any change to the math itself.
The first part of the Yang-Mills problem, the so-called existence question, revolves around whether it’s possible to construct a particular kind of theoretical framework—a quantum field theory, which describes subatomic particles with both quantum mechanics and special relativity—for every type of mathematical symmetry of a certain type. These theories are generally referred to as Yang-Mills theories.
A Yang-Mills theory describes elementary particles and the forces acting between them. Evidence from particle physics suggests that the equations describing particles called quarks have a “mass gap,” where there is a minimum amount of energy required to create a particle such that no particle in a given system can have a mass close to zero. The second part of the Yang-Mills problem is therefore proving that these mass gaps exist for the quantum field theory constructed.
In 2015 a team that included physicist Toby Cubitt of University College London demonstrated that the general problem of determining a mass gap is likely undecidable. But it remains unclear whether Yang-Mills theories, specifically, are indeterminate in this way. Still, experts do not expect AI models to resolve these questions anytime soon.
P versus NP
Mathematicians are least optimistic about finding a solution to the “P versus NP” problem, widely considered the greatest puzzle in modern computer science. In a lecture, University of Texas at Austin computer scientist Scott Aaronson went further, calling it “one of the deepest questions that human beings have ever asked.” This puzzle essentially boils down to: How quickly can a computer solve tasks of a certain complexity?
In computer science, a distinction is made between different “complexity classes,” including P and NP. Problems of the first class can be computed in polynomial time; that is, the effort required to calculate the solution increases to a manageable extent with increasing input. An example of such a P problem is the question of whether a value is a prime number. Modern algorithms can check this in a comparatively small number of computational steps.
The situation is different, however, when the effort required to solve the problem grows exponentially with the length of the input, as is the case with NP problems. Such problems can become so extensive that no computer in the world can solve them in a reasonable amount of time. The NP class is characterized, however, by the fact that a given solution can at least be quickly verified. An example of an NP problem is the prime factorization of a large number: calculating the prime factors is very computationally intensive, but verifying a result—multiplying the supposed prime factors—is done quickly.
The P versus NP problem revolves around the question of whether P and NP are truly different. After all, it’s possible that an extremely fast algorithm for prime factorization exists—but no one has yet discovered it. In that case, an AI might be able to provide a solution. But experts consider this highly unlikely: most are convinced that P and NP encompass distinct problems.
Unlike most other Millennium Prize Problems, experts don’t even have a vague idea of what a possible strategy for proving the inequality of P and NP might look like. This applies to the whole of complexity theory: so far, there are very few proven results in this area that distinguish between complexity classes. Therefore, most experts doubt that AI models will make any significant progress in this area.
And now I ask you, dear readers: Which Millennium Prize Problem do you think will be solved next? And will it be humans or AI that claim the prize?

FBI Director Kash Patel came under intense questioning from U.S. senators Tuesday as lawmakers challenged his leadership of the bureau, pressing him on the Jeffrey Epstein files, immigration-related violence, hiring standards and his lawsuit against a magazine over allegations about his drinking.
Patel defended the Trump administration’s handling of the Epstein files, saying the FBI had complied with the Epstein Files Transparency Act and court orders and released about 3.5 million pages. "We have complied with the statute,” Patel said, adding that the bureau would examine any genuinely new information.
Democrats accused the FBI of protecting President Donald Trump from fallout over Epstein while failing to provide survivors with adequate transparency and accountability.
Patel also defended his decision to file a defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic magazine and journalist Sarah Fitzpatrick over a report alleging he has a drinking problem that interfered with his work. "She printed false material. I’m taking her to court,” Patel said, arguing that he had the right to defend himself as a private citizen.
Asked by Sen. Peter Welch whether the FBI had investigated Fitzpatrick, Patel said no. "The FBI investigates criminals, and the FBI does not investigate personal matters,” he said. The response came after reports that the bureau had opened an investigation into the journalist.
The hearing also focused on the deadly shootings this January of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in the city of Minneapolis, Minnesota during a controversial ICE crackdown. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota pressed Patel on whether the FBI would support criminal investigations and provide information to the families.
"We will fully support all those investigations,” Patel said, regardless of whether they were led by state or federal authorities. Asked whether the FBI would support timely and thorough investigations of officer-involved shootings more broadly, he replied: "When we are the lead agency, yes.”
Soon after the shootings, Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension said the FBI had blocked it from examining evidence in the cases.
Sen. Dick Durbin also challenged Patel over the FBI’s handling of shootings involving federal immigration officers in Illinois, including the shooting of Marimar Martinez by a Border Patrol agent and the killing of Silverio Villegas Gonzalez by an ICE agent.
Patel said investigations were "ongoing” and involved multiple federal agencies, adding that the FBI had to work with state and local partners before the Justice Department could determine what action was appropriate.
Patel further defended a policy change removing certain incidents of bestiality or animal cruelty from before the age of 18 from the FBI’s list of automatic hiring disqualifiers. He said the change was designed to prevent victims of trafficking or coercion from being automatically excluded from consideration.
"We are not going to criminalize and prevent victims from serving the United States,” Patel said.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy questioned why the FBI had addressed the issue at all. Patel acknowledged that his initial reaction was similar but said officials had shown him cases involving people who had been forced into such acts.
Patel portrayed the bureau’s broader record as one of major public safety gains, citing 54,000 violent -criminal arrests, more than 5,000 arrests of child predators and human traffickers, and the seizure of more than 3,200 kilograms (7,055 pounds) of fentanyl.
Democrats disputed his claims and accused Patel of politicizing the FBI. Durbin called him "the least qualified and most partisan FBI director” in US history.

UK changing its approach towards Israel: British envoy to Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:00:48 UTC
02:00:48 KST

The United Kingdom’s new ambassador to Ankara, Jennifer Elizabeth Anderson, said Britain was changing its approach towards Israel following its decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.
“The UK is now changing its approach. There has been unimaginable suffering in Gaza and the West Bank, and this cannot continue,” Anderson told Anadolu in an interview in Turkish.
The ambassador said the UK “will not remain silent while more suffering continues”, adding that the measures were intended to support a two-state solution and prevent illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Anderson presented her credentials to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on September 8 and began her new post in Ankara this month.
She previously served as deputy head of mission at the British Embassy in Ankara. After leaving Türkiye, she said the country “had always been in her heart” and she had continued to follow developments there closely.
Anderson later served as director for consular and crisis operations, coordinating Britain’s assistance efforts in Türkiye following the 2023 earthquakes centred in Kahramanmaras.
UK-Türkiye ties
Assessing bilateral relations, Anderson said ties between Türkiye and the UK were “very strong and becoming even stronger”.
She noted that the two countries had signed a Strategic Partnership Framework in April, followed by a Security and Defence Partnership agreement in July.
“When I first came to Türkiye, our bilateral trade volume was £17 billion ($22.94 billion), but this year it has reached £28.6 billion ($38.59 billion). We are making significant progress,” she said.
Anderson also pointed to an increase in the number of British tourists visiting Türkiye, saying the figure had risen from around 1.7 million in 2020 to 4.4 million this year.
She said negotiations on a new free trade agreement were ongoing, while cooperation was expanding in areas including migration, defence, development, science, technology, innovation and green energy.
“As British ambassador, I am determined to further advance our partnership and friendship,” Anderson said.
She described Türkiye and the UK as two leading NATO allies and said defence cooperation was a key strategic area contributing to economic growth.
Anderson said the Security and Defence Partnership agreement, signed during the NATO summit in Ankara, reflected the two countries’ determination to deepen defence industry cooperation.
UK backs further action
Asked about the decision announced on September 8 by 12 countries, including the UK, France, Norway and Canada, to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, Anderson said Britain was taking a new approach.
“The UK is now changing its approach. There has been unimaginable suffering in Gaza and the West Bank, and this cannot continue,” she said.
“The UK will not remain silent while more suffering continues. The full implementation of a two-state solution is a fundamental policy of the British government. We have decided to take action on this.”
Referring to comments by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham that insufficient steps had so far been taken in response to the situation in Palestine, Anderson said she welcomed statements by Türkiye’s foreign ministry and the Group of Eight.
“As the Foreign Ministry has said, we want to continue working together with countries in the region,” she said.
Asked whether the UK would take further measures to support a two-state solution and prevent Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, Anderson said the new measures had been announced for that purpose.
“Yes. These new measures were announced precisely to support a two-state solution and prevent illegal settlements in the West Bank,” she said.
“We will continue to assess the Israeli government based on its actions. It is very clear that we expect a new approach from Israel, both in Gaza and the West Bank.”

St. Petersburg election officials from Russia’s antiwar Yabloko party were ordered to report to military offices at 9 a.m. on the first day of voting — exactly when polls are scheduled to open
Several Yabloko representatives serving on precinct election commissions in St. Petersburg’s Krasnogvardeysky District have received summonses ordering them to report to military enlistment offices, city election commission member Pavel Shapchits told Fontanka.

Fontanka contacted two commission members who received summonses. Both serve on precinct commissions overseen by Territorial Election Commission No. 44.

Russian authorities are trying to keep Yabloko, which is campaigning under the antiwar slogan “For Peace and Freedom,” out of the elections. A month ago, the Supreme Court removed Yabloko’s federal party list from the State Duma elections on spurious grounds. Courts across the country then began disqualifying the party’s candidates in single-member districts and removing its regional lists. Yabloko has also faced obstruction while campaigning, and the party’s observers have been barred from polling stations.
Russia will hold elections at various levels across the country from September 18 to 20, including elections to the ninth State Duma.

Dutch rail network crippled by suspected sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:58:45 UTC
01:58:45 KST

Dutch rail network crippled by suspected sabotage
THE HAGUE - Rail travel in large parts of the Netherlands ground to a standstill on Sept 15, after what the authorities suspect were coordinated acts of sabotage with tubes attached to train tracks in multiple locations.
Transport by train in most of the central and eastern part of the country was virtually impossible after the authorities discovered items on the tracks in around 30 separate places.
“Materials were found at multiple locations on the track that were deliberately placed there,” said rail operator ProRail in a statement.
“This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved,” added the operator.
ProRail said its computer systems interpret an item on the track as meaning that section is occupied, even though there is no train.
The system then turns all lights in that section red, meaning no trains can pass.
One train did hit one of the tubes but there were no injuries, said ProRail spokeswoman Joke van der Cruysen.
“Who is responsible for this and what the motive is not yet known,” said ProRail, adding that a police investigation was under way.
There was also a knock-on effect on road travel, as level crossings are also malfunctioning due to the sabotage.
By around 3pm local time (9pm Singapore time), the blockages had been removed from the tracks and traffic was able to resume.
Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the alleged sabotage as “disruptive and life-threatening”.
“We must now calmly await the police investigation. The police and the security services are doing everything they can to track down the perpetrators,” added Jetten.
The action coincided with Prince’s Day, when the government lays out its budget plans.
Tuesday also saw protests by farmers angry at the government plans, who set bales of hay alight alongside several country roads.
No roads were closed as a result of the farmers’ protests, according to transport authorities, who also said there were no major delays in road traffic.
The Farmers Defence Force had already announced they would take protest actions to coincide with Prince’s Day, but it is not clear if farmers were also behind the train sabotage.
Climate group Extinction Rebellion was also active, throwing red paint at the route taken by King Willem-Alexander to Parliament to make his Prince’s Day speech.
The group denied having anything to do with the train sabotage, however.
“Placing materials on the tracks is extremely dangerous and unacceptable, and fortunately, it did not lead to any accidents today,” said ProRail.
“ProRail finds the disruption experienced by travellers and shippers today very regrettable.” AFP

EU chief diplomat Kallas says she would answer call from Putin or Lavrov
Kaja Kallas, the EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, has said she would answer a call from Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin or Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov if such a call took place.
Source: Kallas in an interview with Yle, Finland's national public broadcasting company, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kallas pointed out, however, that she does not support starting dialogue with Russia on Russia's terms.
Quote: "Of course, I will talk if such an opportunity presents itself."
More details: Kallas said that she already met Lavrov at international forums, including ASEAN and G20 meetings, and set out the EU's position to him directly.
She said Moscow negotiates skilfully. Kallas believes Russia puts forward maximum demands, issues threats and waits for concessions from the West. Ultimately, she said, the Kremlin tries to secure things it did not previously have.
She also appeared to be sceptical about the efforts of US presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who have travelled to Moscow and Kyiv over the past year and a half in search of ways to bring peace to Ukraine. Kallas believes the process should involve people with a better understanding of how Russia operates.
In her view, if the aim is to end the war quickly, the simplest way is to force the victim to give up what it is defending – namely its land and its people. However, Kallas pointed out that this would not lead to a just and lasting peace.
She also said the European Union cannot currently act as a full-fledged mediator between Ukraine and Russia because it supports Kyiv.
She noted, however, that any negotiations would inevitably include issues whose resolution depends on Europe – for example, the fate of frozen Russian assets.
Kallas said the EU must make it clear that such matters cannot be decided solely through dialogue between Moscow and Washington.
Background:
- It was reported earlier that Jonathan Powell, the UK prime minister's national security adviser, believes it is necessary to maintain contacts with Russia.
- On 6 September, US special envoy Steve Witkoff stated that the task of the American delegation which visited Kyiv and Moscow was to "bring the sides closer together".

US energy chief says Saudi Arabia oil pipeline should be back online within days
WASHINGTON, Sept 15 - Crude oil should be flowing through Saudi Arabia's vital East-West Pipeline within days, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday, after the kingdom was forced to temporarily close it following attacks by Iran-aligned groups.
"It's still a detailed assessment, but I think it will be measured in days," Wright said on the sidelines of a G20 energy meeting in Houston. He said Saudi Arabia is taking steps to move more oil out of the Strait of Hormuz with assistance from the U.S. military.
Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates of how long the pipeline would be offline, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair. Another said it could be fixed sooner and resume pumping partially while repairs take place.
The 1,200-km (745-mile) East-West Pipeline running across the Arabian Peninsula has served as the main route for global supplies of Middle Eastern oil for the past six months while the strait between Iran and Oman has been largely shut by the Iran war. The pipeline had been moving 4 million to 5 million barrels per day, amounting to 4% to 5% of global supply, sparing Saudi Arabia the brunt of the disruption that has crippled other Gulf oil and gas exporters.
Washington has resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support, three sources told Reuters on Monday.
U.S. President Donald Trump said over the weekend he had spoken with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and that Iran-aligned Houthis, who have launched missile and drone attacks on the kingdom from Yemen, had also contacted Washington urging it to stay out of the conflict. REUTERS

Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner after intense grassroots campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:50:54 UTC
01:50:54 KST

The owner of a New York City bodega on Tuesday was reunited with the store’s cat after a couple passing by the establishment five days earlier appeared to abduct the feline in plain view of a surveillance camera and ignited an intense grassroots search effort.
The plight of three-month-old Jabal began on Thursday morning in Brooklyn, when he went just outside the Eighth Street Mini Market where he lives as it opened for the day. A man walking alongside a woman passed the Park Slope market then picked up Jabal, and the pair took off as the kitten visibly squirmed, according to store surveillance video which the bodega’s owner, Imad “Jimmy” Innab, reviewed after he noticed the cat had gone missing.
Dan Janzen, who lives across the street from the Eighth Street Mini Market and is one of its regular customers, said someone immediately ran after the couple and told them the kitten belonged to the bodega – but they were unmoved, stuffed Jabal into a bag and left with him anyway.
As the New York Post and the local CBS affiliate soon reported, Innab and his family subsequently offered a $500, no questions asked reward for Jabal’s safe return, which was announced on a poster. Supporters of the bodega also canvassed the streets of Park Slope for Jabal while the neighborhood’s forum on the Reddit platform provided updates on the search efforts.
One thread dedicated to Jabal’s disappearance had a photo of the couple who took the kitten and was titled, “Anyone Know These Two?” It generated about 1,000 upvotes – which indicate Reddit users’ approval of a thread – and more than 240 comments, with many aiming to help reunite Jabal with the Innabs.
Another thread titled “Stolen Bodega Cat?!?” also called attention to Jabal’s catnapping, along with the news media coverage, which publicized the shocking surveillance footage of the kitten being brazenly snatched.
The campaign paid dividends by Monday, when Janzen – speaking on behalf of Innab’s store – said the bodega had received a call from someone claiming to know who had Jabal. That person said Jabal would be brought back to the store from the Brooklyn neighborhood of Bushwick, according to both Janzen and Innab.
Janzen on Tuesday afternoon then followed up with pictures of Innab holding Jabal, including one in which the bodega owner was planting a kiss on the top of the kitten’s head.
Janzen sent the joyous pictures after spending part of Monday and Tuesday at the store with Innab eagerly awaiting Jabal’s return.
“As much as we love the kitten, we love him more,” Janzen said of Innab. “We were rallying around him to keep his hopes up.”
The Post on Tuesday reported that the woman seen leaving with Jabal arranged for her stepson to bring the kitten to the New York police precinct in Park Slope. Police then brought Jabal back to Innab’s bodega.
Furthermore, the Post reported that the police took the woman into custody on Tuesday, but she was not yet booked with a crime. Innab had previously said he only cared about Jabal being returned safely and did not want to see the pursuit of criminal charges in the case.
Innab also spoke about how had been particularly affected by Jabal’s snatching because the Eighth Street Mini Market’s prior bodega cat, Victoria, had died in June after living there for 17 years. Innab took in Jabal to succeed Victoria, and the kitten was soon due to be given a microchip, which is injected subcutaneously and contains scannable owner and home address information.
Bodega cats are deeply embedded in the fabric of New York City, serving to help keep vermin under control while also acting as living mascots for the stores where they reside. They can be seen lounging among store offerings or roaming along the freezer cases – among assorted other activities – in pictures on certain widely followed social media accounts, including @bodegacatsofinstagram on Instagram.
Janzen on Monday made it a point to say that Innab refused to entertain the thought of not getting Jabal back. As Janzen put, Innab “always said, ‘I have a feeling he’s coming back.’”
“I wish all the stories in the world could end this happily,” Janzen said on Tuesday.
Innab said the way the neighborhood where his store had stood for 39 years supported him after Jabal’s temporary abduction “means everything” to him.
“The people are very beautiful – very good – here,” Innab said of Park Slope. “And I thank everybody who tried to help me.”

How an Israeli cell orchestrated an anti-Qatar campaign
Israeli newspaper Haaretz reports that about 30 people, including influence experts and an ex-Mossad official, were part of an anti-Qatar group.
A group including Israeli influence experts and political advisers worked on a secret campaign targeting Qatar in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, before the initiative was abruptly halted, according to a report by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
The campaign was launched days after the assault on southern Israel and sought to pressure Qatar over its relationship with Hamas, Haaretz reported on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Declassified documents show UK aware of Israeli war crimes for 24 years
- list 2 of 3From hunger crisis to ‘obesity’: how Gaza’s UN data is being twisted
- list 3 of 3How 9/11 helped Israel sell its war on Palestinians to America
“Their goal was to launch a global civilian influence campaign against Qatar,” the newspaper reported.
Those behind it believed international pressure could force Doha to influence Hamas to secure the release of the 251 captives taken to Gaza on October 7, Haaretz said.
According to the report, about 30 people were recruited to the project, including experts in psychological warfare.
A WhatsApp group called Free the Kidnapped was established several days after October 7. The identities of those who initiated the operation “are barred from publication”, Haaretz said.
The newspaper described the effort as a “civilian initiative”.
But Marc Owen Jones, associate professor at Northwestern University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera, “It is unlikely such a campaign would exist without the motivation of an actor like Israel.”
He said he has tracked a campaign against Qatar for the “past three years that sounds exactly like that”.
“I imagine it stopped either because they are pretending it is not happening or outsourced it to another entity for cover.”
Qatar has been the key mediator between Hamas and Israel since Israel’s genocide in Gaza began.
Although Israeli officials have repeatedly travelled to Doha for indirect negotiations with Hamas, the Israeli army carried out a missile strike on the country last year on September 9, targeting Hamas’s negotiating team. Six people were killed, including a Qatari national.
The episode was condemned by countries including France and the United Kingdom.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later apologised for the strike.
The following month, Israel and Hamas agreed to a “ceasefire” deal, which Israel to date has violated hundreds of times.
Since October, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,300 Palestinians in Gaza and injured nearly 4,700.
In total, Israel has killed more than 73,700 people since October 2023, when it launched its genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.
Focusing on Qatar-Hamas relationship
Qatar has repeatedly denied allegations that it funds Hamas, pointing to the strict oversight governing its aid transfers.
“All our aid, financing, and all our support … went to the people in Gaza, and was a very transparent process that the United States is very aware of … [and] Israel was the one facilitating,” Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, Qatar’s prime minister, said last year. “This communication has led to ceasefires, has led to the release of hostages, has led to alleviating the suffering of the people over there.”
Doha, which has long served as a mediator in Middle East conflicts and beyond, has hosted Hamas’s political office since 2012. The decision to host the Hamas leadership came after a request from the United States, according to Qatari officials.
Haaretz reported that one member of the anti-Qatar WhatsApp group asked, “Do we know how much Qatar gives Hamas every year or some other monetary figure that we can hammer home?”
Another responded, “Qatar-ISIS Ltd”.
The message “Hamas is ISIS” was subsequently used on the campaign’s website and Facebook profile, the Haaretz report revealed.
Participants raised donations, produced videos, contacted journalists and arranged media appearances as part of their secret campaign.
A website was also established in several languages and social media accounts were opened.
Haaretz reported that a former Mossad official was also part of the group.
But about a month after it began, the campaign was abruptly halted.
“After a while, it was shut down. We stopped dealing with the Qatar campaign,” one participant told the Israeli newspaper. “I never heard anything more about the campaign.”
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that the story reveals an “extraordinary contradiction at the heart of Israel’s relationship with Qatar”.
“Israel has spent years presenting Qatar as an enabler of Hamas,” he said. “Yet at the same time, successive Israeli governments have relied on Qatar precisely because Doha possesses access to Hamas and other actors that Israel cannot reach directly. Qatar has effectively been both demonised and instrumentalised.”
