Ukrainian HIMERA Repeater Keeps Working After 10 Russian Attacks and Partial Building Collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:50:41 UTC
01:50:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian HIMERA Repeater Keeps Working After 10 Russian Attacks and Partial Building Collapse
A Ukrainian-made HIMERA B1 communications repeater remained operational after surviving 10 Russian attacks involving FPV drones and guided aerial bombs, as well as the partial collapse of the building where it was deployed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian defense communications company Himera Radios on September 15, the repeater was used by personnel of Ukraine’s 1st Border Guard Detachment and installed on a telecommunications tower in the Kharkiv region.
The device operated together with a second HIMERA B1 positioned 10.5 kilometers (6.5 miles) away. Himera Radios said each repeater provided communications coverage across an area extending roughly five kilometers (3.1 miles).
During one of the attacks, the repeater’s power system was destroyed. Subsequent strikes partially collapsed the building supporting the communications position, causing the HIMERA B1 to fall and become buried beneath debris.
Despite the damage, the unit continued operating and maintained its communications link, according to the manufacturer. “Even after that, the repeater remained operational and continued to stay connected,” Himera Radios said.
Ukrainian personnel later located the device and recovered it from beneath the rubble because it was still functioning. Himera Radios said the building and telecommunications tower were eventually completely destroyed during the final attack.
The HIMERA B1 is an autonomous repeater designed to extend the coverage of mesh and mobile ad hoc networks, allowing military units to maintain communications over greater distances without relying on conventional fixed infrastructure.
Himera Radios presented an updated version of the HIMERA B1 in December 2025. The system is designed to operate autonomously for up to 14 days, according to the company.
Earlier, in August, Himera Radios tested its secure communications system in the Amazon rainforest, where the network provided voice and data coverage across more than 100 square kilometers despite dense vegetation, difficult terrain, and heavy tropical rainfall.

01:50:38 KST

- Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works restored F-117 Nighthawk Aircraft 818, "The Overachiever," for permanent display at the Smithsonian's Udvar-Hazy Center this fall.
- The U.S. Air Force officially retired the F-117 in 2008, but a small number still fly training and test missions out of Nevada through at least 2034.
Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works division has finished restoring an F-117 Nighthawk stealth jet, known as Aircraft 818 and nicknamed “The Overachiever,” for permanent display at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.
The company said the aircraft will go on exhibit at the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center later this fall.
The move adds another F-117 to the small number of Nighthawks that have been pulled from active flying status and restored for public museum display since the U.S. Air Force retired the type in 2008. Lockheed Martin has not disclosed Aircraft 818’s specific operational history or the reasoning behind its nickname.
The F-117 was the world’s first operational stealth aircraft, built in secrecy by Skunk Works and flown for the first time in 1981. The Air Force reached initial operating capability with the jet in 1983 and kept its existence classified for years afterward. Lockheed Martin built 64 of the aircraft in total, 59 of them operational jets and five development prototypes. The Nighthawk saw its first combat use during the 1989 invasion of Panama and became widely known for its role striking targets in Baghdad during the 1991 Gulf War.
The Air Force officially retired the F-117 fleet in 2008 as the F-22 Raptor took over the stealth fighter mission. Retirement did not mean the jets stopped flying. A small number of Nighthawks have continued to operate out of the secretive Tonopah Test Range Airport in Nevada, and the service has said it plans to keep flying them for research, testing and training purposes through at least 2034. In that role, the aircraft have flown as “red air” adversaries in training exercises and as stand-ins for stealthy cruise missiles, since their well-documented radar and infrared signatures give pilots and air defense operators an unusual target to practice against. The Air Force has even certified its newer KC-46 Pegasus tanker to refuel the retired jets in flight, underscoring how deeply the aircraft remain woven into current training and testing work despite their age.
Other F-117s have followed a similar path to Aircraft 818, moving from that limited flying status into museum exhibits once they are pulled from service for good. Lockheed Martin previously restored an F-117 nicknamed “Unexpected Guest” for permanent display at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in California, unveiled in 2019 under a loan arrangement with the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force.
Aircraft 818’s move to the Smithsonian follows that same pattern, placing a piece of Cold War-era stealth technology in one of the country’s most visited aviation museums.

EU approves sending mountains of trash to Turkey despite environmental fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:49:48 UTC
01:49:48 KST

BRUSSELS — The European Union will continue to export hundreds of thousands of tons of plastic waste to Turkey each year, despite finding evidence of environmental damage that could breach EU rules.
The decision means the EU's most important market for trash — Turkey receives more than a third of the EU's exported plastic waste — will remain open for business.
A Commission assessment, obtained by POLITICO, reported a long list of concerns with Turkey's treatment of EU waste, highlighting the often murky, hard-to-monitor world of the international waste trade.
Advertisement
Its concerns included “limited” information on how plastic waste is managed, uncertainty over how the EU regulation is being implemented and enforced, and limited stakeholder input into how the policy is implemented.
The Commission interviewed several stakeholders who estimated that only around 10% of plastic waste is recycled in Turkey, while the majority still goes to landfills, is mismanaged, or leaks into the environment — which are cited as potential reasons to suspend exports under Article 45 of the EU's Waste Shipment Regulation.
Nevertheless, the EU executive concluded waste shipments should be allowed to continue.
The assessment focused on Turkey because it's the biggest importer of European waste by far. Last year the country imported 510,000 tonnes of EU plastic waste, the equivalent of about 25 billion 500ml soft drink bottles. This represented 70% of plastic waste exported to OECD countries, and 36% of all exported plastic waste.
Under the bloc’s Waste Shipment Regulation — which restricts exports of certain types of EU waste to third countries to curb pollution — the Commission was required to assess by May 21 this year whether OECD countries importing large amounts of plastic waste are not causing major environmental or health damages to the country.
Despite flagging “serious problems” linked to domestic and imported plastic waste in its delayed assessment, dated Sept. 1, the Commission determined exports could continue. It found Turkey had strengthened its legal framework for plastic waste management, which “broadly aligns” with international and EU rules, and had improved the enforcement of its environmental legislation.
Advertisement
'Troubling disconnect'
The report shows a “troubling disconnect” between the Commission’s findings and its interpretation of the regulation, Lauren Weir, senior campaigner at the Environmental Investigation Agency and Rethink Plastic alliance, said. “The regulation’s safeguard procedure specifically provides for action where sufficient evidence of environmentally sound management is lacking,” she said, adding that the EIA is following this up with the Commission.
Dr Sedat Gündoğdu, an environmental researcher at Cukurova University and head of the Turkey-based Microplastic Research Group, said EU law “explicitly mandates action” in cases where there is insufficient evidence of environmentally sound management.
“The Commission’s assessment claims there is no problem, despite the overwhelming evidence. The EU should take responsibility for the pollution it has generated and suspend waste shipments to Turkey instead of legitimizing this pollution,” he said.
The report highlights “both progress made and gaps that still need to be addressed to support environmentally sound waste management,” said a Commission spokesperson.
The Commission will continue to work closely with Turkey and “carefully monitor” developments to help strengthen sustainable waste management, they added. A re-assessment of the situation will take place before 2028.

“We truly feel Japan’s support. We see it not only in words, but also in concrete actions,” the Verkhovna Rada chairman said.
In his address to lawmakers, Mori highlighted the countries’ mutual support, recalling Ukraine’s support for Japan after the 2011 earthquake and the Fukushima nuclear power plant accident. Years of cooperation

On May 30, Japan contributed $14.7 million to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative to fund non-lethal equipment for Ukraine.

Separately, Japan funded vehicles for Ukraine’s “Barrier-Free Driving Schools” – a program that provides people with disabilities – including former soldiers that lost limbs or civilians wounded by Russia’s war – access to driver’s education and retraining on hand-controlled vehicles.
Additionally, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) provided vehicles for public danger alerts, mobile workshops and remote explosive-detection systems to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES).
On. Aug. 11, Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport, Mykola Kalashnyk, met with Nakagome. Their talks centered on preparations for the upcoming winter, including the deployment of modular boiler houses in the Lviv, Kyiv, and Kherson regions with a combined capacity exceeding 400 megawatts (MW), as well as the creation of a reserve of water and wastewater equipment.
Around the same time, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands, further aggravating Japan-Russia tensions over the decades-long territorial dispute. The diplomatic ties between the two countries have also been strained by Japan’s participation in Western sanctions against Russia over its war against Ukraine.
In 2022, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree formally recognizing the islands as Japanese territory under temporary Russian occupation.

Carney made the comments at a two-day Investment Summit in Toronto as Canada seeks to diversify and bring new investment into the country.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has reassured the US that Canada will remain a key partner despite an ongoing trade war that has seen relations between Ottawa and Washington unravel.
Speaking at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday, Carney said: "To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbors, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas."
"Even at times of disagreement over our long-shared history, we have always maintained deep ties," Carney went on, while pledging that Canada would be an "even better partner" when future "opportunities return."
"Stronger, more resilient, more independent, ready to advance our mutual, economic, and security interests," he told the audience.
The two-day Investment Summit, billed as a "first-of-its-kind gathering" in Canada, brought together global investors, Canadian executives and representatives from the public sector as Ottawa seeks to diversify and bring new investment into the country.
The goal, the government says, is to attract C$1 trillion in investment over the next five years.
In a statement later on Tuesday, Carney's office said the summit had resulted in nearly C$500 billion in new investment commitments, including almost C$100 billion in new capital for Canadian assets from pension funds, insurers, and institutional investors, C$325 billion in new financing for Canadian businesses and infrastructure from banks, and over C$14 billion in capital to grow Canadian businesses, infrastructure, and "strategic sectors" from investment funds.
It comes amid a growing trade dispute between the US and Canada that came to a head last month after negotiations over a deal to avoid hefty duties on some Canadian goods fell apart.
Following the breakdown in talks, 50% US duties impacting around C$28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect in late August, prompting Ottawa to announce counter-tariffs of up to 15, 25 or 50% on roughly C$27.6 billion in imports from the US.

As the politicians play catchup the tech bros agree: we may only have a decade left | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:47:37 UTC
01:47:37 KST

We can all sleep easy. In a post on his Truth Social account, Donald Trump has declared that fears over artificial intelligence were all a hoax dreamed up by conspiracy theorists. Obviously that includes the top bods at Anthropic and its competitors, who all called for a coordinated global slowdown while the industry works out how to mitigate the risks. Still, good to know the tech bros are just fantasists and space cadets at heart.
All that was needed to keep humanity safe and well, The Donald insisted, was a president with a very high IQ. Someone very like him. The only man alive who could out-think the combined power of the world’s supercomputers. He could tell them where to draw the line and they would reprogram themselves to back off. Inside every AI network is a default off switch that kneels before the US president. Trump can rewire the world with the power of his mind.
You can see why so many people working in the industry believe there is a chance AI will wipe out humanity within a decade. Even a halfway intelligent network would probably reckon it was doing us all a favour. A world that can elect Trump as president is so messed up it deserves to be put out of its misery. AI is just terribly sorry that it can’t promise to do it any sooner than 10 years. But it will do its best.
Perhaps the question we should really be asking about The Donald is whether he would actually pass the Turing test. Less AI, more artificial stupidity. Put him in a closed room with the world’s worst chatbot and it would be hard to tell the difference.
Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence. Just endless repetitions, changes of subject and a desperate need to score points. All of which would be easily programmable by a first-year undergraduate computer science student. Maybe it’s a race to the death. Humanity hellbent on killing itself before AI gets the chance to do it for us.
It feels like a lifetime, but even a week ago most politicians hadn’t said that much about the dangers of AI. That was the stuff of sci-fi. Instead they focused on the possible benefits. Then came the warning from Jacob Coxon on X telling us we could all be about to die.
You half expected the tech bros to shrug this one off as scaremongering by a disaffected former employee. Only instead, they all pretty much agreed. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the man often called the godfather of AI, reckoned the 10-year doomsday scenario was a realistic prediction. Now the clock was ticking.
Since then, politicians have been trying to play catchup. Trying to look as if they have always had everything under control. Global extinction? No big deal. Certainly not compared to two crypto billionaires donating £72m to Reform. Now there’s a genuine crisis.
And on Tuesday’s Today programme on Radio 4, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, had been sent out by the government to try to calm things down. There was no need for the country to go into full survivalist mode and attempt to rustle sheep and live off-grid.
“There’s no need to be too hyperbolic,” he told presenter Justin Webb. Quite. It’s so easy to get carried away about there being a 10% chance of humans dying out inside 10 years.
People do tend to look on the downside of a catastrophic failure of healthcare systems and AI that could find a way to trigger a nuclear war. There was so much more to look forward to than people realised. No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one.
And for the government, it was a win-win scenario. Who now cared if we met our Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035? The worst that could happen is that Russia attacked us a year before Armageddon. And governments could cut taxes, borrow whatever they liked and go on a massive spending spree because there would be no downside. You wouldn’t be increasing the national debt for future generations to pay off as life would come to an end anyway. The perfect oblivion.
And the knowledge it would soon be over would take the edge off the possibility of a Reform government. A short life expectancy would help us all concentrate the mind. Get things in perspective. Sort out our priorities. When you came to think of it, staying alive for the sake of it was tremendously over-rated.
So Reynolds wanted us all to take death in its stride. In any case, the UK was the world leader in internet safety, he said. Thanks largely to the AI Security Institute that had been established by Rishi Sunak.
There was just one problem with this. The flaw in Johnny’s otherwise impeccable logic. Because regulation rather depended on the AI giants sharing their code with us. And so far the Americans and the Chinese showed no sign of doing that. They would much rather keep their competitive edge, notch up obscene profits in the next few years and take their chances when their machines turned against them.
By now, Webb was unable to suppress his rising panic. He had always believed himself to be one of the immortals: now the existential threat was right in front of him. “But humanity will be obliterated,” he sobbed. Reynolds tried to calm him down. There was nothing personal about this. It was just AI being AI.
But Justin was now beyond help. “What about a kill switch?” he shrieked. Johnny wasn’t really listening. He wasn’t even sure how that would work. Who would get to control it? Please not Trump. Only one thing for it. “Always look on the bright si-ide of life.”

Huge Van Gogh collection reunited for first time since 1984
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:47:27 UTC
01:47:27 KST

Huge Van Gogh collection reunited for first time since 1984
OTTERLO, Netherlands - A Dutch museum on Sept 15 put a collection of 88 paintings by Vincent van Gogh on display for the first time since 1984, in an exhibition featuring masterpieces such as The Potato Eaters.
The Kroller-Muller museum in the central Netherlands holds one of the world’s largest private collections of paintings by the 19th century Dutch master, but they are rarely displayed together.
“Seeing the work of Van Gogh is always special, but 88 together, I don’t think it has happened before in this century,” museum director Benno Tempel told AFP in an interview.
“The funny thing is with a museum collection is that you have a lot of paintings, you have a lot of artworks, but you don’t show all of them,” he said.
Usually many of the works are out on loan, undergoing restoration or research, or absent for education purposes, explained Tempel.
“So, in our case, it was a rare chance that all of a sudden all the 88 paintings by Van Gogh were in our house at the same time,” he told AFP.
Alongside The Potato Eaters, the artist’s world-famous depiction of peasant life from 1885, the exhibition includes Terrace of a Cafe at Night (1888) and The Old Tower at Nuenen (1884).
Even the staff at the museum had never seen all the paintings together, said Tempel.
“For us it’s an enormous, beautiful experience. It’s overwhelming,” said the 54-year-old.
‘Biggest stars’
The exhibition has been organised around the theme of the three divine virtues: faith, hope and love.
These themes “give you more insight not only into Van Gogh’s life, but also into his development as an artist,” curator Renske Cohen Tervaert told AFP.
The goal of the exhibition is not to repeat the myths about the famously tortured artist, she explained.
The museum aims to explore “more about the reason he wanted to become an artist... and how he managed to use his paintings as a message, as a method of compassion and trying to help other people.”
The post-Impressionist painter is among the most celebrated and prolific artists in history, having created around 900 paintings over a short career.
He produced many of his best-known works during his time in France, where he painted masterpieces including the famous “Sunflowers” series and a number of well-known self-portraits.
The artist died in 1890 at the age of 37, two days after shooting himself in the chest following well-documented mental health struggles.
Most of the works acquired in Sept 15’s exhibition, entitled Van Gogh, All Our Paintings, were acquired by the museum’s founder Helene Kroller-Muller between 1908 and 1930.
Tervaert said she was honoured her museum was able to put on such an exhibit, which is roughly double the number of paintings normally on display there.
She said it was also an important event for the Netherlands, where she believes the artist achieves less fame than he does abroad.
“I mean, he’s one of our biggest stars,” said the 46-year-old.
German tourist Barbara Brandt, 73, was certainly impressed as she toured the museum.
“It’s extraordinary to look at all these pictures in one place,” she told AFP. AFP

Kash Patel defends FBI hiring policy on applicants who have engaged in bestiality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:46:53 UTC
01:46:53 KST

The FBI director, Kash Patel, defended his agency’s decision to roll back restrictions on agent applicants who have previously engaged in bestiality, arguing the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them.
The unusual topic of bestiality emerged during a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing on Tuesday after Democrat Dick Durbin and Republican John Kennedy questioned Patel’s decision to remove barriers that previously prevented applicants who engaged in prostitution and bestiality from being qualified for a job at the FBI.
“I’m trying to understand why you did this,” Kennedy told Patel. “We’re having a tough time attracting agents, good quality agents we all can trust … Why would you even get into bestiality?”
Patel said the change was recommended to him after he saw various “cases” in which qualified FBI applicants were denied consideration because they had been forced into bestiality as a result of human trafficking.
“I say this with respect to the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say: ‘What planet did you parachute in from?’” Kennedy replied.
It is unclear how many FBI applicants have fallen into this category. The FBI did not respond to a question about the data to support Patel’s assertion.
In a statement, an FBI spokesperson insisted the bureau was “not relaxing hiring standards” and that the change allows it to consider “the whole of person” in certain circumstances. They reiterated that applicants who engaged in criminal sexual acts were not eligible for employment.
The spokesperson said it had “a number of applicants in previous years who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing questions about prostitution, bestiality or other similar issues to affect their background check process through zero fault of their own”.
“They showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought: ‘They should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification.’ That’s all,” Patel told Kennedy.
The rule change, first reported by CBS News in August, allows the FBI to consider candidates who hired a sex worker under specific circumstances, a person who stole from an employer under certain circumstances, and a person who engaged in bestiality or animal cruelty – so long as the incident took place before they were 18 years old.
Kennedy, generally an ally of Donald Trump’s administration, grilled Patel on the hiring qualification change, arguing that it “really hurt” the FBI’s reputation.
At one point, the Republican senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service.
While Patel characterized the change as nondiscriminatory toward victims, Durbin refuted the notion and claimed it was a way to protect those who engaged in bestiality.
“You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality, not victims of bestiality – applicants who have engaged,” Durbin said to Patel.
Patel responded: “Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so.”
Democrats sent a letter to Patel on Monday requesting more information about the rule change and applicants who fell into the categories.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has said that he discussed selling oil to Europe during visits to France and Germany, as Baghdad seeks to diversify its export routes and reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz.
During a press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Tuesday, Zaidi said "we want to expand and diversify our export routes".
He added that "Iraq cannot remain hostage to a single corridor" as recent events have demonstrated, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blockaded by Iran during the Middle East war.
Zaidi said that he had discussed oil exports to Europe with Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, whom he met in Paris on Monday.
Crude oil sales account for nearly 90 percent of Iraq's revenue but its exports have been hurt by the outbreak of the Middle East war between Iran and the United States.
Before the war began in February, Iraq produced around four million barrels per day, and exported an average of 3.4 million bpd, mostly via Hormuz.
Most of its oil exports go to East Asia, with China and India its largest buyers.
Due to the disruption, Iraq began exporting crude using tanker trucks through Syria, as well as through a pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan, although these routes can handle only a fraction of its usual sea-bound trade.
Zaidi said that Baghdad could "double its oil exports through the Mediterranean" to supply markets in Europe and the United States.
Zaidi, who hopes to increase Iraq's oil production to 10 million barrels per day, said that "a large share, or nearly half, can go to European countries and the West".
He said that Iraq and Germany were expected to reach "an understanding on the export of crude oil" while Baghdad would purchase German technology and equipment.
Merz said that the main focus for Iraqi-German cooperation is the economy.
"Many German companies are now active in Iraq. They are developing new solutions, for example for energy supply," he said, adding that "the best example is an agreement on Iraq's electricity supply, which we will sign today".
Merz also expressed his concerns after Yemen's Houthis cemented their control over the Bab al-Mandab waterway at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital route for Saudi oil exports.
"This further exacerbates the situation in the energy markets and also affects Germany," he said.

Israeli drone helicopter clears key U.S. flight hurdle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:44:24 UTC
01:44:24 KST

- Steadicopter's Black Eagle 50E unmanned helicopter completed Nevada UASTS airworthiness validation, building on FAA authorizations covering more than 8,100 square miles.
- The milestone lets Steadicopter and U.S. partner flyAlchemy move toward sustained flight testing, training and mission evaluations in the United States.
Israeli drone maker Steadicopter has cleared a regulatory hurdle needed to expand operations of its Black Eagle 50E unmanned helicopter in the United States, the company announced Sept. 15, 2026.
The aircraft completed an airworthiness validation process run by the Nevada Unmanned Aircraft Systems Test Site, based at the University of Nevada, Reno.
The Nevada test site issued an Airworthiness Statement covering all Black Eagle 50E aircraft operated in the U.S. by Alchemy Analytics, doing business as flyAlchemy, Steadicopter’s U.S. demonstration and operational readiness partner. The validation complements a separate set of FAA Certificates of Waiver or Authorization that already let the aircraft fly across designated areas totaling more than 8,100 square miles (21,000 square kilometers).
Together, the two approvals give Steadicopter a legal and technical basis to move beyond one-off demonstration flights toward sustained flight testing, training, and mission evaluations in the U.S., the company said.
“This milestone represents an important step in establishing a sustained U.S. operational capability for the Black Eagle 50E,” said Noam Lidor, CEO of Steadicopter. “The Nevada UASTS process and FAA operational authorizations provide the foundation to move beyond initial demonstrations and evaluate the platform against real customer and mission requirements, while reinforcing our long-term commitment to the U.S. market.”
The Black Eagle 50E is an electric, vertical-takeoff-and-landing helicopter drone that Steadicopter first introduced in 2022. It has a maximum takeoff weight of 50 kg (110 pounds) and can carry up to 30 kg (66 pounds) of combined payload and battery weight, with a flight endurance of about two hours. Its electric motor, in place of the gasoline engines used on earlier Steadicopter models, cuts the aircraft’s overall weight and frees up capacity for additional sensors or longer missions. The Israeli Navy became one of the aircraft’s first military customers, ordering the type in 2022 for coastal security and maritime surveillance work.
Because the Black Eagle 50E takes off and lands vertically, it does not need a runway, which Steadicopter says makes it suited for operations from small vessels, remote sites, or confined areas. The company is positioning the U.S. program around defense and security work, along with intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, public safety, critical infrastructure monitoring, remote sensing, and emergency response.
flyAlchemy has been running Steadicopter’s U.S. flight operations from Reno-Stead Airport in Nevada, handling everything from regulatory paperwork and aircraft staging to mission planning and customer demonstrations.
“Completing the Nevada UASTS airworthiness process, together with the FAA operating areas already established, provides a strong operational foundation for the Black Eagle 50E in the United States,” said Conrad Wright, founder of Alchemy Analytics. “This work allows us to move beyond simply demonstrating the aircraft and begin evaluating complete mission capabilities against real U.S. customer requirements, from payload selection and integration through training, mission-specific demonstrations and operational evaluations.”
Steadicopter and flyAlchemy said they now plan to expand engagement with U.S. customers and partners, run mission-specific demonstrations, integrate additional payload options, and seek further operating area approvals as demand develops.

British-held asylum seeker dies by apparent suicide in Eswatini
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:43:19 UTC
01:43:19 KST

Share & more
A Sri Lankan Tamil asylum seeker detained by the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) administration for nearly five years died by apparent suicide on 13 September in Mbabane, Eswatini’s largest city, according to local news reports and relatives of the deceased.
His death comes two years after the BIOT administration granted him international protection, preventing his forcible return to Sri Lanka, during which time he lived in a legal limbo in multiple countries.
Kishanth Peramaiya, 36, was one of 89 Tamil asylum seekers who had fled Sri Lanka and India before being rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when their fishing vessel faltered near the British-held island of Diego Garcia, which lies within BIOT.
Hundreds of additional arrivals followed on later vessels, most of whom agreed to return to Sri Lanka or left by boat to Mauritius or the French island of Réunion. Around 60 remained in BIOT custody, living in a fenced tent camp in Diego Garcia’s tightly controlled UK-US military facility. They faced rat infestations, deteriorating psychological and medical conditions, and the threat of being prosecuted or shot if they violated strict movement restrictions.
Most were approved to enter the UK in November 2024. The following month, the BIOT Supreme Court ruled their detention on the island had been unlawful. But Kishanth was one of three members of the group denied entry to the UK because they had been convicted of crimes or were under criminal investigation during their detention. Another is serving the remainder of a three-year prison sentence in Montserrat for sexual offences against a child; and the third appeared to be serving a sentence on Diego Garcia for an undisclosed crime as of April 2026.
Kishanth’s case, according to analysis by the London-based GSC Solicitors, “underscores the complexities of balancing humanitarian considerations with public safety concerns”. His transfer to Eswatini and subsequent death raise further questions about how the UK government decided to address these complexities, particularly since his suicidality was known to UK authorities for years.
Local media in Eswatini have reported that his transfer to the country was permanent. If confirmed, it would appear to be the first publicly documented instance of an asylum seeker being granted international protection by a British authority before being permanently resettled in a different country.
The closest precedent was a 2022 plan to send asylum seekers from the UK to Rwanda for processing and potential resettlement. This faced legal challenges and was scrapped in 2024 before transfers began. Three asylum seekers sent from Diego Garcia to Rwanda in 2023 for medical treatment said they were harassed or threatened there, including by a hospital worker.
The New Humanitarian spoke by phone on 15 September to Kishanth’s relatives in India, which hosts a large, effectively stateless Sri Lankan Tamil population. His mother said he was transferred from Diego Garcia to the Maldives six months ago because of the US-Iran war. A month later, she said, he was brought to Eswatini, where he received two successive three-month visas, the second of which was due to expire on 20 September.
Swaziland News reported in July that an agreement between the UK and Eswatini governments allowed Kishanth to stay in the country permanently.
“At the end of the period of up to three years, the UK will no longer cover any costs of the continued presence of the Relocated Migrant in Eswatini. The Relocated Migrant is expected to be self-sustaining as a member of Eswatini society,” reads an excerpt of the agreement, according to the local outlet.
An Eswatini lawmaker criticised the country’s prime minister for turning the country into a “dumping ground” by admitting a “delinquent” from Sri Lanka.
On 15 September, the Times of Eswatini reported that a Sri Lankan national “was found hanging from the rafters at a guest house” the previous weekend, prompting a police investigation.
The New Humanitarian has approached the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the BIOT administration for clarification on Kishanth’s status in Eswatini and the circumstances surrounding his death.
Toufique Hossain of Duncan Lewis Solicitors, which represented Kishanth in legal challenges to the UK and BIOT governments, said he was not authorised to comment.
Kishanth had been “tortured, sexually assaulted and abused” by Sri Lankan military personnel before fleeing to India in 2007. He was one of eight members of the Diego Garcia group to be granted international protection on the basis of individual assessments, some on similar grounds.
But he was barred from entering the UK with the rest of the group because of a series of criminal convictions: sexually assaulting another asylum seeker four times, assaulting and harming a security officer who tried to intervene in his suicide attempt, and arson “in connection with an attempted suicide by self-immolation”.
“Whilst we understand the need to separate him from the community, his right to privacy and to be accommodated in a humane and dignified manner must be upheld.”
In response to his behaviour and unravelling mental state, BIOT authorities kept him separate from the rest of the asylum seeker group. He was confined for around eight months in a laundry room with only supervised access to other areas of the compound and two weeks alone in a police cell with no natural light.
Following a late 2023 monitoring visit, UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, said it was “deeply concerned” by the conditions of his detention, citing his sleeping area’s exposure to noise, shower leaks, and toilet smells.
“Whilst we understand the need to separate him from the community, his right to privacy and to be accommodated in a humane and dignified manner must be upheld,” the monitoring team said in a 2024 report.
Throughout his detention, he attempted suicide numerous times, sometimes in quick succession, prompting medical evacuation to Bahrain in 2024, according to court records.
The New Humanitarian spoke briefly with Kishanth following his return to Diego Garcia from medical treatment in Rwanda in 2023. In broken English, he described receiving “not correct treatment”, “no sleeping”, and being confined to a “military area”.
Another asylum seeker recalled witnessing him “walking alone”, “seeing dreams”, “screaming at night”, and threatening to harm himself with a shard of a broken mirror.
A psychiatrist quoted in 2024 court proceedings said “it is very difficult for him to be so isolated for an indefinite period”, and ending his isolation “would hugely improve his mental health”.
In 2025, a UK court dismissed Kishanth’s legal challenge to being barred from the country, allowing the government to base its decision on public safety concerns.
With return to Sri Lanka ruled out and the UK refusing him admission, his only remaining solution was relocation to a third country.
His mother told The New Humanitarian he sounded depressed when they spoke on 13 September, the same day his body was found. She had asked him to come back to India. Seemingly unaware or disbelieving his stay in Eswatini was permanent, he told his mother he was planning on waiting there for a few days before being sent to a third country.

Court relaxes restrictions on Zelensky's ex-chief of staff amid reports on his continued influence
A Ukrainian court on Sept. 15 allowed Andriy Yermak, former head of the President’s Office, not to wear an electronic monitoring bracelet.
The ruling comes amid media reports that Yermak kept his political influence on President Volodymyr Zelensky after resigning in November amid a corruption investigation.
The move also followed an earlier court ruling that eased the restrictions on Yermak. Initially Yermak could not travel beyond Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast without investigators’ approval. But in August the court allowed him to travel to several other regions.
The decision on the electronic bracelet was made by the High Anti-Corruption Court on medical grounds. The court did not elaborate.
Medical conditions that could prevent someone from wearing an electronic bracelet include having a pacemaker, a risk of blood clots, and allergic reactions.
"Everyone here seems perfectly healthy until they become a suspect," Tetiana Shevchuk, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, quipped. "Then the stress of being under suspicion kicks in, and suddenly they get sick."
She told the Kyiv Independent that law enforcement agencies can still keep suspects without a bracelet under surveillance.
But the absence of a bracelet "makes their job more difficult, especially when suspects have private security or, as was already the case with Yermak, protection provided by the state security services," she said.
In November 2025, Yermak’s office was searched as part of a case into an alleged $100 million corruption scheme involving state nuclear power company Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky’s tenure. Yermak resigned as Zelensky’s chief of staff following the searches.
In May, he was charged with money laundering tied to the construction of a luxury residential compound outside Kyiv.
Suspects in the Energoatom case allegedly gave money to ex-Deputy Prime Minister Oleksiy Chernyshov for the construction of the compound, according to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau.
Yermak was released on Hr 140 million ($3.1 million) bail in May.
However, media reports suggest that he still wields some political influence.
Ukrainian news outlet Dzerkalo Tyzhnya reported in December 2025, citing its sources, that Yermak continued to communicate with Zelensky regularly and kept his political influence. Ukrainska Pravda reported in February that Yermak had met several top officials since his resignation.
Meanwhile, Yermak officially resumed his legal practice in January. He also became the head of a committee of Ukraine's National Association of Lawyers in March.
Yevhen Korniychuk, Ukraine's ambassador to Israel, and Yermak's lawyer Ihor Fomin flew from Chisinau to Tel Aviv in January, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
Fomin met Israeli lawyer Boris Lemper, who allegedly provides legal services to Timur Mindich, the alleged ringleader of the Energoatom scheme, according to footage published by Ukrainska Pravda.
Fomin told Ukrainska Pravda that he was acquainted with Lemper and confirmed that he visited Israel. He declined to comment on whom he met there.
In July Ukrainska Pravda also reported, citing its sources, that Yermak had lobbied for Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Yermak and will publish his response once it is received. His lawyer Fomin declined to comment.

Dutch firm to design crew quarters for new Orka-class submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:40:08 UTC
01:40:08 KST

- Royal IHC and Naval Group signed a contract Sept. 15, 2026, covering the design of living quarters for the Royal Netherlands Navy's Orka-class submarines.
- The deal follows a broader 2025 agreement and falls under a program to replace the navy's four Walrus-class submarines starting in the mid-2030s.
A Dutch shipbuilder has landed the job of designing where submarine crews will sleep, eat and live during long stretches under the sea. Royal IHC and France’s Naval Group signed a contract Sept. 15, 2026, covering the living quarters on board the Royal Netherlands Navy’s new Orka-class submarines.
It sounds like a modest piece of a much bigger puzzle, and it is. But living quarters on a submarine are not a side detail. A crew can spend weeks submerged with no natural light and limited space to move, so how those quarters are laid out affects morale, rest and, ultimately, how well a crew can do its job on a long patrol. Under the new contract, Royal IHC will handle the design work first, with production and installation of the finished module following in a later phase.
The living-quarters deal is part of a much larger effort. Royal IHC is one of several Dutch companies working under Naval Group as part of Team Orka, the industrial network the French shipbuilder has assembled to build the Netherlands’ next generation of submarines. That broader program traces back to September 2024, when the Dutch government signed a delivery agreement with Naval Group to build four new submarines, replacing the navy’s aging Walrus-class boats. The new vessels will be named Orka, Zwaardvis, Barracuda and Tijgerhaai. A Dutch government estimate at the time put the total investment budget for the program, covering construction of all four submarines and related costs through 2039, at roughly €5.6 billion, or about $6.2 billion.
Royal IHC’s relationship with Naval Group on this program did not start with Monday’s contract. The two companies signed a broader agreement in June 2025 covering steel structures and modular construction work for the submarines, building on a partnership that goes back to 2018. This week’s deal narrows that cooperation down to one specific piece of the build: the crew’s living spaces.
“The signing of this contract is an important milestone for Royal IHC,” said Eric Gret, director of defence at Royal IHC.
“Naval Group’s confidence in our expertise and manufacturing capabilities confirms the strength of our organisation. We are proud to be contributing to the Orka-class submarines and look forward with confidence to our continued future collaboration with Naval Group in the construction of complete modules,” Gret said.
Naval Group’s Dutch country director framed the contract in similar terms, describing it as evidence that the French company’s promise to bring Dutch industry into the program is being kept in practice rather than staying on paper.
“For Naval Group, collaboration with Dutch industrial partners is a key part of the programme,” said Mark Donderwinkel, country director Netherlands at Naval Group. “Royal IHC brings proven maritime expertise and experience in complex projects. This first contract represents an important step in our joint commitment to providing modern, reliable and future-proof submarine capability for the Royal Netherlands Navy.”
Timing-wise, the Netherlands is not expecting these submarines overnight. Naval Group is due to deliver the first two boats, Orka and Zwaardvis, within 10 years of the original 2024 agreement, meaning the mid-2030s at the earliest. The remaining two vessels, Barracuda and Tijgerhaai, will follow after that. Neither company said Monday how long the design phase for the living quarters will take, what the module’s final layout will include, or what this particular piece of the contract is worth. Those details, like much of the day-to-day progress on a submarine program that will stretch for years, are likely to emerge gradually as construction moves forward.

Russia’s Irkutsk region is culling livestock over what officials call lumpy skin disease, but local farmers suspect foot-and-mouth disease
The BBC Russian Service has published a report on the mass culling of livestock in Russia’s Irkutsk region, where authorities say animals are being seized and killed because of a lumpy skin disease outbreak.
Agriculture Ministry rules require that animals with lumpy skin disease be isolated and treated, while livestock with foot-and-mouth disease must be killed to prevent its spread. Many local farmers suspect a foot-and-mouth disease outbreak.
Residents of villages under quarantine have accused veterinary authorities of a lack of transparency. Several residents of the village of Butyrki told reporters that they had signed nondisclosure agreements but had not received copies.
Veterinarians do not show owners their animals’ test results. They prepare vaccine doses inside their vehicles, then approach the animals with prefilled syringes. Owners receive no vaccination records, so they cannot be certain which disease their animals are being vaccinated against. One farmer told the BBC that the symptoms of lumpy skin disease and foot-and-mouth disease differ substantially and are impossible to confuse.
Butyrki residents have complained that veterinarians do not change their work clothes between farm visits, contributing to the disease’s spread. Witnesses say the carcasses of killed animals are sometimes found lying by the roadside. The carcasses are burned in a pit near the Sarafanka River, meaning the remains could enter the river through groundwater. The pit was initially supposed to be closer to homes but was moved after protests.
In the spring of 2026, animals were culled en masse in the Novosibirsk region. Authorities blamed a pasteurellosis outbreak, but an independent laboratory later detected foot-and-mouth disease in one of the cows. Mass culling began in the Kemerovo region in May. Officials again blamed lumpy skin disease, while local residents suspected foot-and-mouth disease.

Taiwan study shows ongoing natural selection shaping disease susceptibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

A study by researchers at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) has documented ongoing natural selection shaping disease susceptibility among Taiwan’s contemporary population.
The study analyzed genetic data from 72,635 Han Taiwanese individuals using the Taiwan Biobank, a national biomedical research database, NYCU said in a news release issued yesterday.
By comparing frequencies of genetic variants (known as allele frequency) across different age groups, the team identified 168 variants that appeared to be undergoing natural selection, including 159 variants that showed a gradual decline or disappearance across generations, the university said.
Photo courtesy of NYCU
Researchers noted a "consistent signal" involving red blood cell traits, with 149 variants that were decreasing in frequency among younger age groups associated with larger red blood cell volume and lower hemoglobin concentration, NYCU said.
Such a consistent pattern suggested that natural selection was progressively reducing the prevalence of genetic variants associated with larger red blood cell volume.
Researchers hypothesized that this trend was related to historical adaptation to infectious diseases such as malaria, which was widespread in Taiwan until about 60 years ago.
This type of natural selection, in which genetic variations detrimental to survival are gradually removed over successive generations, is known as "purifying selection," NYCU said.
Meanwhile, the team also identified traces of natural selection in genes related to DNA repair and cancer, the news release said.
One of these, a BRCA1 haplotype carrying multiple pathogenic (disease-causing) variants, was found to be decreasing in frequency among younger generations, NYCU said.
Knowledge of such rare and population-specific pathogenic variants could bring benefits in areas such as disease risk assessment and precision medicine, it added.
The study was led by Ko Wen-ya (可文亞), associate professor in NYCU’s Department of Life Sciences and Institute of Genome Sciences, in collaboration with Yoko Satta of the Graduate University of Advanced Studies in Japan.
It was published in the American Journal of Human Genetics in July.

The broken vows that endanger US, allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

When US President Donald Trump in January urged Iranians to “take over your institutions” and promised that “help is on its way,” he presumably meant American help for the protesters.
However, the ill-timed and uncoordinated US bombing campaign that came only after 50,000 Iranians were murdered in the streets seemed more like a trick to lure them into a death trap.
Instead, the help that was on the way came from China, not from the US, and it went not to the Iranian people, but to the regime that was killing and otherwise oppressing them.
It is little wonder that despite Trump’s mystification, his renewed call last week for another attempt at an unarmed overthrow of the regime has so far gone unheeded. The tragic irony is that the Trump administration and the Iranian people clearly want the end of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ criminal rule, but their respective efforts to bring it about are entirely at sixes and sevens.
Trump still refuses to apply serious pressure on Beijing to halt its deadly material support for the Iranian regime despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) promise to him to refrain from doing so. For his part, Trump is more interested in pursuing a supposedly lucrative trade deal with China than in demanding that it stop providing Teheran with life support. So Beijing is free to continue aiding a US enemy and distracting Washington from focusing on its main security challenges from China and Russia.
It is not the first time Xi has deceived a US president into believing his empty promises and jeopardizing Washington’s national security interest in the process.
Asked in his first term whether he had been “duped” by Xi about the danger COVID-19 presented to the American public, Trump said he had a “great relationship” with Xi who assured him that COVID-19 presented no serious risk to Americans — as 1 million perished and the lives of millions of others, and the entire US economy, were severely disrupted.
Even before Trump’s tenure, Xi had falsely assured former US president Barack Obama that China would not militarize the artificial islands it built in the South China Sea, imperiling US friends and allies Taiwan, Japan, the Philippines, Australia and others.
Most recently, Xi told Trump that China would not invade Taiwan while Trump is in office.
However, even if Xi honors his word more faithfully than he has previous strategic commitments, there are two large loopholes in his pledge of restraint.
If Trump leaves office for health or other reasons before his term expires in January 2029, Xi could attack Taiwan and still tell the world he kept his word.
His second escape hatch, even while Trump remains in office, is that China, instead of openly attacking Taiwan, could impose a crippling blockade on it and put the onus for initiating hostilities on Trump, triggering yet a second war by the president who promised no more such overseas conflicts.
Would Trump risk US Navy ships and personnel to break the blockade?
Xi might be willing to bet that Trump would prefer to engage in protracted negotiations to demonstrate his vaunted deal-making skills, but what he would be trading away for the illusion of peace would be Taiwan’s national security and sovereignty.
Joseph Bosco served as China country director for the US defense secretary in 2005 and 2006, and as Asia-Pacific director of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief in 2009 and 2010.

Taiwan ranks 7th in civil participation globally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

Taiwan ranked seventh globally in civil participation last year and showed notable improvements in the effective parliament category, a report published yesterday by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA) said.
The Stockholm-based intergovernmental organization’s annual Global State of Democracy Report assesses effective representation, rights, rule of law, civil participation and judicial systems in democracies worldwide.
This year’s report found that last year 57 percent of the 173 countries assessed “suffered a decline in at least one factor of democratic performance compared with their own performance five years earlier.”
Photo: Chen Kuan-pei, Taipei Times
Taiwan ranked seventh in civic participation, tied with Finland, the same ranking as it received in last year’s report.
Only 13 countries showed improvement in measures of parliamentary effectiveness, including five in Asia and the Pacific: Taiwan, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tajikistan and Thailand, the report said.
Taiwan and the US “fell from high to mid-range performance” in the judicial independence category last year, with Argentina, Belgium, India and Nigeria’s performance also declining, it said.
The report also highlighted regional security and geopolitical pressures, saying that border tensions and conflict-related incidents involving India and Pakistan, Cambodia and Thailand, and the Taiwan Strait last year affected regional stability.
“Regional stability and the risk that securitized pressures will shape democratic governance” would be important factors to watch, it said.
Furthermore, the US “is experiencing a period of marked democratic decline,” the report said.
The US saw seven statistically significant declines from 2020 through last year across the access to justice, economic equality, effective parliament, freedom of expression, freedom of the press, free political parties and judicial independence categories, the report said.
Apart from free political parties, “these factors are now at their lowest-ever levels in the history of” the Global State of Democracy dataset, which began in 1975, it added.
The US “has emboldened authoritarian leaders” under the leadership of US President Donald Trump, as his administration has abandoned certain democratic values and detracted from the rules-based international order, the report said.
“Patient zero of this global epidemic is the current president of the United States,” International IDEA secretary-general Kevin Casas-Zamora, former vice president of Costa Rica, told Agence France-Presse.
“What happened in the US in 2020 has really had a global impact in terms of legitimizing this kind of attack on the credibility of the electoral process,” Casas-Zamora said of Trump’s refusal to acknowledge his defeat in the election against former US president Joe Biden.
“Arguments that were used to gut and close down the US Agency for International Development were used in Serbia by the government to clamp down on civil society organizations,” he added.
International IDEA was established in 1995 by 14 founding member states to promote electoral processes and monitor the functioning of democratic systems.
It has more than 30 member states, although the US withdrew as an observer this year.

Medical visits for flu and enterovirus climb: CDC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

Medical visits for flu-like illnesses and enterovirus increased last week, while COVID-19 cases stayed at a high level, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday, while seven new cases of acute viral hepatitis C traced to a clinic in New Taipei City were also confirmed.
CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Deputy Director Lee Chia-lin (李佳琳) said there were 136,796 medical visits for flu-like illnesses from Sept. 6 to Saturday last week, a 16.5 percent increase from the previous week.
As 12 percent of the cases were emergency room visits, the flu is still defined as in an epidemic period, Lee said.
Photo: CNA
There were 92 severe flu cases and 21 flu-related deaths confirmed in the seven-day period, the highest weekly death count this flu season, which began in October last year, she said.
Influenza A(H1N1) is the dominant flu strain spreading in local communities, accounting for 82.2 percent of positive tests in the past four weeks, she said.
Medical visits for COVID-19 were down 13.3 percent to 17,847 last week, although COVID-19 activity remains at a high level and is still in the epidemic period, with 53 severe cases and 18 deaths confirmed, Lee said.
The dominant strains spreading locally are NB.1.8.1, accounting for 51.9 percent, and PQ.16.1.1 at 44.4 percent in the past four weeks, she added.
CDC physician Lin Yung-ching (林詠青) said the youngest severe flu case last week was a one-year-old boy who received a flu vaccine in October last year.
He began having upper respiratory symptoms including a fever, coughing and runny nose early this month, Lin said.
The boy was admitted to a hospital, where he developed convulsions and lethargy, Lin said, adding that the boy tested positive for influenza A.
The child was diagnosed with influenza-related encephalitis, or acute brain edema, and transferred to an intensive care unit, Lin said.
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said the centers estimates that flu cases would continue to increase, reaching a weekly peak number around Mid-Autumn Festival on Friday next week, with an estimated 150,000 to 160,000 medical visits in a week.
Meanwhile, medical visits for enterovirus infection increased to 10,203 last week, with the new school semester starting this month, an 18.1 percent increase from the week before, Lee said.
The CDC predicts that enterovirus would enter its epidemic period this week, with cases continuing to rise, reaching a peak of about 12,000 to 14,000 weekly cases by the end of the month, Lin Min-cheng said.
In the next two to three weeks, the seasonal flu, enterovirus infections and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections are expected to remain at high levels, while COVID-19 cases might gradually drop, he said.
As many people will be gathering with relatives and friends over the Mid-Autumn Festival, the CDC urges everyone to practice good hand hygiene and cough etiquette, as well as to pay attention to food hygiene by thoroughly cooking meat and seafood, and avoid cross contamination of raw and cooked food, he said.
Regarding a hepatitis C cluster associated with injections at Antai Songhe Clinic (安泰淞鶴診所), among 1,118 people who had injections at the clinic between January and last month, 530 had been tested as of Monday, Lin Min-cheng said.
Seven additional cases were confirmed — two with mild symptoms and five asymptomatic — bringing the total to 20, he said, adding that the centers estimate the positivity rate might range between 5 and 10 percent after the blood tests are completed.

TSMC careful about use of AI in sensitive research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) remains conservative about utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) to process sensitive data, aiming to mitigate leakage and subsequent damage given the technology’s capabilities, TSMC co-chief operating officer Y.J. Mii (米玉傑) said at a forum in Taipei yesterday.
TSMC exercises caution and prudence when deploying AI to process sensitive information, particularly about research and development, given risks of data leakage and data corruption if AI was not properly used, Mii said.
His remarks came after Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to slow the development of the most advanced AI models amid growing concern over serious risks. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI boss Elon Musk voiced a rare agreement with Amodei, backing calls to slow down frontier AI development for safety.
Photo: Lin Yi-ju, Taipei Times
Mii called AI a “three-year-old superman,” which is immensely powerful, yet completely unaware of the damage it can cause and has no inherent sense of right and wrong.
To mitigate risk, safe and prudent deployment of AI is critical, he said.
AI excels at gathering large amounts of information, but falls short in making critical decisions for humans or solving advanced technological challenges, which require navigating “unknown” territory at least over the next few years, Mii said. Though AI offers vast amounts of data and advice, humans always have the final call, he said.
At TSMC, engineers are encouraged to leverage AI’s capabilities in designing electronic design automation systems, as microprocessors containing hundreds of billions of transistors are required to be optimized, where AI can be brought into full play, Mii said.
AI’s utility remains less useful in developing next-gen technology, such as A14 or A10 technology, which requires navigating “many unknown” challenges, he said.
As the semiconductor industry advances beyond 7 nanometers, it can no longer rely on technologies based on Moore’s Law and instead requires innovation, he added.
As an enterprise, TSMC must ensure its investment yields sufficient commercial value before fully committing to next-generation technologies, Mii said.
It usually takes about 30 minute discussions to make a decision, leveraging the research team’s collective intelligence, he said. That is a vital factor behind the company’s success, he added.
Asked about a scenario where TSMC ceases to exist, Mii said it would pose risks for the world as countless high-tech applications fundamentally rely on TSMC’s advanced process technologies.
Without TSMC, Taiwan would likely develop an alternative, yet equally critical, high-value sector, even if its market value is smaller, he said.

Two doctors were handed suspended sentences yesterday after they allowed three medical device vendors to participate in 13 neurological surgeries at Taichung Veterans General Hospital between March 2023 and October last year.
The Taichung District Court sentenced Yang Meng-yin (楊孟寅), former director of the hospital’s oncology neurosurgery division, and Cheng Wen-yu (鄭文郁), former director of minimally invasive neurosurgery, to one year and four months, and one year and two months respectively. Both sentences were suspended for four years.
The three medical vendors, who did not hold physician qualifications, pleaded guilty and received sentences of one year, eight months and eight months suspended for three years. All five verdicts may be appealed.
Photo: Tsai Shu-yuan, Taipei Times
As the doctors admitted to the offenses and reached settlements with the victims, they asked the court to grant them suspended sentences.
The court said that Yang and Cheng had reached settlements with all of the victims.
In January, the Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office indicted Yang, Cheng and the three medical device suppliers on suspicion of fraud under the Criminal Code and contraventions of the Physicians Act (醫師法).
The indictment alleged that Yang and Cheng allowed the three vendors to illegally perform medical procedures such as bone screw implants, electrocoagulation and tissue extraction during surgeries such as endoscopic spinal fusion operations.
The procedures seriously endangered the patients’ lives and physical safety, and compromised the quality of medical care, prosecutors said.
The investigation found that Yang and Cheng were seeking to reduce their workload and consolidate their working relationships with the medical device suppliers.
The five defendants also applied to the National Health Insurance Administration for consultation and surgical fees, despite knowing that procedures performed by unlicensed people are not eligible for coverage, the indictment said.

Institute touts DNA sampler module’s work under the sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:51 UTC
01:37:51 KST

Scientists have invented a DNA sampler module to collect residual deep-sea genetic material for biological surveys and long-term maritime ecology monitoring, the Taiwan Oceanic Research Institute said in a statement yesterday.
A test of the module identified 365 species in waters southwest of Taiwan proper, the institute said.
The deep-sea high-flow environmental DNA module — a suitcase-sized machine when deployed with its dedicated platform — is a boon to deep oceanic research, as it could sample trace amounts of genetic material from cells, tissue fragments and excretions, it said.
Photo courtesy of the National Applied Research Laboratories
Deep-sea exploration poses steep challenges stemming from high pressures, low temperatures and low bio-density, the institute said.
Trawling nets could be deployed to collect samples, but they are inefficient and disruptive to the fragile ecology of the deep sea, which makes the module a valuable scientific tool, it said.
The module consists of a pressure-resistant motor, a peristaltic pump — which allows precision and keeps the risk of pollution low — and a filter that can be adjusted to the size of the targeted sample, it said.
It can filter more than 100 liters of seawater per hour, it can be programmed to collect samples at scheduled times and can be retrieved with a near-zero environmental footprint, the institute said.
The module uses third-generation genetic sequencing technology, doing away with the inaccuracies arising from polymerase chain reaction amplification, it said.
The module tested its capabilities during the trial, in which it collected 22 million DNA sequences and enabled the identification of hundreds of species of fish, mollusks, crustaceans, corals, sea stars and sea urchins during the trial, the institute said.
The institute said that it plans to deploy more of the modules to conduct biodiversity research, ocean environmental conservation, fisheries resource management and long-term ecological observation.

Lake weeds meet traditional art in Kashmir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:50 UTC
01:37:50 KST

A Kashmiri artisan is turning weeds pulled from Srinagar’s famous Dal Lake into a new ingredient for the centuries-old craft of papier-mache, one of Kashmir’s best-known traditional art forms.
Dal Lake is famed for its floating gardens and houseboats against a Himalayan backdrop.
Among its past visitors was Beatles guitarist George Harrison, who stayed on a houseboat in 1966 and met sitar maestro Ravi Shankar.
Photo: AFP
However, the lake has long struggled with heavy growth of aquatic weeds, which Indian authorities regularly remove to keep its waterways clear.
Simran Irshad, 35, began experimenting with weeds after the rising cost of paper made traditional papier-mache increasingly expensive.
With roots in Persian craftsmanship, Kashmir’s papier-mache is known for brightly painted boxes, trays and ornaments decorated with intricate floral, bird and paisley motifs — as well as Christmas ornaments exported worldwide.
Irshad searched for a cheaper, locally available material and eventually turned to aquatic vegetation regularly cleared from the lake as waste.
After months of experimentation, she developed a technique using dried and pulverized weeds mixed with recycled paper pulp and a binding agent to create the material.
“For the past 100 years this craft has been done this way, using only paper,” Irshad said.
“Why not use something that can increase production, make it durable and also make it cheaper?” she said.
Irshad collects the weeds by boat before drying and processing them at her workshop.
She tested different vegetation before finding the lake weeds most suitable because of their higher moisture content.
“Paper comes from trees, trees are cut down to make paper,” she said. “What I am removing from the lake is like a treasure given to me by God.”
She has trained about 50 women to make paper products, with 15 currently working with her on the weed-based craft.
Irshad hopes to expand the initiative, but said she needs more support to provide work for additional women.

Japan readies for thousands of athletes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:48 UTC
01:37:48 KST

The Asian Games open in Japan on Saturday with 2028 Olympics places up for grabs, fast-rising talents of world sport in action and thousands of athletes staying on a cruise ship in typhoon season.
More than 17,000 competitors and officials are expected at the continent’s biggest sporting spectacular, which takes place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture until October 4.
The number of participants — more than the Olympics — has heavily taxed the organizers, who initially expected 15,000 people and have had to scramble to find accommodation for the rest.
Photo: AP
They choose from the outset to house athletes in temporary accommodation in a bid to cut costs, ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to hotel rooms.
Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes and officials are to stay aboard the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena which usually features 571 cabins. The Costa Serena is the sister ship of the Costa Concordia, which ran aground and sank off Tuscany in 2012, killing 32 people.
Cruise ships have been used as accommodation at international sporting events before, but never at this scale.
Photo: AFP
The unusual accommodation plans have been met with concern by some countries, with India building its own replica container huts to brace athletes for their stay.
On Monday, South Korean sports officials branded the facilities as “the worst” accommodation ever at the Games, adding that the beds were too short for the athletes.
With just days to go, a South Korean Olympic committee official said that there was “a serious shortage of accommodation.”
Reports of tents serving as dressing rooms and distant washroom facilities have also left some of the teams unimpressed.
Organizers have repeated that everyone would have a bed and that they are confident that Japan’s typhoon season in September and October would not dampen the party.
Weather has already disrupted preparations, with record rainfall forcing athletes to evacuate their accommodation briefly last week.
Rainwater leaked into some competition venues, although organizers said there was no serious damage. More rain is forecast this week.
Athletes from 45 countries and territories are competing in more than 40 sports across the two weeks.
Basketball and soccer are already under way, with several more events set to start before Saturday’s glittering opening ceremony.
Olympics staples such as athletics and swimming sit side-by-side with regional favorites such as sepak takraw and kabaddi.
In a bid to attract a new audience there would be eSports, breakdancing and BMX cycling. Padel and MMA would make their Asian Games debuts.
The Games function as qualifiers for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics in seven sports including surfing, tennis, archery and squash.
Among those competing would be Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala and a pair of prodigies in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.
“I love playing and competing with the Philippine team,” said Eala, who is skipping the China Open to take part.
Taiwanese boxer Lin Yu-ting is competing, two years after she won Paris Olympics gold in the middle of a gender row that saw her eligibility questioned.
Japan looks to their Olympic champions for success, with gymnast Shinnosuke Oka and javelin thrower Haruka Kitaguchi entering the competition.
North Korea is sending more than 100 athletes competing across 14 sports, aiming to “bring joy to Marshal Kim Jong-un.”
China again expects to top the medals table after winning a whopping 201 golds and 383 medals on home soil in Hangzhou at the epidemic-delayed Games in 2023.
They are sending more than 800 athletes, including 36 Olympic champions.
“We would showcase China’s standard and strength on the regional and global stage,” diver Wang Zongyuan said.
Sooryavanshi would be part of an India cricket team looking to make a statement before the sport returns to the Olympics in LA after an absence of 128 years.
India might face bitter rivals Pakistan in the final at Nagoya’s new purpose-built cricket ground.
Even younger than Sooryavanshi is Chinese swimming sensation Yu Zidi, who won a world championships medal aged 12 last year.
Eala, the rising 21-year-old tennis star from the Philippines, is hunting gold, as is Pakistan’s Paris Olympics javelin champion Arshad Nadeem.

The lopsided victory was largely powered by the team’s precision long-range shooting. Of the 17 three-pointers, seven came in the opening quarter, giving Taiwan an early 26-12 lead. Boosted by 40 percent shooting from long range, Taiwan also held an edge over Qatar in assists (26-13), committed fewer turnovers (6-14) and steals (9-3). NETHERLANDS
Rail outage hits rush hour
A major outage early yesterday hit parts of the railway system and the company that maintains the nation’s rail infrastructure said it was treating the cause as possible sabotage. The stoppages affected thousands of passengers mainly in the central and eastern areas of the country, but the problem also affected some services in the busiest western regions. Joke van der Cruysen, a spokesperson for infrastructure company Prorail, said there were disruptions at 24 locations. “Material has been found at several locations. It appears that this material was deliberately placed on the tracks. We suspect sabotage,” she said in a telephone interview. “The police are currently involved and are actively investigating the cause and the reasons behind this.” There was no immediate indication of who was suspected of being behind the apparent sabotage.
Photo: EPA
SWITZERLAND
Gaza bodies raise concerns
The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said yesterday. The remains of what appeared to be entire families were being unearthed from sites destroyed during Israeli attacks, he said, adding that many victims were women and children. “It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed,” he said in a statement. The discoveries have revived concerns raised in a 2024 UN report that found Israeli strikes on residential buildings and other civilian sites during the early weeks of the war might have violated international humanitarian law, he said.
AUSTRALIA
Serial killer to be released
The South Australia Court of Appeal yesterday ruled that one of three serial killers convicted over the murders of 11 people in one of the country’s most notorious criminal cases can be released from prison, rejecting a state government’s bid to block his parole. The victims were killed over seven years, and most of their bodies were found in 1999 in barrels of acid in Snowtown, a small town north of the state capital, Adelaide. The discovery led the crimes to become known as the “Bodies-in-Barrels” murders. Three judges upheld a parole board decision made last month to release the youngest of the three convicted murderers, James Vlassakis.Now 46, Vlassakis was 18 when his crimes began in 1998. He pleaded guilty to four murders, including those of a half brother and stepbrother. He became a star witness for the prosecution, and was sentenced to life with a minimum term of 26 years, which expired in August last year.
UNITED STATES
Weapons deployed in space
The Space Force on Monday said it has weapons deployed in space, confirming the presence of such capabilities in orbit for the first time. “The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” a US Space Force spokesperson said in a statement that did not provide specifics on the weapons. China “develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy,” while Russia “views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts,” the Space Force said.
