War pushing demand for long-haul flights, CAL says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:47 UTC
01:37:47 KST

Although the war between the US and Iran has pushed global oil prices higher, it has also increased demand for direct long-haul flights to Europe as people seek safer routes, China Airlines (CAL) said on Monday.
CAL president Kevin Chen (陳漢銘) said that aviation fuel prices have fluctuated significantly since February amid the ongoing US-Iran war, at one point surging to between US$190 and US$200 per barrel.
Prices fell to between US$130 and US$140 per barrel before rebounding to US$160-US$170, Chen said.
Photo: Huang Yi-ching, Taipei Times
The volatility has prompted the airline to reassess the load factor of each flight and adjust aircraft capacity accordingly, he said.
Demand in Southeast Asia for passenger and cargo services is high, prompting CAL to deploy larger aircraft on some routes to maximize cargo space and generate additional revenue, he said.
Despite high fuel prices, the airline expects revenue this year to surpass last year’s, potentially reaching a record, Chen said.
“We still have the fourth quarter to go, but I am cautiously optimistic. I believe my team will deliver results that would not disappoint anyone,” he said.
Some travel agents have expressed concern that demand for short-haul flights could outpace demand for long-haul services as rising oil prices drive up airfares.
However, many people heading to Europe used to transit through airports in the Middle East, but conflicts in the region have prompted them to opt for direct flights to Europe for safety reasons, Chen said.
CAL has benefited from the shift, as it operates six direct routes to Europe, serving Frankfurt, Germany; Amsterdam; London; Vienna; Rome and Prague, he said.
“We have also seen Taiwan emerge as a key hub amid changes in travel patterns triggered by wars, particularly for travelers from Northeast and Southeast Asia heading to North America and Europe,” he said.
“Travelers from Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan can fly to Phoenix, Arizona, Seattle or London with connections in Taiwan. The situation presents a great business opportunity for us,” Chen said.
CAL’s monthly cargo revenue is generally NT$4 billion to NT$5 billion (US$125.5 million to US$157 million), he said.
However, recent monthly cargo revenue has reached NT$7 billion to NT$8 billion, with a peak of NT$10 billion, he added.
Cargo demand has been robust, driven by exports of artificial intelligence and semiconductor-related equipment, the company said last month.

Saudi Arabia yesterday vowed to respond “firmly” to attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, after the Iran-backed fighters wounded 13 people in the kingdom in an assault using ballistic missiles and drones.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Saudi-backed government forces since Yemen’s civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
They seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait last week, which has become vital as the wider US-Iran war chokes the Strait of Hormuz.
Photo: Reuters
Saudi Arabia yesterday issued attack alerts for Mecca — the holy city’s first of the Middle East war — and Jeddah and Taif governorates, before quickly canceling them.
The Saudi Civil Defense had earlier issued short-lived air-raid alerts in six regions.
The Houthis have also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, the world’s leading crude exporter, pushing global oil prices above the US$100 threshold.
A Houthi strike in western Yemen on Monday killed eight government soldiers, two military sources said.
The group also claimed a new large-scale attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” against King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, in southern Saudi Arabia.
A Khamis Mushait resident said he heard “intense blasts” that left fires burning for a “long time.”
“Honestly, we couldn’t sleep at all,” they said.
The Riyadh-led coalition yesterday confirmed there had been missile and drone attacks the previous day on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, reporting 13 civilians wounded and damage to seven houses and two vehicles.
Saudi Arabia responded with more than 50 strikes, as it had the day before, the Houthis said.
As the attacks continue, the UN Security Council was due to meet to discuss the Houthis’ offensive, diplomatic sources said.
The coalition said it would deal with the attacks “firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom” and would take “all necessary operational measures to deter this ... hostile and extremist approach.”
While Saudi Arabia has conducted dozens of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas, it has so far failed to deter the fighters’ lightning offensive.
Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman was expected to hold talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi yesterday.
US media last week reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected a personal request from the crown prince to intervene in the war.
Trump on Saturday said the Houthis had called Washington and asked the US not to get involved.
Meanwhile, the US is facing a shortfall in ammunition as a result of its war against Iran, the US Department of Defense’s inspector general confirmed on Monday, contrasting with Trump’s assertions of full stocks.
In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to the US Congress, the inspector said that between Feb. 28 and June 30, Operation Epic Fury (OEF) had an estimated cost of US$33.4 billion, including US$22.3 billion spent on expended munitions.
“The munitions expenditure on OEF has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” the report said.

Drone academy advancing, MOFA says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:43 UTC
01:37:43 KST

The privately funded Global UAV Academy (GUAVA) is to be registered as a juridical person next week and its offices are to be set up before the end of this year, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said yesterday.
The ministry is assisting in the establishment of GUAVA, which aims to help Taiwan’s diplomatic allies build drone resilience, with the initial phase focusing on pilot training, MOFA said in a policy report submitted to the Legislative Yuan before it starts its next session on Sept. 29.
As the ministry’s drone collaboration with like-minded countries needs to go through non-governmental channels, MOFA is assisting in GUAVA’s establishment, said Department of NGO International Affairs Director-General Chiang Zhen-wei (江振瑋), who is head of the ministry’s drone diplomacy task force.
Photo: Fang Wei-li, Taipei Times
“GUAVA is an incorporated foundation and has been granted an establishment permit, so the juridical person registration is planned for next week,” he said.
Management personnel would be recommended and elected by the private sector, not designated by the ministry or the Industrial Technology Research Institute, he said.
GUAVA is to set up its offices in Taipei and Chiayi County before the end of this year, while the opening of overseas offices would depend on the needs of countries working with the organization, Chiang said.
The focus of GUAVA in its first phase would be training drone pilots, the report said.
Asked to elaborate, Chiang said that during this year’s Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting, the government signed memoranda of understanding with Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu, and Taiwan plans to begin training pilots starting with the Pacific allies from late this year or early next year.
It is estimated that the academy can train up to 30 pilots in Taiwan at the same time, he said.
They can serve as seed teachers assisting in their countries’ talent cultivation after completing training, he added.

Building floodgates rules needed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:42 UTC
01:37:42 KST

Heavy rains have battered Keelung this month, with floodwaters inundating the basements of numerous residential communities. Total losses remain difficult to estimate, while residents blame building management committees and property managers for failing to close floodgates in time.
Floodgates are standard features in many buildings, yet there are recurring stories of their use failing to prevent flooding. In addition to operational and training issues, the decisionmaking structure and emergency response capacity of apartment buildings must also be taken into account to effectively address holes in the system.
Apartment complexes generally cannot make decisions as quickly as buildings under single ownership can. Decisionmaking authority is shared equally among owners and management committees are typically only empowered to handle routine matters of maintenance and management. Building bylaws also often fail to fully authorize management committees or property managers to close floodgates when disasters strike, leaving them in an impossible position when floodwaters approach.
A driver attempting to exit the carpark after the floodgates have already closed could threaten to hold the committee responsible for losses if the gates are not opened. Conversely, someone returning home to closed gates might threaten to hold the property manager liable for any damage resulting from having to leave their vehicle outside.
Decisionmakers can find themselves caught between conflicting demands and having to close and open the gates several times.
Communities also often have no way of knowing how long it will rain, how high the water will rise or whether it is safer to leave their cars in the basement or move them to an elevated area. A local government leader who makes the wrong call in declaring a typhoon day off might face some public criticism, but apartment management committees can come under enormous pressure to directly compensate residents for their losses.
Expecting residential communities, which lack the capacity to forecast weather or assess urban hydrology, to decide when to close floodgates is a recipe for disaster. The government should make that decision instead.
Just as the government issues instructions on when evacuation gates should be closed based on meteorological information, local water-management authorities should use flood-risk assessments to advise residents when and where floodgates should be closed. That would give residents sufficient time to assess their own needs and make preparations.
Residential communities then need only stipulate in their bylaws or committee meeting resolutions that floodgates are to be closed according to government warnings. That would take the decisionmaking risk off management committees and property managers, while preventing disputes between residents over differing personal needs or judgements. Only then can residential floodgates truly function for everyone as intended.
Zou Ho-le is a condominium administration consultant.

Data checks aim to identify medically unfit drivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:40 UTC
01:37:40 KST

Taiwan plans to allow road authorities to use health data to identify drivers who might no longer be medically fit to hold a license, the government said yesterday.
The proposed system would cover drivers with visual impairments, epilepsy and moderate or severe dementia, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said.
Under the plan, road authorities would periodically obtain data on the three conditions held by government agencies, including information collected from people applying for certain government subsidies or insurance programs.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Road authorities would then cross-check the information against driver records.
Drivers identified as potentially no longer fit to drive would be asked to undergo a new qualification review. Those who fail would have to surrender their licenses.
About 47,000 drivers could be affected by the system, which is expected to take effect by the end of this year, the ministry said.
Currently, such checks might not occur until drivers renew their licenses.
The proposed system is intended to address cases in which drivers develop medical conditions or experience age-related changes after receiving their licenses that could affect their ability to drive safely, the ministry said.
The proposal follows amendments to the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例) promulgated in November last year.
Those amendments require drivers to undergo a new qualification review if changes in their physical or mental condition mean they no longer meet the standards required to drive.
The proposed regulations set out what data government agencies would be permitted to provide and how authorities could collect, process and use them.
The information collected would be limited to visual function, epilepsy and moderate or severe dementia, in accordance with the principle of data minimization, the ministry said.
Under current regulations, people with epilepsy can apply for a driver’s license if they provide a doctor’s certificate showing they have been free of seizures for at least two years.

China using extremists to sow division, official says

Unknown Publisher

01:37:39 KST

China is seeking to weaken Taiwan by influencing extremists to enter its democratic system and exploit political divisions, National Security Council (NSC) adviser Alex Huang (黃重諺) said yesterday, warning that the election of just one or two such politicians could make it harder for society to reach consensus.
“The goal is to weaken Taiwan. China does not need to attack you, it just needs to keep you arguing among yourselves,” Huang said in an exclusive interview with the Chinese-language Liberty Times, the Taipei Times’ sister paper.
Chinese election interference overseas is nothing new, with past incidents including attempts to influence the latest US presidential vote, efforts to turn Chinese-Canadian communities against certain politicians in Canada and attempts to fund pro-China candidates in Australia, Huang said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Asked about who are pro-China candidates in Taiwan, Huang said that in a democracy, people should be allowed to run as long as they meet legal requirements.
In Taiwan, candidates must be Taiwanese citizens and give up permanent residency or citizenship in other countries, Huang said, adding that the Central Election Commission and other authorities conduct rigorous checks for Chinese citizenship.
It is certain that China would seek to use such people to enter Taiwan’s political system, he said, adding that Beijing was trying to undermine democracy through its processes.
All China needs is one or two radical political figures to deepen political polarization, making it harder for society to reach consensus, he said.
Once elected, these people could become a source of risk by obstructing important legislations, Huang said.
Revisions to national security laws remain stalled, with some lawmakers seeking to sway public opinion and discredit the measures, while other organizations are being used to prevent legislation from advancing, he said.
Political infighting could prevent the government from obtaining essential uncrewed aerial vehicles and even lead to the leaking of sensitive information to undermine opponents, he said.
Taiwan is like a “real-life encyclopedia” of Chinese election interference, Huang said, adding that Beijing is constantly developing new tactics using artificial intelligence (AI).
These include generating tens of thousands of “live accounts” capable of real-time interaction as well as AI-generated videos targeting President William Lai (賴清德), former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) of the Democratic Progressive Party, he said.
A political party during its chairperson election last year also detected signs of interference, with such operations exploiting gaps in Taiwan’s laws and using content that is difficult to verify to confuse the public, Huang said.
The government is exchanging information with international partners to bolster Taiwan’s information and democratic resilience, and is urging the public to remain alert to suspicious content and avoid sharing it, he added.

Up to 100,000 in Taiwan spying for China: expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

Between 50,000 and 100,000 Chinese spies are operating in Taiwan, far more than the National Security Bureau’s previous estimate of 5,000, German journalist and author Jurgen Kremb said on Monday.
Kremb presented his research, titled “The War of Spies: How China’s Intelligence Services Are Infiltrating Taiwan — and What Europe Must Learn from It,” at a joint event held by the Taiwan offices of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation and the European Values Center for Security Policy.
The report was published in June in the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau’s Prospect & Exploration Monthly (展望與探索月刊).
Photo: Lin Cheng-kun, Taipei Times
By spies, he said he was referring to informants, sources and people who provide intelligence, rather than formally employed intelligence officers, comparing them to “throwaway agents.”
They might not receive monthly payments from the Chinese Ministry of State Security, but could still work on its behalf, he said.
Kremb, a visiting academic in the Human Rights Program at Soochow University in Taipei, also recounted his experience of being surveilled by a spy while traveling in Alishan (阿里山) in Chiayi County in June last year.
He said he was not afraid nor shocked by the incident, as “Chinese spies are everywhere in Taiwan.”
Becoming fearful of them would play directly into China’s hands, helping Beijing to instill fear in people, he added.
A woman who appeared to be about 30 years old asked him to take a photograph of her and the two began talking, during which he noticed she had a northern Chinese accent, Kremb said.
After he asked her where she was from, she said China, but that she lived in Denmark, and from that point he began feel that something was strange and walked back to his hotel, he said.
Along the way, he noticed that the woman was making phone calls, he said.
Two days later, after returning to Taipei, the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau reviewed surveillance footage from the hotel and found that the woman had hidden behind a car and watched Kremb from a street corner, he said.
The bureau determined that the woman was a Chinese spy and forwarded the information to the German Institute Taipei and the German and Danish intelligence agencies, although she had already left Taiwan.
As many as 180,000 intelligence personnel in China work solely on Taiwan-related affairs, Kremb said, citing sources in China.
The agents work under agencies such as the Chinese Ministry of State Security, the Ministry of Public Security, the People’s Liberation Army and the United Front Work Department of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) Central Committee, the report said.
China’s largest intelligence agency is the CCP, which has more than 110 million members who are required to write weekly reports to submit to their superiors even while abroad, which might be passed on to intelligence agencies, Kremb said.
Researchers and overseas communities must not be afraid to express their views, or Beijing would achieve its goal of transnational repression, European Economic and Trade Office in Taiwan head Lutz Gullner said.
Democratic nations must strengthen their capacity to prevent, detect, deter and protect against transnational repression, and boost transparency and awareness in order to bolster democratic resilience, he said.
“The methods Beijing is perfecting in Taiwan — the combination of high-tech espionage, economic blackmail and psychological manipulation — are already being used worldwide against Western democracies,” the report said.
The infiltration of Taiwan is not a local problem, but a “global warning sign,” it said.

Thailand yesterday said that Cambodia was playing the victim in a dispute over maritime resources, as the Southeast Asian neighbors took their feud to international mediators a year after deadly clashes over their land border.
Cambodia, which initiated the case before the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in Singapore, said it hoped the hearings would yield a peaceful resolution for both countries.
In May, Thailand unilaterally pulled out of a bilateral framework agreement that aimed to resolve overlapping maritime border claims, but denied any link to their land dispute.
Photo: Reuters
Cambodia subsequently initiated a UN-backed conciliation process at the PCA, saying it hoped to return to constructive negotiations.
Presenting Bangkok’s case before a five-member panel of international legal experts, Thai Minister of Foreign Affairs Sihasak Phuangketkeow said Cambodia sought to “vilify Thailand through false narratives, distortion of facts and unfounded accusations... including at international forums.”
“It does this by playing the role of a victim with a sense of self-righteousness aimed at claiming the moral high ground,” he said.
Last year’s clashes in July and December left dozens of people dead and displaced more than a million before a truce was agreed.
Thailand has said it withdrew from the framework agreement, called “MOU 44,” because “no progress had been made” in implementing it.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul denied the move was linked to the fighting.
The 2001 memorandum of understanding covers a resource-rich maritime territory of about 27,000km2 to which both Cambodia and Thailand lay claim.
Cambodia said last week that it had resorted to conciliation “after Thailand unilaterally terminated the agreed bilateral framework” through which the two nations had “negotiated their overlapping maritime claims for more than two decades”.
Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet in June said that the move was also to “protect Cambodia’s sovereignty and maritime rights in accordance with international law.”
Cambodian Minister of Foreign Affairs Prak Sokhonn yesterday told the PCA panel that Phnom Penh saw the process “as a means to rebuild trust, not as a form of escalation.”
Cambodia’s goal was to agree with Thailand on a “single, all-purpose maritime boundary,” or alternatively agree to jointly develop and equitably share resources until a boundary is drawn, he said.
“Our overriding objective is to achieve a resolution that serves the people of both nations and contribute to peace, cooperation and share prosperity in the region,” Prak Sokhonn said.
“Cambodia sincerely hopes that Thailand will engage constructively in this process,” he added.
Despite his rhetoric, Sihasak said Thailand was also seeking maritime delimitation and to rebuild trust.
“Thailand stands ready to engage in this process constructively with the aim of achieving with the commission’s assistance a negotiated and equitable solution,” he said.
Analysts have said that Thailand’s withdrawal from the 2001 agreement and Cambodia’s conciliation case were driven by domestic political calculations.
Set up in 1899, the PCA is the world’s oldest intergovernmental dispute-resolution body and resolves issues between countries and private parties by referring to contracts, special agreements and various treaties, such as the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Renoir paintings are not worth a fortune when they are stolen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:37 UTC
01:37:37 KST

Two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings stolen from a small French museum have yet to be recovered, but if the thieves are hoping to cash in on the artwork, they would be hard-pressed to find a buyer.
Selling well-known, stolen art is impossible to do at an auction house or through other public channels without raising eyebrows. Even under the table, the value plummets. Unlike other eye-catching artifacts such as jewels, paintings cannot be chopped up and sold for parts without losing their entire worth.
Art crime experts stress that most buyers simply do not want the liability. In short, the reality looks nothing like the movies.
“People always think that there is this kind of ‘Dr. No’ type from the James Bond movie,” said Arthur Brand, a private art detective based in the Netherlands. “But that’s Hollywood. In the real world, there are no collectors like that.”
Brand, who has investigated art crime for about 20 years, explains that often “nobody will touch” stolen art, particularly high-profile work. Sometimes that means paintings valued at millions of dollars are effectively “worth zero” once they are outside of the museum, if not a small fraction of the price, he added.
Theft at the Renoir Museum on Tuesday last week — the last home of the painter in the French Riviera — marks the latest high-profile art crime targeting collections around the world, and experts warn there could be more.
Cagnes-sur-Mer’s Mayor Bryan Masson said a group of “well-equipped” burglars stole four Renoir paintings from the museum. However, they dropped two of them — Renoir’s Portrait of Madame Pichon and Coco Reading — in the museum garden before they fled, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Police are still searching for the perpetrators.
In the meantime, Renoir’s Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well remain missing.
Masson estimated the value of the combined Renoir works stolen at 9 million euros (US$10.4 million).
However, the probability of profiting off such a heist is “extremely low,” said Erin Thompson, an art crime professor at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice in New York.
In cases that end in arrests, the common takeaway is that “thieves are people who are good at stealing things and bad at thinking through the consequences,” she added.
Some might try to make money from heists in other ways, such as through demanding a ransom or looking for an insurance payout. However, Thompson said many museums do not have insurance, because it is too costly. That is why the practice is so rare in the US, and it would be difficult to negotiate with insurance companies elsewhere without the thieves incriminating themselves.
As a result, if not surrendered or otherwise recovered, stolen paintings might remain hidden — or in some cases eventually destroyed to get rid of evidence, Thompson said.
Brand, who collaborates regularly with law enforcement in his art crime investigations, said that he has still seen limited cases of stolen paintings “floating around in the underworld” — perhaps as partial payments for products such as drugs.
Depending on country-by-country laws, the promise of returning the art has led to reduced sentences of other charges, he said.
“Some more savvy criminal will acquire it as a get out of jail free card, sort of a bargaining chip,” said Christopher Marinello, a lawyer and founder of Art Recovery International. “So, if some drug dealer ever is arrested, he can bargain with the prosecutor and say: ‘Listen, give me a lesser sentence, and I’ll show you where these Renoirs are,’ and that has always worked, and it will work again.”
Stolen paintings are much more difficult to profit from than museums’ other crown jewels — literally.
Jeweled and metal goods have increasingly become a target of theft, because they can be melted down or broken down into parts. Last year, a handful of experts warned that could be the fate of the stunning heist of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris, for example — saying that, if done successfully, smaller pieces could later go up for sale as part of a new necklace, earrings or other jewelry without turning too many heads.
However, of course, such pieces would lose their historical worth and, if actually sold, likely only go for a fraction of their original value. Experts also say that it is far from a simple process overall — and gems might still be identifiable by characteristics such as clarity.
Apart from an emerald-set imperial crown found outside the museum on the day of the heist in October last year, the stolen jewels remain unrecovered.
Paintings, in contrast, do not have the same commodity value that can potentially be parceled off.
“It’s a canvas with some old oil paint on it,” Art Loss Register art theft expert James Ratcliffe said. “You can’t touch it up. You can’t resell it other than for what it is.”
Ratcliffe and others said that has not stopped thefts of famous paintings and other artwork from museums. Just earlier this year, three pieces by Renoir, Paul Cezanne and Henri Matisse worth millions of euros were stolen in Italy, before being recovered last month.
Ratcliffe said that smaller museums, in particular, are harder to secure, because they might not have the funding necessary to invest in the latest technology — or are located in historic buildings that might take more time and effort to install new guardrails.
Still, pressures are piling up, with some warning that future cases of art theft could be likely as vulnerabilities persist.
“We need to change the way we treat small and country house museums before we lose to our cultural heritage permanently,” said Marinello, who stressed that stronger security and enforcement is overdue. “We’re supposed to be preserving our cultural heritage, not allowing criminals to take what they want and using them as shopping malls.”

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:36 UTC
01:37:36 KST

Effective presentations focus on delivering a clear perspective rather than simply listing facts and numbers. To achieve this, you must prioritize logic and visual simplicity over information overload.
Successful speakers follow the principle that every slide should focus on a single core concept. If your content feels crowded, it’s better to split the information across multiple slides so that your audience can grasp the main point within seconds. Furthermore, opt for visuals instead of lengthy descriptions, as a meaningful photo or a clear chart communicates much more effectively than a crowded table. Additionally, maintaining consistency by using the same font, limiting colors to three, and keeping a uniform layout creates a polished, professional look while reducing the cognitive load on your audience.
On the other hand, you should avoid common mistakes that undermine the impact of your presentation. It’s essential to steer clear of excessive animations and low-quality images, as these appear unprofessional and reduce your credibility. Most importantly, avoid putting giant blocks of text on your slides and resist the urge to read every word directly from the screen. These habits not only drain your energy but also weaken your connection with the audience. Remember, your slides are there to support your speech, not to replace it.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
In the end, the most effective presentations are those that communicate ideas with precision and elegance. By embracing the principle that less is more, you can keep your content concise and visually engaging, allowing your confidence to shine through.
有效的簡報聚焦於傳達清晰的觀點，而非單純列舉事實與數字。為了達成這點，你必須優先考慮邏輯與視覺上的簡練，而非資訊過載。
成功的講者遵循每張投影片應聚焦於單一核心概念的原則。若內容令人感到擁擠，最好將資訊拆分到多張投影片中，讓你的觀眾能在幾秒鐘內掌握要點。此外，選用視覺圖像而非冗長的敘述，因為一張有意義的照片或清晰的圖表，比起擁擠的表格更能有效傳達。再者，透過使用相同字型、限制顏色在三種以內，並保持一致的版面來維持連貫性，能營造出精緻且專業的外觀，同時減輕觀眾的認知負荷。
另一方面，你應該避免那些會削弱簡報影響力的常見錯誤。避免使用過多的動畫與低畫質的圖片是至關重要的，因為這些會顯得不專業，並降低你的可信度。最重要的是，避免在投影片上放置大篇幅的文字方塊，並克制自己直接照著螢幕朗讀每個字的衝動。這些習慣不僅會消耗你的活力，也會減弱你與觀眾的連結。切記，投影片是為了輔助你的演說，而非取代它。
總而言之，最有效的簡報是能夠以精準且優雅的方式傳達想法的簡報。藉由擁抱少即是多的原則，你可以保持內容簡潔且具備視覺吸引力，讓你的自信展露無遺。

KEY VOCABULARY
1. logic n. 邏輯
Good logic helps students solve difficult math problems more quickly and correctly.
良好的邏輯能幫助學生更快且正確地解決數學問題。
2. visual adj. 視覺的 & n. 視覺材料（展示或說明用的圖像、影片等）/ visually adv. 視覺上
Bright colors and pictures create a stronger visual effect during presentations.
鮮豔顏色與圖片能在簡報中產生更強的視覺效果。
The report included visuals such as charts, maps, and colorful photographs.
那份報告包含圖表、地圖與彩色照片等視覺材料。
3. core adj. 核心的；精髓的
Trust is a core value in many successful friendships and business relationships.
信任是許多成功友誼與商業關係中的核心價值。
4. concept n. 概念；想法；原則
The basic concept of the game is easy for beginners to understand quickly.
這個遊戲的基本概念讓初學者很快就能理解。
5. grasp vt. 理解；領會
Many students quickly grasp the lesson after practicing the examples several times.
許多學生在多次練習例題後很快理解課程內容。
6. opt vi. 選擇；挑選
Some students opt to study abroad after finishing high school in Taiwan.
有些學生在臺灣高中畢業後選擇出國留學。
7. cognitive adj. 認知的；感知的
Music training may support cognitive skills such as memory and attention.
音樂訓練可能有助於記憶與專注等認知能力。
8. credibility n. 可信度；可靠性
Clear evidence can increase the credibility of a scientific report or news article.
明確證據能提升科學報告或新聞文章的可信度。
9. concise adj. 簡潔的；簡明扼要的
Good speakers usually give concise answers instead of long and confusing explanations.
好的講者通常給簡潔回答，而不是冗長又混亂的解釋。

A “topping out” ceremony was held on Monday at a plant under construction in Germany by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), indicating that the fab is progressing as planned and within budget, the head of a joint-venture company in charge of the project said.
A topping out ceremony is the construction milestone of laying the final beam or structural piece at the highest point of a building, and it honors the construction crew, architects and engineers.
European Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (ESMC) president Christian Koitzsch said that about 2,000 workers from 106 countries are working around the clock at the site in Dresden, and he is confident that construction would be completed on schedule, according to a report by German newspaper Sachsische Zeitung.
Photo: CNA
ESMC is a joint venture between TSMC, Robert Bosch GmbH, Infineon Technologies AG and NXP Semiconductors NV, established to build the advanced semiconductor fab in Dresden, the capital of the German state of Saxony.
The topping out ceremony, or Richtfest as it is called in Germany, being held 25 months after the groundbreaking was an achievement for the construction team, the report cited Koitzsch as saying.
The next milestone for the fab would be the installation of the first manufacturing process equipment in the second half of next year, Koitzsch said.
Before production can begin, the interior of the fab’s cleanroom must be completed, the automated material handling system installed, and infrastructure work completed, including electricity and water supply, the report said.
Saxony Premier Michael Kretschmer, who attended the ceremony, said the state hoped to continue participating in Europe’s semiconductor industry initiatives and that more suppliers and companies would settle in Dresden following the European Commission’s proposal for a Chips Act 2.0, according to the report.
Dresden Mayor Dirk Hilbert estimated that 15,000 to 20,000 workers would move to the area by 2030, including about 600 TSMC engineers and their families, as well as personnel from the company’s suppliers who are expected to move there next year, the report said.
The city is preparing to establish a more systematic economic area to meet projected demand for residential, industrial and commercial land, investment promotion and economic development when fab starts production, he said.
Dresden has held events introducing Taiwanese culture to local residents and to welcome Taiwanese workers, he said, adding that the city hopes to host a Taiwanese night market.

Unknown Publisher

The Legislative Yuan has not submitted this year’s general budget to the president for signature, despite having passed it more than a month ago, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said yesterday, while the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) accused Cho of stoking political discontent.
The budget is 351 days late.
“We are waiting on the budget with bated breath,” Cho told a news conference. “I can only tell my colleagues to hang on.”
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
The government needs President William Lai’s (賴清德) signature on the budget to fund the already-approved supplementary budgets to increase government worker wages and improve welfare benefits.
KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said the premier presents the events surrounding the late budget out of context to manufacture discontent.
“The government is using the lack of funding as a tool to incite the people’s anger against the opposition parties,” she said.
“If the Democratic Progressive Party [DPP] cares about the well-being of 3.9 million people affected by the delay, it should tell them the truth,” she said.
KMT Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) had proposed on Aug. 26 that the legislature send the budget to the government before the new legislative session begins on Sept. 29, as it needed time to organize the budget and other important matters, Hsu said.
The DPP caucus had agreed to this arrangement, and the government has no grounds to complain about it, she added.
“The government, in an act of collective amnesia, is misrepresenting the facts to paint the legislature as boycotting the budget,” Hsu said.
Hsu also accused the media of publishing false stories about the KMT’s and the Taiwan People’s Party’s approach to the budget, saying that the press is failing its duty to monitor the government.
A Cabinet official with knowledge of the matter confirmed that the government has not received the approved budget.
The legislature’s failure to file has ramifications for the implementation schedule of proposed supplementary budgets, they said.
The Cabinet on Sept. 3 proposed a NT$607.63 billion (US$19.08 billion) supplementary budget, which is to increase subsidies for older farmers to NT$10,000 from NT$8,110, and the national pension’s maximum monthly payout to NT$6,715, up from NT$5,437. Those allocations would benefit 530,000 and 1.76 million people respectively.
The supplementary budget additionally includes a 23.5 percent increase to subsidies for mentally or physically disabled people, impoverished older people, disadvantaged children, low-income households and students from poor families, the official said.
These subsidies are to be paid retroactively from July 1, with an estimated 890,000 beneficiaries, they said.
The supplementary budget would give government workers a monthly pay raise, benefiting 720,000 military service members, civil servants, educators and people in supervisory positions.
Since supplementary budgets can only be activated on top of a general budget already allocated for the year, lawmakers would not be able to discuss those proposals until after Sept. 29.
The portion of the general budget that could not be utilized totals NT$299.2 billion.

Most expect housing prices to stabilize in Q4: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:35 UTC
01:37:35 KST

Over 60 percent of respondents to a survey expect housing prices in Taiwan to stabilize in the fourth quarter of this year, while the share who believe it would not be a good time to buy a home over the next two years fell, indicating improving sentiment toward the local housing market, Chinatrust Real Estate Co (中信房屋) said yesterday.
Citing the poll, Chinatrust said 64.1 percent of respondents expected local home prices to remain stable during the October-December period, while 18.3 percent expected prices to rise between 6 and 10 percent, and 9.8 percent said they expected prices to "rise sharply."
Less than 8 percent thought home prices would fall in the fourth quarter, Chinatrust added.
Photo: CNA
The survey also found that 50.2 percent of respondents said the next two years would not be a good time to buy a home, down almost 10 percentage points from a similar poll conducted in June.
With inflationary pressure on the rise, more potential homebuyers were inclined to enter the property market to hedge against inflation, Chinatrust research department deputy head S.M. Chuang (莊思敏) said.
The number of respondents looking to buy a home for their own use also increased, indicating a recovery in confidence in the local housing market, Chuang said.
Ahead of the central bank’s quarterly policymaking meeting tomorrow, the survey found that 41.2 percent of respondents said the bank should ease its selective credit controls for first-time homebuyers and those purchasing homes for their own use, while 17 percent urged the central bank to remove all selective credit restrictions. Another 13.1 percent said the current controls should remain unchanged.
In March, the central bank relaxed its selective credit controls on second-home mortgages for individual buyers following a seventh round of restrictions imposed in June 2024.
Chuang said there is room for the central bank to further ease its selective credit controls on the housing market, as the ratio of home mortgages to banks’ total lending has shown signs of falling.
She said further easing could encourage more potential owner-occupier homebuyers to enter the market and boost market momentum.
The survey found that only 13.7 percent of respondents said the central bank should raise its key interest rates at the upcoming meeting, while 31.4 percent said a rate cut was necessary and 22.2 percent said interest rates should remain unchanged.
Chuang said the poll showed that more than 50 percent of respondents supported either keeping rates unchanged or lowering them, as they hoped to avoid an increase in their financial burden by paying higher interest when buying a home.
She said that with the local housing market showing positive signs, a rate hike could prompt potential homebuyers to delay purchases and slow the market’s recovery.

Beijing might arrange a Taiwan compatriot permit for Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) on his behalf when he attends an APEC ministerial meeting in Nanjing later this month, although the host has already confirmed he is to enter China by presenting his invitation letter, a source said.
The APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting is to commence on Monday next week in Nanjing.
Hung is to attend, making him the first minister in President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration to visit China.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
Asked at a news conference on Wednesday last week whether Hung would need a Taiwan compatriot permit to enter China, Taiwan Affairs Office spokesman Chen Binhua (陳斌華) skirted the question, saying only that Taiwan’s participation in APEC meetings and activities has always been handled in accordance with the “one China” principle, and the provisions and practices of APEC memorandums of understanding.
The source said Taiwan has a liaison mechanism involving senior APEC officials and recently received the invitation letter through the mechanism.
The authorities would provide it to the Ministry of Labor, and Hung would enter China using the invitation letter, the source said.
APEC is an international forum, and Beijing would not arbitrarily arrest someone attending the event, the source said, adding that Hung is not among those Beijing has designated as a “Taiwan independence diehard.”
Several APEC ministerial meetings have been held in China, with more than 200 Taiwanese officials attending over the years without incident, the official said.
However, the source cautioned that China’s legal system continues to regard Taiwanese nationals as citizens of the People’s Republic of China.
Even if Hung neither applies for nor receives a Taiwan compatriot permit, Chinese authorities may, without his knowledge, arrange for someone to obtain one on his behalf, the source said.
That is a longstanding practice of the Chinese government, the source said, adding that Taiwanese officials who previously traveled to China for APEC meetings also had Taiwan compatriot permits secretly obtained for them and were treated as Chinese citizens.
Democratic Progressive Party caucus secretary-general Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) yesterday said that the Chinese government obtaining a Taiwan compatriot permit for Hung would not turn a Taiwanese official into the kind of Chinese citizen Beijing considers him to be.
When Taiwan joined APEC in 1991, the memorandum did not contain any so-called “one China” principle, Chuang said, adding that Beijing was taking advantage of this year’s meeting being held in China to take liberties with Taiwan.
Beijing could obtain a Taiwan compatriot permit for Hung if it wants to, but Hung does not have to accept it, he added.

Okinawa vote likely to boost Japan’s defense buildup, Taiwan security: Scholars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

The anti-Henoko "All Okinawa" camp’s 12-year hold on the Okinawa governorship ended Sunday when former Naha deputy mayor Genta Koja unseated two-term incumbent Denny Tamaki in a six-candidate race.
The conservative-backed 42-year-old won 59.4 percent of valid ballots after campaigning largely on livelihood issues.
However, the local election could have consequences far beyond Okinawa.
Photo: AFP
Two academics on Monday said that Koja’s victory could quicken Japan’s defense preparations across its southwestern islands — a development both viewed as favorable to Taiwan.
From local vote to first island chain
Lim Chuan-tiong (林泉忠), a research fellow at the University of Tokyo’s Institute for Advanced Studies on Asia, called Koja’s victory "a source of reassurance" for Taiwan amid growing Chinese military pressure.
Okinawa Prefecture lies along Japan’s southwestern island chain, a key section of the first island chain, while the Miyako Strait is an important route into the Pacific for Chinese warships, he said.
Koja’s willingness to work with Tokyo should smooth defense efforts, Lim said.
Kuo Yu-jen (郭育仁), vice president of the Institute for National Policy Research, said Koja could not have won had opposition to relocating Futenma remained decisive, adding that his victory should ease friction between Okinawa and Tokyo over base relocation and other defense projects.
"In Japan, there is only one government, and that means the central government in Tokyo," Kuo said.
Prefectural authorities can nevertheless delay projects through administrative and environmental procedures, he added.
An echo of 1998
Lim said 12 years of lawsuits over Henoko and confrontation with Tokyo had exhausted voters, who were also concerned about possible cuts to central government subsidies.
"What happened this time was a repeat of 1998," Lim said, comparing Tamaki’s loss with anti-base Governor Masahide Ota’s defeat.
The 1995 rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by US servicemen triggered protests, after which Ota refused to renew leases for US military land and clashed with Tokyo.
In 1996, the US and Japan agreed to return Marine Corps Air Station Futenma once a replacement was ready.
A 2006 bilateral roadmap designated Henoko, a less populated coastal area of Nago, as the replacement site.
All Okinawa considers it another permanent base and an environmental threat, while Koja accepts the relocation.
Lim said then-Japanese prime minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned that subsidies could be cut if Ota continued refusing lease renewals, prompting voters to waver.
"They felt that nothing could be accomplished if this continued," Lim said.
China: A harder ’Ryukyu card’ to play
Koja’s victory could also make it harder for China to play what Lim calls the "Ryukyu card" by exploiting local discontent.
Lim coined the term to describe Beijing’s use of state-linked media and academics to question Japan’s sovereignty over the Ryukyu Islands.
Lim identified four waves since 2005: during disputes over then-prime minister Junichiro Koizumi’s Yasukuni Shrine visits and wartime history; amid Senkaku/Diaoyutai (釣魚台) tensions around 2013; during Tamaki’s 2023 Beijing visit and debate over a Taiwan contingency; and after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Taiwan-related remarks last year.
Tamaki attended a meeting between a Japanese trade delegation and Chinese Premier Li Qiang (李強) in 2023.
"Tamaki was not particularly pro-China," Lim said. "But he actively engaged with China, rarely criticized Beijing, opposed US military bases and had poor relations with the LDP. Taken together, all of that was very much in line with what Beijing wanted."
Koja’s victory gives Beijing less room to maneuver, Lim said, adding that Beijing may now emphasize trade, exchanges and Okinawa’s ties with China while saying less about political status.
"The Ryukyu card will not disappear," Lim said. "But the strategy and approach will change."
Changes expected by 2027
Kuo traced Japan’s current defense direction to its 2013 National Defense Program Guidelines and three key security documents adopted in 2022.
Planned revisions could enable Japan’s Self-Defense Forces to respond more proactively to regional contingencies, including scenarios involving Taiwan.
Koja’s victory would not alter that strategic direction, but could ease its implementation in Okinawa, Kuo said.
Projects include reorganizing the Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade into a division, expanding military access to airports and ports, and adding anti-ship and air-defense missile sites across the southwestern islands, Kuo said.
Those measures would help deter China’s navy and air force, especially its aircraft carriers, he said.
"If progress is slowed, Taiwan would lose its shield to the east and northeast," Kuo said.
With the Defense Buildup Program running through next fiscal year and Takaichi seeking to revise the three security documents by the end of this year, Kuo expected implementation to accelerate.
"I think we will see fairly immediate and visible results in 2027," Kuo said.

Belarus criminal justice system ‘weaponized’: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

Belarusian authorities are using the country’s criminal justice system as an instrument of repression to systematically target government opponents, UN investigators said yesterday.
A group of independent UN experts at the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights tasked with probing the rights situation in Belarus determined that the country had for years “weaponized” its judicial system, “creating a system of punishment and legal sanctions against any form of dissent, real or perceived.”
“What emerges is not a picture of isolated violations, but of a system in which state institutions have systematically been used to suppress dissent and fundamental freedoms,” group chairwoman Karinna Moskalenko said in a statement.
Photo: Reuters
“Criminal justice processes are an integral part of a broader machinery of repression,” she said, adding that “their impacts are felt not only by those arrested, prosecuted or imprisoned, but by an entire society being warned about the price of dissent.”
The expert group was created in April 2024 by the office to investigate violations committed in Belarus since 2020, when the country was gripped by unprecedented anti-government demonstrations followed by a brutal crackdown.
In their first report last year, the experts determined that some of the abuses by Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s government since then amounted to crimes against humanity.
The latest report looked specifically at the judicial system, documenting abuses at every stage of the process.
Arrests were often “arbitrary” and “violent,” and carried out by plain-clothes officers without warrants, who frequently denied arrestees access to lawyers and forced them to record humiliating “repentance” videos, the experts said.
Detainees were held in “overcrowded, excessively hot and unsanitary cells, often without enough beds and infested with bedbugs, while being deprived of adequate food and sleep,” the report found.
It highlighted gender-specific abuses, including invasive strip searches of female detainees in view of male guards and the deliberate denial of basic menstrual hygiene products.
Trials against political opponents, journalists and rights activists in particular were riddled with systematic violations of fair-trial guarantees, with defendants kept in metal cages in the courtroom and their defense lawyers often disbarred or detained, the experts found.
Once convicted, detainees held on politically motivated grounds were marked with yellow tags and systematically subjected to “discrimination, inhuman conditions of detention, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and incommunicado detention,” the report said.
Among other things, former detainees interviewed for the report described facing repeated punishment for “alleged disciplinary violations,” including being held in frosty isolation cells, referred to as “torture by cold.”
State persecution continued even after release, with courts frequently ordering lengthy and intrusive preventive supervision, the report said.
That exposed former prisoners to nighttime raids by security forces, movement restrictions and immediate rearrest for minor schedule deviations, it found.
“Releases ... cannot be mistaken for an end to repression,” expert Monika Platek said in the statement.
The experts called on Belarusian authorities to immediately release all those held on politically motivated charges and to promptly investigate and prosecute all allegations of rights violations. They also urged other countries to step up pressure on Belarus.
“The international community must not look away,” expert Susan Bazilli said. “Those responsible for serious human rights violations must know that impunity is not a permanent shield, and victims must know that their rights have not been forgotten.”

Wildlife conservation groups yesterday urged the government to incorporate ecological considerations into policymaking rather than responding only after environmental harm has occurred, ahead of the Walk for Wildlife march, which is to be held in Taipei on Saturday.
The march, organized by Taiwan Walk for Wildlife (TWW), is to be held outside the Legislative Yuan and is scheduled to begin at 2pm on Saturday under the theme: “Wildlife cannot wait, incorporate ecology into public policy.”
At a news conference in Taipei, TWW chairman Lee Tsung-chen (李宗宸) said this year’s campaign builds on calls from the previous two editions in 2023 and 2024 for better management of stray dogs and cats, and stronger legal tools to address ecological conflicts.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
“We eventually realized that the problem was not simply that one measure was missing, but that different policies were operating independently, with ecological concerns only addressed after the damage had already been done,” Lee said.
The problem extends beyond animal protection, with ecological concerns often left out of decisionmaking by central and local governments on issues such as land use, energy and public works, he added.
Wild at Heart Legal Defense Association researcher Kuo Chia-wen (郭佳雯) cited the endangered Taiwanese humpback dolphin as an example of ecological concerns being sidelined in development policy.
Taiwan has invested substantial resources in researching the species, but coastal industrial development, offshore wind farms and land reclamation projects have continued along the west coast — the dolphins’ only habitat — without adequately taking their ecological impact into account, Kuo said.
“We’re not saying Taiwan should stop developing, nor are we saying people should stop using electricity,” she said. “The question is how we can truly achieve coexistence.”
Among TWW’s demands for the march is the establishment of a biodiversity committee jointly by central and local governments, with authority to coordinate across agencies and track implementation.
“Any policy that could affect the environment should be subject to review, with scientific data and expert opinions considered before decisions are made,” Lee said, outlining the committee’s role.
Saturday’s event is to run from 11am to 5:30pm, with conservation groups operating booths from the morning.
Following the about one-hour march through streets near the Legislative Yuan, participants are to return to the event site for a series of talks on wildlife and conservation issues.

How China turned Taiwan tensions into a top-rating TV spy drama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:30 UTC
01:37:30 KST

After shaking off the people trailing her through a crowded market and emerging from a bathroom in disguise, the double agent appears to have escaped. But a sip of water on a plane eventually gets her. She is poisoned after Taiwan’s military intelligence service discovers that she has been working secretly for China.
The plot comes from a new Chinese spy drama co-produced by the Ministry of State Security. Since its premiere on Sept. 6, it has become a TV hit, with a fictionalized take on a subject rarely treated so directly: the modern history of tensions with Taiwan.
The series, which will run for 40 episodes, is officially titled The Long Watch in English or Jiaofeng, meaning clashing or “crossing swords” in Chinese. It follows two decades of spies, double agents and intelligence operations between China and Taiwan from the mid-1990s.
Photo: AP
Jiaofeng mixes fictional characters and locations with real ones such as Taipei, the capital of Taiwan. Yet it remains difficult for analysts to verify how closely the drama follows real events as new episodes continue to be released.
While Taiwan’s intelligence services are portrayed as an adversary capable of obtaining sensitive missile information, the drama casts Chinese state security officers as the heroes defending the country against infiltration and theft.
By making these dramas, Chinese authorities are “essentially creating their own historical narrative,” says Li Fu-chung, a historian at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University whose research includes Chinese Communist party history and film history. “Through a dramatic format, people can very easily be brainwashed, not only in China but potentially in Taiwan as well.”
Billed as drawing on declassified national-security cases, the series’ writers said they interviewed retired state-security officers and studied 27 case files while developing the script.
Within about a week of its premiere, the series topped the daily prime-time drama ratings on China Central Television five times. Online, it surpassed 50 million views across platforms within a week, according to Chinese entertainment data provider Maoyan.
Chinese viewers have described the series as unusually “bold” for addressing real political figures and depicting details of espionage operations on both sides.
“One reason China has been making more dramas on this subject in recent years is simply that espionage makes for good drama. Another is that they want to emphasize patriotism,” Lisays.
“Since the story involves Taiwan trying to turn Chinese officials into agents, there will be negative and positive characters. That contrast helps show who is patriotic and who is betraying the country,” Li adds.
SPIES, LIES AND CROSS STRAIT TENSIONS
Set in 1994, the first episode opens with a newsreader’s voice playing over a cityscape in China, reporting that Taiwan’s then president Lee Teng-hui () had made remarks that “incite separatist sentiment” and “undermine the foundations of cross-strait relations.”
“This is seriously bold!!! It’s exciting from every angle and really doesn’t shy away from anything,” one Chinese viewer wrote on the microblogging platform Weibo, surprised at the direct mention of Lee.
Lee, who later became Taiwan’s first directly elected president, was viewed by Beijing as a major “separatist.” His visit to the US sparked Chinese missile tests and military exercises that developed into the 1995-96 Taiwan strait crisis, during which the US sent aircraft carrier groups to waters near the island.
Jiaofeng, however, is not the first state-backed Chinese spy drama to draw on cross-strait relations. Last year, another TV series called Silent Honor, also made with guidance from the Ministry of State Security, portrayed espionage set against the backdrop of the end of the Chinese civil war.
Despite the historical narratives, the shows help play into current events. In a commentary about Jiaofeng, published on Sept. 8, the state-run Global Times described cross-strait espionage as a “hidden front” and said “the struggle on this front will only truly end when the complete reunification of the motherland is achieved.”
On Chinese social media RedNote, one user posted a video saying the drama had taught him a hard lesson about the spy game.
“One moment of misplaced trust, one casual conversation or one flash of greed could be enough to pull you into the whole trap,” he said.
‘THIS IS JUST PROPAGANDA’
So far, however, the drama appears to have caused barely a ripple in Taiwan.
Little discussion is evident across social media, despite the series being available there through Chinese streaming service Tencent Video and on YouTube.
Last year, Taiwan’s own drama about cross-strait security threats performed strongly, becoming the most-watched drama of the year. The government-subsidized series Zero Day Attack imagined a Chinese blockade and invasion, with storylines involving sleeper agents and media infiltration.
Annie Hsieh, a 26-year-old Taiwanese postgraduate student, has never heard of Jiaofeng; nor would she be interested in watching it, given the topic.
“Who knows what they’ve made out of it,” she says.
Another Taiwanese graduate, Liang Tian-jun, says Chinese romance dramas were more popular among his peers, but that “watching dramas wouldn’t make them feel more open or receptive towards China.”
A poll conducted last month found that only 7.4 percent of Taiwanese respondents had a favorable view of the Chinese Communist party, down from 9.6 percent in July.
“Taiwan is, after all, an open and free society, so some people will be influenced by propaganda from across the strait,“ Li says, “But most Taiwanese can see that this is just propaganda.”

One approach to handling this obstruction is to circumvent it by building robust drone capabilities across a wide swathe of the population. Taiwan is doing just that, but more is needed. Is Saudi Arabia recruiting Syrian fighters to fight the Houthis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:28 UTC
01:37:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Is Saudi Arabia recruiting Syrian fighters to fight the Houthis?
Saudi Arabia has transferred hundreds of Syrian fighters to its southern border for possible deployment against Yemen's Houthis, according to a Lebanese media report, although experts speaking to The New Arab have cast doubt on whether any such deployment has yet taken place.
Lebanon's Al-Akhbar reported this week that hundreds of Syrian fighters had recently arrived in southern Saudi Arabia, including men who took part in the "Deterrence of Aggression" offensive that toppled Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
The report comes as Saudi Arabia faces renewed pressure from the Houthis, who have made significant territorial advances in Yemen and launched attacks on Saudi territory.
There has so far been no confirmation from either Riyadh or Damascus that Syrian fighters have been deployed, while several pieces of purported evidence circulating online have been found to be false or misrepresented.
Maysaa Shuja Al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab that she had independently heard of discussions within Saudi circles about bringing Syrian fighters into the conflict, but said she was not aware of the proposal having been put into action.
"I heard that the Saudis are thinking about that, but they haven't brought Syrians. They haven't done anything in practice," Shuja Al-Deen said.
Aron Lund, a Middle East analyst with the Swedish Defense Research Agency, told The New Arab that the Al-Akhbar report seems "improbable and overblown", warning that claims of foreign extremist involvement are a "propaganda classic" in regional conflicts.
However, Lund said the possibility could not be entirely dismissed, noting that Syrian mercenaries were previously deployed to Libya and Saudi Arabia had used foreign troops in Yemen.
There was therefore potentially "some little fire behind the smoke", he said, such as Syrian trainers or drone experts, but stressed that this remained speculation in the absence of tangible evidence
Shuja Al-Deen said numerous proposals were circulating as Riyadh considers how to respond to the deteriorating position of forces opposed to the Houthis, including discussions in some Saudi and Western circles about encouraging the UAE to return to a greater role in Yemen.
"There are many talks and discussions and suggestions here and there," she said.
Would Syrian fighters change the war?
Shuja Al-Deen said she had also specifically heard discussion of bringing Salafi or "jihadi" fighters from Syria to Yemen, although she strongly questioned the military logic of the proposal.
"As I told you, there are many talks and discussions here and there, and one of them, as I heard, is that they are going to bring some Salafi or jihadi fighters from Syria," she said, describing the proposal as "the most silly idea for me".
She argued that the anti-Houthi camp's principal problem was not a shortage of fighters or weapons, but the fragmentation of the numerous Yemeni forces opposed to the group.
Yemen's mountainous geography would also present a very different battlefield for Syrian fighters accustomed to fighting in Syria, she said, while the anti-Houthi camp already contains substantial numbers of experienced Yemeni fighters, including Salafi forces.
"I don't think it will help or do anything different, because the issue was not about the military capacity of these groups," Shuja Al-Deen said. "They were big troops. They were capable militarily. They have weapons."
Instead, she said recent battlefield setbacks had exposed longstanding divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.
"The big issue that led to this defeat was the lack of coordination and the absence of unified leadership," she said. "It's important that all of the soldiers of the different military factions receive one order from one leader, which has not happened."
Shuja Al-Deen said disagreements between commanders during recent fighting had left forces without a coherent chain of command.
"The soldiers were lost. There is no one order for everyone," she said. "It was a political issue regarding the division, or the lack of coordination, between the different groups that are fighting the Houthis."
She said that if Syrian fighters were ultimately deployed, she expected it to happen in coordination with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is heavily dependent on Saudi Arabia.
"If it happens, definitely it will happen in coordination with the government," she said, describing the Yemeni government as "a puppet in the hands of the Saudis".
Would Damascus be involved?
The identity of any Syrians potentially being considered for deployment would be significant.
Syria's former opposition factions have undergone a complicated process of incorporation into the country's new armed forces since Assad's fall, meaning the recruitment of former factional fighters would not necessarily indicate an official deployment by Damascus.
There is currently no evidence that the Syrian government has authorised or facilitated the reported plan.
Damascus has, however, publicly backed Saudi Arabia amid the recent escalation. Syria's foreign ministry condemned Houthi attacks on the kingdom earlier this month and expressed solidarity with Riyadh and its right to take measures to protect its security.
The reports emerge as Saudi Arabia struggles to contain a renewed Houthi offensive that has dramatically altered the military picture in Yemen.
The Houthis have captured the strategic port city of Mocha and strengthened their position around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including taking control of Perim and the Hanish Islands.
They have also stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting energy and military infrastructure, while Riyadh has reportedly sought greater US military assistance against the group.
Washington has resisted Saudi requests for direct US attacks on the Houthis, according to Reuters, while continuing to provide intelligence support.
The reported discussions over Syrian fighters come as Riyadh considers how to shore up an anti-Houthi camp that has suffered major battlefield setbacks despite possessing significant numbers of fighters and weapons.
Shuja Al-Deen said bringing in additional foreign fighters would not address what she identified as the central problem - the absence of unified political and military leadership among the Yemeni factions fighting the Houthis.

EDITORIAL: The real patriots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:37:24 UTC
01:37:24 KST

Chinese poet Bei Dao (北島) wrote in The Answer (回答) that “debasement is the password of the base, nobility the epitaph of the noble.”
A Hong Kong court on Friday sentenced three former leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China — which held annual vigils to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown — to prison terms of up to seven years and three months for “inciting subversion” under a Beijing-imposed National Security Law.
Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤), 41, a barrister; Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人), 69, a former legislator and labor union leader; and Albert Ho (何俊仁), 74, a former legislator, were charged in September 2021 and had been behind bars for at least 1,300 days. They are expected to be released between 2028 and 2030. The alliance, which was disbanded in 2021, was fined HK$1.5 million (US$191,238).
The ruling was lauded by Hong Kong officials and condemned by human rights groups. Friends and families of those convicted called it a “sad day” and that the three should not be in prison “even for a single day.”
The court said that the National Security Law “has no retroactive effect,” yet the judges said the defendants had “all along been hostile toward the Chinese Communist Party [CCP] and the central government under its leadership.”
What was deemed so “hostile” and “subversive” that prompted the court to hand down such heavy sentences?
The alliance, established in 1989, upheld five central tenets: release the dissidents; rehabilitate the 1989 pro-democracy movement; demand accountability of the June 4th massacre; end one-party dictatorship; and build a democratic China.
The alliance had for three decades organized annual vigils at Victoria Park in Hong Kong after the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s bloody crackdown on protesters at Tiananmen Square in Beijing.
The Hong Kong government in 2020 cited COVID-19 pandemic curbs to ban the vigils — the only large-scale, public commemorations in China — which had drawn tens of thousands of people for decades and did the same again the following year.
Since 2023, pro-establishment groups have held market carnivals at the park on June 4.
What is considered “patriotic” and “hostile” in Hong Kong in that time is quite telling. A carnival that draws vendors selling Chinese products at a former commemoration site is considered “patriotic,” while a vigil remembering the dead is considered “hostile.”
Lee’s wife said that his lifelong struggle was not out of any hatred of the CCP, but was based on a belief that Chinese deserve democracy, freedom and human rights.
Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo (劉曉波), a Nobel laureate who helped draft Charter 08, wrote: “I have no enemies and no hatred” in a statement two days before he was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2009 for “inciting subversion of state power.” Liu said he was optimistic about a future in China in which everyone could fearlessly speak their mind without being politically persecuted.
Liu, who died at age 61 in 2017 after battling liver cancer, was not “the last victim of China’s endless literary inquisitions” as he hoped he would be.
The court did not merely sentence three prominent democracy advocates, it also put millions of Hong Kongers on trial for holding a candlelight vigil to remember those who were sacrificed under a brutal regime.
As Chow put it in her mitigation, “the 206-page judgement, after all, boils down to saying that pursuing democracy is a crime... A law of this nature is nothing more than a euphemism for tyranny.”
The verdict does not just serve as a CCP warning, but also poses a question to everyone who believes in freedom and democracy: Do you uphold your beliefs when it comes with a heavy price?
Chow gave a clear answer: “To plead or apologize for everything you believe in is the most hypocritical thing imaginable and it is an insult to everyone who shares those beliefs.”
“If the law truly cannot accommodate our beliefs, then I would rather be a criminal than a person who betrays their conscience,” she wrote.
The true hostility lies in the CCP regime against its people. It is so profoundly insecure that it sees hostility at every turn and relies on hatred to maintain its grip, as Chow put it.
Those who dance with the CCP’s rhetoric are opportunists. The real patriots love their country so much that they are willing to sacrifice their own freedom in pursuit of the greater good.
In the face of the CCP’s authoritarian expansion, it is time for Taiwanese to prepare their own answer.
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It
