Syria to reinstate 14,000 teachers who lost jobs under Assad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:24:04 UTC
01:24:04 KST

Breadcrumb
14,000 Syrian teachers who lost their jobs under Assad to be reinstated
Around 14,000 teachers who were dismissed from their jobs for taking part in the revolution against the ousted Assad regime will be reinstated, Syria’s Education Minister Mohammad Abdel Rahman Turko said Monday.
Turko made the announcement during remarks to the People’s Assembly, Syria’s parliament, according to the state-run news agency SANA, saying a plan to permanently reinstate the teachers had reached its final stages and would soon be referred to the assembly for approval.
The move is part of a wider effort to overhaul Syria’s education system after decades of Baathist rule, when schools and textbooks promoted regime ideology.
"It’s great that these thousands of teachers who were sacked for opposing Assad are being reinstated, that’s a good thing," political commentator Robin Yassin-Kassab told The New Arab.
The regime of longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad, which witnessed a dramatic collapse in December 2024 following a lightning rebel offensive, used extensive repression to punish Syrians who took part in protests against it.
Hundreds of thousands of people were detained or killed by the regime, and many more lost their jobs.
The Syrian conflict grew out of anti-regime protests in March 2011 that were violently suppressed by Assad’s forces. The war drew in several foreign armies and militant groups, killing more than 500,000 people – according to conservative estimates – and leaving much of the country in ruins.
Turko said reinstated teachers would be entitled to work at the school closest to their place of residence. He also said top university graduates would be appointed as teachers without having to sit for a competitive exam, with lists of their names expected to be issued within days.
Dismantling Baathist education
Yassin-Kassab said the reinstatement of teachers was part of a broader transformation of Syria’s education system under the new government.
The ministry has removed the "Qawmiya" or nationalist education subject from the curriculum, he said, describing it as a heavily propagandistic subject designed to promote Baathist ideology.
"The new education ministry has gotten rid of the Qawmiya subject in school – which everybody hated so much – [it] was very propagandistic, and it was all designed to indoctrinate people in Baathist propaganda," he said.
Other propaganda material had also been removed from school textbooks, he added.
Corporal punishment has also been officially banned in schools, although Yassin-Kassab said it remained unclear how consistently the ban was being enforced.
"Corporal punishment has officially been banned in schools, which is great," he said. "I don’t know how much of that is being observed, or how little it’s being observed, but it’s great that it’s now being recognised as a problem."
During a debate in parliament on Monday, however, some lawmakers said they supported corporal punishment, while others argued that it made students afraid to go to school.
Another lawmaker complained that there were too many women working in schools, saying he opposed the "feminisation" of education.
Turko reiterated his outright rejection of corporal punishment.
The lawmakers' comments drew criticism from many Syrians on social media, who accused them of being disconnected from reality.
The overhaul is also stirring debate on long-standing questions over minority languages.
Kurdish-language education in particular remains controversial, with many Kurds in northeast Syria seeking greater access to education in their native language.
Yassin-Kassab said he sympathised with Kurdish demands for children to be educated in their mother tongue, while noting that the availability of Kurdish-language education in Kurdish-majority areas would nevertheless represent a significant departure from the Baathist era.
"That was of course completely banned under the Baathist education system," he said.
Balancing old and new
The changes to education are taking place amid a broader debate over what should replace the ideological framework that dominated Syria’s public institutions under Assad.
"Education is one of the areas where this kind of push and pull is happening between secularists and Islamists," Yassin-Kassab said.
He said some secular Syrians were concerned that Baathist ideology could be replaced by Islamist interpretations that might affect how certain subjects, including science, are taught.
The debate extends beyond education to the wider restructuring of Syria’s public sector, including the dismissal of workers associated with the former regime.
The new government has said that some employees linked to the Assad regime were effectively on the state payroll without having proper jobs. But Yassin-Kassab said there were also concerns that some dismissed workers had held legitimate positions, with some members of Syria’s Alawi community feeling they had been unfairly or disproportionately targeted.
The issue remains controversial as the new authorities attempt to dismantle the structures of the Assad era while rebuilding state institutions.
Rebuilding Syria’s schools
On curriculum development, Turko said the ministry had completed the national standards for developing new curricula six months ago. The standards are currently before parliament, and work on drafting the new curricula will begin once they are approved.
The minister expects the number of students to reach six million this year, up from 5.3 million last year and 4.3 million before the fall of the former regime.
According to the figures he cited, the expected increase is 700,000 students compared with last year, or around 13.2 percent.
Turko attributed the rise to "the return of refugees and students who had dropped out returning to school," adding that accommodating the growing number of students was among the challenges facing the ministry.
He estimated that around two million students had dropped out of school, citing economic and social factors, as well as a lack of schools in some areas, among the reasons for the high dropout rate.

ECB staff raise stability concerns about rumours of Lagarde's early departure

01:23:00 KST

Concerns are mounting that Europe's central macroeconomic institution might not be ready for turnover at the highest level.
In a letter seen by Euronews, European Central Bank staff members have questioned the institution’s stability in the face of rumours of the early departures of its president, Christine Lagarde, and board member Isabel Schnabel.
The staff calls the board to provide "appropriate clarity regarding potential leadership transitions", as discussions of major departures can affect both monetary policy and ECB internal reforms.
"We do not take a position on the accuracy of these reports, nor do we question the right of any individual to consider future professional or public responsibilities," the staff members write, referring to press coverage of the rumours. "However, when such possibilities concern members of the Executive Board, and specifically the ECB President, they inevitably raise institutional questions."
In early February, the Financial Times, which also first reported on the letter, spread the news about a possible early departure by Lagarde before the end of her mandate in October 2027.
What she would like to do next is not certain, but she has floated some options herself, telling Euronews that she would like to play a role in French presidential election campaign – albeit not by standing as a candidate.
Another possibility is her taking the helm of the World Economic Forum, which the Wall Street Journal first reported in February.
Another board member, Isabel Schnabel, might depart before the end of her term, as she is in negotiation to take a senior role at the International Monetary Fund, the German outlet Handelsblatt reported in early September.
These rumours are circulating just as other ECB leaders prepare to depart on schedule. Among them is Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose mandate ends in May 2027.
"Prolonged uncertainty regarding the future of the institution's senior leadership can therefore affect trust in the ECB's communications, create concern among staff and stakeholders, and complicate the orderly planning of leadership succession and strategic priorities," the letter says.
The potential reshuffle also comes in a moment of high uncertainty for the eurozone.
The volatility of energy prices due to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are making the job hard for the ECB to keep inflation low. Last week, Lagarde announced an interest rate hike to keep inflation low, that the ECB's 2% inflation target will not be met by the end of 2027.

Spain's Supreme Court refuses to apply amnesty to Catalan leader Puigdemont
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:21:55 UTC
01:21:55 KST

Puigdemont, who fled to Belgium to avoid detention after the referendum and is still the target of an arrest warrant, has been accused of misusing public money to organise the 2017 independence referendum.
Spain's Supreme Court has refused to apply amnesty to Puigdemont for the alleged offence of embezzlement in the "procés" case — Catalonia's independence movement, which peaked in the 2017 referendum and unilateral declaration of independence. The court is also keeping in force the national arrest warrant for Catalonia's former president.
Investigating judge Pablo Llarena, who is leading the case, has dismissed the request filed by Carles Puigdemont following the ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on 16 July.
The court agreed with the Socialist-led government's argument that the 2024 amnesty law for Catalan separatists complies with EU legislation.
But Puigdemont, who headed Catalonia's regional government when it held a banned independence referendum and attempted to secede from Spain, was excluded on two grounds: that Puigdemont had intended to obtain personal financial gain, and that the events had harmed the EU's financial interests.
The EU court said granting amnesty for the misuse of funds did not undermine the bloc's financial interests.
However, Llarena maintains that the European ruling doesn't affect his other ground for excluding the amnesty: the alleged intent to obtain personal financial gain.
The ruling stresses that the new request isn't being rejected because the CJEU's interpretation is irrelevant, but because that interpretation doesn't reach the second argument underpinning his refusal to apply the amnesty.
Llarena also notes that Spain's Constitutional Court has not yet ruled on how the Amnesty Law should apply specifically in this case. Those rulings, he says, have neither overturned nor specifically endorsed his finding of personal financial gain — and he adds that he cannot predict the outcome of the appeals still pending before that court.
Puigdemont's arrest warrant remains in force
The defence had asked for the national arrest warrant to be withdrawn on the grounds that the case might be closed, that the amnesty should apply, or that pursuing the men twice for the same acts would be unlawful.
Having rejected all three grounds, Llarena finds no basis to lift the warrant either. He notes, though, that this doesn't rule out reviewing the measure in future if circumstances change, nor does refusing the amnesty by itself justify any tighter restriction.
Because the warrant is national in scope, Puigdemont and Comín can be arrested only if they enter Spanish territory.
Supreme Court refuses to transfer the case
Llarena also rejects requests to transfer the case to the High Court of Justice of Catalonia (Catalonia's own regional high court) or to courts in Barcelona.
He likewise dismisses the request to close the case on grounds of "non bis in idem" — the legal principle barring double punishment for the same act — which the defence argued applied because an accounting-liability case is already underway at Spain's Court of Audit.
As a result, Llarena maintains that the CJEU's ruling doesn't touch the argument he says still blocks the Amnesty Law from covering the embezzlement charges against them.

Lebanon prosecutor seeks charges for Michel Aoun over port blast

Lebanon prosecutor requests charges for ex-president Michel Aoun over port blast: official
A Lebanese prosecutor on Tuesday requested that former president Michel Aoun be indicted over the 2020 Beirut port blast that killed more than 200 people, a judicial official told AFP.
The prosecutor at Lebanon's Court of Cassation asked the judge overseeing the case, Tarek Bitar, to "press charges against (former) president Aoun," said the official, requesting anonymity.
The official added that charges were being sought against Aoun because he "had prior knowledge of the presence of ammonium nitrate at the port and its danger, without taking the necessary measures" or referring it to the country's Higher Defence Council.
Aoun, founder of the mainly Christian Free Patriotic Movement, was Lebanon’s president between October 2016 and October 2022. He is not related to current President Joseph Aoun.
The massive explosion on 4 August 2020 killed more than 230 people, injured more than 6,500 and laid waste to swathes of the capital.
Lebanese authorities have said the explosion was triggered by a fire in a warehouse where tonnes of ammonium nitrate fertiliser had been stored haphazardly for years, despite repeated warnings to senior officials.
Nobody has been punished for the blast despite public anger and families of the blast victims demanding justice in a country long plagued by official impunity.
In March, a judicial official told AFP that judge Bitar had completed his probe.
He referred the case to the public prosecutor who was to study it, and prosecutor Mohammad Saab submitted his review on Tuesday, the official said.
The review specified the responsibility of more than 70 defendants, including current and former politicians, security and military officials, and civil servants, some of whom were previously charged by Bitar.
The charges remain up to Bitar, who could issue them in the coming weeks.
The case had been bogged down by political and legal wrangling since 2023, after Iran-backed Hezbollah led a campaign demanding Bitar's removal and dozens of lawsuits also sought to remove him from the case.
However, Bitar resumed his investigations last year as Lebanon's balance of power shifted.
President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam took office following a 2023-2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah, which weakened the armed group. That conflict is ongoing, with continued Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon.
Since then, several legal impediments to Bitar's work have also been removed, including the lifting of a travel ban against him.

As Russia closes in on Sloviansk, this taxi driver keeps working
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:18:12 UTC
01:18:12 KST

As Russia closes in on Sloviansk, this taxi driver keeps working
Oleksandr behind the wheel of his work car, in Sloviansk, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 17, 2026. (Lisa Bukreyeva / The Kyiv Independent)
SLOVIANSK, Donetsk Oblast — From a brick-walled garage that barely fits the blue car parked inside, Oleksandr Richak carefully backs his taxi cab out onto the narrow street.
The 42-year-old usually starts work around 8 a.m., once the early-morning rush hour of deadly Russian drone activity in the eastern front-line city subsides.
As he briefly parks the car outside a damaged one-story house, his wife, Nataliia, walks over and hands him a bottle of lemon-flavored water. Her worried eyes follow Richak as he drives off, watching until he disappears from view.
"Before it was fine, but now with the FPV (first-person view) drones hitting so many cars…" she says, unable to finish the sentence.
"Whenever I hear (a loud explosion), I immediately call him."
As Russian troops gradually advance toward Sloviansk, the security situation in what was once a relatively safe haven in the eastern Donbas region has significantly worsened this year. Now only around 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Russian troops, an intensifying barrage of glide bombs and FPV attacks is gradually destroying the city.
Many Sloviansk residents are now doing something that until recently, they had never contemplated — fleeing.
Every day brings more reminders of the potential cost of staying. Richak drives past new ruins, and the number of shops, cafes, and restaurants still opening their doors each morning is dwindling.
"Every night, something gets hit," Richak says, driving past a series of destroyed and damaged buildings.
Richak drives for five minutes before arriving at the eerily empty Sloviansk central bus station. Alongside a few other remaining Sloviansk taxi drivers, he waits for bookings, lighting up a cigarette and opening the OnTaxi app on his phone.
Another taxi arrives at the bus station, driven by 54-year-old Ruslan Kuzmenko. The two men greet each other on the station square.
Suddenly, they're interrupted by the unmistakable buzzing of an FPV drone.
"It is an interceptor drone," Kuzmenko says calmly, just seconds before a loud explosion blasts out from the direction of a nearby market.
"Turns out it's not," he says.
"It hits, and someone is just unlucky."
Richak and Nataliia both studied in Sloviansk when they were younger, and in 2006, after completing 18 months in the military, he returned to the city. Nataliia and their one-year-old daughter followed a year later. They added a son to the family in 2013 and bought their first home in 2018.
"There was such life here," he says fondly.
Before the full-scale war broke out in 2022, Richak drove a truck, delivering cakes and pastries from the local confectionery factory Valensiya all across the country. The war forced a change of career, and four years ago he swapped the truck for a taxi to supplement his main job as a gas repair worker.
His first booking comes in, and he jumps in the cab to pick up a 40-year-old soldier named Yurii, who needs to view a potential new apartment as its current tenant has decided to leave Sloviansk.
During the drive over, Yurii, who asked to disclose his first name only as his family still lives in Russian-occupied territories, mentions he is originally from the now-occupied town of Velyka Novosilka in Donetsk Oblast.
Richak's face lights up at the mention of a place he frequently visited for work before the war. They share memories of the town and discover they both know the same woman from there. Richak remembers her from the police academy.
"What a small world!" Yurii says, laughing as he hands cash to Richak and leaves the taxi.
read also
Up until 2014, Richak worked in the police for 10 years. In a country strained by corruption, in need of Western reforms, and still under the strong influence of the Kremlin, he hoped he could make a small but positive contribution to his homeland.
The rest of his roughly 25-man police unit had other ideas. When Russia invaded Donbas in 2014 and its proxy troops occupied Sloviansk, all but two of them defected in what he believes was a prearranged plan.
"We were placed on alert, but I learned that my entire unit had gone over to the side of the (Russian proxy forces), including the commander," he says.
Richak was not surprised — he had heard their views during the 2013-2014 Euromaidan Revolution, and knew how they felt about Ukraine moving closer to Europe and away from Russia.
A week into the occupation, he walked out of the city to escape.
Pro-Russian sentiment persists among some Sloviansk residents, typically from the older generation who grew up in the Soviet Union. Even to this day, under constant Russian bombardment, there are occasionally clients who support Russian President Vladimir Putin, and blame President Volodymyr Zelensky for Moscow's war.
Richak says he encounters someone like this about once a month. Often, they will rant during the drive, insist that he speaks Russian, and, when he refuses, slam the door in anger when they leave.
His response as they exit his taxi is the same one he gives to everyone.
"Have a nice day."
Richak's second booking buzzes his phone into life. Fifty-nine-year-old retiree Lyudmila Hurkina rarely leaves her house these days. Her husband suffered a stroke in May, is bedridden, and she tries to leave him on his own as little as possible.
But she can't avoid errands like buying food or picking up his medicine, and a taxi allows her to get back home as quickly as possible.
She already knows what it's like to flee, forced to leave the city of Horlivka when it fell to Russian proxy forces in 2014. If she has to do it again, she doesn't know how she will afford it — two weeks of her husband's medicine costs UAH 3,000 (about $67), nearly the full amount of her pension.
"I might have to leave again and start all over," she says as they arrive at the hospital.
"But now I am 59. I don't know whether I can start over in a new place and build up a life."
The stories that are shared in taxis in Sloviansk are often understandably heavy, centered on survival in a city Russia seems determined to destroy.
Richak says he often feels like a therapist, listening to people's problems and giving them advice when he can. But it can also work the other way, with Richak hearing useful information about the situation in the city.
"We drive on the road, and there is the feeling of having known them for 10 years," Richak says.
A regular working day in Sloviansk will see Richak take around 15 bookings. He tries to wrap up and be home by 8 p.m., before the 9 p.m. curfew and the inevitable increase in Russian drones as night falls.
On a typical day, he'll take in around UAH 3,000 ($70), but after taxi app commission and expenses like fuel, he takes home around half.
His main job as a gas repair worker is no less dangerous than driving a taxi around a city constantly in the sights of Russian glide bombs and drones.
On 24-hour standby, he and his team rush to repair gas pipelines damaged in Russian attacks. The threat of double-tap strikes, a deliberate tactic Russia uses to target emergency workers, is ever-present.
On Aug. 19, a Russian Molniya drone exploded three meters away from him as he responded to a call. Though his team survived and he escaped with a concussion, the experience further heightened his anxiety.
"Next time it might hit me directly," he says. "These are weapons that can take life away from you at any moment."
Another booking comes in — three generations of one family, a grandmother, her daughter, and her granddaughter.
Seven-year-old Aliya is on her way to perform a song in church alongside some of the other remaining children in Sloviansk.
"The Russians stole their childhood."
"The children act as though they are okay, but it is still stressful for them," 52-year-old grandmother Oksana Mykhalchyk says.
"The Russians stole their childhood," Aliya's mother, Khrystyna, adds.
As the family exits the taxi, the sounds of air defense fire echo across the city. Richak parks his car under a tree in the courtyard of a residential building to wait out the danger.
After a while, he returns to the bus station. "There are very few taxi drivers today," he says.
Richak knows that as Russia further encroaches on the city, there will be less and less work for him. The once-bustling streets were packed with entertainment venues and hosted a Christmas market he recalls with fondness.
Despite growing up in Kharkiv Oblast, Sloviansk has always been his second home; he used to visit the city during school breaks and stay at his aunt's. Coming from a village, Richak saw Sloviansk as a big city, and he watched it grow as he built a family of his own.
He feels certain that Russia will reduce Sloviansk to rubble before the urban fighting begins, much like other cities in the Donbas.
"I don't think there is another scenario," Richak says. "We are mentally preparing for a time when we are not going to return to the city."
Shortly after spending the day with Richak, his wife and daughter left Sloviansk, joining their son in Kharkiv Oblast.
After his shifts, Richak has to return each day to an empty home — he can only leave Sloviansk if the gas service relocates him elsewhere.
Richak tries to distract himself from thoughts of fear with his work, talking to people and staying busy.
"You still think about it constantly anyway," Richak says. "Every day, it never leaves you."
All the taxi passengers interviewed in August for this story later told the Kyiv Independent they had since decided to leave Sloviansk due to near-misses amid ever-intensifying Russian drone and glide bomb attacks.
Richak remains, mentally adjusting to each passing day and the ever-present possibility of death.
"It hits, and someone is just unlucky," Richak says. "That is how we live."
A note from the author:
Hi, this is Asami, the author of this article. Thank you for reading it until the end. It was a completely different experience to head to Sloviansk and Kramatorsk this summer compared to most of my previous trips to the east since 2023, when those cities were still considered safe havens. But meeting local residents, such as Oleksandr, and hearing their stories of resilience reminded me why Donbas holds a special place in my heart. At the Kyiv Independent, we try to shed light on the reality of the war from a range of perspectives, including human-focused stories like this one and my usual front-line pieces.

‘Not all roads lead to Rome’: Study shows marvels of the Roman Empire’s road network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:17:43 UTC
01:17:43 KST

‘Not all roads lead to Rome’: Study shows marvels of the Roman Empire’s road network
ROME - Augustus, ancient Rome’s first emperor, placed a gilded monument called the Milliarium Aureum, or Golden Milestone, in the Roman Forum in 20BC to mark the symbolic starting point for all roads in the sprawling empire.
These roads indeed were the backbone of the world’s first continental-scale transportation system.
Now, researchers have conducted a detailed structural analysis of the empire’s road network, spanning roughly 300,000km of routes crisscrossing Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.
The study showed the old adage “all roads lead to Rome” was not exactly true, and the empire’s later imperial capital Constantinople – present-day Istanbul – was a better fit for that maxim.
While the Romans preferred building straight roads, difficult terrain sometimes frustrated that goal, it found.
The researchers also documented a correlation in many regions between the old Roman roads and modern highways.
The Romans, master engineers and builders, constructed roads stretching from the Moroccan and Arabian deserts in the south and east, all the way to Scotland and the Atlantic Ocean in the north and west.
These roads were linked to navigable rivers and sea lanes to form a comprehensive transportation web.
“This infrastructure meant that a vast region became more tightly integrated: it provided a continent-sized platform for people, animals, pathogens, goods and ideas to spread,” said classical archaeologist Tom Brughmans of Aarhus University in Denmark, who helped lead the study published on Sept 15 in the journal Nature Communications.
“The Roman legions marched over roads to respond to threats, relieve colleagues and colonise new territories.
Radical new ideas like early Christianity moved with people over land and sea. But the roads themselves were most used for the frequent commutes between farm and field, or to local markets for selling produce,” Brughmans said.
Some roads were very durable, constructed with a combination of materials including crushed stone, lime cement, gravel and paving stones.
Traffic consisted mostly of people walking and riding on animals including horses, donkeys, mules and camels, as well as pack animals and animal-drawn carts and carriages.
Road distances from Rome were measured from the Milliarium Aureum. But was this ancient megalopolis really the centre of the network?
“All roads lead to Rome? Not really,” Brughmans said.
“Rome is centrally located for Mediterranean shipping, but not particularly central in the Roman road system. We found that provincial capitals were exceptionally well located on the roads in their province, facilitating effective provincial administration and tax collection.”
Some of these provincial capitals included Ankara in Turkey, London in Britain and Corinth in Greece.
“Rome itself was centrally located on the roads on the Tyrrhenian coast of Italy.
But when we consider all movement within the entire Italian peninsula, we were shocked to discover that the most central road actually follows the opposite Adriatic coastline, bypassing Rome altogether,” Brughmans said.
A new capital
In the early fourth century AD, the Emperor Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople.
“This new capital was strategically located where Europe and Asia meet, and our research has revealed that it was exceptionally central for empire-wide overland travel – way more so than Rome,” Brughmans said.
“It’s on the Bosporus, and we know of ferries that crossed this strait in antiquity, effectively connecting European and Asian road traffic.”
Roman engineers used tools and techniques to make roads as straight as possible, with the Via Appia south of Rome a prime example.
“But even the Romans had to bow to nature. We found that Roman roads tend to be straight only if the local topography allows for it, such as in the rather flat areas of Belgium, northern France or the Po Valley in Italy.
On the whole, they did not move mountains just to build a road,” Brughmans said.
These ancient roads structured interactions among hundreds of millions of people for more than two millennia, given the continued use of many long after the Western Roman Empire fell in 476AD and the Eastern Roman Empire, also called the Byzantine Empire, succumbed in 1453.
“The persistency of the Roman road network can be demonstrated for many regions, from Britain to the Near East,” said Adam Pazout, a postdoctoral fellow at the Autonomous University of Barcelona who helped lead the study.
“And these roads in many places served as the main communications throughout the medieval period until development of the railroads in the 19th century and highways in the 20th century.”
Many modern highways trace ancient roads.
“A great example is the Via Augusta, which goes from Cadiz in the south of Spain to the Pyrenees.
The road passes under a triumphal arch called the Arc de Bera between Tarragona and Barcelona, where you can clearly see it has the same course as the modern N-340 motorway,” Brughmans said. REUTERS

ICC must be ‘decolonized’ – human rights advocate (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:16:24 UTC
01:16:24 KST

ICC must be ‘decolonized’ – human rights advocate (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) needs sweeping reform to ensure that powerful countries are held to the same standards as the rest of the world, human rights advocate David Lopez has said.
The Hague-based ICC was established in 2002 under the Rome Statute to prosecute genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression. It has long faced accusations of political bias and selective justice.
Speaking to RT on Tuesday, Lopez said that over the past two decades, cases in Africa and the Global South have received disproportionate attention, while alleged crimes involving powerful Western countries have gone unpunished.
He referenced the 2003 Iraq war, claims of CIA torture, and the conflict in Gaza as examples, noting that alleged US crimes in the case of Afghanistan were set aside due to pressure from Washington.
“Justice with no power over the powerful is colonial administration of the law,” he said.
The court must be “decolonized” through structural reforms that give Africa, Asia, and Latin America greater representation and reduce its financial dependence on Western countries, Lopez argued.
The ICC currently has 125 member states, but major powers, including the US, Russia, China, and India, are not among them. Israel also rejects its jurisdiction.
Washington has sanctioned ICC judges, prosecutors, and other staff over cases involving US and Israeli nationals. The court issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The institution is also facing growing opposition from member states. Venezuela and Chad have recently announced plans to withdraw, bringing to five the number of countries seeking to leave over the past year, alongside Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. The three African states have accused the ICC of selective justice and neocolonialism.

While Xi hinted at interest in potentially playing an explicit US-Iran mediation role in his BRICS speech, he did not explicitly announce any such imminent diplomatic initiative.
Instead, the Chinese president once again promoted a broad four-point plan for de-escalation in the Middle East, which is centred on peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adherence to international law, and balancing development and security.
Analysts have pointed out that while China wants to see an end to a war that has brought tumult to financial and energy markets, it has traditionally avoided deeply entangling itself in third-party conflicts and potentially failed diplomatic initiatives.
Inside Iran, there have been varied opinions on the significance of Xi’s latest remarks.
Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said on Sunday that Xi’s “constructive initiatives offer timely openings to de-escalate tensions” and show that multilateral diplomacy “is the only viable path to stability”.
But Hamed Vafaei, professor of Chinese literature at the University of Tehran and a China researcher, said that perceiving Xi’s remarks as an offer to mediate between Iran and the US was more of a “free interpretation” of his words than reality.
Nuclear file, sanctions and military cooperation
Araghchi is also expected to discuss Iran’s nuclear programme with China, as Washington attempts to renew focus on Tehran’s activities.
Last week, the US and its European allies, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, successfully pushed the board of the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), to refer Iran to the UN Security Council.
The last such referral came 20 years ago and was followed by six UN Security Council resolutions being passed against Iran, and sweeping sanctions that hit the country’s economy hard.
This time, however, the move is expected to be largely symbolic. China and Russia have strongly opposed it, and can veto any new Security Council measures.
Western pressure on Tehran is continuing elsewhere. Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami was barred from attending this week’s IAEA General Conference in Vienna under “snapback” sanctions reimposed by European powers last year.
The US has continued to build on its own sanctions against Iran, launching “Operation Economic Outcast” to further isolate the Iranian government from the international community as it also tries to choke off the country through a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports.
A large number of China-linked refineries, companies and financial channels allegedly facilitating dealings with Iran have also been targeted as part of the sanctions, although larger Chinese banks have not been hit so far.
But on Monday, the US Treasury designated Russia’s VTB Bank under the Iran sanctions. It did not name China in its statements, but the second-largest Russian bank is the only one with a licensed branch in mainland China, with direct access to China’s national payment system.
China remains the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil and has vowed to protect its own interests despite the sanctions. It has continued purchasing Iranian oil stored beyond the reach of the US blockade.
China’s links to Iran’s military capabilities also drew attention in the US this week, after the Wall Street Journal reported that Iran had obtained high-resolution satellite images from Chinese entities before carrying out an attack on a US military base in Jordan that killed three American soldiers.
Trump downplayed the incident when he was asked about it by reporters, saying that the Chinese were “basically doing what we do”.
“I think he’s behaved reasonably well,” Trump separately said about Xi. “When they say that China spies on us, I say you’re right, and we spy on them, too”.

Election in Philippines’ Bangsamoro region ends in hung parliament
No party wins majority in first parliamentary polls in southern Philippines’ Muslim-majority region, unofficial results show.
Marawi City, Philippines – The first parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines has resulted in a hung parliament as no single party managed to secure a majority, according to unofficial results.
With more than 99 percent of votes counted as of Tuesday evening, the two rival parties that emerged from the separatist Moro Islamic Liberation Front each had more than 30 percent of the vote, showed the partial count of GMA News, one of the country’s largest news networks. Neither secured the 41 seats needed for a majority in the 80-member parliament.
The front signed a peace agreement with the Philippine government in 2014 after decades of conflict for independence and self-governance. It served as an interim government after voters approved the autonomous region in 2019. But last year, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr replaced longtime Moro Islamic Liberation Front chairman Al Haj Murad Ebrahim with Abdulraof Macacua, a former front commander, as chief minister, in a move that worsened internal divisions in the Muslim-majority region.
Macacua, who leads the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, has acknowledged that a coalition with other parties is “an unavoidable situation” following Monday’s vote.
Ebrahim told reporters after casting his ballot that he hoped his party – the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) – would clinch most of the seats, but expressed openness to negotiating with other parties.
“If the party does not get majority of the seats, we will look for parties who can be our allies so that we can form a coalition,” Murad said.
Some voters had feared a return to fighting if the UBJP failed to get a commanding lead, especially because the front has halted the disarming of former fighters, citing the government’s failure to provide aid as promised.
“One of the commanders of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front has said that if they don’t win the election, there might be war again,” Alinair Aracaya said.
The commander he was referring to was 64-year-old Abdullah Macapaar – also known as Commander Bravo and notorious for being one of the most defiant front leaders. On Monday, Macapaar, who was also running to become a member of parliament, voted for the first time in his life.
In a Facebook post, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, who led peace negotiations with the front on behalf of the government, commended the participating parties “for their great effort to build their capacity to enter the field of electoral politics and play by the rules of the electoral process”.
Authorities said the elections were generally peaceful, but security forces will remain on high alert in the coming days. Multiple shooting incidents on election day left at least three people dead and several wounded.
“We will still hold our deployment in place even after the proclamation of winners. We are trying to ensure that the security situation will remain stable,” said Brigadier General Jemuel Siason, deputy police director of the Bangsamoro region.
After years of negotiations, the Philippine government and Moro Islamic Liberation Front signed a peace agreement that paved the way for autonomy in the region.
Voter Aracaya’s wife, Norhailyn Madayan, remembers a childhood spent fleeing conflict. “Just the sight of soldiers terrified us because that meant there might be clashes again. There were also clan wars,” Madayan said.
Aracaya and Madayan said peace has allowed them to build a life. They have a thriving business and a newly constructed concrete home. But they also say peace has been fragile. In 2016, ISIL-linked fighters briefly took control of their town.
The following year, the same group laid siege to Marawi City. The military responded with air attacks.
Asraf Balt, a resident, was only nine years old at the time. But because shots rang out every now and then, he said he did not immediately realise the gravity of the situation until he saw what happened to their home.
“We got displaced, and our house got destroyed. Like, heavily destroyed to the point that we had to rebuild it,” Balt said. His family has moved back to their home, but hundreds of others remain in temporary shelters.
Analyn Pangandaman said her family cannot afford to rebuild their home without reparation from the government. She has been waiting to get compensated for nearly nine years.
Now, she says, she cannot even visit her mother, even if she lives just a few towns away.
“I used to see my parents a lot, but I don’t any more because I can’t afford the commute. We used to be able to visit them because we had a car,” Pangandaman said.
With the Bangsamoro region having been able to conclude its first election, Pangandaman hopes to receive what the government owes her family soon. And it’s only possible, she says, if winning parties set aside differences and work together towards peace and progress.

19 Russian defense companies remain outside international sanctions, helping sustain Russia’s war machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:13:52 UTC
01:13:52 KST

Ukraine's military intelligence agency, HUR, published data on 54 Russian enterprises within KRET, a defense holding under Russia's state-owned Rostec corporation, on 15 September. More than a third of KRET's enterprises face no sanctions from any country in the international sanctions coalition, HUR reported on 15 September.
Russia's defense industry is vast, and sanctions have targeted companies and individuals across the sector in multiple rounds since the full-scale invasion to restrict its ability to produce and finance weapons. But complex networks of state-owned holdings and subsidiaries can leave gaps, allowing some companies involved in military production to remain outside international sanctions. An August report by the anti-corruption organization NAKO found that the EU had sanctioned only 23% of 482 Rostec-linked entities.
What KRET makes for Russia's military
- KRET makes electronic warfare systems, friend-or-foe identification systems and onboard electronics for Russian fighter jets and helicopters, HUR said. Its companies also make other military equipment, including anti-drone systems and remotely operated machine guns.
- KRET also supports Russia’s missile production. The Signal plant in Stavropol makes compact jamming stations for 9M723 Iskander-M missiles, and the Kaluga Research Radio Engineering Institute makes electronic protection systems for 3M22 Zircon missiles.
- KRET’s main organization covers funding shortfalls for state defense contracts carried out by its companies, according to HUR.
Unsanctioned companies make missile and drone parts
HUR also named several of the 19 unsanctioned companies that it says are involved in Russian weapons production.
Among those firms, HUR identified manufacturers of navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion drones, gyroscopes for 9M727 cruise missiles used in the Iskander system, and electric motors for drones.
The enterprises include JSC Inertial Technologies of Technokompleks, JSC Tambov Plant Elektropribor, and JSC Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association.
HUR calls for broader sanctions
The intelligence agency called for more defense companies to be added to international sanctions lists, better monitoring of compliance, and punishment for violations. KRET is the 10th Rostec holding whose enterprises HUR has published on its War&Sanctions portal. The portal now lists 764 Rostec enterprises, UNN reported.
On 8 September, HUR published data on 155 enterprises belonging to Roselektronika, another Rostec holding. Nearly half were not under international sanctions.

FBI’s Kash Patel defends hiring policy change on bestiality, prostitution
Policy change sparks heated Senate debate; critics question its timing amid challenges in attracting new FBI agents.
United States FBI Director Kash Patel has defended the bureau’s loosening of hiring requirements regarding prostitution and bestiality, saying the changes were meant to enable victims of those acts to apply for employment without fear of automatic disqualification.
The FBI quietly issued guidance this past spring lifting a categorical hiring ban on applicants who had previously engaged in prostitution, and said that it would instead consider the context of the behaviour in at least some cases. The bureau made a similar change regarding bestiality.
Pressed about the moves at a Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing, Patel on Tuesday denied that the changes reflected a lowering of employment standards and insisted they were designed to protect victims forced to engage in that conduct and to prevent automatic disqualification.
“We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked. We did not want to make it an automatic disqualification for the FBI to consider you,” Patel said.
The answer did little to satisfy Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, who grilled Patel on the rationale for a change the FBI director said subordinates proposed to him.
Kennedy asked Patel why, given the FBI’s current difficulty attracting new agents because of negative public sentiment, Patel would make these changes now.
“Why would you even get into bestiality?” Kennedy said.
Patel replied it was a way of supporting victims, and that some people who were “forced into” bestiality should not be disqualified.
The Republican-led panel tried to keep the focus on Patel’s efforts to combat violent crime, counter drug trafficking and pursue the Trump administration’s agenda from his perch at the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency.
But Democrats seized on the tumult inside the FBI over the last year, including sweeping firings of agents who participated in investigations into President Donald Trump, the bureau’s efforts to investigate Trump’s perceived political adversaries and Patel’s travel schedule, which has blended private leisure with professional responsibilities.
“Mr Patel is the least qualified and most partisan FBI director in our nation’s history,” Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, the panel’s top Democrat, said in his opening statement at the hearing. He accused Patel of wielding the bureau’s law enforcement powers to seek retribution against Trump’s political opponents and pursue the president’s grievances, including his false claims that the 2020 election he lost was stolen.
Patel has made multiple appearances before Congress while serving as director, including to testify about the FBI’s budget, but this was his first time since last September before the Senate committee that has primary oversight jurisdiction over the bureau.
That hearing featured feisty and personal exchanges with Democrats, with Patel at one point shouting over Senator Adam Schiff of California, calling him an “utter disgrace” and a “coward”.
“You can make an internet troll the FBI director, but he will always be an internet troll,” Schiff shot back.
Tuesday’s hearing was expected to be no less contentious given Democrats’ fierce criticism of his leadership and conduct. Durbin called for Patel to be replaced as director in April following an article by The Atlantic magazine that raised allegations of excessive drinking.
Patel later filed a $250 million defamation lawsuit, calling the article false and a “malicious hit piece”. The Atlantic said it stood by its reporting and would vigorously defend against the “meritless lawsuit”.

Train service across much of the Netherlands was disrupted after metal pipes were placed on the tracks. The rail operator suspects sabotage.
Train service has been severely disrupted across much of the Netherlands. Rail infrastructure operator ProRail suspects sabotage, NOS reports.
ProRail said it learned of the problems at about 5:30 a.m. on September 15. Signaling and safety systems malfunctioned at at least 30 locations, making it impossible to determine whether a train was on a particular section of track. Because trains could not operate safely under those conditions, the signals turned red.
According to ProRail, the disruption was caused by metal pipes that someone had attached to or placed on the tracks.
Service was disrupted mainly on routes connecting Utrecht with the northern and eastern parts of the country, but the effects were felt nationwide, ProRail said. Trains are still running on some routes, but at very low speeds.
The disruption could also affect road traffic. If the safety system determines — correctly or mistakenly — that a train is approaching a railroad crossing, the barriers come down.
It is unclear when train service will be restored. “We know which sections of track are affected, but not exactly where the problems are. So we have to walk the entire stretch of track to find and fix the problem,” ProRail said. The company referred questions about who might be behind the suspected sabotage to the police.
The disruption occurred on Prince’s Day, NOS reports. During the annual event, the king of the Netherlands visits parliament and delivers the Speech from the Throne. Prince’s Day is held in The Hague on the third Tuesday of September, which fell on September 15 this year. The BBC notes that the event is often accompanied by protests by various activist groups. It remains unclear, however, whether the disruption was directly connected to the event.

What Greece and Israel's defence deal means for the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:13:07 UTC
01:13:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Achilles Shield: What Greece and Israel's defence deal means for the Middle East
Greece's decision to spend roughly €3 billion on an Israeli-built integrated air-defence network is about more than adding another layer of protection to its armed forces.
The proposed “Achilles Shield” comes as Greece’s relationship with Turkey worsens, while Athens deepens ties with Tel Aviv.
Greek proponents see Israeli technology as a way to modernise Greece's defences against drones, aircraft, and missiles. Critics, however, warn that the deal could bind Athens more closely to Israel at a time when Tel Aviv is increasingly isolated worldwide because of its rogue actions in Gaza and elsewhere.
There are also questions to raise about whether systems developed for Israel’s very different geography and security environment are right for Greece.
The result is a major defence purchase with implications well beyond the battlefield. The deal could significantly impact Greece’s relationships with Turkey, Israel, the United States, and fellow European Union (EU) members.
A critical question relates to whether Athens is buying an integrated shield for its territory, or a deeper strategic commitment to Israel.
Turkey the central factor in Greece's defence planning
For all the uncertainty surrounding Greece's security environment, Turkey remains the central reference point in Athens's defence planning. The two NATO members have spent decades at odds over the Aegean, Cyprus, maritime boundaries, and competing territorial claims, even as periods of diplomatic calm have periodically reduced tensions.
Tony Rigopoulos, an Athens-based journalist and political analyst, sees the Greek-Turkish rivalry as the most important explanation for this historic defence deal.
“Greece’s main and long-lasting threat comes from Turkey; even in periods when tensions were low, Greek governments have been using the ‘Turkey card’ to justify expensive defence deals,” he told The New Arab.
“In the case of the Achilles Shield deal, the conservative government of the ‘New Democracy’ party and its friendly media exhibited very low interest in analysing any potential threat from Iran and focused once more on Turkey.”
As Rigopoulos explained, comments from Turkish officials about “taking” Greek islands and the upcoming vote on the “Blue Homeland” law in Turkey’s parliament are, from Athens’ perspective, a grave threat to Greece’s sovereignty.
Dr George Tzogopoulos, a lecturer at the European Institute of Nice (Cife), offers a less exclusively Turkey-focused interpretation. In his view, Greece is modernising its armed forces because its strategic environment has become more unpredictable, rather than because Athens expects an imminent confrontation with Turkey.
That distinction matters. Greece may regard Turkey as its principal long-term military challenge while recognising that the immediate security environment has also changed. The US-Israeli war on Iran, for example, creates risks for Greece even though Athens maintains positive relations with Tehran.
Greece hosts important American military facilities and is closely aligned with Washington, potentially making it vulnerable to conflicts in which it is not a direct participant.
Stavroula Pabst, an independent analyst, similarly cautions against reducing the deal to Greek-Turkish tensions. While Athens is concerned about Turkey’s expanding military capabilities, she points out that both countries have repeatedly expressed an interest in managing their disputes through dialogue.
“Achilles Shield” may therefore be less a preparation for war with Turkey than an attempt by Greece to hedge against a range of threats.
“I am wary of saying this is primarily driven by Turkey but am forced to acknowledge this is a major factor for Athens. I believe Athens feels threatened by Turkey’s advancements in defence as of late, where Turkey is putting significant effort into fielding weapons like ICBMs, and armed drones,” she told The New Arab.
“But even as this occurs, I also want to point out that there are reasons to believe level heads will prevail here: Greece and Turkey have repeatedly made it clear that they would like to work on their grievances with each other [with the Cyprus issue being an example] among themselves. I don't know if these weapons deals will change that,” added Pabst.
Nevertheless, the Turkish question remains unavoidable. The more sophisticated Ankara’s weapons become, the greater the pressure on Athens to ensure its own defence apparatus does not fall behind. “Achilles Shield” can therefore be understood both as a response to Turkey and as part of a broader effort to preserve Greek options in a less predictable regional environment.
Can Israel's air-defence model work across Greece's islands?
Israeli defence companies have been able to market their systems to foreign governments on the basis that they have been used repeatedly in real-world conflicts, including against drones and missiles.
For Greece, which is seeking to rapidly modernise its defences, that experience is potentially a powerful selling point. Dr Tzogopoulos argues that Israel’s technological expertise and battlefield experience are precisely what make its systems attractive, even though many details of “Achilles Shield,” including the precise systems to be deployed and their locations, remain unknown.
Dr Ioannis E. Kotoulas, an adjunct lecturer in geopolitics at the University of Athens, similarly argues that Israel’s battle experiences are particularly valuable for Greece because of limitations within Europe itself.
“Israel’s battlefield experience and technical expertise, especially concerning air and missile defences, is very important for Greece since the EU has not yet managed to develop similar levels of technical assistance and suffers from bureaucratic obstacles. This is a fast way to obtain advanced defence capabilities,” he told The New Arab.
But the meaning of “battle-tested” is worth addressing. Israel’s recent experience against Iran does not necessarily demonstrate that its air-defence architecture could independently withstand a comparable attack.
In Rigopoulos’ assessment, Israeli defences required substantial assistance from the United States and other allies to deal with large numbers of Iranian missiles and drones. He also points to a fundamental difference between Israel and Greece’s environments.
Turkey and Greece share land and maritime borders, while Iran and Israel are separated by thousands of miles and several countries. Turkey’s ability to produce large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones and missiles could therefore present a different challenge from the one for which Israeli systems were designed.
Geography creates another complication. Greece’s territory is dispersed across hundreds of islands, with many in the Aegean and some considerably closer to the Turkish mainland than to mainland Greece. A centralised architecture that makes sense for Israel may require significant adaptation to work across Greece’s fragmented territory. Some Greek defence specialists question whether a network of smaller, geographically distributed systems might be more appropriate.
This highlights the danger of treating combat experience as a guarantee of effectiveness in a different strategic environment. The relevant question is whether Israeli systems can be integrated into Greece's existing defences and adapted to its geography and Turkey’s military capabilities.
Greece has presented the project as an integrated national air-defence network capable of responding to ballistic missiles, aircraft and drones. However, the precise architecture, deployment timetable and relationship between its various systems have not been fully disclosed.
The system’s effectiveness will therefore depend heavily on interoperability. Greece already operates a mixture of American, European and other weapons systems, and the value of a new shield will depend on how effectively those systems can communicate.
Israeli technology can be interoperable, but the details of Greece’s plans have not been made public. The same uncertainty applies to command and control. An integrated network could give Greek commanders a more comprehensive picture of incoming threats and allow different defensive systems to respond in coordination. However, its effectiveness will ultimately depend on how much information can be shared and how quickly decisions can be made.
There is also a more fundamental question about technological sovereignty. Rigopoulos has drawn attention to comments by Moshe Patel, director-general of Israel’s Missile Defence Organisation, concerning Greece’s access to the system’s source code and Israel’s continuing role in support and maintenance.
If Athens lacks full access to the underlying software and remains dependent on Israel for substantial technical support, the meaning of “national” control over the shield becomes more complicated.
Foreign military systems routinely require supplier support, so dependence is not unusual. But the more central “Achilles Shield” becomes to Greece’s national defence, the more significant that dependence could become.
That question also illustrates why the deal is more than a conventional arms purchase. An integrated defence architecture involves software, command systems, training, maintenance, upgrades and long-term technical cooperation.
If “Achilles Shield” becomes deeply embedded in Greece's military infrastructure, Israel could consequently become an indispensable partner in Greek national defence for decades. The strategic significance of the agreement may therefore lie as much in the relationship it creates as in the weapons Greece receives.
Greece faces a growing divide over its ties with Israel
The strategic case for closer cooperation with Israel exists alongside a significant political problem: Greek public opinion toward Israel has deteriorated sharply amid the Gaza genocide.
Polling data from February-May 2026 shows 65 percent of Greeks expressing an unfavourable view of Israel, while there have been hundreds of pro-Palestinian demonstrations across the country since October 2023.
Pabst expects substantial opposition to “Achilles Shield,” arguing that the Greek public has broadly opposed closer cooperation with Israel because of its conduct in Gaza. The contrast between public sentiment and government policy is striking. While Athens has continued to deepen its relationship with Israel, many Greeks appear increasingly uncomfortable with a country whose technology will now play a significant role in their national defence.
Yet, opposition to Israel does not necessarily translate into opposition to the defence relationship. Dr Tzogopoulos makes an important distinction between attitudes toward the current Israeli government and perceptions of Israel as a useful strategic and technological partner.
“Greek citizens are concerned about the future trajectory of Greek-Turkish relations. In that regard, closer collaboration with Israel, which goes beyond the Achilles Shield, is considered important in the context of the national interest,” he told The New Arab.
“The image of the current Israeli government in Greece is being deteriorated because of the Gaza war, but this is different from considering Israel a partner in the process of modernising armed forces - both at the political and public opinion level,” noted Dr Tzogopoulos.
Rigopoulos similarly describes the relationship as something that parts of Greek society may regard as a “necessary evil”, essentially constituting a partnership that is politically uncomfortable but difficult to reject if believed to strengthen Greece’s security.
That tension could become increasingly important as the defence relationship deepens. Arms agreements are unusually durable forms of foreign policy, involving large financial commitments and creating networks of military, technological, and institutional cooperation that can last for decades.
Pabst argues that this could eventually make it more difficult for Greece, or even other European governments, to distance themselves from Israel or hold its government accountable for its actions. The more Greek defence planning depends on Israeli technology, the greater the political cost of disrupting the relationship.
'Achilles Shield' entrenches Greece's partnership with Israel
Domestic politics aside, “Achilles Shield” is the latest step in a Greece-Israel relationship that has deepened for more than a decade, alongside increasingly close ties with Cyprus. Joint military exercises, energy cooperation, and defence links have given the relationship a strategic dimension, while deteriorating Israeli-Turkish relations have made the Greek-Israeli partnership more conspicuous.
From Athens' perspective, cooperation with Israel offers access to advanced military technology while strengthening ties with a regional actor whose interests overlap with Greece’s on several issues. “Achilles Shield” is therefore not an isolated procurement decision but another piece of a broader Eastern Mediterranean security network.
Dr Kotoulas describes that network in more explicitly strategic terms, arguing that “Achilles Shield is an important upgrade of Greek defence capabilities and functions as a factor of deterrence for any Turkish regional aspirations.” He also noted that “the network of Greece-Cyprus-Israel in the Mediterranean creates an important military counterweight to any regional hegemonic attempts”.
It would nevertheless be premature to describe this network as a formal anti-Turkish alliance. Dr Tzogopoulos rejects the idea that regional alliances are necessarily forming, arguing instead that states are building partnerships around overlapping interests.
Israel’s disagreements with Turkey are also different from Greece's: Israel's disputes with Ankara centre heavily on Syria and the Palestinian question, while Greece's concern the Aegean, maritime boundaries and Cyprus.
“Israel will not help Greece in a Greek-Turkish crisis,” he told The New Arab, adding that he will “not be surprised if Israel and Turkey will be able to better manage their relationship in the future”.
Even without a formal alliance, however, defence agreements, exercises, intelligence relationships, and military technology can alter perceptions of the regional balance of power. “Achilles Shield” adds another layer to that process, making Greece and Israel more deeply connected militarily and giving Turkey another reason to watch their relationship closely.
The implications of “Achilles Shield” extend beyond Greece, Israel, and Turkey. For the United States, stronger Greek air defences are broadly compatible with Washington's interest in strengthening the military capabilities of a key ally on NATO's southeastern flank.
At the same time, Washington has its own defence industry to consider, and greater Greek reliance on Israeli systems could mean fewer opportunities for American weapons manufacturers. Greece’s broader modernisation strategy, which also involves military cooperation with the United States, France, and Italy, suggests that Athens is attempting to diversify its partnerships rather than replace one major supplier with another.
Dr Kotoulas sees the strategic relationship from an Israeli perspective as even broader. “Greece along with Cyprus function as the strategic depth of Israel in the Eastern Mediterranean,” he told The New Arab.
For NATO, the equation is similarly complicated. A more capable Greek military could strengthen the alliance's southeastern defences, particularly against drones and missiles. But “Achilles Shield” also raises questions about interoperability and dependence on a non-NATO supplier.
Those questions become more significant if the Israeli system is eventually integrated deeply into Greece's wider command-and-control infrastructure. The system’s value to NATO will depend not only on what it can intercept, but also on how effectively it can communicate with the alliance's existing networks and other weapons systems.
The EU faces a different dilemma. Greece's growing dependence on Israeli defence technology comes at a time when European governments remain divided over Israel's conduct in Gaza. Pabst's concern is that arms agreements can create relationships that are much harder to unwind than ordinary diplomatic partnerships.
If Israeli technology becomes critical to Greek or wider European security, governments seeking to place political or economic pressure on Israel could face an additional constraint: the practical consequences of disrupting an increasingly important defence relationship.
Turkey, meanwhile, is likely to view the deal with suspicion even if it does not regard “Achilles Shield” as evidence of an imminent Greek-Israeli military alliance. The system could contribute to an arms competition in the Eastern Mediterranean if Ankara concludes that Greece is acquiring capabilities specifically intended to offset Turkish military advantages.
Dr Tzogopoulos, however, stresses that conflict is not inevitable. Greek-Turkish communication channels remain open, and both countries have an interest in preventing disputes from escalating into a military confrontation.
The United Arab Emirates and other regional actors will also be watching the Greece-Israel relationship, particularly against the backdrop of the intensifying US-Iran confrontation. But perhaps the most important geopolitical implication is the one that is easiest to overlook, which is the fact that “Achilles Shield” could make Athens’ relationship with Tel Aviv substantially more difficult to reverse.
Once a country relies on another state for critical military technology, maintenance, upgrades, and expertise, the relationship acquires an institutional momentum of its own. Therefore, the significance of the deal may lie in the possibility that Israel is becoming embedded in the architecture of Greek national defence.
What exactly is Greece buying with 'Achilles Shield'?
“Achilles Shield” is ultimately difficult to understand as a response to any single threat. Turkey remains the most important long-term concern in Greek defence planning, but the US-Israeli war on the Islamic Republic has demonstrated broader risks arising from Greece’s position in a volatile region and its close relationship with Washington.
At the same time, the system’s suitability for Greece remains tied to unanswered questions about geography, interoperability, effectiveness, and technological sovereignty.
What is clearer is that the €3 billion project represents more than a conventional arms purchase. It is another step in Greece's military modernisation and toward a deeper, potentially more durable strategic relationship with Israel. That relationship may provide valuable technology and capabilities, but it also creates dependencies with political consequences well beyond the battlefield.
The central question, then, is what kind of security architecture Greece is building, and how much of that architecture is Athens prepared to place in the hands of a foreign partner seen throughout much of the world as a rogue state guilty of genocide?
In an Eastern Mediterranean already defined by overlapping rivalries and shifting partnerships, the answer could prove highly complicated.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics.

Two years after COP29, Azerbaijan turns climate commitments into investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:10:59 UTC
01:10:59 KST

The country has committed €540 million to climate-resilient irrigation and launched an AI-based farmer-scoring system, developed with the FAO, to channel subsidies to smallholders who adopt water-saving and soil-regenerating techniques.
Azerbaijan has committed up to 1 billion manat (€540 million) to climate-resilient irrigation infrastructure under its 2026-2030 state programme, as the country hosted a regional climate week two years after staging COP29 in Baku.
The figure, announced by Agriculture Minister Majnun Mammadov at Baku Climate Action Week, represents nearly 40% of the state agricultural budget earmarked for climate adaptation.
The funding will support modern irrigation systems across the South Caucasus, where water shortages, shifting growing seasons and soil degradation are accelerating.
The government also launched an AI-based farmer scoring system this year, developed in partnership with the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
First piloted in 2024 and tested in 2025, the digital platform distributes advance subsidy payments to smallholder farmers managing between five and 100 hectares.
Mammadov said eligibility is assessed across three criteria: adoption of modern farming practices, the economic value of the chosen crop, and whether the farmer uses water-saving or soil-regenerating techniques.
"The scoring system evaluates three fundamental pillars," Mammadov told Euronews. "First, the adoption of modern agricultural practices, second, the economic value and profitability of the crop for the farmer and the wider economy."
"And third, ecological impact. How the selected crop interacts with soil health and whether the farmer utilises climate-supporting subsidies like soil-regenerating or water-saving techniques."
Smallholder farmers are the most exposed to climate volatility across the Caucasus, where minor shifts in temperature or water availability can destroy yields.
Mammadov said international investors in local farming infrastructure would receive the same subsidy access as domestic operators.
"Agriculture is in a very unique position, it is causing climate change, and it is being affected by climate change," FAO Representative in Azerbaijan Nasar Hayat said.
'Opportunity to build'
Separately, the UN Industrial Development Organisation urged Azerbaijan to prioritise domestic industrial use of green hydrogen before pursuing European export ambitions.
Petra Schwager, chief of UNIDO's climate and technology partnership division, said pipeline exports to Europe would take years because the infrastructure does not yet exist.
In the short term, she said, green hydrogen derivatives such as green ammonia could be used in domestic fertiliser manufacturing and shipping fuels.
"The true benchmark of success for industrial decarbonisation is not policy pledges or technology partnerships, but verifiable CO2 emission reductions," Schwager said.
On financing, Turkey announced two new mechanisms ahead of COP31 in Antalya: BRIDGE, a technical support platform for developing countries to structure investment-ready projects, built alongside the UN Development Programme, and SURF, which adapts a Turkish municipal lending model to scale low-cost credit lines to cities across developing nations.
Fatma Varank, CEO of COP31 and Deputy Minister of Turkey's Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, pointed to the long-term cooperation between host nations.
"Along our shared journey from Baku to Antalya, we have an opportunity to build on this foundation and achieve stronger outcomes by sharing experiences, deepening partnerships and channelling climate finance towards tangible implementation," Varank said.
Azerbaijan's Deputy Foreign Minister Yalchin Rafiyev confirmed that a Black Sea subsea cable project to carry renewable electricity from Azerbaijan and Central Asia to European markets remains a priority.
"Continuity between the COPs is extremely important in order to keep the legacy for the host country, but at the same time, globally it is very important," Rafiyev told Euronews.
He said COP29's legacy had brought Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan forward with specific green grid proposals.
At COP29 in 2024, wealthier nations agreed to provide at least $300 billion (€258 billion) per year by 2035 to help developing countries cut emissions and manage climate impacts.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said at the time the deal provided "a base on which to build" but fell short of what the crisis required.
According to Jens Nielsen, Founder and CEO of the World Climate Foundation, global climate diplomacy is undergoing a structural evolution, which is “changing from the politics of climate change to the economics of climate change."
"We need to move beyond commitments and action straight into bankable financial transactions," Nielsen told Euronews.
Baku Climate Action Week was held in parallel with the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change regional climate week for Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

The UN is considering moving aid shipments for Ukraine to underground storage facilities following strikes on warehouses
Kyiv • UNN
Russian strikes this year destroyed millions of dollars’ worth of UN property at 10 warehouses. The organization is strengthening protection for personnel and supplies.
The UN humanitarian coordinator in Ukraine said on Tuesday that his organization was considering moving humanitarian aid supplies to underground storage facilities to avoid Russian strikes. Such attacks have already hit 10 of the organization’s warehouses this year, destroying property worth millions of dollars, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Earlier this month, one of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) main warehouses, where medical supplies were stored, was hit, while other attacks destroyed hygiene kits and school supplies for children, UN humanitarian coordinator in Ukraine Matthias Schmale told Reuters in Geneva.
"These targeted attacks on warehouse facilities (...) are a new trend of the past few months," he said after a briefing for states on Ukraine’s needs in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
According to him, the organization is considering moving supplies to underground bunkers and postponing the procurement of humanitarian aid until the last possible moment in order to minimize the risk of them being hit.
"There is an increasing sense that the front line is moving into the airspace," he said. "This also means additional costs for taxpayers, who ultimately pay for the goods brought in by the UN and other humanitarian organizations." He added that such expenses had not been included in the organization’s $2.3 billion humanitarian aid budget for 2026.
The UN is investing in equipment to protect personnel — including purchasing more armored vehicles and drone-detection systems — and is also considering requests from the Ukrainian side to install mobile shelters from drones on the streets (for example, near bus stops) amid the rising number of civilian casualties, Schmale said.

Herzog condemns Smotrich's AI video of Supreme Court chief being dragged, warning: ‘Elections are not a civil war’
Unknown

16:04:49 UTC
