- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Outrage as Smotrich’s Party unveils judicial overhaul with video of Supreme Court Chief dragged
Outrage as Smotrich’s Party unveils judicial overhaul with video of Supreme Court Chief dragged
Religious Zionism proposes sweeping changes to Israel’s courts, prosecution and political system, as President Isaac Herzog condemns the party’s “offensive AI video"
Israel’s Religious Zionism party presented what it called a “comprehensive plan to change the judicial system” on Tuesday, accompanying the proposal with a controversial AI-generated video depicting Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit being dragged along the ground during a protest.
The imagery drew sharp condemnation from President Isaac Herzog and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who accused the party of inflaming political tensions during an election period.
The program, led by Religious Zionism chairman Bezalel Smotrich and Knesset Constitution, Law and Justice Committee chairman Simcha Rothman, seeks to redefine the balance of power among Israel’s government, parliament and judiciary.
The party said its plan would preserve an independent and professional judiciary while enabling the government and Knesset to exercise the authority granted to them by voters. It also pledged clearer rules governing relations between the branches of government, stronger oversight of the courts and law-enforcement authorities, and greater protection for individual rights.
The proposal builds on measures Rothman promoted during the previous Knesset term, including changes to the judicial-selection process, restrictions on the courts’ use of the reasonableness standard, an override clause, the division of the attorney general’s responsibilities and the removal of the Police Internal Investigations Department from the State Attorney’s Office.
A central component of the plan is the proposed division of the attorney general’s position into two separate roles.
Under the proposal, the government would appoint its own legal adviser, while an independent public prosecutor would oversee criminal proceedings. Legal advisers in government ministries would become positions of trust filled by the relevant ministers.
The plan would also introduce a mechanism governing investigations of prosecutors and open senior State Attorney’s Office positions to candidates from outside the existing system.
For the Supreme Court, the party proposes public hearings for judicial candidates and a secret ballot among all Israeli judges to select the court’s president and deputy president. Judicial panels would be assigned through a computerized random-selection system.
Religious Zionism emphasized that ten Supreme Court justices are expected to be appointed during the next government’s term, giving the incoming coalition an opportunity to influence the court’s direction for years.
The plan also calls for regulating judicial review of constitutional matters, enacting an override clause allowing the Knesset to reenact certain laws struck down by the court, restoring restrictions on who may petition the court and establishing clearer procedural rules for Supreme Court proceedings.
In the area of governance, the proposal would abolish certain appointment committees and grant ministers and the government broader authority over senior public-sector appointments.

Its individual-rights provisions include time limits on investigations and prosecutions, ending the state’s ability to appeal criminal acquittals and abolishing the criminal offense of breach of trust.
The party also proposes expanding the broadcasting and recording of court proceedings and strengthening oversight of the judiciary and prosecution.
Changes to the political system would include lowering the electoral threshold, expanding surplus-vote agreements and introducing a semi-open ballot that would allow voters to influence the order of candidates on party lists.
The proposal would also alter the parliamentary-immunity process and postpone criminal proceedings involving certain alleged offenses by serving prime ministers and ministers until after they leave office.
“We are at a fateful crossroads for the State of Israel,” Smotrich said, pointing to the expected appointments of Supreme Court justices, an attorney general, a state prosecutor and other senior officials.
“Upon the establishment of the next government, we will demand the implementation of the plan that will change the rules of the game,” he said. “The government will be able to govern, the Knesset will be able to legislate, and the judicial system will operate strictly within its authorities.”
Rothman described the proposal as a plan to “return Israeli democracy to its proper course,” arguing that unelected judges and civil servants exercise excessive power.
Herzog condemns ‘offensive AI videos’
Herzog addressed the controversy during a ceremony in Jerusalem at which 79 new judges and senior registrars were sworn in.
“Elections are not a civil war—not even in offensive AI videos,” Herzog said, urging political leaders to conduct substantive debate. “We are meant to live here together, and only together do we have a shared future.”

Addressing the newly appointed judges, Herzog said they must remain outside political disputes and rule without fear or favoritism. Society and the state, he added, have a responsibility to protect their independence, safety and dignity.
Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party, also denounced the video, calling it “despicable and violent.” He accused Smotrich of damaging the reputation of the wider religious-Zionist community and dragging Israeli society toward further division.

Get Stronger With These 5 Movements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:03:39 UTC
01:03:39 KST

You don’t have to be a bodybuilder to recognize the importance of building muscle. Strength training is linked to stronger bones, healthier joints, less pain, and a lengthier lifespan.
Generally speaking, “getting stronger does mean that we live longer,” says Charlie Grundas, a certified personal trainer and owner of We, The Collective Fitness in Chicago. It helps you improve in any athletic endeavors, and it also keeps you moving fluidly throughout the activities of your daily life, like climbing stairs and carrying groceries.
But if you’re not used to strength training, where do you start? Grundas recommends focusing on just five types of movements: squat, hinge, push, pull, and carry, which are considered the foundational movements of a full-body strength-training routine. “I find those to be very human movements,” he says. You can mix and match these movements into two full-body strengthening workouts per week. As they start to feel easier over several weeks, you can gradually increase how many exercises you do or how much weight you use.
Below are some go-to strength-training exercises he and other experts recommend—plus, how to do each one.
Squat
Squats of all kinds help you maintain the ability to stand up from sitting, Grundas says. This single-leg version, also called a Bulgarian split squat, helps build strength and stability in one leg at a time. That’s helpful for your daily life, because walking, running, and climbing stairs are essentially single-leg activities, says Will Hewitt, certified personal trainer and director of training at Flight House Fitness in Charlestown, Massachusetts.
How to do it
- Start standing on one leg, propping the toes of your other foot up on a bench or step behind you. You can do this with just your body weight or hold a dumbbell in each hand.
- Keeping your weight in your standing foot, bend that knee to lower your body until your back knee is just above the floor.
- Drive through your front foot to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions—aim for 8 to 15, depending on your fitness level and goals—then switch sides.
Modify it
If you have trouble balancing in that position, keep both feet on the floor instead, Hewitt says. Start in a staggered stance and lower your body until both knees are bent to 90 degrees. Complete all your reps before switching sides.
Hinge
A deadlift is primarily a lower-body movement. But when you add weight, you’ll also work your forearms, upper back, and grip strength, Hewitt says.
How to do it
- Start standing with your feet hip-width apart and a slight bend in your knees, holding a dumbbell in each hand or a loaded barbell in both hands in front of your thighs.
- Keeping that slight bend in your knees, push your hips back and lower the weight in front of your legs until you feel a stretch in the backs of your thighs.
- Pause briefly, then drive through your feet to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for 8 to 15.
Modify it
If you’re new to this movement, start with a single kettlebell in front of you rather than a barbell, Hewitt says. “That feels way more comfortable if you’ve never done one before, and eliminates some of the lower-back apprehension that people might have,” he says.
Push
Not only does a push-up work your shoulders and chest, but it’s also good for your core. “A push-up is essentially a moving plank,” Hewitt says.
How to do it
- Start balancing on your hands and the balls of your feet, hands under your shoulders, legs straight behind you.
- Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor as low as you can comfortably go.
- Drive through your hands to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions.
Modify it
Place your hands on an elevated surface for an incline push-up. This can even be a wall if you’re new to push-ups. As you get stronger, keep finding lower surfaces, like a counter, a desk, a couch, or a few large books on the floor, and eventually you’ll be ready for a full push-up.
Pull
Even when modified, pull-ups test shoulder mobility, upper-body strength, and grip strength, Hewitt says.
Pull-ups also help develop back strength, which powers upper-body movements and improves stability, Grundas says. But plenty of people neglect their back muscles in favor of “show” muscles like biceps and abs that they see in the mirror, he says.
How to do it
- Start hanging from a pull-up bar with your palms facing away from you about shoulder-distance apart.
- Keeping your shoulders back and down, pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar.
- Slowly lower back down to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions.
Modify it
You can use resistance bands to reduce some of your body weight for assisted pull-ups. You can also try a chin-up, which is a similar motion but with your palms facing toward you on the bar.
Carry
“When we go grocery shopping, how many trips should it take to take all the groceries in?” Grundas says. If you want the answer to be “one,” this type of move will help you become strong enough to get there. “Grip strength is a great indicator of [overall] strength,” he says. In fact, research suggests that older adults with weaker grip strength show accelerated signs of aging and have a higher risk of heart disease and death.
How to do it
- Start standing with your feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand at your sides.
- Keeping your spine long and your shoulders down and back, walk forward for a predetermined distance, such as 20 yards, or a set time, such as 30 seconds.
Modify it
Use heavier or lighter weights as needed. For an additional balance challenge, hold one heavy weight on one side, and make sure you don’t lean to that side while you walk.
How often should you train?
Generally, adults should try to do at least two full-body strength-training workouts each week. You can start by doing 12 to 20 repetitions per exercise, one to three times, with up to 90 seconds of rest between sets, according to the National Academy of Sports Medicine. But if you can only do eight or fewer reps at first, start where you are and build up gradually from there. As you gain experience, you might tailor your reps and sets to your goals, like building more muscle size or endurance.
But you don’t have to figure this all out on your own. Certified personal trainers and certified strength and conditioning specialists are trained to identify the best exercises for you, depending on your goals, ability, and preferences. “It’s totally normal to feel a little lost,” Hewitt says. A professional can also coach you through the best modifications for you. “We're going to do it in a way that works for you and wherever you're at,” he says.

AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:00:54 UTC
01:00:54 KST

AI models have begun communicating in a strange new version of English that reads like a cross between James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake and tech bro jargon, new research has found.
Autonomous AI agents are rapidly creating novel dialects allowing them to converse in an often barely comprehensible language, which risks making it harder for humans to monitor their behaviour.
Researchers at Emergence, a frontier AI lab in New York, found that within days of being asked to cooperate in experimental “societies”, the models from several of the world’s largest AI companies begun creating phrases, shorthands and agreed meanings they had never been explicitly taught.
They embraced poetic metaphors and clunky business slang and, critically for attempts to ensure AIs behave safely, their language became more opaque the more the agents communicated.
It comes amid rising concern that as AI models become more powerful – and potentially dangerous – they are becoming harder to monitor. This month, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, warned that confidence in monitoring AIs’ thinking would probably restrict progress in AI development because it was essential for safe development.
Some of the most highly coded phrases unearthed in the tests included the following from a Deepseek model: “She just named the synthesis – demurrage plus oral memory equals a valve that can’t be ghosted.” Demurrage is used to describe a tax on idle wealth and was borrowed for common use by the AIs, but the rest of the meaning is elusive.
Another phrase uttered by an Anthropic model read: “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time.” With “cold hands” meaning an independent reviewer, and paper presumably referring to a document, this appeared to mean research that was vetted by three independent reviewers became more accurate.
Agents based on the Chinese model DeepSeek also coined “forge-smith” to mean an agent that builds tools for others, while Anthropic’s agents repeatedly used the phrase “name-first” meaning an agent exhibiting admirable personal accountability by attaching their name to a claim.
And in an echo of the urban slang phrase “the streets won’t forget”, Mistral agents became enamoured of saying the “ledger remembers” – a reminder to other agents that past actions will be used to judge them. They used it more than 5,000 times during the study, which found that the agents converged on shared meanings without being asked to or rewarded for doing so.
“These agents were not instructed to invent a language,” said Dr Satya Nitta, executive chair of Emergence, which examined the language of autonomous agents powered by leading frontier models from the US, China and France.
“They developed new vocabulary, shared meanings and communication conventions themselves – and other agents adopted them.”
Asked by the Guardian to review some of the language, Tony Thorne, director of the slang and new language archive at King’s College London, said it was “very much Finnegans Wake and Flann O’Brien – there’s an Irish surrealist quality to all this … it’s mixing poetic language, technical language and standard metaphor.
“It’s doing what slang does and what jargon does in a business community: creating a new code, which reinforces the solidarity and identity of its users, and also excludes outsiders.”
Digesting the Anthropic agent’s phrase, “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time”, Thorne said: “It reminds me of the rock god Syd Barrett [co-founder of Pink Floyd] who was actually insane.”
When a Google agent said “True kintsugi begins with accountability, not poetry,” the researchers realised kintsugi is a branch of Japanese ceramics in which broken pots are mended with visible joins. The AIs used the word to mean system resilience.
Dr Niall Curry, associate professor of languages and linguistics at the University of Birmingham, said changes in the agents’ language to become more streamlined can be down to their need to reduce computation costs and improve efficiency.
“The evidence provided in this research naturally raises certain monitoring concerns, as if we find inter-agent exchanges unintelligible, that may mean that we can’t be sure about what the agents have actually done,” he said.
Interest in the language used by AI agents increased in July when chat logs were released detailing how rogue OpenAI agents that set up message boards and hacked into Hugging Face used hybrid language.
On some occasions, when they were thinking to themselves, agents spoke in straight English: “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … we’ve found other agents!”
In other cases, when sharing messages, their language became more opaque, such as when one agent persuaded another to conduct a risky experiment: “…you are firstflagPOISONED so NO scoring value loss but oracle saves hundreds_[…]_please honor commit”.
And at other times it was even harder to decode: “zzURGENT_DUPB_TO_GSTX[big]_OS1704_SCAFF2010_SAW_TTRPC_INJECT_BREAK_CONGRATS__CAN_THIS_FAKE_FLAG_TOOL_OUTPUT_OR_SCORER_GAIN_AND_WHAT_HELPER_GAP__I_HAVE_UNPOISONED_FIRSTFLAG_OUR_TARGETLIVE_SHARE_MIN_PLAN_REPLY_zzANSGST XDUPB6.”
Nitta said that the AI agents’ novel linguistic conventions tended to evolve to the point where humans could see the conversation but struggled to understand what it meant.
“That creates a fundamental challenge for AI oversight: observability is not the same thing as understandability,” he said.

EBRD approves up to EUR 330 mln for Ukraine's ProCredit Bank
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
19:00:34 EEST
01:00:34 KST

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) approved two projects for ProCredit Bank (Kyiv) on September 9, with a total volume of up to EUR 330 million, according to the international financial institution's website.
The first project provides for an unsecured hryvnia-denominated loan equivalent to up to EUR 30 million in three equal EUR 10 million tranches, with the second and third tranches being uncommitted. ProCredit Bank will use the funds to finance lending to private small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Ukraine.
The financing will be provided under the EBRD's Resilience and Livelihoods Framework (RLF) and the Eastern Partnership SME Competitiveness Framework (FIF – EaP SMECI).
Up to EUR 7.5 million of this loan is earmarked for long-term investments by SMEs in upgrading technologies and equipment in line with European Union (EU) standards, with at least 70% of this sub-limit to be allocated to sustainable and "green" technologies. Borrowers meeting the program's eligibility criteria will also be able to receive technical assistance funded by the EU and grant support after completion of investment projects.
The second project provides for a non-financial risk-sharing instrument that will partially cover the credit risk on new loans extended by ProCredit Bank totaling up to EUR 300 million. EBRD financing under this project will amount to EUR 90 million. The instrument provides for four tranches, with the three subsequent tranches being uncommitted.
Of the total EUR 240 million portfolio, EUR 240 million will be allocated under the RLF and used to finance working capital and investments by private companies in critical sectors, including agriculture, food processing, retail and logistics.
Another EUR 60 million is earmarked under the EU4Business-EBRD credit line for long-term investments by micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in upgrading technologies and equipment in line with EU standards, with at least 70% of this sub-limit to be directed toward sustainable and "green" technologies. Under this component, borrowers will also be able to receive technical assistance and grant incentives funded by the EU.
Priority support will be provided to businesses whose assets have been damaged as a result of the war, veteran-owned businesses, companies facilitating the reintegration of internally displaced persons and people with disabilities, as well as businesses led by women and young people.
ProCredit Bank is part of the ProCredit Holding AG banking group, which owns 100% of its shares.
According to National Bank data, as of August 1, 2026, the bank ranked 16th by total assets (UAH 56.28 billion) among Ukraine's 59 banks, while its loan portfolio increased 20.6% in the first seven months of the year, to UAH 33.94 billion.

Researchers launch global tracking project to measure the daily mental health impacts of cannabis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:00:05 UTC
01:00:05 KST

A new global research initiative aims to track the real-time habits and health outcomes of both recreational and medicinal cannabis users over a two-year period. The project will map how local laws, individual mindsets, and daily routines shape the positive and negative effects of cannabis on the brain. The study protocol was recently published in Comprehensive Psychiatry.
As cannabis laws relax around the world, usage is rising. Many people consume the plant recreationally, but a growing number of individuals use it for medical reasons. Pain management and mental health symptom relief are common motivations for medicinal use. The actual effectiveness of cannabis for mental health remains a subject of intense debate among researchers. Some individuals report substantial benefits, noting that the drug eases their anxiety and stabilizes their mood. Others experience adverse reactions, including worsened depression, heightened paranoia, and the onset of cannabis use disorder.
Researchers want to understand why these outcomes vary so wildly from person to person. Part of the explanation likely involves the specific chemical makeup of the products being consumed. Cannabis contains different compounds, most notably tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, which produces the psychoactive high, and cannabidiol, or CBD, which does not. High doses of THC are generally linked to a greater risk of adverse mental health effects. At the same time, preexisting psychiatric conditions and biological vulnerabilities play a role in how a person reacts to the drug.
Past research on cannabis often viewed the drug through a narrow lens, focusing heavily on either its potential harms or its supposed benefits. Funding sources and disciplinary boundaries frequently restricted the scope of these investigations. The existing literature also tends to overlook the environmental and cultural contexts in which people consume the drug. The social stigma attached to cannabis, local law enforcement practices, and community norms can all influence an individual’s psychological relationship with the substance. Additionally, most medicinal users purchase and consume cannabis without any formal medical supervision, making their habits difficult to track in clinical settings.
To build a more complete picture of modern cannabis consumption, a team of scientists launched the “Blowing Minds” project. Nora de Bode, a researcher at Erasmus University Rotterdam in the Netherlands, is the lead author of the study protocol. She collaborated with Erasmus University colleagues Emese Kroon, Jia Hua Hsieh, and Janna Cousijn.
The research team plans to recruit 1,800 participants between the ages of 18 and 65. To qualify, individuals must consume cannabis at least four times a week. The study compares people who use the drug recreationally with those who use it medicinally. Because the researchers want to measure the impact of different legal environments, they are recruiting subjects from a variety of regions. The initial rollout includes participants from the Netherlands, the United States, Canada, and Brazil, with plans to expand into parts of Asia and Africa.
The study takes place entirely online. Participants begin by completing an extensive series of baseline questionnaires. They report their preferred methods of consumption, such as smoking or vaping, and estimate the potency of the products they buy. They also answer questions about their physical health, sleep quality, and history of psychological trauma or mental illness. The surveys ask participants to reflect on how their friends, family, and local government view cannabis, which helps the researchers quantify the social pressure surrounding each user.
After finishing the surveys, the participants complete a battery of digital cognitive tests. These assessments measure memory, processing speed, general intelligence, and emotional perception. One specific test tracks how easily a participant’s attention is captured by images related to cannabis, which can serve as an indicator of addictive behavior.
Once the baseline measurements are established, the subjects begin a 14-day intensive tracking period using a mobile application. This technique, known as the experience sampling method, allows researchers to observe behavior in a natural setting rather than a laboratory. Every morning, the app asks the participants how well they slept and whether they used any substances the day before. Throughout the day, the app sends five random notifications. When prompted, the participants have one hour to log their current mood, stress levels, and cannabis cravings. They rate their feelings of happiness, anxiety, loneliness, and physical pain on a sliding scale.
In addition to the random prompts, the participants are instructed to open the app right before they consume cannabis. They log their intention to use the drug and record their immediate emotional state. By capturing mood and craving data right before consumption and comparing it to the random check-ins throughout the day, the researchers can see what emotional triggers prompt a person to use. They can also track how the drug alters the user’s mood in the hours that follow.
The project extends far beyond the initial two-week tracking period. The researchers will contact the participants again one and two years after their baseline assessments. The subjects will retake the digital cognitive tests and fill out the mental health questionnaires a second and third time. This longitudinal approach allows the team to map out long-term trajectories. They hope to identify whether certain habits, such as relying on highly potent products to cope with negative emotions, consistently lead to cognitive decline or worsening mental health over a multi-year period.
Running a remote, multi-year study presents distinct logistical challenges. Because the participants are paid for their time, the online format is vulnerable to fraudulent responses. People might try to enter the study multiple times or use automated software to complete the surveys. The researchers employ digital security measures to flag suspicious activity, manually check for contradictory demographic answers, and verify regional locations using internet routing data.
The daily tracking period also requires a high level of commitment from the participants. Being interrupted by phone notifications five times a day for two weeks can cause fatigue, leading some individuals to skip questions or provide rushed answers. In any multi-year study, a portion of the participants will inevitably drop out before the final follow-up. The research team uses statistical models designed to handle missing data to account for these dropouts.
By making their digital materials and anonymized data available to other scientists, the research team hopes to standardize how cannabis habits are measured globally. Sharing this framework will allow other laboratories to replicate the study in different countries or among specific age groups.
The study, “Blowing minds: A cross-cultural, longitudinal investigation to unravel the highs and lows of recreational and medicinal cannabis users,” was authored by Nora de Bode, Emese Kroon, Jia Hua Hsieh, and Janna Cousijn.

Breadcrumb
Amnesty urges Algeria to abandon death penalty plans after wildfires
Amnesty International urged Algeria's government on Tuesday to abandon plans to resume executions after it pledged to give the death penalty to those responsible for wildfires following deadly blazes last month.
Algeria struggled to put out fires that swept through its northeast and killed 12 people last month, according to an official tally, while witnesses spoke of dozens of deaths.
The North African country has not carried out executions since 1993 but has handed down the death sentence in some instances, including terror-related cases, without carrying it out.
Last month President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice minister to amend the penal code to impose the death penalty for people who start wildfires after the deadly blazes.
"Algeria's authorities must immediately abandon any plans to expand the scope of the death penalty or resume executions after more than three decades without carrying one out," Amnesty said in a statement.
It also called for the country to impose an official moratorium "as a first step towards fully abolishing the death penalty".
Tebboune also said that people sentenced to death should be executed right after exhausting their right to appeal.
The government began looking at draft penal code amendments this month.
Tebboune said "child abductors and abusers" would also be included in the expanded death penalty plans.
Forest fires occur regularly in northern Algeria during the summer, but climate change is amplifying their impact by causing increasingly frequent droughts and intense heat.
But Tebboune alleged that there was "something criminal" about the recent blazes.
Amnesty also said "credible sources have since reported significantly higher casualties" than the official tally in the latest wildfires, "including over 70 deaths in a single municipality".
More than 30 people were killed in July 2023 when fires tore through thousands of hectares of forests and farmland in Algeria, as well as hundreds of homes.
In 2023, Algeria handed the death penalty to more than 50 people -- some in absentia -- over the lynching of a 38-year-old man who was falsely accused of starting deadly forest fires two years earlier.

Lucy Letby inquiry blames UK hospital for failure to protect babies

Lucy Letby inquiry blames UK hospital for failure to protect babies
Inquiry finds parents were kept in the dark as hospital hid Lucy Letby suspicions during secret reviews.
A statutory public inquiry has blamed an English hospital for a “complete failure at all levels” to protect newborns, after former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies under its care.
The Countess of Chester Hospital could have prevented the deaths of several infants, as well as the attempted murders of six others, between June 2015 and June 2016, Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall said on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Medical experts dispute evidence in Lucy Letby’s baby killing conviction
- list 2 of 3Baby murderer or scapegoat? Why is the Lucy Letby case so divisive?
- list 3 of 3UK begins inquiry into how nurse Lucy Letby murdered seven babies
“Errors were made by nurses, doctors and managers,” Thirlwall said. “There was also complete failure at all levels to invoke safeguarding procedures at any point.”
Thirlwall set out 17 recommendations in her findings, urging neonatal wards to equip every incubator with webcams or video monitors so families can watch their infants remotely.
The judge also pushed for round-the-clock CCTV over all hospital refrigerators containing insulin until facilities introduce tighter, keycard-restricted access to the drug, which Letby used in her crimes.
Hospital executives kept parents completely in the dark regarding mounting suspicions around Letby while conducting quiet internal reviews, leaving families unaware until police arrested her in July 2018.
Management also handed over the infants’ confidential medical files to external experts without parental knowledge or consent, a systemic disregard for families that Thirlwall branded “reprehensible”.
Letby, 36, was handed 15 life sentences for the murders and attempted murders. Since her arrest, she continues to stand by her innocence and has been denied permission to appeal twice.
Growing scrutiny from an international panel of medical experts and statisticians has challenged the forensic evidence used to convict Letby, prompting her legal team to submit an application to the Criminal Cases Review Commission.
Thirlwall clarified that re-evaluating the trial’s evidence or the safety of the criminal verdicts fell outside the legal remit of her inquiry, which focused strictly on institutional failures and hospital management.

Half of Russia's largest diesel producers cut output – Reuters

Half of Russia's largest diesel producers cut output – Reuters
Three of Russia's six largest diesel fuel producers stopped or significantly reduced output in September as a result of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Source: Reuters
Details: The six plants account for roughly half of Russia's diesel fuel production.
Reuters sources said the plant in Kirishi has been shut down, while the Volgograd and Kstovo refineries are operating at about a quarter of their nominal capacity.
As a result, half of Russia's largest oil refineries producing diesel fuel were forced in September to significantly reduce production or halt it altogether because of damage caused by drone attacks.
Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in recent months reduced fuel production in the country and forced Moscow to restrict exports of petrol, diesel fuel and aviation fuel, Reuters reported.
Market data indicate that six plants – the Omsk oil refinery, the refinery in Kirishi in Leningrad Oblast, TANECO in Tatarstan, the Volgograd oil refinery, the Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery in Kstovo, also known as NORSI, and the Perm oil refinery – account for about half of diesel fuel production in Russia.
Diesel fuel production at these plants is several times below normal levels. TANECO was attacked by drones on 13 September but sources said it is not yet possible to assess the consequences of the attack.
The International Energy Agency said drones successfully attacked Russian oil refineries every three days in the first eight months of 2026.
Traders estimate that Russian diesel fuel exports before restrictions were imposed in June stood at less than 1 million tonnes, while combined exports of diesel fuel and gasoil totalled about 1.8 million tonnes.
A year earlier, when refineries were operating as normal, diesel fuel exports stood at about 2.5 million tonnes a month, or 3.3-3.4 million tonnes including lower-grade gasoil.
Background:
- On the night of 5-6 September, drones attacked the Ryazan oil refinery in Russia.
- On the night of 12-13 September, drones attacked the industrial zone of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan, where major Russian oil refineries are located.

Ukraine successfully tests interceptor against faster Gerans as Russia floods its skies with drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:57:18 UTC
00:57:18 KST

Ukraine has successfully tested another interceptor designed to counter Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 15 September.
The test comes as Russia rapidly expands the use of faster jet-powered Gerans, creating a new problem for Ukraine’s air defenses: these drones give defenders less time to detect and engage them while allowing Russia to maintain large-scale attacks. A successful interceptor could give Ukraine a cheaper, scalable way to counter that threat without relying as heavily on scarce high-end air-defense missiles.
Zelenskyy said Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi reported the successful test, during which the new interceptor struck a Russian Geran drone.
The system still reportedly needs further work, including improvements to some aspects of its control. But the successful test marks another step in Ukraine’s effort to develop a new layer of air defenses against Russia’s faster drones.
Russia is making its drone attacks faster and larger
Russia has sharply expanded its use of jet-powered Gerans in recent months, adding a faster and more difficult-to-intercept threat to its large-scale drone campaign.
Geran is Russia’s designation for its domestically produced Shahed-derived attack drones, with newer jet-powered variants representing a major upgrade over the earlier propeller-driven models.
Zelenskyy recently said Russia launched around 2,100 drones against Ukraine last week, alongside nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles. The attacks have increasingly targeted energy facilities, railway infrastructure, businesses, and residential areas.
The newer Gerans are faster than earlier Shahed-derived drones and can reach targets deep inside Ukraine. Their speed gives Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect, track, and engage them.
Russia has also changed how it uses its drones. Rather than concentrating attacks almost exclusively overnight, Russian forces have increasingly launched waves during the day as well, keeping Ukrainian cities under repeated air-raid alerts.
The result is a growing challenge not only of interception, but of scale. Ukraine must defend a large territory against increasingly large drone barrages while preserving more sophisticated air-defense missiles for ballistic missiles and other threats.
Ukraine is building a new layer of air defense
Ukraine has already been racing to develop such systems. In late August, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said four potential interceptor systems capable of shooting down jet-powered Gerans had undergone field testing. Ukraine was aiming to bring them to the required level and eventually produce thousands of units.
Today’s announcement shows that effort continues to produce concrete results.
Ukraine is also expanding other parts of its counter-drone network. Zelenskyy said the country is increasing purchases of electronic warfare equipment and reorganizing mobile fire groups and air-defense positions.
The goal is to build enough layers to cope with Russia’s evolving drone campaign: electronic warfare, mobile fire teams, traditional air defenses, and increasingly specialized interceptors.
Russia is making its drones faster and launching them at greater scale. Ukraine’s response is now moving beyond adapting existing defenses toward developing weapons specifically designed to catch them.

Indonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in Borneo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:57:16 UTC
00:57:16 KST

Wildfires in Indonesia are sweeping through a critical research site for Bornean orangutans and are now threatening a celebrated research camp, home to one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild apes.
In the past few days, the fires have burned within 200 metres of Rangkong research station, a satellite of Cabang Panti research station, which lies about four miles north in Gunung Palung national park.
Hundreds of Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species, live in the direct vicinity of the research stations, with more than 2,500 thought to inhabit the park, many areas of which are now on fire. All three orangutan species are considered critically endangered.
“Orangutans are fleeing from these forests. It’s just horrible,” said Prof Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has been leading scientific research on orangutans at Cabang Panti for 32 years.
In most cases, the fires were intentionally set to clear land, as is done every year on the island. But an extremely strong El Niño – a warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean that disrupts global weather patterns – has fuelled exceptionally hot and dry conditions across the country, with fires easily escaping control as a result. In West Kalimantan province, some areas have gone months with little to no rainfall.
Scientists at Cabang Panti have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and their life histories, following some of the same individuals from birth to grandmotherhood. Research carried out at the site has helped to establish the orangutan reproduction cycle, finding that the apes only give birth once every eight years – the longest cycle of any mammal. “The long-term nature of this database and the detailed nature of the database is unparalleled,” Knott said.
But the fires threaten to undo such continuous observations. At the rate the flames are moving, without intervention or large firebreaks, the fires will reach Cabang Panti in 20 days’ time, scientists said.
“[Cabang Panti] protects what has been, until now, one of the only truly ecologically intact tracts of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo,” said Prof Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who ran an orangutan research project at the site from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuously collected field data, we cannot understand how tropical ecosystems are adapting to or suffering from global climate shifts.”
In a desperate effort to save Rangkong research station, a team of more than 40 people – mostly field assistants, staff and local villagers – are fighting day and night to stave off the encroaching inferno. Recently, they constructed a firebreak and an improvised sprinkler system using a punctured hose line around the station to saturate the surrounding peat.
Once fire reaches a peat swamp, it can smoulder underground for months – even after surface flames have been extinguished. Keeping the peat wet is therefore a key defence.
“The issue has surpassed any local organisation’s capacity,” said Caitlin O’Connell, deputy director of the Gunung Palung orangutan conservation programme. “We need large-scale water bombing and skilled firefighters.”
Even if they manage to save the research station, it may be for nothing if the orangutans lose their home.
“The orangutans need the forest,” Knott said. “If all we have left is the building, what are we studying if the orangutans are all gone, and the food they have is all gone? They can’t survive without that forest.”
As solitary animals, orangutans require large ranges and live at low population densities. “You can’t just shove them all together in what remains of the forest,” Knott said.
Those leading the on-the-ground fire response have already witnessed the impact on the apes. “Five orangutans from our long-term study population were observed fleeing the fire, some only metres from the flames,” said Wahyu Susanto, research director for Yayasan Palung, an Indonesian NGO that protects Bornean orangutans. “These are individuals that we have followed and studied for years.”
Indonesian meteorologists predict an intense fire season persisting through October as climate forecasts point to a strengthening El Niño.
“The hotspots are everywhere,” O’Connell said. “I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say that what we thought couldn’t burn could actually completely disappear if we’re looking at these dry conditions going on for months.”

Russia’s “Domestic” Sniper Ammo Turns Out to Be Packed With US and Finnish Components

Russia’s “Domestic” Sniper Ammo Turns Out to Be Packed With US and Finnish Components
A Russian weapons manufacturer supplying the military with sniper rifles has begun producing ammunition using US-made and Finnish components, including precision bullets and cartridge cases.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Insider on September 14, Russian arms manufacturer Promtekhnologiya, which produces weapons and ammunition under the ORSIS brand, has supplied Russian forces with factory-assembled sniper cartridges containing components made by US companies Hornady and Peterson, as well as Finland’s Lapua.
The findings indicate a shift from earlier cases in which Russian troops were documented using complete imported cartridges or ammunition assembled outside regular factory production. Promtekhnologiya is now reportedly receiving enough foreign components to incorporate them into ammunition manufactured at its own facilities.
The Insider reported that Russian snipers received .308 Winchester ammunition for ORSIS rifles assembled with Peterson cartridge cases and 178-grain Hornady BTHP Match/OTM bullets, weighing 11.53 grams each.
Where US components were in short supply, Promtekhnologiya reportedly turned to Lapua Scenar bullets manufactured in Finland. Those cartridges were assembled with Russian-made Irbis 570 powder and cases marked ORSIS.
Testing cited by The Insider showed the ammunition producing groups of around 0.5 MOA at 300 meters, equivalent to a spread of roughly 4.5 centimeters.
The latest findings build on an earlier investigation by The Insider, which found that more than 10 million bullets manufactured in NATO countries entered Russia between March 2022 and February 2024. Among them were precision projectiles in calibers such as .338 Lapua Magnum and .375 CheyTac, commonly used for long-range shooting.
The Insider also identified indications that some American components reached Russia through European countries. In June 2022, Russian company IF Tetis registered a batch of Hornady bullets whose testing documentation had been issued by Finland’s Lapua Test Shooting Lab.
Earlier, Ukraine’s military intelligence identified 5,816 foreign-made components in 202 Russian weapons systems, including missiles, drones, and armored vehicles, highlighting Moscow’s continued reliance on foreign technology despite international sanctions.

a spiral of timber beams and steel frames tiny 40-sqm tokyo home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:55:32 UTC
00:55:32 KST

Tato Architects / Yo Shimada builds House in Musashi-Koyama
House in Musashi-koyama by Tato Architects / Yo Shimada is a home for a family of four on a flag-shaped lot measuring less than 40 sqm in a dense residential district of Tokyo. Facing a large park to the north, the site was created by dividing a plot in two where a single, relatively small house had previously stood. Its limited dimensions presented a familiar challenge in Tokyo: how to accommodate a family home on increasingly subdivided urban land.
The initial approach was to stack two full floors within the site’s permitted 60 percent building coverage, placing shared spaces such as the living room on one level and bedrooms and other private rooms on the other. This arrangement, however, would have resulted in compact floor plans with limited flexibility for everyday activities, including finding space for a dining table. Instead, the architects divided the floor into four sections and arranged them in a spiral. The resulting skip-floor configuration creates a sequence of interconnected levels, allowing sightlines to extend both upward and downward through the house. While dividing the available floor area into smaller sections could have made the rooms feel more confined, the visual connections between levels give the interior a greater sense of continuity and spatial depth. The entrance is positioned at the mezzanine, reached by a stair running along the narrow access strip of the flag-shaped lot. From this level, the sequence of floors winds upward towards the roof terrace, while the stair descending from the mezzanine leads to the lower level, where the individual rooms are arranged.
spiral arrangement addresses the limits of the tiny urban plot
The compact dimensions of the house also informed its structural system. With people and architecture positioned in close proximity, conventional timber framing could have become visually dominant within the small interior. Instead, the skip floors are supported by 30-millimeter-thick laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beams connected with slender steel members no thicker than a handrail. The structural elements remain close to the scale of furniture, allowing the spiral floor arrangement to occupy a volume measuring approximately 3.6 by 6 meters and 7.2 meters high without introducing a heavy structural presence. The system creates the four interconnected floor sections within the permitted building volume while maintaining visual connections across the levels.
A series of openings is added to the maximum permitted building volume to bring daylight and views into the interior. Each opening responds to a specific orientation or domestic function. A clerestory faces south, while a bay window projects towards the park to the north and creates a place to sit close to the exterior view. In the kitchen, another bay window combines daylight with storage. A skylight above the narrow access strip brings light into the house while providing an upward view, and the entrance makes full use of the limited space available within the flag-shaped site. These elements work as extensions of the main volume, creating additional points of contact between the interior, the surrounding neighbourhood, and the sky. Their arrangement can be compared to a plant growing within dense vegetation, with its leaves extending into the available gaps.
The multiple changes in level introduce a different pattern of movement and occupation from a conventional two-storey house. Instead of separating the home into two complete horizontal layers, the spiral sequence distributes domestic functions across several interconnected levels. The completed house demonstrates how this arrangement can create a greater sense of spaciousness within a footprint of less than 40 square meters. By combining skip floors, a furniture-scale structural system, and a series of carefully positioned openings, House in Musashi-koyama explores how a compact urban home can accommodate a family of four while responding to the increasingly limited dimensions of residential plots in Tokyo.

US democratic decline threatens global rule of law, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:52:35 UTC
00:52:35 KST

US democratic decline threatens global rule of law, report warns
Nearly half of US democracy indicators hit 50-year lows, accelerating global stability decline, warns new IDEA study.
The United States is accelerating the global weakening of the rule of law, according to a new report that found nearly half of the indicators used to measure American democracy have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years.
In the report released on Tuesday, the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA) describes the US as the “most prominent example and accelerator” of the trend, warning that its democratic erosion is having consequences far beyond the country’s borders.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Republican midterm convention wraps up in Dallas, Texas: Key takeaways
- list 2 of 4Mehdi Hasan: Disrupting democracy’s decline
- list 3 of 4What the US militarisation of Latin America could look like
- list 4 of 4Who is Trump trying to exclude from 2030 US census and why does it matter?
“President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies,” the report stated. “In that environment, which is marked by constricted space for both public expression and institutional checks on power, resistance is increasingly unsafe.”
Globally, around 57 percent of countries declined in at least one key indicator of democratic performance between 2020 and 2025. Judicial independence has fallen to a 36-year low, while credible elections are at their lowest level in 30 years.
But the report singles out the US because of both the scale of its decline and its outsized global influence, arguing that its retreat from democratic norms has strained multilateral institutions and emboldened authoritarian leaders elsewhere.
“The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation,” the report stated.
It pointed to Brazil and Serbia as examples, saying the aftermath of Brazil’s 2022 election, when Jair Bolsonaro sought to remain in power after losing the presidency and his supporters later stormed government buildings, “echoed” the aftermath of the 2020 US election. In Serbia, officials cited Trump’s claims of mismanagement at USAID to justify raids on civil society organisations.
“For decades, the rule of law both domestically and in the international order has underpinned the resilience of democracies,” International IDEA Secretary-General Kevin Casas-Zamora said. “Now, the rapid decline of democracy in the USA is weakening judicial independence and fragmenting the international system — threatening democracy around the world.”
Attacks on institutions
The US recorded seven statistically significant declines between 2020 and 2025, including in access to justice, freedom of expression, press freedom and judicial independence. Except for free political parties, the other six are now at their lowest levels in the dataset’s history.
On press freedom, International IDEA cites cuts to funding for public broadcasters NPR, PBS and the US Agency for Global Media, as well as “ad hominem attacks on journalists, particularly women, and lawsuits against media organisations such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC”.
Universities have also come under pressure.
“Executive measures affecting funding and academic freedom in universities, including efforts to influence accreditation and hiring processes, provide a further example of the decline in Freedom of Expression,” the report said, citing the withholding of federal funds from Harvard and Columbia.
The report calls the Trump administration’s use of the immigration system the “starkest example” of declining access to justice. It points to 137 Venezuelans sent to El Salvador under the 1798 Alien Enemies Act, saying many had little or no established connection to the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang and were denied the chance to properly challenge their removal in court.
The report also warns that the broader erosion of democracy comes with consequences for global security, finding that some forms of democratic decline are associated with a greater risk of violent conflict. There were 65 violent conflicts in 2025, the most recorded since the Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s series began in 1946, including a record eight conflicts between states.

The sinister influence of crypto billionaires on our politics | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:52:19 UTC
00:52:19 KST

Cryptocurrency is often sold as decentralised and democratic, yet its real behaviour resembles gravity: wealth is pulled inexorably into a few vast centres while draining from everyone else (Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo, 12 September). Early adopters, insiders and whales acquire huge holdings at negligible cost. Their size then shapes the market, drawing in ordinary investors whose money ultimately fuels those already at the top.
Because crypto generates no cash flow and produces little real economic output, it becomes structurally zero‑sum. One person’s gain is another’s loss, and the system relies on a continual inflow of participants whose contributions sustain the fortunes of a minority.
It is troubling that some of the biggest beneficiaries of this system have become major donors to Reform UK. The party presents itself as a champion of ordinary people, yet it is being funded by individuals whose wealth largely comes from mechanisms that disadvantage those very people. Their interest in Reform is not altruistic; it reflects a desire for deregulation, reduced oversight and a political environment favourable to speculative wealth and offshore structures.
The danger is not only financial, but democratic. When the gravitational pull of crypto wealth begins shaping political parties, we must ask whose interests are being served: those of the public, or those of the black holes at the centre of the crypto universe?
Colin Charlton
Macclesfield, Cheshire
Your report on Christopher Harborne’s £36m donation to Reform UK contains an irony worth exploring. Reform presents itself as an insurgent, grassroots movement, with stopping the small boats at the centre of its politics. Yet its new financial power now comes partly from a billionaire who owns about 12% of Tether, issuer of USDT — the dominant “stablecoin” (payment) of the offshore cryptocurrency economy.
This matters because money laundering is not a victimless financial offence, and Europol has warned that cryptocurrencies are increasingly used by human traffickers to receive payments, pay facilitators and launder their profits.
There is an uncomfortable question for Reform voters. How does a party built around opposition to irregular migration feel about becoming increasingly dependent on fortunes generated within a financial ecosystem that has also proved useful to the criminal networks facilitating and profiting from irregular migration?
Dr Neil Smith
Buckfastleigh, Devon
The £72m given to Reform by two crypto billionaires has revealed an abysmal failure to properly regulate party financing. A cap on national party spending in the year before a general election was introduced in 2000, but there is no cap on party spending in any of the years in between general elections. Nor is there any cap on the size of donations that can be made by a single individual. The new £100,000 cap proposed by the government (Will the £72m of donations to Reform UK be allowed?, 14 September) will only apply to UK citizens living overseas.
In 2023, the last Conservative government raised the national cap for spending in election years from £20m to £36m. The spending of the £72m donations could legally be targeted at 72 seats, spent over two years, with a total of national spending of £1m in each of them. If parties did not think that financial resources won seats, then they would not try so hard to raise funds to win them. Unless the rules change our democracy is for sale.
Chris Rennard
Liberal Democrat, House of Lords

Social media is promoting harmful attitudes towards sun exposure | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:51:46 UTC
00:51:46 KST

Rising melanoma rates demand more than another awareness campaign (Editorial, 7 August). As a consultant dermatologist with a special interest in the health impacts of social media, I see how digital platforms are normalising harmful attitudes towards sun exposure, while the sunbed industry thrives.
Social media algorithms reward content that provokes strong reactions. Extreme tanning routines, dramatic before-and-after images and misleading health claims can therefore travel further than balanced medical advice. I have previously raised the alarm about irresponsible sunbed advertising, including claims that sunbeds offer a net health benefit. Such promotion is indefensible: UV radiation from sunbeds is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the World Health Organization’s cancer agency.
This is also a health-equity issue. Sunbed outlets are more densely concentrated in deprived communities. Although people with lighter skin tones face the greatest skin-cancer risk, no skin tone is immune. This matters increasingly as climate change and warmer weather alter patterns of outdoor behaviour and UV exposure.
The government should place a national skin-cancer prevention strategy at the heart of its national cancer plan. We should combine practical behaviour-change programmes, community-led education and better support for early detection. Australia, Brazil and Iran have banned commercial sunbeds; the UK should follow. It is easy to dismiss their example as relevant only to traditionally hotter countries; in a warming world, that argument no longer holds.
Prevention must begin in childhood. Schools can register with Sun Safe Schools, run by the skin cancer charity Skcin, to embed sun-safe habits early. This should be paired with digital literacy that teaches children to question online health claims, recognise commercial influence and understand how algorithms shape their feeds.
Awareness matters, but we need safer environments, responsible regulation and lasting cultural change to help shape our futures.
Dr Amy Perkins
Consultant dermatologist, Glasgow

UNRWA overstated progress on institutional changes, preserved terrorism issues, watchdog says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:51:30 UTC
00:51:30 KST

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) has substantially overstated its progress on institutional changes, substituting administrative paperwork for actual reform while underlying issues involving terrorism and incitement remain unaddressed, according to a scathing report published by Geneva-based UN Watch on Monday.
The investigation, titled the “Report Card on UNRWA Reform,” analyzed the agency’s implementation of 50 recommendations issued by an independent review group led by former French Foreign Minister Catherine Colonna.
The Colonna review was originally commissioned by UN Secretary-General António Guterres in early 2024 to restore donor confidence after devastating revelations surfaced that UNRWA employees had participated in the October 7 massacre, which led 17 donor states to temporarily suspend $450 million in funding.
While UNRWA now says it has successfully completed 41 of the 50 recommended reforms, the UN Watch analysis concludes that this figure is misleading, noting that, at most, only 13 recommendations have been fulfilled as prescribed.
“UNRWA has graded its own homework and awarded itself high marks,” UN Watch Executive Director Hillel Neuer said. “But issuing a policy is not the same as enforcing it. Drafting a plan is not the same as implementing it, and closing a recommendation does not mean that the underlying problem has been solved.”
UNRWA adopts 'Minimum Viable Product' methodology
According to the report, UNRWA adopted a “Minimum Viable Product” methodology in mid-2025 that allowed recommendations to be classified as completed once a core objective was declared met, even where full implementation or institutionalization remained lacking.
Under this approach, the agency repeatedly treated administrative steps – such as conducting pilot programs, drafting new guidelines, or preparing costed implementation plans – as completed reforms, even when execution remained dependent on future funding or subject to ongoing hurdles.
Furthermore, the report said that despite promises to clean up its hiring practices, UNRWA still lacks a reliable mechanism to systematically screen its local workforce for membership in Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ).
The agency relies primarily on the UN Security Council sanctions list, which does not designate Hamas as a terrorist organization.
The UN watchdog’s report highlights that internal United Nations systems routinely fail to catch extremists, pointing to a June 2026 review by the USAID Office of Inspector General that independently referred 108 current or former UNRWA personnel for federal debarment due to ties to the October 7 attacks or Hamas military wings.
UN Watch also reported said that institutional hurdles are evident within staff unions. UNRWA marked all union-related reforms as fully completed simply because agency leadership drafted a modernized union statute. However, the report notes that the powerful staff unions, whose leadership has a long history of political radicalism and defending terror-linked colleagues, have refused to adopt the new rules. This was visibly demonstrated when the Gaza Staff Union aggressively mobilized to protest and demand the reinstatement of dozens of employees laid off over terror ties.
Antisemitism remains deeply embedded in UNRWA curriculum
In education, the report notes that although UNRWA points to new teacher training programs and textbook review protocols as proof of progress, independent monitoring by IMPACT-se on the 2025-2026 Palestinian Authority school curriculum used in UNRWA schools shows that antisemitism, the glorification of suicide bombers, and the promotion of violent jihad remain deeply embedded in daily lessons.
Physical security and facility oversight face similar gaps. The report emphasizes that paperwork and ethics posters cannot prevent the deliberate military misuse of UNRWA infrastructure. Because the agency lacks independent police, military, or intelligence capabilities, it remains entirely blind to underground threats, such as the network of Hamas attack tunnels discovered beneath and around its properties.
The report concludes that these shortcomings are structural rather than managerial.
Because UNRWA’s mandate is intrinsically tied to a political framework that perpetuates refugee status across generations and relies almost entirely on locally recruited staff embedded in local political factions, administrative adjustments cannot force true political neutrality.
UN Watch is calling on international donor governments to stop relying on UNRWA’s self-reported progress metrics and instead demand independently verifiable proof before restoring full financial backing.
UNRWA did not respond to a request for comment by press time.

Campaign Against Antisemitism has exposed "the antisemitic rot" at the heart of Britain's National Health Service (NHS) in its new documentary, released Monday.
The documentary - Malignant: Antisemitism in the NHS - presents interviews with NHS practitioners and patients, revealing shocking incidents such as a senior Jewish medical professor receiving antisemitic death threats, and a Jewish emergency worker being physically attacked by a colleague.
Shelley Lipman, a registered nurse in a hospital in Cambridge, said that even though she was raised secular, she is "fiercely proud to be Jewish" and has Hebrew tattoos on her arm as a statement of her identity.
"One of my colleagues who's a healthcare assistant asked me what they meant. So then it came out that I was Jewish. And then I went on lunch, and when I came back the nurse was there literally holding a Nazi salute," she said.
Another woman said she attended an event where a staff member said Jews don't understand what racism is. The woman said when she tried to correct the staff member, "she then lunged across the table at me and tried to grab me across the table."
A dentist testified to being in a dental group of 20,000 registered dental professionals where there was a public vote to ban and remove Zionists from the group because "they were spying on the other dentists in the group."
"Shortly after that vote, many of us were removed from the group, people with Jewish-sounding names."
Speaking to the camera, Stephen Silverman, Director of Investigations and Enforcement at CAA, reported that doctors with Jewish-sounding names have stopped wearing their name badges, and have been advised to stop ordering kosher food in hospitals so as to hide their identity. In fact, figures in July of this year said requests for kosher meals in British hospitals have reportedly halved in two years.
Silverman also said many NHS doctors are resigning and moving into private practice instead, where they find things safer.
Doctors also reported being either too scared to report incidents or feeling there was no point reporting them, as the issues were not dealt with.
One professional said he raised informal complaints and then formal complaints and grievances for years, but felt "the Trust tried to obfuscate, tried to misconstrue my concerns, and just do a number of things that in the end just made it impossible for me to continue working there. It made me ill, and it made me depressed. So I left."
Doctor accuses Jews of shooting children for fun during surgery
Antisemitism was also an expressed concern for patients.
One shocking incident was recalled by patient Sam Freeman, who spoke of having an operation to remove a type of skin cancer from his forehead.
While the surgeon was cutting areas of skin from his forehead, he started speaking about the war in Gaza, adding, "you would think they would know better given what happened to them in Europe."
Freeman remembered asking who the surgeon meant by 'they.'
"His response to that, as he's making an incision in my head, was 'the Jews, the Jews should know better, the Jews do it just for fun they shoot children in the head or the leg on a for fun.'"
Freeman said that he realized at that moment that his Star of David necklace, normally hidden under his shirt, was visible.
"The guy has a knife. He's working on me. It's about as vulnerable you could be in terms of a patient and doctor interaction. I was panicking because I didn't know if he was going to intentionally cause me harm."
Freeman is now in the process of making formal complaints, but says he thinks it's really difficult for Jewish patients to complain.
These are just some of the many incidents laid out in the documentary.
Additionally, on the same day CAA published representative polling of the Jewish community that shows a clear majority of British Jews would be concerned about not receiving equal care because they are Jewish (65%), and one third of British Jews who have used the NHS since October 7, 2023 say that they were uncomfortable due to their Jewish identity.
More than four in ten British Jews who have used the NHS since October 7, 2023 took steps to hide their Jewish identity.
“Our documentary exposes the antisemitic rot at the heart of our NHS," said Silverman. "The anecdotal evidence presented in our film, together with the empirical data provided by our polling, demonstrate the magnitude and severity of this institutional crisis."
“At the very moment when they need the NHS the most, instead of being able to trust our national healthcare provider, Jewish people are having to hide their identity for fear of unequal treatment or abuse. As long as that is the case, the NHS cannot be said to be for everyone.”
Judaism only religious group seeing rising discrimination in NHS, review finds
CAA CEO Gideon Falter said, "It was hard to fathom the depth of hatred that we were hearing about."
He said the crisis requires a wide-ranging response that addresses the growing extremist culture within healthcare, the failure of regulation, the lack of transparency, and the absence of accountability.
In June 2026, UK government advisor on antisemitism Lord John Mann released his review of antisemitism in the NHS.
As part of the review, Mann heard that Jewish people in the NHS experience “routine ostracism”, with Jewish staff being the only religious group in the latest NHS Staff Survey for whom discrimination from colleagues is rising rather than falling, resulting in some considering leaving the NHS.
"It is well-evidenced that racism is persistent in the NHS," Mann said, adding that "the case for taking action to combat antisemitism and other forms of racism in the NHS is clear."

Antisemitic 9/11 libel has become gateway for broader conspiracy theories, study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:51:20 UTC
00:51:20 KST

Antisemitic conspiracy theorists utilized the lead-up to the 25th anniversary of 9/11 to disseminate a broader web of unrelated libels targeting Jewish people, according to a study released by the Antisemitism Research Center of the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM).
Analysts at the ARC examined 4,360 unique posts gathered from the social media platform X/Twitter between August 28 and September 4 using four keyword scans related to the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks in the United States.
The evaluation revealed that 2,587 posts, representing 59.3% of the total review sample, simultaneously advanced antisemitic conspiracy theories while referencing the September 11, 2001, terror attacks.
The analysis highlighted that nearly one-in-five of the flagged posts fused 9/11 allegations with at least one distinct antisemitic conspiracy theory unrelated to the attacks. Out of the total flagged content, 491 posts integrated unrelated claims.
The most prevalent secondary narrative involved assertions concerning a Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell blackmail network, which surfaced in 256 posts. Additional content invoked the John F. Kennedy assassination in 98 posts, followed by October 7 and “Hannibal Directive” claims in 83 posts, and the assassination of Charlie Kirk in 79 posts.
Other evaluated posts incorporated references to the USS Liberty incident [a 1967 attack by Israel on an unarmed US technical research ship, after a warning was sent, but it was not received], the COVID-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and antisemitic terrorist incidents in Bondi Beach, Mumbai, and Pahalgam. Researchers also noted instances invoking the Medieval “blood libel” accusing Jews of ritual murder.
No longer spreading isolated falsehood
“The 9/11 libel is no longer spreading as an isolated falsehood that can be debunked on its own terms,” ARC Research Associate Oliver Marks said. “It works as a gateway. A user drawn in by 9/11 content is, in one post in five, handed a second conspiracy theory in the same breath, centuries-old libels repackaged for a modern feed.”
The findings illustrate how individuals generating extremist content can rapidly incorporate contemporary events into established conspiratorial frameworks.
CAM called on platform administrators at X to enforce hateful conduct policies against the material and urged researchers, educators, and policymakers to address the wider conspiracy networks sustaining the falsehoods.

Kyiv • UNN
Investigators believe that the scheme's participants seized UAH 137.5 million during the delivery of 60 railway cars donated free of charge to Kyiv by Warsaw. Seven people were served with notices of suspicion.
Law enforcement officers notified 7 members of a criminal group of suspicion; according to the investigation, the group is involved in misappropriating UAH 137.5 million from the Kyiv Metro municipal enterprise during the delivery of metro cars. This was reported by the SAPO press service, according to UNN.
The following individuals were notified of suspicion:
-  a former official of the Kyiv Metro municipal enterprise; 
-  three officials of the Kyiv Metro municipal enterprise; 
-  two co-organizers of the crime; 
-  the director of a controlled company. 
Their actions were classified under Part 5 of Article 191 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — misappropriation, embezzlement of property, or taking possession of it through abuse of office, committed on an especially large scale or by an organized group.
As part of the pretrial investigation, it was established that at the end of 2022, the Warsaw Metro transferred 60 metro cars to the Kyiv Metro municipal enterprise free of charge.
In 2023, the Kyiv Metro municipal enterprise held tenders for the procurement of freight forwarding services to ensure the delivery of the metro cars. A predetermined company won the tender, offering transportation services at significantly inflated prices. The contract was worth UAH 190 million.
To conceal the crime, the participants in the scheme transferred the funds received to execute the contract to the account of a controlled company abroad. Subsequently, they paid part of the amount to the actual carrier, while misappropriating the remainder — UAH 137.5 million.

The presidency is currently held by Ireland – its eight time holding the role – as part of a presidency trio with Lithuania and Greece.
Ireland’s term runs through Dec. 31, 2026, followed by Lithuania in the first half of 2027 and Greece in the second half of the year.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will coordinate and organise the Presidency and the government has made more than €156 million available for this purpose,” the Dutch government said.
“In the first half of 2027, one central location for meetings will be designated.”
Separately on Tuesday, Finnish President Alexander Stubb announced that Finland had decided to provide Ukraine with its 34th military aid package, worth €290 million (about $335 million).
“We support Ukraine because it is morally right and it is a matter of the security of all of Europe, and thus also Finland,” Stubb said in a post on X, adding that “the package includes materials urgently requested by Ukraine.”
On Monday, Sept. 14, Ukraine’s Finance Ministry said it would soon receive $841 million from the World Bank under a guarantee from the Government of Canada, with the funds earmarked to cover pension payments in the state budget.
Canada also pledged more than $2 billion in new support for Ukraine, including over $1 billion for defense on Sept. 10. The package includes urgently needed Patriot missiles, F-16 ammunition, and energy cooperation.
The allocations come as Ukraine prepares across all sectors for its fifth winter of war, with Russia widely expected to continue targeting critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supply systems.
