Kim pro quo: North Korea is emerging from international isolation by backing Russia’s war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:25:13 UTC
00:25:13 KST

In early September, Russia and North Korea opened a road bridge across the border river Tumen. Analysts note that the structure could become a key gateway for transporting North Korean troops and weapons for the war against Ukraine. Since 2023, military aid deliveries to Russia have become a key source of revenue for North Korea’s budget, fueling unprecedented economic growth. As Pyongyang has drawn closer to Moscow, China has also entered the competition for influence over North Korea — even though it backed sanctions against the country together with Russia back in 2017. Combined, these factors have strengthened Pyongyang’s position enough that it no longer needs to seek a thaw with the United States. At the same time, Donald Trump has shown readiness for talks, which, should they take place, could cement North Korea’s status as a nuclear power.
In July, South Korea’s central bank estimated that North Korea’s economy had grown by more than 3% for a third consecutive year, its best results since a comprehensive sanctions package took effect in 2017. The turnaround would have seemed improbable only a few years ago. North Korea emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic impoverished and more isolated than ever after sealing its borders, while international restrictions continued to limit trade as its nuclear program deepened the country’s estrangement not only from the West, but even from its traditional Chinese and Russian allies. Yet renewed trade with China, ambitious state-led development programs and, increasingly, military cooperation with Russia have produced North Korea’s strongest sustained growth in years. At the same time, Moscow has turned Pyongyang from an international liability into a useful military partner, while Donald Trump’s return has revived the possibility of direct diplomacy at the leader level. The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) represents perhaps the most striking example of a state rejecting the post-Cold War world, and its sudden breakout from isolation serves as a signal that the order which once marginalized North Korea is beginning to unravel.
An unlikely recovery
North Korea’s recovery began, in part, by simply reopening the country. Trade with China had collapsed from nearly $2.8 billion in 2019 to $539 million in 2020— and it was just $318 million in 2021 after Pyongyang responded to COVID-19 by virtually sealing its borders. However, freight traffic gradually resumed in 2022, and by 2023 bilateral trade had recovered to around $2.3 billion. That reopening restored supplies of fuel, fertilizer, machinery, and consumer goods while allowing North Korean exports back onto the Chinese market. At the same time, the state poured resources into construction and industry, and improvements in agricultural production also helped pull the economy out of its pandemic slump. Russia would soon add an entirely new source of demand and foreign revenue, but North Korea’s recovery was already far from dependent on the wartime relationship with Moscow alone.
The domestic component of North Korea’s sudden relative prosperity has been remarkably visible. Since 2021, Kim Jong Un has made construction and regional development a central priority for the government, combining a five-year program to build 50,000 new apartments in Pyongyang with an extensive rural housing drive. With even grander ambition, in 2024 the DPRK’s Supreme Leader launched the “Regional Development 20x10 Policy,” calling for the modernization of factories in 20 cities and counties every year for a decade, with an emphasis on food processing, clothing, and everyday consumer goods. This represents a notable turn away from the focus on heavy industry traditionally favored by the state. Even more worrying for its neighbor to the south (and for the power of UNSC sanctions more broadly), however, is the fact that these programs are difficult to dismiss as propaganda. Satellite imagery has shown construction beginning within weeks of its announcement, and factories were installed in all 20 communities targeted during its first year. Building on its initial success, in 2025 the 20x10 program expanded into hospitals, leisure facilities, farming infrastructure, and other local projects, again opening all of its intended projects before the end of the year.
This headline policy represents a significant shift for a nation that has historically experienced extremely uneven economic development, with the capital, Pyongyang, and strategic heavy industries absorbing a disproportionate share of state investment while much of the country’s provincial economy remained dependent on Cold War-era factories or the nation’s growing informal economy. The 20x10 program, by contrast, is an explicit attempt to narrow that divide and invest in creating local provincial centers capable of processing regional materials into basic consumer products. It also seeks improvements in food production, agricultural mechanization, and housing. Whether these new industries can survive the country’s harsh shortages of electricity, machinery, and several raw inputs remains to be seen, but its focus on provincial economies and light industry is a significant departure from traditional party doctrine and seems to have borne early fruit.
That shift in emphasis, however, has not come at Pyongyang’s expense. At the same time the government has redirected investment toward provincial cities, it has continued an enormous reconstruction of the capital. In February, the government announced the completion of the aforementioned program to construct 50,000 new housing units, much of it concentrated in the brand new Hwasong district, where the program transformed former agricultural land into dense high-rise neighborhoods. The more striking changes, however, are taking place at the street level rather than on Pyongyang’s prominent skyline (which itself has long been a Kim family prestige project). Foreign visitors returning after the pandemic described the city as shockingly different from its pre-COVID self, with app-based taxis, QR-code payments, food and medicine delivery services, new storefronts and restaurants, and a far more visible smartphone economy. For the first time, the city’s wide streets and parking lots have been tested to capacity as the country experiences an influx of largely Chinese vehicles, imported despite UN sanctions. The most important new source of resources behind this expansion, however, came from outside the country.
Beginning in the summer of 2023, Pyongyang became a major supplier of artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to Russia, eventually providing more than 15 million artillery rounds, according to South Korean intelligence estimates.
The resources for North Korea’s economic upturn largely came from military cooperation with Moscow
The Institute for National Security Strategy (INSS), a think tank affiliated with South Korea’s intelligence service, estimates that weapons exports alone earned North Korea more than $10 billion between mid-2023 and the end of 2025 — an extraordinary sum for a country whose entire annual GDP is estimated at only around $27 billion. The subsequent deployment of roughly 15,000 North Korean soldiers to Russia added hundreds of millions more, even if INSS says only a fraction of the proceeds has been confirmed as payment in kind, while much of the remainder may consist of sensitive military technology, components or materials, or may still be owed.
More consequential than the scale of the payments themselves, however, is the extent to which the relationship has begun to dismantle the economic constraints imposed on North Korea over the previous decade. The sanctions adopted after 2016 derived much of their force from the unusual willingness of both Russia and China to participate in isolating Pyongyang — restricting its access to fuel, machinery, foreign currency, overseas labor, and many of the export markets on which it had previously depended. Russia has now reversed that situation by becoming a major customer for the same military-industrial complex that the sanctions were intended to constrain while simultaneously supplying North Korea with many of the resources those measures sought to keep out. In short, the DPRK’s recent recovery is not simply a rebound from the extraordinary deprivation of the pandemic years, but the result of a much larger change in the country’s international position.
Pyongyang’s place in the new world
North Korea’s problem was never a lack of powerful backers. When it was nearly destroyed by the U.S.-led coalition during the Korean War, Communist China intervened in large part out of fear of having an American-aligned state and military presence on its border, and to this day the DPRK-PRC alliance remains China’s only mutual-defense commitment. What it couldn’t secure were powerful friends that truly needed anything it could provide. For most of the post-Cold War era, Pyongyang had little to offer in exchange for its dependence on Chinese and Russian trade and diplomatic protection — a meagre workforce, a domestic market too poor to absorb high-end imports, and an endless stream of diplomatic liabilities generated by its nuclear program and recurring foreign provocations. However, the war in Ukraine has begun to reverse that imbalance, turning qualities that had made North Korea a diplomatic liability into assets that its allies increasingly covet.
The shift is clearest in relations with Moscow. In 2017, Putin insisted that Russia “unequivocally condemned” North Korea’s nuclear tests and pledged “fully complied with the UN Security Council resolutions” imposed on the DPRK. And yet, by 2024 he was in Pyongyang signing a mutual-defense treaty as Russia purchased billions of dollars’ worth of North Korean munitions. The change soon reverberated to international institutions that had been designed to constrain the DPRK. In March of that year, Russia vetoed the renewal of the UN Panel of Experts responsible for monitoring sanctions on North Korea, dismantling one of the central mechanisms through which the Security Council could apply pressure on the country.
In March 2024, Russia vetoed one of the central mechanisms through which the UN Security Council could apply pressure on the DPRK
Of course, for Pyongyang the benefits go far beyond munitions export revenue and diplomatic protection. North Korea also receives access to fuel, materials, and advanced military equipment. According to some South Korean and Western assessments, the partnership also includes transfers of military technology in areas ranging from air defense to missile and satellite development. For the Korean People’s Army (KPA), which is still overwhelmingly reliant on Cold War-era Soviet designs and indigenous attempts at their modernization, such cooperation offers one of the few plausible routes toward modernizing the capabilities that North Korea cannot readily develop on its own.
The benefits of friendship with Russia also affect North Korea’s other international relationships. If anything, Pyongyang’s growing independence from Beijing appears to have made China more attentive when it comes to preserving its own influence. After starting to cool off during the pandemic, relations with Beijing grew dramatically closer starting in late 2025. As a result, in June 2026, Xi Jinping made his first visit to Pyongyang in seven years, pledging that China would not waver in its support for North Korea and agreeing to deepen cooperation in various fields. Rather than displacing Beijing, Russia’s entry has made North Korea more valuable to China by giving Pyongyang a realistic alternative source of support. Kim is now in a position to draw economic backing from Beijing and military and diplomatic benefits from Moscow while reducing the degree to which either power can take its influence over the DPRK for granted.
By the time Trump returned to office, he found the conditions that had enabled his famous first negotiations with North Korea largely absent. Back then, the DPRK was largely isolated from the rest of the world, and Western offers of sanctions relief and moves toward normalization were actually enticing. Now, Pyongyang has retained its nuclear arsenal, expanded its missile program, rebuilt much of its foreign trade, and secured relationships with Moscow and Beijing that are far more economically valuable than the recognition America once promised. While none of this removes negotiations or even potential steps to rapprochement from the table, it has shifted the starting point decisively in Kim’s favor. Trump’s America is still interested in talking to North Korea, but Kim’s North Korea has less of an incentive to reciprocate.
Trump’s gambit
Trump’s most consequential move toward Pyongyang so far took place on August 16. Only hours before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were scheduled to begin, the president ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” America’s participation, arguing that the drills were costly and that they sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, a country he described as having been “unthreatening and respectful” during his first term. The eleven-day exercise was subsequently cut to five days and its field component reduced; Washington later cancelled a separate upcoming joint Marine Corps exercise. For Pyongyang, which has spent decades portraying the exercises as rehearsals for an invasion and demanding their termination — along with the end of America’s presence in South Korea — Trump demonstrated immense goodwill without even requiring Kim to meet him.
Trump has shown readiness to engage with Pyongyang since returning to the White House
While it’s unclear how much Trump’s apparent frustration with South Korea’s lack of backing for American action in Iran contributed to the cancellation, the move itself isn’t entirely unprecedented. Days after his first summit with Kim in Singapore in 2018, Trump announced the suspension of Ulchi Freedom Guardian and several smaller exercises, similarly adopting Pyongyang’s description of the drills as “provocative” while arguing that their cancellation would save the U.S. money. However, the circumstances surrounding the two decisions could hardly be more different. In 2018, Trump’s suspension came amid perhaps the most dramatic thaw in inter-Korean relations since the division of the peninsula, with Moon Jae-in and Kim Jong Un having already met at Panmunjom, where they declared that “there will be no more war” between the two Koreas and that reconciliation, economic cooperation, and even the eventual reunification of the peninsula were desirable.
Today, nearly every condition that made such a gesture logical in 2018 has disappeared. The inter-Korean rapprochement surrounding Singapore has given way to Pyongyang’s formal abandonment of reunification, its designation of the ROK as a hostile state, and even the destruction of sections of the road and railway links that Moon and Kim had once promised to reconnect. At the same time, North Korea would enter any renewed negotiations with a growing nuclear arsenal, a mutual-defense treaty with Russia, and considerably less dependence on the sanctions relief that once formed Washington’s principal bargaining chip.
Despite offering little in return, Pyongyang does not appear to have ruled out renewed talks. Following Trump’s move, South Korean intelligence assessed that another Trump-Kim summit could be arranged “at any time.” However, unlike in 2018, North Korea now treats its nuclear arsenal as a permanent component of the state and the ultimate guarantor of its sovereignty. Analysts argue that, from Pyongyang’s perspective, America’s war against Iran vindicated a lesson already drawn from Libya and earlier attacks on Tehran: a credible nuclear deterrent is a necessary guarantee against potential American attack. This leaves any renewed summit with a much narrower window for discussion, particularly given Washington’s enduring policy calling for the complete denuclearization of North Korea (which is mirrored by South Korea).
Regardless of whether Trump’s gambit produces another summit, the larger reversal has already taken place. Less than a decade ago, North Korea faced a sanctions regime endorsed by Washington, Beijing, and Moscow, and the country depended almost entirely on China for its economic survival while remaining a liability even to the powers most interested in keeping it alive. Today, Pyongyang has already hosted two of the three most powerful leaders on Earth and is within reach of another meeting with the third. For the beleaguered hermit kingdom, it is a break in the storm clouds perhaps unmatched at any point this millennium.
A shrinking peninsula
For all of North Korea’s vast newfound advantages, the peninsula clearly leans in South Korea’s favor. For the DPRK, the enormous Korean People’s Army KPA remains central to the state, but the South Korean armed forces are still judged to hold the conventional advantage, as they are built around cutting-edge technology as opposed to the North’s heavily aged stockpiles. The economic imbalance is even more lopsided, with South Korea’s nominal GNI coming in at 56 times that of the North’s in 2025. Seoul’s annual defense budget alone now exceeds the estimated value of North Korea’s entire economy, giving the South a capacity to modernize, replace losses, and sustain high-end weapons systems on a scale Pyongyang cannot realistically match.
The one area where this overwhelming disparity is beginning to matter less, however, is manpower. South Korea’s fertility rate stood at just 0.80 children per woman in 2025, and the demographic collapse which for decades loomed as a distant economic problem has now reached the pool from which the ROK draws its soldiers. Between 2019 and 2025, the number of 20-year-old men fell by roughly 30%, while the active-duty military shrank by a fifth (to around 450,000 personnel), leaving a manpower shortfall estimated at roughly 50,000 troops. Seoul has been able to soften the consequences through force restructuring, expanded recruitment of women and career personnel, and a growing reliance on technology, but none of these measures change the arithmetic behind a conscription system which is drawing each successive intake from a substantially smaller generation than the last.
From 2019 to 2025, the number of young men in South Korea fell by 30%, and the size of the active-duty military by 20%
North Korea has also struggled demographically, though not as severely as its neighbor. The UN estimates its fertility rate at 1.8 children per woman in 2025, far above the South’s but still below replacement level. As the much smaller generation born during and after the famine of the 1990s reached enlistment age, the government reportedly loosened physical requirements for military service and also drew increasingly heavily on women. The country’s working-age population is estimated to have begun shrinking by almost 1% annually after 2020, and similar shortages have appeared outside the military, leading the state to increasingly direct young people toward mines and farms and mobilizing married women into factories and other production sites where the supply of workers has begun to thin.
The demographic balance between the Koreas is consequently moving in two directions at once. In the near term, South Korea is losing military-age manpower far faster, allowing Pyongyang to preserve one of the few quantitative advantages which Seoul’s economic ascent never completely eliminated. Over a longer horizon, however, the North is facing the same problem, only with much less room to absorb it. A smaller South Korean generation still enters an economy capable of sustaining increasingly capital-intensive production and defense, whereas a smaller North Korean generation has to be divided between an oversized military and a civilian economy in which agriculture, mining, construction, and large parts of manufacturing remain unusually dependent on labor. What currently looks like a durable Northern advantage is therefore better understood as a delayed disadvantage, albeit one which may matter considerably for the military balance during the decades before the DPRK’s own demographic contraction fully catches up with it.
Over a longer horizon, however, the North is also facing a demographic decline, only with much less room to absorb it
That reversal extends far beyond the demographic balance. North Korea’s reinvigorated economic growth, wartime partnership with Russia, renewed importance to China, and reduced dependence on what Washington can offer have together placed Pyongyang in perhaps its strongest international position since before the end of the Cold War. The country remains vastly poorer and conventionally weaker than the South, and its own demographic decline may ultimately prove more difficult to absorb, but it no longer approaches the outside world from the position of near-total dependence which shaped Trump’s first negotiations with Kim. If the two return to the negotiating table, Trump will therefore confront not the isolated North Korea he encountered in Singapore, but a state which has found in the unraveling of the post-Cold War order considerably more room to survive on its own terms.

Egypt, Saudi leaders meet as Houthis threaten Red Sea shipping

2026-09-15

Breadcrumb
Egypt, Saudi leaders meet as Yemen's Houthis threaten Red Sea shipping
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called for freedom of navigation in the Red Sea during talks in Cairo on Tuesday as a lightning offensive by Yemen's Houthis threatens to cause fresh disruption in the vital shipping corridor.
The Iran-backed group has effectively taken control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait after seizing control of Yemen's Red Sea coast, threatening Saudi oil exports and Egypt's revenues from the Suez Canal.
During Tuesday's talks, the two leaders "emphasised the importance of ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, the presidency said in a statement.
Al-Sisi also reaffirmed Egypt's support for measures taken by Riyadh "to protect its security and stability", it said.
Bin Salman travelled to the Egyptian capital on Tuesday on what Saudi media called a "working visit".
Saudi Arabia has become heavily reliant on the Red Sea to export oil since the US-Israeli war on Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis' takeover of the Bab al-Mandeb - the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal – coincided with a drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, which the country has used to ship crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and bypass Hormuz.
Since the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in July, the kingdom has routed oil to the Mediterranean via Egypt's overland Sumed pipeline. Crude is shipped from Yanbu to Egypt's Ain Sokhna, where it is transported via pipeline to the eastern Mediterranean at Sidi Kerir.
The attack, which Saudi authorities said was launched from Iraq, has taken the East-West pipeline offline, forcing the kingdom to now rely exclusively on covert shipments through Hormuz assisted by the US military.
Disruption in the Red Sea could also have a major impact on Egypt, which is reliant on ships transiting the Suez Canal for foreign currency revenues.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Aty said last week Egypt has lost almost $11 billion in revenues due to the disruption.
Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia have raised speculation about whether the kingdom may ask Pakistan and Turkey to intervene under their recently signed mutual defence pact.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement includes a provision similar to NATO's Article 5 that treats an attack against one of the countries as an attack against all.
Egypt has coordinated closely with the three countries over regional issues in recent months but has stopped short of joining the alliance.

Investigation confirms data fraud by Japanese nuclear plant operator
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
23:21:19 CST
00:21:19 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Japan's Chubu Electric Power Co. has engaged in serious misconduct, including falsifying earthquake data during the screening process for restarting reactors at the Hamaoka nuclear power plant in Shizuoka Prefecture, central Japan, an investigative report released Monday confirmed.
The report, released by a third-party committee composed of external lawyers, found that at least 208 of the 225 seismic ground motion assessments suspected of containing problems involved improper practices, including false explanations and concealment.
The report said that in order to pass the regulatory screening by Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority (NRA) for the restart of reactors at the Hamaoka plant, Chubu Electric, the plant's operator, manipulated data while determining the maximum seismic ground motion that could potentially occur.
According to the committee, the company told regulators that it had generated 20 sets of seismic waves using different calculation conditions and selected the one closest to the average as the "representative wave."
In reality, however, its employees cherry-picked one specific seismic wave as the "representative wave" and then selected the remaining 19 waves to make the "representative wave" appear closest to the average, the report said.
The Hamaoka plant is the only nuclear power station operated by Chubu Electric. Because the plant is located in an area where a Nankai Trough megaquake in the Pacific is expected to occur, all of its reactors were shut down at the Japanese government's request following the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, which was triggered by a massive earthquake and tsunami.
Chubu Electric applied to the NRA between 2014 and 2015 for screening to determine whether the No. 3 and No. 4 reactors at the Hamaoka nuclear power plant complied with new, stricter safety rules, aiming to restart the two reactors.
In January this year, however, the company acknowledged that its maximum seismic ground motion evaluation may have involved deliberately selecting data favorable to the company and underestimating earthquake risks.
In light of the scandal, Chubu Electric announced Monday that its president and chairman will step down at the end of this month to take responsibility for the misconduct, and the company will withdraw its application to restart the reactors.
Local media said the scandal could reignite public doubts about the safety of nuclear power plants and cast a long shadow over the Japanese government's plans to revive nuclear power as the resource-poor nation seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on fossil fuels. ■

News Analysis: Cardiff pact adds pressure on British Labour gov't
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
23:21:16 CST
00:21:16 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhao Jiasong, Larry Neild
LONDON, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Britain's Labour government is facing another constitutional headache after nationalist party leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland met in Cardiff on Monday to press for greater self-determination.
Scottish First Minister and Scottish National Party (SNP) leader John Swinney, Welsh First Minister and Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, and Northern Ireland First Minister, Sinn Fein vice president Michelle O'Neill and Sinn Fein President Mary Lou McDonald signed a memorandum as party leaders setting out areas for closer political cooperation.
The meeting came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pursues a wider devolution agenda. It also followed remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump in support of a united Ireland, adding another sensitive constitutional issue for the British government to handle.
A COMMON CALL FOR SELF-DETERMINATION
The memorandum used unusually strong language. It said "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and called on the British government to "prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change."
It also said people in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland should be free to decide their constitutional future. No Westminster government should stand in the way of that choice, according to the document.
The parties also agreed to cooperate on the economy, energy and relations with Europe. They blamed Brexit for lost economic opportunities and said they saw their nations' future in the European Union.
But public opinion is less clear-cut than Monday's show of unity might suggest. Recent polls across the three nations have not shown majority support for leaving the United Kingdom.
The longer-term trend has still caused concern among supporters of the union. The Guardian wrote in June that Britain's decision to leave the European Union had "bolstered support for Scottish independence." Support has remained close to half of Scottish voters for much of the period since Brexit.
A SHOW OF UNITY, DIFFERENT PATHS
Experts believed that the immediate constitutional effects of the Cardiff meeting were much more limited. The memorandum itself does not change the distribution of powers inside Britain or provide any new legal route to independence.
Laura McAllister, professor of public policy and the governance of Wales at Cardiff University, said that the significance lies in the fact that the first ministers of all three devolved nations now favour greater autonomy and, ultimately, constitutional change.
She said the choice of the broader term "self-determination" was deliberate because Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are at very different points in their constitutional debates.
"This is the first time that the nations of the United Kingdom are attempting to drive the constitutional question rather than the centre," she said, adding that England's absence would become a major issue in any wider review of the United Kingdom.
Those differences leave a large gap between a common political message and a common route forward. Scotland held an independence referendum in 2014 and voted by 55 percent to 45 percent to remain in the United Kingdom. Wales has never held such a vote. Northern Ireland's constitutional arrangements are tied to the Good Friday Agreement and its principle of consent.
Public opinion is another constraint. The electoral strength of nationalist parties does not automatically translate into majority support for breaking up the United Kingdom.
Jon Tonge, professor of politics at the University of Liverpool and an expert on Northern Ireland, told Xinhua that the nationalist parties now hold unusually strong political positions across the three devolved nations.
He cautioned that public opinion in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland still remains, "to varying degrees," in favour of staying within the United Kingdom.
Huang Fei, an associate professor at the School of International Studies at Renmin University of China, told Xinhua that the meeting was held by the participants in their roles as party leaders. The memorandum has no legal force, and as a result, its short-term impact on Britain's constitutional arrangements is likely to be limited, she said.
PRESSURE ON THE LABOUR AND BURNHAM
The Cardiff initiative also lands directly in the middle of Burnham's own effort to move power away from Westminster.
Since taking office in July, Burnham has put devolution near the center of his domestic agenda. In his first speech as prime minister on July 20, Burnham pledged to move power out of Westminster and into communities across the country.
Three days later, Burnham began working from "No10 North," a new government office in Manchester. The office is intended to coordinate regional growth and devolution, with Burnham saying the days of Whitehall resisting devolution were "over, for good."
His government has also promised greater powers and financial freedom for English mayors. Burnham has described the changes as a major transfer of power from Westminster, while ruling out fresh independence referendums.
That distinction is now being tested by nationalist leaders. Swinney said in Cardiff that Burnham's own political logic -- that decisions should be taken closer to the people affected by them -- should lead him to recognize Scotland's right to decide its constitutional future.
Yang Fang, a researcher at the Institute of European Studies of the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, said that the nationalist parties are, to some extent, making use of Burnham's devolution agenda to advance their own demands.
Burnham's programme was mainly designed to transfer powers within England, she said, adding that the SNP, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Fein can use the broader argument for decentralization to press for further powers and self-determination in their own nations, and such a campaign may also help the parties mobilise support among their respective electorates.
Ian Scott, a professor at the University of Manchester, said Burnham now faces the danger that deeper devolution itself could encourage demands to go further.
The three nationalist movements also face difficult questions of their own, including public services, taxation, population, defence and possible future EU membership. Their objectives are far from identical, he argued.
Downing Street has so far held its ground. Burnham's spokesperson said Monday the government is focused on "addressing the issues that matter most to families, including easing pressures on household finances and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums."
The issue is unlikely to disappear. According to British media, Burnham is expected to meet the leaders of the devolved administrations in the coming weeks.
Scott described that meeting as an important staging post for deciding the timetable and pace of further devolution. The question for Burnham is how far power can move away from Westminster without giving fresh force to parties that want to move much further, he said. ■

In a five-year plan on further expanding tourism, China targets 8.3 billion domestic trips and 7.7 trillion yuan in domestic tourism spending by 2030.
To address difficulties in implementing small tourism projects, supportive policies will be introduced for the construction of public service facilities such as gas stations and service areas in remote or rural areas.
The guideline also stressed that land use must be strictly determined in accordance with territorial space planning. It is strictly prohibited to arbitrarily change the current land status or planned use under the pretext of tourism projects for building villas, private estates, other forms of real estate and golf courses, among others. ■

Sweden May Change Prime Minister, But Support for Ukraine Remains Strong

Sweden’s election could return Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson to the prime minister’s office. For Ukraine, the result is unlikely to mean a change in support.
Backing for arming Kyiv extends across Sweden’s political spectrum, including parties that disagree sharply on immigration, taxation, and NATO. That gives Ukraine greater confidence in the durability of Swedish commitments as political opposition for assistance grows elsewhere in Europe.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The preliminary count following Sunday’s election put Andersson’s opposition bloc ahead by 176 parliamentary seats against 173 for the parties supporting Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. That is a three-seat advantage in a 349-seat parliament, with the center-left best positioned to take power, according to Reuters.
As of Tuesday, neither the final result nor the next government was settled.
A possible Andersson return
Late and overseas ballots, due to be counted on Wednesday, could still affect the outcome. With most districts counted, Andersson has the fastest route to office, according to the Associated Press.
Her immediate problem is reaching an agreement with the Greens, Left Party, and Center Party.
Together with the Social Democrats, they would have enough seats to replace Kristersson if the preliminary result holds. But the Center Party opposes the Left Party’s participation in government, complicating negotiations over cabinet positions, according to the Guardian.
Ukraine Successfully Tests New Interceptor Against Russian Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
A Social Democrat-led minority government, supported by other parties from outside the cabinet, is one possible solution. However, no such arrangement has been agreed upon.
Under Sweden’s parliamentary rules, a proposed prime minister can take office unless an absolute majority votes against the appointment. Parties can therefore permit a government to form by abstaining without joining it.
The election also brought a setback for the nationalist Sweden Democrats, whose parliamentary support sustained Kristersson’s government. Their preliminary vote share fell to 17.6%, from 20.5% in 2022, as reported by Reuters.
Ukraine support across the political spectrum
The Sweden Democrats backed the outgoing government’s multi-year military support framework for Ukraine, allocating approximately $7 billion over three years.
At the other end of the spectrum, the Left Party explicitly supports Swedish military, financial and humanitarian assistance to Kyiv. Its published Ukraine policy calls for tougher sanctions against Russia and action against its shadow fleet in the Baltic Sea. It also says Ukraine must determine its own future, including whether to seek EU and NATO membership.
While Swedish parties may disagree over individual weapons, spending levels, and alliance policy, their support for Ukraine is not waning, unlike in Germany and France.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government remains committed to Ukraine. However, anti-Ukraine AfD, which is on the rise, campaigns for a different relationship with Moscow. Its co-leader Alice Weidel has called for restoring ties and ending the boycott of Russian oil and gas, telling Reuters that her party aims to lead a national government.
France’s presidential election next year presents another risk to continuity, as Kyiv Post examined in “Just How Likely Is Le Pen to Win?”
Marine Le Pen has condemned Russia’s full-scale invasion, but that has not removed concerns about her party’s willingness to sustain assistance. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, prioritizes negotiations and French non-alignment, resisting a more NATO-centered defense policy.
Swedish commitments extend beyond the election
The next Swedish government will inherit defense agreements reaching well beyond the immediate fighting.
On June 30, Ukraine and Sweden signed an agreement for the procurement of 16 Gripen E fighter jets, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2029, according to Ukraine’s presidential office.
The aircraft are a long-term investment in Ukraine’s air force, however, they will not resolve Kyiv’s current air-defense shortages.
Separately, Sweden announced in May that it intended to donate up to 16 older Gripen C/D aircraft. That proposed donation is distinct from the June procurement agreement, but does not mean the aircraft have already arrived.
More immediate assistance includes a military package worth approximately $1.42 billion, announced in February, covering air defense, drones, long-range weapons, and ammunition.
Sweden has also redirected civilian aid toward Ukraine. In December, it announced plans to phase out development assistance to five countries and use the money to increase support for Kyiv, including rebuilding energy infrastructure. According to Reuters, aid to Ukraine was to reach at least $1.06 billion in 2026.
These commitments leave a new government with procurement contracts, funding decisions, and delivery schedules to implement. Broad political support reduces the risk of reversal, although future budgets and individual purchases will still require agreement.
A reliable partner for EU membership
Sweden also matters to Ukraine as a member of the EU, where support from the largest countries alone cannot secure accession.
As Ukraine’s membership negotiations proceed, opening talks are only the beginning. Kyiv must implement reforms and persuade member states that its institutions can meet the bloc’s requirements.
Every EU government must agree to conclude negotiations, and every member state must ratify the eventual accession treaty. The European Commission’s rules give Sweden a necessary voice in that process.
While Ukraine may count on Sweden’s support, it cannot continue failing key reforms. Continued pressure on independent institutions and unfinished reforms shows why diplomatic goodwill cannot substitute for credible courts and anti-corruption safeguards.
For now, Sweden’s election leaves the leadership question open, but offers considerably more certainty about policy towards Ukraine. Whoever forms the government will have to face the practical test of delivering the assistance already promised.

====================================================================================================

Zelensky’s political endgame has begun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:15:06 UTC
00:15:06 KST

Zelensky’s political endgame has begun
Although Ukrainian authorities have rejected any idea of unity between the peoples of Russia and Ukraine, the best metaphor for their country’s modern political system is a traditional Slavic winter game called ‘King of the Mountain’. In this game, any player who manages to reach the so-called ‘mountain’ (dominating height) must defend it at all costs against rivals. When another player knocks off the ‘king of the mountain’, he takes his place until the next ‘king’ topples him, and so on.
Much like in this children’s game, leaders have quickly succeeded one another in modern-day Ukraine – in fact, former President of Ukraine Leonid Kuchma (the first to promote the state concept “Ukraine is not Russia”) was the only Ukrainian leader to serve two consecutive presidential terms. Today, there is no democratically elected head of state: Vladimir Zelensky’s term ended in 2024.
Since then, Zelensky has invested all of his political capital into suspending elections, which for him would mean ‘political suicide’. Apparently, Ukraine’s political system has ceased to disguise itself as a democracy, as was the case in 2004, when an unconstitutional third round of elections was held to secure Victor Yushchenko’s victory; now, however, there is nothing but a ruthless struggle for power in the country. In this uncompromising fight, which disregards the genuine aspirations of the Ukrainian people, the reigning ‘king of the mountain’ exercises authority not for the good of the nation but rather to eliminate any potential ‘contenders’ who threaten the established status quo.
Road to the ‘mountain’
In this context, it’s hard to accuse Zelensky of political opportunism; he knows better than anyone in Ukrainian politics how to storm the heights of power. Born in the city of Krivoy Rog, Zelensky long sought to conquer another Olympus: Moscow, the former capital of the once-unified USSR. However, he encountered setbacks, like failing to be admitted to the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (an alma mater of many Russian officials and leaders of post-Soviet countries).
His team was defeated in the KVN semifinals, and had a falling out with the show’s host, Aleksandr Maslyakov, who had turned the post-Soviet comedy sketch contest into a mass cultural phenomenon and an important tool of Russia’s soft power. Then, Zelensky’s Studio Kvartal-95 was gradually pushed out of the Russian entertainment industry.
All this forced the enterprising young man to carve his own path in Kiev. Zelensky’s big opportunity came in the latter half of the 2010s with the release of the TV series ‘The Servant of the People’. It told the story of a modest high school teacher who was elected president after his video exposing Ukraine’s corruption issues went viral. In real life, Zelensky, who had skillfully crafted an image of a ‘Ukrainian Ronald Reagan’ from the earliest days of his presidential campaign, rose to power by means of skillful criticism of his predecessor, Pyotr Poroshenko, and promises of peace in Donbass.
However, even before the start of Russia’s military operation aimed at demilitarizing and denazifying Ukraine and protecting Donbass, it became clear that Zelensky’s election promises would remain unfulfilled. Following the start of the war, he consciously missed opportunities to resolve the conflict at earlier stages – such as during the April 2022 talks in Istanbul.
Protecting the dominating height
Today, Ukraine’s political discourse revolves around the possibility of presidential elections, which Zelensky would likely lose due to war fatigue and valid concerns about Ukraine’s approach to negotiations with Russia. As Moscow adopts a harder stance following each round of negotiations, Ukrainians have justifiably begun to question the price paid for fighting “to the last Ukrainian,” especially since the final terms of settlement become less favorable as time passes.
Zelensky’s main rivals will attempt to hold his team accountable for the lost territories, the devastated economy, and the depletion of the nation’s population. At the same time, they will push the narrative that Zelensky’s policies were not merely misguided but effectively criminal, driven by a desire for self-enrichment. These are the reasons behind the series of anti-corruption investigations involving Zelensky’s inner circle, including figures like co-owner of Studio Kvartal 95 Timur Mindich, and former head of Zelensky’s office Andrey Yermak.
Against this backdrop, there has been a notable surge in activity among those vying for Zelensky’s position. Valery Zaluzhny, the former Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces and presently Ukraine’s Ambassador to the UK, is by now a familiar figure with seemingly limited chances for victory.
However, the emergence of Mikhail Fyodorov in the upper echelons of Ukrainian politics has become the biggest sensation of the year and triggered the biggest political crisis during Zelensky’s presidency. Born in the village of Vasilyevka in Zaporozhye region (now part of Russia), 35-year-old Fyodorov gained recognition when he became Minister of Digital Transformation and later Minister of Defense. He proposed high-tech methods for waging war against Russia – views that clashed with those of then-Commander-in-Chief of the AFU Aleksandr Syrsky.
Sensing a threat to his own power from the young, up-and-coming politician, Zelensky reshuffled his cabinet and dismissed both Fyodorov and Syrsky. The seemingly unjustified removal of a minister who enjoyed unprecedented popularity among Western media sparked a wave of civil unrest in several Ukrainian cities and was dubbed the “Cardboard Maidan.”
Despite Fyodorov’s appointment as advisor to the Italian Minister of Defense and the rapid decline of protests in Ukrainian cities, this episode is now rightly regarded as the most significant domestic political challenge for Zelensky since 2019, and is perceived by many analysts as a final warning ahead of a potential power transition.
The King’s fall is coming
This is particularly relevant when viewed in the context of US President Donald Trump’s recent uptick in diplomatic activity. Facing the risk of losing the fragile Republican majority in Congress following November’s midterm elections due to his failed operation against Iran – one that not only paralyzed the Strait of Hormuz and exposed the limits of American influence in the Middle East but also triggered a severe energy crisis leading to soaring fuel prices in the US – the Trump administration, in need of a resounding foreign policy success, has decided to return to resolving the Ukraine crisis. Despite repeated claims by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about the demise of the “Spirit of Anchorage”, the US has made several attempts to revive negotiations.
This included CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s discreet visit to Moscow, followed by talks between US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent and his counterpart, Russian Minister of Finance Anton Siluanov, on the sidelines of the G20 summit. Most recently, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made visits to Moscow and Kiev. So far, the most tangible outcome of these diplomatic efforts has been the announcement of a resumption of trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US set for October, immediately after the Russian legislative elections. So what does Trump’s renewed activity around Ukraine mean for Kiev?
The Anchorage agreements may have indeed become less relevant; however, this should not be seen as a testament to the effectiveness of Ukrainian diplomacy in bringing Trump back into the realm of “Euro-Atlantic solidarity.” Rather, it may signal a looming shift at the front: the Russian Armed Forces are close to liberating the Slavyansk-Kramatorsk urban agglomeration.
As we may recall, Zelensky’s refusal to withdraw Ukrainian forces from the remaining areas under Kiev’s control in Donetsk region was a key sticking point that prevented the implementation of the “Anchorage Formula.” The loss of Donbass – especially in light of Russia’s effective strikes against Ukrainian port infrastructure that have essentially cut off Ukraine’s access to the Black Sea – places Zelensky’s regime on the brink of collapse. Consequently, there is a strong likelihood that a final settlement agreement will be signed by a new “yellow-blue king of the mountain”...

International Day of Democracy: why this observance remains relevant today
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:13:13 EEST
00:13:13 KST

International Day of Democracy: why this observance remains relevant today
Kyiv • UNN
On September 15, the world marks the International Day of Democracy, established by the UN in 2007. In Ukraine, its development is complicated by martial law.
Every year on September 15, the world marks the International Day of Democracy. It was established by the UN General Assembly in 2007, designating this date as an occasion to remind people of the value of democratic governance and the need for its constant protection.
Today, UNN tells its readers about the history and significance of the observance.
Why the UN established the International Day of Democracy
The day was first observed in 2008. The initiative is also linked to the Universal Declaration on Democracy adopted by the Inter-Parliamentary Union in September 1997.
The UN proceeds from the premise that democracy is a universal value based on the freely expressed will of people to determine their own political, economic, social and cultural development. At the same time, the Organization emphasizes that there is no single model of democracy, but its fundamental principles should be shared – respect for human rights, the rule of law, citizens’ participation in decision-making, government accountability and political pluralism.
The main principles of democratic governance, or Why democracy is not limited to elections
Free and competitive elections remain one of the key mechanisms of democracy. However, by themselves, they do not make a state democratic. Equally important are independent courts, the separation of powers, freedom of speech and the media, the right to peaceful assembly and association, the protection of minority rights, as well as the ability of citizens to oversee the authorities and influence their decisions.
In his address for the 2026 International Day of Democracy, UN Secretary-General António Guterres specifically emphasized that democracy is the daily practice of ensuring human rights, the rule of law and people’s meaningful participation in public and political life. This year, the UN’s focus is on deliberative democratic processes, that is, engaging citizens from different groups in society in discussions of important decisions.
The state of democracy in the world
International studies in recent years have recorded a sustained deterioration in democratic standards. According to Freedom House, global freedom declined for the twentieth consecutive year in 2025: deterioration in political rights and civil liberties was recorded in 54 countries, while improvement was seen in 35. Only about 21% of the world’s population lives in countries that the organization classifies as "free".
V-Dem also states in its 2026 report that the level of democracy enjoyed by the average person on the planet has returned approximately to the levels of 1978. The causes include the spread of authoritarian practices, the concentration of power, pressure on independent media and civil society, the weakening of judicial independence and electoral institutions.
International IDEA, for its part, notes that over a five-year period, more than half of the countries studied experienced deterioration in at least one of the key components of democracy. The decline in press freedom was particularly notable: deterioration was recorded in nearly a quarter of the countries.
Ukraine: democracy during wartime
For Ukraine, the issue of democracy has a particular dimension because of the full-scale war. Martial law has been in effect in the country since Russia’s invasion in 2022. Under these conditions, presidential, parliamentary and local elections are not held, while certain rights and freedoms may be temporarily restricted for security reasons.
In its 2026 report, Freedom House gives Ukraine a score of 51 out of 100 and classifies it as a "partly free" state. The organization points to the war’s negative impact on political rights and civil liberties, while also noting the continuation of reforms aimed at strengthening democratic institutions. Remaining problems include corruption, the state of the judicial system and ensuring effective oversight of the authorities.
In its 2025 report on Ukraine, the European Commission, for its part, noted that the overall legal framework remains suitable for holding democratic elections after martial law is lifted, when circumstances permit. At the same time, the EU emphasized the need to strengthen the rule of law and prevent any weakening of the independence of the anti-corruption system.
What challenges does democracy face today
Modern democracies face both traditional threats in the form of authoritarianism or political violence and disinformation, social polarization, manipulation on social media, declining trust in state institutions, and attempts by politicians to weaken the system of checks and balances.
New technologies pose a separate challenge. Artificial intelligence can simplify access to information and citizens’ participation in political life
However, at the same time, it creates new opportunities for the mass dissemination of disinformation, fabricated audio and video, and covert influence on public opinion.
For Ukraine, the conditions of war add to these problems: the need to simultaneously ensure the country’s defense, maintain democratic control over the authorities, media freedom, the parliament’s capacity to function, the independence of anti-corruption institutions, and prepare rules for future post-war elections. At the same time, it will be necessary to take into account the participation of millions of Ukrainians abroad, military personnel, and internally displaced persons.
However, at present, for Ukraine, the protection of democracy is directly linked to the protection of state sovereignty.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has moved his flagship foreign policy conference from Sochi to Moscow Oblast amid growing concerns over Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes, the Financial Times reported on 15 September.
The decision is likely an indirect acknowledgment of the impact of Ukraine’s ongoing deep-strike drone campaign. Russian officials may not publicly admit that Ukrainian drones pose a serious threat, but their actions suggest otherwise: Putin has increasingly avoided areas within range of Ukrainian drones, and now a major Kremlin event is being moved out of Sochi because of security concerns.
The annual Valdai Discussion Club meeting was originally planned for Sochi, but the venue was changed after Putin’s security service insisted on the move, according to four people familiar with the decision cited by the FT. Ukraine is targeting the defenses behind Russia’s rear
Ukraine has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to strike targets in Russia’s rear. Its drones have reached energy and logistics infrastructure thousands of kilometers from Ukraine, while Sochi and other areas of Russia’s Black Sea coast have come under repeated attack.
The latest strike came on 13–14 September, when Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the 92N6 multifunction radar of a Russian S-400 air defense system in Sochi, according to Ukraine’s General Staff. The radar tracks aerial targets and guides the S-400’s missiles, making it a critical component of the system defending the area.
The strike followed a 4 September Ukrainian attack on Sochi that hit two fuel depots and an air defense position near the Abkhazia border. Satellite imagery later showed nine destroyed fuel storage tanks and damage at the air defense position.
Putin’s movements show the threat is changing
The relocation also fits a broader pattern in Putin’s movements. The Russian president has spent much of his time in Moscow, St Petersburg and his residence near Lake Valdai in Novgorod Oblast, while making more trips east of the Urals – areas farther from Ukraine’s long-range drone reach.
The Valdai forum will still take place from 28 September to 1 October, but now in Moscow Oblast rather than Sochi. Putin traditionally attends the final day and holds a lengthy question-and-answer session.
The Kremlin does not need to say Ukrainian drones are a serious threat. Moving Putin’s major foreign-policy forum away from Sochi says it for them.

China leads trade with Ukraine but faces steep public backlash – Active Group, Experts Club poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:11:05 EEST
00:11:05 KST

Canada ranked first in terms of the balance of positive and negative attitudes among Ukrainians toward the 50 largest trading partners of Ukraine, while China, which leads in trade turnover, received the lowest score, and attitudes toward Poland deteriorated significantly, according to the results of a study by Active Group and the Experts Club information and analytical center.
According to the published ranking, Canada's balance of positive and negative assessments stood at plus 73.8 percentage points. It was followed by Sweden at plus 70.6 p.p., the Netherlands at 69.7 p.p., Finland and Norway at 69.3 p.p. each, France at 69.1 p.p., Italy at 67.1 p.p., Lithuania at 65.9 p.p., and Switzerland and the United Kingdom at 65.6 p.p. each.
This indicator is the difference between the shares of positive and negative responses. In particular, 76.3% of respondents expressed a positive attitude toward Canada, 2.5% a negative attitude, and 19.2% a neutral attitude.
The worst balance was recorded for China, at minus 25.4 p.p.: 18.2% of respondents assessed it positively, 43.6% negatively, and 33.9% neutrally. Negative figures were also recorded for India, at minus 14.3 p.p., Hungary, at minus 12.7 p.p., and Lebanon, at minus 9.2 p.p.
Olha Bezrukova, Doctor of Sociology and head of the Kyiv branch of the Sociological Association of Ukraine, called the People's Republic of China a telling example of the gap between the scale of economic interaction and the public image of a country.
"We saw that China is Ukraine's largest economic partner in terms of total trade turnover, but this in no way translates into a positive public image. This shows that Ukrainian citizens clearly distinguish between the pragmatism of economic interaction and their overall assessment of a country. Economic dependence and interaction do not equal public sympathy for this country," she said at a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Tuesday.
One of the most notable changes was the deterioration in attitudes toward Poland. While the balance of assessments stood at plus 41.7 p.p. in March 2026, in August positive and negative responses were virtually equal, with a slight predominance of negative ones. A positive attitude was expressed by 34.6% of respondents, a negative attitude by 37%, and a neutral attitude by 25.4%.
"At the beginning of the invasion, Poland was perceived almost as the main partner. We asked about bringing Ukraine and Poland closer together, politically and economically, and even about uniting in some kind of common alliance, and we saw enormous positive results. And here we see that Poland still seems to remain a key partner, but they have already forgotten about unification; we see a steady negative attitude," said Active Group founder Andriy Yeremenko.
He linked the deterioration in assessments to the position of part of the Polish authorities, which he considers anti-Ukrainian.
At the same time, the balance of attitudes toward Hungary improved from minus 33.6 p.p. in March to minus 12.7 p.p. in August, although negative assessments still prevail. As for the United States, the figure increased from plus 19.4 to plus 38.4 p.p. A positive attitude toward the United States was expressed by 55% of respondents, a negative attitude by 16.6%, and a neutral attitude by 25.6%.
Asked who contributes most to achieving peace in Ukraine, 44.6% of respondents named European Union countries, 25.2% the United States, 23.3% the United Kingdom, 4.1% the PRC, 1.8% India, and 1% Brazil. When asked which countries should be prioritized for the development of trade and economic relations, 69.9% chose EU countries and the United Kingdom, 11.9% the United States, and 8.4% the PRC.
According to Bezrukova, assessments of the U.S. role in achieving peace remained relatively stable over the three waves of the study.
"Overall sympathy for a country and an assessment of its functionality at the international level are related, but they are not identical. Country images are multidimensional. A person may change their emotional attitude toward a state while continuing to recognize its international weight," the sociologist explained.
Another model, she said, is demonstrated by India: 48.3% of respondents expressed a neutral attitude toward it, but among those who had formed an opinion, negative assessments prevailed – 31.5% versus 17.2% positive.
Economic indicators were presented by Experts Club founder, deputy director of the Interfax-Ukraine news agency and Candidate of Economic Sciences Maksym Urakin. According to data from the State Customs Service cited by him, in the first half of 2026, Ukraine's trade turnover amounted to $70.3 billion, exports to $21 billion, and imports to $49.3 billion. The negative balance in trade in goods reached $28.3 billion.
"If we compare this with the first half of 2025, there was also an imbalance then, but now exports have increased by approximately 5%, while imports have risen by almost 30%. In other words, the deficit increased by more than $10 billion over the year. Therefore, it is very important for us to analyze our main partners," he said.
According to the materials presented, trade turnover with China amounted to about $14.68 billion in January-June. Ukraine exported $778 million worth of goods to the PRC and imported $13.90 billion worth, resulting in a deficit of approximately $13.12 billion. Poland remained the largest buyer of Ukrainian goods, with $2.38 billion. Türkiye ranked second among export markets at $1.78 billion, and Italy third at $1.28 billion.
In terms of total trade, after the PRC came Poland at $7.05 billion, Türkiye at $4.90 billion, Germany at $4.48 billion, and the United States at $3.07 billion. Yeremenko highlighted Türkiye as an example of a combination of significant trade turnover and predominantly positive perceptions: 52.3% of respondents expressed a favorable attitude toward it, while 7.4% expressed a negative attitude.
Urakin separately drew attention to partners with which trade provides Ukraine with a positive balance. In the first half of the year, the largest positive balances were recorded with Spain at $578.1 million, Egypt at $527.1 million, and Moldova at $467.2 million. They were followed by Algeria at $309.2 million, the Netherlands at $221.5 million, and Lebanon at $220.5 million. Libya, Tunisia, Iraq and Yemen also made the top 10.
At the same time, neutral attitudes prevail toward a number of these partners. Egypt was assessed neutrally by 61.3% of respondents, Algeria by 65.8%, and Tunisia by 67.3%. The participants in the press conference attributed this to Ukrainians' insufficient awareness of these countries and emphasized the need for more active economic and public diplomacy.
"More needs to be done to develop not only general awareness. First and foremost, business associations, the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs need to work on developing bilateral relations and improving the balance. At a time when Ukraine already lacks funding and, essentially, lives on external borrowing, we need to expand cooperation with countries with which we can have a positive balance," said Active Group Director Oleksandr Pozniy.
Urakin recommended that embassies accredited in Ukraine ensure full-fledged communication in Ukrainian, openness to the media, and regular communication of the results of cooperation.
"The first recommendation is to regularly demonstrate specific projects, specific actions, the presence here of foundations, embassies, teams and diplomats in the humanitarian sphere and in science. The second is to be open to questions and requests from the media and the public. We also need to use our sociological research to draw conclusions and cement our relations, primarily our trade relations," he added.
This is the third wave of the study; previous surveys were conducted in August 2025 and March 2026. The survey was conducted in August 2026 using self-administered online questionnaires through the SunFlowerSociology panel. A total of 800 Ukrainian citizens aged 18 and older were surveyed. According to the organizers, the sample is representative by age, gender and region, and the stated maximum theoretical margin of statistical error at a 95% confidence level is 3.5%.

‘Do you know where Ceuta is?’: EU Parliament erupts over migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:10:40 UTC
00:10:40 KST

The European People’s Party and Socialists clashed in a heated European Parliament debate, with shouting and mutual accusations exposing deepening divisions over migration within the coalition backing Ursula von der Leyen.
A European Parliament debate on the situation in Ceuta on Tuesday descended into a bitter internal clash between the political groups backing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, just one day before her landmark State of the Union address.
The two main groups underpinning the centrist majority — the European People’s Party (EPP) and the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) — clashed over the aftermath of the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave on 30-31 July, when around 80,000 people crossed the border irregularly and more than 150 people died.
“The EPP has been exploiting Ceuta for more than a month with the sole aim of attacking the Spanish government,” Socialist leader Iratxe García Pérez said in a direct attack on the centre-right group.
S&D MEPs rallied behind Sánchez’s government while criticising other EU countries for what they described as a failure to show solidarity with Spain.
Some lawmakers targeted the Italian government, which came under fire for extending by another 15 days its reintroduction of checks at air and maritime borders with Spain.
“Meloni asked for solidarity for Lampedusa and denies it for Ceuta,” Italian Socialist MEP Sandro Ruotolo said, accusing Rome of applying a double standard on migration.
EPP lawmakers, meanwhile, largely used their interventions to criticise Sánchez, accusing his government of allowing an “invasion” of European territory by failing to prevent the mass influx.
Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report suggested that Moroccan forces had played a role in pushing migrants towards Ceuta, adding pressure on Madrid and fuelling criticism from the EPP.
“The police warned him. The intelligence services sent reports. [...] Sánchez knew it and went on vacation for 25 days,” Spanish MEP Dolors Montserrat said.
Centre-right lawmakers also used the debate to attack the Spanish government’s broader migration policy, including its plan to regularise thousands of undocumented migrants, although the measure is not directly linked to the Ceuta crisis.
“Sánchez asked for solidarity after resisting common tools needed to prevent crises and initiated mass regularisation even though there was no agreement on this in Europe,” Dutch EPP MEP Jeroen Lenaers said.
A resolution on the issue is due to be put to a vote next Thursday, with a political battle over amendments expected to determine its final wording and expose further divisions between the two main centrist groups.
The EPP is expected to push for critical references to Spain’s handling of the crisis, while the Socialists are likely to seek to soften the language of the accusations.
Migration is also expected to feature in the State of the Union address, where von der Leyen is likely to propose further restricting measures on asylum rights and a boost to the EU border agency Frontex.
Far-right and left clashed in chaotic debate
Beyond the EPP-S&D clash, several MEPs from the far right and radical left also took the floor with provocative remarks and counter-accusations, sparking heated exchanges.
Podemos MEP Isabel Serra Sánchez accused far-right colleagues of turning Ceuta into a “hate laboratory” by calling for migrants to be “hunted”, which she said had contributed to attacks against migrants in the exclave.
Diego Solier, of the Spanish nationalist party The Party Is Over, challenged her, asking whether she cared about women who had allegedly been sexually assaulted by migrants in the autonomous city.
Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé Villalba shouted during an intervention by Green MEP Jaume Asens, while non-attached MEP Alvise Pérez claimed he had been insulted by left-wing colleagues. Pérez was then reprimanded for having previously insulted The Left’s Irene Montero, prompting an unusual exchange with Parliament Vice-President Younous Omarjee.
After a passionate speech warning of an “invasion” of Europe by irregular migrants, League MEP Susanna Ceccardi was challenged by Swedish liberal MEP Abir Al-Sahlani, who hit back with a pointed question: “Do you know where Ceuta is?”

Israel and Saudi Arabia are engaged in CENTCOM-mediated talks on intelligence support against the Houthis, a regional diplomat tells i24NEWS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:09:58 UTC
00:09:58 KST

Israel and Saudi Arabia are engaged in CENTCOM-mediated sharing intel against the Houthis
A source familiar with the details of the discussions told i24NEWS: "The talks went well."
Israel and Saudi Arabia are engaged in direct dialogue facilitated by the United States Central Command over potential Israeli intelligence assistance to Riyadh against the Houthis, a regional diplomat told i24NEWS.
The information was provided directly to i24NEWS, rather than attributed to an earlier Israeli media report. The diplomat said the discussions are intended to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ability to confront the growing Houthi threat, with Israel potentially supplying intelligence on the group’s military positions, weapons infrastructure and operational plans.
The disclosure comes shortly after CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper visited Saudi Arabia and met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other senior officials. A source familiar with those discussions told i24NEWS that “the talks went well,” without providing further details.
Cooper’s visit and CENTCOM’s reported role in facilitating the Israeli-Saudi dialogue point to intensified American efforts to coordinate regional security responses as Houthi attacks place increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia and threaten navigation through the Red Sea.
The Houthis have sharply escalated their attacks against the kingdom over the past week. The group reportedly launched drones at Saudi oil pipelines and pumping facilities, causing a partial disruption to operations along a major pipeline.
Houthi forces have also been accused of attacking Saudi civilians at a mosque and nearby buildings close to the border with Yemen.
At the same time, the group seized several strategically located Red Sea islands and prevented Saudi vessels from passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a critical route for international trade and energy shipments.
The restrictions have increased economic and political pressure on Riyadh while raising broader concerns about maritime security in the region.
Regional security officials have warned that the escalation is alarming not only Saudi Arabia but also other governments that could face similar threats.
Those countries are reportedly concerned that Washington may eventually reach separate understandings with Iran and the Houthis, leaving its regional partners exposed to continued attacks without a comprehensive security arrangement.
Israel’s potential contribution would likely center on its intelligence and surveillance capabilities. The Israeli military has demonstrated an ability to monitor Iranian and allied forces across the region and has previously assisted the United States in developing intelligence on Iranian military deployments around the Strait of Hormuz.
Another unresolved issue is President Donald Trump’s decision to permit Saudi Arabia to develop a civilian nuclear program. Israeli security officials have raised concerns with the Trump administration about the program’s long-term strategic implications, even if it remains exclusively civilian.
Trump has sought to connect progress on the Saudi nuclear program with normalization between Riyadh and Jerusalem. The newly disclosed security dialogue suggests that practical cooperation may be advancing in response to the Houthi threat even as the larger political negotiations remain unsettled.
