Breadcrumb
'Find a moral compass': Ed Sheeran urged to cancel 'compromised' US tour
British singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran should "find a moral compass" and stand up to wealthy supporters of Israel's war on Gaza, an artists' advocacy group has told The New Arab, following rapper Macklemore's exit from Sheeran's US stadium tour.
Artists for Palestine UK condemned Sheeran after Macklemore said he had been removed from the remainder of the singer's Loop tour amid pressure over his pro-Palestine stance.
The group, which has received backing from figures including actor Brian Cox, former Loose Women panellist Nadia Sawalha and singer Charlotte Church, said it supported "Palestinian calls for Ed Sheeran to cancel the rest of his now compromised US tour".
"We urge Sheeran to find a moral compass and stand up to billionaire-supporters of genocide and apartheid," Artists for Palestine UK told The New Arab.
"While artists certainly come under enormous pressure to be silent about the ongoing genocide, Macklemore continues to build an audience of millions precisely because he speaks truth to power," the group added.
It praised Macklemore's sustained advocacy for Palestinians through his music and public statements about the situation facing Palestinians under Israeli occupation.
The rapper has been notably vocal since releasing his 2024 track 'Hind's Hall', which was inspired by pro-Palestine student protests at universities across the United States over Israel's war on Gaza.
"His statement [on Monday] makes clear that artists of his profile and wealth, and of Ed Sheeran's profile and wealth, are well placed to take a lead in refusing to bow to wealthy bullies," Artists for Palestine UK said.
Macklemore said in a social media post that he had been removed from the remainder of Sheeran's Loop tour after allegedly being warned against performing.
He also stressed that the controversy should not overshadow the suffering of Palestinians in the occupied territories.
The announcement followed a series of onstage statements by Macklemore in support of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, including calls for a "free Palestine".
His departure prompted widespread criticism from pro-Palestine supporters online, including calls for Sheeran to address the decision.
Robert Kraft, the pro-Israel billionaire owner of the New England Patriots whose Kraft Group owns Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, reportedly contacted Sheeran and said the rapper would not be allowed to perform at the venue.
Artists for Palestine UK criticised the influence of wealthy pro-Israel figures over the arts, saying they try to restrict freedom of expression and criticism of Israel.
"Billionaires like Robert Kraft and Miriam Adelson are destroying the planet, funding political misinformation and genocidal policies against Palestinians in Gaza - and trying to shut down freedom of expression in the arts," the group told The New Arab.
"This level of crude and deeply anti-democratic censorship should be resisted by Sheeran and by all of us, together, for the sake of Palestine, but also for the sake of communities everywhere."
Artists rally behind Macklemore
Ms Rachel, a children's educator, entertainer and human rights activist, also criticised Sheeran in an Instagram post.
"Ed Sheeran had an opportunity to show that we won't be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine," she wrote. "Instead, he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza."
Climate activist Greta Thunberg also expressed solidarity with the Grammy-winning rapper on social media.
"Full solidarity and free Palestine. Artists' very active silence in the face of injustice and genocide will not be forgotten," she wrote.
Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, has also received support from fellow musicians, including Irish rap trio Kneecap.
Responding to his Monday post, Kneecap wrote: "Free Palestine. They can never silence the truth."
The group also shared a photograph with Macklemore, captioned: "All love and solidarity to @macklemore. FREE PALESTINE."
Rock band Garbage also criticised the decision, describing Macklemore's removal as "sheer madness".
"This is so wildly unjust. Can I remind everyone that nothing Macklemore actually said was violent or hateful or remotely radical," the band wrote.
"Those who exile, silence and censor others are never the good guys. No matter what you tell yourself. Just because you ignore the truth doesn't make the truth go away or make it any less potent. It is all so utterly obscene."
Sheeran's Ukraine support scrutinised
Criticism of Sheeran has also drawn attention to his previous public support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion in 2022.
Posts resurfacing on social media included a video of Sheeran responding to Ukrainian band Antytila, whose members had joined the war effort following Russia's invasion.
In the clip, filmed ahead of Sheeran's appearance at the 'Concert for Ukraine' benefit event in Birmingham, the singer told the band and the people of Ukraine: "I love you, I stand with you."
Sheeran later headlined the fundraiser, collaborated with Antytila frontman Taras Topolya on a reworked version of his song '2step' and donated royalties from the track to a humanitarian appeal for Ukraine.
British lawyer Shola Mos-Shogbamimu criticised what she described as a contrast between Sheeran's response to Ukraine and his position on Palestine.
"Ed Sheeran saying 'I Stand With Ukraine' is being 'apolitical'?" she wrote in an X post. "Not taking sides uh? But when it comes to genocide of Palestinians you side with the oppressor Israel."
Sheeran addresses criticism
In a lengthy Instagram post, Sheeran defended himself against the continued backlash, asserting that he does not use his professional platform for politics.
The famed singer said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and framed the nearly three-year Israeli war on Gaza as "suffering and pain caused on both sides".
However, Sheeran stressed that he does not publicly share his personal views, despite his previous public statements of support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion.
"I am not complicit," his statement read. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."
Sheeran said his audiences often include children and young people "from all backgrounds", which he said was why he does not use his stage for political statements.
He also said the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour was made by the promoted and venues hosting upcoming concert dates, rather than by him.
Sheeran confirmed Macklemore's account that venues had contacted him to say they would cancel the gigs if the rapper remained involved.
He said he was "involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue's and promoter's decision was final."
Despite his reluctance to speak publicly about Palestine, Sheeran said he respected Macklemore's "strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes".
However, he also argued that "there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace".
He concluded: "If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."

Reiche Länder müssen sich laut OECD noch weitere 20 Jahre lang auf Covid-Folgekosten einstellen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:52:44 UTC
23:52:44 KST

Die gesundheitlichen und wirtschaftlichen Auswirkungen von Covid-19 werden laut einem heute veröffentlichten Bericht der reichsten Industrieländer der Welt voraussichtlich noch zwei weitere Jahrzehnte andauern.
Im Zuge der Pandemie stiegen die Raucherquoten, der Alkoholkonsum und ungesunde Ernährungsgewohnheiten, während die Versorgung von Menschen mit chronischen Erkrankungen unterbrochen wurde. All dies belastet die heutigen Volkswirtschaften und Gesundheitssysteme weiterhin, wie es in einem Bericht der Organisation für wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit und Entwicklung (OECD) heißt.
Und während die Länder weiterhin unter dem durch Covid bedingten Druck auf ihre Haushalte leiden, besteht für sie zudem eine Wahrscheinlichkeit von 50 Prozent, dass es in den nächsten 25 Jahren zu einer weiteren Pandemie ähnlichen Ausmaßes kommt.
Advertisement
Das Dokument, das die wirtschaftlichen Argumente für die Pandemievorsorge und -bewältigung untersucht, erläutert, warum frühzeitiges Handeln notwendig ist, um die schlimmsten gesundheitlichen und wirtschaftlichen Folgen abzuwenden.
Von 2020 bis Mai 2023 starben fast sieben Millionen Menschen an Covid, während die Weltwirtschaft im Jahr 2020 im Vergleich zum Vorjahr um fast vier Prozent schrumpfte. Das ist ein Rückgang, der mit der Finanzkrise von 2008 vergleichbar ist, heißt es in dem Bericht.
Die Autoren modellierten Ausbrüche von Viren wie Ebola, Vogelgrippe, Influenza A, Corona und Masern, um Gesundheitssysteme und Volkswirtschaften einem Stresstest zu unterziehen.
Ohne Behandlungen oder Impfstoffe könnten in den ersten neun Monaten ein Prozent der Bevölkerung an einem dem Coronavirus ähnlichen Ausbruch und mehr als fünf Prozent an einem Influenza-A-ähnlichen Ausbruch sterben.
Demgegenüber würde das Bruttoinlandsprodukt bei einem Ausbruch eines Coronavirus-ähnlichen Virus um 2,7 Prozent schrumpfen, bei einem Masern-ähnlichen Virus hingegen um 16,2 Prozent.
„Transport und Lagerung, das verarbeitende Gewerbe sowie Verwaltungs- und Unterstützungsdienstleistungen würden durchweg zu den am stärksten betroffenen Wirtschaftssektoren gehören“, heißt es in dem Bericht.
Aus diesem Grund seien frühzeitige Maßnahmen im Bereich der öffentlichen Gesundheit wie etwa Händewaschen, das Tragen von Masken und Abstandhalten von entscheidender Bedeutung, um Leben zu retten und die Wirtschaft am Laufen zu halten – und damit die Notwendigkeit späterer drastischerer Maßnahmen zu verringern, heißt es in dem Bericht.

EU unveils digital platform to ease recognition of social security and professional qualifications
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:52:07 UTC
23:52:07 KST

The European Commission estimates that a system allowing faster and easier recognition of working documents could save billions of euros by the end of the next decade.
In a proposal put forward on Tuesday, the European Commission has set out plans for a digital European platform that citizens can use to get their working documents recognised across the bloc.
The aim of the platform, which will be known as the "European Social Security Pass", is to overcome delays that cross-border workers face when they need to receive working documents or get them recognised in member states other than their home countries. Those delays often result in basic rights being violated.
With the new package, workers will be able to more easily claim their social security and health insurance benefits, as well as have their professional qualifications recognised in other EU countries without unnecessary red tape.
The proposals also aim to protect mobile workers and to address challenges faced by companies when recruiting talent from abroad within the EU.
"The single market must also become a genuine skills market with more opportunities for workers and businesses," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement.
Commission data from 2024 showed that around 14 million Europeans lived in EU countries other than those they were born in; 10 million of them were of working age. A recent Eurobarometer survey, meanwhile, found that 18% of Europeans want to move abroad.
European Commission Vice-President for Social Rights Roxana Mînzatu told Euronews that a new EU platform will save “talented" people from “wasting their skills” when they move across EU borders.
The Commission estimates that the platform could deliver as much as €6 billion in benefits by 2040.
"Over 12 years, digitisation could save up to €64 million for businesses, €69 million for healthcare providers, and €72 million for labour inspectors through faster cross-border verification. Digital signatures could avoid up to €277 million in fraud over the same period," the Commission said in a statement.

Carney visits Europe: Can Canada seek refuge with the EU amid US trade war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:49:42 UTC
23:49:42 KST

Carney visits Europe: Can Canada seek refuge with the EU amid US trade war?
Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking a ‘unique alliance’ with Europe as transatlantic relations sour.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is visiting Europe this week as his country seeks a closer strategic alliance with the European Union amid its bitter trade war with the United States.
At the same time, once-reliable transatlantic relations between Europe and Washington have been strained by US President Donald Trump’s threats of tariffs and his aggressive bid to acquire Greenland, as well as the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, which European countries have refused to join.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Mark Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid US trade war
- list 2 of 4Apple changes name of Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ in maps app
- list 3 of 4How Canadians are bracing for the impact of Trump’s trade war
- list 4 of 4Why has the Netherlands moved $10bn of its gold from the US?
Carney is set to visit Strasbourg in France, and Liverpool in the United Kingdom between September 15 and September 17, according to an official statement.
Here’s what we know about his European ambitions:
What do we know about Carney’s visit to Europe?
Carney has said Canada is seeking opportunities to diversify trade and investments, but has not revealed much else officially.
In meetings with members of the European Parliament, the prime minister will seek to “strengthen Canada’s ties with the EU in trade, investment, and security”, a government statement announcing his visit read.
While some in Carney’s cabinet and in the EU have floated the idea that Canada might be seeking an “associate EU membership”, the prime minister has said that is not an option.
“We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” Carney said, speaking to reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday. Rather, Canada is looking to start discussions on what he called a “unique alliance”.
“We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths,” Carney continued.
A senior Canadian official, however, told The Associated Press news agency that the aim of the visit is to strengthen Canada’s sovereignty; thus, the country would not be willing to give up “our rights to Brussels”.
Canada will, however, push for an arrangement that would allow Canadians to live and work in Europe without visas, and that investment would be at the core of the deeper partnership, the official added.
Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre in an X statement on Sunday said the prime minister was “out of touch”.
What would closer ties mean for Canada?
Carney has emphasised Canada’s over-reliance on the US as a trading partner and the need to diversify amid the increasingly fraught trade war with the Trump administration, which has seen both sides impose tit-for-tat trade tariffs. Last month, Trump even renamed Lake Ontario – which lies along the US-Canada border – “Lake America”, in a fit of pique.
Closer ties with the EU could achieve this by generating significantly more trade with Brussels instead of the US, which currently imports more than 70 percent of all Canadian goods, worth more than $300bn a year.
Canada’s trade with the EU is currently a distant second to the US and was worth 130 billion euros ($150bn) in 2025. Canadian passport holders can enter the Schengen zone as tourists for only 90 days but will require a permit for longer stays.
It could also mean more travel, work and retirement opportunities for Canadian citizens, analysts say.
Similar arrangements between the EU and non-EU member countries within Europe exist. Switzerland, for example, is associated with the EU through several bilateral treaties that mean it has access to the EU single market and the Schengen open border area.
Why is this significant?
Experts say Canada and the EU are both looking for ways to strategically shield themselves from fallouts with the US.
A deeper alliance appears part of a global trend of new powers and orders, analysts say, as Washington’s traditional allies find it much harder to rely on Trump.
A 2017 EU-Canada trade agreement already eliminated duties on Canadian products entering the EU and vice versa. It also made investments easier for firms on both sides to invest.
Both sides also already hold yearly Canada-EU summits. At last year’s meeting, they signed a defence pact stipulating joint responses to international security emergencies or stabilisation missions and interoperability between Canadian and European armed forces.
What has caused Canada-US and EU-US relations to sour?
Canada’s issues with the US began before Carney took office, when Trump unleashed his trade war on several countries, including Canada, at the start of his second term.
When imposing new trading tariffs on other countries, Trump has repeatedly cited the trade deficit that the US has with most of them.
According to the Office of the US Trade Representative, goods trade with Canada totalled $715.5bn in 2025. Exports to Canada were $333.6bn, compared with imports from Canada of $381.9bn. The US goods trade deficit with Canada was $48.3bn, a 21 percent decrease ($12.9 billion) over 2024.
Trump also accused Canada, however, of not doing enough to stem the flow of fentanyl, a highly addictive synthetic opiate drug, into the US.
Under former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, Canada enforced retaliatory duties in response.
More recently, a new wave of US tariffs erupted after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed in August. Trump has since slapped 50 percent tariffs on $20bn-worth of Canadian goods imported into the US.
When Canada retaliated with matching tariff rates, the US president moved to ban imports of certain products like whey, some alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and mopeds. He has also directed government agencies to declare Canadian products ineligible for long-term US government contracts.
Although Carney has warned that the US’s trade war could hollow out the economy, the Canadian public has largely rallied behind him and supports retaliatory measures.
Trump has separately irked the Canadian public by repeatedly floating the idea of making Canada a 51st state. He has also launched personal attacks on Canadian leaders and last month signed an executive order to change Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.
Why are Europe-US relations fraught?
The US-EU relationship is similarly fraught, although Brussels exports mostly to the US. Trump has slapped a 15 percent tariff hike on the bloc since 2025.
Trump, who has repeatedly questioned the utility of the NATO security pact, was angry about EU member countries’ refusal to join the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran. Last year, tensions also arose over Trump’s insistence on seizing control of Greenland, the self-governing Arctic territory which is part of Denmark.
In January this year, seven European leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer, issued a joint statement saying the mineral-rich Arctic island “belongs to its people”, which also irked Trump enough to threaten yet more tariffs against European countries standing in his way. Later that month, he walked back these threats, saying he had agreed to a framework for a future deal over the island state with NATO chief Mark Rutte.
Earlier this month, the EU said it had signed a declaration with Greenland, promising a stronger partnership and announcing a 200 million-euro ($232m) investment package to soothe anxiety caused by Trump’s repeated threats to annex it.

US could hit Putin's Arctic gas empire by sanctioning 14 LNG tankers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:47:27 UTC
23:47:27 KST

The House of Representatives could vote this week on a bill that would allow the U.S. to sanction vessels transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), including 14 specialized tankers serving the Yamal LNG project, sanctions-monitoring NGO Urgewald told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 15.
The bill, which targets Russian energy, could put the vessels that transport LNG from Russia's Yamal Peninsula under U.S. sanctions review. The measure comes as Europe prepares to fully ban Russian LNG imports and continues to account for the vast majority of Yamal LNG cargoes.
The Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed the Senate 86-11 in August and was advanced by the House Rules Committee on Sept. 14. Further consideration in the House is scheduled for this week.
The legislation would not automatically sanction all 14 Arc7 tankers serving Yamal LNG. Instead, it would require U.S. President Donald Trump to review vessels covered by the bill and determine which meet the criteria for designation.
Under the Senate-approved version, Trump would have 30 days after the bill's enactment to review the vessels and designate qualifying ships as blocked property.
The legislation would also allow sanctions against foreign port owners or operators that knowingly provide services to Russia's sanctioned vessels.
"Sanctions offer Washington a way to support Western security in the High North without putting American troops in harm's way," Alexander Kirk, a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, said.
Yamal LNG is one of Russia's largest LNG projects and accounts for more than 60% of the country's LNG exports. Despite partial restrictions on Russian LNG, European countries remain the main destinations for the cargo.
European ports received 136 of the 140 Yamal LNG cargoes shipped in the first half of 2026, worth an estimated 5.96 billion euros ($6.82 billion), according to previous Urgewald analysis.
The EU is due to impose a full ban on Russian LNG imports in January 2027. Until then, European demand continues to provide an important market for Russia's Arctic LNG exports.
The 14 Arc7 tankers are specially designed to navigate the harsh winter conditions around Russia's Yamal Peninsula. Disrupting even part of their trade routes could have substantial consequences for Russia's ability to export LNG and generate revenue from the industry.

What will Luke Lindberg mean for WFP and humanitarians?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:45:31 UTC
23:45:31 KST

Share & more
The Trump administration dismantled aid and attacked the global system as wasteful. Now a Trump pick looks set to lead one of the world’s biggest humanitarian agencies.
US agriculture official Luke Lindberg will be named the new head of the World Food Programme, two aid officials familiar with the selection process told The New Humanitarian.
Officially, the UN secretary-general and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s director-general choose the WFP leader, in consultation with WFP’s executive board. A special session of WFP’s board is scheduled for 18 September.
A letter shared within humanitarian circles also confirms Lindberg as the pick. News of Lindberg’s pending appointment was first reported by Devex over the weekend.
Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader?
It follows months-long delays in choosing a new executive director at WFP – and for some, worry over what putting a Trump-aligned pick at the heart of the emergency aid system will mean.
WFP has been without an official executive director since Cindy McCain announced her departure earlier this year, citing health concerns.
Lindberg’s selection would continue a long history of opaque UN appointments and American dominance at the helm of WFP. The executive director role has been held by an American since 1992, under the UN’s practice of backroom horse-trading key roles.
It’s also another example of top leadership jobs going to the politically connected, whether at UN agencies or big NGOs. Lindberg is the son-in-law of US Senate majority leader John Thune, and currently undersecretary for trade and foreign agricultural affairs in the US Department of Agriculture.
Lindberg appears to have no experience in emergency response, but he will join a UN agency that is often seen as the lynchpin of the international humanitarian system.
His public record so far contrasts sharply with the neutrality and impartiality principles that the humanitarian sector often foregrounds. Lindberg has voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (who has an active arrest warrant for war crimes accusations), and touted weapons exports amid the Israeli military’s onslaught on Gaza.
Critics say the US is increasingly co-opting the humanitarian system along ideological lines – using funding and policy to align aid with geopolitical interests, and to sideline reproductive health and equity, for example.
Lindberg will lead a key agency at a time of deep budget cuts, severe hunger, and spiralling emergencies – in some cases in crises provoked by US military actions and US government policies. Some 151.6 million people face crisis levels of hunger or worse, according to famine analysts.
Crises are spiralling, deepened by conflict, climate change, and the flouting of international laws. At the same time, donor funding cuts have left the global emergency response system at a breaking point, triaging budgets to target only a fraction of the more than 239 million people said to need emergency aid. WFP’s projected funding this year sits at around $6.4 billion – less than half of what it was in 2022, and its lowest in about a decade. The US funds about 30% of the agency’s budget.
Here are four key questions:
Who does Lindberg answer to?
Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader?
The Trump administration has used foreign aid funding as a hammer: It steers its humanitarian and health money to align with geopolitical interests instead of needs; and sharpened its discriminatory global gag rule to sideline reproductive health and equity programmes funded by other donors.
This has put an extra spotlight on the delayed search for a new WFP chief. Will they be beholden to Washington, or to the organisation’s humanitarian mandate?
“We never really had to ask this question before for a UN appointee quite so explicitly,” said Sam Vigersky, a former US humanitarian adviser and now a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a New York-based think tank. “That to me in itself is a concerning development in our field.”
Before the Trump administration backed Lindberg for the UN role, other rumoured candidates had pushed to make US support to WFP conditional on aligning with foreign policy interests, Vigersky said. Lindberg hasn’t outlined such plans, and should be judged based on what he does when he starts at WFP, he said.
“Is Lindberg able to unlock sums of money from the Congress and the Trump administration that otherwise would be sidelined because there wasn’t an insider at the helm… or does this end up being an appointment to a multilateral agency that ends up running a political operation for the Trump administration to potentially be punitive towards NGOs they think are critical of the administration,” Vigersky said.
“A lot of the aid coming out of [the] State Department has directly framed how they are making decisions. So I’m going to be looking for the firewall between the two.”
Many of the issues at the heart of WFP’s work may contradict the current US administration’s interests – from climate change as a cause of crises, to famine declarations that are politically inconvenient for allies like Israel, to pushing back on aid cuts.
Still a US government official for now, Lindberg’s recent public comments have defended the cuts as a sort of “level-setting”.
”This idea that we’re retreating is an unfair characterisation of the pause that was taken to re-evaluate and re-design some of the structures and the way in which we do business,” Lindberg said during a CFR briefing this month. A study in The Lancet estimated that donor cuts could lead to 9.4 million deaths by 2030.
In his short time in the agriculture department, Lindberg has been open about using US aid for US interests.
The USDA-managed Food for Peace programme, which sends US commodities as food assistance, now targets only a handful of countries, after a restructuring overseen by Lindberg. It notably leaves out several countries facing severe levels of hunger – such as Mali, Somalia, Sudan, or Yemen – while including some that are not. These choices balanced hunger needs, the availability of distribution partners, and “the geopolitical interests of the United States”, Lindberg said.
How do other humanitarian agencies see Lindberg?
Lindberg is mostly unknown in humanitarian circles, but his social media feed has done most of the talking so far.
His personal accounts have been peppered with pro-Israel posts, pics of Lindberg grinning and gripping a rifle to be exported to the Israeli military, and plenty of cowboy hats.
A newer Twitter account created for his WFP bid presents a milder image, tinted with shades of UN blue, frequent retweets of WFP posts, and inoffensive statements about resilience and ending hunger.
Lindberg is “obviously MAGA” and the gun pics are concerning, but he appears to be less risky than other names floated for key positions, one aid official told The New Humanitarian.
“Basically, I think he’s someone we can work with,” said the official, who compared Lindberg’s potential to that of David Beasley, the former South Carolina governor appointed as WFP executive director during Trump’s first term. Beasley’s reputation is that of a prolific fundraiser; his time as WFP head overlapped with a years-long surge in donor government support for the humanitarian system as a whole.
How do staff see Lindberg, and how will people in crisis now see WFP?
But Lindberg’s politics are a deep concern for many, and an agency’s leader reflects on the entire organisation.
WFP’s staff of 20,000 stretches across the globe, from Central America to the Pacific Islands, or from Afghanistan to Sudan and Gaza. Like many humanitarian organisations, most are local staff, often from the communities they’re trying to help.
Some staff have expressed outrage about leadership positions on Gaza, or WFP’s choice of partners like Boston Consulting Group or Palantir. In conversations with The New Humanitarian, they have also expressed unease about US influence on the organisation, and about Lindberg.
Then there’s whether a WFP led by Lindberg changes how communities in crisis see a humanitarian organisation that often says it relies on its perceived neutrality to operate.
The agency’s likely new leader is an enthusiastic supporter of Netanyahu, whose government and military has inflicted harm in crises where WFP is asked to alleviate hunger.
“We are exporting freedom and prosperity to our friends,” Lindberg wrote in a social media post while clutching a South Dakota-made sniper rifle – one of several pics that have been widely shared among WFP staff and other humanitarians. At the time, Lindberg was a trade official for the US state.
The world’s leading genocide scholars say Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity against Palestinians.
Where does Lindberg push WFP on data, tech, and partnerships?
WFP faces growing criticism for its relationship with Palantir, the data analytics firm and military contractor.
Its private sector partnerships, and its ambitions around harnessing sensitive data of deeply vulnerable populations, are especially under the microscope as Big Tech and artificial intelligence corporations grow to dominate economies, culture, and power – and as WFP forms the backbone of international humanitarian logistics.
WFP’s envelope-pushing experimentation and data strategy have been encouraged by multiple leadership teams, and by several different donors.
Lindberg’s recent comments suggest the agency will continue full speed ahead on the same path.
“In a resource-constrained environment, you have to do more with less,” Lindberg said during the CFR briefing, mirroring existing WFP leadership talking points on tech partnerships and AI.
“I think there’s all kinds of tools out there in the world today that can make even the best organisations a little bit better,” he added.
The USDA signed a $300 million deal with Palantir earlier this year.

Russia said on Tuesday it is important that statements about an energy ceasefire with Ukraine, which US President Donald Trump announced a day prior, are “translated into action.”
In response to a question by Anadolu, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told a briefing in the city of Yekaterinburg that she does not think further comments on the topic are needed as the Kremlin has already issued statements on the matter.
“Now, the most important thing is for these declarations to be translated into action,” Zakharova said at the briefing, which took place on the sidelines of the 2026 International Festival of Youth.
She said Russia has always honored and adhered to ceasefires announced during the war, but argued that “cannot be said of” Kyiv.
“Therefore, all words must be backed by concrete actions that back them up,” Zakharova added.
On Monday, Trump said in a statement on Truth Social that both Moscow and Kyiv agreed to not hit each other’s energy infrastructure, while attributing a surge in global diesel prices primarily to the ongoing conflict that began in February 2022.
The Kremlin said earlier on Tuesday that it backed Trump’s idea of the truce, noting that Russia remains in contact with the US on the initiative.
“We certainly consider it a very good idea overall,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a press briefing. The energy truce and measures to ensure the safe operation of oil refineries alone, he said, would not resolve the main problem affecting global oil product markets.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an evening address late Monday that Kyiv is ready to take de-escalatory steps if Washington can “ensure that Russia is genuinely ready to stop this war aimed at destroying life – and to do so for real and for the long term.”
“Peace is needed. Energy, food routes, critical infrastructure – all of this must be part of the discussion on ending the strikes … We expect specifics from our partners,” Zelenskyy added.

VRT was expected to confirm its participation by Tuesday, Sept. 15, in line with Eurovision regulations.

Reports have circulated that Belgium's French-speaking public broadcaster RTBF could take over the country's Eurovision participation if VRT withdraws.
RTBF, however, denied the reports.

This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:43:23 UTC
23:43:23 KST

This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
Burned grasses preserved in an Australian cave reveal ritual traditions that may stretch back an astonishing 25,000 years.
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site.
- Share:
The GunaiKurnai, an Australian Aboriginal nation, are recognized as the traditional custodians of Gippsland and the southern Victorian Alps. Caves within their lands have long been linked to spiritual practices. Accounts recorded in the 19th century, together with oral traditions, describe them as places where powerful learned women and men known as 'mulla-mullung', along with other spiritual practitioners, carried out rituals involving magic, healing, and cursing.
Archaeological evidence now shows that one of these sites, Cloggs Cave, was used for such activities over an extraordinary span of roughly 25,000 years.
"Here we show that the Old Ancestors selected whole grasses from the wider landscape and carried them into Cloggs Cave to spread out in thin layers and burn. Over time, sediments covered these burnt layers, preserving each layer on top of another over thousands of years," said Dr Elle Grono, a postdoctoral researcher at the Australian National University and the corresponding author of a new study published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.
Microscopic Clues From Ancient Plants
Grono and researchers from Australia, France, and New Zealand examined phytoliths recovered from buried sediments inside Cloggs Cave. Phytoliths are microscopic silica structures that form within plant tissues and can survive long after the plants themselves have disappeared.
The research grew out of archaeological excavations carried out in 2019 and 2020. Those excavations were designed to determine how people collected and used plants inside the cave in the distant past. The work was requested by the GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, and GunaiKurnai representatives were involved in the research design, fieldwork, interpretation, and communication of the findings.
"Unlike pollen, which is dispersed by wind or insects, phytoliths mostly accumulate at the spot where a plant decays. No plants grow inside the cave due to a lack of light, so the phytoliths must have been carried in by people or by animals such as possums on their fur or through their scats," explained Grono. "We focused on half-burnt phytoliths from ashy layers, which can only have been brought in by people, as unburnt ones might have arrived through either means."
Because vegetation cannot grow naturally inside the dark cave, the burned plant remains offered especially strong evidence that people had intentionally carried grasses into the site.
Layers of Ash and a Standing Stone
Using microscopy, the researchers classified thousands of phytoliths collected from two excavation pits measuring 1.5 m and 2.3 m deep.
The upper sections of those pits contained 73 thin layers of ash deposited by people between approximately 4,400 and 1,600 years ago. Researchers established those ages using optically stimulated luminescence and carbon dating via accelerator mass spectrometry.
Hidden among the layers was another striking discovery: a standing stone measuring 28 cm high. Later analysis showed that Old Ancestors had intentionally placed the stone inside the cave for ritual purposes around 2,000 years ago.
Grasses Were Carefully Chosen
The team identified 29 different kinds of phytoliths representing grasses, herbs, and woody plants. Many were exceptionally well preserved, including delicate silica structures such as hair cells.
Grass phytoliths dominated the samples, accounting for as much as 97% of the total. They included members of the Pooideae subfamily, which favor temperate or cool conditions, as well as Panicoideae grasses, which generally thrive in warmer and more humid environments.
Phytoliths from Chloridoideae grasses, which tolerate drought and are adapted to warm, dry arid conditions, appeared less frequently. Remains from herbs and woody plants were also uncommon.
The pattern suggests that Old Ancestors did not simply gather whatever vegetation was nearby. Instead, they deliberately selected particular grasses.
Before European settlement, the landscape around Cloggs Cave included riparian forest and open woodland containing many different plant species. Yet those plants were largely absent from the archaeological deposits. The people using the cave instead chose grasses growing relatively close to its entrance.
"The phytoliths found at Cloggs Cave were from different parts of grass plants such as stems, leaves, flowers and roots, indicating that whole grasses were brought in, including the inedible parts," said Grono.
Evidence of Ritual Burning Across Millennia
As much as 18% of the phytoliths showed signs of burning or melting. Those altered plant remains occurred throughout the dated deposits, suggesting that people repeatedly carried vegetation into the cave and burned it there across the span of the past 25,000 years.
The finding fits with other archaeological evidence indicating that Cloggs Cave was a place of long-lasting ritual activity rather than an ordinary living site.
Professor Bruno David from Monash University, who co-led the excavations with GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, concludes that "their burning is consistent with GunaiKurnai traditional practices of using ash to perform magic and rituals, and also to track the footsteps of anyone coming in, including spirit-Beings. Other macro-botanical evidence, such as fat-smeared, trimmed wooden sticks from Casuarina trees, was also found in deeper and older deposits, indicating that other kinds of rituals using woody plants were also performed."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Elle Grono, Bruno David, Russell Mullett, Janelle Stevenson, Fiona Petchey, Jean-Jacques Delannoy, Matthew C. McDowell, Declan J. Miller, Mike W. Morley, Joanna Fresløv, Dylan Jenkin. Phytoliths from Cloggs Cave, GunaiKurnai country (southeastern Australia) reveal the gathering of whole grasses for burning practices inside the cave. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 2026; 5 DOI: 10.3389/fearc.2026.1871928

Bonnie Blue’s baby outrage – and the dangers of our extreme attention economy | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:43:09 UTC
23:43:09 KST

Bonnie Blue has made millions of pounds by having sex with thousands of men. I suppose that last part isn’t particularly unusual for a sex worker; it’s basically the job description. But Blue has reached an unusual level of fame for the profession through grotesque stunts such as having sex with 1,057 men in 12 hours and preying on young men with “barely legal” content and university “bang bus” tours. She’s notorious enough that she was the subject of a Channel 4 documentary last year.
In short, Blue (real name: Tia Billinger), possesses two of the most important qualities for financial success in the modern world: shamelessness and a keen understanding that you’ve often got to go to extremes to cut through in today’s attention economy. She is exploiting the idea that it is profitable to “enrage to engage”: the business model baked into every social media algorithm.
Now it seems that Blue, who gave birth to her first child (father unconfirmed) last month, is carrying that enrage-to-engage ethos into motherhood. She has been sharing postpartum content with her subscribers and recently escalated to posting a video where she is holding a baby and is surrounded by men in balaclavas while promoting her sexual content. It is unclear if it’s actually her baby or a doll in the video but, either way, it’s disturbing. So much so that it’s even got me agreeing with the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, for perhaps the first time ever. Speaking to Sky News last week, Badenoch said that the video was a “safeguarding issue”. She added that while it is tempting to ignore the whole disgusting affair, doing so risks “normalising babies in porn adverts”.
In response, Blue sent Sky News a statement insisting “my baby is loved, protected, and incredibly well cared for”. Blue may love her baby but there is obviously nothing protective about using your child to entice people to watch you perform sexual acts. Clearly there should be an investigation into this child’s welfare.
While she has taken it to a dangerous extreme, Blue isn’t the only parent to be recklessly using their child as a prop on social media to make a buck. There are endless family influencers who share intimate details of their kids’ lives and splash their images all over the internet without their informed consent. Then there are all the budding “momagers” who run Instagram accounts for their young girls, hoping it will lead to a modelling or influencer career down the line. In 2024, the New York Times analysed 5,000 mum-run accounts of young girls and found that while “men accounted for about 35% of the audience overall”, many large accounts with “more than 100,000 followers had a male audience of over 75%”.
The NYT also documented many instances of grown men sending explicit messages to these underage accounts or reposting pictures, with “even some egregious violations [leading] to no action by Meta”. Which isn’t surprising when you look at the company’s history. In a July 2020 internal chat, which was made public in court documents, one employee asked what the company was doing about child grooming. Another replied: “Child safety is an explicit non-goal this half.” Gotta concentrate on ramping up profits so Mark Zuckerberg can build a bigger bunker! Instagram has since instituted more content guardrails for child safety but still faces questions about whether it could do more.
Blue is obviously incredibly problematic. But the broader problem here is that the digital economy, with its warped incentive structures, rewards this sort of depraved and extreme behaviour. And while shamelessness can now be a lucrative career path, the traditional route to a comfortable middle-class life has been destroyed. The UK has seen more than a decade of wage stagnation while house prices and the cost of living have rocketed. The job market is grim, particularly for new graduates. AI, if it doesn’t kill us all, is going to make everything worse. It’s no wonder so many people want to be influencers, and no wonder so many people will chase online fame no matter how low they have to stoop to achieve it. Blue’s latest stunt is obscene, but so too is this brave new world the tech bros have forged. It feels as if we’re all screwed.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

How to Tell When Caregiver Stress Is Harming Your Health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:40:35 UTC
23:40:35 KST

Sue Ryan had been her husband’s sole caregiver for just under five years before her facade of keeping it all together first began to crack. It was a long time coming. She’d spent countless nights up late correcting mistakes in the household finances—a task her husband had handled before Alzheimer’s disease made it difficult. She no longer went to the gym, or on walks, or to her own medical appointments. She waved away every offer of help with some version of No, no, I’ve got this.
So when Ryan watched the potato chip fall from her husband’s lunch plate, she felt a flash of anger: I’ve been doing all these things for you. You can’t even keep a potato chip on your plate?
She didn’t say it. She gave him more chips, told him, “Honey, I’ll be right back,” and retreated to the bathroom, where she sat down and began to shake. “Oh my gracious,” she remembers thinking. “What just happened?”
Ryan, who has spent 40 years caring for various family members and co-founded the caregiver-support organization The Caregiver’s Journey, had been sacrificing pieces of her own life without tallying the toll. “I didn’t realize the impact of giving up a little bit here, shaving this off, shaving that off,” she says.
Caregiver stress can have serious consequences for physical and mental health. It’s associated with anxiety, depression, sleep problems, mood disorders, and burnout, says Dr. Aditi Nerurkar, a stress expert and lecturer in the division of global health and social medicine at Harvard Medical School.
But how can you tell when caregiving is starting to take a toll on your health—and what can you do?
Pay attention to what’s changed
The clearest warning sign isn’t one terrible day or week—it’s a pattern. Are you regularly struggling to fall asleep, barely eating (or wolfing down five doughnuts a day), snapping at people you love, or unable to focus on the novels you once loved? Maybe you’ve stopped calling friends because you don’t have the bandwidth for chit-chat.
What matters is whether these changes have become “consistent and persistent,” says Diane Mariani, a licensed clinical social worker and director of Caring for Caregivers at Rush University Medical Center. Your friends and family members might notice them first. If they tell you that you don’t seem like yourself, resist the automatic “I’m fine” and seriously consider what they’re seeing.
Poor sleep deserves particular attention. Even when Ryan slept, she says, she didn’t truly rest. It felt like she always had “one eye half open,” waiting for the next problem. “There’s a layer of stress even when you think, ‘I’ve got this,’” she says. “You’re waiting for the other shoe to drop.”
Notice when your own medical care has become optional
Caregivers often postpone their own screenings, brush off symptoms they would normally get checked out, or let chronic conditions go unmanaged.
“You keep pushing things out,” Mariani says. Perhaps you cancel a mammogram because your loved one is in the hospital, or you don’t have anyone who can stay with them while you’re away. Next thing you know, you’re a year overdue.
Caregiving also disrupts the habits that help people stay healthy. “What we hear a lot from caregivers is the change in their sleeping, eating, and even exercise,” Mariani says. Over time, poor sleep and chronic stress can affect blood pressure and immune function, she adds, while missed appointments make it harder to catch new problems or manage existing ones.
That doesn’t mean every headache, stomachache, or other symptom is caused by caregiving stress. New, persistent, or concerning symptoms need medical evaluation. Mariani and her colleagues routinely ask caregivers whether they have a primary-care doctor and when they last saw them. If you can’t remember the answer—or you’ve repeatedly canceled your own care—that’s a warning sign.
As Nerurkar puts it, caregivers often land “at the bottom of that to-do list—and often they’re not even on the list.”
Don’t mistake suffering for resilience
Caregivers often de-prioritize their own health because they believe that’s what a strong, loving person does. If the situation feels unbearable, they might decide they simply need to become more resilient.
Nerurkar calls this “toxic resilience”: a mind-over-matter approach built around “productivity at all costs, ‘all systems go’ all the time.”
Real resilience accounts for human limits and the brain’s need for rest and recovery. “It is a myth, categorically untrue, that people who are resilient cannot get burned out,” she says. “They can and they do.”
Guilt can reinforce the same pattern. A spouse may have promised years ago never to move their partner into a care facility. An adult child might believe they’re responsible for managing everything alone. In some families and cultures, that responsibility traditionally falls to one person, often the oldest daughter.
Ryan calls some of these commitments “promises you’re not meant to keep.” They’re made out of love, before anyone knows what a serious illness will eventually require. “It becomes, ‘I should take care of him. I promised him I would do this. I’m not going to go back on a promise,’” she says.
Ryan once made a promise like that. But she ultimately moved her husband into a care community because his dementia had progressed, and he needed more social interaction than she could provide at home. It was, she says, “the wisest choice for his lifestyle, and his safety and mine.”
Identify what needs to change
Mariani suspects that most caregivers can already tell when a situation has become unsustainable. “I think most caregivers do kind of know,” she says. “They just don’t know the solution.”
Ask yourself: “If nothing changes, can I continue living this way for another three or six months?” Then identify which part is wearing you down most. Is it getting up four times a night? Managing medications you don’t understand? Never being able to leave the house? Handling every appointment while your siblings offer advice from several states away?
“I took this on. I want to do this. This is meaningful for me,” caregivers often tell Mariani. “I just don’t know if I can sustain it.”
That’s why she avoids lecturing people about “self-care.” To someone who’s already overwhelmed, it can sound like “another task for their long list,” she says—or another reminder that they’re still not doing enough.
Instead, Mariani asks: “What’s something you would like to have time for?”
Maybe you miss your morning walk or reading before bed. Start there, and figure out what would have to change to bring it back. If you can’t walk because your loved one can’t be left alone, ask someone to stay with them for 30 minutes. If you keep missing your own appointment because you’re responsible for your parent’s transportation, ask a relative to drive them.
Try: “I want to keep doing this, but I can’t sustain it exactly as it is. Could you handle the grocery shopping for the next few weeks?” Or: “Could you stay with Mom on Tuesday so I can make it to my appointment?”
But it’s easier said than done, and our society doesn’t currently provide enough support for caregivers, experts argue.
Give every offer of help a job
Before the potato-chip incident, Ryan routinely—and politely—turned down friends who offered to lend a hand. “I can lie to myself, and I can believe it,” she says. Her best friend, Lynn, was less convinced. After Ryan told her what had happened, she asked Lynn to become an accountability partner—a person who could tell her when she was taking on more than she could handle.
Ryan also wrote a list of what someone could do if they had five minutes, 10 minutes, half an hour, two hours, half a day, or overnight. Then she contacted people who had previously offered to help and asked what they would be willing to take on.
The tasks don’t have to involve hands-on care. Someone could pick up groceries, schedule appointments, call the insurance company, bring over dinner, research respite-care programs, or sit with your loved one while you leave the house.
If you’re supporting a caregiver, offer something specific: “I’m going to the grocery store tomorrow—send me your list.” “I can take Dad to his appointment Thursday.” “I’ll stay with Mom while you get your mammogram.”
If the person you want to help resists, Mariani suggests telling them: “I really care about you, and it would mean a lot to me if I could do something for you.” Then offer a task instead of asking them to invent one.
One thing to avoid: dispensing advice from the sidelines. Caregivers often hear some version of “Why don’t you…” or “Have you tried…” from people who don’t understand their daily reality. “You don’t know, because you’re not here,” Mariani says. Start by listening.
Bring in professional support
If you’re dealing with ongoing changes to your sleep, mood, appetite, relationships, or overall health, contact your primary-care doctor and let them know you’re a caregiver. Don’t dismiss new physical symptoms as “just stress,” or assume a worsening health problem will improve once life settles down.
Ask the health system treating your loved one whether it offers caregiver specialists, social workers, counseling, or support groups. Local and condition-specific organizations may also provide respite care, meal delivery, transportation, or in-home assistance.
Support groups can be particularly useful because “everybody gets it,” Mariani says. Caregivers can trade practical advice without having to explain why an outsider-supplied solution won’t work.
If researching resources feels like one responsibility too many, hand that job to someone who keeps asking how they can help: “Find out what caregiver support is available through Mom’s hospital, and send me the three best options.”
Accepting help ultimately benefited both Ryan and her husband. He was highly social, and when friends stopped by, he got more company and stimulation. Ryan, meanwhile, stopped reflexively turning everyone away.
“I went from, No, I got this, to yes,” she says. “People wanted to lean in. They wanted to help. I got out of my own way.”

Philosophy for an Ending World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

Samuel Scheffler’s well-known Death and Afterlife (2013) invites us to consider whether, knowing that human extinction is immanent due to wide-spread infertility, we can continue to find many of the projects and activities that animate our lives to still be meaningful. His answer is that we cannot: too many of our projects and activities make sense to us as worth pursuing because they aim at things that matter. But much of what we take to matter tacitly assumes that humanity will continue into the indefinite future. Scheffler’s conjecture is that knowledge of humanity’s immanent extinction would undermine our confidence that there are things that matter and we would collectively lapse into a state of anomie and despair.
The insight that animates Tim Mulgan’s exciting and carefully argued new book, Philosophy for an Ending World, is that a small change to Scheffler’s thought experiment brings into view a new series of challenging questions that reward philosophical exploration. What he proposes is that we consider the implications of knowing that, due to a cataclysmic event many light years from earth, human extinction (and the extinction of all life on earth) is certain but not immanent. Humanity can count on another two centuries before its story comes to an end. Despair and anomie might still be apt responses to the reality of this post-cataclysm world. But there are other plausible ways of responding to it that are live possibilities because there is time to adapt to the loss of future-dependent meaning.
Mulgan introduces the range of plausible ways of thinking about the significance of the cataclysm through a debate between the various positions. In these early chapters we meet, amongst others, the character of the Perennial Pessimist, who holds that life has always been meaningless and is inclined to embrace anti-natalism; the Presentist, who accepts that the cataclysm robs humanity of some ways of living that can give life meaning, but believes that there remain a sufficient number of goods available to be pursued in life that do not presuppose humanity’s continuing into the indefinite future to make life meaningful; the Post-Cataclysmic Pessimist, who holds that knowing that extinction is on the horizon, even if it is still a way off, undermines the possibility of leading a meaningful life, given our current conceptual repertoire for how one might lead a meaningful life; and finally, the multigenerationalist.
The core of the book is an extended argument for multigenerationalism. The view agrees with the Post-Cataclysmic Pessimist in holding, against the Presentist, that meaningful lives are not possible if the kinds of goals, projects, and activities that constitute leading a meaningful life are completely severed from any connection to future people. Not all goals and projects are, of course, multi-generational in character in the way that, say, curing cancer is a multi-generational project. But even present-focused activities get their point from intergenerational traditions in which they are embedded. Multigenerationalism insists, however, that we need not wallow is pessimism because the possibility of meaningful lives need not come to an end because we know extinction is on the horizon. For though leading meaningful lives requires intergenerational sources of meaning, it is both possible and feasible to reorient these sources in a way that frees them from the assumption that humanity will continue indefinitely. That is, meaningful lives are possible post-cataclysm if we develop intergenerational, time-limited projects of the kind that living meaningful lives requires.
Crucially, these new intergenerational projects must be able to sustain meaningful lives for even the last generation of humans. The multigenerationalist claim is that living meaningful lives requires participating, either directly or indirectly, in intergenerational projects and traditions. For this reason, one might think that, in fact, procreation is not permissible after the cataclysm. If procreation is allowed to continue, there will be a last generation that do not have the possibility of leading meaningful lives. Arguably, producing that generation is impermissible. But once this is granted, we quickly reach the conclusion that procreation is impermissible after the cataclysm, on pain of participating in an intergenerational Ponzi scheme. But if procreation is impermissible after the cataclysm, it follows that it also marks the end of people being able to lead meaningful lives.
Three of the book’s central chapters, on procreative ethics, argue that both consequentialist and non-consequentialist approaches to theorizing permissible procreation concur that we need not accept this conclusion. Procreation is permissible if multi-generational projects that support intergenerational meaning are feasible. To respect the constraints that Mulgan uncovers through his nuanced discussion of procreative ethics, suitable projects must involve intergenerational co-operation, allow future people the hope of a flourishing life that are hopefully better, and at the very least, not worse than that enjoyed by past generations, and allow the last generation to find meaning in the fact that they are contributing to a co-operative project of bringing the history of humanity to a fitting end.
A consequence of the constraints on permissible post-cataclysm procreation is the need for moral progress and transformation. The values and moral outlook we now have are poorly suited to enable humanity to cope with extinction because they presuppose humanity continuing into the indefinite future. Simply bequeathing them to the next generations is not, therefore, compatible with the constraint that we do our best to ensure their lives are at least as good, if not better, than the ones past generations have enjoyed. If the history of humanity is to be continued for the next two centuries before it comes to an end, different values will need to be taken up, values that are better adapted to navigating the changed circumstances of knowing that humanity will come to an end in the next two centuries. We cannot know what these values will look like from our current vantage point.
Uncovering these new or adapted values is an exercise in intergenerational moral creativity and imaginativeness. That a successful reimagining or moral transformation of this kind is in fact possible is illustrated, as Mulgan sees it, by the example of the Crow Indian Chief Plenty Coups, as portrayed by Jonathan Lear in his Radical Hope (2006). As Lear describes him, Plenty Coups was confronted with the task of leading the Crow through a period of cultural devastation in which the way of life presupposed by their values disappeared. Exercising a kind of imaginative courage, Plenty Coups drew on Crow teachings and traditions to transform Crow morality, reimagining what, for example, a good Crow life that exemplified the virtue of courage could be like under a radically changed circumstances in which the Crow no longer engaged in war. The permissible continuation of humanity after the cataclysm requires an intergenerational commitment to a similar imaginative moral transformation. Given the scale of what is involved, it cannot be successfully realized within a single generation.
What I have covered here are just some of the main ideas of Philosophy for an Ending World. There is a lot more in it. I have, for example, skipped over the very interesting discussions of religion, of whether the best way to ensure the flourishing of the last generations is for them to upload their consciousness into a virtual world, and of the kind of utopia towards whose realization by the last generation some multigenerational projects might aim. That Mulgan covers so much ground is both a strength and weakness of the book. It is a strength in that it exhibits the fecundity of the slowly ending world thought experiment.
But it is also a weakness, in two respects. First, because it covers so much ground and at times engages with recent work on, for, example, procreative ethics in great detail, it is likely to be off-putting for non-academic readers. Given the importance of its subject, that is to be regretted. As Mulgan points out at the end of the book, even if one doubts that humanity is on the precipice of extinction, it is easy to believe that the possible futures for our descendants will be radically different than anything humanity has experienced and that is all one need accept to find the questions Mulgan pursues in this book to be important. A much shorter version of it that just presented a broad overview of these questions and the complexity involved in thinking through them would certainly find a wider audience.
Second, the scope of coverage comes at the cost of certain key premises of the book’s overall argument being insufficiently defended. For example, the case for the importance of intergenerational meaning seemed to me to call for a more extended defense than it receives. Some of what I take to be meaningful in life, such as the exploration of philosophical ideas, is in part meaningful because I am participating in a venerable tradition that will continue after I am gone. But I don’t see why I should find it less meaningful if I knew the tradition would soon come to an end. Why isn’t it enough for me to feel that I am participating in a meaningful activity whose meaning transcends me that there are at least still some others who value philosophical inquiry as I do?
I would have also welcomed some discussion of the idea of ‘bringing the story of humanity to a fitting end.’ The idea that the cataclysm makes salient humanity and its history as something that enters our consciousness as an object of evaluative concern has a great deal of intuitive plausibility. But what it is that is of concern is ill-defined, in a way that invites skepticism that the appearance of plausibility can survive scrutiny. Some discussion of whether humanity and its history is in fact a defensible object of concern would have been welcome and is something hopefully we will hear more about from Mulgan and others working in this area.
REFERENCES
Lear, Jonathan (2006). Radical hope: ethics in the face of cultural devastation. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.
Scheffler, Samuel (2013). Death and the Afterlife. Edited by Niko Kolodny. New York, NY: Oxford University Press.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday slammed the Supreme Court after it declined to allow the US Postal Service to enforce a rule putting tighter restrictions on mail-in ballots before November’s closely watched midterm elections.
"This Supreme Court is bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left into making decisions that have set America back at least a hundred years," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

The Trump administration says the rules are necessary to fight voter fraud.

The Perils of Mind-Reading in the Taiwan Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:39:00 UTC
23:39:00 KST

Less than two weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s high-stakes visit to Washington, Beijing reportedly threatened to cancel the planned summit with U.S. President Donald Trump if the United States approved further arms sales to Taiwan. Despite the White House’s silence on arms sales, its top envoy to Taipei last week called securing peace in the Taiwan Strait “one of its top priorities” for the United States.
Beneath this routine exchange of rhetoric lies a persistent problem: For all the attention Beijing and Washington devote to Taiwan, sustained communication over the issue remains thin. With both sides heralding their own version of strategic ambiguity, much of what passes for communication instead takes place at arm’s length – through public statements, arms sales, military deployments, and exercises. Consequently, strategic mind-reading has become a routine part of the relationship.
But constant guessing can harden assumptions more than sharpen judgment, creating precisely the kind of miscalculation that pushes a crisis toward conflict. For all their differences, neither Beijing nor Washington is immune to the risk.
Beijing would seem to have an advantage in the mind-reading game. Unlike China, the United States exposes much of its internal friction in public: issues like defense spending, weapons stocks, and industrial buildout are openly debated and scrutinized. Washington’s apparent difficulty in mobilizing resources and coordinating allied efforts over Ukraine and Iran, set against increasingly fractured domestic politics, can easily be read as evidence of American power in decline.
That perception has likely fed into Beijing’s calculations over Taiwan, where one of the hardest questions is not whether the United States has the capability to intervene, but whether it would do so quickly enough to shape the course of a crisis. Chinese strategists may therefore be tempted to treat signs of American political dysfunction and mobilization delays as evidence against timely U.S. intervention. Already, China’s leading government advisers have highlighted the practical obstacles to timely U.S. intervention, from defense-production bottlenecks exposed by the war in Ukraine to Washington’s reliance on allied bases and logistical support.
But precedent shows such readings can be dangerously incomplete. During the 1995-96 Taiwan Strait crisis, Beijing reportedly interpreted Washington’s restrained response to earlier Chinese military exercises as evidence that the United States would limit itself to diplomatic protest. Instead, as tensions escalated, the Clinton administration sharply raised the stakes by deploying two carrier battle groups toward Taiwan, reportedly catching Beijing by surprise.
Those in Beijing who doubt Washington’s willingness to intervene may take further confidence from China’s growing military advantages close to home. But the broader warning still applies: familiar patterns of American restraint can become unreliable guides once a crisis changes the political stakes. If Beijing mistakes visible constraints on American power for a reliable forecast of U.S. behavior over Taiwan, it could overestimate how much room remains for coercion before provoking an unexpected response.
Information asymmetry leaves Washington at least as dependent on mind-reading. The search for a Chinese “timeline” on seizing Taiwan has become something of a cottage industry. Some assessments have focused on 2027, when Xi has instructed the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to meet important modernization goals; others now look to Taiwan’s 2028 election cycle; still others have inferred a much longer horizon from Beijing’s linkage of unification with “national rejuvenation,” a goal associated with 2049. The proliferation of competing dates reveals how uncertain outsiders are about the logic that actually drives Beijing’s decisions on Taiwan.
That uncertainty naturally pushes Washington toward what it can observe. Chinese military activity around Taiwan offers an obvious proxy: the frequency and scale of drills and patrols are all being scrutinized for clues about Beijing’s intentions. Yet those signals are becoming harder, not easier, to interpret as China normalizes a higher tempo of military activity around the island. The same exercise can function at once as coercive signaling, contingency preparation, and rehearsal for operations Beijing may – or may not – someday choose to execute.
The result is an uncomfortable ambiguity. More intensive PLA activity does not necessarily signal a decision to use force, while routine activity may mask a meaningful change in intent. As once exceptional behavior becomes normalized, Washington risks misreading signals in both directions: seeing imminent action where there is only coercion, or dismissing a real shift in Beijing’s intentions as just another exercise.
The greater danger is that these two forms of misreading can reinforce each other in a crisis. If Beijing expects Washington to respond slowly, it may push coercion further in the belief that there is still room to maneuver. Washington, seeing a sharper escalation than expected, may interpret it as evidence that Beijing has already crossed a political threshold and respond more forcefully. That response, in turn, could convince Beijing that U.S. intervention is becoming imminent, narrowing the space for restraint on both sides.
The next crisis would leave little time to sort signal from intent. That is why sustained political and military communication – now beginning to regain momentum amid renewed high-level engagement between Xi and Trump – should be pursued even in the absence of deeper strategic trust, if only to strengthen deterrence and reduce the risk of miscalculation. Regular contact gives both sides a chance to explain what particular actions are meant to convey, learn how those actions are being received, and correct dangerous interpretations before they begin shaping the next move.
Beijing and Washington will continue to watch each other closely across the Taiwan Strait. They should also leave themselves a way to ask what they are actually seeing.
