Can the Houthis hold on to Yemen’s strategic western coast?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:28:31 UTC
23:28:31 KST

Can the Houthis hold on to Yemen’s strategic western coast?
Houthi coastal advances face hurdles: geography, local resistance and fierce government counterattacks.
Following rapid territorial gains on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, the Houthi movement’s ability to maintain control over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area now faces major military and logistical tests.
The military escalation, which has intensified over the past two and a half months, recently altered a map of control that had remained almost static for the past four years. But while Houthi forces have successfully pushed into coastal territories, seizing the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands and Mayyun Island, retaining these gains presents a deeply complex challenge.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands flee to Djibouti amid renewed Yemen fighting
- list 2 of 3Benchmark US government bond yield hits 19-year peak as oil prices surge
- list 3 of 3Saudi Arabia promises to respond to Houthi attacks ‘firmly’
Saeed Thabit, Al Jazeera’s bureau chief in Yemen, said that the group’s geographical achievements also bring with them immediate structural vulnerabilities.
“We are talking about an area extending from Hodeidah to Mocha and Bab al-Mandeb, in addition to the islands in the Red Sea,” Thabit said. “Securing this extension requires large forces and continuous supplies, especially since the open nature of the coast makes it easy for aircraft to monitor and target movements.”
This vast geographical hurdle was echoed by Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera’s Yemeni affairs editor.
“This is a very large area for fighting,” al-Shalafi said.
Ali al-Dahab, a military and security strategic affairs expert, told Al Jazeera that the group employs specific tactics to overcome this coastal exposure.
“The Houthis’ military doctrine is primarily based in guerilla warfare, and the necessary tactics related to adapting the terrain,” al-Dahab said. “They compensate for their weakness in the coastal areas by ascending to mountainous areas and controlling them, and setting up firing positions to defend these coastal areas.”
Attrition and counterattacks
To disrupt the Houthi hold on the coast, Saudi Arabia-backed Yemeni government forces have initiated a series of counteroffensives designed to stretch the group’s resources.
Recently, government-aligned forces reported destroying a Houthi military convoy on the al-Waziyah front and clashing with fighters on the outskirts of al-Mudaraba in Lahj province, an area adjacent to the Houthi-captured Dhubab district. Simultaneously, government forces struck Houthi positions and equipment in Dhubab and al-Khokha along the Red Sea coast.
“Government forces are able to reorganise their ranks and launch counterattacks, benefitting from air cover and their knowledge of the region,” Thabit told Al Jazeera. “These attacks may force the Houthis to distribute their forces between the coast, the islands and other fronts, which exhausts their capabilities and depletes their forces.”
Al-Shalafi said that government forces appeared to have shifted their operational tactics.
“[The Yemeni government is focused on] attacking the Houthi group in the Mocha and Bab al-Mandeb areas,” al-Shalafi said.
Al-Dahab explained that the Houthis attempt to absord these counterattacks through a ruthless deployment strategy, utilising local fighters before sending in their elite forces.
“They push the people of the regions who they are able to influence to the frontlines so that they can exhaust government capabilities, then after that they push forward their elite force,” al-Dahab said. “They always rely on the theory of ‘victory at any cost’, and they do not care about losses at all.”
Expanding fronts and local resistance
Faced with these counterattacks, the Houthis have attempted to alleviate pressure on the western coast by heavily escalating attacks on Marib and Lahj.
Lahj province serves as the primary northern and western gateway to the government’s interim capital of Aden, housing the historic al-Anad airbase just 60km (37 miles) away.
However, holding the newly acquired coastal areas involves more than just military deployment. Thabit highlighted the movement’s lack of societal integration in these specific territories compared with their northern strongholds.
“The Houthis do not have in these areas the social and security influence that they accumulated in their old areas of control, and they may face popular local resistance targeting their forces and supply routes,” Thabit noted.
Despite the lack of local influence, al-Dahab warned that the group’s coastal presence bolsters its logistical lifelines and smuggling networks.
“The outskirts of the Gulf of Aden and the southern Red Sea are now in direct contact with smuggling sources and non-state actors that supply them with weapons,” al-Dahab said.
The international flashpoint
Beyond local dynamics, the coastal advance has triggered significant international alarm. The Bab al-Mandeb strait has become an increasingly vital waterway for global energy shipments, particularly as the ongoing United States-Iran war causes major disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
This sensitivity has already drawn heavy regional military responses. The Saudi-led coalition recently promised a firm response to Houthi cross-border strikes, while the Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia launched 54 air raids across multiple governorates, including Taiz and Lahj, in a single 24-hour period.
Al-Shalafi emphasised the severe global economic implications of this specific theatre of war.
“You are facing a major economic crisis that the Houthi control over these areas could create,” al-Shalafi told Al Jazeera.
With international actors heavily invested in maritime security, Thabit warned that the group’s presence near the strait could trigger severe consequences.
“Regional and international powers are monitoring Houthi movements near this navigational corridor, and any threat to ships may prompt a broader military response,” Thabit stated. “Therefore, reaching these areas is one thing, and the ability to protect and retain them is another.”

JAKARTA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia is seeking an additional 26 billion to 27 billion U.S. dollars over the next five years to finance the transformation of its national health system and increase life expectancy, Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin said Tuesday.
Speaking at the fourth Indonesia Health Partners Meeting, Sadikin said the government aims to raise life expectancy to 76 years and healthy life expectancy to 65 years, in line with targets set by President Prabowo Subianto.
The health system transformation is estimated to require 223 billion dollars, with about 203 billion dollars already secured from the government and the health system. Of that amount, 177 billion dollars has been allocated to the transformation, leaving a funding gap of 26 billion to 27 billion dollars over the next five years, Sadikin said.
Indonesia is seeking to close the gap by strengthening cooperation with international development partners and philanthropic organizations.
"We are trying to build trust with our global partners and philanthropists," Sadikin said, noting that international cooperation has helped expand access to health technologies.
Recent initiatives include the distribution of about 300,000 anthropometric devices to community health posts, 10,000 ultrasound machines to health centers and X-ray machines for tuberculosis screening.
Indonesia is also deploying near point-of-care testing technology, providing free health checkups and expanding genomic testing as part of efforts to strengthen disease prevention and early detection. ■

He also urged African development finance institutions to increase project-preparation funding and provide financing instruments suited to first-of-a-kind projects, while calling on prospective buyers to turn non-binding interest into credible long-term offtake agreements.
South Africa has launched the first wave of six priority green hydrogen projects, the president said, noting that the Saldanha Bay electro-sustainable aviation fuel project led by Phelan Green Group has reached a final investment decision, with construction expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

World Insights: Canadian PM's "Super Week" turns strategic pivot to Europe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
22:27:13 CST
23:27:13 KST

TORONTO, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney kicked off an extraordinary week in transatlantic relations on Monday.
Carney inaugurated the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto to attract global capital and is set to travel to Europe to address the European Parliament and meet with British and French leaders.
These high-profile engagements coincide with the formal implementation of the 50 percent tariffs imposed by the United States on Canadian goods.
This series of events highlights Carney's strategy: boosting domestic economic resilience through foreign direct investment, defending national interests against U.S. tariffs, and deepening diplomatic and security ties with Europe to reduce Canada's long-standing reliance on the American market.
TAPPING ASIAN, EUROPEAN MARKETS
First announced in April, the Canada Investment Summit was designed to attract fresh capital for national infrastructure projects -- a cornerstone of Carney's strategy to expand economic links with non-U.S. partners.
Speaking on the summit's opening day, Carney described the gathering as part of a broader government roadmap aimed at bringing foreign capital into Canadian manufacturing while bolstering trade with Asia and Europe.
"Canada has immense opportunities in both Europe and Asia. And we have not fully realized our potential in these markets," Carney said.
The summit aims to mobilize 1 trillion Canadian dollars (about 726 billion U.S. dollars) in total investments over the next five years.
To pitch global investors with roughly 300 business leaders, including executives from the world's largest asset management firms, the Canadian government unveiled a catalog of priority projects spanning energy, critical minerals, advanced technologies and major infrastructure.
According to a prospectus disclosed by Canadian media, the package features more than 160 major projects across eight sectors, including 11 conventional energy projects, 31 clean energy projects, 63 mining and metals projects, among others.
Notable projects include a 35 billion-Canadian-dollar oil pipeline extending from Alberta to the Pacific coast and a 28.5 billion-Canadian-dollar liquefied natural gas project in British Columbia, and a 79 billion-Canadian-dollar expansion of the Port of Churchill on Hudson Bay.
"We are launching an investment super-cycle that this country needs," Carney said.
A report by TD Bank predicted that with the right government execution, Canada could enter an investment "super-cycle" lasting a decade or longer, driving job creation and lifting output per capita by 12,000 Canadian dollars.
SEEKING UNIQUE ALLIANCE WITH EUROPE
Following the summit in Toronto, Carney will depart for Europe on Tuesday for a three-day visit.
He is set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, and attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's State of the European Union address, the first non-European leader invited to such an event.
Carney will also hold his first bilateral meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool to discuss defense and security, energy transition, AI governance and critical minerals.
On Sunday, he will travel to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French archipelago south of the Canadian island of Newfoundland, to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron.
Carney and Macron will discuss deepening the Canada-France partnership in strategic sectors, including aerospace, energy and critical minerals, and advanced technologies such as quantum, satellites and supercomputing, according to a press release by Carney's office.
Canada will host the Canada-EU Summit on Oct. 29-30 to sustain momentum in trans-Atlantic cooperation, the office has announced earlier.
Although Carney clarified that Canada "is not seeking to join the European Union," the two sides are forging what officials describe as a "unique alliance."
At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney argued that the post-war international order had suffered a "rupture" and called on middle powers to form coalitions of overlapping interests. While his remarks sparked frictions with Washington, they resonated across Europe.
Canada achieved a significant breakthrough earlier this year by becoming the only non-European nation admitted to the EU's Security Action for Europe defense procurement framework, allowing Canadian defense contractors to bid directly on European rearmament contracts.
Carney's efforts to strengthen ties with Europe are gaining public support. According to an Abacus Data survey, conducted from Sept. 4 to 9, as many as 80 percent of Canadians say Canada should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU on foreign policy, defence and economic priorities.
"Now, Carney was accelerating Canada's pivot to Europe, matchmaking a shotgun marriage to offset the pain of its divorce with America. In effect, a threat to make Canada the 51st state is pushing America's northern neighbor so close to Europe that leaders have begun to half-in-jest dub it the EU's newest member," said the Wall Street Journal.
Trump's tariffs and policies toward NATO and Greenland have accelerated efforts by Canada and Europe to diversify their economic and security ties, the Associated Press (AP) reported, citing Ian Lesser of the German Marshall Fund in Brussels.
However, it warned that Carney is carrying to Europe a message that has won praise there but that European governments have been reluctant to follow: Middle powers should be willing to resist economic coercion and walk away from a bad deal.

MPs call for action over debanking of defence firms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:27:04 BST
23:27:04 KST

Defence companies are being refused bank accounts because of the sector they work in, and the practice should be brought to an end, according to a report by the Scottish Affairs Committee which describes the situation as unacceptable.
The committee heard during a private roundtable with small and medium-sized enterprises that defence businesses are often viewed by financial institutions as carrying reputational risk, and that one of the companies giving evidence had been debanked because of its connections to the sector.
Participants suggested defence businesses are treated as undesirable by some institutions and support bodies. The committee also heard of landlords who will not rent properties to defence companies.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, acknowledged the problem in oral evidence, telling the committee the department had seen examples of “good defence businesses supporting our national security” being debanked, which he said was “not acceptable in a time of increasing risk”. He expressed hope that financial institutions would increasingly support defence firms and ensure they have access to appropriate banking services.
The committee’s recommendation states: “It is unacceptable that SMEs working to deliver the UK’s national security objectives are being denied access to financial services through so-called ‘debanking’. The UK Government should assess the impact of this practice on Scotland’s defence industry and engage with the financial services sector to end this practice, which is damaging to the UK’s national security objectives, SME growth, and the provision of highly-skilled jobs in Scotland’s defence sector.”
The Scotland Office is asked to report back to the committee within six months on the findings of that work and the actions taken in response.
In its summary, the committee says it is “especially concerned by reports of defence businesses being denied access to banking services, which risks undermining investment and growth in the sector”.
Debanking sits within a broader section of the report on how the sector is regarded, which the committee found continues to affect recruitment and business sustainability.
Some witnesses expressed a view that Scottish Government policies have contributed to detrimental perceptions. The committee describes the sector’s negative public image as one of its most persistent barriers to recruitment.
On the government side, the report records plans for Destination Defence, a communications campaign intended to increase awareness of careers in the industry, which the department says is seeking to improve the sector’s reputation and attract new talent. John Howie of Babcock, who is involved through the Defence Industrial Council, drew a comparison with Destination Nuclear, which he said had increased applicant numbers by raising awareness of less visible roles.
The committee concludes that the Defence Industrial Strategy called for a public conversation on the importance of defence but that sufficient progress has not been made, and asks the government to set out in its response how it plans to deliver that conversation in Scotland.

LONDON, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Britain's unemployment rate for people aged 16 and over was estimated at 4.9 percent in the three months to July, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) on Tuesday.
The rate was up 0.2 percentage points from a year earlier but largely unchanged from the previous three-month period. The number of payrolled employees fell by 84,000, or 0.3 percent, year on year, and by 39,000, or 0.1 percent, from the previous quarter.
The data showed 3.9 percent annual growth in total earnings, including bonuses, in three months to July, down from 4.2 percent in the previous three-month period.
From June to August, the estimated number of job vacancies fell by 8,000 to 702,000, compared with the March-May period, the ONS said. Excluding the COVID-19 pandemic period, job vacancies were last at 702,000 or lower in the three months to October 2014.
Although the labor market remains broadly stable, payrolled employee numbers continued to edge down, with falls over the past year particularly evident in the retail and hospitality sectors, said ONS Director of Economic Statistics Liz McKeown.
"Vacancies remain at their lowest level outside the pandemic period for more than a decade, with smaller businesses continuing to report that increased labor costs are affecting hiring decisions," she commented.
McKeown added that total pay growth has eased in recent months, with a notable difference between public- and private-sector pay growth. ■

No individuals have been charged or are under investigation, Telenor said in a stock exchange announcement.
The company said the investigations were a continuation of a long-standing dialogue with Norwegian prosecutors and that it had provided authorities with extensive documentation and information.
“Telenor will do its utmost to clarify the case to the extent possible,” the company said.
Telenor cites risks to employees
Telenor said conditions in Myanmar had become increasingly difficult after the military seized power in February 2021.
“Our employees risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty if the military authorities’ orders were not followed,” Telenor Chief Information Officer David Fidjeland said in a statement.
Telenor received a mobile licence in Myanmar in 2013 and began operations there in 2014.
The company later sold its Myanmar business after writing down the value of its investment by 6.5 billion Norwegian kroner ($700 million).
“This is a complex case that has also previously been investigated by the police. We will therefore let the police carry out their work and await the further process before commenting further,” Fidjeland said.
The investigations follow a parliamentary inquiry opened last year into Telenor’s operations in Myanmar around the time of the military coup.

South Africa secures $1 bn loan from BRICS bank
South Africa has secured a $1 billion loan from the BRICS-founded New Development Bank (NDB) to reform failing water, electricity and waste services across all eight of the country’s metropolitan municipalities, the National Treasury has announced.
In a statement released to the media on Tuesday, National Treasury said the loan would support the government-led Metro Trading Services Reform Programme, which focuses on improving the governance, financial sustainability and operational performance of municipal services.
The program covers key trading services including water and sanitation, electricity and energy, and solid waste management.
”The financing supports a government-led, performance-based reform program implemented through South Africa’s existing legal, fiscal and institutional framework,” Treasury said.
”This is a performance-based loan with financing linked to institutional strengthening and the achievement of independently verified measurable performance targets that are approved by metro councils for their trading service.”
Treasury added that NDB’s financing forms part of the government’s broader efforts to reform municipal trading services in metropolitan municipalities and offers favorable concessional financial terms. The financing would have a maturity period of 15 years, including a five-year grace period, with the interest rate linked to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR).
The concessional financing would help reduce the cost of funding the reforms while supporting metropolitan municipalities to strengthen the financial and operational performance of their trading services, according to the department.
The program applies to South Africa’s eight metropolitan municipalities: Buffalo City, Cape Town, Ekurhuleni, eThekwini, Johannesburg, Mangaung, Nelson Mandela Bay and Tshwane.
”The NDB loan was prepared in coordination with development partners active in South Africa’s infrastructure sector. National Treasury extends its appreciation to the NDB for its support to this government-led reform towards better services for residents and stronger, more sustainable cities.”

Is Greece’s Israel alignment risking its long-term security?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:22:00 UTC
23:22:00 KST

As Israel continues to expand its genocidal war on Palestinians from Gaza to the occupied West Bank, where illegal settlers have attacked both Christian and Muslim villages, Greece, a country whose priests have also faced attacks in Jerusalem, signed a major defence deal with Israel on August 31.
The Achilles Shield agreement, worth approximately €3 billion, will see Israel supply Greece, an EU member, with air-defence technology including David’s Sling, SPYDER and the BARAK MX system.
“This is the largest defense export deal in the history of Israel-Greece relations, and one of the largest in the history of the State of Israel,” Israel’s Ministry of Defence said in a statement. The ministry also cited “the extensive operational experience Israel's defense establishment has gained during the war” as part of the cooperation underpinning the agreement.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has portrayed the growing relationship between the two countries as part of his so-called “hexagon alliance”, extending from India to Greece, the Greek Cypriot Administration (GCA) in South Cyprus and Africa, and potentially encompassing breakaway regions such as Somaliland in the strategic Horn of Africa.
Experts see the Greece-Israel defence deal as both a significant development in its own right and an extension of the countries’ growing strategic cooperation.
“This should not be read as an ordinary arms purchase,” Oral Toga, a researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies, tells TRT World, referring to the Achilles Shield.
In April, both states also signed the PULS deal, a €650 million ($750 million) contract on missile systems.
“Greece is not buying a battery. It is buying the sensor, command and control layer. In other words, the nervous system of its future military,” says Toga.
Greek Defence Minister Nikos Dendias described the Achilles Shield as “a transition from a collection of weapons systems to a holistic deterrence system”, underscoring the extent of Athens’ growing defence cooperation with Israel.
“A non-NATO actor is acquiring decades of visibility into the airspace management of a NATO member state,” says Toga.
Greek designs
Dendias also signalled that Greece’s new ships and aircraft, equipped with Israeli systems, would no longer be confined to the narrow defence of the Aegean and would assume a broader deterrence role.
The shift has implications for the Aegean, where Türkiye maintains that several Greek islands must remain demilitarised under treaties governing their status.
“That is not a procurement statement. It is a doctrinal one. This is where the matter begins from Ankara's perspective. Turkey has a longstanding legal objection here based on the demilitarised status of the eastern Aegean islands under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and of the Dodecanese under the 1947 Paris treaties,” says Toga.
“The existence of Greek-Turkish problems is no secret. But the real question is not whether those problems get solved tomorrow. It is whether a third party (Israel) will slip through the cracks they open with an agenda of its own. The confrontation of the two NATO allies serves only those who want the alliance weakened.”
In March, following joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Greece deployed an American-made MIM-104 Patriot air-defence battery to the southeastern Aegean island of Karpathos, prompting a protest from Türkiye, which argued that the island should remain demilitarised under international law.
Following Türkiye’s objections, Greece relocated the air-defence system to Crete, easing tensions in the Aegean.
With Greece now acquiring Israeli air-defence and missile systems, the question could resurface over where “the components of this multi-layered architecture will actually be deployed,” says Toga.
He points to the possibility that Athens could deploy Israeli equipment on islands that Türkiye argues should remain demilitarised, potentially adding another layer of tension to longstanding disputes in the Aegean.
The recent acquisition of Israeli weapons systems is, in this sense, further evidence of deepening Greece-Israel cooperation extending from the Aegean to the gas-rich Eastern Mediterranean.
Greece, Israel and the Greek Cypriot Administration have also developed cooperation over energy resources and maritime arrangements in the region.
“Greece cannot find another partner capable of helping it offset Türkiye’s rapidly developing domestic defence industry,” Gokhan Batu, an expert on Israeli politics, tells TRT World.
In recent years, Ankara has significantly expanded its domestic defence industry, developing drones, aircraft and warships that have increasingly reached international markets. It has also moved to restore relations with Egypt, another key Eastern Mediterranean state.
Türkiye has strongly opposed Israel's actions in Gaza and its broader military policies across the region, including in Lebanon, Syria and Iran.
It has also sought to expand its regional diplomatic and security ties through a series of agreements, including the latest defence pact in Mecca with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
“What Greece and Israel share is their discomfort with Türkiye’s growing military capacity and strategic autonomy,” says Batu.
“The course of Türkiye-Israel ties and financial considerations are shaping Greek policy. Athens is concerned that it may struggle to find a sponsor for its maximalist policies in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean in the upcoming years.”
More risks for Greece
Greece and neighbouring Türkiye remain divided over longstanding disputes, including the status of Aegean islands, Cyprus, and other regional issues.
Yet rather than reaching a comprehensive settlement with Ankara, Athens has accelerated efforts to strengthen its ties with Israel, as relations between Israel and Türkiye have become increasingly strained.
Batu argues that the growing Greece-Israel partnership poses greater risks for Athens than for Israel, which, he says, has a history of leveraging relationships with other states to advance its strategic interests across regions stretching from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and the Gulf.
“Israel is not offering Greece any tangible security guarantees,” he says, referring to the two countries' defence agreements.
Batu warns that Israel has previously prioritised its own interests, even when doing so has conflicted with those of its partners, pointing to efforts to establish the US-backed Middle East Air Defense Alliance (MEAD) between Israel and Gulf states.
The initiative was intended to strengthen regional coordination against Iranian drones and missiles, with Israel playing a significant role in the proposed air-defence architecture.
Batu argues, however, that subsequent developments have exposed the limits of the security assurances such cooperation can provide Gulf states.
Although Iranian attacks on Israel ended after the US-Iran ceasefire in early April, countries across the Gulf, including Bahrain and the UAE — both of which have normalised relations with Israel — continue to face the threat of Iranian retaliation against US military bases in the region.
“Israel sought to develop a joint air-defence framework with the Gulf countries, yet it failed to provide a clear commitment concerning the defence of Gulf airspace.
“Moreover, despite this agreement and the wider rapprochement, Israel strongly opposed the UAE’s attempt to acquire F-35 fighter aircraft and lobbied against the sale,” says Batu.
“A similar issue can now be seen in the Achilles Shield project. The air-defence umbrella being provided to Greece still leaves Athens dependent on source codes controlled by Israel.
“The theatres and circumstances change, but Israel’s demands at the negotiating table and its way of doing business remain largely the same.”
Eastern Mediterranean: a critical arena
Experts say the most consequential effects of Greece-Israel cooperation could arise in the Eastern Mediterranean, an energy-rich region where both Türkiye and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) also have significant interests.
Greece has “a habit of developing ties with countries which have animosity towards Türkiye,” says Ismail Bozkurt, a leading Turkish Cypriot political analyst and former member of the TRNC presidential advisory council involved in negotiations with the Greek Cypriot Administration(GCA), to TRT World.
Israel, meanwhile, faces mounting constraints on its Middle East policy and is seeking partners such as Greece to expand its influence in the Eastern Mediterranean, Bozkurt says.
Cyprus occupies a particularly important position in this strategy, he adds, noting that some early Zionist figures had considered the island a potential site for Jewish settlement.
Since October 7, thousands of Israelis have reportedly moved to areas under GCA control in southern Cyprus, a development that has fuelled what Bozkurt describes as the Greek Cypriot population’s “growing concerns about Israelisation of the island.”
Bozkurt argues that Israel, Greece and the GCA are seeking to establish an energy corridor linking their interests in the Eastern Mediterranean, while failing to adequately account for Türkiye’s role as a guarantor power and the interests of Turkish Cypriots.
Before Türkiye began normalising relations with Egypt, Greece and the GCA sought to capitalise on tensions between Ankara and Cairo to deepen their Eastern Mediterranean cooperation with Israel. At the time, Israel was also in a stronger regional position following the signing of the Abraham Accords, which expanded its diplomatic ties with several Arab states.
“Today, the regional landscape is quite different. Türkiye’s relations with the US, the Gulf states and Egypt have improved on several fronts. At the same time, Israel’s regional gains from the Abraham Accords have suffered a serious setback since 7 October,” says Batu, adding that Ankara has also made substantial progress in several major defence projects.
As a result, while the potential risks posed by growing Greece-Israel cooperation across the Eastern Mediterranean, Syria and other areas should be “taken seriously”, Türkiye’s “confidence is not unfounded,” Batu says.

Five states and Union Territory of Delhi signed an agreement on the long-pending Kishau Project
NEW DELHI: Five states and Union Territory of Delhi on Tuesday signed an agreement on the long-pending Kishau Project, which is expected to regulate water availability in the wider Yamuna basin and increase flows downstream, benefitting the national capital and Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan in one way or another. The water stored in the Kishau reservoir will augment drinking water supply for Delhi.The Kishau multi-purpose project is a proposed dam and hydropower project on the Tons river, a major tributary of the river Yamuna, flowing along the border of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Besides supplying drinking water, the multi-purpose project will also provide irrigation water for 97,000 hectares of land in riparian states and generate 1,476 million units of hydroelectric power.The agreement was signed here by all six chief ministers in the presence of Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah, who said the Centre and the chief ministers of these six states/UTs of Yamuna basin are committed to complete the project at the earliest.Calling it a “historic agreement”, Shah said Delhi will be the biggest beneficiary of the project and it will also contribute to environmental conservation by ensuring environmental flow of river Yamuna.
Under the Kishau Multipurpose Project agreement, an around 232-metre-high concrete gravity dam will be constructed on Tons. It will have a water storage capacity of 1,562 million cubic metres.Shah said the Centre that declared the Kishau Multipurpose Project a “national project” will bear approximately 90% of its financial burden, while the remaining 10% will be borne by the participating states in accordance with the 1994 agreement.Shah, on the occasion, recalled the signing of several other agreements on water issues and said that the period from 2018 to 2026 will be remembered as a period in which almost all water disputes, from Kashmir to Uttar Pradesh, were resolved. The foundation for these resolutions was laid in meetings of the Zonal Councils and the Ministry of Jal Shakti efficiently took these agreements forward, he added.
Citing examples, Shah recalled that first, in August 2018, the dispute over the Lakhwar Multipurpose Project was resolved. In the same month, the dispute over Shahpur Kandi Dam Project was settled. In 2019, the dispute over Renukaji Multipurpose Dam Project in Upper Yamuna Basin was resolved. In 2021, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh reached an agreement on the Ken-Betwa Link Project, benefiting the water-stressed region of Bundelkhand, he added.The other projects in this league are the revised Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal River Link project in 2024; the scheme for transferring water from Hathnikund to the Yamuna through an underground pipeline in Feb 2024; resolving dispute over the rehabilitation of families displaced by the Narmada Project in July 2026; and settling the dispute over water sharing between Bihar and Jharkhand in the river Son Basin in Aug 2026.

He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Netanyahu’s plane to avoid JFK over fears Mamdani could disrupt New York visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:19:28 UTC
23:19:28 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s official aircraft will not land at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport when he travels to the United States next week for the UN General Assembly, ynet has learned, amid Israeli security concerns over a possible confrontation with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Security officials decided that the “Wing of Zion,” Israel’s official state aircraft, should avoid JFK because they fear Mamdani could seek to prevent it from remaining on the ground there throughout Netanyahu’s visit.
In previous years, allowing an official aircraft to remain at JFK for the duration of a leader’s visit was a privilege granted to the leaders of Israel and Iran.
Netanyahu’s visit is expected to take place under unusually stringent security arrangements. The U.S. Secret Service has significantly increased its involvement in protecting the prime minister and is expected to accompany him from the moment he lands until his departure.
Protests are planned outside Netanyahu’s hotel and near the United Nations during his address, while Jewish groups are organizing demonstrations in support of the Israeli prime minister.
Mamdani, who previously said he would seek Netanyahu’s arrest before later backing away from that position, has encouraged New Yorkers to protest the prime minister’s visit.
That creates an unusual situation in which the mayor is publicly encouraging demonstrations against Netanyahu while the NYPD, which operates under the city administration, will also take part in securing the visit.
With JFK ruled out, Israeli officials are examining alternatives including Newark Liberty International Airport in neighboring New Jersey or a nearby military airfield.
Either option would allow the “Wing of Zion” to remain parked throughout Netanyahu’s stay in the New York area.
Netanyahu is expected to arrive in the United States on Wednesday, Sept. 23, around midday. His address to the UN General Assembly is scheduled for Thursday, Sept. 24, at 2 p.m. New York time, 9 p.m. in Israel.
Israeli officials are preparing for possible protests inside the General Assembly hall, including delegates demonstratively walking out during Netanyahu’s speech or attempting to interrupt him.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet U.S. President Donald Trump during the trip because Trump is due to leave New York before the Israeli prime minister arrives, although several meetings with other world leaders remain possible.
Under the current schedule, Netanyahu is expected to leave the United States on Thursday night in order to return to Israel before the start of Sukkot.

The Cabinet of Ministers plans to increase the minimum wage by 900 hryvnias next year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:17:15 EEST
23:17:15 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers plans to increase the minimum wage by 900 hryvnias next year
Kyiv • UNN
The government plans to raise the minimum wage to 9,546 hryvnias from 2027. The subsistence minimum for one person will be 3,559 hryvnias.
In the draft state budget for 2027, the Cabinet of Ministers plans to set the minimum wage at 9,546 hryvnias, which is 899 hryvnias more than this year. MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported this, according to UNN.
The minimum wage from January 1, 2027, is planned at 9,546 hryvnias (+899 hryvnias)
Zhelezniak also reported that the subsistence minimum per person will amount to 3,559 hryvnias per month from January 1, 2027 (+350 UAH, +10.9%).
For able-bodied persons – 3,691 hryvnias; for persons unable to work – 2,878 hryvnias.
It should be noted that from January 1, 2026, the minimum wage in Ukraine is set at 8,647 hryvnias, while the hourly rate is 52 hryvnias.
Also, from January 1, 2026, the subsistence minimum per person per month is 3,209 hryvnias, while for the main social and demographic groups of the population:
-  children under 6 years of age - 2,817 hryvnias; 
-  children aged 6 to 18 years - 3,512 hryvnias; 
-  able-bodied persons - 3,328 hryvnias; 
-  persons who have lost their ability to work - 2,595 hryvnias; 
-  persons who have lost their ability to work, which is applied to determine the amount of additional payment for residence in areas contaminated by radioactive pollution pursuant to court decisions, - 1,600 hryvnias. 
For able-bodied persons, which is applied to determine the basic amount of the official salary of a judge, the official salary of a prosecutor of a district prosecutor's office, the official salaries of employees of other state bodies whose remuneration is regulated by special laws, as well as employees of tax and customs authorities, - at the level established for the respective state body as of December 31, 2025.
The subsistence minimum is the monetary value of a set of food products sufficient to ensure the normal functioning of the human body and preserve its health, as well as the minimum set of non-food products and the minimum set of services necessary to meet a person's basic social and cultural needs.
The subsistence minimum is used for:
-  a general assessment of the standard of living in Ukraine, which serves as the basis for implementing social policy and developing individual state social programs; 
-  establishing the amounts of the minimum wage and the minimum old-age pension, determining the amounts of social assistance, assistance to families with children, unemployment benefits, as well as scholarships and other social payments based on the requirements of the Constitution of Ukraine and the laws of Ukraine; 
-  determining the right to receive social assistance; 
-  determining state social guarantees and service standards and provision in the areas of healthcare, education, social services and others; 
-  establishing the tax-free minimum income of citizens; 
-  forming the state budget and local budgets. 
The subsistence minimum also affects the amount of the minimum pension, which is calculated based on the subsistence minimum for persons who have lost their ability to work; that is, the minimum pension this year will be 2,878 hryvnias.
In June, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a bill that forms part of Ukraine's commitments to strengthening the rule of law and cleansing the judiciary of unscrupulous elements. In addition to introducing new rules for vetting judges, the document establishes that a judge's salary is calculated only on the basis of the full subsistence minimum.

Trump lashes out at US Supreme Court justices after ballot ruling

Trump slams ‘horrible’ Supreme Court mail-in ballot ruling
- President Trump criticised the Supreme Court for blocking his plan to restrict mail-in voting, calling the decision “horrible” and accusing justices of yielding to Democrats.
- The court ruled that states need more time to implement changes before the November elections, with most conservative justices agreeing and only two dissenting.
- Trump baselessly claimed mail-in voting enables fraud, despite its global use and security, and warned this ruling harms Republicans ahead of crucial midterm elections.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump assailed the Supreme Court on Sept 15 after it denied his request to lift an order halting his divisive plan to restrict mail-in voting, accusing the court of allowing itself to be cowed by Democrats.
“Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America,” he posted on his Truth Social network, calling the decision “horrible” and “highly political”.
Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting, ahead of midterm elections in November, saying without evidence that it is vulnerable to fraud. The order quickly prompted multiple legal challenges.
Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that, under the US Constitution, states – and not the federal government – retain broad control over the administration of elections.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a concurring opinion with the majority, said late on Sept 14 Trump’s plan may ultimately be legal in the long run, but “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”
Only two of the six conservative justices on the nine-member panel offered a dissent.
Trump claimed baselessly that the US mail voting system, which is secure and has no significant problem with fraud, was a “laughing stock all over the World”, and lamented that the United States was “the only country that has to endure such a Nation Destroying SCAM”.
More than 30 countries worldwide offer citizens the opportunity to vote using a mail-in ballot.
“It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats’, on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do. And now they have an open field to do so! The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!” said Trump.
Trump has repeatedly denounced mail-in voting as corrupt while using it himself, including to vote in Florida’s Republican primary in August.
The fight, alongside disputes over partisan redistricting in around a dozen states, comes with high political stakes ahead of the Nov 3 elections.
Republicans hold narrow congressional majorities, but Democrats are favoured to capture the House and possibly the Senate as Trump’s approval ratings remain weak and voters voice frustration over living costs and the continuing war with Iran. AFP

UN accepts Trump nominee to head World Food Programme
GENEVA, Sept 15 - United Nations chief Antonio Guterres has accepted Trump nominee Luke Lindberg from among dozens of candidates to lead the World Food Programme, a document showed and a U.N. official confirmed on Tuesday.
• Lindberg, a senior U.S. agricultural official, was recommended by Guterres and Qu Dongyu, a Chinese national heading the Food and Agriculture Organization, according to a September 11 letter to the head of the WFP board.
• Some 54 candidates applied for the job, according to the letter, which did not name them. Nine were shortlisted.
• U.N. spokesperson Farhan Haq confirmed to Reuters that the organisation had accepted a recommendation for the role from a hiring panel, transmitted that recommendation to the WFP, and was waiting for the board's response.
• A U.N. official said the nomination, first reported by Devex, was expected to be confirmed by the WFP board on Friday.
• The White House and State Department had no immediate comment.
• Nearly 300 million people face crisis levels of hunger this year, the WFP says, with the Iran war exacerbating the situation.
• The World Food Programme, established as a joint project of the U.N. and the FAO, is aimed at providing an emergency response to global food shortages.
• Despite cuts by U.S. President Donald Trump, the U.S. remains the WFP's biggest donor, and it has traditionally been led by an American from the Republican party.
• Some U.S. donations to the Rome-based agency are in-kind or specify that food must be of U.S. origin, which also provides support for U.S. agricultural businesses. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Health secretary says plans for cot cams in baby wards being developed ‘urgently’ after Lucy Letby inquiry report – latest updates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:16:26 UTC
23:16:26 KST

Health secretary says plans for cot cams in baby wards being developed ‘urgently’ after Letby inquiry report – as it happened
Yvette Cooper says this must ‘be a turning point for the NHS’ and tells the Commons she is ‘profoundly sorry’ for mistakes highlighted in Thirlwall report
Yvette Cooper says plans for cot cams in neonatal units to be 'urgently' developed
The health secretary said she has asked officials to develop plans to install “cot cams” in neonatal units.
She told the House of Commons:
On safety and reassurance for parents, Lady Justice Thirlwall recommends the introduction of video baby monitors for neonatal units. I agree.
I have asked my officials to urgently develop plans for cot cams, which can also help parents feel better connected to their babies when they aren’t able to be with them in person.
The government takes the recommendations from the Thirlwall inquiry “very seriously”, Cooper added.
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has told the Commons she is “profoundly sorry” for the failures set out in the Thirlwall Inquiry report, which was prompted by Lucy Letby’s crimes. In a statement, Cooper said: “On behalf of the government and the health service, I am profoundly sorry for the failures set out so clearly in this report, for the harm, distress and unthinkable loss for their families, and for the failures to keep their babies safe. Our responsibility now is to act.”
Cooper added that officials have been instructed to develop plans to fit “cot cams” in neonatal units, following a recommendation in the report. She told the House of Commons: “On safety and reassurance for parents, Lady Justice Thirlwall recommends the introduction of video baby monitors for neonatal units. I agree.”
The health department “is setting up a recommendation hub to properly track” its progress in addressing concerns raised by the inquiry, the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said, as she warned the publication of the long-awaited report must be “a turning point for the NHS”. “The safety and safeguarding and wellbeing of babies must never again be treated as a side issue,” she said, adding that maternity and neonatal services can no longer “operate on the margins” of the healthcare system.
Three babies might have survived and seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses and doctors had taken action over concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby, the Thirlwall inquiry found.
The report found a “complete failure” in safeguarding to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital, where Letby worked.
The inquiry, which was chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall, also found parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed.
Thirlwall said the report described dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.
A total of 14 recommendations were made in the report, including the fitting of baby monitors in all cots and incubators in neonatal units and CCTV cameras focused on insulin storage fridges.
But the inquiry chair said she was not reassured that ministers would act on her recommendations after the abolition of NHS England and little clarity on which body would take responsibility.
Letby, who maintains her innocence, is serving 15 whole-life terms for the murders of seven babies and attempted murders of seven others by various means between June 2015 and June 2016. The 36-year-old was twice denied permission to appeal against her convictions in 2024.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission is considering evidence presented on her behalf by an international panel of medics who claim poor medical care and natural causes were the reasons for the babies collapsing.
The Care Quality Commission (CQC), which is in charge of inspecting hospitals in England, has admitted some of its inquiries and record-keeping fell short when it came to the Countess of Chester Hospital and the Thirlwall Inquiry. Dr Toli Onon, CQC’s chief inspector of hospitals, said in a statement: “Our focus now must be on what additional safeguards need to be put in place to ensure that patients are better protected from this kind of harm.”
Tamlin Bolton, from Irwin Mitchell who represents seven children harmed by Lucy Letby, said: “Lady Thirlwall’s report paints a damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on. In her own words, a dispiriting and at times shocking account of multiple and repeated failings by organisation and individuals.”
Dr Tom Dolphin also said non-medical managers across the NHS “remain the only major part of the NHS workforce which is not regulated and this needs to change”.
He added:
We are glad to see the inquiry recommend a full statutory regulation system for managers and a system to disbar those who fail.
We also welcome the tougher requirements to end the ‘revolving door’ system that allows inadequate managers to simply find employment at another hospital.
Dr Tom Dolphin, chairman of the British Medical Association (BMA), said major reforms to NHS safeguarding and culture are needed in the wake of the Thirlwall Inquiry.
He said: “The events at Countess of Chester hospital a decade ago were some of the most appalling we’ve had to face in recent NHS history.
“This tragedy stems from systemic failure and major reforms to NHS culture and safeguarding are now required to make the NHS safer for all in future.”
He said the report showed “the hospital’s management was simply not up to the task of keeping patients safe”.
He added: “After multiple senior doctors raised concerns, they were palmed off and told to stop causing a fuss. This is sadly not unusual in the NHS.
“We have represented many whistleblowers who have been silenced by management for raising safety concerns and who have suffered career-ending consequences.”
We firmly believe that the changes we have made, as set out in our evidence to the inquiry, have created a safer environment for our patients and staff. We acknowledge, however, that there is more to be done.
We will now carefully consider the entire content of the Thirlwall report and its recommendations, working with NHS colleagues to embed the learning locally and across the wider NHS.
Our priority is to ensure that we address the Thirlwall report’s recommendations as swiftly as possible, whether through ensuring that actions we have already taken are sustained or by taking further action where needed.
'We are a different organisation today,' Countess of Chester Hospital Trust says in wake of damning inquiry
We can now bring you a statement from Jane Tomkinson, chief executive officer at the Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, which runs the hospital where Lucy Letby carried out her crimes. Tomkinson said in a statement:
Today, as the Thirlwall report is published, our thoughts remain fully with all of the families and the babies who came to harm or who died because of Lucy Letby’s crimes at the Countess of Chester Hospital in 2015 and 2016.
We recognise the enduring impact on them and the courage and dignity they have shown in ensuring their experiences are heard.
We know that no apology or action can undo what happened at our hospital. We are, however, truly sorry for the events that occurred in 2015 and 2016.
We acknowledge the findings of the Thirlwall report and will approach its recommendations with openness and a firm commitment to build on the progress we have already made in improving our hospital’s governance, safety and culture since that time.
We are a different organisation today with new leadership, stronger governance and safety processes, and a more open culture where speaking up is encouraged and acted upon.
Cooper also said that it is the government’s “intention” to publish a full response to the Thirlwall Inquiry within six months.
Her answer came in response to shadow health secretary Damian Hinds, who described the report as “thorough and devastating”.
He also raised concerns that the system to speak up in the NHS is “uneven” and the Health Bill will abolish the council of governors at NHS trusts and NHS England, leaving whistleblowers few places to turn. Cooper said she plans to review the details of the current system investigating patient safety concerns.
'This must be a turning point for the NHS,' health secretary says
The health department “is setting up a recommendation hub to properly track” its progress in addressing concerns raised by the inquiry, the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said, as she warned the publication of the long-awaited report must be “a turning point for the NHS”.
“The safety and safeguarding and wellbeing of babies must never again be treated as a side issue,” she said, adding that maternity and neonatal services can no longer “operate on the margins” of the healthcare system.
Poorly-performing NHS managers to be removed under new barring system, Cooper says
Cooper also told MPs that she will legislate to bring in a barring system to remove poorly-performing NHS managers “as soon as parliamentary time allows”.
The health secretary said:
The government has consulted on and confirmed plans to apply a barring scheme to senior leaders and managers, not just to clinicians.
So, we will legislate to introduce the scheme as soon as parliamentary time allows and we will consider (Lady Justice Thirlwall’s) recommendation to expand it further.
In line with one of the recommendations in the report, the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said all NHS trusts are signed up to roll out the national bereavement care pathway in 2027, which is meant to ensure high quality and consistent bereavement care throughout the UK, ending the current postcode lottery of provision.
“The report recommends the national bereavement care pathway for neonatal death should be rolled out in 2027 – I agree and can confirm that all trusts are signed up to implement it,” Cooper told the House of Commons.
“I will ensure that it is repeated in all versions of the NHS planning framework while I am the secretary of state.”
Yvette Cooper says plans for cot cams in neonatal units to be 'urgently' developed
The health secretary said she has asked officials to develop plans to install “cot cams” in neonatal units.
She told the House of Commons:
On safety and reassurance for parents, Lady Justice Thirlwall recommends the introduction of video baby monitors for neonatal units. I agree.
I have asked my officials to urgently develop plans for cot cams, which can also help parents feel better connected to their babies when they aren’t able to be with them in person.
The government takes the recommendations from the Thirlwall inquiry “very seriously”, Cooper added.
Cooper says she is 'profoundly sorry' for failures set out in report
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has told the Commons she is “profoundly sorry” for the failures set out in the Thirlwall Inquiry report, which was prompted by Lucy Letby’s crimes.
In a statement, Cooper said:
Let me address the issues for the families and the parents directly, because the suffering endured by these babies and their families is impossible to comprehend.
On behalf of the government and the health service, I am profoundly sorry for the failures set out so clearly in this report, for the harm, distress and unthinkable loss for their families, and for the failures to keep their babies safe. Our responsibility now is to act.
She added that officials have been instructed to develop plans to fit “cot cams” in neonatal units, following a recommendation in the report.
Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, said health leaders across the NHS “will share in the widespread sense of dismay and deep sorrow over the events that unfolded at the Countess of Chester hospital, and the determination to improve safety and accountability in the NHS”.
He added:
They will recognise the inquiry’s strong words on the upheaval caused by successive reorganisations, the complex regulatory landscape, staff shortages, unacceptable ‘revolving door’ appointments and the inadequacies of under-funded NHS IT systems.
They will welcome the call to strengthen managerial accountability while also implementing better training and support for managers.
We look forward to working with the government as it aims to develop a regulatory system for managers that is effective, equitable and fair, and that is fit for purpose for its intended aims.
Tamlin Bolton, from Irwin Mitchell who represents seven children harmed by Lucy Letby, said: “Lady Thirlwall’s report paints a damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on.
“In her own words, a dispiriting and at times shocking account of multiple and repeated failings by organisation and individuals.”
She said there had been direct and frank criticism of all those at senior management level and a description of a chief executive officer “with an intention throughout to stall or obstruct a police investigation”.
She said:
The families recognise that no system can guarantee that deliberate criminal acts will never occur. But when concerns are raised about patient safety, they must be listened to, investigated properly and acted on without delay.
The report today and the criticisms and failings highlighted in it cannot be the end of the matter. The families deserve more than expressions of regret and promises of change.
She said translating the inquiry’s recommendations into “meaningful and lasting change” would honour the children at the centre of the inquiry.
In a joint statement, Sue Hodkinson, Alison Kelly, Ian Harvey and Tony Chambers, the former senior managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital, said: “We are carefully reviewing the Thirlwall report and its recommendations.
“Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time.
“Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital.”
Dr Toli Onon, who joined the CQC as chief inspector of hospitals last year, said it was sorry for shortfalls in the evidence it could present to the inquiry.
She said:
We are truly sorry for the fact that there were significant shortfalls in CQC’s document management that impacted the evidence we were able to provide to the inquiry.
An independent external review of our information and records management practices has since been undertaken, and learning from that review is being used to improve CQC’s information management practices and document management systems.
The Thirlwall report makes very clear the need to focus on our core purpose and develop teams that work to achieve that purpose.
We are absolutely committed to improving how we work with others to keep people safe and improve care, how we use information to assess quality, identify risk and take appropriate action, and how we give people assurance about the services they rely on.
We will ensure the learning from this report is embedded in the turnaround process CQC is currently engaged in. We are committed to working with the Department of Health and Social Care and wider system partners to play our part in taking forward the recommendations set out by Lady Justice Thirlwall and her team.
The Care Quality Commission (CQC), which is in charge of inspecting hospitals in England, has admitted some of its inquiries and record-keeping fell short when it came to the Countess of Chester Hospital and the Thirlwall Inquiry.
Dr Toli Onon, CQC’s chief inspector of hospitals, said in a statement:
My deepest sympathies go out to the families who continue to suffer as a result of these horrifying crimes. Everyone who has a role in delivering, leading or regulating healthcare services must actively consider the findings of this report to help prevent another situation where premeditated harm goes undetected.
Our focus now must be on what additional safeguards need to be put in place to ensure that patients are better protected from this kind of harm. Our 2016 inspection of Countess of Chester Hospital did not identify an increase in neonatal mortality. Crucial information was not shared by the hospital – however, what is also very clear is that we as the regulator, did not take an approach which was sufficiently investigative and inquiring.
We have learnt from this and our assessment approach has been significantly strengthened since that point in time.
She added:
We now employ a more probing and evidence-led assessment model, with greater emphasis on clinical expertise. We have also made changes to our assessment approach to improve oversight of neonatal services.
Neonatal care is now inspected as a standalone service aligned to maternity, with relevant neonatal data presented to inspectors separately from data for other services – ensuring the whole team has clear and direct access to all intelligence as part of their assessment.
We have added to the range of mortality data sets that we review and are in discussion with NHS England about accessing additional data they hold, to allow more active tracking of mortality.

agricultural waste forms complete building system in new york house by LTL architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:15:42 UTC
23:15:42 KST

one straw system does it all in ltl architects’ residence
LTL Architects completes the All Straw House in New York, a prototype residence developed with Guy Nordenson and Associates and Princeton University that turns highly compacted straw boards into a structural building system. Prefabricated over two months at Princeton’s Architecture Lab, the house is assembled from 16 large straw units whose material properties determine the geometry of the walls and roof. At approximately 370 kilograms per cubic meter, the compressed straw reaches more than three times the density of conventional straw bales and performs simultaneously as structure, insulation, and interior finish.
Straw is a rapidly growing byproduct of grain agriculture and stores carbon as it grows, giving the material a different relationship to construction than mineral- or fossil-based assemblies. Here, however, the density of the material, its ability to be compressed and stacked, and its limits in forming the building all become design parameters. The research is developed through a learning-by-doing process involving a dedicated group of Princeton student researchers.
The construction of the house, designed by the team at LTL Architects, begins with the cutting, stacking, and compression of straw boards into large prefabricated elements. Inside, 111 layers of straw remain exposed as a smooth interior surface, while wood ring beams are introduced every 22 layers to provide lateral stability. The result avoids the sequence in which insulation disappears behind layers of drywall or other interior finishes. Instead, the material that performs the building’s thermal and structural work also becomes its visible interior surface.
The exterior follows the same logic. Thirty-three prefabricated thatch panels form a rainscreen, each overlapping the panel below by 21 inches. The panels are smoothed together into a continuous coat, while the elongated windowsills extend over the tapered thatch beneath them. Between six and eight inches thick, the thatch contains tens of thousands of linear reeds, producing a textured field across the exterior.
The combination of compressed straw and thatch makes the building read like a single material system. The walls and roof merge into one continuous assembly, with the structural straw continuing upward and the thatch responding to the requirements of drainage.
the All Straw House is wrapped in a continuous thatched rainscreen
material constraints determine form
The geometry of the All Straw House occurs from those material constraints, as the straw panels can only be corbeled to a certain degree, while the thatched roof requires a sufficient slope to shed water. Instead of concealing these limitations, LTL Architects uses them to establish the form of the building.
At the interior, the exposed straw makes this construction logic particularly legible. The repeating layers register the process of fabrication, while the timber ring beams mark the structural organization of the wall. Around the walnut sink, tadelakt plaster is applied directly to the straw to create a waterproof backsplash, extending the experiment into the smaller details of the domestic interior.
The All Straw House operates as a research project scaled to the size of a dwelling. Its significance lies less in the novelty of building with straw alone, a material with a long history in construction, than in the attempt to develop a contemporary tectonic system around its properties. Prefabrication allows the compressed panels to be assembled efficiently, while the exposed material reduces the number of separate layers normally required to complete a wall.
111 layers of compressed straw remain exposed inside the house
the interior brings together exposed straw panels, timber framing, and a compact living space
a walnut counter and tadelakt backsplash add contrasting materials
the thatched rainscreen meets a timber-framed window
the steeply tapered form follows the structural limits of the compressed straw panels

Putin moved the "Valdai" forum from Sochi to Moscow due to the threat of Ukrainian drones - FT
Kyiv • UNN
The "Valdai" forum was moved to Moscow amid fears of drone attacks. Putin's security service insisted that the decision be made.
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin decided to hold this year's Valdai Forum in Moscow instead of Sochi. The venue was changed at the last moment due to concerns about possible drone attacks. Financial Times reports this, citing sources familiar with the organization of the event, reports UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the Russian president's security officials insisted on moving the forum. About 120 invited participants have already been notified that they do not need to travel to Sochi.
FT sources explained the change in plans as being motivated by security considerations. Drones were one of the specific threats taken into account by the presidential security service.
Putin, meanwhile, had not visited Sochi for more than a year. According to the publication, he last traveled to the resort city in October 2025, when the previous Valdai Forum was held there.
Thus, this year's event, which traditionally brings together Russian officials and invited guests from abroad, will be held in Moscow.
The Kremlin uses the Valdai Discussion Club as a platform for promoting Russian interests and ideological narratives abroad. Russian senior officials, foreign journalists, political scientists, and experts are invited to participate.
This year, participants are expected to include Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, and Putin aide Maxim Oreshkin.

How fish has BJP's plate full in West Bengal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:14:12 UTC
23:14:12 KST

Bengal CM prayed at Kalighat temple and had fish-basanti pulao prasad.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari last week offered prayers at the Kalighat Temple on the occasion of 'Kaushiki Amavasya' and partook of a traditional bhog that included fish and 'basanti pulao'. Interestingly, the timing of the visit gave the ritual a political context.The meal came amid a political controversy over Bageshwar Dham chief Dhirendra Krishna Shastri's recent appeal to Bengali Hindus to refrain from eating non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja. As expected, the remarks kicked up a political storm, forcing the BJP’s Bengal unit to publicly distinguish itself from Dhirendra Shastri’s position on food.Chief minister Adhikari, who had shared a stage with Shastri earlier this month and invited him to establish a centre in Bengal, then got into the balancing act.“A religious figure is entitled to express his opinion, but whether people accept it or not is a personal matter,” the chief minister said after his Kalighat visit.Adhikari also referred to his own practices, saying he follows a sattvik diet on Ashtami and during Kartik, while accepting fish offered to Goddess Kali as bhog and goat meat as prasad.
"A saint or a religious leader is entitled to express their opinion. People may choose to accept it or not. On Mahashtami, when I worship Maa Durga, I consume sattvik food. During the month of Kartik also, I consume sattvik food. At the same time, as a Bengali, I accept the bhog offered to Maa with fish. I also accept the prasad of goat sacrifice. Today, whatever was offered to Maa in the afternoon, the temple priests gave me the same. There was fish head and fried fish, along with basanti pulao," he said.
From Liluah to Kalighat
All this began on September 4, when Adhikari shared the stage with Shastri at a Hanumant Katha programme at the Liluah Workshop Ground in Howrah.
Dhirendra Shastri on Durga Puja.
Addressing Shastri, Adhikari said: "Baba Maharaj Ji, please open a centre here. There should also be a Bageshwar Dham centre. This is the land of saints and of spiritual awakening."Two days later, on September 6, Shastri appealed to Hindus in Bengal not to sell, cook or eat non-vegetarian food near Durga Puja idols during Navratri. He described those consuming such food as "pakhandi" and called for opposition to the practice."I am appealing to the Hindus of Bengal, that during Navratri, even if you don't keep the idols of the Goddess, do not sell or consume non-veg near the idols. I do not like it when dirty non-vegetarian food is eaten during Durga Puja and at gatherings linked to the festivities. I want the Hindus of Kolkata to awaken and boycott such people. These people cannot be considered religious; they are pakhandi (hypocrites). Wake up and expel those people," he appealed.
BJP pushback
The remarks triggered criticism from the opposition and prompted the Bengal BJP to distance itself from the dietary prescription.State BJP president Samik Bhattacharya said no one could decide what Bengalis should eat."How can Bengalis not have fish and meat?" he said, adding that people in Bengal would continue with their traditional food practices. He also invoked Swami Vivekananda while defending the consumption of meat and fish in Bengal’s religious traditions.
BJP dismissed all anxieties over Durga Puja.
Other BJP leaders, including Dilip Ghosh, also said food choices were a matter of personal preference and referred to the place of meat in some Bengali religious traditions.The Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) also found itself navigating the controversy following statements made during an interactive session with Kolkata puja organizers. Swami Nirgunananda, a member of the VHP's central advisory council, had suggested that non-vegetarian food stalls be kept away from the immediate area around Durga idols and situated in designated spaces outside pandals to maintain sanctity and cleanliness.When his comments were interpreted as an official organisational diktat restricting meat sales, VHP International president Alok Kumar issued a formal clarification. "Vishva Hindu Parishad has not issued any directions regarding the arrangements at Durga Puja pandals... worship of the Goddess should take place according to tradition and the atmosphere should be one of love and devotion," it said.The Kalighat temple is associated with Bengal's 'Shakta' tradition, in which offerings can include fish and meat. The bhog included several varieties of fish, along with other vegetarian dishes and goat meat.That tradition sits somewhat differently from the vegetarian dietary practices associated with Navratri in several parts of north and west India.
The not-so-new ‘maach-bhaat’ row
The controversy over Shastri's remarks comes months after fish and meat had already become part of the BJP-TMC contest over Bengali identity during the assembly election campaign.Mamata Banerjee repeatedly alleged during the campaign that a BJP government would restrict what Bengalis could eat. At a rally in Purulia on March 29, she said: "BJP says can't eat fish, meat, eggs." She subsequently argued that restrictions on meat and fish sales in some BJP-ruled states showed what could lie ahead for Bengal.The issue became prominent enough for senior BJP leaders to address it directly. Amit Shah clarified that "consumption of fish, eggs will not be stopped" if the BJP came to power in Bengal, calling Mamata's claim a rumour.Prime Minister Narendra Modi also sought to engage with the issue, though from a different direction. At a rally in Haldia, he spoke about Bengal's fish production and said the state could become self-sufficient in fish under a BJP government. "In 15 years, TMC couldn't even give you fish. We created a separate ministry for fisheries," he said, contrasting Bengal's production with that of Bihar and Assam.The BJP’s campaign also included more visible efforts to counter the perception that it was opposed to Bengali food habits. Leaders publicly ate fish and meat, while BJP candidates and workers used fish in campaign imagery. On Poila Boishakh, TMC organised a "Maach-Bhaat-e-Bangali" procession, alleging that the BJP would impose restrictions on fish and meat.The argument did not remain confined to the two parties. TMC leaders presented food as part of the broader question of Bengali identity. BJP leaders, in turn, sought to emphasise that dietary choices would remain a matter of personal freedom.
The Bengal and Bengali dilemma for Suvendu
Months after the BJP swept Bengal in assembly elections, the opposition has sought to use the same "outsider" charge to try and alienate the saffron party from the voters. Congress filed a police complaint against Shastri, alleging that his comments hurt Bengali sentiments, while invoking the “outsider” argument that the TMC had used against the BJP during the election. Congress’s complaint described his remarks as an affront to Bengali traditions and social harmony.The TMC, which had made fish and meat part of its cultural-identity campaign against the BJP, is also again using the remark against the party.As CM, however, Adhikari has also taken a position on protests against Shastri.On September 10, he directed the Kolkata Police commissioner to arrest those who allegedly burnt Shastri’s photographs during a protest in Bhawanipur. "Not in Bengal," he said, making clear that burning photographs as a form of protest would not be tolerated.The move has produced another political contest. Congress has criticised the arrests and accused the government of protecting Shastri while acting against those protesting his remarks. One Congress leader, Atanu Das, was subsequently arrested.
The recent row has brought an old question back for the BJP in Bengal: how does the party's Hindu politics sit with the state's own traditions?Bengal has a strong Shakta tradition, centred on Kali and Durga. In this tradition, the line between what is considered religious and what is considered non-vegetarian is not always drawn in the same way as it is in northern/western India. Fish, and in some places meat, can be part of offerings and rituals.That makes food an unusually sensitive issue in Bengal. And for many Bengalis, it is tied to family customs, festivals and a sense of what is distinctly 'Bengali'.Suvendu Adhikari is leading the first BJP government in Bengal. For now, he might be able to shut down critics by consuming fish bhog at Kalighat. But it will be interesting to see how he manages BJP's national Hindu politics in Bengal while also balancing the "Bengaliness".
