El Nino reaches super status: Where will it bring rain, drought and heat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:10:26 UTC
22:10:26 KST

El Nino reaches super status: Where will it bring rain, drought and heat?
Forecasters say the Pacific Ocean warming pattern could be the strongest on record. Here is what that means for you.
A powerful El Nino is taking shape in the Pacific, and it is reshaping weather across the globe.
El Nino is a natural climate pattern caused by warmer-than-usual water in the central and eastern Pacific.
Data from the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), released on September 14, 2026, shows El Nino has breached the temperature rise threshold of 2C (3.6F), thus becoming “very strong”, informally known as a super El Nino.
This year’s El Nino began developing in June 2026 and is expected to peak by early 2027, with forecasters warning it could be one of the strongest ever recorded. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center expects it to persist through March-May 2027.
According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), El Nino happens every two to seven years. It usually starts between March and June, peaks between November and February, and can last up to 18 months.
How could El Nino affect your country?
A very strong El Nino tends to bring heavier rain to East Africa, South America and the southern US, drought to South Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and Southern Africa, as well as warmer temperatures almost everywhere.
Select your country from the dropdown below to see where rainfall is likely to increase or decrease.
Where could it rain more?
El Nino typically brings heavier rain to East Africa, South America and the southern US.
East Africa is expecting heavier rain than usual between October and December. The IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre, based in Ngong, Kenya, puts the chance of wetter conditions in southern Ethiopia, central and southern Somalia, and northeastern Kenya at 90 percent. These rains can supply up to 70 percent of the region’s annual rainfall, so heavier rain also means a higher risk of flooding.
El Nino typically brings more rain to parts of South America and the southern US too, with wetter conditions expected along the coasts of Ecuador and northern Peru in early 2027, then spreading to southern Brazil, Uruguay and northeastern Argentina between September 2026 and January 2027.
Where could it turn drier?
El Nino typically brings drier conditions to South Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and Southern Africa.
India and Pakistan’s summer monsoon has fallen short. Rainfall across India was 15 percent below average between June 1 and September 9, according to the India Meteorological Department.
Indonesia faces a drier season and higher wildfire risk. Its meteorological agency, BMKG, recorded 5,019 hotspots by late July, with Sumatra and Kalimantan at the highest risk.
Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology expects below-average rainfall across southern and eastern parts, with warmer temperatures raising the risk of wildfires.
The South African Weather Service expects below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures across most of the country through spring and summer.
How could El Nino affect food supplies?
The World Food Programme (WFP) warns that El Nino could push at least 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of 2027.
That would raise the total across the 45 countries it analysed from 225 million to 274 million. Eastern and Southern Africa and Latin America face the largest increases.
The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization says maize, rice and other rain-fed crops are most at risk. Dry conditions threaten harvests from Southern Africa and the Sahel to South and Southeast Asia.
“El Nino is a massive threat to the food security of millions who are already vulnerable,” said Carl Skau, WFP’s acting executive director.
Will El Nino make it hotter?
Yes. The phenomenon usually warms the planet, with the biggest effect felt the year after it develops.
The WMO expects warmer-than-normal temperatures almost everywhere from September to November. It also sees an 86 percent chance that at least one year between now and 2030 beats 2024 as the hottest on record.
“There is an El Nino predicted for the end of 2026, which increases the chances of the following year, 2027, being the next record-breaking year,” said Leon Hermanson, who led the forecast.
What about snow?
El Nino’s biggest effect on North American winters comes through the jet stream – the fast, high-altitude winds that steer storms.
During El Nino, the strongest part of this jet shifts south and stretches farther east, pushing storms across the southern third of the continent.
NOAA scientists call El Nino “the great snowfall suppressor” for most of the continent.
In past El Nino winters, snowfall dropped below average around the Great Lakes, interior New England, the northern Rockies, the Pacific Northwest, western Canada and Alaska. The southern US, especially at higher elevations, tended to get more.
NOAA notes these are past patterns, not a forecast, and can vary widely year to year.
The link is weaker in Europe. The United Kingdom’s Met Office expects a higher chance of wetter, stormier conditions in Northwest Europe this autumn and early winter, while the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts has linked El Nino to colder late winters in Northern Europe.
What else could change?
A strong El Nino usually calms the Atlantic hurricane season. NOAA’s August outlook gave a 75 percent chance of a below-normal season, noting that every strong event in recent history has been linked to below-average activity.
Forecasters stress that no two El Nino events are alike. The WMO warns that the strength of an event does not translate directly into the scale of its impacts in any single region, since conditions in the Indian and Atlantic oceans also play a role.
“El Nino is being supersized before our eyes,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a WMO statement. “The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”

Saudi crown prince lands in Egypt to meet Sisi: Egyptian state-linked media
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman arrived in Cairo on Tuesday ahead of meetings with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Egyptian state-linked media said, as the kingdom vowed to respond to attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
The regional powers are expected to discuss the threat posed by Houthi control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route vital to both Saudi oil exports and Egypt's Suez Canal revenues.
The de facto Saudi ruler "arrived in Egypt on an official visit", reported Al-Qahera News, which is close to Egyptian intelligence services. Riyadh's foreign ministry said Sisi received the crown prince for a "working visit".
Last week, the Houthis seized control of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, threatening the last direct route to Asian markets for the world's largest oil exporter.
Bab al-Mandeb, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and Egypt's Suez Canal, has become essential for Saudi oil exports this year, with the Strait of Hormuz blocked by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Since the Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, Saudi Arabia has relied more heavily on Egypt to export oil, chiefly through its overland Sumed pipeline.
Crude is transported from the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu to Egypt's Ain Sokhna, and carried overland through the pipeline to the eastern Mediterranean at Sidi Kerir.
But a recent drone attack, which Riyadh said was launched from Iraq, forced it to shut the East-West pipeline that feeds Yanbu, pushing global oil prices above the $100 threshold.
Disruption to Bab al-Mandeb could land Egypt with heavy losses too, with Cairo reliant on Suez Canal tolls for crucial foreign revenue.
Revenues from the waterway are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis started attacking ships in 2023, in what they said was an act of solidarity with Palestinians during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said last week Cairo's Suez Canal losses stood at $11 billion.

Lebanon, Israel envoys to meet in Washington as south burns
Lebanon's and Israel's ambassadors to Washington are expected to meet at the US State Department on Tuesday, as Israel continues its attacks and occupation in southern Lebanon and questions grow in Beirut over the value of negotiations that have so far failed to secure an Israeli withdrawal.
Lebanese Ambassador Nada Mouawad and Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter are expected to discuss recent developments and the implementation of a US-sponsored framework agreed between Lebanon and Israel in June.
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab that the meeting was intended to keep communication between the two sides open following recent setbacks in negotiations. They said no decisions or agreements were expected to emerge from the talks.
Lebanon will reiterate its demand for an end to Israeli attacks and military operations, including the bulldozing, destruction, demolition and booby-trapping of areas in the south, the sources said.
Beirut is also expected to push for agreement on a second "pilot zone" to be handed over to the Lebanese army.
The meeting comes despite growing doubts in Lebanon over negotiations with Israel, which has continued military operations inside the country while refusing to fully withdraw from Lebanese territory.
A US State Department official said earlier that the ambassadors would discuss "current developments" and the continued implementation of the trilateral framework, describing it as the only viable mechanism for restoring Lebanese sovereignty and Israeli security.
The next round of formal negotiations is due to take place in Rome in October. The eighth round of negotiations between Lebanon and Israel had been scheduled for September but was postponed until October.
A Lebanese government source told TNA that Israel had shown little enthusiasm for negotiations and continued to favour military action in southern Lebanon.
"Israel refuses to withdraw from Lebanon and insists on remaining in the south," the source said, adding that Israel sought to maintain its presence for as long as possible as part of a wider regional project.
US ambassador visits southern Lebanon
Against this backdrop, US Ambassador to Beirut Michel Issa visited southern Lebanon on Tuesday accompanied by representatives from the Lebanese government's Council for Development and Reconstruction.
Arriving under heavy security, Issa visited the Our Lady of the Annunciation Monastery in Zawtar al-Gharbiya in Nabatiyeh district. An Israeli drone reportedly flew overhead during the visit.
Issa later stopped in Qaaqaaiyat al-Jisr, where he inspected a newly constructed bridge replacing one destroyed in an Israeli airstrike.
The visit comes as Washington seeks an expanded role in shaping post-war security arrangements in southern Lebanon while continuing to back Israel, whose forces remain inside Lebanese territory.
Issa, who is of Lebanese origin, recently met Lebanon's vice president of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council, Sheikh Ali Al-Khatib. The meeting was viewed by some as an attempt by Washington to engage Lebanon's Shia community while maintaining its campaign against Hezbollah and pressing for the group's full disarmament.
Hezbollah is designated a terrorist organisation by the United States. The group has rejected demands to surrender its weapons while Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanese territory and carry out attacks.
Zawtar al-Gharbiya is among three villages where the Lebanese army deployed this summer under the June framework agreement. The US-sponsored plan calls for Israel to hand over designated "pilot zones" to the Lebanese army, which is then expected to ensure they have been cleared of Hezbollah weapons and military infrastructure.
Implementation has proceeded slowly amid continued Israeli attacks and occupation. Beirut has repeatedly demanded that Israel halt its military operations and withdraw from Lebanese territory.
Israeli attacks continue
The diplomatic activity comes as Israeli forces continue attacks across southern Lebanon.
Since midnight on Tuesday, Israel has carried out artillery shelling in Wadi Zibqin, al-Mansouri and Kfar Tibnit, as well as detonations in Kounine, Baraachit and al-Mansouri. Israeli operations have remained concentrated around Nabatiyeh despite the Lebanese army reinforcing its deployment in the area.
Fears have also grown over a possible Israeli push towards Nabatiyeh after Israeli forces captured the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge overlooking the city.
Israel's military currently occupies a border zone extending several kilometres into Lebanon, which it calls the "Yellow Line". Dozens of Lebanese towns and villages in the area have been destroyed, preventing large numbers of displaced residents from returning home.
In al-Bayyada in the Tyre district, Israeli forces have been burning what remains of homes, according to Lebanon's state-run National News Agency, while the nearby village of al-Mansouri has faced months of attacks.
On Monday, a resident of Baraachit was killed after Israeli forces opened fire with machine guns in the area.
According to Lebanon's Health Ministry, more than 4,300 people have been killed since all-out fighting between Israel and Hezbollah resumed on 2 March. Since the conflict began in October 2023, close to 9,000 people have been killed in Lebanon and more than 30,000 wounded.

‘You’re Simply Forced to Sit Within These Four Walls’: Kyiv Residents Living Under Constant Drone Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:06:00 UTC
22:06:00 KST

For much of the war, Kyiv’s air-raid routine followed a grim but predictable rhythm: Russian drones arrived at night, missiles struck before dawn, and the city dusted itself off to restart in the morning.
That pattern has now been shattered by recent events.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Since Aug. 27, Russia has been sending waves of drones toward Kyiv throughout the day and night, including faster, jet-powered models and larger Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones, alongside frequent ballistic attacks.
There was only a brief pause on Sept. 6-7, when Russia and Ukraine agreed to a temporary hold on strikes on Moscow and Kyiv as US President Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow.
For those two days, Kyiv briefly returned to something resembling normal life.
Then the drones came back.
The result is not simply a city under attack. It is a city where the line between an emergency and everyday life is disappearing.
Air raid alerts can last for hours. The subway stops running across the Dnipro River. Bridges close to traffic. Schools move children into shelters. Kindergartens send toddlers into basements. Shops and cinemas shut. Public institutions suspend their work.
Every alert carries an economic cost: delayed workers, interrupted production, closed businesses, suspended deliveries and disrupted public transport.
Russia is also targeting the logistics networks that keep Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities supplied, with warehouses, delivery infrastructure, and gas stations increasingly coming under attack.
Russian Casualties in 2026 Top 300,000, Ukraine Says
For Kyiv residents, the consequences are deeply personal.
“That is how we live every day”
Viola lives in Kyiv with her nine-year-old daughter, Oleksandra, while her husband serves in the military in southern Ukraine.
Her daughter started fourth grade in September. Viola says she feels safer knowing the girl is at school than she would on the first floor of their apartment building.
But the school spends much of the day in its shelter.
“There can be up to 10 air raid alerts a day,” Viola said.
She works from home, which makes the situation somewhat easier. But staying in or leaving the apartment has become a calculation.
Before going anywhere, she checks news channels and the Shahed flight map. If drones are not heading towards their area, she and her daughter leave for school, the store, the post office or wherever they need to go.
The most frightening moments come when the warning arrives after they have already left.
Recently, Viola and her daughter were returning from school when she received a report that a Shahed was entering their area. They were near a car wash, garages and a large shopping mall.
“There were practically no reliable shelters and nowhere to hide,” she said.
They simply walked faster toward home, listening for the drone and looking for somewhere they could take cover if air defenses began firing.
“That is how we live every day.”
At home, the family has adapted to the possibility of a major attack. Viola keeps an emergency backpack packed with documents, medication, masks, a flashlight, emergency blankets, tourniquets, spare keys, food and water.
Shoes are kept nearby in case they need to evacuate quickly. So are carriers for the family cats. The car is kept fueled.
Even ordinary household routines now require preparation.
“We have to check that all your gadgets, EcoFlow, lamps and batteries are charged,” she said.
Her daughter also has her own ways of coping. They play board games, read books, watch movies downloaded from Netflix, go for walks with friends and light candles and fairy lights.
But the exhaustion remains.
“You want to sleep through the whole night in your own bed, plan trips outside without looking at air raid maps, and have children study somewhere other than shelters and freely live their childhood,” Viola said.
“For now, we are adapting to constant change.”
‘You Aren’t Able to Hear the Teacher’
For 15-year-old Maria, the disruption is most visible at school.
She studies at the lyceum, where an air raid alert used to mean one thing: classes stopped and students went to the shelter.
The shelter is small and crowded, its conditions are far from comfortable.
“The toilet in the shelter is not great. It is dirty and always smells,” Maria said.
A year ago, she said, there was no toilet at all – just a bucket and a curtain.
Students are not allowed to leave school on their own during an air raid alert. Parents have to collect them.
Maria now follows a blended schedule, spending one week studying remotely and one week at school.
During remote learning, classes continue under a lower-level alert as long as students are in safe places. If the danger level rises to red, the lessons end.
In-person lessons are supposed to continue in the shelter. Maria does not see how that can work.
“Everyone is shouting and you’re not able to hear the teacher,” she said.
The shelter is also hot and poorly ventilated.
“Sometimes I feel sick if we have to sit there for two hours or more,” she said.
‘We Feel Guilty’
For parents of younger children, the choice can be even harder. Liubov, 34, is an English teacher and the mother of a four-year-old daughter.
Her daughter has barely attended kindergarten over the past three weeks because children can spend almost the entire day in the shelter.
Liubov’s daughter attends a private kindergarten where children have lessons, meals and activities even while sheltering. Compared with many other children in Kyiv, their situation is relatively good.
But the parents still feel guilty.
“We as parents still feel guilty about making her stay there all day,” Liubov said.
Whenever they can, they keep their daughter home.
Both Liubov and her husband work from home, so they take turns looking after their child and trying to keep up with work.
“It’s hard because the work still needs to be done, and juggling everything is challenging,” she said.
They also try to take their daughter outside every day, but stay close to home so they can return quickly if a major attack begins.
When they hear explosions or air raid alerts, they try not to panic in front of the child – but they have also stopped pretending that the noise is simply thunder.
The girl has begun to ask questions about what is happening in Ukraine.
“It’s a difficult balance – trying to give her a sense of safety and normality while knowing that we can’t completely shield her from what is going on around us,” Liubov said.
‘I’m Already Running Out of Strength’
For Anastasia, 31, the past three weeks have been almost unbearable.
Her four-and-a-half-year-old daughter attends kindergarten, but the facility does not have a properly equipped shelter.
During alerts, the children cross the road to a residential building and shelter in its basement. That was manageable when it happened occasionally.
It is very different when children spend four or five hours there at a time, which since Aug. 27, Anastasia said, has become the reality.
When she realized the situation was not improving, she took her daughter out of kindergarten and began keeping her at home.
That solved one problem and created another as Anastasia works full time.
“Being with a child 24/7 and maintaining my functionality and effectiveness at work is extremely difficult,” she said.
“So far, thank God, I’ve managed. But I can already feel that I’m running out of strength.”
Her daughter is also struggling with being confined to the apartment.
Anastasia cannot simply take her outside during the workday. Even after work, going out may be too dangerous when drones are moving over the city in large numbers.
At home, she says, at least there are concrete walls between them and falling debris. Outside, there is nowhere to know for certain that you are safe.
The disruption has spread into the most ordinary parts of life.
Going grocery shopping requires planning. Going to a shopping mall has become difficult. Even ordering a package can feel risky as Russian attacks increasingly target logistics infrastructure.
Sometimes, Anastasia said, the situation creates a feeling of absolute despair.
“You see empty shelves in stores, you can’t take your child to kindergarten or any extracurricular activities, you can’t take her anywhere to have fun, not even to a children’s play area.”
“You’re simply forced to sit within these four walls, look at each other and wait for all of this to end.”
“And whether it will actually end – that’s completely unclear.”
‘Now Half of My Family Became Refugees’
For Mariia, 32, the constant attacks eventually forced a decision about where her family could live.
Leva arrived in Kyiv on Aug. 23, initially planning to stay for about a month.
The first few days were unusually quiet. She said the calm coincided with Russia putting on a show of restraint around the visit of foreign diplomats.
Being back home felt good.
She wanted to spend more time with her family and her one-year-old niece. She began considering staying longer, or even partially moving back.
Then the attacks intensified.
Her family has now left Kyiv for Uzhhorod, where they found an apartment and moved out within days.
The family still owns an apartment in Kyiv. They want to come home.
But they do not believe it is safe to raise a small child there under the current conditions.
“It’s impossible to sleep here with kids because parents worry about their safety nonstop,” Leva said.
The alternative, she said, is spending night after night in the metro or a dusty basement – and even that does not guarantee safety.
Her brother and sister-in-law made the decision to leave with their young daughter.
“They want to come back home,” Leva said. “Just because they like it here and because they want my niece to grow up with her grandparents, aunts and uncle, cousins around.”
But for now, they are gone.
“Now half of my family became refugees.”
Her mother and younger brother left for Germany after the full-scale invasion began.
Leva says there is something particularly painful about the fact that being able to leave is itself a privilege.
“I’m supposed to be happy that my family can be in a safer place now. Because for most of the people there is no such an option.”
“But I just want them to be home, because they want to be home.”
A City That Cannot Stop
The effects are not limited to families with young children.
Myroslava, a culture correspondent at Kyiv Post, said a Sept. 2 Russian drone attack on the National University of Food Technologies came while classes were taking place.
Some 160 students and faculty members were unharmed because they were in the shelter.
But the attack reopened a broader question for Kyiv’s universities: should students continue attending classes in person when the city is under near-constant attack?
The decision is left to individual institutions.
For Myroslava’s family, the question was personal. Her daughter is a fourth-year architecture student at the Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture in Solomianskyi District, one of the areas facing a high level of threat.
Until recently, professors had required students to attend in person.
Only on Sept. 9 did the university administration decide to move classes online for a limited period until Sept. 25.
The same pressure is being felt across Kyiv’s cultural life.
Museums and theaters have struggled to operate under the dense schedule of air raid alerts.
Myroslava and her family eventually managed to attend an anniversary exhibition dedicated to composer Borys Liatoshynsky at Ukrainian House – on their fourth attempt.
The previous attempts were disrupted by security concerns.
Relearning the lessons of survival
For much of the war, Kyivans learned how to live with air raid alerts.
People knew what to do when the sirens sounded. They knew where to shelter. They knew that eventually the alert would end, the trains would start to run again, shops would reopen and the city would return to work.
Now that rhythm is breaking down. The question for Kyiv residents is no longer just how to get through one more night of attacks.
It is how to live when the next interruption can come at any moment – and when there may be no clear end to the interruption at all.

Former spokesman of Greek ultra-nationalist party Golden Dawn, Ilias Kasidiaris, speaks to his supporters after his release from prison. (AFP Photo)
The former spokesman of Greek neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn, Ilias Kasidiaris, was released from prison on Sept. 15 and vowed a return to politics, having already drawn attention from Elon Musk.
Kasidiaris, 45, had been handed a 13-year sentence as a leading member of the violent outfit that for years carried out beatings of migrants and political opponents, and the 2013 murder of anti-fascist rapper Pavlos Fyssas.
Raising his fist and holding a folded Greek flag, Kasidiaris said he was returning to a “new, strong national party, such as those dominating all of Europe.”
“Today I am back. And from what I see, I am not alone,” he said outside Domokos prison in central Greece.
He called his incarceration “an underhanded and dirty conspiracy” by his political opponents, and added that he would announce the name of his new party on Sept. 14.
Dozens of cheering supporters, several holding Greek flags, were waiting for him.
“Ilias, we are with you,” many chanted. “We will make you prime minister.”
Formerly a Golden Dawn MP from 2012 to 2019, Kasidiaris was jailed for six years and worked off the rest of his sentence while behind bars.
He had previously spent a year in pre-trial detention in 2014 before his incarceration in 2020.
Even during his incarceration, the former food chemist never ceased his political activity on social media, particularly on his YouTube channel, which has 162,000 subscribers.
In July he drew the attention of Musk, whom he has praised as “the most eminent personality in the world.”
The multibillionaire, who backs far-right groups in Europe including AfD in Germany, noted on X on July 17 that Kasidiaris’ continued incarceration was “messed up.”

Palestinian woman prisoner gives birth in Israeli detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:02:37 UTC
22:02:37 KST

Breadcrumb
'Left to struggle through her pregnancy': Palestinian woman gives birth in Israeli jail
A Palestinian woman has given birth to a baby girl inside an Israeli prison while being held under administrative detention, the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said on Monday.
Dana Joudeh, 35, from Iraq al-Tayeh near Nablus in the occupied West Bank, was detained while pregnant and spent six months in Israel's Damon Prison without charge or trial, the commission said.
Joudeh is due to be released on Tuesday with her newborn daughter after completing her six-month administrative detention order. She is currently reportedly receiving treatment at a hospital in Ramallah.
The Palestinian Prisoners' Society said Joudeh has another child and was detained while pregnant before being placed under administrative detention.
The Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs accused Israel of leaving Joudeh to go through her pregnancy without adequate healthcare or medical attention, describing her detention and treatment as violations of international law.
"Leaving her to struggle through her pregnancy without any health or medical care constitutes a crime that violates all international norms and laws," the commission said.
It also noted that forcing Joudeh to give birth inside the prison as a "double crime" and said the Israeli prison administration treats Palestinian women prisoners "brutally".
Joudeh's case comes amid wider allegations of abuse and mistreatment of Palestinian women held at Damon Prison.
In June, the Palestinian Prisoners' Media Office reported that women detained there had faced physical abuse and torture, including being forced to lie on the ground with their hands tied behind their backs before being beaten.
The office also reported poor-quality food and medical neglect among female prisoners.
Israel holds hundreds of Palestinians in administrative detention without charge or trial, with detention orders that can be renewed indefinitely.
More than 9,400 Palestinians are currently held in Israeli prisons, including 370 children and 92 women, according to the Palestinian Prisoners' Society.

Paris ex-mayor says 'collective failure' led to wave of child abuse

Paris ex-mayor says 'collective failure' led to wave of child abuse
PARIS, Sept 15 - Former Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo said on Tuesday "collective failure" at institutions had opened the door to a wave of child abuse at state nurseries and primary schools in the French capital over more than a decade.
Police have been examining more than 200 allegations of mistreatment, violence and sexual abuse of young children during lunch breaks, rest periods and after-school activities.
Hidalgo told a Senate hearing the number of victims was unacceptable and that she understood the sense of abandonment amongst families.
'INSTITUTIONS FAILED TO PROTECT OUR CHILDREN'
"If we are standing before you here today, it is because our institutions... despite the actions taken and despite a genuine awareness of the sexual abuse suffered by our children in this country, have failed to protect our children. And this is a collective failure," she told senators.
The first allegations of abuse surfaced in 2014. A year later, the Paris General Inspectorate, an inter-departmental supervisory body, published a report warning of the risk of such offences being committed by city employees against minors.
Parents groups say their concerns about abuse fell on deaf ears in City Hall for years. Paris Public Prosecutor Laure Beccuau told France Inter radio last week she has opened investigations into Hidalgo and current mayor Emmanuel Gregoire over their alleged failures to assist a person in danger of abuse.
On Tuesday afternoon a Paris court sentenced a former after-school activity supervisor to five years in prison with four years suspended.
The offender had admitted sexually assaulting nine girls aged six to 10 at a Paris elementary school.
Senator Agnes Evren, who led the Senate's hearing, listed shortcomings in City Hall's actions detailed in the Inspectorate's report, including a four-year pause in systematic reporting of complaints, and said the Inspectorate's recommendations had only been partially implemented.
Parents' collective SOS Periscolaire expressed disappointment at Hidalgo's answers, which it said failed to deliver facts.
"We are unfortunately not surprised by these answers, which always point to the failures and responsibilities of others, but never her own," SOS Periscolaire said in a statement.
Barka Zerouali, the cofounder of a second parents' group, #MeTooEcole, told Reuters: "Once we drop our child off at school they are supposed to be safe, all the more so when we're talking about a public service." REUTERS

South African police probe killings of seven women, Ramaphosa vows action
JOHANNESBURG, Sept 15 - South African police said on Tuesday they were investigating the deaths of seven women whose bodies were found near Johannesburg over the past two months, with some stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual violence.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed "no stone will be left unturned" in the investigation into their deaths, which have caused widespread alarm.
The victims are mostly aged in their 20s or 30s, and one was identified as a woman who disappeared after leaving home for an afternoon run.
Violence against women is one of the country's most entrenched social problems, despite years of government pledges to tackle it.
Police are investigating whether the killings in and around Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, were carried out by a single perpetrator, multiple suspects or copycat criminals.
Some bodies were found naked, others partially clothed. One body was decomposing when discovered.
The killings have sparked widespread condemnation from civil society and sporting bodies. Police have not yet established a motive for the killings.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world, averaging about 60 a day, according to official crime statistics. Violent crime is a persistent source of public anger and anxiety as the country prepares to hold municipal elections in November. REUTERS

Luana Lopes Lara Is on the Frontlines of Evolving Prediction Markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:45 UTC
22:01:45 KST

Luana Lopes Lara is inherently an optimist—perhaps because Brazilians, she says, have a more positive outlook than people from other countries. That trait has served her well as chief operating officer of Kalshi, the New York-based prediction market that has boomed in recent years as people take up placing money on everything from what words the President will use in his speeches to the price of a Costco hot dog.
“I probably wouldn’t be here if I hadn’t had this Brazilian culture and background,” says Lopes Lara, 30. “I’m very optimistic and positive, but it’s not a blind optimism—it’s more like I believe that in the end, things will work out.” She still leans on some Brazilian traditions, like always trying to get out of bed on her right foot and then taking a few hops on it, eating lentils for New Year’s, and jumping over seven waves in the ocean for good luck.
Lopes Lara put her optimism to work when the company decided to sue Kalshi’s regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, arguing that the company should be allowed to list political event contracts. Kalshi won the case in September 2024, which allowed the platform to feature the 2024 elections, with users favoring Donald Trump over Kamala Harris when polls were forecasting an even race. Since then, the company’s valuation has grown to $22 billion, and in December 2025, Lopes Lara unseated 31-year-old Scale cofounder Lucy Guo to become the world’s youngest self-made woman billionaire at 29, according to Forbes.
Lopes Lara’s parents, a math teacher and an electrical engineer, pushed their two daughters to be financially independent, so they would never need to rely on partners for money. But her parents’ vision of success included going to a public university in Brazil and getting a job as a doctor, engineer, or lawyer, she says. She wanted more for herself: “I always wanted to do bigger things.”
Lopes Lara was accepted into the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard, Yale, and Stanford while she was performing as a ballet dancer in Austria, having trained at the only official affiliate school of the Russian Bolshoi Theater outside of Moscow. She chose MIT, she says, because people there seemed more passionate about what they were pursuing than students did at Harvard. It was at MIT that Lopes Lara got to know her Kalshi co-founder, Tarek Mansour, when he sat next to her in the first row in an algorithms class so he could learn from her, she says.
These days, Mansour handles many public-facing tasks as CEO and Lopes Lara handles internal operations. The role has forced her to unlearn some of the perfectionist tendencies she honed for so long as a ballerina, she says, where tilting your finger a centimeter in the wrong direction can ruin the aesthetics. “For a startup, you need the opposite,” she says. “You need to move very fast.”
The speed at which Kalshi is moving has caught the eye of regulators outside the federal government, resulting in court challenges in states including New York and Washington. So far, its federal regulator has remained steadfast in holding that Kalshi can legally operate. Lopes Lara says she believes Kalshi’s case will prevail—after all, it was a President Biden-appointed judge who first gave the company the green light to list elections, and it’s the Trump Administration that continues to support the company. “At the end of the day, it’s because we’re right on the law,” she says. Many state attorneys general disagree, making her position, unquestionably, what an optimist might say.

How Netflix Star Sofia Carson Brings Her Identity to Work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:44 UTC
22:01:44 KST

In the 2025 Netflix romance My Oxford Year, Sofia Carson plays Anna De La Vega, an American student studying abroad at one of England’s most prestigious universities who, like Carson herself, is of Latin American descent. Anna’s Colombian, Argentine, and Cuban heritage is woven naturally into her character’s everyday life instead of being treated as a barrier she has to overcome. It’s a distinction that Carson, who has four consecutive global #1 Netflix hits to her name, says is nonnegotiable when it comes to the roles she chooses to take on.
“All the Netflix films I have been a part of that have gone on to make streaming history have been led by myself, a Hispanic American actress telling the stories of Latin women,” says Carson, who also starred in the music-heavy romance Purple Hearts (2022), action thriller Carry-On (2024), and romantic drama The Life List (2025). “Within those stories, that heritage isn't a tattooed stereotype, but rather an organic part of existence.”
Born in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., to Colombian immigrant parents, Carson, 33, got her big break starring in the massively popular 2015 Disney Channel musical Descendants and its sequels. “I think back to my earliest memories and it wasn’t a choice that I made, it was always who I was,” Carson says of her lifelong Hollywood ambitions. “I remember being a little girl, as young as 3, and music, storytelling, performing, dancing, that was just what I did. It was undeniable.”
She has since parlayed that initial success into a diverse, multi-hyphenate career—establishing herself as one of Netflix’s most valuable movie stars, serving as an executive producer on several film projects, and building a recording catalog, including a self-titled album and songs from her films, that has surpassed 4 billion streams worldwide. Beyond her work on screen and in music, Carson is an advocate for young people’s education and empowerment through her roles as a U.S. Ambassador for UNICEF and the first global ambassador for the Latin GRAMMY Cultural Foundation.
“I recognized very early on in my career that I had a responsibility to use my voice to stand for goodness and to stand for justice,” she says.
Next up, Carson is set to co-star in the Wagner Moura-directed indie dramedy Last Night at the Lobster as part of an ensemble cast featuring award-winning actors like Elisabeth Moss and Brian Tyree Henry. “What’s most important to me is to shift the misunderstanding that to be a Latin woman is to look one way, to be one thing, to be one [type of] woman, body, skin color, accent,” she says. “In reality, we are a kaleidoscope of cultures, of talents, of thoughts, of passions. That has been such an important guiding light in my career.”

Mónica Ramírez Is Teaching Migrant Women How to Organize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:44 UTC
22:01:44 KST

Growing up around the rows of corn and soybeans in Fremont, Ohio, Mónica Ramírez spent her earliest days being looked after by her maternal bisabuela, or great-grandmother, Virginia Guardiola. From her home in town, Guardiola served as an informal, one-woman welcome committee for farmworkers who arrived in Fremont, disoriented and alone. Guardiola would tell these newcomers where to find jobs and fill them in on what they needed to know about Ohio.
From her great-grandmother, Ramírez says she learned “the importance of having information to share, so that people could actually get jobs—and get safe.” Ramírez saw the vulnerability of those who followed the harvest to a place like Fremont. Many were women living far from their families, who often worked without legal status, which made it risky for them to speak out against exploitative foremen in the fields or predators in the worker barracks. It mattered, she says, for them to have “trusted community members.”
Some 40 years later, Ramírez is an internationally recognized attorney and feminist, with degrees from Ohio State and Harvard. The founder of the advocacy group Justice for Migrant Women, Ramírez has made powerful allies, including celebrities like Eva Longoria and America Ferrera; she was Laura Dern’s guest at the Oscars in 2018. Yet to this day, she still lives within miles of the agricultural fields in Fremont.
When Ramírez founded Justice for Migrant Women in 2014, she’d spent a decade as an attorney helping farmworkers fight for their rights in court. But Justice for Migrant Women is not a legal aid clinic. Instead, it performs the service Ramírez saw her bisabuela perform in Fremont: it provides information. Ramírez helps workers access the knowledge they need to organize and fight for their own rights.
She sees herself more as a neighbor than a charity giver, and the neighborliness goes both ways. One of the women who most inspired Ramírez was a farmworker named Bernice, who had been sexually victimized in a labor camp and later evicted. Homeless and injured, Bernice decided to return to her home county rather than file a criminal complaint, despite Ramírez’s offer to fight for her. In all their calls, Bernice always began conversations by asking Ramírez the same question: “Are you happy?” For Ramírez, it was a model. Today, she says she starts every new conversation by considering the dignity of the person she is speaking with, taking account of the fullness of their life.
Ramírez sees a role her organization can play in the twists and turns of politics and culture, working to ensure that Justice for Migrant Women is there for people who need support as the political landscape shifts and new challenges arise. In 2017, as the Me Too movement took off, Ramírez helped write the “Dear Sisters” letter, which ran in TIME under the headline “700,000 Female Farmworkers Say They Stand With Hollywood Actors Against Sexual Assault.” It read, in part: “Even though we work in very different environments, we share a common experience of being preyed upon by individuals who have the power to hire, fire, and blacklist.” And amid the Trump Administration’s mass deportation campaign, as some farmworkers feel they have to choose between enduring sexual abuse in silence or coming forward and risking the trauma of detention and family separation, Ramírez is working in community meetings and trainings to help them understand their rights.
One of Ramírez’s projects, the “Humans Who Feed Us” dinner series, brings people together and highlights the interdependence of our broader communities. In Ohio and around the country, she sets large tables for farmworkers, line cooks, delivery drivers—immigrant workers who support the nation’s food system—and then invites business leaders and other community members to join them.
“We’re too far apart, and I think that that space between us is what’s leading to hate and misunderstanding,” Ramírez says. She sets the table the way her great-grandmother would for any newcomer in town. “Back in the day,” she says, “people relied on their neighbors.”

Ana Valdez Is Making Business Leaders Recognize Latino Economic Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:44 UTC
22:01:44 KST

Sometimes, when Ana Valdez walks into a C-Suite office and introduces herself, she can see the person taking in her Mexican accent and her last name with some surprise. “They were expecting somebody different,” Valdez says. It can get “old, and a little annoying” to re-introduce herself—to explain she’s a CEO who has worked for the United Nations in Geneva and President Bill Clinton’s Administration in Washington, D.C.—but, Valdez says, in some ways, she’s happy to do it: “I like this part of my job. I’m proud to represent whom a Latino should be regarded as.”
Today, as president and CEO of the Latino Donor Collaborative, that representation is Valdez’s job in more ways than one. The LDC is a clearinghouse for original research and what Valdez describes as “data-driven Latino economic advocacy.” In practice, this is what that advocacy looks like: Valdez walks into CEOs’ offices and tells them that, when they think about their Latino customers, they need to transform the image that comes into their heads. Valdez puts the LDC’s data in front of them, and explains that, according to their research, U.S.-based Latinos represent a $4.4 trillion economy. If measured as their own country, U.S. Latinos would rank as the fourth-largest economy in the world.
She is often met with disbelief. “People are saying, ‘It can’t be that my housekeeper produces $4.4 trillion,’” Valdez recounts, laughing. “I mean, literally, these are the kind of comments I hear.”
Valdez grew up in Mexico City and studied at the prestigious Tecnológico de Monterrey, housed on a modernist campus south of Monterrey’s skyscrapers. Later, back in Mexico City, she worked as a senior account executive with Nielsen. It was there that Valdez saw the power of market research to change the look of entire cities. Nielsen would tell multinational companies where untapped customers lived, and those companies would then flood those markets with commercials, new stores, and billboards to reach them.
In 1996, Valdez became an immigrant, moving to the U.S. to work for the Clinton Administration. She moved to Los Angeles to support Clinton and Vice President Al Gore’s reelection campaign in ’97 and has called L.A. home ever since. Even with a high-powered background, Valdez had to fight the feeling that she was starting over in the States. In Mexico, saying she went to Tec meant something; in the U.S., it went over people’s heads. That personal experience, as much as her background, made her a natural fit for the LDC.
The LDC was founded in 2010, when a small group of business leaders and former politicians decided to push back against “harmful stereotypes” about Latinos among the business community. The officially nonpartisan organization pursues this goal using market research—the kind of work Valdez did at Nielsen. It might not look like a march in the streets or a political campaign, but the central thesis of LDC’s work is that transforming the way businesses see their Latino customers can change the world: it evolves the TV people watch, the stores they walk into, the language they use.
Valdez began as a development consultant with the LDC before becoming president and CEO in 2015. She says that, in boardrooms and corner offices, her pitch is easy: ditch Latino stereotypes and get rich, or hold onto them and fail. She points to the growing popularity in the U.S. of Latin music and Mexican food-and-beverage brands, from Bad Bunny to Modelo beer. “For those decision makers that know the numbers, and are tracing the source and the root of pop culture today, they’ll be in great position in the coming years,” Valdez says. “Those who don’t recognize it,” she warns, “will not.”

Jose Alvarado Brought Puerto Rican Pride to the NBA Championship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:44 UTC
22:01:44 KST

As the New York Knicks mounted one of the greatest comebacks in sports history, erasing a 20-point fourth-quarter deficit in Game 4 of the NBA Finals in June against the San Antonio Spurs, Knicks reserve guard Jose Alvarado refused to overthink the moment.
Alvarado, who at a generously listed 6 ft. checks in as one of the shortest players in the NBA, electrified the celebrity-soaked Madison Square Garden crowd; his defensive effort, two critical three-pointers, and a driving layup down the stretch helped the Knicks chip away at San Antonio’s seemingly insurmountable lead. “I kid you not, I was not once nervous in that game,” says Alvarado, 28. “Not once. It was like, ‘Let’s do it, let’s go have fun, and let’s enjoy this moment.’ And that’s exactly what I did.’”
Three nights later, Alvarado fulfilled an impossible dream: he won an NBA title with his hometown team. The Knicks ended their 53-year championship drought, and Alvarado, a hard-nosed spark plug of Puerto Rican descent who grew up honing his game in the playgrounds of Brooklyn and Queens, came to embody the resilience of not only the team he suited up for but also the people of his city—especially his fellow Puerto Ricans, whom he’s so proudly represented in the global spotlight.
At every stage of Alvarado’s career, he was written off. “Everyone was telling me, ‘Coach, you’re in the ACC. You can’t take this guy,’” says Josh Pastner, the former Georgia Tech coach who recruited Alvarado out of Christ the King High School in Queens. “‘He’s too small. He’s not quick enough. Come on, man.’” Alvarado was named conference defensive player of the year in 2021; Georgia Tech won the ACC tournament championship that season. “Winning is more important than breathing to him,” says Pastner, who now coaches at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.
“I don’t pass the eye test,” Alvarado admits. He knows he doesn’t look the part. But he’s now an NBA champion who signed a three-year deal, worth more than $14 million, with the Knicks this summer.
So: “I wouldn’t trust the eye test.”
Alvarado credits his success to his New York City outer-borough upbringing. “I got my toughness and my grittiness from Brooklyn,” he says. “I got a lot of my skills playing great opponents from Queens.” Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, which disrupted the seasons of many college players, in 2021 Alvarado could have returned to Georgia Tech for a fifth year of eligibility. He asked Pastner for $60,000 in name, image, and likeness money—chump change in today’s lucrative college sports economy. But five years ago, NIL rules hadn’t been formally put in place, so Pastner didn’t pay him. Alvarado bet on himself and went into the NBA draft. “Thank God I did,” he says.
“I wish I paid him the 60 grand,” says Pastner. “I mean, guys are asking me for a million dollars who average one point and can’t win a game. I would maybe have a Final Four underneath my belt.”
Although Alvarado didn’t get drafted in 2021, the New Orleans Pelicans signed him to a contract: in the Big Easy, he carved out a role as a defensive specialist, earning the nickname Grand Theft Alvarado.
Then, in February of this year, Alvarado learned that the Pelicans had traded him to the Knicks. “I automatically got water eyes because it was like, ‘Wow, I’m going to my hometown team,’” says Alvarado.
Leaving his teammates in New Orleans was bittersweet, but Alvarado fit right in with the Knicks: less than a week after the team acquired him, Alvarado scored 26 points, with eight three-pointers and five steals, against Philadelphia in just 19 minutes off the bench; he was the first reserve NBA player in history to record such sterling stats. These efforts, and the Knicks’ title, now offer him cult-hero status in New York. “After the championship, I can’t walk the streets,” he says. In late June, Alvarado brought the NBA championship trophy to Puerto Rico, where fans snapped his picture as he arrived at the airport. The governor honored Alvarado at a ceremony.
Alvarado also led Puerto Rico to an appearance in the 2024 Olympics, and was named Athlete of the Year at the 2025 National Puerto Rican Day Parade in New York City. He plans on returning to the Olympics with Puerto Rico in 2028 in Los Angeles.
As for this upcoming NBA season? The reigning champion isn’t planning to take it easy. “What makes the story better,” asks Alvarado, “than to do it again?”

Xochitl Gonzalez’s Novels Put the Spotlight on Latina and Black Creatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:43 UTC
22:01:43 KST

When Xochitl Gonzalez was reading literature to research her third novel, she noticed something that didn’t quite feel right: there weren’t enough scenes featuring characters of color having a ball together. Even in tough times growing up, the writer recalls, her family always found reasons to celebrate. “My grandfather recycled bottles to pay for my communion party when I was 7,” says Gonzalez, 48. “So often, our stories are more about suffering than joy. But what I knew—and what shaped so much of my personality—was being at parties.”
So for her third novel, the best-selling author of Olga Dies Dreaming and Anita de Monte Laughs Last wrote a book rich in colorful party scenes. Last Night in Brooklyn, a Great Gatsby retelling set in 2007, conjures a version of Brooklyn just before a new wave of gentrification made it unrecognizable. The novel, which was published last year, follows Alicia, a young woman trying to shrug off the weight of her mother’s traditional values. Alicia wants to let the city sway her toward new experiences and new people—particularly her neighbor La Garza, a local fashion designer and legendary party host. La Garza’s glamorous gatherings pull Alicia into a world full of young Latino and Black creatives working to make their mark on a rapidly changing world.
Gonzalez, who was born to a Puerto Rican mother and Mexican American father, and raised in Brooklyn by her maternal grandparents, infuses her books with explorations of both identity and culture. Her love of New York City shines through her stories about characters discovering who they are and where they belong. And she likes imagining how her novels might literally fit into readers’ busy routines. She knows from her own experience as a reader hustling around the city that a book that’s easy to carry or a well-narrated audiobook can make a difference in how many people engage with her work. “I’m making art that’s meant to be consumed, so I try to keep in mind the lives that people are living,” she says. “Beautiful language means a lot to me—I also want to deliver a satisfying story that keeps people wanting to turn the page, because we’re in competition with people’s time. When I’m editing my own work, I’m like, ‘Is this book worth lugging around the city? Is it worth the schlep?’”
In a past career, Gonzalez worked for about 13 years as a wedding planner. Orchestrating events for different kinds of clients across New York gave her insights into human nature and power. She decided to become a writer in her early 40s, funnelling her breadth of experience into stories filled with characters finding their way through the world and toward their dreams while contending with the intersections of privilege, race, and class, much like she has. Her next book, Need Blind: A Memoir of Class and Climbing in America—her first nonfiction book, coming in 2027—will examine this journey even more closely. “I was able to take all of that time observing people and how things work,” says Gonzalez, who was a Pulitzer finalist for her columns in The Atlantic. “Now, I can use it.”

These Two Brothers Are Fighting to Protect Immigrant Families After a Tragedy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:43 UTC
22:01:43 KST

For years, the Salgado house in Houston has been the place where the family gathers—for birthdays, holidays, and especially for New Year’s. “It's a house that my dad built for all of us,” says Ronaldo Salgado, 29. His father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, moved to the U.S. from Mexico more than 30 years ago with his wife and began working in construction, saving up for a home large enough to host future generations: their three sons and any grandchildren they might one day welcome.
This summer, the house was full again. Not for a celebration, but to mourn the death of Salgado Araujo. On the morning of July 7, the 52-year-old small-business owner was shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent while driving his crew to work. In the aftermath of the shooting, Ronaldo and his brother Lorenzo Jr., 27, estimate that 14 relatives from across Texas, Mexico, Alabama, and North Carolina convened at their family house. Now, it’s quiet. Salgado Araujo’s wife spends long hours at the altar the family created, sitting in silent mourning.
In their grief, the family is also awaiting answers. What they do know is that Salgado Araujo had breakfast and left to pick up his brother and other members of his crew. They know that two unmarked SUVs approached and pursued Salgado Araujo’s van, and that, eventually, an agent shot through the passenger-side window, striking him in the abdomen. Video footage shows him lying on the ground beside the van, surrounded by officers and calling for help. He died in the hospital.
There are critical questions that still need to be answered. ICE’s version of events conflicts with statements from the witnesses who were in the van that morning. An ICE spokesperson told TIME that Salgado Araujo refused directives from agents, rammed one of their cars, and attempted to run over an officer, who fired in self-defense. The passengers, all of whom were detained by ICE and have since been released, have said that no officers were in front of the vehicle or in any danger when he was shot. The agents were not wearing body cams. A department spokesperson stated that Salgado Araujo was not the person agents were looking for that day. The FBI, the Texas Rangers, the Harris County District Attorney’s office, and the ACLU, in partnership with the family, are all investigating the events of July 7. Harris County DA Sean Teare has said a grand jury will determine any charges. In an interview with TIME, Houston ACLU attorney David Donatti says the organization intends to file a claim.
“The lack of answers is an indignity in of itself,” Lorenzo Jr. says.
He and his brother don’t believe their father would have driven away if he’d been able to tell the SUVs were government vehicles. The family had a plan in place, on the off-chance Lorenzo Sr., who was undocumented, encountered ICE agents. He was supposed to call Ronaldo or his wife at the first opportunity. He kept paperwork in his van from his lawyers, meant to show he was pursuing the ability to work legally in the U.S.
“It’s that fear that people go to work with every day, that they’re going to be detained and won’t be able to see their family that evening,” Lorenzo Jr. says. “That used to be our biggest fear: my dad would get picked up, and we’d have no idea where he was for a few days.” He hangs his head for a moment and exhales. The family’s reality is so much worse than they ever thought to fear.
“Everyone has the inalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. For immigrants trying to achieve the American dream, regardless of status, they're entitled to that. Also, they’re entitled to due process,” Ronaldo says. “Unfortunately, the Department of Homeland Security, specifically ICE, isn’t following through on that promise.”
A spokesperson for DHS says, “All illegal aliens receive due process. We are applying the law as written by Congress. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them.”
Often, family members of those detained, injured, or killed by ICE are limited in how much they can speak out, for fear of having their own immigration status examined. Ronaldo and Lorenzo Jr. were born U.S. citizens, and feel a sense of responsibility to use their voices to call for change. Ronaldo has spoken at press conferences beside politicians; he and Lorenzo Jr. have appeared on broadcast news and testified at a congressional forum. Ronaldo wants to work on state legislation that will protect immigrant communities.
“I’m trying to use that anger and channel it in a more positive way,” says Ronaldo. “I feel right now that I can’t slow down, that I have to continue taking on these meetings, doing these interviews, doing anything I can just to get my dad's name out there, to shine a light as to what happened, to who my dad was, and the injustices that my dad experienced—that we're still experiencing to this day.”
Salgado Araujo had the equivalent of a middle school education when he came to the U.S. His sons say his greatest pride was their commitment to education. Ronaldo, a high school geography and history teacher, was set to move to Dallas for a “dream job” on Aug. 1. He was the last son still living at home with his parents, and he looked to the examples of his brothers—Lorenzo working as an engineer in D.C., their younger brother in college in Pennsylvania—and wanted to start a life in a new city like they did. The timing made sense: his father was talking about slowing down at work, and his parents were going to enjoy more time together, to enter the next phase of life. “I always had that fear: What if they need me? But it got to a point where I was like, You know what? My mom and dad, they’re fine. They have each other, and they’ll always have each other,” Ronaldo says, voice breaking. He resigned from the job he was set to begin so he can focus full-time on the work he’s doing in his father’s memory.
“This is not anything that any of us ever imagined happening, especially to us, especially to my dad, who was a decent citizen, regardless of status,” he says. “He loved this country, regardless of how much it discriminated against him.”
Ronaldo visits the site where his father was killed at least once a day, and every day he finds someone there who wants to talk. Sometimes it’s a neighbor, but often it’s a traveler from other parts of Texas, from Arizona, from New Mexico, from Minnesota. They tell Ronaldo their immigration stories and about the loved ones they’ve lost, they say that he and his brothers remind them of their own kids, or that Lorenzo Sr. reminds them of their own fathers. A few community members have dedicated themselves to tending to the makeshift memorial, watering the flowers, bringing their dinners outside to watch over things as the day winds down.
“This is all just to try to remember a man who worked all his life to give his family a better life,” Ronaldo says, “and to give his kids something to be proud of.”

How Cástulo de la Rocha Built an Affordable Health Care Empire
Unknown

When Cástulo de la Rocha arrived at the East LA Barrio Free Clinic in 1977, he had just moved back from Berkeley, where he’d gone to law school. “I pulled up in my old beat-up Volkswagen. I had long hair for sure, holes in my pants and things like that. So a very typical hippie,” he recalls. At the clinic, started by activists to provide free health care in Spanish to the Latino community, “I saw long lines of people waiting to get a number—a ticket early in the morning, so that they may see a volunteer physician at 4:30, 5:00 in the afternoon,” he says. “It could have been my mother, could have been my sisters. It could have been one of my family members.”
De la Rocha, who was born in Chihuahua, Mexico, and immigrated to East LA when he was 10 years old, was just a few years out of college and there to be the group’s first employee. Whether he’d still have a job after the first three months depended on whether he, as executive director, could drum up funding. For the next five decades, that’s what he did, as the small clinic expanded into what is now known as AltaMed Health Services, a major provider of health care in southern California and the nation's largest nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Center. Today, de la Rocha is CEO and president, and he estimates that AltaMed employs about 10,000 people and serves 700,000 patients over about 2 million visits annually.
Throughout his time at AltaMed, he has remained inspired by the energy and vision of the clinic’s founders and board members, who were young activists in their early 20s passionate about social justice. “They said we can make a difference,” he says. “There was a need for health care, and as long as we kept our doors open, continued to support the community, people kept coming. Here we are today. AltaMed is a very different organization, but we’ve never forgotten our roots and our commitment to the community.”

Marina Larroudé Is Disrupting the Fashion Industry One Shoe at a Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:43 UTC
22:01:43 KST

Despite having worked in the fashion industry for more than 25 years, Marina Larroudé, the co-founder and creative director of footwear brand Larroudé, has never been one to wear black. She chalks it up to her Brazilian upbringing.
Growing up in São Paulo, it was so hot that “wearing black was not even an option,” says the former fashion director turned shoe designer, 46, who has called New York City home for half her life. Out of both personal taste and necessity, she built herself a wardrobe full of lightweight fabrics in bold patterns and candy-colored shades. She now believes her whimsical style, a proud product of her background, was the key to her success in the fashion industry. “Having a different point of view was actually a strength—I really used that to my advantage,” she says.
Larroudé has taken that same approach with her namesake global footwear brand (pronounced lah-roo-DAY), which offers luxury shoes for between $290 and $590.
Larroudé and her co-founder, CEO, and husband, Ricardo Larroudé, then both unemployed, launched their debut collection in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic with just $4,000 and a Shopify site. They offered a selection of four styles: a knee-high boot, a chunky platform, a mule, and a pointed-toe ballet flat. The shoes came in black, ivory, and a few playful patterns, including a daisy print. While the floral pattern was more her style, the mother of two knew from her previous job working as vice president and fashion director at Barneys New York that neutral colors always sold best. Yet something unexpected happened after the COVID vaccine became available and people started going out again: the daisy print sold out. “It was like a revenge shopping situation,” she says.
The self-financed brand leaned into Marina’s style, designing shoes for those who were looking to have fun with fashion without sacrificing comfort. “I don’t want someone to buy a shoe from us and not wear it,” she says, which is why she hired a fellow Brazilian woman as head engineer to construct her shoes, which include wider toe boxes and memory foam soles, from scratch.
Building the construction internally instead of buying an existing model, which is the industry norm, was an expensive move that ended up paying off for the brand, whose famous fans include Taylor Swift, Selena Gomez, Alicia Keys, and former First Lady Jill Biden. As an entrepreneur, Marina believes she has to take risks in order to succeed. “If I play by the old playbook, I’m not going to get anywhere,” she says. “We are here to disrupt what no longer works.”
It’s not the only risk Marina took to grow her brand, which also designs handbags. At Ricardo’s suggestion, she moved away from the wholesale business model—the industry standard which prioritizes bulk orders from major retailers—and adopted a more sustainability-minded direct-to-consumer model. Customers are able to pre-order upcoming styles months in advance, allowing the company to streamline production processes and ensure minimal waste. “We see what the customers are responding to,” she says. “And then we chase that demand.”
By 2023, demand was so great that Marina and Ricardo opened a nearly 100,000 sq ft factory in Sapiranga, Brazil, where production, logistics, marketing, and administration all happen under one roof. In less than five years, Larroudé has grown from a five-person team to an operation of 750 employees. The brand with nine-digit revenue currently manufactures 500,000 shoes a year with a goal to manufacture a million pairs annually by 2028.
As the business continues to expand, supporting the Brazilian people behind the brand remains a priority. “To give prosperity back to a country,” Marina says, including by providing employees with comprehensive health benefits and opportunities for growth, “that, for me, is the silver lining.”

Ultimately, Zegler refuses to let anyone put her in a box. “I love playing fully formed humans with complexities,” she says. “Human beings deserve to be represented for their flaws as well as the things that make them wonderful—I kind of think they’re one and the same.”

Nelson German Has a Recipe for Shaking Up the Oakland Restaurant Scene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:42 UTC
22:01:42 KST

Chef Nelson German doesn’t believe in the idea of the “self-taught” culinarian.
“How can you really teach yourself?” asks the Dominican American executive chef and restaurateur. “Even if you’re learning from watching somebody on YouTube, that person taught you. A dishwasher, a prep cook, a server who instills you with some kind of knowledge—you’re learning from everybody around you.”
German, whose culinary career spans over two decades, cut his teeth training in several esteemed New York City kitchens. His profile as an emerging chef continued to rise after a stint on Season 18 of Bravo’s Top Chef in 2021, and today, German is best known for his steadily expanding culinary presence in Oakland, Calif. German believes his current portfolio, a trio of conceptual eateries inspired by and in celebration of his Afro-Latin roots, was only conceived because he stepped away from New York.
German, 45, grew up in the Washington Heights neighborhood of Manhattan, a cultural enclave for the Latin Caribbean community. In 2010, he relocated to the San Francisco Bay Area, his wife’s hometown. German says the culture shock coming from “Nueva Yol”—where it seems there are members of the Afro-Caribbean diaspora on every block—was jolting.
When homesickness hit a peak, German decided to harness the nostalgia and embrace his cultural heritage by honoring “the ingredients I missed the most” in his restaurants, alaMar Dominican Kitchen and Sobre Mesa.
“As chefs, to be recognized—at least back in the day—we were always taught to focus on European-centric food,” German says. “That [was] the only way to be well-known, to get the recognitions, to get the awards. That’s not true anymore.”
What has now earned German a Michelin recommendation and recognition from the James Beard Foundation is his innovation of traditional Afro-Latin dishes without compromising the flavorful Caribbean spice the culture is known for—in spite of the notion that fine dining must serve a flatter, Western palate. German’s promise to deliver cuisine authentic and accurate to history and cultural memory is in line with what he believes is a growing trend among chefs of color: deviating from the mainstream to create culinary experiences that are culturally and regionally hyperspecific.
The latest addition to German’s distinct offerings is the Ethiopian and Dominican fused Meski, a collaboration with entrepreneur Guma Fassil and Golden State Warriors forward Draymond Green, which opened in April 2025.
“We’re telling a real story,” German says.
The story that he wants to define his legacy is one of community, whether it’s nurturing young minds through culinary training programs or fostering togetherness through Caribbean fare. His first book, Caribbean Cocktails: Drinks and Bites from the Afro-Latino Diaspora, released in June, offers modern takes on familiar libations and is meant to inspire readers to “host the way we do it, as Caribbeans,” German says. Maintaining ancestral traditions is how he honors Sankofa, the Ghanaian principle adopted widely throughout the African Diaspora: “You always look back and celebrate your past while always continuing to move forward, and moving forward with love and kindness,” German says. “Always giving tribute to the people that paved the way for you.”

Julián Castro Is Bolstering Latino Communities One Grant at a Time
Unknown

2026-09-15

22:01:42 KST

Julián Castro has gotten a few things from his mother: a last name, a twin brother, a general sense of optimism, and a penchant for serving his community.
Maria del Rosario Castro, a now 79-year-old Mexican American activist, was once a member of La Raza Unida, a prominent Chicano political party in Texas. Her two sons, who were born in San Antonio in 1974, often accompanied her to rallies and meetings when they were young. “[She] raised my brother and me with this sense that you should always do well for yourself, but also do good for others,” Castro says.
For more than a decade, Castro used politics as an avenue to act on that sense. (The same goes for his brother, Joaquin, who has been a Texas congressman since 2013.) His resume includes a stint on the San Antonio city council, five years as mayor of the city, an appointment to President Barack Obama’s cabinet as the U.S. Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, and a 2020 presidential campaign.
But Castro, 51, recently started a new chapter in his career. He’s left politics behind—for now—and has entered the world of philanthropy. Since 2024, he has served as CEO of the Latino Community Foundation, an organization founded in 1989 that funds Latino-serving and Latino-led nonprofits in the U.S. He says that this opportunity has presented him with “a new way to do good for the community.”
One in five Americans are Latino, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center report, and the Latino Donor Collaborative found that this group alone was responsible for 28.2% of all U.S. economic growth in 2024. But this national impact is not reflected in the amount of philanthropic dollars invested back into the Latino community, which often remains below one percent.
Castro says that LCF is in the business of disrupting this status quo. “The country can only prosper if the community does well.”
In March, LCF, which primarily funds nonprofits based in California, announced a plan to expand its grant-making efforts nationally and establish a $250 million endowment—a sizable increase from the organization's current, "modest" $35 million endowment. Castro says that this new plan would ensure an annual grant-making baseline of $10 million and the ability “to serve many more organizations consistently.”
Castro says that as the Trump Administration and Immigration and Customs Enforcement continue their sweeping, sometimes fatal immigration crackdown across the U.S., the work of nonprofits has never been more important. In February, LCF launched the Community Protection Fund, issuing grants to grassroots organizations in California, Nevada, and Minnesota that are either offering assistance to families impacted by ICE’s actions or challenging detention abuses in court. This initiative was a no-brainer for Castro.
“Immigrant families and mixed-status families are under attack by an Administration absolutely determined to target both legal and undocumented immigrants, and sometimes even citizens. And so we decided to double down on investing in immigrant-serving nonprofits,” he says.
Though Castro feels deeply disappointed by how changes in immigration and deportation policies have affected Latino communities in the U.S., he hopes that Americans who feel the same will use this time to imagine a diverse, inclusive, and equitable future: “My hope is that the Latino Community Foundation, as it grows, can help accelerate that progress.”

Lukashenko dismisses rumors of political arrests following release of other prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:01:41 UTC
22:01:41 KST

MINSK, September 15. /TASS/. During talks with US Special Envoy for Belarus John Cole, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko dismissed as baseless reports that political arrests are taking place in the country following the release of people convicted of extremist-related crimes.
"Our 'runaways' are promoting this narrative in the West. From what I hear, I sense they have led you to believe that while we are releasing some people, we are simultaneously detaining twice as many to replace them as part of ongoing repression. I want to state publicly that this is absolutely untrue," Lukashenko said. A video clip of the talks was published by Pul_1, a Telegram channel close to the presidential press service.
"We have no intention of sending new people to correctional labor colonies to replace those who have been released. We do not have such a problem. We are not doing this, nor will we. These are our fellow Belarusians," Lukashenko emphasized.
He also pointed out that Belarus has no political prisoners, as the country’s legislation contains no such legal category.
"If any Belarusian citizens - or foreign nationals present here - violate Belarusian laws, we will certainly respond in accordance with the law. If they need to be placed under investigation or sent to correctional labor colonies, that is where they will be. But this has absolutely nothing to do with politics," Lukashenko stressed.
He said there was "no need to persecute anyone for political reasons" today.
