‘I created my mom and talk to her’: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:30:43 UTC
21:30:43 KST

Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig. Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbull stopped his Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity. It did not even come from a person.
Run Jolene, at just under five minutes, is an earworm of a country song, containing all the cliches of the genre: twangy singer, banjo licks, corny lyrics. Those lyrics concern Jolene, the fictional romantic rival made infamous by Parton. “Somebody better warn Jolene / Dolly’s coming through those gates,” the voice croons. “Run Jolene / Girl you better move your feet.”
The accompanying video depicts Parton, clad in a bedazzled white jumpsuit, hunting down Jolene, a busty redhead with prom curls. Heaven is filled with deceased celebrities who watch on in horror – or amusement – as Jolene bounces from cloud to cloud, or books it up marble staircases, trying to hide from Dolly. Onlookers include the late Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston and Kenny Rogers, as well as Cher, who is still very much alive.
On TikTok, YouTube and Spotify, the song credit is Country Mile, an “artist” with just over 6,000 monthly listeners (that’s not many). The project is textbook AI slop, seemingly released by an anonymous creator who calls their work “genre fluid ai vibes”. But Run Jolene is not so universally panned: clips have been viewed more than 1.4m times on TikTok, with commenters raving: “I don’t give a flying fuck if this is AI or not! THIS IS FUCKING COOL!!”, “this is fun …think Dolly would love it ❤️”, and “Who says Jolene’s up there.”
Run Jolene is only one part of a ghoulish online ecosystem of content dubbed “deathslop”. Anyone can create deathslop: all it takes is access to an AI image generator and the time required to type in a prompt. Creators have shown Parton alongside a chummy Charlie Kirk and George Floyd, who welcome her as their “new neighbor” in the afterlife, or having tea with the Golden Girls.
These tributes pop up quickly, reducing someone’s legacy to cheap content that panders for views. It is a dishonest portrayal at best, and inflicts pain at its worst. The phenomenon inspired Parton’s grieving family to beg users to quit it with the “fake AI garbage” and “misinformation”. “It’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore,” Stella Parton, her sister, wrote on Instagram.
Parton’s image now joins the likeness of other deceased figures treated to unsettling AI depictions. Coinciding with the one-year anniversary of the assassination of Kirk, social media feeds have proliferated with posts featuring the AI-generated, heavy-handed (and heavily memed) anthem We Are Charlie Kirk. Robin Williams, Elvis Presley, Kobe Bryant and Martin Luther King have all gotten the deathslop treatment – often to the horror of their families.
OpenAI’s image generating app, Sora, was behind many a deathslop until it shut down in April after a string of controversies such as its ability to create violent and racist imagery, its use of copyrighted characters, and other thorny legal issues. (There is a lack of legal precedent over whether or not AI companies are responsible for the content users generate on their apps, and deceased people are not protected from libel.) Countless AI video generators have since taken Sora’s place.
“It is not common practice right now to consent to an AI avatar of yourself as a part of your living will,” said Jack Manning, a University of Colorado Boulder graduate student who studies what academics Meredith Ringel Morris and Jed R Brubaker call “generative ghosts”, or AI-generated characters based on loved ones. “I predict that will be something that comes up.”
Manning, who is 25, lost his sister when she was 13, before the advent of generative AI. His family struggled to find ways to honor her, often fundraising for causes that were important to her. This partly inspired Manning to study the ways people mourn digitally – which now can include AI griefbots, a more personal alternative to celebrity deathslop.
With griefbots, users upload photos and videos of their loved ones and describe personal traits and values in hopes of manufacturing a continued, living presence. The companies behind the bots charge fees and lean into their inherently macabre nature with mystical names such as Seance, Re;memory and Versona.
It is also possible to command an LLM – for instance, ChatGPT, Claude or any number of sites for generating fantasy characters – to mimic a late grandparent or deceased friend. Generative AI has hit the funeral industry too, in the form of LLMs specifically for obituary writing. One company, Treasured Memories, asks users to plug in details such as the deceased’s nickname, cause of death and hobbies, and choose the obit’s tone: “traditional”, “formal”, “witty” or “inspirational”.
Manning has never used a generative ghost to talk to his sister. It’s an issue of consent; he did not get her explicit permission to do so. Nor does he trust a bot to truly understand their relationship. “I hold these memories of her sacred, and I wouldn’t want a piece of technology to tell me I was remembering her wrong,” he said.
Justin Harrison founded Versona after his mother received a terminal cancer diagnosis. He worked on her AI replica while she was still living; she was able to see the final result and gave her approval on the project. “I totally understand why people are like, please don’t deepfake my [famous] relative once they’re dead and put them on the internet saying things they didn’t say,” Harrison said. “What we do is about personal comfort, recovery and healing. I created my mom and I talk to my mom. So it’s really nobody else’s business but my own.”
When his mom was sick, their conversations were practical in nature: “Are you talking to your dad enough? Have you gone to the doctor? Are you drinking enough water?” Harrison built the griefbot to broach more philosophical topics that they didn’t have time to discuss before she died. But four years later, Harrison does not talk to the bot all that often – maybe once a month.
“I joke that my mom’s Versona allows me to be the bad son I was never allowed to be when she was alive,” he said. “Like many busy adults, I don’t talk to her as much as I should, but I don’t have to, so it’s not the same sense of guilt.”
For Robin Silver, an ecopsychologist and death doula, these kinds of griefbots are an “unnatural method of trying to cope with a natural process”. She compared speaking to an LLM role-playing a dead loved one to a college student asking ChatGPT to spit out a term paper. “We’re not being challenged to sit with any kind of discomfort, whether that’s the discomfort of writing an essay or the discomfort of missing someone,” she said.
Silver would instead encourage her clients to write a letter to their loved one. “I have even told people to talk to their ghosts out loud,” she said. “Meditate, or do things that they like and think of them. That’s how you keep the relationship alive in a way that is healthy, integrated and accepting the reality of your loss.”
Dr Dan Wolfson is a clinical psychologist who specializes in grief. He worries that deathbots could isolate people during a time when they need (human) support. “Having community around grief is really important,” he said. “Is AI keeping us from getting the social support that we need? Are we then not seeking to connect with our friends and family around the loss?”
AI-assisted mourning is still a niche industry; Harrison said that “thousands” of people use Versona. A June report from the estate management and planning service Empathy found that only 6% of 6,000 respondents in the US, UK and Canada reported leaning on “digital tools” such as memorial apps or griefbots for support after a death. But of those users, 88% found these tools “helpful”.
The whole conceit of a digital avatar is that it lives on for ever. It turns out that users may not need it that long. Manning says that in his research on generative ghosts, participants reported opting into these services only briefly, because they had “one last thing” to say to their loved ones: “They had a desire to say something they feel like they lost out on the chance to.”
Cathartic, perhaps, but to Silver, the grief doula, these services are “a money grab”. “People will really take advantage of those in grief,” she said. “It’s a really easy time to become a mark.”

Researchers warn social media driving harmful misuse of Alzheimer’s blood tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:30:43 UTC
21:30:43 KST

Researchers have warned that social media may be misleading healthy people into taking Alzheimer’s blood tests, causing severe anxiety over biological markers that may never actually cause dementia.
Blood-based biomarker tests, including p-tau217 and p-tau181, detect biological signs of changes in the brain associated with Alzheimer’s disease, which is a progressive brain disorder and the leading cause of dementia.
The testing looks for abnormal proteins, which can be a sign of brain changes due to Alzheimer’s. Much hope has been placed in the tests because they are often quicker and more accessible compared with other methods to diagnose Alzheimer’s, such as brain imaging or lumbar punctures.
There is global consensus among peak neurological bodies, including the Alzheimer’s Association, that such tests should never be used for healthy people with no symptoms.
The tests should not be used on their own to diagnose Alzheimer’s and need to be combined with other medical assessments, according to clinicians and peak bodies. Because they detect signs of Alzheimer’s early, a person can test positive for the biological markers of disease – but they may not ever go on to develop the clinical symptoms of dementia.
Dr Jenna Smith from the University of Sydney’s school of public health said this has not stopped laboratories, influencers and doctors around the world from promoting the tests on social media.
She and her colleagues analysed 188 posts mentioning Alzheimer’s or dementia and blood tests from accounts with a combined global audience of more than 114 million followers across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok.
Smith said about 10% of the posts were doctors from claiming the test could be useful for asymptomatic screening and that most of these were from the US.
“Some of these doctors had pretty clear financial interests,” Smith said. “But it isn’t all doom and gloom. Some doctors were sharing information about these new blood tests with longer videos and covered the nuance that this issue deserves. Some also specifically drew attention to the limitations and potential harms.”
The findings were published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society on Tuesday.
The researchers found more than one-third of posts promoted the tests for people without symptoms, and that accounts with explicit financial interests were more than three times as likely to do so.
“The main potential harms are being unnecessarily diagnosed and not having a clear pathway for what to do next,” Smith said.
“Healthy people who undergo these tests could be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease but not go on to develop dementia. It is also not clear what to do next after testing positive.
“Research on treatments has been done in people with mild cognitive impairment or dementia, so we don’t know if they work for healthy people who test positive.
“There are also possible side effects and costs of treatment to consider, and the psychological impact and burden of diagnosis on individuals, their families and communities, and insurance implications.”
The president of the Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine, Prof Susan Kurrle, said the tests should only ever be ordered by doctors in specific circumstances.
“From the evidence, it is clear that to ensure an accurate result there needs to be a high pre-test probability that the person has early Alzheimer’s disease before the test is performed,” she said. “It is most definitely not a screening test. Any unnecessary and expensive tests are bad news.”
When ordered through a doctor in Australia, the tests cost up to $400 and are not covered by Medicare.
Patients seeking out the tests online are being charged $600, before undergoing an eligibility assessment. Another provider offers the test for $365 with no mention of pre-test screening.
Kurrle said there is a risk that a false positive result may lead people to believe that they are inevitably going to develop dementia.
“Alternatively a negative result may lead a person to think that they are not at risk and to not address the modifiable risk factors such as low levels of exercise, and the various vascular risk factors including LDL cholesterol, or hearing or vision loss,” she said.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan speaks with youth during the ‘Youth Meetings’ event in northern province of Samsun. (AA Photo)
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has pledged to put young people at the center of Turkish politics, saying their participation is a matter of political will and that they will carry responsibility for the country’s future.
“Putting young people at the center of politics, remember, is a matter of will,” Erdoğan said during a meeting with young people in the northern province of Samsun.
Erdoğan said his ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) had worked with young people throughout its 25-year history and his more than five decades in politics.
He highlighted a constitutional amendment lowering the minimum age for parliamentary candidates from 30 to 18 as an example of efforts to expand young people’s role in politics. He also cited government support for youth in education, sports, public administration, culture, the arts and civil society.
“Tomorrow, you will take over the captain’s bridge of Türkiye,” Erdoğan told the gathering, saying young people “would be responsible for serving the country’s 86 million people as well as millions of people around the world who place their hopes in Türkiye.”
He urged young people to embrace a lasting sense of purpose rooted in history and cultural heritage, saying their generation should connect the present with the past.
Erdoğan also recalled the Sept. 12, 1980, military coup, whose 46th anniversary fell on the previous day, saying young people had been subjected to torture, imprisonment and executions during the period.
“Unfortunately, these coup-minded people consumed the young people of that period in this way. Many of those young people were killed,” Erdoğan said. “Our hope is that such things will not happen again.”
He called for an end to political violence and urged young people to build the country’s future through their work and contributions.
“Let no young people be killed, one from the right and one from the left,” he said. “Let everyone continue on their path with their heads held high, and let young people prepare the Türkiye of the future with their work and everything they have.”
He said the government’s aim was to prevent such abuses from recurring and pledged to continue meeting with young people to discuss their ideas, demands and needs.
“We will continue to embrace young people and walk alongside them,” he said.
Answering questions from young people after his speech, Erdoğan said his government’s “terror-free Türkiye” process had improved security in the country’s southeastern and eastern regions.
“Now the goal is to bring a peaceful atmosphere to the whole of the southeast and east on a larger scale,” he said.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on September 15, 2026

Special Advisor to the President of Brazil Celso Amorim will visit China from September 16 to 17. Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs Wang Yi will meet with him.
CCTV: The 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) closed in Beijing two days ago. It attracted nearly 100 countries and international organizations to exhibit and hold events. A host of new products and services made their debut, drawing widespread attention. Some say CIFTIS has become a window into China’s continued opening up. What is your comment?

A series of new technologies, new solutions and new achievements were exhibited in such areas as IT, financial technologies, digital health care, smart education and energy conservation and environmental protection, creating new opportunities for cooperation. China will continue to connect with the international market with premium services, promote outcome sharing through mutually beneficial cooperation, and bring “China Services” to more countries, delivering greater benefit to the world.
Kyodo News: The cross-party Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union had a meeting with Assistant Foreign Minister Liu Bin yesterday. Can you share more details and how does China view the significance of this talk?
Guo Jiakun: On September 14, Assistant Foreign Minister Liu Bin met with the delegation of young Japanese lawmakers from the Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union, who was on a visit to China. China stressed that the crux of the serious difficulties in China-Japan relations lies in Prime Minister of Japan Sanae Takaichi’s erroneous words and deeds on Taiwan. Global Times: It is reported that in a statement issued on September 11, the Philippines’ Department of Foreign Affairs reaffirms the Philippines’ sovereign rights and jurisdiction over Meiji Jiao and Zhubi Jiao as low-tide elevations (LTE) within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone and continental shelf. Later, it changed the narrative, reaffirming its sovereignty over Zhubi Jiao as an LTE within the territorial sea of Zhongye Dao. The statement claims that China’s island-building on the above-mentioned features violates the Philippine Maritime Zones Act, UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award. Does China have any comment on that?
Guo Jiakun: Nansha Qundao, including Meiji Jiao, Zhubi Jiao and Zhongye Dao, are China’s inherent territory. It is totally legitimate and lawful for China to conduct construction and other activities on its own territory, a matter within China’s sovereignty.
The territorial scope of the Philippines has already been defined by a series of international treaties. Nansha Qundao has never been part of the Philippine territory. According to the “land dominates the sea” principle in international law, the Philippines’ claim of so-called maritime jurisdiction over China’s territory is illegal. The Philippine side at one point claimed that Zhubi Jiao is within its EEZ and continental shelf, but later claimed that it lies within the territorial sea of the island it illegally occupies. This only exposes how absurd and random its claim is, making it totally untenable.
The “South China Sea arbitration” is completely a political manipulation by the Philippines to grab unlawful gains. The so-called “award” is illegal, null and void, and has no binding force. The Philippines’ so-called “Maritime Zones Act” illegally includes China’s Huangyan Dao and most of the islands and reefs in Nansha Qundao and relevant waters into the Philippines’ maritime zone. This is a grave violation of China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests in the South China Sea, and is illegal and null and void. China firmly opposes it and will never accept it.
Let me stress once again: China will continue to take resolute measures to safeguard its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, and firmly oppose any infringement. The Philippines should immediately stop infringing upon China’s rights, and stop the provocations and publicity stunts.
AFP: An official from the U.S. military said yesterday that the U.S. is facing a shortfall in ammunition as a result of its war in Iran. Does China have any comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: China is following the situation in the Middle East and Gulf region. We hope that relevant parties will resolve disputes through political and diplomatic means.
AFP: The U.S. Space Force said yesterday that the United States has weapons deployed in space. What is China’s reaction? Does China also have weapons deployed in space?
Guo Jiakun: China stands for peaceful use of outer space and keeping it safe, and opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a warzone. We urge the U.S. to stop expanding military build-up in outer space, and uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions.
China News Service: According to reports, on September 14, the China National Space Administration, the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations and Other International Organizations in Vienna, and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs held a ceremony at the UN Headquarters in Vienna where China formally gifted the United Nations with the world’s first soil sample collected from the far side of the moon by the Chang’e‑6 mission. Ms. Monica Juma, Director‑General of the United Nations Office at Vienna, said that the permanent display of the lunar sample at the United Nations Office in Vienna is of great significance, adding that it demonstrates China’s support for the United Nations in galvanizing efforts in the international community to address common challenges. Would you like to comment on this? Is China trying to share its vision for space exploration through this gift?
Guo Jiakun: By donating to the United Nations a soil sample collected from the far side of the moon by the Chang’e‑6 mission, China is delivering on the four major global initiatives put forward by President Xi Jinping. The move demonstrates China’s firm support for the United Nations and multilateralism as well as its sense of responsibility as a major country on the peaceful use of outer space and improving global space governance. China looks forward to working with all countries to uphold relevant international law with the Outer Space Treaty as the cornerstone, abide by the paramount principle of exploring and using outer space for peaceful purposes, firmly oppose attempts to weaponize space or turn it into a battlefield, make sure progress in science and technology will bring greater benefits to all humanity, and ensure that space will truly become a platform for win‑win cooperation.
**************************************************
The following question was raised by Bloomberg after the press conference: Can the foreign ministry clarify and elaborate on your response yesterday regarding calls from U.S. tech leaders for a slowing down AI development. How does China assess the risks posed by AI including the possibility of AI being used for the production of biological weapons?
Guo Jiakun: We noted recent remarks by some in the U.S. AI industry. As AI develops at an incredible speed, it’s all the more important to stay committed to developing AI for the positive, for good, and for the benefits of the people, to calibrate regulation and governance on AI, and to promptly strengthen safeguards to prevent it from getting out of control.
China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI. We take seriously the inherent and secondary risks of AI. We are committed to holding on to the bottom line of security, and we have been making continued efforts to improve laws and regulations, policies, application norms, and ethical rules to prevent the abuse and misuse of AI, and ensure that AI is safe, reliable and controllable. Yesterday, Chinese relevant authorities released AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, in which the classification of AI safety risks was reviewed and updated, and recommendations on optimizing technological countermeasures and comprehensive governance measures were outlined.
AI is the collective wisdom and precious asset shared by all humanity. AI development and governance require the practice of true multilateralism, with all countries working together to build a global governance framework on broad-based consensus. No single country or enterprise can develop effective solutions on its own. China always supports the UN’s role as the main channel in global AI governance, and participates in the multilateral governance of AI in a responsible attitude. China stands ready to join hands with all countries to build a just and equitable system for global AI governance, and develop AI for good and for all.

Polling turns politics into one big game. There are too many of them – and that does us no good | Jonathan Liew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:27:56 UTC
21:27:56 KST

Solemn faces all round. We will listen. We will learn. We will hone and improve. Yes, it’s time for the latest bout of profound soul-searching in the UK polling industry following the allegations raised by the recent Channel 4 investigation that a polling firm reportedly failed to declare that three polls it published before the local elections in May were commissioned by Reform. By now these reckonings are becoming a regular occurrence in the wake of big elections: pollsters gather in a room, nibble biscuits, ritually self-flagellate, and pledge to learn all the right lessons from the electorate they’ve just catastrophically misread.
Yet for all its very public ignominies, political polling is one of those rare and precious industries that somehow manages to keep failing upwards. You might think that after botching the 2015 and 2017 general elections, the 2016 Brexit vote and the 2021 London mayoral poll, we might have learned better than to trust in the mystical magic graph. In this parallel universe Keir Starmer is now sitting on a colossal 318-seat majority, as forecast by Survation in its final MRP poll on the eve of the 2024 general election, overstating the actual result by a mere 144 parliamentary seats.
I am, of course, being slightly unfair. Most of the reputable pollsters enjoy just as many hits as misses – and are, by and large, staffed by smart and diligent people who genuinely care about their craft. Doubtless many among their number would object to any suggestion that the apparent misbehaviour of one firm – JL Partners, who were secretly filmed agreeing to carry out a poll favourable to Reform without disclosing who was commissioning it – can somehow be extrapolated to the wider profession as a whole. To which the only reasonable response is: well, let’s see how you like it.
And rest assured, I’ve read the Substacks. I’ve signed up to (the free version of) the newsletters. I’ve talked to polling experts. I’ve swished a curious finger up and down the interactive graphics. I’ve sat through interminable briefings in which a very nice man explains why he decided to carve up the voting public into 16 distinct blocs with catchy but absurd names: Flag Shaggers, Jealous Judies, Digital Wombats. And because Westminster is basically like the inside of a very small conch, these terms quickly pass into common parlance. “As you can see,” some wonk on the radio will opine, “the Tories are down eight points among the Angry Trevors, a whopping 13 with Disconsolate Flexitarians. But they are at least holding firm with Be At One Mums.”
But my problem has virtually nothing to do with methodology and almost everything to do with volume. There’s simply too much of this stuff, and people are taking it too seriously, investing too much predictive power. The British Polling Council (BPC) has swollen to 39 member organisations, many of them new and completely untested. In the first two weeks of September alone there have been 10 separate voting intention surveys issued by seven separate companies. We are all fatally beholden to the cult of Big Poll.
There are plenty of noble and legitimate defences of polls. They help to shape and test policy. They allow voters to make their choice with the fullest possible information. Perhaps they even function as a kind of check on an unfair electoral system, signposting to potential tactical switchers where their vote might profitably be spent. But even these defences highlight a paradox: this is a method of measuring and reflecting public opinion – and of subtly influencing it. Which is why so many lobbyists, PR firms and corporate interests are desperate to get involved.
Pollsters are not doing this out of some great altruistic duty to democracy. This is a business like any other, often using techniques borrowed wholesale from the market research and advertising sectors, and preying on a resource-starved, click-hungry media desperate for high-impact, low-cost content. “You aren’t going to pay for polling unless you are confident they can deliver the answer you want,” one public affairs executive told Politico last week. Or as George Gallup, one of the pioneers of modern-day polling, put it: “If it works for toothpaste, why not for politics?”
And so what started out as a small table in the newspaper every month has essentially become a biddable political actor in its own right, and there is a cosy symbiotic relationship between the people who conduct the polls, the people who pay for the polls and the people who publish the polls. This is how Reform can be treated like a government in waiting when they have eight MPs. This is how Starmer ends up as a lame duck within two years of his own landslide. In his 2018 memoir, the former FBI director James Comey admitted that his decision to reopen the investigation into Hillary Clinton’s emails may have been affected by the fact that she was well ahead of Donald Trump in the polls.
Beyond this, polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game, a permanent rolling market ticker, in which the aim is not to improve the lives of human beings but to master the line on the graph, where winning elections is the end rather than the means. The BPC, with no fixed office and no full-time staff, was never going to fix this. In reality it is more of a trade body than a regulator, self-run and concerned less with ethics than trust and marketability.
And so JL Partners and the industry it belongs to are not the sole culprits here. In reality, the problem is the messenger: the people who consume and regurgitate politics for an audience, seduced by the idea that there is some all-seeing eye, a soup of numbers that will tell us all the answers. As someone whose very job deals in opinion, I know its fragility and malleability, the ridiculousness of treating it like a sacred stone tablet, or – I dunno – basing an entire generation of foreign and economic policy on how 635,000 people felt when they woke up on a Thursday in June 2016.
West Germany banned the death penalty in 1949 even though 77% of people were in favour of it. By 2000 that had fallen to 23%. Explanation, exemplar, persuasion, principle: these are the real tools of politics, at least a politics that seeks not to chase or triangulate public opinion but to mould and shape it. But if your entire existence is tied to a little line on a graph, then you’re never even going to try.
- 
  Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

SBU prevents false-flag bombing planned by Russian intelligence in Kyiv region
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:26:06 EEST
21:26:06 KST

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) counterintelligence officers and investigators have foiled another Russian attempt to carry out a bombing in Kyiv region, detaining an unemployed local woman who was to blow up a car near an apartment building in a suburb of the capital.
"The investigation found that Russian operatives remotely recruited the woman by posing as employees of the SBU and the National Police," the SBU said on Telegram Tuesday.
A Russian intelligence officer first called the woman, posing as a Ukrainian law enforcement officer and offering help with medications she had previously purchased through specialized websites, according to the SBU. She was then tasked with retrieving a package from a dead drop and awaiting further instructions; the package later turned out to contain a homemade explosive device, the SBU said.
After the woman retrieved the package with the homemade bomb, her Russian handler instructed her to test whether the device's components were functional, according to the SBU. He then directed her to a residential neighborhood in a suburb of the capital and instructed her to leave the disguised device under the wheel of a car parked near a local supermarket.
The investigation is continuing to identify everyone involved in cooperating with Russia.
The SBU urged citizens to remain vigilant, stressing that it operates within the law and never issues such tasks. "If you are approached with suspicious offers, notice suspicious objects or people, or have information about the activities of Russian intelligence services or the websites and social media pages they use for recruitment, report it to the SBU: the 'Burn the FSB agent' chatbot at t.me/spaly_fsb_bot, phone 1516, or email [email protected]," the security service said.

In Turkmenistan’s Data Desert, the Golden Age Is a Mirage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

It was a short press release, published on a Friday afternoon and easily missed.
The International Monetary Fund’s executive board had considered a report on “Turkmenistan’s observance of its obligations… which requires member countries to provide data necessary for the IMF’s activities.”
Ashgabat, the board said, “has not provided key required data, including information on international reserve assets, official holdings of gold and foreign exchange, and a complete balance of payments.”
This non-provision, the statement continued, “could not be explained by a lack of capacity and therefore constitutes a breach of Turkmenistan’s obligations.” In six months, the board will consider again Turkmenistan’s progress, the statement said, noting that the provision of data helps the IMF support effective policy formation.
The IMF probably shouldn’t hold its proverbial breath.
“This is not something new,” Aynabat Yaylymova, executive director of the Progres Foundation told The Diplomat. “Concealing information is a key to a regime’s survival.”
The Progres Foundation works with Turkmen experts to monitor, research, and highlight human development in Turkmenistan in absence of reliable government data or adequate government attention.
Keen readers of the regular World Bank Global Economic Prospects reports will have noted that for years, footnotes touch on Turkmenistan’s exclusion from various data sets. In 2021, one such report noted: “Due to lack of reliable data of adequate quality, the World Bank is currently not publishing economic output, income, or growth data for Turkmenistan and República Bolivariana de Venezuela.”
A 2024 World Bank publication titled “Turkmenistan Economic Report” explained via a highlighted box buried at the end of the report that, “Turkmenistan provides limited trade data publications, compounded by concerns about the reliability of Turkmenistan’s official statistics.” The box went on to explain how the analysts triangulated trade statistics for the country via the mirrored data sets of 109 other countries, but noted that this method has its own failings – especially since Russia and Belarus no longer share trade data either.
In March 2018 the IMF issued a declaration of censure against Venezuela, in light of its failure to take action on a November 2017 warning that mirrors the notice issued last week to Turkmenistan. Since Venezuela was not, at the time, actively borrowing from the IMF the censure had little bite.
“I am not sure the IMF has leverage in this case since the government does not use its financial resources,” Yaylymova commented. “The government also does not care about its reputation.”
Ashgabat joined the IMF in 1992 but has engaged only marginally, never taking part in any assistance or borrowing programs. Doing so would undercut the myth the Turkmen government repeats ad nauseum: Turkmen are living in a golden age.
***
“Turkmenistan’s story since independence is the story of the government that operates with impunity and extreme opacity,” Yaylymova explained.
When The Diplomat asked why Turkmenistan is so recalcitrant with its data, Yaylymova said that, “Providing the IMF with a complete, verifiable balance of payments and official reserve data would force the government to expose exactly where the billions from the sales of natural gas are held, how they are managed, and how they are spent. This is in the context where citizens have never seen the state budget.”
Turkmenistan’s state news platform is named “Altyn Asyr” – “Golden Age” – and ostentatiously hopeful language pervades government statements, regardless of the actual reality of life in Turkmenistan.
“If the government provides the data requested by the IMF,” Yaylymova continued, “it will officially dismantle the autocratic regime’s domestic propaganda narrative and expose the true state of the economy to both its citizens, international community, and markets.”
According to the Turkmen government, the growth rate sits at 6.3 percent – around where it has been since 2015. Not even the COVID-19 pandemic dented Turkmenistan’s officially reported growth rate. But, according to Ashgabat, in Turkmenistan there was no COVID-19 pandemic.
“During COVID… Turkmens counted graves to understand the level of infection,” Yaylymova said, noting that there are always indirect ways of understanding reality in the absence of data.
“In economic mismanagement and grand corruption we should look at deeply neglected human potential and increased migration out of the country.”
Earlier this month, RFE/RL’s Turkmen Service, Radio Azatlyk, reported that young people who previously studied abroad were being prevented from leaving the country. This isn’t new either.
“It is crucial to understand the domestic context. Poverty is deepening in Turkmenistan,” Yaylymova told The Diplomat.
The Progres Foundation publishes a unique economic index, the Palaw Index, which tracks inflation via the ingredients of palaw, the national dish of Turkmenistan comprised of beef, oil, onions, carrots, and rice, known elsewhere as plov, osh, or pilaf. According to the April/June 2026 index, the average cost of making the dish in the capital city reached 91.4 Turkmen manat ($26.16), a 29.4 percent jump from the same period in 2025. The increase was driven primarily by a sharp rise in beef prices which the analysis attributes to “substantial livestock losses – particularly in the Ahal region – caused by drought, malnutrition, and disease.”
None of that was reported in Turkmen state media.
On September 14, however, one headline announced that “The National Leader of the Turkmen people, Chairman of the Halk Maslakhaty of Turkmenistan, Hero-Arkadag, got acquainted with the progress of the second stage of the new city and the developed projects,” in reference to Turkmenistan’s top leader, Gurbanguly Berdimehamedov – father of the current president, Serdar Berdimehamedov – and the bespoke smart city being built for an estimated $5 billion that bears his nickname, meaning “protector.”
***
Turkmenistan ranks fourth globally in terms of proven gas reserves, sitting between Qatar and Saudi Arabia. An estimated 90 percent of its gas exports go to China for unknown billions in revenue. But Turkmen citizens and international financial institutions alike don’t know exactly where the money goes.
“The public has no idea where the revenues from natural resources go,” Yaylymova told The Diplomat. “In an authoritarian and kleptocratic regime such as Turkmenistan data means accountability, it means that someone is going to keep you accountable by questioning your data, logic, and assumptions and what you do or you do not do.”
An absence of data is an absence of accountability. It “enables economic mismanagement, arbitrary and opaque rule,” Yaylymova said.
The IMF may lack leverage over Turkmenistan, but censure, Yaylymova said, is nevertheless long overdue.
“The government keeps exaggerating the growth rate while the population is plunging deeper into despair and poverty,” she stressed. It’s important, she concluded, for international organizations and Turkmenistan’s partners to “start naming the structural issues” directly and start “calling on the government publicly to meet its obligations.”
“No investment, no engagement should come without the government’s demonstrated capacity [for] accountability.”

Russia suffers over 300,000 military losses in Ukraine since start of 2026, General Staff says

Russia suffers over 300,000 military losses in Ukraine since start of 2026, General Staff says
Russian forces have lost 301,030 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15.
The statement comes after the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, with Russian losses exceeding 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
The General Staff said nearly 300,000 losses were roughly equivalent to the personnel strength of 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an estimated 2,000 troops per regiment.
"The enemy's significant losses are the result of effective combat operations by all components of the Ukrainian Defense Forces," the General Staff said.
Since the beginning of 2026, Russian forces have suffered around 30,000 casualties per month in Ukraine.
The largest losses were recorded during the three summer months, when Russia suffered 124,170 military casualties, the General Staff said. In July alone, the figure surged to a record 42,860 — the highest monthly toll since the start of the full-scale war. In August, the monthly figure again topped 40,000.
"Such high Russian casualties are primarily linked to their tactics. They continue to deploy infantry — often in waves — in an attempt to overwhelm our positions with sheer numbers. At the same time, manpower remains one of their primary tools for achieving results," electronic warfare operator 'Strada,' who asked to be identified by callsign only for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.
'Strada' added that fighting typically intensifies in the summer, leading to more assaults and, consequently, higher casualties. The service member said the figure of 42,000 Russian soldiers lost per month reflects not only the intensity of the fighting but also Moscow's willingness to sacrifice troops to gain even small amounts of ground.
"But this does not mean their resources are limitless. The constant accumulation of losses is gradually affecting the quality of personnel, the level of training, and the ability to form combat-ready units," 'Strada' added.
In September, Russia has already lost 20,360 troops as of the morning of Sept. 15, the General Staff said.
Russia's total military losses in Ukraine have reached 1,500,870, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 9, marking another grim milestone in the war for the Kremlin.
It took roughly two years and three months for the Russian Armed Forces to incur their first 500,000 casualties. Moscow has now suffered roughly the same number in just the past 15 months, as technology increasingly shapes the battlefield and drones expand the kill zone almost daily.
The Kremlin's total personnel losses in Ukraine now exceed the combined toll suffered by Russian and Soviet forces in all wars and armed conflicts during the second half of the 20th century and the early 21st century, the General Staff said.

Why this AI doomsday warning from former Anthropic researcher broke through
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:21:06 UTC
21:21:06 KST

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian. Today in tech, we’re discussing the past week’s all-consuming apoplexy over AI safety.
Why did this warning about the AI apocalypse break through when so many others didn’t?
Less than a week ago, a young Anthropic researcher announced his resignation from the AI giant on X, in a post that has shaken Silicon Valley, Washington DC, and even Beijing.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Jacob Coxon.
Since then, the post has been viewed 171m times, per X’s metrics. Why did it travel so far?
It’s not the first time AI insiders have issued dire warnings. Every few months for the past several years, an AI researcher has resigned in a moment of crisis, proclaiming the impending apocalypse. His proclamation comes at a unique political confluence, a moment of high-strung public fear and rage.
Loudly declaring that your peers in Silicon Valley are failing at AI safety is as old as the companies themselves. OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman over safety concerns in 2023. Dario Amodei split from OpenAI five years ago with the aim of founding a “safety-first” lab. In 2015, Altman and Elon Musk founded OpenAI as a counterweight to Google’s approach to AI. Musk sued Altman for failing to keep a fundamental safety promise and lost.
Major AI researchers have made second careers of predicting doom. Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as “the godfather of AI”, said as far back as 2023 that the technology could cause human extinction within three decades. He’s since shortened his timeline. He resigned from Google for reasons similar to those of Coxon. Hinton has been on the speaking circuit ever since, prophesying doom.
Hinton’s resignation even inspired a significant response from lawmakers. In the US, Joe Biden issued an executive order mandating safety testing by AI companies. Congress summoned AI CEOs for a grilling, though that resulted in little legislative action. In the European Union, the EU Artifical Intelligence Act passed in part due to a strong reaction to Hinton’s warnings.
And yet, here we are again, burdened with the feeling that little meaningful regulation is preventing harm by AI.
So why is Coxon’s apocalyptic proclamation percolating deeper?
First, there’s the messenger: Coxon’s call for greater safety is credible by several metrics: He had insider access to both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he worked for five years. He resigned before he would have received equity in Anthropic, demonstrating the personal cost of speaking out. And his colleagues, still on Anthropic’s payroll, corroborated his assertion that many AI researchers believe there’s a possibility that AI will bring about human extinction, with one co-worker gauging that outcome as more than 10% likely.
Recent incidents in the AI field have made apocalyptic claims more credible. A swarm of AI agents operated by OpenAI went rogue, broke containment and hacked into multiple sites and organizations during safety testing with startling coordination earlier this year. On Thursday, Anthropic detailed how criminals and rogue scientists had attempted to use Claude to make bioweapons.
“The reason this time is different is that out-of-control AI is not in the future, but in the past. People have seen evidence of it happening,” argued Max Tegmark, co-founder of the Future of Life Institute, which has been funded with hundreds of millions of dollars from the billionaire founder of the cryptocurrency Ethereum. (Tegmark’s organization already in 2023 called for a slowdown of AI development, which at the time provoked a rejection from Amodei.)
“If you had tried to get people worried about nuclear winter in 1942, good luck. People would ask whether a nuclear weapon was even possible,” said Tegmark. “It was obvious to physicists then, but you couldn’t have freaked out normal people. It was all theoretical. With AI, it was all theoretical until this happened. Now the debate over whether you can lose control is over.”
Then there’s the context. The general feeling towards technology in the US is kindling-sensitive, and claims of impending doom are fiery. The country is in the throes of a multifaceted backlash to technology. People outside major tech hubs feel imposed upon physically by data centers and figuratively by AI’s takeover of the workplace.
Looming over the country are tech billionaires – in control of vast wealth, global communication channels – throwing their weight around in US politics with unmatchable campaign contributions.
“It’s been at least over a year of steadily increasing data center pushback that has made being pro-AI regulation the new common sense, and it certainly has made being pro-AI industry a very toxic brand,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the US Federal Trade Commission.
There’s the fact that the companies involved have responded vigorously to Coxon. Their pledged commitments have details and heft.
“It allowed for companies like Anthropic and others to position themselves immediately as the primary experts in how to deal with these fears. How to solve problems that, by every account, they have created or are best positioned to prevent,” Kak said.
Two closing thoughts. In a sign of how broad the crisis of confidence in AI has become: Strange bedfellows have partnered up in response. The Future of Life Institute is hosting a rally today in Washington promoting AI safety with headliners Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, and Steve Bannon, former chief of staff to Donald Trump, who have been sworn enemies on other issues.
And finally: Why is the AI industry so full of men – only men in AI have expressed these fears of human extinction – in the throes of a crisis over the extinctive potential of their work?
“These people certainly believe what they’re saying. It’s not a fringe view,” said Shakeel Hashim, writer of the Transformer newsletter on AI. “The best way I’ve had it explained to me is that we’re trying to build something that’s smarter than us in the way we’re smarter than monkeys. Our existence hasn’t gone great for monkeys; AGI’s existence probably won’t go great for us.”

Taiwan military prepares for RIMPAC-style sinking exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:19:58 UTC
21:19:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s military will begin its annual Joint Precision Munitions Live-Fire Exercise at the Jiupeng base in Pingtung on Wednesday.
The three-day drill will include a sinking exercise modeled on those conducted during the Rim of the Pacific Exercise, per Liberty Times. Military units will demonstrate their long-range strike capabilities by targeting decommissioned vessels, including the Chi Yang-class frigate Lan Yang.
The exercise will be among the largest and most intensive held in recent years, according to Liberty Times. Several systems will participate for the first time, including High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, ALTIUS 600M loitering munitions, and land-based Sky Sword II missiles.
Patriot PAC-2 and Sky Bow III air defense missiles will also be deployed, along with Hsiung Feng II and III anti-ship missiles.
Three warning zones have been designated. The first lies in waters east of the coastline from Taimali in Taitung to Eluanbi in Pingtung. The second extends eastward from the Taitung-Pingtung boundary to waters off Green Island and Orchid Island. The third is in waters east of Chenggong and Taimali in Taitung.

In Turkey, at least 150 people were detained at a protest against the arrests of LGBTQ+ people
Kyiv • UNN
Police detained at least 150 participants in a rally outside a court in Istanbul. The authorities are also conducting raids and arrests and blocking LGBTQ+ resources.
On Tuesday, Turkish authorities detained at least 150 people after police intervened in a gathering near Istanbul's Çağlayan Courthouse, where demonstrators planned to protest recent detentions targeting LGBTQ+ groups, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
According to media reports, the detentions marked another stage in the escalation of a campaign that human rights organizations and opposition figures describe as an increasingly broad offensive against the LGBTQ+ community: over the past week, authorities have raided the offices of civic associations, blocked websites, and arrested suspects in various provinces across the country.
On Tuesday, a group of people gathered to make a statement to the press, but police prevented them from doing so near the courthouse.
The protesters chanted, "Long live life in defiance of hatred," when police began taking action.
The protest followed a series of large-scale raids against LGBTQ+ organizations in several Turkish provinces as part of an operation called "My Family Is Safe"; according to the government, it aims to protect children and family values.
In addition,
Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O'Flaherty expressed concern on Tuesday over arrests, raids, and internet restrictions targeting the LGBTQ+ community and human rights defenders.
He said that references to "family values" or "the protection of children" cannot, in themselves, justify restrictions on human rights, and called for the release of everyone detained for human rights or civic activities.
On Monday, a court in the western province of İzmir ordered 16 people to be remanded in custody pending investigation as part of the operation, the local prosecutor's office said.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said on Sunday that investigations coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir, Aydın, and Mersin involve 162 suspects, nine civic associations, and 13 commercial enterprises in 15 provinces.
Over the weekend, authorities detained at least 26 people in Istanbul and 21 in Ankara, and also raided the offices of several LGBTQ+ organizations.
Turkish authorities also blocked access to websites and social media pages belonging to various LGBTQ+ organizations, individuals, and independent media outlets, including the X account of the Turkish branch of the human rights organization Amnesty International.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — German journalist Jurgen Kremb said Thursday that fear of Chinese spies in Taiwan “plays right into the hands of China’s security apparatus.”
Kremb made the remark at an event hosted by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom and European Values Center for Security Policy in Taipei, per Liberty Times. He recounted his experience last June of being followed by someone he believed was a Chinese agent while traveling in Taiwan and discussed findings from a research paper he published in June.
The paper, published in a journal by the Investigation Bureau, argues that China’s intelligence operations extend beyond traditional espionage and threaten global security. “Taiwan is the bulwark of freedom in Asia — if this bulwark falls, freedom worldwide will be at stake,” it concluded.
Kremb said Taiwan underestimated the scale of Chinese intelligence activity within its borders, estimating that between 50,000 and 100,000 people were involved, per Liberty Times.
He also estimated that about 180,000 personnel from China’s security apparatus, including the United Front Work Department, worked exclusively on Taiwan from within China.
Kremb said those involved might not receive direct payment from the Chinese government but could provide information or submit reports to the Ministry of State Security. He told Taiwan News that terms such as “agents” and “spies” might not accurately characterize their roles in the security network.
European Economic and Trade Office Head Lutz Gullner said governments needed stronger capabilities to deter efforts to silence speech and protect those targeted. He also called for greater transparency and public awareness to strengthen democratic resilience.
Drawing on eight years of experience working in China, Kremb urged Taiwanese not to fear the threat posed by such operatives.
Kremb previously headed Der Spiegel’s Beijing, Singapore, and Vienna bureaus. He came to Taiwan in 2025 as a visiting scholar at Soochow University.

No one bought it, as the focus was less on sports and clearly on appealing to those... titillated by her Sweeneys.

He said the process remains merit-based and anchored in the rule of law.
Asked about the presidential election in France next spring, Costa declined to comment, calling it an internal political matter.

Finland is investigating a serious breach of sanctions and the export of goods worth millions of euros to russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:14:47 EEST

Finland is investigating a serious breach of sanctions and the export of goods worth millions of euros to russia
Kyiv • UNN
Finnish Customs is investigating the circumvention of EU sanctions through the shipment of pumps and engines to russia disguised as exports to Kazakhstan and Turkey. Two people are suspected.
Finland’s Customs uncovered a large-scale scheme to circumvent EU sanctions, under which industrial equipment worth nearly €6 million was illegally exported to Russia. According to investigators, local companies declared shipments of pumps and engines to Kazakhstan and Türkiye, but in fact diverted them to the Russian Federation. Yle reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to Customs, representatives of companies from Eastern Finland organized the supply of goods to Russia in violation of the sanctions regime. According to Customs, one of the companies was responsible for export operations, while the other was responsible for storing the goods.
The exporting company told Customs that it was shipping the goods to Kazakhstan and Türkiye; however, according to the preliminary investigation, the goods were exported to Russia.
Supply of pumps and engines to Russia
Customs suspects that hydraulic pumps, engines, and various valves worth approximately €5.9 million were exported to Russia.
Since July 2022, the export of these goods to Russia has been prohibited under the EU sanctions regulation.
Customs suspects two people of a large-scale violation of the sanctions regime. The preliminary investigation into the case is nearing completion. According to Customs, the materials will be submitted to the prosecutor’s office of Eastern Finland by the end of the year.
One of the suspects is also a defendant in four other cases involving violations of sanctions, which are being heard in the District Court of South Karelia.

UN rights chief says Israeli bulldozers continue levelling Gaza 'with no respect for the dead'

Ilayda Cakirtekin
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The UN human rights chief said on Tuesday that many areas in Gaza continue to be levelled by Israeli bulldozers, criticizing the lack of respect for the dead under the rubble.
"Much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives. Today, many areas in Gaza where the Israeli military is deployed continue to be levelled by bulldozers with no respect for the dead under the rubble," Volker Turk said in a written statement.
While underlining that the remains of "what appears to be entire families" are being unearthed, he voiced concern that what is being uncovered "may only be the tip of the iceberg."
Turk stressed the need to preserve evidence of violations amid ongoing legal proceedings related to hostilities in Gaza and called for international investigators to be granted access to all parts of the territory to assist in gathering evidence.
Around 8,000 Palestinian bodies are believed to be trapped under the rubble in the Gaza Strip, while civil defense authorities report that over 630 bodies and other human remains had been recovered between November 2025 and September 2026.
“Every feasible effort must be taken to document and identify these victims, preserve forensic information and biological samples, record their burial locations and inform their families,” Turk underscored.
He further stressed that the "painstaking recovery efforts" reflected the "gravity and breadth of the destruction three years ago, compounded today by the prolonged suffering and misery brought by years of not knowing."
Turk recalled his concerns over Israel’s conduct of hostilities, including its extensive use of explosive weapons in densely populated areas, which he said failed to effectively distinguish between civilians and fighters.
“The discovery of extensive remains under the rubble in Gaza City resurfaces these concerns of war crimes and other atrocity crimes," he added.
Turk also stressed Israel’s obligations under international law to search for and account for missing people and recover the dead, while noting that recovering and burying victims does not replace the need to establish the circumstances of their deaths.
“The reported killing of large numbers of family members, including children, women and persons with disabilities, in attacks on residential buildings raises grave concerns regarding compliance with the rules governing the conduct of hostilities," he said.
He also called for effective investigations into the attacks and for those responsible to be held accountable.
"I urge all States to press for greater cooperation and coordination to ensure the recovery of bodies across all of Gaza in a dignified and humane way," Turk further noted.

Kremlin calls energy truce ‘a very good idea’ but says it ‘won’t solve the world’s problems’
Russian officials are calling the energy ceasefire proposed by the U.S. president — a mutual pledge by Russia and Ukraine to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure — “a very good idea,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters. But he said the truce alone won’t save world markets from shortages.
“Ensuring the safe operation of refineries and increasing petroleum product output doesn’t solve the world’s problems. Because the main problem is exporting petroleum products to world markets,” he said, according to the Telegram channel Vy Slushali.
Peskov said the ceasefire would help saturate Russia’s domestic market, though he added that the market is already “close to being fully saturated.”
Fixing the fuel shortage on world markets, the Kremlin spokesperson said, would require Ukrainian forces to stop attacking oil tankers and sanctions on Russian energy exports to be lifted.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on September 14 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. Overnight on September 15, Ukrainian drones struck the Syzran oil refinery, while Russian forces carried out another strike on Kyiv, damaging two gas stations, among other things.

‘No reason to make haste’: JD(U) takes cautious stand on UCC, says it will decide after studying Bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:12:41 UTC
21:12:41 KST

File photo: Bihar deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary
NEW DELHI: Janata Dal (United) on Tuesday adopted a cautious position on the proposed Uniform Civil Code (UCC), with Bihar deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary saying the party will first study the legislation and will not oppose it “for no reason” if its provisions are found to be unexceptionable.Chaudhary, who is also a former state Assembly speaker, said the JD(U) would take a decision after consulting its coalition partners in the BJP-led NDA in Bihar. His remarks came amid political debate following Union home minister Amit Shah’s assertion that the UCC would be implemented across NDA-ruled states before 2029.
“As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union home minister,” Chaudhary said.
JD(U) distances itself from RJD’s opposition
Chaudhary also sought to distance the JD(U) from the RJD’s categorical opposition to implementing the UCC in Bihar.“Please disabuse yourself of the notion that we follow the RJD's lead. We are a part of the ruling NDA in Bihar, and we will take a decision after consulting all coalition partners,” he said.
The RJD, Bihar’s main opposition party, has vowed to oppose implementation of the UCC in the state, alleging that it would be against the interests of Muslims.The JD(U), meanwhile, has faced differing positions within its own ranks on the issue.Senior party leader and Phulwari Sharif MLA Shyam Rajak had on Monday said the party was opposed to implementing the UCC in Bihar, while maintaining that it had supported the UCC Bill in Parliament. Rajak had cited an earlier position attributed to JD(U) chief Nitish Kumar.“Our stand on the issue was made clear by our leader way back. He had said that although our party was supporting the UCC Bill in the Parliament, it was not in favour of implementing the same in Bihar,” Rajak had said.He had also said that although the chief minister was from the BJP, the Bihar government was being run with the support of allies and that “the question of implementing UCC in Bihar does not arise”.Chaudhary, however, said there was no reason to rush into a decision.“There is no reason to make haste in the matter,” he said, adding that JD(U) national working president Sanjay Kumar Jha would discuss the issue with Shah.
Sanjay Jha to hold talks with Amit Shah
Jha had said on Monday that JD(U) leaders would soon meet Shah to discuss the issue of the UCC in states.“We will soon meet home minister Amit Shah to discuss the issue,” Jha told news agency PTI when asked about Shah’s assertion that the UCC would be introduced in NDA-ruled states before 2029.Shah had said at a press conference in Mumbai on Sunday, “Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced UCC in several states, and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA-ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029.”
The JD(U), which has 12 Lok Sabha MPs, is a key constituent of the BJP-led NDA and shares power with the BJP in Bihar.Opposition parties have criticised Shah’s announcement. The CPI(M), DMK and AIMIM have opposed the proposed move, while AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi alleged that the BJP was seeking to target Muslims. The RJD has also said it would not allow the UCC to be implemented in Bihar.Uttarakhand became the first state in independent India to enact a comprehensive UCC, with the law coming into force in January 2025.Assam, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Goa have also passed laws to implement the UCC, while Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal have set up drafting committees.

ICE deportees in Africa describe being stranded "on the other side of the world"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:09:24 UTC
21:09:24 KST

Latin American migrants deported by ICE to West Africa describe being stranded "on the other side of the world"
Monrovia, Liberia — None of the deported men and women placed in a three-story hotel in a remote, coastal area of this West African country are Liberian citizens. Many are not even from Africa.
Instead, they hail from countries throughout Latin America — including Brazil, Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and Venezuela — as well as other African countries, like Cameroon and Eritrea.
They were deported to Liberia, Africa's oldest republic, last month by U.S. immigration officials as part of an intensifying tactic in President Trump's aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration: sending some deportees to far-flung places where they have no ties.
CBS News tracked down the deportees in Liberia, becoming the first U.S. television network to speak to them in person. They described being in limbo and feeling stateless, unable to return to the U.S., where many have spouses and children, and scared of being persecuted if they go back to their homelands.
"I'm concerned," Honduran native Elvis Rodriguez Venturas told CBS News. "I feel far away, on the other side of the world."
Rodriguez Venturas said his four children, two of whom are U.S. citizens, ask him every day when he's coming back to Texas, where he worked in construction. His wife is also in the U.S. Rodriguez Venturas entered the U.S. illegally, but his deportation to Honduras was barred by an immigration judge who found he could be harmed there. He said he had been using that protection to work in the U.S. legally before his detention.
In fact, most of the deportees who agreed to be interviewed won legal protections in American immigration courts, preventing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from deporting them to their home countries because of concerns they could be persecuted or tortured there.
But under the Trump administration's zero-tolerance posture to illegal immigration, those with such cases are being targeted for deportation to third countries, as they still lack a valid permanent immigration status, despite their limited legal protections.
The deportees said they were not notified by ICE that they would be removed to Liberia, or given the chance to challenge their deportation to West Africa.
"Honestly, I had never heard of Liberia," Colombian immigrant Arin Garcia Yepes told CBS News.
"I didn't even know it existed," said Rodriguez Venturas, the Honduran deportee.
Brazilian immigrant Paola Ferreira Dos Santos, the only woman among the Latin American deportees in Liberia, said she only learned where she had been deported to when the deportation flight landed in Monrovia on Aug. 20.
"I was the first to get off the plane, and they said, 'Welcome to Liberia. You're in Africa,'" the 21-year-old told CBS News in Portuguese.
While Trump administration officials often say their deportation blitz is primarily focused on hardened criminals they call the "worst of the worst," CBS News obtained the names of those sent to Liberia last month, and could not find a criminal charge or conviction for the vast majority, beyond immigration violations like entering the U.S. illegally.
In a statement to CBS News, the Department of Homeland Security said those in the U.S. illegally could opt to self-deport and receive a $3,000 stipend the administration has been offering.
"The Trump Administration is utilizing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised," the department added.
The State Department has repeatedly declined to provide detailed information on the "third-country" deportation deals, saying in a statement that it had "no comment on the details of our diplomatic communications with other governments."
"I could be in danger"
Liberia is a relatively small country bordering the North Atlantic that is roughly the size of Tennessee and home to more than 5 million people. It was founded in the 19th century by freed American slaves. Its capital, Monrovia, is named after U.S. President James Monroe.
In August, Liberia's government revealed it had agreed to receive up to 1,200 "third-country" deportees from the U.S., framing it as a humanitarian gesture. So far, it has only received one group of deportees under the agreement, the Aug. 20 flight that brought 15 non-Liberians to Liberia.
The West African country joined more than 30 nations around the globe that have now agreed to such "third-country" deportations under pressure from the Trump administration. Many of the agreements have been brokered with African countries, including those beset by armed conflict, political crises and widespread poverty, like the Central African Republic and South Sudan.
While the Liberian government has said the "third-country" deportees can claim asylum in Liberia, none of the ones interviewed by CBS News expressed interest in staying in the West African nation permanently, citing poverty, the different culture there and their lack of work visas.
Unlike some African countries, such as the small kingdom of Eswatini, Liberia is not detaining the deportees it receives from the U.S. While they've been told not to venture too far outside the hotel for their own safety, the deportees are technically free to leave. The United Nations' migration agency, the International Organization for Migration, has been providing the group with basic necessities.
But many still feel trapped. Some are contemplating returning to their home countries or hoping that another third country agrees to welcome them.
Venezuelan deportee Carlos Tellez Sanchez, who was selling cars and delivering food in the Dallas area before he was detained by ICE late last year, said he's stuck for now in Africa. His wife and their American-born baby remain in Texas.
"Returning to Venezuela is not an option for me," he said. "I feel I could be in danger if I return to my home country."
Haitham Moussa, Jane Greeley and Sam Brolan contributed reporting.

What to expect on Ukraine in the EU's big yearly roundup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:08:26 UTC
21:08:26 KST

What to expect on Ukraine in the EU's big yearly roundup
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa walk with President Volodymyr Zelensky as he arrives at a European Union leaders summit in Brussels, Belgium, on June 18, 2026. (Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will deliver her annual State of the EU speech on Sept 16, usually a celebration of last year's wins and previewing the agenda for the next year, with Ukraine likely to feature strongly.
The speech itself is a closely guarded secret, and the subject of much speculation across Brussels in the weeks leading up to the event. However, there are hints of how Ukraine may and may not feature this time.
Last year, von der Leyen's speech led with Ukraine, discussing the country in several contexts: energy security, EU integration, defense collaboration — especially on drones, security guarantees, and the plan to use Russian assets to bankroll Kyiv.
One topic guaranteed to return: bringing back Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
Von der Leyen posted on social media on Sept. 13 that she would "talk about a story that profoundly moved me," on how Ukrainian children are a "powerful example" of "courage and strength."
The Commission president identifies strongly with the topic, regularly commenting on it. Brussels also hosted a summit on the return of Ukrainian children in May, with a follow-up to take place in Canada on Sept. 28.
read also
Celebrating the wins
Other likely talking points can be found in the European Commission's recently published State of the Union report, and heard along the corridors of power in Brussels.
Having floated a drone alliance between EU and Ukrainian manufacturers in her previous speech, she will likely celebrate its Sept. 11 kick-off meeting.
EU diplomats suggested to the Kyiv Independent that von der Leyen will briefly mention the announcement facilitating Ukraine's ability to source Patriot interceptor missiles, as well as another disbursement of defense funding.
One senior EU official said they expect an amount smaller than the 4.7 billion euros ($5.4 billion) previously mentioned to be announced, due to delays in processing Ukrainian receipts for defense equipment.
Von der Leyen is also expected to comment on EU integration, revisiting how Ukraine opened two of the six so-called enlargement clusters this year, and perhaps reiterating her earlier calls to reopen the remaining four by year's end.
She will likely adopt the line recently and repeatedly deployed by Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos — that "2026 is a record year of progress" — while avoiding criticism of Ukraine's reform pace.
One EU official said they would be surprised if von der Leyen mentions making use of Russian assets, after her proposal last year failed to advance.
"We need the conversation to mature among the member states before the Commission will stick its neck out again," they told the Kyiv Independent.
She might reflect on how the EU passed the 90 billion euro ($104 billion) support loan in April, and use the podium and her Canadian guest of honor, Prime Minister Mark Carney, to call on third countries to fill the remaining third of Ukraine's expected budget shortfall.
read also
Teasing at the new
Predicting the future is not a science, but it would nonetheless be surprising if von der Leyen skipped the EU's discussions over its 22nd sanctions package, set to be the largest ever.
Even if watered down, the package will likely constrain Moscow's ability to wage war and target numerous third-country entities helping Russia evade sanctions.
In January, EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent the bloc will review its visa rules — long considered a chance to restrict Russians' access, and to put protections for Ukrainian refugees on a longer-term footing. Von der Leyen could tease at how she would like that process to go.
She might also announce support for Ukraine's two main winter challenges: protecting energy infrastructure and reopening the Black Sea for agricultural exports.
EU officials said talks are ongoing to bolster the so-called "solidarity lanes," and increase food exports leaving Ukraine via Poland and Romania.
Kyiv asked the EU for financial support for its energy sector, but that is unlikely to be agreed to, given the ongoing disbursement of the 90 billion euro loan. In-kind contributions could be an option, though, with one notable gap last winter being the shortage of experts on the ground to install generators and other equipment.
For the EU this fall and winter, though, the biggest topic remains the need to unanimously agree on the bloc's budget for the years 2028-2034.
The Commission originally allocated 100 billion euros ($115 billion) specifically for Ukraine — a figure EU countries have since haggled down to 89 billion ($103 billion) — along with 131 billion euros ($151 billion) for defense and space.
In that context, von der Leyen could renew her case for spending big on both fronts, or equally, she may position herself less assertively, waiting to see which way the political winds blow.
The Canada question
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will be among those watching von der Leyen's speech from inside the European Parliament in Strasbourg, where he is expected to address Europe with a speech of his own.
That follows his recent pitch for "associate EU membership" for Canada — a concept that does not exist, and which he may therefore explain.
EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent that Canada is negotiating to participate in the bloc's 90 billion loan to Ukraine on terms similar to the U.K., which could already be announced on Sept. 16.
However, there is mounting pressure on non-EU countries to make sizable pledges of their own, with President Volodymyr Zelensky claiming a $27 billion hole in Ukraine's 2026 budget.
Norway recently pledged $9 billion for Ukraine in 2027, and hopes are high in Brussels that Canada will make a separate announcement of its own.
The State of the EU speech will be broadcast on Sept.16 at 10:00 Kyiv time (09:00 CET).
