Germany’s secretive ‘Sonderstab Ukraine’ fast-tracks weapons deals for Kyiv in as little as two weeks, FT reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:43:49 UTC
20:43:49 KST

Germany’s secretive ‘Sonderstab Ukraine’ fast-tracks weapons deals for Kyiv in as little as two weeks, FT reports
A small, standalone unit inside Germany’s Defense Ministry known as the “Sonderstab Ukraine” can arrange weapons deals for Kyiv in just two weeks — a fraction of the time other departments take when bogged down by the bureaucracy of domestic procurement, the Financial Times reports.
The unit’s head, Brigadier General Joachim Kaschke, said, “We have extremely short decision-making chains. That makes us agile and flexible.”
The Ukraine unit was formed in 2022, a few months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and quickly earned a reputation as a responsive, efficient body, the FT writes. Because Ukraine’s government — not Germany’s — signed the contracts, the unit sidestepped German procurement rules.
Since then, the unit’s role has shifted several times as Germany moved from cautious support to becoming one of Kyiv’s main partners. Over the past year, the Sonderstab has become a hub where the German and Ukrainian defense ministries and defense companies exchange experience and technology.
The unit remains compact today, employing fewer than 20 people. “It’s got a bit of a start-up vibe,” said a source familiar with the team’s work. “They have a very deep knowledge of systems: what works . . . and what is overpriced, glitzy nonsense.”
Germany is one of Ukraine’s key allies. In September, German authorities decided to transfer some of their own stockpiled anti-aircraft missiles for American Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine, which needs them to repel Russian missile strikes. A recent ARD-Deutschlandtrend poll showed that 39% of respondents in western Germany consider weapons deliveries to Ukraine excessive, compared with 54% in the east.

WTO warns global trade fragmentation could slash world GDP by over 5%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:43:48 UTC
20:43:48 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The World Trade Organization (WTO) warned on Tuesday that the geopolitical fragmentation of the global trading system into aligned blocs could shrink global gross domestic product (GDP) by 5.1% and reduce global exports by 18.6%.
In an even worse scenario, a total breakdown of multilateral cooperation that replaces the WTO with an unstructured network of bilateral free trade agreements would reduce global GDP by 6.9% and cut global exports by 26.9%.
Conversely, reinforcing multilateral trade cooperation could boost global output by 2.9% and expand global exports by 17.9%, the report showed.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala stressed that global trade faces its most severe period of disruption in 80 years as non-discriminatory rules come under increasing strain.
Okonjo-Iweala noted that around 72% of global merchandise trade still operates under most-favored-nation tariff terms, down from roughly 80% in 2022.
The report emphasized that integration into the multilateral trading system has helped expand trade between members by 140% since 1995 and driven faster economic growth across low- and middle-income economies.
However, gains remain unevenly distributed, with least-developed countries accounting for less than 1% of world trade and facing trade costs in manufacturing and services that exceed those of high-income economies by 50%.
Looking ahead, the report projected that artificial intelligence could increase global trade by 40% by 2040 and add more than 13% to world GDP over the next 15 years, particularly driving growth in digitally deliverable services.

Boeing wins first production deal for Navy’s carrier drone tanker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:43:26 UTC
20:43:26 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Boeing a $562 million contract for the first three low-rate production MQ-25A Stingray drones, with deliveries expected in 2029.
- The program of record calls for 76 MQ-25A aircraft, which will refuel carrier-based F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and other aircraft.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Boeing a $562 million contract to begin low-rate production of the MQ-25A Stingray, the service’s first carrier-based unmanned refueling drone.
The Fixed Price Incentive contract covers three Lot 1 aircraft and includes advance funding to buy long-lead components for three more Lot 2 aircraft. Boeing expects to deliver the first Lot 1 aircraft in 2029.
“Awarding this first LRIP contract marks a pivotal transition from development to operational reality and is a testament to the focused effort of our joint government and industry teams,” said Capt. Daniel Fucito, Unmanned Carrier Aviation program manager.
“MQ-25A will deliver the advanced reach, lethality, and survivability our warfighters need to outpace evolving threats and dominate the future battlespace,” Fucito said.
The contract follows a Milestone C decision in May, when Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao approved moving the MQ-25A into full production and deployment. That approval cleared the way for the Navy to commit funding beyond the test and development aircraft already under contract.
The MQ-25A is designed to fly aerial refueling missions from aircraft carriers, a job currently handled in part by manned F/A-18E/F Super Hornets. Freeing those jets from tanker duty lets them fly more strike missions and reduces wear on the Super Hornet fleet, extending its service life.
The Navy’s program of record calls for 76 MQ-25A aircraft total, including four Engineering Development and Manufacturing airframes and five System Demonstration Test Articles built earlier in the program. Seven test aircraft are currently in production, split between Boeing’s St. Louis facility and a dedicated MQ-25 production line in Mascoutah, Illinois.
The Stingray is built to operate as the first fully integrated unmanned aircraft flying routinely from a carrier deck alongside manned jets. The Navy has described the program as a template for how unmanned aircraft will be folded into carrier air wings going forward, beyond the tanking mission the MQ-25A is starting with.
Program office PMA-268 oversees both the MQ-25A air vehicle and the ground-based Unmanned Carrier Aviation Mission Control System used to command and control it.

====================================================================================================

Nepal floods leave thousands homeless as climate finance lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:41:11 UTC
20:41:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Nepal's deadly floods leave communities devastated as climate finance falls billions short
Sarita Pyakurel was working in her fields on the morning of 26 August when she received a call from her nephew, who told her that a flood was coming and that she should return home.
The 48-year-old farmer had seen floods before and didn’t think much of it, assuming that even if the Trishuli River rose, the water would only reach the fields.
She was making her way back to her home in Nuwakot, which lay about 500m from the river, when she saw a torrent of water sweep the local bridge away.
Shocked and in a daze, she rushed the other way up the hill and into a nearby forest.
"We could never have imagined a flood like this," she told The New Arab. "Everyone thought it wouldn’t be very big."
On 26 August, a glacial flood that began up in the Himalayas tore through villages and towns along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in central Nepal, causing widespread devastation. As of 15 September, more than 1,395 people have died, and another 5,130 are still missing, according to Nepali authorities.
Sarita had lived in her Nuwakot home for 34 years. She was unable to salvage anything; all she could do was watch as everything was washed away before her eyes.
"We worked for years to build our house," she said, "and it was destroyed within seconds."
The land she once knew so well had turned into a muddy, silty swamp.
Now she can no longer recognise her village, unable to point out where her house, farm, pasture, or neighbourhood used to be.
Her two sisters-in-law, aged 55 and 57, and her 20-year-old nephew were among those swept away. They are still missing.
Sarita told The New Arab she is now staying in a shelter run by her village's rural municipality, where she sleeps in a room shared with 20 others.
"We have nowhere else to go," she said, adding that she wishes the government had provided better accommodation.
A 'climate-driven disaster'
"[River] Bhotekoshi’s devastating floods, which claimed lives and destroyed homes, are a climate-driven disaster,” Dr Maheshwar Dhakal, who leads the Climate Change Management Division under Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, told The New Arab.
"While Nepal’s contribution to global carbon emissions is negligible, we are bearing the consequences of emissions from wealthy, industrialised nations. In that sense, we are victims of others’ actions, not our own."
According to glaciologist Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, global warming is heating the Himalayas faster than most regions, accelerating glacier melt and raising the risk of more frequent and severe glacial lake outburst floods and other ice-related disasters.
Between 1990 and 2020, glaciers in the Himalayas and the nearby Hindu Kush range contracted in area by approximately 12%, contributing to a total ice-thickness loss of about 24 meters since 1974, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
Researchers who reviewed 493 floods caused by bursting glacial lakes up to 2024 found that the risk of these outbursts is exacerbated by climate change.
They found that the number of glacial lake outburst floods has jumped fivefold since 1950, from an average of 7 per decade to 38, and flagged 407 glacial lakes as potentially dangerous and at risk of bursting.
A disaster-prone country
Nepal is no stranger to climate catastrophe.
In April 2015, a 7.8-magnitude earthquake triggered an ice-and-rock avalanche that buried Langtang village, killing around 300 people.
A decade later, on 8 July 2025, the bursting of a temporary glacial lake in Tibet unleashed a surge of water down the Lhende Khola River, killing at least nine people and sweeping away the Miteri Bridge on the Nepal–China border.
Less than a month later, on 30 July, the Bhotekoshi River flooded, damaging roads and other infrastructure along the same corridor.
Initial assessments showed that the latest flood had damaged 7,570 private homes, 48 government buildings, 18 schools, and seven health facilities, affecting roughly 84,270 people across six districts.
The deluge also devastated hydropower infrastructure, damaging multiple projects and reducing generation capacity by 431 MW — approximately 10% of Nepal’s total output.
An analysis by the Kathmandu-based think tank Change Initiative estimated preliminary losses at between $1.38 and $ 2.70 billion, roughly equivalent to 4% of Nepal’s GDP.
A climate funding gap
Experts said the August 2026 Bhotekoshi–Trishuli disaster was not just a natural shock — it was the predictable outcome of a long-standing climate finance gap.
For years, Nepal’s efforts to adapt to the worst effects of climate change have been constrained by insufficient and fragmented financing, leaving the country without the systems needed to protect people living in the path of glacier- and flood-related hazards.
Nepal has received only about $400 million in total climate finance to date.
But its government estimates it will need roughly $46 billion by 2030 alone to implement its National Adaptation Plan to adapt to the expected effects of climate change, such as floods, landslides, and similar disasters.
This leaves a shortfall of around $45.6 billion, meaning the country’s climate finance needs are more than 100 times what it has received so far.
Furthermore, 61% of the climate finance Nepal receives is in the form of loans, deepening its debt even as climate impacts escalate.
This funding model severely limits support on the ground.
A key $49.9 million project aimed at protecting 2.4 million people in glacial river basins, such as Sarita's community, has only $9.2 million — all of which was disbursed to the UNDP for early-warning and risk-reduction activities.
Global safety nets offer little relief when disasters strike. By July 2026, 119 countries had filed funding requests totalling $2.8 billion with the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), but only $342 million was available for its active pilot phase.
The Fund, established at COP27 in Egypt, has been pledged $822 million by donor nations but has received only $485 million.
The erosion of international support
Alongside the funding gap, vital international support is being rapidly withdrawn.
The SERVIR–Hindu Kush Himalaya initiative, a USAID-funded regional hub that provided critical satellite data and tools for disaster monitoring across the region, was “formally concluded” in January 2025 following a stop-work notice from the United States, despite its contract running till the end of 2026.
A few days after the flood, former USAID official Jeremy Konyndyk noted that DOGE-led actions "killed $420m worth of climate work at NASA" and, in the process, cancelled all seven Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) projects in Nepal — dismantling early warning mechanisms that could have alerted farmers like Pyakurel before the waters rose.
Birendra Bajracharya, former director of the SERVIR-HKH project, told The New Arab that "funding cuts had stalled efforts to improve avalanche situational awareness during heavy rainfall."
"The work to detect slope speeds for avalanche forecasting also could not be completed," he added.
The programme was identifying areas at risk of glacier lake outburst floods so downstream communities could better prepare for potential disasters. Then Donald Trump cut its funding.
Closely watching USAID funding cuts, Dr Ramesh Poudel, Associate Professor in the Central Department of Economics, said that the recent USAID cuts have eroded Nepali trust in America, despite Nepal’s significant contributions of manpower to the United States.
According to him, thousands of Nepalis have worked as security guards, drivers, cooks and base‑support staff for private contractors supporting US operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Nepali doctors, nurses and other health workers are employed in US hospitals and care facilities; many other Nepalis in the United States work in informal and low‑wage sectors.
"Imported development and parasitic consciousness do not always benefit us. We must become self-reliant," he said.
Dr Ramesh warned that when international aid is abruptly halted, existing projects collapse and progress is set back by a decade, because Nepal has historically outsourced its development. Filling the massive funding gaps left by the US withdrawal remains highly unlikely in the near term, he explained.
"Climate finance must fund technology and capacity-building across all three pillars — mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage," Raju Pandit Chhetri, Executive Director of Prakriti Resource Centre, told The New Arab.
"Mitigation avoids or reduces greenhouse gas emissions; adaptation helps communities adjust to a changing climate; and when adaptation is no longer possible, as in the Bhotekoshi flood, the result is loss and damage."
Raju said that the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement oblige developed countries to provide climate finance to developing nations, which have contributed far less to the crisis, face its worst impacts, and have the least capacity to respond.
"From a climate justice perspective, climate finance must therefore flow from developed to developing countries and be implemented effectively," he added.
Uttam Babu Shrestha, director of the Global Institute for Interdisciplinary Studies (GIIS), told The New Arab that developing countries have made climate-finance promises they haven’t kept, and the money they pledged has largely not materialised.
"Even the money that’s available is hard to access, while our needs keep growing dramatically. Because mitigation efforts in developed countries have fallen behind, temperatures are rising, and climate impacts are worsening," he said.
'The real solution is to cut carbon emissions;
An Oxfam report from May 2026 showed that developing countries will need about $2.4 trillion per year in climate investment by 2030, rising to roughly $3.2-3.3 trillion per year by 2035 to meet the Paris Agreement and development goals.
Yet adaptation remains severely underfunded, and finance for loss and damage is still largely uncosted and poorly tracked.
Wealthier nations frequently overstate their climate finance contributions by using ambiguous reporting rules and counting loans at full face value.
Many climate finance providers adopt a risk-averse approach.
Consequently, around 90% of climate finance is directed toward middle-income, high-emission countries, leaving lower-income, fragile, and conflict-affected nations with only a fraction of the funding they need.
"The key point is that we’re not looking to the Western world to solve all our problems. Some things can be funded from our own budget and the private sector," Raju said.
Climate analyst Manjeet Dhakal said that the real challenge is staying true to the international climate process, honouring what countries have agreed to and responding to the needs and courage of future generations.
"The real solution is to cut carbon emissions. If we keep emitting carbon, climate disasters will only get worse. Climate finance can help us cope in the short term, but it doesn’t solve the root problem; it just delays it," Manjeet said.
He added that reaching out to the climate finance community isn’t about handing out money to vulnerable communities.
"It’s about enabling them to live with dignity, continue their education, and access rehabilitation and other essential support," he stated.
For people like Sarita Pyakurel, the climate finance debate is not just about figures on a balance sheet — it’s about whether the international system can turn its promises into meaningful support for people like her.
She has felt the effects of disaster more than most.
Nepal’s 2015 earthquake destroyed her home, the 2025 floods wiped away her fields, and this latest deluge carried away what she had left.
"I do not know where to turn," she said.
Sunita Neupane is an independent investigative journalist based in Kathmandu, Nepal. She specialises in high-impact reporting on human rights, public health, and climate justice

According to the ministry, approved methods of UAV interception will include "technical devices, use of force and firearms".
"The proposal would also expand the Finnish Defence Forces' ability to provide executive assistance to the police in intercepting the movement or operation of an unmanned vehicle and other cooperation between authorities," the ministry explained.

Pentagon research arm opens new push into radio-spectrum sensing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:39:17 UTC
20:39:17 KST

- DARPA will hold a BEAMERS program Industry Day on September 30 in Arlington, Virginia, with registration closing September 23.
- The program seeks analog signal-processing methods to reduce data loads in wideband electronic-support systems before digitization.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency will hold an Industry Day on September 30 in Arlington, Virginia, for a new program aimed at building next-generation electronic-support systems that can watch across wide swaths of the radio spectrum without needing to digitize and process every signal they detect.
The program is called BEAMERS, short for Beam-Space Analog Processing for Multifunctional Enhanced RF Systems. It falls under DARPA’s Strategic Technology Office and is run by program manager Dr. Stefano Galli. Companies interested in bidding on future BEAMERS work can register for the event through September 23 at 5 p.m. Eastern time.
Electronic-support systems are used to detect, locate and characterize radio frequency signals in the environment, a function that spans warning systems, situational awareness and sensing missions across different platforms. DARPA says these systems increasingly rely on “staring” architectures that continuously monitor wide bands of spectrum, which generates far more data than current hardware can practically digitize and process in full.
BEAMERS is built around a different approach. Instead of converting every beam, frequency channel and polarization output into digital data, the program wants systems that filter and reduce that information while it is still in analog form, then send only the signals worth digitizing downstream for processing. DARPA is looking for expertise in analog beamspace processing using lenses, gradient-index structures and phased-array-fed lenses, along with integrated radio frequency and microwave photonics, wideband channelization, and event detection.
The Industry Day will run from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Strategic Analysis Inc. Executive Conference Center on Wilson Boulevard, split into two parts. The bulk of the day will consist of government presentations classified at the SECRET level, open only to U.S. citizens holding a Department of Defense SECRET clearance or higher. Attendees must submit their clearance information through the Defense Information System for Security and present government-issued photo identification at the door.
A separate Industry Showcase Poster Session will follow at 3:30 p.m., held at the unclassified but controlled level. That portion is intended for small businesses and emerging companies to display posters and materials about their capabilities and network with other attendees and potential teaming partners.
DARPA capped attendance at 120 registrants, with no more than three representatives per organization. Foreign nationals who want to attend must submit a separate DARPA Form 60 and supporting documentation by the same September 23 deadline. There is no registration fee, and DARPA will not reimburse travel or other costs tied to the event.
The agency was explicit that showing up does not commit anyone to anything. Attendance is voluntary, and companies do not need to attend the Industry Day to submit proposals if DARPA later issues a formal solicitation tied to BEAMERS. No solicitation has been published yet, and the notice does not disclose a program budget, contract vehicle or expected timeline for follow-on work.

Explainer-Who is Lucy Letby and why is her case so controversial?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:37:24 UTC
20:37:24 KST

Explainer-Who is Lucy Letby and why is her case so controversial?
LONDON, Sept 15 - A British public inquiry concluded on Tuesday that hospital managers could have prevented nurse Lucy Letby killing more babies in her care had they taken action against her sooner.
Letby is serving life in jail after being found guilty of murdering seven newborns and attempting to murder eight more between June 2015 and June 2016 while working at the Countess of Chester Hospital (CoCH) in northern England.
The convictions made her Britain's worst serial child killer of modern times. She has always maintained her innocence and in recent years there has been a growing campaign arguing she was a victim of a miscarriage of justice.
Here are details about her, the controversy around her convictions and the public inquiry.
WHO IS LUCY LETBY?
Letby, 36, was born in Hereford in central England. She completed a nursing degree at Chester University in northwest England and after qualifying, she began to work in the neonatal unit of the city's Countess of Chester Hospital.
WHAT IS THE LUCY LETBY CASE ABOUT?
Over 18 months from January 2015, there was a significant rise in the number of babies dying and suffering serious collapses at the neonatal unit.
Senior doctors became worried as many of the babies had deteriorated suddenly and unexpectedly, and then did not respond to appropriate resuscitation. Other babies, who suddenly collapsed and did not die, recovered, with both their collapse and recovery defying usual medical norms.
The police and medical experts were called in and as they looked for a cause, they eventually focused on one common factor - Lucy Letby.
She was first arrested in July 2018, and then again in June 2019 and November 2020 when she was charged with murdering seven babies and attempting to kill another 10 between June 2015 and July 2016.
WHAT WAS LETBY CONVICTED OF DOING?
Prosecutors said Letby attacked 17 babies who had been on the ward. Some she was said to have poisoned with insulin. Mostly she was accused of injecting air into their bloodstream or stomachs, or giving them excessive milk.
The victims included twins and triplets, and in one case, she killed two siblings on consecutive days. The youngest baby she murdered was just a day old. The oldest was 11 weeks old, a baby girl who she attacked four times before she died.
Although the babies had been born prematurely, some were regarded as being in reasonable or good condition before they suddenly deteriorated, mainly during night shifts when Letby was working.
Letby attacked a number of the babies shortly after their parents had left their bedside, prosecutors said.
Police said she had kept medical records at her home with reference to some of the babies involved and had also carried out social media searches for their parents and families.
She denied any wrongdoing and blamed poor conditions on the hospital unit and doctors working there.
She was convicted in August 2023 of seven murders and seven attempted killings and acquitted of two charges of attempted murder while jurors could not agree on six other suspected attacks.
The following year she was convicted of trying to murder another newborn baby following a re-trial. Police said they had been unable to find a motive for the attacks.
THE THIRLWALL INQUIRY
Amid shock at her convictions, the British government set up an inquiry to examine how the killings went undetected, and review the hospital's response to concerns raised about Letby before her arrest.
Its chair, Kathryn Thirlwall, concluded that there had been "complete failure" to protect babies at the hospital and some of the deaths could have been avoided if the dysfunctional management had acted sooner on concerns. She had said its remit was not to examine Letby's culpability.
IS LUCY LETBY INNOCENT?
Letby has always maintained her innocence, saying she never harmed or intended to harm any child in her care.
She has launched a series of appeals against her convictions but these have all been rejected by the courts.
However in the three years since she was found guilty there has been a growing campaign, particularly online, arguing that she was the victim of a miscarriage of justice.
Some medical specialists have queried the evidence given at her trial with one, neonatal doctor Professor Shoo Lee, saying his research had been misused and that he and other international experts did not believe any babies had been attacked.
They said there had been medical mistakes and failures at the hospital.
The case has now been referred to the Criminal Cases Review Commission which is considering whether her convictions are safe. There is no timescale for it to conclude its work.
MORE VICTIMS, MORE POLICE INVESTIGATIONS?
Since her convictions police carried out a review of Letby's career at the Countess of Chester Hospital and at the Liverpool Women's Hospital where she had spent part of her training to see if there was evidence other babies had been attacked.
In January, prosecutors said they would not bring any new charges, a decision which police said was disappointing.
However, an investigation into the Countess of Chester Hospital's managers remains ongoing with three senior members of the leadership team arrested last July on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter. REUTERS

China’s weak domestic demand, worse-than-expected unemployment threaten growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:35:27 UTC
20:35:27 KST

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu and Emir Yildirim
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
China’s slowing retail sales growth and fixed-asset investment and rising unemployment rate indicated a slowdown in domestic demand, fueling expectations that Beijing may have to introduce additional fiscal and monetary measures to support economic growth.
China’s retail sales grew 0.4% year-on-year in August, short of estimates, while falling compared with the previous month. Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2% at the same time, worse than expected.
China’s unemployment rate came in higher than expected at 5.3% in August. The country’s industrial production rose 5.2%.
The loss of momentum, especially in consumption and investment, could complicate the path Beijing will have to take to meet its growth targets.
Lynn Song, chief China economist at ING Group, said in a recent ING Think article that consumption and investment remained low due to weak domestic demand in the country. He expected gross domestic product (GDP) growth to likely stagnate in the third quarter and said the 4.6% growth forecast for 2026 may have to be revised downward.
Song said positive developments in industrial activity were driven by external demand, while China’s improvements in its tech and industrial sectors continued to support growth.
He noted that sectors focused on high tech and external demand continue to perform well, while most other categories continue to underperform.
“Auto sales were the biggest drag on retail sales, down 18.5% YoY,” he said. “Despite strong exports, China has been both the largest producer and the largest consumer of electric vehicles, and the drop in domestic demand has weighed on the auto sector this year.”
He noted that furniture sales declined 7.9%, but household appliance sales saw their first positive growth since September 2025, rising 2.3% on an annual basis.
Gold and jewelry sales fell 17.5% year-on-year despite the rebound in gold in August, dropping to their lowest level in the past four months.
He mentioned that recent measures taken to stimulate consumption include interest rate subsidies on consumer loans, which are expected to have a modest impact on overall consumption growth.
“Moving forward, as the drag from the trade-in policy weakens, we may see some stabilization in retail sales, but a more significant turnaround will likely require additional support,” he added.

Up to 8 years for “drops” — Parliament backed introducing liability for handing over bank cards
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:32:52 EEST
20:32:52 KST

Up to 8 years for “drops” — Parliament backed introducing liability for handing over bank cards
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament approved in the first reading a bill on criminal liability for handing over bank cards and access to accounts. For repeated offenses, up to 8 years in prison is proposed.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted bill No. 16013 as a basis to strengthen the protection of citizens’ bank accounts against cyber fraud. The document provides for criminal liability for transferring cards and access to accounts. This was reported by UNN, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
According to the bill, amendments are planned to Article 200 of the Criminal Code, including changing its title to "Illegal actions involving payment instructions/payment messages/payment orders, payment instruments and other means of access to a bank and/or payment account".
In particular, the counterfeiting or falsification of payment instructions/payment messages/payment orders, payment instruments, other means of access to a bank and/or payment account, electronic wallets, or individual account information will be punishable by a fine of UAH 51,000 to UAH 85,000, restriction of liberty for a term of two to four years, or imprisonment for the same term.
It is also proposed to establish that the misappropriation, theft, acquisition through deception or abuse of trust, or acquisition by any other criminally unlawful means of payment instruments, individual account information or other means of access to them, as well as unlawful access to a bank and/or payment account or electronic wallet, will be punishable by a fine of UAH 85,000 to UAH 136,000, restriction of liberty for a term of three to five years, or imprisonment for the same term.
The bill supplements the Criminal Code with Article 200-1, "Transfer, receipt, acquisition, storage or other acquisition of payment instruments for the commission of a criminal offense."
Thus, the transfer, receipt, acquisition, storage or other acquisition of payment instruments, data for accessing them, bank or payment accounts, or electronic wallets, if carried out with the aim of committing fraud or another criminal offense, will carry a fine of UAH 5,100 to UAH 17,000.
For receiving, purchasing, storing, selling or transferring another person’s payment instruments for criminal purposes, a fine of UAH 51,000 to UAH 170,000, restriction of liberty for 2–5 years, or imprisonment for 2–6 years is proposed.
If committed repeatedly or by an organized group, the punishment will be imprisonment for 5–8 years.
Let us recall
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted two bills to the Verkhovna Rada on strengthening liability for organizing fraudulent call centers, as well as for organizing schemes involving "drops".

DOE calls for stronger global action to protect ozone layer, tackle climate change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:32:50 UTC
20:32:50 KST

DOE calls for stronger global action to protect ozone layer, tackle climate change
TEHRAN – Shina Ansari, the head of the Department of Environment, has called for stronger international cooperation to address the harmful effects of ozone-layer depletion and climate change, saying that global participation, strong commitment to obligations, and dedicated financial resources can produce real, tangible, measurable, and monitorable results.
Speaking at a ceremony on Tuesday, marking World Ozone Day, she said, “We have gathered today to reaffirm our commitment to fully restoring and rebuilding the Earth’s protective shield and safeguarding life against harmful solar radiation. We must take more effective steps toward our shared goals of addressing global environmental challenges, both in protecting the ozone layer and in mitigating global warming.”
Referring to the Montreal Protocol, Ansari said it is a global agreement aimed at controlling the production, trade, and consumption of chemicals that deplete the ozone layer, with the ultimate goal of protecting life on Earth through the gradual phase-out of ozone-depleting substances.
The official added that the landmark agreement, adopted in 1987 and entering into force in 1989, is now regarded as one of the world’s most successful environmental agreements and an inspiring model for environmental cooperation.
“Thanks to the joint efforts of countries around the world, the ozone layer is currently on a path toward recovery and restoration, and significant progress has been made in this regard,” she said.
The protocol has demonstrated that science-based policymaking, global participation, effective international cooperation, strong commitment to obligations, and dedicated financial resources can produce real, tangible, measurable, and monitorable results, Ansari noted.
She added that this process has not only made ozone-layer protection possible but has also enabled countries and industries to move toward safer, more environmentally friendly alternatives while supporting economic development.
Kigali Amendment
Referring to the Kigali Amendment, Ansari said this year marks the 10th anniversary of the amendment, the latest amendment to the Montreal Protocol, which was adopted to gradually reduce global emissions of powerful greenhouse gases known as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and accelerate the transition to more efficient and safer refrigerants.
Over the past decade, implementation of the amendment in various countries has demonstrated how the promotion of efficient technologies, the strengthening of industrial capacity, and support for innovation in the refrigeration sector can help advance development priorities, she said.
Ansari predicted that full implementation of the amendment could prevent between 0.5 and 1 degree Celsius of global warming by 2100, describing it as one of the most important approaches to mitigating climate change in the present century.
She said that, in line with the protocol’s new objectives of aligning ozone-layer protection with efforts to reduce global warming, issues such as new technologies, increased energy efficiency, equipment modernization, and the development of environmentally friendly technologies have been prioritized, taking into account the country’s current circumstances, economic considerations, industrial capacity, market needs, and access to safe technologies.
Given the structure of the Montreal Protocol and the cooperation of its implementing agencies and financial mechanisms, Iran can use the implementation of its international environmental commitments as an opportunity to modernize and develop domestic technology, the DOE head said.
Referring to this year’s World Ozone Day theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet,” Ansari said the slogan reflects the international community’s efforts to protect the ozone layer and the need to continue this path with future generations in mind.
“These efforts offer us the prospect of successfully implementing the Montreal Protocol and creating the necessary conditions and capacities to help address global environmental crises,” she said.
The official stressed that, as an inspiring agreement, the Montreal Protocol symbolizes humanity’s ability to cooperate.
“When humanity reaches consensus and demonstrates a firm determination to resolve one of the major global environmental crises, it becomes clear that such an achievement is possible,” she said.
Ansari added that the agreement has succeeded in realizing this goal, expressing hope that the international community would, through greater cooperation and the responsible conduct of officials, take steps toward addressing the environmental challenges currently facing the world, including habitat and biodiversity protection and plastic pollution as a global concern.
“We hope that this global cooperation can also pave the way for consensus and collaboration on other issues and challenges that have emerged as crises around the world,” she said.
Iran’s environmental commitments
Ansari said the Islamic Republic of Iran has taken effective steps in this direction in recent years through cooperation among national and international executive bodies, as well as governmental and nongovernmental sectors.
She added that various industries using substances covered by the Montreal Protocol, along with other stakeholders, have taken significant and commendable steps. Such progress has been made possible through a shared and responsible approach to fulfilling the country’s commitments under these international treaties, she said.
The head of the Department of Environment further noted that the country is also facing another environmental challenge: the damage and losses caused by two imposed wars waged against Iran over the past two years.
“These two unjust wars, in addition to the many forms of damage they have inflicted on the country, have damaged infrastructure, and unfortunately, civilian targets have also been attacked,” she said.
“Cultural and historical heritage sites have been targeted, scientific and research centers have been damaged, and irreparable losses have unfortunately been inflicted on the country’s natural habitats, coastal ecosystems, biodiversity, and even our environmental protection facilities.”
From this perspective, Ansari stressed, the harmful effects and consequences of wars—which can constitute a serious obstacle to the implementation of international agreements—must also be taken into account, as they can have extremely damaging repercussions.

====================================================================================================

WWII Podcast to Which Putin Should Have Listened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:32:00 UTC
20:32:00 KST

The twice-weekly UK-based WWII podcast “We Have Ways of Making You Talk” (WHW) has addressed almost every aspect of WWII in more than 1,000 episodes since it began in April 2019. It is hosted by comedian Al Murray, who read modern history at Oxford University, and the professional historian James Holland, the latter of whom has been sanctioned by Russia in response to his published views on the war in Ukraine.
The podcast, which also often includes guest historians and analysts, primarily focuses on the causes of WWII and examines the history, campaigns, personal stories, and the decisions made by the political and military leaders. At the same time, it often draws overt and implied parallels between the lessons from WWII and more modern conflicts including Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This level of analysis is nowhere more apparent than in the eight recent episodes it dedicated to Operation Barbarossa, which draws parallels between Adolf Hitler’s catastrophic miscalculations on the Eastern Front and those made during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s so-called “special military operation” against Ukraine.
Putin frequently equates the Soviet Union’s defeat of Nazi Germany during the “Great Patriotic War” to justify his invasion of Ukraine. The current lack of success in reaching his aims, the podcast argues, is his failure to pay attention to the lessons of Operation Barbarossa combined with the structural inadequacies within both Hitler’s and Russia’s autocratic regimes.
Trump Claims Ukraine, Russia Agreed to Halt Energy Infrastructure Strikes
Battle of Kursk
The WHW podcast draws a number of similarities between the Battle of Kursk in 1943 and Putin’s invasion.
Putin’s current strategy is a giant pincer maneuver around the Donbas salient, just as Hitler attempted to surround the Soviet Kursk salient. The defenders now and then had months to prepare extensive fortifications and knew exactly the direction of attack.
Despite the protests of their military, the dictators insisted on head-on assaults straight into those prepared defenses. Putin, like Hitler, believed that force of numbers would allow them to successfully overrun the defenders. Both drastically underestimated the will and ability of the defenders to stand and fight even against the most formidable of armies.
The war has now reached an effective stalemate – Russia’s armor has been largely neutralized by the use of artillery, anti-tank guided weapons and, most of all, by the development of drone technology, sophistication and tactics.
Underestimating the enemy
WHW argues that both dictators assumed their enemies were inferior in every way and that a rapid political collapse and a swift military victory would follow. For Hitler, this was as much necessity as design: He wanted success before Stalin could mobilize the numerical and industrial advantages he could call on.
They also failed to understand the nature of their opponents’ fierce national pride and the level of resistance this would engender. This was made worse by the brutality of the treatment their forces inflicted on the local population, even those who were potentially sympathetic to the invaders – in WWII, many Ukrainians and Belarusians had no love for the USSR.
Hitler’s indiscriminate brutality encouraged resistance among the civilian population in occupied areas. This has been mirrored by Putin’s forces, which have carried out widespread torture and murder of civilians, blocked humanitarian relief convoys, bombed hospitals, shopping malls, apartment buildings and even the theater in Mariupol marked “children” in Russian and have resulted in uniting Ukrainians against the invader.
Fixation with politics
Both Hitler’s Germany and Putin’s Russia are driven by a political orthodoxy that saw the desire to take and control “real estate.”
In Hitler’s case, this was encapsulated in the philosophy of “Lebensraum,” or living space. While this was largely driven by the theories of Friedrich Ratzel, who claimed society’s evolutionary needs required expansion of territory to thrive, in Hitler’s case there was also the reality of Germany’s lack of raw materials, particularly rare metals and oil.
In Putin’s case, despite his suggestions that the invasion was to protect Russian-speaking minorities, it is in fact his desire to recover the lost hegemony of the defunct Soviet Union and his desire to recover Russia’s “historical lands.”
In both cases, the prioritization of symbolic geographic gains over sound strategic and tactical military drivers has led to fatal errors and losses to their forces. Hitler could not be persuaded from seizing Stalingrad (now Volgograd) simply because it bore the name of his adversary.
Flawed logistics
Hitler’s forces, because of their initial rapid advances, overextended their supply lines as a result of poor logistical preparation and eventually ground to a halt – which proved fatal when the Russian winter hit. German soldiers were forced to fight wearing summer uniforms, relying on newspaper and straw as insulation against freezing temperatures and to eat horses, dogs and rats – the plan for Barbarossa called for Soviet forces to be destroyed before autumn.
Similarly, Putin’s columns outran their own supply capabilities during their initial invasion, with Russian forces increasingly unable to adequately feed, fuel and equip themselves.
Russian troops became lost and disoriented using outdated mapping, have looted supermarkets in search of food, their vehicles have run out of fuel and broken down, ammunition shortages have impacted their attacks, and the use of cellphones in place of inadequate military communication has led to attacks against troop concentrations and senior officers.
As the war has become ever more static, modern weaponry – particularly drones and long-range artillery and missiles – has enabled Ukraine to strike factories, refineries and supply lines ever deeper into the occupied areas and beyond, which has further exacerbated the resource issues Putin’s forces, and now the civilian population, face.
Faulty intelligence
The nature of 1940s Germany’s and 21st century Russia’s autocratic command structures discourages dissent, with subordinates telling their leaders what they want to hear, which has led to the development of strategic blind spots.
The obvious representation of this is the reports that, prior to the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian security agencies assured Putin that his troops would be welcomed with open arms.
Where professional military advice contradicts the dictators’ preconceptions, they often ignore it to make grand, politically motivated decisions themselves. Putin has and continues to receive information that the war on the frontline is going to plan, and the avowed tactical and strategic aims are being met – even when all the evidence is to the contrary.
Justification for war
Putin claimed in a 2021 essay titled “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians” that Ukraine was an artificial creation and was historically part of Russia. In fact, Ukraine had existed for several centuries before the creation of modern Russia. He also accuses Ukraine of fighting a proxy war on behalf of NATO.
This echoed many of Hitler’s claims from “Mein Kampf,” which claimed Germany’s lost greatness was a result of a global conspiracy.
In reality, Putin’s war against Ukraine is one of imperialism resulting from the Kremlin’s nostalgia for past Soviet dominance, exacerbated by a fear of the eastward march of Western democratic political systems, reinforced by a deep-seated xenophobia that calls for Ukrainian society to be “de-nazified” and purged of Western influence.
The WHW podcast suggests that Hitler’s miscalculation has been repeated by Putin and continues to be made – it remains to be seen if his war will suffer the same outcome.

Syria's Al-Sharaa to head to New York for UNGA meetings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15

Breadcrumb
Syria's Al-Sharaa to head to New York for UN General Assembly meetings
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa will travel to New York on 21 September for a four-day official visit to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly and deliver Syria's address to world leaders. Al-Sharaa is also expected to hold political meetings and participate in events on the sidelines of the General Assembly.
According to sources cited by Syria's official Al-Thawra newspaper, his programme includes a bilateral meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 22 September to discuss several shared issues.
His meeting with Rubio is expected to cover Syrian-US relations as well as political, economic and security issues of mutual interest, as ties between Damascus and Washington continue on a path of renewed engagement and openness.
The Syrian president will also take part that day in a dialogue organised by the Atlantic Council in New York on Syria's future, reconstruction, economic recovery and regional role.
The Atlantic Council said on its website that its dialogue with Sharaa would address his vision for Syria's future and his government's priorities for reconstruction, economic recovery and institutional reform. It would also cover developments in Syrian-US relations, efforts to strengthen state institutions and Syria's continued regional reintegration.
Sharaa is scheduled to deliver Syria's address during the General Assembly's general debate on 23 September, alongside more than 150 heads of state and government taking part in the session.
Syria's priorities
Sharaa is also expected to use his participation in the General Assembly and bilateral meetings to raise issues that are a priority for Damascus, including developments in southern Syria and Israeli attacks and interventions.
Reconstruction, economic recovery, investment and strengthening Syria's international relations are also expected to feature during the visit.
Syrian political activist Ayman Abdel Nour told The New Arab that Syria's repeated participation in UN meetings provides an opportunity to raise Syrian issues internationally and strengthen coordination with the US administration.
He described the visit as important because it occurs at the centre of the annual global political event, noting that Sharaa's General Assembly session is scheduled for the morning, when delegations are active and media coverage is stronger.
Abdel Nour said the president's programme also includes media meetings, visits to research centres and meetings with members of the Syrian diaspora.
Al-Sharaa is also expected to attend a general meeting of heads of delegations with US President Donald Trump, with a brief meeting between the two presidents possible on the sidelines, as happened last year.
The Syrian president is also scheduled to meet between five and 12 heads of participating delegations, Abdel Nour estimated, providing an opportunity to strengthen relations with those countries.
Second consecutive year
Sharaa's participation in the General Assembly this year carries particular significance as it marks his second consecutive appearance, following his participation in the 80th session in September 2025.
He was the first Syrian president to attend the General Assembly since 1967.
During his previous participation, Sharaa held a series of meetings with leaders and officials, including Trump. He also used the General Assembly platform to outline his vision for Syria's new phase, call for sanctions to be lifted, and urge support for reconstruction and greater international engagement.
The UN General Assembly's 81st regular session opened on 8 September, with the general debate scheduled to begin on 22 September. It will bring together leaders, heads of government and delegations from member states.
The session will address a wide range of international issues, including sustainable development, climate change, a just transition, rising sea levels, the right to development, economic inequalities, financing and debt, as well as pandemic prevention and health emergency preparedness.
The meetings will also address human rights, combating racism and nuclear disarmament, alongside challenges linked to artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.
Sharaa's participation comes as Damascus seeks to consolidate its international presence and expand its political and economic relations following a series of diplomatic moves aimed at ending its international isolation and strengthening ties with Arab, regional and international states.

Three babies might have survived if hospital had acted over Lucy Letby concerns, inquiry finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:30:41 UTC
20:30:41 KST

Ministers have promised sweeping changes to the NHS after a “devastating” official review concluded that three babies might have survived if hospital bosses and doctors had acted on concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby.
A public inquiry found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.
In a series of findings, the inquiry chair, Lady Justice Thirlwall, said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner.
Thirlwall said a third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses might have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said she was “profoundly sorry” for the “devastating” failures revealed in the report, telling MPs: “This must be a turning point for the NHS.” She said she had asked officials to urgently take forward plans for “cot cam” monitors for neonatal units in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation.
However, Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald, told the Guardian the government had “moved with too much haste” and acted before the outcome of her challenge to her convictions was known.
Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in the year to June 2016.
The former neonatal nurse is fighting to overturn her convictions, which have been described by the senior Conservative MP David Davis as a “clear miscarriage of justice”.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is reviewing a dossier of evidence submitted by experts on her behalf before deciding whether to refer the case back to the court of appeal, which has twice rejected her legal challenges.
Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, where families of some of the babies had gathered, Thirlwall said: “My report describes dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.
“There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. This was because no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.”
Families of the babies who died or were injured said the report painted a “damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on”.
Tamlin Bolton, a solicitor at Irwin Mitchell representing seven of the families, urged ministers and the NHS to act on the report’s recommendations, saying: “It cannot be the end of the matter.”
Richard Scorer, of the law firm Slater and Gordon, which represents three of the families, said: “Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust. This cannot be allowed to happen again.”
In her 822-page report, Thirlwall said it was “inexcusable” that successive governments had failed to act on reforms proposed by other public inquiries into NHS scandals stretching back 30 years.
Thirlwall is said to believe that “cot cams” – allowing parents to monitor their newborn around-the-clock – could have prevented all seven of the deaths as medics would know they were being monitored.
Samantha Dixon, the Labour MP for Chester North and Neston, whose constituency includes the hospital, said the inquiry revealed a “truly appalling state of affairs” that needed “the firmest response possible from government”.
Ministers are working on the urgent introduction of other CCTV in hospital neonatal units as well as cot cams, in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation, and stricter rules on the storage of insulin.
Hospital executives who are found to have failed in their responsibilities will be prevented from working again in the NHS under new regulation to stop managers being transferred to another part of the country.
And they will roll out a single tracker to monitor the delivery of recommendations made by inquiries into maternity and neonatal scandals.
McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “The government has moved with too much haste. They have made the same mistake as Thirlwall not to pause and wait for the new evidence to be considered.”
However, others said the inquiry’s findings and recommendations must be taken seriously irrespective of Letby’s legal challenge.
Dr Tom Dolphin, the chair of the British Medical Association, said it stemmed from “system reform” within the NHS and that it required “major reforms” to the culture of the health service.
Leaders of NHS trusts and other bodies said the inquiry had shone a light on the “upheaval caused by successive reorganisations, the complex regulatory landscape, staff shortages, unacceptable ‘revolving door’ appointments and the inadequacies of underfunded NHS IT systems”.
Letby was first linked to baby deaths in June 2015. That month, three newborns died in unexplained circumstances within two weeks – the number usually expected on the neonatal unit in a year.
Senior doctors became concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives. However, the inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police.
Rather than being believed, Thirlwall said, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016.
Parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry found. Thirlwall described their treatment as “reprehensible”.
The inquiry chair accused hospital executives of overseeing “an exercise in spin” by downplaying the rise in deaths to the board of directors. Their failure to contact police before April 2017 – nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths – suggested that protecting the hospital’s reputation was “prized more highly” than the doctors’ concerns, she found.
Three hospital executives, who have not been named, were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter. Cheshire police said its investigation into the former bosses, and a parallel investigation into corporate manslaughter, was ongoing.
Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, said it was “clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier”. She said the precise number of deaths that might have been prevented would never be known for sure.
However, the inquiry concluded that if Letby had been removed from duties in October 2015 – when senior managers were made aware of the concerns – then the twin boys known as babies O and P would not have died in June 2016 and five further babies would not have suffered harm.
Thirlwall said it was possible that three newborns would not have died and seven others would have been protected if a senior doctor had not “disregarded” an insulin result for a week-old baby boy in August 2015, whom Letby was later convicted of attempting to murder by poisoning him.

Denmark accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its military helicopters over the Baltic Sea, the government said Monday, Sept. 14, 2026.
The helicopter was tracking the vessel as part of what Denmark described as a routine monitoring operation when the flares were fired.
The Danish government summoned the Russian ambassador to protest the incident. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the Russian action “reckless” and said it was designed to “intimidate and divide.”
Denmark has not said which type of helicopter was involved, where in the Baltic Sea the incident took place, or whether the flares came close enough to pose a direct risk to the aircraft or its crew.
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, said this was not the first time Danish Air Force helicopters had carried out what he described as dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships operating in open water outside Denmark’s territorial waters, according to Russian statements on the incident.
The confrontation adds to a run of incidents between Danish forces and Russian vessels in the Baltic Sea and the straits connecting it to the North Sea. In December 2024, a Russian warship fired a flare at a German military helicopter on a routine patrol in the same waters, an episode NATO also treated as a warning sign about the growing frequency of close encounters in the region. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service has separately reported that Russian warships have aimed weapons and tracking radars at Danish naval vessels and air force helicopters while transiting the Danish straits, incidents it has called deliberate provocations.
Denmark has also dealt with a string of drone incursions and unexplained naval activity near its coast over the past year, including a Russian landing ship that lingered off the island of Langeland during a period of airport disruptions in September 2025. Danish officials have not tied Monday’s flare incident to those earlier episodes, and the government has not announced any additional military or diplomatic measures beyond summoning the ambassador.

Pezeshkian pushes for drafting Iran-China action plan to combat desertification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:30:08 UTC
20:30:08 KST

Pezeshkian pushes for drafting Iran-China action plan to combat desertification
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian has highlighted the need to draft a five-year Iranian-Chinese action plan to manage airborne dust and combat desertification in line with a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by the two countries.
The MOU was inked in the last month of spring in 2025, in Lanzhou, China, to promote scientific cooperation and address sand and dust storms (SDSs) challenges, IRNA reported.
Following specialized meetings and an assessment of scientific and operational indicators, a five-year action plan is scheduled to be developed, and two regions have been designated as pilot sites for implementing joint efforts.
The selected areas include Salehiyeh Wetland, a major dust source affecting Alborz, Qazvin, and Tehran provinces, and Tabas desert, another main dust hotspot in the country, chosen due to their roles in the expansion of desertification, sandstorms, and their impacts on agriculture and infrastructure.
Highlighting the importance of protecting natural resources and the environment, Pezeshkian called for taking action against unauthorized construction and illegal activities that undermine regulations and lead to environmental consequences, as well as benefiting from the capacities and expertise of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in implementing pilot projects.
The official made the remarks in a meeting held on Monday to give an account of the progress in the bilateral MOU.
Moreover, the president urged the University of Tehran to maintain constant collaboration with the Chinese Academy of Sciences and develop a joint action plan to be assessed and discussed in the next meetings. The official also asked the Plan and Budget Organization to secure funds required for the studies and measures in the five-year action plan.
Dust storms are significant environmental challenges that adversely affect food security, human health, and the sustainable development process at national and regional levels.
Being located in an arid and semi-arid area, Iran has been negatively impacted by climate change. The rise in temperatures, drop in precipitation, intensified droughts, and frequent SDSs have not only threatened the ecosystem and biodiversity but also jeopardized the country’s food security by exacerbating soil erosion, expanding desertification, and declining agricultural productivity.
Iran chairs intl. event on combating SDSs
Iran’s ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations, Amir-Saeed Iravani, chaired a high-level event held to mark the International Day for Combating Sand and Dust Storms (SDSs) in New York on July 10.
The event was organized by the Permanent Missions of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Iraq, the Republic of Senegal and Mongolia, in cooperation with members of the United Nations Coalition on Combating Sand and Dust Storms, providing a platform to exchange experiences, strengthen partnerships and identify actions to advance implementation at the national, regional and global levels.
At Iran’s initiative, in 2023, the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed July 12 as the International Day of Combating Sand and Dust Storms, recognizing that SDSs and their negative impacts at different scales are issues of international concern.
This year, the day was marked under the theme: ‘From Source to Impact: Protecting Land and Life from Sand and Dust Storms’. The event brought together Member States, United Nations entities, regional and international organizations, experts and other stakeholders to strengthen international cooperation and accelerate action to address the growing impacts of sand and dust storms.
As highlighted by the four host countries, dust storms, beyond degrading land and the environment, have severely impacted human health, food and water security, agriculture, transportation, infrastructure, economic activities, biodiversity, and the achievement of sustainable development goals.
Addressing the event, Iravani highlighted that dust storms have become a global challenge affecting development, health, food security, transportation, the economy, climate change, and the environment, which requires a comprehensive, preventive approach based on broad international cooperation to be dealt with, IRNA reported.
Besides climate change, drought, desertification, land degradation, and the unsustainable use of natural resources, conflicts and wars, particularly in the West Asia, have resulted into land degradation, deterioration of natural resource management, and emergence or expansion of dust and sandstorm hotspots, he noted.
Highlighting the impact of unilateral coercive measures and sanctions on the capacity of developing countries to protect their environments, Iravani stressed the need to eliminate barriers to environmental cooperation and ensure equitable access for affected countries to necessary resources, technology, and knowledge.
The official welcomed the regional programs of the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific as well as the inter-regional cooperation between the Commission and the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia.
He described the United Nations Decade on Combating Sand and Dust Storms (2025–2035) a significant opportunity to convert political commitments into practical, results-oriented actions.
During the interactive dialogue session, representatives of UN member states called for strengthening scientific, technical, and financial collaborations, developing early warning systems, ensuring sustainable land management, combating desertification, and enhancing the resilience of vulnerable communities.
The participants noted that SDSs know no political border, and that no individual country can tackle the challenge on its own. Accordingly, enhancing the role of the UN, fostering cooperation among source countries where dust originates, transit countries, and destination countries that receive dust, as well as effectively supporting developing countries, are essential to achieve sustainable responses.
The four countries, Iran, Iraq, Senegal, and Mongolia, issued a joint statement reaffirming their commitment to promoting regional and international cooperation to combat dust storms. They called for governments, the UN, financial institutions, regional organizations, scientific centers, private sectors, and other stakeholders to enhance their cooperation in areas like prevention, monitoring, early warning, land restoration, knowledge and technology transfer, capacity building, and securing financial resources.

Belarus has sought to have U.S. sanctions lifted since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year. The Biden administration had introduced many of the sanctions in response to the 2020 election crackdown in Belarus and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.S. has negotiated the release of hundreds of Belarusian political prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief since Coale initiated talks with Minsk last year. Tuesday marked Coale’s first visit to Belarus in six months.
At the latest meeting, which Belarusian state media said lasted around three hours, Coale told Lukashenko that Trump “fully supports everything we’re doing.”
Before traveling to Belarus, the American envoy met with Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys in Vilnius and freed Nobel laureate Ales Bialiatski in Washington to discuss regional security and ongoing prisoner releases.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake, take them,” Lukashenko told reporters last week, expressing frustration that U.S.-Belarusian talks are “stuck” on the issue of releasing political prisoners.

Public Broadcasting has begun accepting applications for the national selection for the international song contest "Eurovision 2027," which will take place in the city of Burgas (Bulgaria), UNN writes.
Applications may be submitted from September 15 through November 2, 2026, inclusive. The winner will be selected in February 2027. The format will be developed taking into account security risks and possible challenges during the winter period
Artists who will be 18 years old as of May 3, 2027, may participate in the national selection; both solo performers and groups of no more than 6 members may apply; the selection requirements stipulate that songs must be no longer than 3 minutes; only original songs created without using other works will be eligible; a song competing in the national selection must not have been previously published or performed publicly; there is no limit on the number of songs submitted by one participant; demo versions may be submitted.
In addition, participants in Ukraine's national selection may not take part in selections conducted by other countries participating in the contest.
Following the nationwide preliminary selection, a longlist of participants who will continue in the national selection will be formed. The list will include up to 12 performers. Longlist participants must attend an audition, with personal attendance being mandatory. Based on the audition results, a shortlist comprising at least 6 participants will be selected. The shortlist will be published on the Public Broadcaster's platforms by December 4
Next, a ranked online vote will be held among the longlist participants who do not make the shortlist, determining one more shortlist participant.
The full shortlist will be published on the Public Broadcaster's websites no later than January 22, 2027.
It is noted that musician and composer Dmytro Shurov (Pianoбой) has become the music producer of the 2027 national selection.

Russian Tu-95 Strategic Bomber Repair Hub Reportedly Targeted in Taganrog Missile Strike
A missile attack struck the Russian city of Taganrog overnight on September 15, with preliminary reports indicating that the Beriev aviation complex, a key facility involved in repairing and modernizing Russia’s Tu-95 strategic bombers, may have been among the targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rostov region governor Yuri Slyusar confirmed what he described as a large-scale missile attack on the city. According to his statement, the strike damaged agricultural warehouses, an Ozon logistics warehouse, a commercial building, a grocery store, a gas pipeline, several residential buildings, and an educational facility. Several fires were also reported.
According to Supernova+ and other monitoring channels on September 15, explosions and smoke were reported near the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex. The channels also reported that Russian military aircraft were undergoing repairs at the facility at the time of the attack.
The exact extent of any damage to the aviation complex has not yet been independently confirmed.
The Beriev plant is one of Russia’s major military aviation maintenance facilities and has been involved in repairing and modernizing Tu-95MS strategic bombers, aircraft used by Russia to launch long-range cruise missiles against Ukraine.
Defense Express previously reported that documents leaked in 2025 revealed a contract worth approximately $200 million for the repair of three Tu-95MS bombers at the Taganrog facility. The work was valued at roughly $66 million per aircraft.
According to Defense Express, the nature of the work indicated that the aircraft could have been undergoing modernization toward the Tu-95MSM configuration, which includes upgrades allowing the bombers to carry additional Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles.
The Beriev complex also repairs and modernizes other Russian military aircraft and operates its own Taganrog-Yuzhny airfield. The city is also home to the Taganrog-Central military airfield and the 325th Aircraft Repair Plant, making it an important aviation maintenance hub for the Russian military.
The Beriev facility has been targeted previously. In November 2025, Ukrainian forces struck military-industrial facilities in Taganrog. Ukraine’s General Staff later reported that an experimental A-60 aircraft may have been destroyed during the attack.
The September 15 strike followed another attack on Taganrog several days earlier, when fires were reported near aviation and industrial facilities in the city.
Earlier, satellite imagery confirmed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant after a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strike. The facility supplies materials used in Russian weapons production, including components linked to Iskander-M, Kinzhal, Kalibr, Grad, Smerch, and Tornado-S systems.

Kremlin welcomes Trump’s idea of energy truce with Ukraine, calls for sanctions removal

Kremlin welcomes Trump’s idea of energy truce with Ukraine, calls for sanctions removal
MOSCOW - The Kremlin said on Sept 15 it welcomed a US proposal for a Russia-Ukraine moratorium on attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, while saying it was also necessary to protect seaborne exports and remove “illegal” sanctions on Russia.
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other’s energy targets, though neither side has confirmed such an agreement.
Russia hit petrol stations in Kyiv on Sept 15 and Ukraine said it struck a Russian oil refinery.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Trump’s suggestion was a “very good idea”, but it would take more than that to bring down global fuel prices.
“It is necessary to ensure safe commercial shipping and navigation here, including for oil tankers. The Kyiv regime has so far shown no inclination to guarantee such security,” Peskov said.
“And the second thing that needs to be done is, of course, to lift sanctions (against Russia) and these unlawful restrictions on energy supplies. Only then will the world be adequately supplied with these petroleum products, global markets will stabilise, and prices will move lower.”
Peskov said Russia would stay in touch with the Americans about Trump’s proposal.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Kyiv was ready to support an energy ceasefire only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to end its war on Ukraine.
Ukrainian strikes on energy facilities have led to a summer of fuel shortages in Russia, causing it to restrict exports.
That has added to shortages of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel on energy markets, pushing up prices and stoking global inflation.
Ukraine, which faces regular Russian attacks on its own energy infrastructure, says refineries are legitimate military targets.
Trump urged Zelensky on Sept 13 to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks were causing a diesel shortage that is “hurting the world”.
The Kremlin said on Sept 14 that the global market upheaval was mainly due to the conflict in the Gulf.
Trump launched military strikes on Iran in February and Tehran responded by largely closing the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies had previously passed.
Russia and Ukraine have also been also hitting each other’s cargo vessels in the Black and Azov seas.
The escalation has driven up the price of grain, of which both are major exporters. REUTERS
