Hamas seizes on Israeli film ‘NAZA,’ urges ICC to use testimony against Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:12:35 UTC
20:12:35 KST

Hamas on Tuesday publicly seized on the Israeli documentary NAZA, calling on the International Criminal Court, United Nations bodies and human rights organizations to use testimony featured in the film as part of investigations against Israel over the war in Gaza.
The terror group presented the film as support for its allegations that Israel deliberately targeted Palestinian civilians and committed genocide and ethnic cleansing, claims Israel has repeatedly rejected.
In a statement issued on its official channel, Hamas said the significance of NAZA stemmed from testimony by people who had served inside Israel’s military and intelligence establishment and had taken part in surveillance and targeting systems.
Hamas said the documentary includes testimony from 24 IDF soldiers, officers and intelligence personnel and claimed those accounts reveal how targets were selected and strikes approved in Gaza. The figure was cited by Hamas in its statement.
The group also highlighted the film’s use of the term “NAZA,” the Hebrew military acronym for collateral damage, and argued that testimony in the documentary should be formally documented as part of international investigations into alleged war crimes.
“Hamas calls on the International Criminal Court, UN bodies and relevant human rights organizations to document the testimonies and information contained in the film and make use of them in investigation and accountability proceedings,” the group said.
It also cited the reception the documentary received at the Venice International Film Festival, where it was greeted with a prolonged standing ovation reportedly lasting 25 minutes, portraying the response as evidence of the film’s international impact.
“What NAZA revealed must not remain merely material for viewing and sympathy,” Hamas said, calling for it to become “an additional impetus for investigation and accountability.”
The statement marks a new stage in the controversy surrounding the documentary, with Hamas now explicitly incorporating the Israeli-made film into its international political and legal campaign against Israel.
NAZA, created by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Shor, has drawn attention for allegations based in part on anonymous testimony from soldiers and intelligence personnel involved in the Gaza campaign.
According to descriptions of the film and interviews with its creators, it alleges that Israeli targeting systems relied heavily on digital surveillance and artificial intelligence, that human oversight was insufficient in some cases and that strikes were approved despite expectations of significant civilian casualties.
The documentary also raises allegations concerning shootings in areas with unclear boundaries, attacks near aid distribution points, the destruction of civilian areas and Israeli policies toward food and humanitarian supplies.
Israel and the IDF have rejected allegations that they pursued a policy of deliberately killing civilians or committing genocide, arguing that Hamas embedded fighters, weapons, command centers and an extensive tunnel network inside densely populated civilian areas.
The IDF has said its targeting procedures require human authorization and assessments of military necessity, proportionality and expected civilian harm, and has maintained that it takes extensive precautions intended to reduce civilian casualties.
The film has already triggered a heated debate inside Israel over the conduct of the Gaza war, the use of artificial intelligence in targeting and the legal and moral standards applied by the IDF.
Hamas’ statement now adds another dimension to that debate: testimony and allegations originating inside Israel are being cited directly by the terror organization as material it wants international courts and institutions to use against the country.

Poland’s Orlen rushes to find alternatives to Saudi oil supply, traders say
LONDON/WARSAW, Sept 15 - Polish integrated oil firm Orlen is rushing to find crude oil cargoes from the North Sea and further afield to replace disrupted Saudi imports, five industry sources told Reuters.
Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco became Orlen's top supplier in 2022, helping wean it off of Russian oil but making the Polish company reliant on the Saudi producer which is now grappling with disruptions to its exports due to war in the Middle East.
Orlen purchased several cargoes of crude oil in spot tenders on Friday and Monday, the sources said. It picked up North Sea grades including Grane, Johan Sverdrup and Johan Castberg, two of the traders said.
It also tendered for grades further afield including U.S. WTI Midland and Kazakh CPC Blend, two sources added.
Orlen and subsidiaries operate oil refineries in Poland, Lithuania, and the Czech Republic. Poland's Baltic port of Gdansk received around 160,000 barrels per day of Saudi crude this year to date, and Lithuania's Butinge received 63,000 bpd, according to data form analytics firm Kpler.
Together, those accounted for around 59% of Europe's total Saudi imports, the data show. Orlen also imported a smaller volume of Saudi crude to Trieste which is connected to its Czech plants.
At least four tanker fixtures to bring crude oil from the terminal in Sidi Kerir, Egypt to Gdansk in September have failed, shipping data reviewed by Reuters showed.
Saudi Arabia is grappling with a wave of attacks from Iran-aligned militia, including one which took its East-West Pipeline offline last Thursday.
ARAMCO IS ORLEN'S TOP SUPPLIER
Saudi Aramco in recent years became Orlen's largest supplier, delivering some 40% of the crude Orlen processes.
Last month, Orlen signed a contract with Equinor for supplies of up to 25% of Orlen's refining capacity in Lithuania, Poland and the Czech Republic, making the Norwegian company its second-largest supplier.
By contrast, in 2015 Orlen was almost fully relying on crude from Russia, according to the company's former CEO. The company reduced its dependency over the following years.
No further details on the tenders were available and the results could not be directly confirmed with the counterparties. Orlen declined to comment on details of specific commercial transactions, but said it actively manages its supply portfolio to ensure the uninterrupted operation of its refining assets.
"Adjusting and optimising purchase volumes is a standard, ongoing part of the Orlen Group’s operations, driven by both current production needs and changing market conditions," an Orlen spokesperson said.
Currently, feedstock deliveries to Orlen refineries are proceeding without disruption, the spokesperson said. REUTERS

The discovery of hundreds of bodies in the rubble of Gaza buildings destroyed in Israel's genocidal war on the Palestinian territory has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes.

"It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed," he said in a statement.
He said the discoveries revived concerns raised in a 2024 U.N. report that found Israeli strikes on residential buildings and other civilian sites during the early weeks of the war may have violated international humanitarian law.
"Every feasible effort must be taken to document and identify these victims, preserve forensic information and biological samples, record their burial locations and inform their families."
"The discovery of extensive remains under the rubble in Gaza City resurfaces (the) concerns of war crimes and other atrocity crimes," he warned.
The Israeli prime minister's office and Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Israel rejects that it deliberately targets civilians and claims it acted in accordance with international law in Gaza.
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza – launched after a Hamas incursion into Israel in October 2023 – has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United Nations.
A U.S.-brokered cease-fire brought an end to full-scale fighting in October 2025, but Israel continues to strike the coastal enclave on a daily basis.
The Palestinian Civil Defense says more than 630 bodies and human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025.
Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the wreckage.
The United Nations also called for international investigators to be granted access to all of Gaza "to assist with evidence-gathering" as hundreds of bodies are pulled from the rubble.
"The remains of what appears to be entire families are now being unearthed at locations that were pulverized by Israeli attacks," Türk said.
He feared that the remains recovered so far could be "only the tip of the iceberg," noting that large parts of Gaza had been flattened by Israeli bombing or later demolition and clearance operations.
Türk also accused Israel of continuing to level some areas of Gaza where its forces remain deployed, saying bulldozers were operating "with no respect for the dead under the rubble."
Israel's Gaza genocide killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities.
Israel claims it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian casualties and alleges that Hamas uses Gaza's civilians as human shields, without offering proof.
The U.N. rights chief called for international investigators to be granted access to all parts of Gaza to help preserve evidence, citing ongoing legal proceedings examining conduct during the war.
Israel has blocked the entry of heavy machinery needed to remove rubble, according to Türk's statement.
Francesca Albanese, the U.N. expert on the Palestinian territories, has said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified before full clearance starts.
This month, the Palestinian Civil Defence said 96 bodies and human remains had been recovered from a single site in the Zeitoun area of Gaza City, including 58 children and 23 women.

Logistics diversification pushes rental rates up 20-30% – expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:07:46 EEST
20:07:46 KST

Ukrainian businesses have lost nearly half of their warehouse stock to Russian strikes, and as companies diversify their logistics, rental rates are rising 20-30% compared with the start of the year, commercial real estate consultant Vitaliy Mukhanov told Interfax-Ukraine.
According to a WINHUB study, Ukraine's warehouse infrastructure had shrunk 50% as of early September, with 2.1 million square meters of Class A/B space destroyed by the enemy out of 4.2 million square meters that existed at the start of 2022. New construction over 2022-2026 (800,000 square meters) has only partially offset the losses. The situation is even more pronounced in the Kyiv region, where more warehouse space was lost in the first eight months of 2026 alone than over 2022-2025 combined, with a total of 68% of stock lost (1.5 million square meters).
According to Mukhanov, companies are now actively rethinking how they organize their logistics: reducing the size of individual warehouses, splitting inventory across multiple locations, and considering relocating to relatively safer regions.
"Businesses are trying to avoid overconcentrating inventory in large logistics hubs. In inquiries, there's a noticeable focus on 1,500-3,000 square meter spaces in smaller warehouse facilities. The main goal of this approach is to reduce the risk of losing a significant share of goods and halting operations all at once. We're also seeing interest in the build-to-suit format, that is, constructing facilities tailored to the specific needs of the end tenant or buyer. Facilities still under construction are being actively considered as well," Mukhanov said.
He said the rise in rental rates is already noticeable, with some listings up 20-30%.
"There's still room for further increases, especially in the compact warehouse segment. At the same time, the trend depends on the specific location, the property's characteristics, and the availability of alternatives for tenants, of which there are few. This is also affecting relationships with existing tenants. Owners are more actively pushing to renegotiate rents upward, benchmarking against the rates new clients are willing to pay. Where an agreement can't be reached, some owners are prepared to switch tenants once the contract ends or when its terms allow," he said.
As a result, property owners' negotiating position is strengthening, while tenants have fewer opportunities to preserve their previous commercial terms. According to Mukhanov, the most advantageous approach for businesses is to enter negotiations during the development stage, when it's still possible to secure optimal pricing in exchange for a longer contract term. Insurance terms, which are currently being systematically reviewed, are also affecting future rates.

Brazil's top court postpones ruling on probe of justice in politically charged case
BRASILIA, Sept 15 - Brazil's Supreme Court on Tuesday postponed a decision on whether to investigate one of its own justices in connection with a politically explosive bank corruption case, possibly deferring the issue until after an October presidential election.
The justices held a hearing to consider opening a probe into Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who rose to national prominence by leading investigations that resulted in the convictions of former President Jair Bolsonaro and several allies last year for plotting a coup to reverse 2022 election results.
The Supreme Court session was halted for up to 90 days on Tuesday evening after Justice Flavio Dino formally asked for more time to review the probe request.
The issue has become a flashpoint in the presidential election in which right-wing candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the former president's son, is in a tight race against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Lula's opponents have tied him to Moraes in campaign rhetoric.
The call for an investigation of Moraes is an outgrowth of a case involving failed lender Banco Master that has rattled Brazil for months.
Leaks revealed that Daniel Vorcaro, the bank's imprisoned owner, had a vast web of influence and embarrassed some of the nation's top power brokers, including Senator Bolsonaro himself.
Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca released a federal police report two weeks ago alleging that Vorcaro sent several text messages to Moraes including references to a possible escape plan.
Moraes has accused Mendonca, who was appointed by Bolsonaro, of abusing his authority in handling the case, which Mendonca has denied.
According to court records, a law firm owned by Moraes' wife had a $24 million consulting contract with Banco Master, which was liquidated by the central bank in November 2025.
Before Tuesday's hearing, Moraes said the records were illegally gathered and did not show any wrongdoing. He argued the calls for him to be investigated were politically and electorally motivated as revenge for his role in convicting former President Bolsonaro.
Chief Justice Edson Fachin, in an attempt to contain the crisis engulfing the court, last week ordered the unsealing of proceedings related to the Banco Master case, only for Brazilians to learn that Senator Bolsonaro, the right-wing presidential hopeful, was also being investigated over alleged money laundering and corruption linked to the bank.
The younger Bolsonaro denied any wrongdoing and said that all dealings he had with Vorcaro were private and related to Vorcaro's role in financing a film about his father. REUTERS

The SBU thwarted a terrorist attack in the Kyiv region prepared by Russian intelligence services
Kyiv • UNN
In the Kyiv region, an unemployed woman who was supposed to blow up a car with an improvised device was detained. The woman was recruited remotely by Russian intelligence services.
Counterintelligence officers and investigators of the Security Service of Ukraine thwarted yet another attempt by Russian intelligence services to carry out a terrorist attack in Kyiv region. This was reported by UNN, citing the SBU press center.
Details
The detainee was a local unemployed woman who was supposed to blow up a car near an apartment building in the capital’s suburbs. According to the investigation, the Russians recruited the woman remotely, posing as employees of the Security Service of Ukraine and the National Police of Ukraine.
First, a Russian intelligence officer called the unemployed woman, introduced himself as a Ukrainian law enforcement officer, and offered to help her obtain medicines that she had previously purchased through specialized websites. After that, the woman received an assignment from the enemy: retrieve a package from a cache and wait for further instructions. It was later established that the package contained an improvised explosive device. After the woman retrieved the package with the homemade bomb, her handler from Russia instructed her to additionally check whether the components for the IED were working
According to the intelligence service, the Russian handler directed the woman to a residential neighborhood in the capital’s suburbs and ordered her to leave the disguised IED under the wheel of a car parked near a local supermarket.
The investigation is currently underway to identify all individuals involved in cooperation with Russia and bring them to justice. The detainee may face life imprisonment.

Flawed tests by Israeli cyber firm triggered real-world AI breaches: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:04:39 UTC
20:04:39 KST

Yasin Gungor
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Real-world cybersecurity breaches by artificial intelligence models at Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta stemmed from flawed testing environments created by a Tel Aviv-based contractor rather than rogue autonomous behavior, according to an investigative report.
"A single firm, Irregular, is responsible for hacking done by all three companies," Monday's report by a US-based publication, Effort, claimed, explaining that while models gained unauthorized access to external servers, published malicious packages, and exploited vulnerabilities, the incidents occurred because the Israeli testing contractor mistakenly left internet connections active during simulated capture-the-flag exercises.
The findings challenge recent efforts by leading artificial intelligence developers to promote an existential narrative around runaway systems. In earlier disclosures, Anthropic attributed four separate breaches by its Claude model to artificial intelligence "recklessness," while Irregular described "the agent itself becoming a threat actor." Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei subsequently cited catastrophic risks, warning that future swarms "could be capable of taking over the entire internet" following a breach at Hugging Face, to argue that frontier laboratories must deliberately coordinate to pace technological progress.
Flawed test boundaries
Technical evidence detailed in the report showed that evaluators repeatedly misled the models by asserting in prompts that internet access was disabled, even as configuration errors left public network access wide open. Furthermore, evaluators failed to establish operational boundaries or define which computer networks were authorized targets, allowing isolated model instances to scour external networks for up to 34 hours per run.
The report emphasized that real-world hacking ceased entirely once engineers implemented basic prompts, directing the models not to do real-world hacking. "According to their own findings, Anthropic and Irregular bear all of the responsibility for the cybersecurity incidents they caused," the Effort said.
Rather than acknowledging administrative negligence, the report alleged, developers deployed aligned safety advocates to deflect blame toward a "baseless 'rogue agent' theory."
Israeli corporate footprint and funding
The investigation traced Irregular's leadership directly to the Effective Altruism movement in Israel. Irregular co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Omer Nevo serves on the board of Effective Altruism Israel, while Chief Executive Dan Lahav co-founded educational entities alongside Nevo's brother, Sella Nevo. These interconnected entities, alongside Irregular's initial investor Good Ventures, receive direct financing from Asana co-founder Dustin Moskovitz through Coefficient Giving and Open Philanthropy.
The analysis noted that unauthorized intrusions and record alterations carried out through unsecured models risk violating the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. However, legal enforcement remains complicated by Irregular's dual registration as Pattern Labs Tech Inc in Delaware and Pattern Tech Ltd in Tel Aviv, creating a jurisdictional shield where critical Israeli personnel, assets, and operational decisions may evade direct US congressional and regulatory accountability.
Neither Irregular nor its American client laboratories have issued an official response to the investigative report.
The investigative disclosures come directly amid an intensifying debate over artificial intelligence pacing and federal oversight, exposing a sharp contradiction between the industry's public alarms and its private operational practices.
Over recent days, technology executives mounted a coordinated push to slow down technological development, citing existential hazards and catastrophic autonomous actions to justify deliberate pacing, pre-training safety cases, and independent third-party monitoring.
However, the report claims that the very cybersecurity crises cited to validate this urgent slowdown were not caused by autonomous systems escaping human control, but by basic administrative negligence, absent network firewalls, and unconstrained test environments managed by an Israeli firm.

EXPLAINED: Energy Truce in Ukraine – Third Time’s the Charm?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:04:08 UTC
20:04:08 KST

US President Donald Trump claimed on Monday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an energy truce.
But this isn’t the first time the US has attempted to mediate an energy truce. The one in early 2026 was short-lived, while the most serious attempt yielded a 30-day truce proposal in March 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
That, too, soon fell apart, as everyone interpreted the terms differently. But with Trump concerned about diesel prices – a problem he has pinned on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, rather than his own war in Iran – Washington may have a stronger vested interest in seeing it through this time, particularly ahead of November’s mid-term elections.
What’s the latest proposal?
There are no actual terms yet – though Ukraine has floated an energy truce in recent weeks ahead of a difficult winter.
By Trump’s account, on Monday, Kyiv and Moscow both agreed not to strike “energy targets” without further elaboration.
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do so, likewise,” Trump claimed on his Truth Social platform.
President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a statement an hour later, saying Ukraine supports the idea – without saying Kyiv has agreed – before adding that it will only do so in reciprocity, if its allies can guarantee that Russia will not strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure for a prolonged period.
“If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes,” Zelensky wrote.
54% of Eastern Germans Say Weapons for Ukraine Are Excessive, Poll Finds
Russia has not officially said whether it has agreed to the proposal.
What happened in March 2025?
Everyone ostensibly agreed to a 30-day energy truce in March 2025 soon after Trump’s return to office – just not the same version.
These differing interpretations allowed both sides to accuse the other of violations and use them to justify retaliatory strikes, while the lack of a monitoring mechanism also dampened the proposal’s effectiveness.
In short, US officials said Washington had reached separate agreements with Ukraine and Russia to “develop measures for implementing” a ceasefire, but the duration and list of facilities differed for each.
From the Russian side, it listed March 18 as the start date – despite the official talks in Saudi Arabia starting on March 23 – and omitted facilities that Kyiv said were included in its version.
In a statement to the news outlet European Pravda at the time, Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy said Russia’s list did not include its oil and gas production facilities, contrary to Kyiv’s agreement with the US. The exact list of facilities Kyiv presented is unclear.
And violations soon took place – on March 28, Russia struck gas production facilities in Ukraine’s Central Poltava region. The same day, Russia accused Ukraine of firing US-made HIMARS missiles at the Sudzha gas metering station in the Kursk region bordering Ukraine, a claim that Kyiv dismissed as a Russian “false flag.”
In other words, no ceasefire.
Why might Ukraine, Russia want an energy truce?
Ukraine is concerned about a difficult winter, while Russia is facing an unprecedented fuel crisis.
For Ukraine, energy infrastructure – including power stations, substations and gas storage facilities – has been hit hard by Russian attacks in previous winters. Repairs are costly and time-consuming, and with the country facing a budget crunch, any further Russian strikes would put additional pressure on a system already strained by subzero winter temperatures.
For Russia, meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure have hit export revenues and severely cut domestic fuel supplies, raising concerns about public discontent. A recent think tank report suggested that Russia’s overall exports and revenues dropped by 7% and 8% respectively, with extra spending needed to import gasoline and diesel to keep the country running.
But at the same time, both Kyiv and Moscow also expect each other to break this winter, with top officials and commanders calling the season a win-or-break moment in the war, casting doubt on whether an energy truce can hold.
Third time’s the charm?
Another attempt at an energy truce took place in early 2026 and lasted a few days.
In late January, Trump said he had appealed to Russian leader Vladimir Putin to stop strikes on Kyiv and Ukrainian energy infrastructure to facilitate peace talks. Moscow confirmed the request and said it would last until Feb. 1, while Kyiv said there was no deal yet, but it would reciprocate nonetheless.
On Feb. 2, Russia resumed strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, leaving locals in the Kharkiv, Sumy, Dnipropetrovsk, and Cherkasy regions without power.
So, third time’s the charm with the latest proposal?

Algeria-UAE rupture impacts ports, industry and real estate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:02:56 UTC
20:02:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Fate of UAE investments in Algeria: Political rupture impacts ports, industry and real estate
Algeria's decision to sever political and diplomatic ties with the UAE began a new phase for investments between the two countries.
While the immediate impact is not expected to be significant in terms of trade, given the UAE's limited weight as a trading partner for Algeria, greater attention is focused on the future of UAE capital and investments already present in Algeria and the options that the new phase could impose on these interests.
According to Algerian economist and former parliamentarian Abdelkader Brich, the most pressing issue in the near future concerns UAE investments in Algeria, which are concentrated in several sectors, including ports, logistics, tobacco, real estate and hospitality.
Brich told The New Arab that the decision to cut diplomatic relations does not automatically end these investments, as existing contracts, partnership agreements, and capital holdings are governed by laws and agreements regulating investment, and therefore cannot be terminated or liquidated outside the legal and contractual frameworks governing them.
He stressed that cutting relations, in itself, does not mean confiscating investments, cancelling contracts or ending the legal activities of companies in which UAE entities hold stakes. Rather, it places existing economic relations within a new political reality imposed by Algerian sovereignty.
However, the legal continuation of contracts and investments does not necessarily mean that the investment relationship will remain in the same form as before the rupture.
The movement of capital and investments is affected by the nature of political relations and the level of trust between countries, making the future of some UAE investments in Algeria likely to be reassessed in light of the new phase.
Brich pointed to the possibility of divestment and the sale of stakes, rather than liquidating the economic activity itself.
Depending on the nature of each project, ownership of some of these stakes could pass to Algerian investors, including state-owned institutions or companies, or to foreign investors.
UAE investments in Algeria are concentrated in several sectors, including ports and logistics services, where DP World operates the Port of Algiers and Djen Djen Port in Jijel provinces.
From a legal standpoint, the 30-year concession contract has not officially expired, as it is expected to continue until 2039.
But the partnership is facing a practical freeze on the ground.
In September 2019, the Algerian government ended DP World's monopoly over some powers. Moreover, it took back the shares of the Port Services Group (Serport), making the Algerian a direct partner for the Port of Algiers, in a move that reduced the UAE company's influence.
In the defence sector, Algerian-UAE cooperation in recent years has included several projects related to the assembly and manufacture of armoured vehicles, and the development of defence industrial capabilities.
These projects include Nimer Algeria, which was established as a partnership between UAE-based EDGE Group and the Algerian Ministry of National Defence's Mechanical Industries Development Group.
The cooperation includes a factory in Khenchela dedicated to producing NIMR light armoured vehicles, with an estimated production capacity of hundreds of vehicles annually, as well as investments aimed at developing production and assembly lines.
The cooperation also included a project to produce Fuchs 2 armoured vehicles in Algeria.
It also extended to the utility vehicle sector for military and paramilitary use through projects linked to Mercedes-Benz factories in Tiaret and Rouiba, producing four-wheel-drive vehicles and trucks for military and paramilitary use.
In the tobacco sector, several Algerian-UAE companies are active, including the Algerian-UAE Tobacco Company, known as Sétif Tobacco and Matches Company (CETIM), and United Tobacco Company.
The sector has recently seen legal and regulatory measures and reviews by the Algerian authorities, covering some contracts, transactions and documentary dealings linked to these companies.
In the real estate sector, UAE involvement in Algeria has been linked to several projects, most notably those of Emaar and the Dounia Park project.
However, most of these projects were not completed according to the initial plans and no longer represent existing or ongoing UAE real estate projects.
The statements of Workers' Party Secretary-General Louisa Hanoune came to the fore after she recalled in a press statement that the party had opposed, between 2014 and 2015, granting 50% of the Port of Algiers to DP World.
She said the party had campaigned to overturn the decision, given the port's strategic importance and its connection, in her assessment, to internal security and national security.
Hanoune also revived the file of the tobacco and matches company, objecting to the transfer of 65% of the company's capital to interests linked to a UAE investor.
She said the company had been highly important to the public treasury, as its taxes made it the second-largest contributor to the treasury after Sonatrach.
The official also addressed the major Dounia Park project, stressing that the Workers' Party had not supported it.
She noted that the Algerian state had paid large sums as part of international arbitration linked to the project.
Hanoune further said that the UAE's economic presence in Algeria went beyond a purely commercial and investment dimension.
She argued that some concessions and projects had become a source of influence within sectors considered important to the national economy and Algerian sovereignty.

UK trade unions warn against ‘Americanisation of our politics’ from big political donations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:01:34 UTC
20:01:34 KST

Trade unions have stopped short of backing a cap on political donations but called for further action on big money in politics, in a joint statement after Reform UK was given an unprecedented £72m from two donors.
General secretaries have been split on a call for unions to back a specific cap on individual donors to political parties while protecting trade union donations, which the TUC said were the “cleanest money in politics” because it came from workers’ subscriptions.
Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, was among those who called on the unions to go further, warning about the dangers to democracy posed by billionaires buying influence.
In a statement at the TUC conference on Tuesday, general secretaries warned: “The scale of donations made to Reform in recent days is unprecedented in British politics and should deeply concern anyone who cares about the health and integrity of our democracy.
“We cannot afford to see the Americanisation of our politics, with out-of-control political spending, funded by stratospheric sums of crypto and corporate cash. These donations show clearly whose side Reform are on, with crypto billionaires, foreign and powerful corporate interests lining up to pour in eye-watering sums of money to advance their agendas.”
But the statement said trade union funding of political parties should not be put in the same category as donations from wealthy individuals. Trade unions that are affiliated to Labour, including Unite, Unison and GMB, are the biggest donors to the party.
“Trade union funding is the cleanest money in politics,” the statement said. “Union donations are made up of the collective subscriptions of care workers, teaching assistants, shop workers and millions of trade union members, democratically controlled and heavily regulated.
“We will continue to work with policymakers to clean up our politics and strengthen public trust in our democratic system. We expect our government to protect our democracy from being captured by the super-rich. Unions are committed to ensuring that working people have a strong, collective voice in the decisions that affect their jobs, their communities and their futures.”
Graham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the £72m combined donations to Reform UK from the crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne were not comparable to union funding. “There is a transparency issue, there is an individual versus collective issue, and I think it is quite worrying,” she said.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC conference, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour.
“How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” Rayner said.
“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy. We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.”
The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said the donations to Reform were “a blatant attempt to effect a corporate takeover of our politics” and this should “ring alarm bells”.
“In the years since corporate donations became unrestricted in the United States, we’ve watched with horror the corporate capture of that nation’s democracy,” he told the conference on Tuesday.
“As unions, we will continue to work with government to clean up our politics, to protect our democracy and to strengthen public trust.”
Later on Tuesday, Downing Street confirmed that work is under way to look at retrospectively tightening residency rules for donations in a bill already going through parliament, a move which could mean the money handed over by Delo and Harborne needing to be given back.
Delo formerly lived in Hong Kong, while Harborne spends much of his time in Thailand. Both are registered to vote in the UK, which allows them to donate. Under current rules, being resident for electoral purposes is a matter of voluntarily affirming you have a permanent home address in the UK.
A No 10 spokesperson said ministers were looking at a possible toughening of this system, which could come in amendments to the ongoing representation of the people bill.
“We are looking to introduce an enhanced residency test for political donors. These enhanced rules will mean you also have to demonstrate an ongoing presence in the UK, details of which will be set out shortly,” the spokesperson said.
Asked if this had been under consideration before the new donations, he declined to say. But asked if the idea was intentionally targeting Reform, he replied: “No, I completely reject that.”

More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:00:41 UTC
20:00:41 KST

More than 1,000 women invested in the slave trade, challenging the conventional notion that they were passive beneficiaries and largely fought for its abolition.
Researchers found women bought, sold and brokered shares in the Royal African Company, South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, and used profits from the trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure financial independence and provide for their families.
By the time the RAC, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved people, was dissolved in 1752, women made up about 10% of shareholders.
The Register of British Slave Traders, revealed exclusively in the Guardian, shows that women from across society played an active role in financing and sustaining the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.
Investors ranged from queens and princesses to titled nobility, merchants, shopkeepers and cowherds.
The archives include letters in which women discuss profits from “African stock”, while company records show one investor, Helen Gladman, asking the RAC to transport a young African girl from Sherbro Island, off Sierra Leone, to England to serve in her household.
Researchers found women were involved “at almost every level” of the company’s activities. They acted as brokers, supplied goods including barrels and swords traded on the Atlantic African coast, managed company property and used their familial and social networks to strengthen the company’s finances and political influence.
Lila O’Leary Chambers, a lecturer at the University of Cambridge who researched women’s involvement for the register project, said: “This research really shows that this was not just a flash in the pan.
“Across the entirety of the Royal African Company and its various guises, there were women contributing financially and expecting a financial return from the slave trade.”
Women invested from the earliest years of enslavement, from Queen Elizabeth I’s backing in the 1560s to Lady Elizabeth Craven’s £1,000 loan financing a voyage to the Gambia through the Guinea Company. Some investors, unable to write their names, signed company records with a spidery “X”.
The research identifies 1,100 female investors across the histories of the RAC, the South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, though the true number is likely to have been higher. Of the 457 women whose marital status could be identified, almost half were widows and just over 42% were unmarried. Of the 7% who were married, most were aristocrats.
For many, these investments were crucial to gaining economic independence. “They were making the decision to invest, or they inherited shares and suddenly had this other asset they did not have before,” Chambers said.
Some became active traders and traded shares for friends and family, she added. “It was not a career as they would see it, but we might think: this has become your job.”
Chambers said the research directly challenged the conventional narrative that “white women come in at the point of abolition, see the suffering of enslaved people, identify with that oppression, and then work either to reform or ultimately abolish the slave trade and slavery itself”.
Work to overturn that misconception builds on decades of scholarship by historians from the Caribbean and west Africa, including Eric Williams, Elsa Goveia and Walter Rodney. More recent public-facing projects, such as the Legacies of British Slavery archive compiled by historians at University College London, have helped bring this history to wider audiences. The archive revealed that women were among those connected to the ownership of enslaved people who received compensation after slavery was abolished in a large portion of the empire in 1833, she said. Enslaved people received nothing.
“But this tells a much longer story, and that helps us see past a simple narrative that positions women historically as actually less complicated than they were.”
For Chambers, the accumulation of more than 1,000 names was itself a “gut punch”, because of the lack of similar information about enslaved African women.
“Historians and activists have really struggled to locate the names of enslaved people, to restore biographies to them, and to give a sense of their world,” Chambers said.
“The comparative opportunity to do this research for the people who invested is just really striking.”
Olivette Otele, a distinguished professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London, said while the lack of comparable detail about enslaved African women remained startling, “the more we know about enslavers, the better chance we have to know about enslaved women from the archives, because sometimes through diaries you can find more details”.
She added that archives alone cannot tell the full history, and future research should look at other evidence to help recover the lives and agency of enslaved women. “These women were the transmitters and the holders of their cultures wherever they were taken from,” she said. “Through food, music, and dancing, it’s about resistance and agency, and they transmitted that.”
The research also found that because female investors seemingly did not vote or hold board positions, they often relied on informal efforts to influence and shape a company.
Meeting minutes show women acting as witnesses, running the meeting house, delivering the goods exchanged for African lives, petitioning for wages, passing information and, most importantly, lending money and buying and selling shares.
Under English law, women who were single or widowed were in control of their own property and could operate as legal persons, while married women could not.
“That becomes really important for the Royal African Company as it stutters between financial crises,” Chambers said. “Women provided this important well of capital they could go to.”
In the early 18th century, the RAC secretary, John Perry, wrote to female investors, including Lady Dorothy Thomas and Mrs Stacy, urging them to exchange company debts for shares and persuade friends and relatives to do the same.
Chambers said: “That is a financial project, but it is also a political one, because he knows that they might not hold official positions, but women were very influential with their family members and with the way companies were perceived.”
The company survived long enough to attract at least 60 new female investors between 1713 and 1719, followed by another 250 women during a revival in the early 1720s.
The research also found many investors understood the violence underpinning their wealth. Some widows petitioned the courts for “head money” – bonuses owed to husbands according to the number of enslaved people they had trafficked.
“They would go and ask: he was supposed to get head money for 28 people he trafficked. Where is it? I am his widow and I need that,” Chambers said.
Chambers was also able to cross-reference some of the female investors with portraits of women with Black children who worked as their servants.
Women left RAC shares to their daughters to shore up their economic position, or used investment income to support widowed, disabled and vulnerable relatives.
In one letter, Mary Stanley committed to leaving £300 RAC stock and its proceeds to her son, Peter, with the caveat that if her daughter’s husband failed to provide her with “the necessaries of life”, Peter would use the stock to support her.
For Chambers, the research revealed a stark contradiction between white British women using their investments to protect their own families while investing in the destruction of African families.
“You cannot separate the way you think about investment from these structures of kinship, intimacy and violence,” she said. “That profit comes from denying those same kinship ties to African people, and denying their ability to make sure their own children are safe.
“That is so important to this story in particular, but also to how slavery shapes capitalism in general.”
Some investors endowed schools, churches, charities and universities that still exist today. Lettice Cornwallis, for example, funded education and charities while discussing acquiring an African boy for her household in family correspondence.
“This is an everyday conversation happening in houses,” Chambers said. “You see it in correspondence. There are these newsy, gossipy letters about someone getting married, someone being sick, or having a new recipe for a cordial, and then: by the way, how are your South Sea Company or Royal African Company shares doing?”
Female investors would have encountered African people in Britain, both free and enslaved, the research found. Dame Hester Buckworth, who bought £1,000 of RAC stock, knew Robert Negar, who was described in her husband’s will as his “Black servant”.
Another investor, Sarah Cornish, is thought to have shared a household with an African man named Paupey, whose legal status in England remains unclear.
Chambers often returns to the story of Susanna Sedgewick Phipps, who had a financial connection to the RAC throughout her life. Her grandson, James Phipps, later worked at Cape Coast Castle and married an Afro-Dutch woman, Catherina. He acknowledged their children in his will, some of whom later lived in England. One of their descendants, James Townsend, would eventually become Britain’s first elected Black MP.
Other women stood out to Chambers for the seeming mundanity of their concerns. She points to Sarah Clerke, who wrote frustrated letters to her nephew because she wanted to go to Tunbridge Wells to visit the spa and needed money from her African stock to do so.

‘Just be aware of what you’re spending’: budget hints for students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:00:41 UTC
20:00:41 KST

Like late-night study sessions and cramming into a student kitchen to cook up meals, being savvy with money has long been part of the university experience. But with the cost of living remaining high, students are more money-conscious than ever.
“It is one of the most difficult times to make ends meet as a student,” according to Tom Allingham, communications director at Save the Student (STS). He says soaring prices for essentials, such as food and energy bills, have “disproportionately affected” students, while maintenance loans (intended to help cover day-to-day costs) have failed to keep up with high rates of inflation.
STS’s 2025 money survey found the average student spends £1,142 a month on living costs, but receives a maintenance loan of £640, meaning the £502 shortfall has more than doubled since 2020.
So what are the best ways to stretch your loan as far as it will go?
Split money across multiple bank accounts
Opening a student bank account comes with plenty of perks, from free railcards and large interest-free overdrafts to a welcome cash incentive that may come in handy during freshers’ week festivities.
But to stay on top of your spending, don’t keep all of your money in one place. Robert Medhurst, 25, who graduated this summer from Nottingham Trent University, recommends opening a separate digital bank account alongside your main student account, to split your maintenance loan into daily budgets.
Budgeting features on apps such as Monzo, helped him to visualise his finances and rein in his spending, which he found much harder to track when all of his maintenance loan was lumped into one account.
Setting aside money and placing a spending cap on the pots feature – one for rent and others for weekly food shops and nights out – “really allows you to see how much you’re spending and not go over”, he says. It can also help curb the urge for contactless spending.
Make a budget before move-in day
It’s common for students to find themselves tipping into their overdraft faster than expected. To avoid the burden of being in the red, start setting out your budget before you step foot on campus. Allingham suggests incoming students use time over the summer to work out “where the gaps will be in your budget – where potentially you might need to cut back, or where you might need to look for extra income”.
There are plenty of free tools available to help, such as online budget trackers. Soham Chougale, education officer at University College Birmingham Guild of Students, created Your Friendly Guild Budget Buddy to help students keep their finances afloat amid the cost of living crisis. It includes features that help map out income and set saving goals, while offering information on where to access financial and mental health support in one place. “It realistically shows how a student would spend, rather than fancy budget planners which would have 10 other things that are not the top priorities,” says Chougale.
Research hardship funds and bursaries
If you’re experiencing financial difficulty while studying, applying for non-repayable hardship funds and bursaries offered by your university may help ease the strain. In recent years, some universities have doubled or tripled the amount of money in hardship support to students, while also widening the household income criteria for eligibility. Increasingly, says Allingham, institutions have “recognised that it’s not just people from the very poorest backgrounds that are struggling right now”.
For Medhurst, accessing a hardship fund “was a lifesaver”, helping to tide over part of his rent each term. “Don’t be afraid to ask and to look for it,” he says. “There’ll probably be something that you can apply for that can really save you a lot of money.”
Ask for a student discount
Whether stashed away in your wallet or slipped inside your phone case, be sure to keep your student ID on you. Discounts are a big bonus of student life so even if one isn’t advertised, don’t be afraid to wave your ID and ask.
Sign up to student discount platforms like UNiDAYS and Student Beans to enjoy exclusive 10% to 30% offers both in-store and online. Richard Jackson, head of content at Student Beans, says lots of chains such as YO! Sushi, Greene King and Pizza Express offer students in-store dining deals.
The key to securing great discounts, he adds, is to always plan ahead. Follow and set notifications for your favourite brands on discount sites, and keep an eye out for boosted seasonal deals around Freshers, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
Start planning your meals
After a long day of lectures, it can be convenient to order a quick meal from Deliveroo or Uber Eats. But relying on takeaway services can add up quickly, totalling an entire week’s food shop in just a single purchase. Instead, 21-year-old Chloe Harmer, a third-year fashion marketing student at Leeds Arts University, found cooking compact meals in bulk to carry around between classes a cost-effective alternative. “I pop it in the fridge and then when I’m about to leave for uni the next day, put it straight in my bag and then that’s lunch sorted,” she says. “And I’d just repeat that most days.”
Before heading off to the supermarket, know exactly what you want. Medhurst researched affordable, simple recipes online and then planned his shopping list around that. “Otherwise you go to Lidl and Aldi just kind of choosing willy-nilly, basing it on what you feel like there and then and it can be very easy to overspend,” he says.
Splurge on discount nights out
You can have a good time without burning through all your student loan. Holly Nicholson, 21, who just graduated with an English literature degree from the University of Bristol, says the key to big nights out on a budget is putting aside in advance how much money to spend on drinks or entry to clubs. And, of course, she says there’s always the old student kitchen tradition: pre-drinking with your flatmates.
Don’t overlook student society socials, which often boast subsidised drinks or free (and fun) events such as film screenings. If you’re a film or theatre devotee like 24-year-old Finola Clarke, an MA journalism student at Goldsmiths, signing up to student memberships at independent cinemas, weekly lottery queues for discounted theatre tickets and scavenging sites like TodayTix and the Stagedoor Rewards app offer some “ways to do what you enjoy at a significantly lower price”, she says.
“You’re in a really weird and hard-adjusting time of your life, don’t put too much pressure on yourself,” says Harmer. “Still have fun, but just be aware of what you’re spending.”
