Economic Watch: Reliable mainland market for Taiwan fruits challenges DPP's push for cross-Strait economic decoupling
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:50:54 CST
19:50:54 KST

This photo taken with a mobile phone on Sept. 9, 2026 shows pomelos at a pomelos garden in Juisui Township of Hualien County, southeast China's Taiwan. (Xinhua/Ma Xinran)
TAIPEI/BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- When fruit harvests peak, Taiwan farmers not only need favorable weather but also buyers capable of absorbing large volumes quickly. For an increasing number of them, these buyers are on the Chinese mainland, with its proximity, vast consumer market and measures to facilitate agricultural trade.
In Juisui Township of east Taiwan's Hualien County, farmers are racing to harvest and pack pomelos, a seasonal fruit with a mildly sour and sweet aftertaste. For growers like Yang Ju-huang, who cultivates more than 10,000 pomelo trees across a 22-mu (about 1.47 hectares) orchard, securing sales channels is as important as producing a good crop.
The pomelos grown in Juisui have relatively thick peels and can undergo a post-harvest process in which moisture gradually moves from the peel back into the flesh, making them well suited to long-distance transportation.
"That gives our pomelos a particular advantage in reaching consumers across the Taiwan Strait," Yang said.
Access to the mainland market has expanded this year. On Aug. 25 and Sept. 1 respectively, mainland authorities added more Taiwan pomelo orchards and packing facilities to the list eligible to export to the mainland.
The Farmers' Association in Juisui said that exports to the mainland and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region are expected to further grow this year.
For farmers, the significance lies not only in individual orders, but also in the predictability of demand.
"Pomelos exported to the mainland have stable sales, which gives farmers greater peace of mind," said Chen Ting, a Hualien grower.
This demand is increasingly visible beyond the orchards. Hualien pomelos have been showcased at major trade and agricultural events in Beijing, south China's Dongguan and Nanjing in east China this season, giving producers direct access to consumers and distributors in mainland cities.
"The good harvest this year coincided with sluggish sales of some fruits in the local market, making mainland demand particularly valuable," said Tsai Yao-cheng, director of Taiwan Farmers' Association Development Co., Ltd. "Taiwan pomelos are now arriving in Nanjing every week, while Guangdong in south China and east China's Fujian are also actively seeking to introduce Taiwan fruits."
The same market dynamic is even more pronounced for pineapple custard apples, one of Taitung's signature agricultural products.
Pineapple custard apple orchards stretch for more than 100 km across the county. Roughly 95 percent of the island's overseas shipments of the fruit have gone to the mainland, making this market a key part of the industry's sales structure.
Lin Chao-hung, head of a fruit growers' cooperative group in Beinan Township, Taitung, told Xinhua that her group established a stable partnership with a mainland warehouse retailer two years ago, enabling the fruit to reach mainland shelves from the orchard in as little as nine days.
The mainland has traditionally been a major market for Taiwan farm produce. In 2019, the mainland was the largest export market for such produce, taking up a share of 22.9 percent of the island's total farm produce exports.
However, driven by a cross-Strait economic decoupling policy, Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities intentionally abandoned the mainland market that is geographically close, connected by relatively short shipping routes, and capable of absorbing large volumes of seasonal produce.
Meanwhile, the mainland has never stopped trying to reconnect and promote agricultural exchanges across the Strait.
The mainland in April rolled out a package of 10 policies and measures to promote cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation. One of these measures aims to facilitate the entry of Taiwan agricultural and fishery products that meet quarantine requirements and supports their participation in mainland trade fairs to expand sales channels.
Implementation has since moved beyond policy announcements to concrete trade facilitation. At the Straits Forum in June, a matchmaking and signing event brought together Taiwan agricultural and fishery producers and mainland buyers. Mainland companies signed procurement agreements with enterprises and industry associations from several Taiwan localities covering products ranging from pineapple custard apples to pomelos and tea.
Figures point to a broader trend. According to Taiwan's agricultural authorities, the island's total agricultural exports declined in the first half of 2026, as shipments to the United States and Japan fell. By contrast, exports to the mainland rose 11.3 percent in this period, with pineapple custard apples among the main growth items.
Yet the expansion of agricultural trade has not been matched by an equally open and facilitating approach from Taiwan authorities.
When mainland enterprises placed orders for Taiwan agricultural and fishery products, including pineapple custard apples from Taitung and groupers from Pingtung, at the Straits Forum matchmaking event, the DPP authorities accused the mainland of using agricultural products as a political tool and launched investigations into five Taiwan agricultural and fishery organizations that participated in the event.
This episode underscored the gap between the commercial nature of cross-Strait agricultural exchanges and the political lens through which they are viewed by the DPP authorities.
A similar pattern has emerged in tourism and other areas covered by the 10 measures. While the mainland has sought to promote people-to-people exchanges and expand business links, the DPP authorities have imposed additional political conditions and administrative barriers on such contacts.
"The 10 measures fully align with the common interests of people on both sides of the Strait," said Sheng Jiuyuan, director of the center for Taiwan studies at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in east China. These measures, he said, are pragmatic steps to promote the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations and deepen integrated development, with benefits reaching grassroots farmers and fishermen, small and micro businesses, young people and other groups in Taiwan.
After the measures were released, the DPP authorities immediately launched a campaign to discredit them, Sheng said, arguing that such efforts deliberately fueled confrontation across the Strait and played up the so-called "mainland threat" to divert attention from governance problems.
"The DPP authorities' actions were driven entirely by the party's own political interests at the expense of the island's overall development and the well-being and livelihoods of its people," Sheng noted.
For Taiwan's fruit growers, however, the calculation is more straightforward: when harvests arrive, a reliable market matters. For an increasing number of them, the mainland remains a market large enough, close enough and stable enough to make a tangible difference.
"A sufficient and stable market is the most practical guarantee," Lin Chao-hung from Taitung said. ■

Xinhua Headlines: 30 years of partnership narrows China's regional divide
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
18:50:41 CST
19:50:41 KST

* In 1996, China launched a pairing initiative linking coastal Fujian Province with landlocked Ningxia as part of the country's east-west poverty alleviation collaboration program.
* The east-west collaboration program is part of a broader national strategy to narrow regional development gaps and promote common prosperity.
* Through this model, the country has formed an all-round pattern of poverty alleviation and targeted support at various levels, providing a "Chinese solution" for countries around the world to address poverty.
YINCHUAN, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- A lifelong farmer from northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Wang Guozhong has taken on a new role at the age of 64 by stepping onto the stage as an actor.
He now stars as the lead in a play at "See Minning Drama Village," China's first theater complex themed around the country's fight against poverty.
Located in Minning Town in Ningxia's Yongning County, the complex stages more than 100 performances a day, featuring 36 original productions. Many of the plays are inspired by Minning's history of resettlement and development, with performers like Wang bringing their firsthand experiences to the stage.
"When we cry on stage, it is because we really went hungry back then. When we laugh, it is because we are now living a life we once could only dream of," he said.
Wang was born in Xihaigu, a place the United Nations deemed the "most unfit place for human settlement" in the 1970s due to severe drought and ecological fragility.
Three decades ago, China launched a pairing initiative linking coastal Fujian Province with landlocked Ningxia to target poverty alleviation as part of the country's east-west poverty alleviation collaboration program. At the time, Fujian's GDP stood at 260 billion yuan (about 38 billion U.S. dollars), dwarfing Ningxia's 20.29 billion yuan to roughly one-thirteenth.
In 1997, construction began on Minning Village on barren land near Yinchuan, the regional capital. The cross-provincial effort transformed Minning, named after the abbreviations of Fujian and Ningxia, into a modern town, with a population rising from some 8,000 to over 60,000, mainly living on growing wine grapes, mushrooms, and goji berries and raising cattle.
The theater complex has become another source of employment. Since its opening in July, it has helped create jobs and boost incomes for around 2,500 local residents.
"For me, earning 4,000 yuan a month means I can have a stable income without leaving home," Wang said. "More importantly, I can tell our story to audiences and let more people know how east-west collaboration has changed ordinary people's lives."
Wang's personal transformation mirrors a broader historical shift. Figures show that the east-west collaboration has helped Ningxia eradicate absolute poverty, lifting 803,000 rural residents out of destitution.
Since 1996, Fujian has channeled 7.68 billion yuan in aid, guided over 1,600 enterprises to invest in Ningxia, with actual invested funds exceeding 100 billion yuan. Today, nearly 6,000 Fujian-based enterprises operate steadily in Ningxia, laying a solid foundation for the region's socioeconomic development, according to Wang Jian, head of Ningxia's regional department of agriculture and rural affairs.
In 2025, Ningxia's per capita GDP reached 78,000 yuan, nearly 19 times higher than in 1996, underlining a compelling story of success.
Guided increasingly by market forces, the two regions are facilitating a two-way flow of resources. Their digital cooperation stands out as a prime example, as Ningxia's computing resources are meeting Fujian's rising demand while helping to ease Fujian's energy constraints. This synergy is not only transforming Ningxia's resource advantages into new economic drivers but also establishing a new model for east-west digital cooperation.
China's east-west collaboration program is part of a broader national strategy to narrow regional development gaps and promote common prosperity.
Over years of experimentation, the program has developed a relatively mature system featuring joint coordination, paired assistance, financial support, exchanges of officials and professionals, and broad participation from businesses and society.
By combining capital and markets from the east with resources from the west, the initiative has helped spark thriving local industries.
For instance, the partnership between the eastern Jiangsu and northwestern Shaanxi transformed Ankang, a city in Shaanxi Province, into a "plush toy capital," with over 800 enterprises generating an annual output of 10 billion yuan and employing nearly 20,000 people.
Similarly, the economic powerhouse of Guangdong and the less developed Guizhou in southwest China created a "guitar capital" in Guizhou's Zheng'an County through a cross-regional model linking Macao's design, manufacturing in Zheng'an and sales in Guangdong's Hengqin, boosting exports to 248 million yuan in 2025.
Furthermore, agricultural trade has evolved from emergency charity sales to stable market integration, with Shanghai now hosting over 300 direct outlets for Yunnan's specialty products.
As a long-term institutional arrangement for promoting coordinated regional development and common prosperity, the east-west collaboration has been upgraded from phased poverty alleviation measures to long-term and stable cooperation mechanisms.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) released this year underscores the need to optimize the east-west collaboration. As 2026 marks the first year of implementing regular assistance, Chinese leadership urges drawing on the valuable experience gained from the Fujian-Ningxia partnership to further refine these mechanisms and broaden the scope of cooperation.
Maierdan Mugaiti, vice minister of agriculture and rural affairs, said China would maintain the long-term pairing of eight eastern provincial-level areas with 10 western ones. Additionally, economically developed eastern counties will be linked with key western counties for rural revitalization, ensuring paired assistance reaches a wide range of people.
Through this model, the country has formed an all-round pattern of poverty alleviation and targeted support at various levels, providing a "Chinese solution" for countries around the world to address poverty.
In July, officials, experts and scholars from more than 50 countries visited Ningxia to decode Chinese modernization by exploring and learning from local poverty alleviation stories.
Ghulom Halimzoda, chairman of the Socialist Party of Tajikistan, valued most from the Ningxia trip a complete set of institutions and mechanisms for socioeconomic operation, which could be borrowed by Central Asian countries.
"The core inspiration China's experience brings us is not simply that huge resources were invested. The continuity of policy, the governance capacity to coordinate and mobilize all forces, and, most crucially, the people-centered principle are what matter most," he said. (Video reporter: Lyu Ze; Video editors: Hong Ling and Li Qin) ■

Russia is ready to resume negotiations over its war against Ukraine and believes talks could be restarted if Kyiv is willing, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Tuesday, Sept. 15.
“We have never refused negotiations,” Lavrov said during a diplomatic roundtable on the war, according to TASS. “If our colleagues are ready, I think it is quite possible to resume them. We have something to say.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Lavrov claimed previous rounds of negotiations had been halted “not on our initiative,” without acknowledging Moscow’s role in launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He also reiterated Russia’s longstanding demands, saying Moscow was prepared to seek “reasonable compromises” but had not changed its fundamental position.
Among those demands, Lavrov listed what he called Russia’s need to ensure its security, prevent NATO from appearing on its borders and protect the rights of Russian and Russian-speaking people in Ukraine.
Russia already shares land borders with six NATO members: Norway, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland.
Lavrov also repeated Moscow’s claims about “denazification” and “demilitarization” – rhetoric Russia has used to justify its invasion of Ukraine.
Energy truce in sight?
Lavrov’s comments came as Washington pushes for renewed de-escalation efforts between Kyiv and Moscow.
Putin Resists Energy Truce Announced by Trump
US President Donald Trump claimed Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy truce.
But it would not be the first US attempt to broker such a deal. The one in early 2026 was short-lived, while the most serious attempt yielded a 30-day truce proposal in March 2025.
That agreement also quickly unraveled as Kyiv and Moscow interpreted its terms differently.
But with Trump concerned about diesel prices – a problem he has pinned on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, rather than his own war in Iran – Washington may have a stronger vested interest in seeing it through this time, particularly ahead of November’s mid-term elections.
An hour after Trump’s announcement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a statement, saying Kyiv supports the idea but stopping short of saying Ukraine had agreed to it.
Zelensky said Ukraine would only halt such strikes on a reciprocal basis if its allies could guarantee that Russia would refrain from attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure for a prolonged period.
“If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes,” Zelensky wrote.
The Kremlin on Tuesday welcomed Trump’s proposal, with presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov calling the energy truce a “good initiative.”
Peskov said a truce could help stabilize Russia’s domestic fuel market, although he acknowledged that Moscow was already taking measures to secure its refineries and other energy facilities.
He also claimed Ukraine attempted to strike a Russian energy facility overnight on Sept. 15, after Trump announced the proposed truce.
Abu Dhabi in Focus
Russia sees Abu Dhabi as a priority venue for a possible resumption of negotiations, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said earlier.
The possibility of restarting talks was discussed after Russian President Vladimir Putin met US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, in Moscow on Sept. 5.
The meeting lasted more than three hours, with the sides discussing what Washington could “actually do” to help end the war, according to the Kremlin.
The following day, the US delegation traveled to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian officials.
Witkoff described the discussions with Putin as constructive and said Washington had heard “new ideas” from Moscow, while Kushner referred to a broader “peace package.”
Zelensky called his talks with the US envoys “very substantial” and said Kyiv was ready to move toward trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia. National security advisers from Britain, France and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
Zelensky also said Kyiv and Washington are working toward a trilateral negotiating format.
“We agreed with the American side: let’s prepare all this among ourselves first, and then communicate it publicly,” he said.
Previous rounds of trilateral talks were held in the United Arab Emirates in January and February, followed by a third round in Switzerland in February.
A fourth round was planned for March in Abu Dhabi but was postponed amid fighting in the Middle East.

Doomers vs boosters: Who's who in the global fight over the risks of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:49:35 UTC
19:49:35 KST

Anthropic's Dario Amodei warns AI could wipe out humanity, while Nvidia's Jensen Huang calls it nonsense. Meet the key players shaping the world's fiercest tech debate.
The furious debate over artificial intelligence has hardened into warring camps, with a cautious middle caught between them.
Here is a look at the battle lines in the war over a technology that is now the backbone of the economy and could decide the future of the planet.
Both terms grew out of online AI debates on X and internet forums rather than formal usage, borrowing the slang habit of tech and crypto communities that coin shorthand for opposing camps.
'Doomer' describes those forecasting catastrophe, while 'booster,' sometimes used interchangeably with 'accelerationist,' describes those pushing for AI's rapid, unrestrained development.
The doomers
Fear of technology's dangerous consequences for society goes back far in history.
OpenAI was founded in part because its backers, including first investor Elon Musk, feared that AI's development would end up in the hands of Google, which they believed could not be trusted with the technology.
Today, most of the doomers warning against the impact of artificial intelligence come from inside the companies themselves, from academia, or both.
Those inside the industry are best represented by Dario Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic, now a major AI giant heading toward a historic IPO.
He left OpenAI because he felt the Sam Altman-led company was not taking the technology's potential and dangers seriously enough.
His stance is decried as hypocritical, coming from a company that is itself pushing out cutting-edge technology.
Former Google researcher Geoffrey Hinton and fellow computer scientist Yoshua Bengio led the warnings about AI's threats in the months after the release of ChatGPT in 2022, which kickstarted the latest AI frenzy.
MIT physicist Max Tegmark, who heads the Future of Life Institute, organised the open letter in 2023 that called for a six-month pause in the development of the most advanced AI systems, drawing thousands of signatures, including Musk's.
Further outside the industry is Eliezer Yudkowsky, a self-taught theorist who has spent two decades arguing that a sufficiently powerful AI would wipe out humanity.
Build, build, build
Diametrically opposed to the doomers are the accelerationists, who believe in technology's advancement, its inevitability and its fundamental benefit for society, and who also make their fortunes on its success.
The ethos is widespread in Silicon Valley, but it is best represented by venture capital figures with considerable sway in the White House, such as Marc Andreessen, the influential head of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, and David Sacks, the former White House AI czar.
Personally and philosophically aligned with tech figure Peter Thiel, the group is fundamentally opposed to regulation and battles behind the scenes and on X against what it calls a well-financed doomsday "cult."
They accuse doomers of being a front for companies seeking to use regulation to crush rivals.
Garry Tan, who runs the startup incubator Y Combinator, is among the loudest of those voices, casting safety-driven regulation as a threat to the small companies that cannot absorb its costs.
Andreessen and his allies lavishly fund political action committees that donate to Republican and Democratic lawmakers promoting AI growth, with Anthropic now leading an effort to match that spending through its own fundraising.
In the same go-faster camp is Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are the bricks and mortar of the AI revolution, housed in the gargantuan data centres now meeting opposition across the United States.
Huang dismisses talk of AI-driven extinction as "complete nonsense," though he has broken from some accelerationists in calling for a unified federal AI framework and industry-run peer review, rather than no regulation at all.
Also worth noting is Yann LeCun, who shared the Turing Award with Hinton and Bengio and has spent years dismissing their warnings of existential danger as overblown.
Proceeding with caution
Many big tech companies try to proceed carefully, in a positioning more typical of large corporations that do not want to be caught on the wrong side of a political fight.
At its founding in 2015, OpenAI was structured to ensure that researchers, and not investors, would have the final say on how the technology was deployed, with safety for humanity the guiding philosophy.
But under Altman, who survived an in-house coup in 2023 led by safety-focused colleagues, the company now toes a more complicated line, speaking to AI's dangers while still accelerating and cozying up to a no-holds-barred White House.
Google, Microsoft and Amazon are veterans of talking about safety in tech while navigating Washington successfully to keep regulation to a minimum.
With AI, they are still walking that fine line.

the hacienda must be built: on spectacle and wonder in a disenchanted world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:49:11 UTC
19:49:11 KST

I went through most of 2017 thinking about the night. My master’s thesis had started as an attempt to understand nightclubs, and a good part of the research happened standing at the edge of dancefloors, trying to work out why a badly lit basement with a good sound system could reorganize how a few dozen people behaved toward each other. What I ended up arguing was that, across decades, these places have done real sociopolitical work for those who had nowhere else to go, and that we should keep fighting for their existence.
To make that argument properly, though, I had to go further back than the clubs themselves, into the night that made them possible in the first place. And the night turned out to be a much stranger thing than I had assumed. Design historian Lucius Burckhardt called it a man-made construct, assembled out of opening hours and closing times, price scales, timetables, habits and streetlamps. The night is not a darkness that falls at the end of the day, but a set of decisions, many of them commercial, about when we are ‘allowed’ to be awake, where we may go, and what it will cost us to stay.
Ivan Chtcheglov had seen it coming decades earlier in the Formulary for a New Urbanism, a short and feverish text he wrote in 1953, at nineteen, which would later become a founding document for the radical avant-garde collective, Situationist International. Artificial light had banished darkness, he said, and air conditioning the seasons. Dawn was disappearing, and night and summer were losing their charm. People in cities believed they had escaped from ‘cosmic reality’ but had been handed nothing in return, no corresponding expansion, as he put it, of their dream life. ‘The reason is clear: dreams spring from reality and are realized in it.’ In the early nineties, a team of Russian scientists proposed putting an enormous mirror into orbit, reflecting sunlight onto the dark side of the earth to extend the working day and cut the cost of lighting cities, and in 1992 they tested it successfully. Among the objections was that the night sky is a commons, and that seeing the stars is a basic human right no company should be able to switch off. Yet, if the night sky is indeed a human right, then, according to Jonathan Crary, who tells this story in his book on sleep and late capitalism, this right is already being violated for half the world’s population living ‘in cities that are enveloped continuously in a penumbra of smog and high intensity illumination.’
The mirror never went up, but the impulse behind it did not need a satellite. In the decades since, the same logic has worked its way inward, from the streets and the sky into the hours themselves, and finally into the body. Our phones tell us how long we slept and how well, our watches count steps and calories and minutes spent standing, and our feeds know what we will click on before we do. Our days are measured, optimized and increasingly predictable, and almost everything we look at now arrives pre-sorted, ranked by how likely it is to hold us. We have never been exposed to more images, and rarely felt less enchanted by them.
the 20-metre wide space solar mirror, Znamya-2, after its deployment | image by RSC Energia, via Wikimedia Commons
Guy Debord, who by then was leading the Situationists, gave this a name in 1967. The spectacle, he argued, is not the images themselves but what has quietly taken the place of the things that used to happen directly between people, and he described the slide in stages: an economy that first taught us to measure a life by what it owned rather than by what it was, and then moved again, until what counted was no longer having but appearing. Everything lived directly recedes into representation, and of the spectator he wrote that the more he contemplates, the less he lives. Debord was not asking for less to look at. The Situationists spent their years building what they called situations, moments constructed to be lived through rather than watched. We are not short of things to look at. Between the immersive rooms, the light festivals and the pop-ups built for the photograph, there is more spectacle available now than at any point in history, and much of it asks nothing of us beyond turning up and taking a picture. What feels missing is the kind of spectacle that cannot be scrolled past, with real stakes and an uncertain ending, closer to a rite than a product. What if we are not overwhelmed by spectacle, but starved of it?
‘You’ll never see the hacienda. It doesn’t exist. The hacienda must be built,’ wrote Chtcheglov in that same 1953 text. Thirty years later, Factory Records took the phrase and gave it to a nightclub in Manchester, handing the interior to Ben Kelly, who built it out of materials lifted from outside, using hazard stripes, bollards and the signage of a working industrial city, brought indoors and repurposed for dancing. What he wanted, Kelly said later, was that the people who came could ‘almost take the place over’. They did. The Haçienda has a reasonable claim to being the room where British rave culture began. It closed after fifteen years, was demolished, and there are flats on the site now, sold under its name.
The Haçienda interior by Ben Kelly for Factory Records, Manchester, 1982 | image courtesy of Ben Kelly
Italy got there first, where a generation of young architects who spent the sixties attacking modernism found that the discotheque was one of the few things they were actually allowed to build, and filled those rooms with projections, performers and, in one case, a vegetable garden, treating light and noise and the crowd itself as building materials. Gruppo 9999 built Space Electronic in Florence on Marshall McLuhan’s theories, out of his idea that electric media had produced a kind of all-at-onceness where time stops and everything arrives together, while in seventies New York, David Mancuso ran his parties without clocks or mirrors, so that people lost track of time and stopped checking themselves.
Observing a club night for that 2017 thesis, I wrote that the crowd was captivated by a spectacle of which they were both performers and watchers at once. This collapse of spectator and spectacle is what our new chapter follows, moving beyond the dancefloor to a museum gallery arranged so precisely that the room becomes a living psychological environment, to a garment that turns the body into a walking act of rebellion, to a crowd that gathers around a temporary monument and becomes the reason to look. It happens in a fashion show that exists for eleven minutes, in a film set built to be believed rather than lived in, and in a procession that turns a street into a stage.
Florence’s revolutionary Space Electronic by Gruppo 9999, inaugurated in 1969 | image via designboom article here
The rooms in this chapter are not escapes from the world, they are the working distance you need in order to see it. It is very hard to recognize what should change in a life you never once step out of, and there is a quiet protest in simply being somewhere you are not meant to be, moving in unconventional ways the established order has no use for. Spectator and Spectacle asks how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away.
the first stop of our new travelling series brought together designers, architects, collaborators, and friends for a week of conversations and hands-on activities.

Russians make the best of a struggling economy before vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:47:11 UTC
19:47:11 KST

Russians make the best of a struggling economy before vote
YAROSLAVL, Russia, Sept 15 - As a bustling tourist hub on the Volga River whose town centre and roads are being rebuilt with state funding, the picturesque medieval city of Yaroslavl may be better shielded than most from Russia's economic stagnation.
But even here, 250 km northeast of Moscow, locals voting in parliamentary elections this week face a growing list of daily challenges to their livelihoods and businesses — whether they believe those are connected to the war with Ukraine or not.
In Russia's tightly controlled political environment, and with anti-war candidates largely barred from the ballot, few expect the election to change much. But the Kremlin sees it as a gauge of fatigue from a war now well into its fifth year.
Stubbornly high inflation, high borrowing costs, stagnating output and fuel shortages form the everyday backdrop to economic life in Russia. Yet businesses in Yaroslavl say they could still get by — if only they could find the labour.
"We have a lot of work here," said Angelika, the owner of a chain of sewing shops who gave only her first name. "The problem is that there are no workers," she added, noting a dearth of young people willing to enter the sector despite decent wages.
Confectioner Gilles Walter agreed, complaining of difficulties recruiting for his nearby production facility.
"They cannot even make an omelette or cook pasta," Walter, a Frenchman who settled in Russia in the 1990s, said of graduates he tried to hire from the local culinary college.
"Very few here are ready to begin work at three in the morning so that fresh croissants are ready in time."
TIGHT LABOUR MARKET, TIGHT PURSE-STRINGS
Neither wanted to link the labour shortages to mass army recruitment and heavy losses in the fighting, as evidenced by hundreds of fresh graves at the local military cemetery with raised flags honouring the war's dead.
But with official unemployment just above 2%, others draw a link between the lack of young workers coming onto the labour market and the steady decline in Russia's fertility rates. Some fear the situation will get worse as people are reluctant to give birth while the war drags on.
Lubov, a meat trader from the village of Dyudkovo, about 50 km from Yaroslavl, recalls that in May 2012 when she gave birth, there were four children born in the village. Now, she says, there was only one child born in two years.
"People just don't want to give birth while this is going on," she said in reference to the war in Ukraine.
At the Yaroslavl central market, pensioner Varvara, 68, sells dried porcini mushrooms collected in the forests outside the city to augment her 17,000-rouble pension, which she says is not enough to live on.
As she searches for words, she instinctively switches to Ukrainian, blushes and whispers that Ukrainian is her native language as she moved here 40 years ago from Poltava.
"Dried mushrooms have become a luxury now. People are buying less this year; their purchasing power has shrunk," she says.
FUTURE PROSPECTS DOWNGRADED
After a sharp fall in economic growth in 2025 to 1% from 4.9% the previous year, followed by another slight contraction at the start of 2026, the government is forecasting full-year growth of 0.6% — not much lower than the 0.9% that the European Central Bank sees the euro zone generating this year.
But the bigger picture is still bleak, with the Economy Ministry earlier this year slashing forecasts through to 2029 on an expected slowdown in industrial output, capital investment and consumer spending.
While down from the double-digit highs of last year, Russian inflation at just above 6% means the central bank is having to keep rates at an eye-watering 14%, making borrowing punitive for both businesses and households.
President Vladimir Putin has scolded officials for their failure to turn the economy around, and the Kremlin promised earlier this month that it was not considering raising taxes again to help patch over an above-target budget deficit.
The business people Reuters spoke to in Yaroslavl said recent tax hikes, introduced to compensate for growing military expenditure, were painful enough but something they could still cope with, provided taxes do not go up again next year.
UKRAINIAN DRONES HIT ECONOMIC TARGETS
Perhaps tougher — and harder to control — are the rising prices in essentials from food to fuel arising from everything from international sanctions to the war in Ukraine and wider troubles, to which the Iran war has added since February.
This summer was the most difficult for Russians since the war started in 2022, as Ukrainian drones struck at the heart of the Russian economy, hitting sectors such as oil refining and retail, e-commerce, agriculture and tourism.
People queued for fuel for hours, inflation spiked, thousands of small businesses saw their goods burn at e-commerce warehouses, domestic tourism shrank by 6%, and farmers had grain unsold as trade via the Black Sea became too dangerous.
Valery, a retired military accountant who now keeps bees, complained that the sugar he buys in autumn to feed the bees before winter had doubled in price over the last two years.
"For me, it is critically important. I am afraid of instability. More stability and confidence in the future would have been better," he said.
Yaroslavl's centre, lined with ancient churches and 17th- and 18th-century merchants' houses, contrasts sharply with the sprawling refinery, Russia's fifth largest, on its outskirts.
The cost of the added security now required is unmistakable: The refinery's most sensitive units are shielded from drones by walls made of sea shipping containers, while thousands of thick metal wires run between its pipes to trap approaching drones.
A short walk from the refinery, Evgeny, whose house was heavily damaged by a shot-down drone, says he will be too busy to take part in this week's election.
His main task, he said, will be to install a new metal door into what remains of the house. REUTERS

‘I Felt Super Violated’: Men Wearing Meta Glasses on Dates Is an Instant Red Flag
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Courtney McAnuff was out of a year-long relationship in the summer of 2024 and starting to date again when she agreed to grab drinks with a potential suitor.
They met at a bar in midtown Manhattan. He arrived wearing a baseball cap pulled low and sported a pair of black-framed glasses, she says. As conversation flowed, from discussions about navigating life in New York to past relationships, he mentioned that his glasses were Meta Ray-Bans.
“I wasn’t familiar with them,” McAnuff, a 28-year-old project manager who now lives in Toronto, tells WIRED. It was her first time seeing the smart glasses up close, which can record images and video from the wearer’s viewpoint. He let her try them on and even showed her a couple of videos that he’d taken previously, she says. “That was it. We stopped talking about it after that. I figured that was the end of the use.”
The next day, checking her Instagram, McAnuff noticed she’d been tagged in one of his story posts. To her surprise, it was footage of them at the bar and on the subway together, en route to a basketball game uptown. In the video, McAnuff is captured from an above angle, sitting across from her date who is holding a drinking glass; WIRED has seen screenshots of the footage. “I felt super violated,” McAnuff says. “Like, what if I don’t want everyone knowing what I’m up to? He felt so free to film me and post it. There was no conversation about it.”
Meta sold more than 7 million pairs of the Ray-Bans in 2025, as its smart glasses have infiltrated public spaces thanks to pranksters with dreams of viral fame, some of whom even film people while they’re at work. The phenomenon, which has also spread to pickup artists hitting on women, has earned the hardware the nickname “creep glasses.”
Among singles, and particularly women, Meta’s AI-powered eyewear has become a recurring nuisance, as people share a spreading unease about being covertly filmed on dates.
“Ban those glasses completely,” posted a young woman on Bluesky in August, writing that her date “leaned over to show me pictures he took of me I had no idea he was taking.” One TikToker claimed in a video after a date that she “immediately felt uncomfortable,” questioning why people are “so comfortable videoing everything. It’s a terrible way to portray yourself, wearing a fucking camera on your face and you’re sitting in my face.”
In a Reddit post from August, users debated the ethics of the trend, wondering if it was OK to continue a date when someone showed up wearing them; in a separate thread, one person said they had ghosted a guy after realizing he’d worn the glasses on their date. “I didn’t notice until toward the end of the night. I kissed him while he was wearing the glasses,” they said. In July, a man was put under investigation in Seoul, South Korea, for allegedly filming four women he had gone out with and later uploading clips to social media, according to The Korea Herald.
In many regards, dating has been reframed by our dependency on technology. Apps connect people. Chatbots are used for all sorts of things these days: as wingmen and for role-play. Smartphone cameras capture important moments together. But while a phone being held up to someone’s face gives them a clear opportunity to object, smart glasses largely erase that opportunity. (Meta’s glasses do have a front-facing LED that switches on when the glasses are recording, but the light is the only warning, and it can be disabled by hacking the hardware.)
For McAnuff, the trend is about more than privacy instructions. She was worried about what would happen with the footage afterward. “He didn’t ask if I wanted to be recorded or if I wanted my face uploaded. And now he has this video file of me forever. It’s definitely a big trust issue,” she says.
In a 2025 YouGov survey of US adults focused on factors contributing to successful relationships, trust ranked the highest, with 94 percent of respondents categorizing it as “very important.”
Gary Lewandowski, a psychology professor at Monmouth University whose research focuses on the science of romantic connection, says adding covert cameras to the mix will only make building trust harder. He says beyond posting for the ’gram, a number of factors could be driving men to do this. The most logical, non-creepy reason may be tied to post-date analysis, in that the glasses can help men identify blind spots around their own behavior.
“A lot of men out there are eternal optimizers. They want better, more efficient ways of doing things, so reviewing game tape allows them to learn from mistakes,” Lewandowski says. “But I do wonder if some are doing it to build a case instead of a connection—why they’re right and the other person is wrong—or to help better identify red flags.” That type of surveillance “makes the date less about getting to know each other and more about fact gathering,” he adds.
The trend has also reanimated discussions around consent when it comes to dating. Yue Xu, cohost of the Dateable podcast, believes new social norms are needed to keep up with our evolving tech. “It’s bringing in a third party, which is disturbing. It just shows that this person lacks respect for the integrity and privacy of the date,” Xu says, adding that she fears that the glasses are triggering a future “where people have no more anonymity.”
Concerns have intensified as issues about the device have continued to make headlines. Meta and EssilorLuxottica, which owns Ray-Ban, are facing a class action lawsuit alleging that they captured and stored users’ private data without consent. This month, Semafor reported that Meta disabled the recording function for thousands of users who tampered with the light that notifies people that the Meta Ray-Bans are filming. Following the addition of an unreleased face-recognition feature called NameTag to its eyewear earlier this year, revealed by a WIRED investigation, Meta scrubbed the code from its app in June and is facing another proposed class action over allegedly breaching Illinois and California privacy laws by collecting biometric information from users’ photographs without their knowledge.
“This lawsuit is without merit and misrepresents our work,” a Meta spokesperson tells WIRED in reference to the NameTag lawsuit. “We've been transparent about how we use people's information to build and improve our AI products. As for NameTags, nothing has shipped to consumers, and no final decision has been made on what to do here, if anything. If we do decide to roll something out, we will take a thoughtful approach and do so with full transparency. One decision we can be clear about—we are not building a universal face database.”
EssilorLuxottica did not respond to a request for comment.
According to Meta, if people tamper with the recording light, including placing blockers over it, the camera will not turn on. Additionally, the company says it removes accounts and content that violate its policies when it becomes aware of them, including content meant to degrade or shame others. In August, Meta expanded its public awareness efforts through a social media campaign focused on helping people identify when someone is recording with the glasses.
“We don't want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform. So we're trying to fight that every way we can,” Meta's head of Instagram Adam Mosseri said in July.
That hasn’t stopped regulators around the world from pushing to enact harsher privacy laws for consumers. A California bill just passed both chambers that mandates visible recording indicators on recording devices and bans users from turning them off. Likewise, Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is asking tech companies to automatically blur people’s faces recorded with their smart glasses, writing that “as smart glasses evolve and become more common, they may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content.”
When McAnuff realized footage of her had been uploaded without her approval, she confronted her date over text. He apologized for his actions but she says that “he didn’t think it was that serious.” She hasn’t seen him since.
For McAnuff and many others, Meta’s smart glasses have simply become the latest privacy issue hiding in plain sight.
“Being in each other’s physical space is such a beautiful experience in itself. We don’t need to have gadgets around,” McAnuff says. “I don’t think that every moment needs to be captured.”

85% of Wang Fuk Court owners sign sale deals as flat selection moves ahead
Housing Bureau holds computerised ballot to set flat-selection order, posts results online as rehousing scheme moves into next phase
More than 85 per cent of owners at the blaze-hit Wang Fuk Court have signed agreements to sell their flats to the Hong Kong government as authorities move ahead with flat selection under a special rehousing scheme.
Authorities said on Tuesday that 1,702 households – 85.8 per cent of flat owners across blocks A to H at the estate – had signed sale and purchase agreements as of Monday.
On the same day, the Housing Bureau held a computerised ballot to determine the selection sequence for subsidised flats under the scheme.
“The Housing Bureau conducted separate computerised random-ordering ballots for the two batches of applicants to determine the sequence of the last two digits of the application numbers held by the applicants,” a spokesman said. “Based on the ballot results, the Housing Bureau randomly generated the order of all applicants.”

Syria was 'born again' after sanctions were lifted, President al Sharaa says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:43:07 UTC
19:43:07 KST

Syrian President Ahmed al Sharaa stated on Tuesday that Syria was “born again” after sanctions against the country were lifted, saying their removal opened the way for economic recovery, foreign investment and a stronger regional role.
Speaking at the Arab Media Summit 2026 in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates, al Sharaa said Syria had faced an exceptionally extensive sanctions regime, with some restrictions dating back to 1979, leaving generations unfamiliar with international financial transactions and banking guarantees.
He said mediation efforts involving Arab and regional leaders, as well as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in contact with US President Donald Trump, contributed to what he described as a “historic decision” to lift the sanctions.
“I believe Syria was born again after the sanctions were lifted and the road ahead was opened. In other words, the restrictions were broken,” he said.
“What remains now is to adopt the right policies and procedures and make sound choices,” he added.
Economy, Gulf investment
Al Sharaa said Syria is transitioning from an economic system resembling a socialist model, characterised by bureaucracy and corruption, towards a more liberal economy supporting the private sector, acknowledging that the shift could initially require difficult decisions.
He said the Syrian economy stood at around $60 billion in 2010 before falling to roughly $20 billion by 2024, then growing to $32 billion in 2025. It could reach $50 billion this year and return to its 2010 level by 2027, he added.
“Our programmes aim to bring the economy to around $200 billion over the following five to 10 years,” he said, provided international conditions remain stable.
Al Sharaa said investors from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait are among those moving into Syria, with several memoranda of understanding signed and some projects already under implementation.
He also cited planned investments involving Emirati businessman Mohamed Alabbar and DP World’s investment in the Port of Tartus on Syria’s Mediterranean coast.
Al Sharaa said Syria’s geographical position could make it an important part of alternative trade, energy and supply routes linking East and West.
He also described Syria as a potential regional food basket, saying it could produce enough food for 70 million to 75 million people without advanced agricultural technologies and more than 100 million with modern technology.
‘Syria follows its own interests’
Al Sharaa stressed the independence of Syrian decision-making, saying Damascus does not intend to become subordinate to any outside power.
“Syria does not necessarily need to be aligned with any particular side. Syria follows its own interests,” he said, while stressing the importance of Syria’s Arab and Islamic surroundings.
He said Syria wants to benefit from successful Arab experiences in economic and institutional development rather than starting “from zero.”
Al Sharaa cited the operation that eventually led to the capture of Damascus as evidence of independent Syrian decision-making.
“When we made the decision to liberate Damascus, we were on our own,” he said.
“Our decision was entirely our own — distinctly Syrian — and we relied on ourselves in every respect,” he added.
Bashar al Assad, who ruled Syria with an iron fist for nearly 25 years, fled to Russia on December 8 2024, ending the Baath Party’s decades-long dictatorship that began in 1963. A transitional administration led by al Sharaa was formed in January 2025.
Al Sharaa warned that Syria’s recovery could be affected by expanding wars and instability elsewhere in the Middle East.
“What concerns us most is the possibility that the wars could expand further and create broader instability across the region,” he said.
Damascus is working with Arab countries to reduce the impact of regional conflicts and mitigate future risks, he said, adding that Syria has a “pivotal role” to play.
“Syria’s stability today does not benefit Syria alone; it benefits the entire region. It is a shared interest for everyone,” he said.
Rebuilding state apparatuses
Al Sharaa said Syria is also rebuilding state institutions and public trust following decades of poor governance and years of war, while dealing with damaged infrastructure, energy shortages, economic difficulties and risks of internal division.
He said his vision is for Syria to become a “normal country” with strong economic growth while protecting the dignity and independence of its citizens.
“Our greatest asset is society itself,” he said.
“Our policy is one of continuous and serious work,” he added, saying the government would “work day and night” to serve Syrians.
Turning to the media, al Sharaa described journalism as a serious public trust and urged media professionals to prioritise credibility and reliable information and avoid politicisation.
“People’s minds are, in a sense, entrusted to journalists,” he said, noting their influence over public opinion during periods of crisis and uncertainty.
“How can people be expected to remain patient with something they do not fully understand?” he asked, stressing the need to provide societies with accurate information.
“I believe this is, above all, the mission of journalists as messengers: to convey the facts to people as they are,” he said.
The Arab Media Summit 2026 is being held at the Dubai World Trade Centre, bringing together media leaders, policymakers and industry figures to discuss developments and challenges shaping the Arab media landscape.

Ukraine Launches ‘Vivaldi’ Counteroffensive in Donetsk as Russian Forces Face Setbacks Near Lyman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:43:01 UTC
19:43:01 KST

Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps has launched an offensive operation in the Donetsk region aimed at pushing back Russian forces and dismantling their infiltration tactics, Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, the corps’ commander, said Tuesday.
In a video address on Sept. 15, Biletsky said the operation, codenamed “Vivaldi,” was now underway but that Ukrainian forces were maintaining strict information silence around its progress.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“In recent weeks, there has been talk regarding the retreat of Russian troops in the Donetsk sector and the elimination of the so-called Lyman salient. Settlements that have come under the control of Ukraine’s Defense Forces are being named, and military maps are being updated,” Biletsky said.
Biletsky said he believed the attention surrounding the operation was not helping Ukrainian forces as it was just gaining momentum.
“Indeed, the 3rd Army Corps has launched an offensive operation in this sector codenamed ‘Vivaldi.’ For now, please remember that word. This operation is proceeding under conditions of strict information silence,” he added.
“Vivaldi” offensive targets Russian infiltration tactics
Biletsky said the operation was designed in part to counter Russian “infiltration tactics,” which he said had allowed Russian troops to penetrate deep into Ukrainian positions in some areas.
“Thanks to meticulous planning and the heroism of the 3rd Army Corps’ troops, a heavy blow has been dealt to the combat effectiveness of Russia’s 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies,” he said.
Drone Attacks in the Ukrainian-Polish Border Region
Biletsky said Russian forces considered their so-called “infiltration tactics” to be one of their advantages, with troops in some areas penetrating tens of kilometers deep into Ukrainian combat formations. He said dismantling this approach was therefore one of the 3rd Army Corps’ primary tasks.
According to Biletsky, Ukrainian search-and-strike missions eliminated Russian infiltration pockets around Novoselivka, Yarova, Koroviahyi Yar and Oleksandrivka.
He said the liberation of Serednie in the Donetsk region was a “shaping, preparatory phase” of the operation. The settlement, he added, had been “de-occupied” and was now fully under Ukrainian control.
Biletsky also said a key objective was to disrupt Russian supply lines. According to him, successful strikes by the corps’ unmanned systems units forced Russian forces to relocate fuel and lubricant supply operations to Russia’s Voronezh region, across the Ukrainian border.
Ukraine claims heavy Russian losses
Biletsky claimed that Russian forces suffered significant losses during the first phase of the operation, including 1,500 troops, 12,000 drones and several hundred armored vehicles and artillery systems.
He also claimed that Ukrainian forces had cleared approximately 75 square kilometers (29 square miles) of territory of Russian infiltrators and liberated more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) of territory.
These battlefield claims could not be independently verified.
Biletsky said open-source reports had speculated that the operation’s ultimate objective was to reach the Chornyi Zherebets River, but suggested that the Ukrainian military had not disclosed its actual plans.
“However, our operation is named ‘Vivaldi.’ And as everyone knows, Vivaldi has four seasons. This is merely the first one,” he said.
He urged the public and media to wait for official updates.
“So, stay tuned for our official updates and please hold off on spoilers. Good news is coming, but for now, our actions require silence,” Biletsky added.
The setback comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin reportedly expects his military to fully capture the Donetsk region within the next six months.
Sources close to the Kremlin told Bloomberg that Putin has set the new target after previously setting the end of this year as a deadline. According to the ISW, Putin has changed his “deadlines” for capturing the Donbas at least 15 times since the beginning of the full-scale war.
Russian milbloggers acknowledge setbacks
Russian milbloggers have also acknowledged a deterioration in the situation near Lyman and described the tactical situation as worsening.
The Russian Telegram channel Rybar earlier blamed the setbacks on “systemic lying in reports to superiors” and a “flawed assessment of the situation.”
“Based on the experience of the Kupyansk sector – where similar problems were addressed through ill-prepared assaults – this will lead to further losses,” the channel wrote, as cited by The Moscow Times.
Rybar added that diverting reserves to plug gaps near Lyman could weaken Russian defenses elsewhere, creating vulnerabilities that Ukrainian forces would likely exploit.
Russian military expert Valery Shiryaev similarly said the Russian army’s retreat could be confirmed, with Ukrainian forces gradually pushing settlement after settlement into the “gray zone.”
Ukrainian forces breached a “very old defensive line” and moved into the rear of the Russian force near Lyman, according to Shiryaev. Russian troops in the area found themselves “effectively encircled,” he said.
Shiryaev also compared the situation with Russia’s earlier setbacks around Kupyansk.
“In exactly the same way, the commander of the ‘West’ Group, Kuzovlev, reported successes in Kupyansk and even received the title of Hero of Russia. Then the situation reversed, yet the command and top political leadership had already announced the ‘success’ to the whole world… The situation now is far worse than it was in Kupyansk,” he said.
Russian military analyst Yan Matveyev called the developments a serious but localized crisis for Russian forces.
“A disastrous summer for the Russian army has ended, and autumn is beginning with a massive scandal surrounding Sviatohirsk,” Matveyev said.
“For Russian troops, this crisis is relatively localized, but it is a crisis nonetheless – denying that would be foolish. Meanwhile, significant opportunities are opening up for Ukrainian forces along the entire Sloviansk axis,” he added.
Meanwhile, Shiryaev said a sustained Ukrainian foothold near Lyman could eventually allow Ukrainian drone operators to strike the rear of Russian forces advancing toward Mykolaivka and Sloviansk.
“If the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) succeed – fully establishing a foothold there without interference, bringing in their drone operators, and seizing the entire area – the situation will shift regarding firing ranges,” he said.
Ukrainian drone operators could potentially gain an additional 10-15 kilometers (6.2-9.3 miles) of effective first-person-view (FPV) drone range, allowing them to launch mass strikes against the rear of the Russian group advancing toward Sloviansk, Shiryaev added.
Notably, Putin claimed on Sept. 1 that Russia’s Northern Group of Forces had captured Svyatohirsk after Russian troops advanced to within 13 kilometers (8.1 miles) of the city in late spring and early summer.
Biletsky has denied Putin’s claim: in a video recorded on Sept. 7 in the city center with the Holy Assumption Svyatohirsk Lavra visible behind him, he said the 60th Mechanized Brigade remained in full control of the city.
OSINT analysts report larger Ukrainian gains near Lyman
It is also worth noting that some OSINT analysts have reported significantly larger territorial gains than those cited by Biletsky.
Clément Molin, who was among the first to report the development on X, said Russian forces in Ukraine had been forced to abandon more than 200 square kilometers (77 square miles) along the main axis of the Ukrainian counteroffensive in the Donetsk region.
“After four months of the Lyman counter-attack, Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps managed to cut off the Russian salient north of Lyman and liberate more than 200 km². This is one of Ukraine’s most important victories of 2026, and it will delay the offensive on northern Donbas,” he wrote.

The figures should therefore be treated as unconfirmed by official Ukrainian sources.

“We assess that Russian forces have lost control of approximately 240 km² there. By comparison, they have lost approximately 430 km² in the Dnipropetrovsk region since February. However, Russia’s southward advance from the Dobropillia axis is continuing.”

FAA boss set to discuss air traffic reform as airlines urged to better handle delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:42:06 UTC
19:42:06 KST

FAA boss set to discuss air traffic reform as airlines urged to better handle delays
Sept 15 - Airlines affected by air traffic control staff shortages should do more to prevent delays from snowballing into broader disruptions, a pilots' union and an aviation consultant said, as lawmakers prepared to discuss U.S. sector reforms on Tuesday.
Federal Aviation Administration boss Bryan Bedford is set to testify before a U.S. House appropriations subcommittee about a planned $12.5 billion air traffic control overhaul, a day after a government watchdog warned about spending shortfalls.
Air traffic control-related disruptions have caused flight delays and cancellations in the U.S., Australia and Britain due to staffing shortages and technology issues, posing challenges for airlines around the world.
New York-based airline JetBlue Airways said last week its air traffic-related flight cancellations nearly doubled in the Northeastern U.S. this summer compared to the average of the prior three summers after the region was hit by storms and controller shortages.
According to data from consultancy Cirium, JetBlue's July performance lagged other major U.S. airlines, with an 8.3% cancellation rate compared with less than 3% at rivals including Frontier, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.
In correspondence reviewed by Reuters, JetBlue's pilots' union, which is currently in contract negotiations with the airline, urged the carrier to take additional steps to prevent flight delays and cancellations from spiraling.
"This summer took a toll with long days, repeated disruptions, and too much seemingly preventable chaos," said a September 7 message from Wayne Scales, president of the JetBlue arm of the Air Line Pilots Association.
Pilots have urged JetBlue to design a plan to prevent operational challenges that left crew waiting for reassignments and hotel accommodations in July, Scales wrote.
"Storms and air traffic constraints will happen; no airline can fully eliminate operational disruptions," he said. "What management can control is how prepared JetBlue is to respond — and how effectively it recovers."
AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL CONSTRAINTS
JetBlue said in a statement it put extensive preparation into its summer operation based on prior years' weather and air traffic control performance, but storms and missing controllers could upset even the best planning.
"The unpredictability of weather and air traffic control constraints makes it significantly harder to plan ahead and can cause disruptions to compound quickly," the carrier said. "This is exacerbated for JetBlue given our outsized footprint in the Northeast."
U.S. airline industry consultant Bob Mann said airlines operating in Northeast airspace — the most congested in the nation — risked delays. He said software was available that could reduce the domino effect of delayed and canceled flights, but it was not widely used by airlines.
Bedford met last Thursday with the CEOs of major U.S. airlines to discuss the FAA's plans to use advanced software to overhaul flight scheduling and improve flight management.
The SMART system, which uses predictive analytics, could more effectively reschedule flights that were canceled due to bad weather.
JetBlue said it was encouraged by the system, "which has the potential to give both the FAA and airlines better information and tools to anticipate constraints earlier, make better operational decisions and recover more effectively when disruptions occur." REUTERS

Russia accuses Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships, RIA reports
MOSCOW, Sept 15 - Russia has accused Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships in the Baltic Sea and handed an official note to Copenhagen complaining about such incidents, Russia's ambassador to Denmark said on Tuesday, according to Russia's RIA state news agency.
Vladimir Barbin, the ambassador, was speaking after the Nordic NATO member's military said that a Russian frigate had fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Denmark on Monday, narrowly missing the aircraft.
RIA cited Barbin as blaming Denmark for the episode.
“I demanded that the Danish side take the necessary measures to prevent such incidents from recurring in the future, and handed over a note to that effect,” it cited Barbin as saying.
Asked about the matter, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have details and was not in a position to comment.
Barbin, the ambassador, was quoted by RIA as saying he had complained about another similar incident last year.
"In September 2025, during a meeting at the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, I was forced to draw attention to dangerous fly-bys and low-altitude hovering carried out on 27 August by a Danish Air Force helicopter over the large anti-submarine ship ‘Vice-Admiral Kulakov’," RIA quoted him as saying.
Such manoeuvres posed a collision risk and could have interfered with the Russian ship’s equipment, he added, saying the helicopter had not established radio contact or responded to warnings at the time. REUTERS

TIME Trailblazers Toast to What Gives Them Hope for the Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

At a dinner event celebrating the 2026 TIME Trailblazers at the ARIA Resort & Casino in Las Vegas on Sept. 14, some of the honorees offered toasts to their collective achievements in shaping a brighter future and reflecting on what continues to inspire them.
Professional climber Alex Honnold said that while he was proud of his athletic feats in his nearly two-decade career, he believes those will all someday be surpassed. But his work at The Honnold Foundation, a nonprofit supporting solar energy use in communities, “has a real impact on human lives, and that can’t really be taken away.”
Traveling around the world and seeing communities in need of reliable power sources has helped Honnold see access to energy as a basic human need as important as shelter and food.
While the organization has over $11 million committed to 75 solar projects just this year, Honnold says that it is “literally a tiny, tiny drop in the bucket in terms of the global transition of renewables.”
But he said what gives him hope is the power of “dreaming small,” and he continues to draw inspiration from communities that need better access to energy. “These are people that know the solutions to their problems, and all they really need is the opportunity to execute their vision,” he added.
Marine biologist and National Geographic Explorer Erika Woolsey, another honoree, said she draws her hope from the reef-building coral. To her, the anemone look-alikes lift much of the weight in rebuilding seabeds and coastlines wrecked by massive storms and bleaching events.
Woolsey said that years ago, as she co-founded The Hydrous, a nonprofit devoted to helping people appreciate the marine environment by creating 3D models of them, one of her previous study sites at the Great Barrier Reef was wiped out by a cyclone. In her recent return, Woolsey witnessed the marine site grow anew, populated with corals and fish.
“This was in a well-protected region, and when an ecosystem has time and space, it can persevere,” Woolsey said. “This gives me tremendous hope in the work I do.”
Labor organizer and human rights strategist Saket Soni, meanwhile, celebrated recovery workers and responders—those who help rebuild communities and restore homes after natural disasters like fires and hurricanes—whom he called the country’s “white blood cells” and “indispensable workers of the climate era.”
Witnessing the sordid living and job conditions of these workers was once evidence of what Soni called the U.S.’s “false promise of hope,” but a mentor reminded him that it was his job to make that hope real.
Soni said his nonprofit Resilience Force, which works with third-party contractors to ensure recovery workers get better pay and safety standards, has made a new, “highly skilled, dignified profession” out of the job.
He also touted how the years-long reconstruction and adaptation jobs these workers do are irreplaceable, not even by automation or artificial intelligence. “We’re making resilience work a way to build not just homes,” Soni said, “but to build hope.”
Soni then directed his toast to the dinner attendees: “Standing here with all of you, I can see that we’re not alone. You are building hope—out of 3D-printed homes in Texas, innovative reconstruction after the Los Angeles fires, greenhouses in India … To truly rebuild, it will take all of us in this room and outside of it.”
The TIME Trailblazers Dinner: Designing and Making the Future was presented by Autodesk.

TIME Trailblazers Put People First in Designing a Better World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

While much talk about what the future could look like focuses on emerging and rapidly advancing technologies, speakers at the TIME Trailblazers Dinner in Las Vegas on Monday urged focusing on people.
Aicha Evans, the chief executive officer of autonomous vehicle company Zoox and a 2026 TIME Trailblazers honoree, talked about how the design of her company’s robotaxis—or “toasters,” as she jokingly called them, in apparent reference to how boxy they look—prioritizes the rider experience and tries to eliminate the thought of driving altogether.
“We have a very simple view: when you are in our purpose-built robotaxi, if you thought about driving, we actually failed,” Evans told moderator Kelly Conniff, TIME’s deputy editor and head of creative at TIME Studios. “We want you to be you. To some people, that’s hanging out. … To some people, like me, it’s probably the only time when I feel alone in a good way.”
Evans added that Zoox also takes its responsibility to keep riders safe seriously, given how there are nearly 40,000 deaths in the U.S. each year related to motor vehicle crashes.
Fellow panelist and 2026 TIME Trailblazers honoree, entrepreneur Jason Ballard, whose construction-technology firm ICON specializes in 3D-printed housing, discussed how his own experiences with hurricanes in the Texas Gulf Coast made him think deeply about what decent human shelter looks like. He added that the way houses are built today is still “inhuman,” “sterile,” and “repetitive,” and that he envisions a world where housing can be both “affordable” and “beautiful.”
Ballard argued that technology can reconcile values that otherwise appear to conflict. “What advanced technology is supposed to do is maybe bring our values out of conflict,” he says. “Right now you have to choose between affordability and beauty, or you have to choose between speed of construction and sustainability. But wouldn’t the purpose of technology be that we can have all of our values?”
Steve Blum, executive vice president and chief operating officer of software company Autodesk, which is a presenting partner for the event, also participated in the panel and touched on current concerns about artificial intelligence and automation replacing humans.
Blum said that at his company, “AI is here to augment the human, not replace the human,” adding that it gives people more time to do activities they love and to hone their expertise.
“Everywhere around the world I travel, folks are saying they can’t go after all the projects they want to go after because they do not have the capacity and people,” Blum said. “AI will help by getting more out of each of the humans and allow them to do more work.”
Ballard wrapped up the panel discussion with a vision for this people-focused future, and presented an optimistic view of technology’s role in bringing dignity to people’s lives.
“There’s a lot of maybe scary, fearful things in the air right now around advanced technologies and AI,” he said. “But I think when you look at the things that are actually being done with the tools today… it’s a very cool time to be alive.”
The TIME Trailblazers Dinner: Designing and Making the Future was presented by Autodesk.

Western leaders ‘don’t end up’ in ICC – ex-MEP (VIDEO)
Western leaders are far less likely to face the International Criminal Court (ICC) for conduct comparable to that alleged against officials from weaker states, former MEP Gunnar Beck has told RT. The “defeated” and “powerless” are most at risk while leaders of major nations are largely shielded, he argued.
The ICC was established in 2002 under the Rome Statute to try individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, but has faced longstanding accusations of political bias and selective justice.
In an interview with RT on Tuesday, Beck said that “major powers don’t end up” in the ICC, adding that international organizations remain “largely dominated by Western powers and their sort of allies and vassals.” Invoking Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s famous dictum that “victors are not judged,” he argued that the court’s record largely reflects the same principle.
“The same acts committed by a head of state of a major power, and especially a Western power, are far less likely, if not to say are altogether unlikely, to be prosecuted or brought before the court,” he said.
He argued that the pattern extends beyond whether countries formally belong to the court. Russia, China, the US, and India are not parties to the Rome Statute, but Beck said political power also affects the likelihood of prosecution.
“If you ask me, is a Russian leader more likely to be at least prosecuted before the court than an American leader, I’d say yes, even if that were for similar deeds,” he said. “So we certainly see a discrepancy here.”
Criticism of the ICC has intensified in recent months. Venezuela, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger have moved to withdraw from the court, accusing it of political bias and “neocolonial repression.”
Russia, which is not a party to the Rome Statute, rejected the ICC’s authority when the court issued warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in 2023 over the alleged unlawful transfer of Ukrainian children.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has pledged to “systematically dismantle the threat posed” by the ICC to US sovereignty. Israel has likewise rejected the court’s jurisdiction, although the ICC issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza
