Nairobi to make history as first African host of World Athletics Championships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:21:39 UTC
19:21:39 KST

Nairobi will host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, becoming the first African city to stage the global outdoor track and field event, World Athletics announced on Tuesday.
The Kenyan capital beat bids from London, Munich and Rome for the 2029 championships, while Munich was selected to host the 2031 edition following a World Athletics Council meeting in Budapest.
“We were fortunate to have four outstanding bids for 2029 and 2031, and this was not an easy decision for the Council,” World Athletics President Sebastian Coe told a news conference.
The 2027 championships have already been awarded to Beijing.
‘Historic’ first for Africa
Coe called Nairobi’s selection a historic moment for African athletics and praised the city’s bid as compelling.
“Taking our championships to Africa for the first time will be historic,” Coe said, adding that Nairobi had shown it was ready to help accelerate the development of athletics in Kenya and across the continent.
The decision means the next three editions of the championships will be staged across Asia, Africa and Europe, with Beijing in 2027, Nairobi in 2029 and Munich in 2031.
Nairobi builds on athletics legacy
Kenya previously bid unsuccessfully to host the 2025 championships but has a long record of staging major international athletics events.
Mombasa hosted the 2007 World Cross Country Championships, while Nairobi hosted the World Under-18 Championships in 2017 and World Under-20 Championships in 2021. The capital also staged the 2010 African Athletics Championships.
Coe said Nairobi had returned with a stronger bid after learning from its previous campaign.
The city’s Kasarani Stadium is undergoing a major renovation ahead of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, further strengthening its infrastructure for the championships.
Coe said Nairobi had demonstrated that “this is their moment” to create a lasting legacy for athletics in Kenya and across Africa.

UN experts say Belarus justice system used to target Lukashenko opponents
The experts say courts, police, security services, prosecutors, and prison authorities work together to silence real or perceived government critics.
United Nations experts have found that Belarusian state institutions have worked together to repress government critics through arrests, imprisonment, and surveillance since 2020.
In a report to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council this week, the independent experts said courts, police, security services, prosecutors, and prison authorities had worked together to silence real or perceived opponents of President Alexander Lukashenko, who has been in power since 1994.

The experts said they found “systematic” violations of international human rights obligations from arrest through to detention, conviction, and post-release supervision.
They cited arbitrary arrests, torture, denial of legal safeguards, closed trials, and the continued harassment of former detainees.
“The patterns of violations described in this paper continue to the present day,” the report said.
It added that the judiciary had played a key role by legitimising abuses and denying victims effective remedies.
According to the report, Belarus has previously rejected UN criticism of its human rights record and did not cooperate with the experts, who said requests to visit the country and engage with authorities went unanswered.
The experts said Belarus violated multiple international treaties. They reiterated earlier findings that some abuses committed since May 2020 could amount to crimes against humanity, including persecution and imprisonment.
The findings come three years after mass protests erupted following the August 2020 presidential elections, which saw Lukashenko win once again. The opposition and Western governments condemned his electoral success, calling the vote rigged.
In the crackdown on protesters, thousands of people were arrested, and rights groups continue to document political prisoners in the country.
While Lukashenko denies holding political prisoners, describing them as “bandits”, former political prisoner and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Ales Bialiatski told the Reuters news agency last month that despite recent prisoner releases secured through United States engagement with Minsk, “the machinery of repression keeps running.”
On Tuesday, US envoy John Coale arrived in Minsk for his first talks in six months with Lukashenko to negotiate the release of political prisoners.
According to the Belarusian human rights group Viasna, more than 900 political prisoners are still being held in Belarus.

US Air Force personnel supporting Operation Epic Fury in the Middle East weathered 1,200 "Alarm Red" conditions amid Iranian missile and drone attacks, completed 48 runway repairs, and conducted more than 400 unexploded ordnance sweeps, a senior military official has said.
The operation will be studied for its scale, precision and speed, Gen. Ken Wilsbach, chief of staff of the Air Force, said at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.
He noted that in over 38 days of combat missions, the Joint Force hit more than 13,000 military targets.
A fleet of 500 aircraft executed 10,000 sorties, maintaining a daily tempo of more than 250 flights, while personnel managed emergency repairs and conducted more than 420 reportable ordnance disposal missions under fire, he added.
The combat missions occurred during the US war on Iran, which began February 28 with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iranian leadership and infrastructure.
While the campaign degraded Iranian positions, American bases across the Gulf and Jordan have sustained retaliatory missile and drone barrages that heavily depleted interceptor stockpiles and caused operational damage.
The combat operations form part of the six-month-old Iran war, which has left 18 US service members dead and 824 wounded since February 2026. Meanwhile, thousands have been killed in Iran.
The US has formally separated Operation Epic Fury from the ongoing hostilities with Iran, while continuing to conduct strikes and maritime operations under different labels such as Project Freedom and Overseas Operations.
To counter evolving threats, Wilsbach announced the establishment of the Point Defence Weapon System, which integrates kinetic and directed platforms to bolster base security, alongside a specialised point-defence career field.

Veterans Affairs Ministry: Ukraine will not copy American veterans support model
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:19:28 EEST
19:19:28 KST

The Ministry of Veterans Affairs has stated that Ukraine will not copy the American model of veterans policy, but will instead build its own system tailored to the demands of the war and Ukrainian society.
"The main outcome of the meetings is that Ukraine will not copy the American model, but will build its own system tailored to the demands of the war and Ukrainian society. At the same time, utilizing years of international experience will allow us to cover this path much faster," the ministry reported following a working visit to Washington, D.C. (USA) by Minister of Veterans Affairs of Ukraine Vitaliy Kim.
It is noted that for Ukraine, which is developing its own veterans policy amid a full-scale war, U.S. experience is extremely valuable.
The ministry recounted that during the working visit, it was important for the Ukrainian delegation to study this system from the inside: what works effectively and where problems have accumulated over decades that should be avoided.
"One of the key events was a meeting between Minister of Veterans Affairs of Ukraine Vitaliy Kim and U.S. Secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins. This is the first bilateral meeting between the heads of the two countries' veterans agencies in a long time... During the meeting, the discussion focused on the U.S. veterans medical system, which unites 170 centers and over 1,000 outpatient facilities. U.S. experience in prosthetics, treatment of polytrauma, and psychological rehabilitation is important for Ukrainian specialists. The parties agreed on further exchange of experience at the level of teams and specialized experts," the report states.
Also, together with leading American research centers RAND Corporation and CSIS, the Ukrainian delegation discussed the challenges and practical aspects of the functioning of the U.S. veteran system.
In particular, experts from RAND discussed the creation of an economic model for the reintegration of veterans, and the involvement of Ukrainian analytical centers in joint research projects was also addressed.
In addition, CSIS specialists shared their experience in the field of financial support for veterans policy and outlined issues that Ukraine can take into account when shaping its own institutional decisions.

Joint exhibition of Chinese, Mongolian sculptors opens in Mongolia's capital
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:31:30 CST
11:31:30 KST

ULAN BATOR, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- A joint exhibition featuring works by Chinese and Mongolian sculptors opened on Tuesday in Ulan Bator, the capital of Mongolia, showcasing works by 14 Chinese and eight Mongolian sculptors.
Upon entering the exhibition hall, visitors are greeted by works from both countries, thoughtfully arranged to complement one another. The exhibits encompass a variety of forms, including bronze and figurative sculptures, and explore a wide range of themes and artistic styles.
Chinese sculptors draw inspiration from the richness of traditional Chinese culture, blending elements of the northern grasslands and the Silk Road with modern aesthetics. Their works combine intricate craftsmanship and refined textures with a sense of grandeur. Mongolian sculptors, meanwhile, delve deeply into the rich heritage of grassland culture, with their works featuring themes such as swift horses, vast grasslands, and nomadic life.
"This exhibition is not merely a joint display of artworks, but also a profound dialogue encompassing creative philosophies, artistic techniques, and cultural perspectives," said Li Zhi, counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Mongolia and director of the China Cultural Center in Ulan Bator. ■

MADRID, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Substitute Carlos Espi scored an injury-time winner as Real Madrid came from behind to beat Elche 3-2 in the sixth round of La Liga on Tuesday.
The result gives Jose Mourinho's side 15 points from a possible 18, drawing it level with FC Barcelona ahead of Barca's home game against Racing Santander on Wednesday.
Real Madrid took the lead in the 25th minute when Arda Guler's free kick was parried into his own net by Elche goalkeeper Matias Dituro. Kylian Mbappe made it 2-0 eight minutes later, heading in from a Yan Diomande cross. Mbappe then had a goal ruled out for a tight offside three minutes before halftime.
Elche rallied after the break. Ariel Osorio pulled one back with about 20 minutes remaining after getting the better of Dean Huijsen, and Fer Nino leveled in the 83rd minute following a defensive lapse by Marc Cucurella. Just when it looked as if Elche would salvage a draw, Espi combined with Jude Bellingham and Mbappe before slotting home in the 91st minute.
Valencia claimed its first win of the season, beating Deportivo Alaves 1-0 under B-team coach Oscar Sanchez, who took charge following Carlos Corberan's dismissal on Sunday.
Luis Rioja scored the only goal in the 78th minute after fine work from Javi Guerra but had to be withdrawn injured shortly afterward. Arnaut Danjuma had a first-half goal ruled out for Valencia, while Alaves wasted several chances.
Rayo Vallecano and Espanyol kicked off the day, with Rayo ending its exile at Leganes' Butarque Stadium with a 2-1 victory. Alvaro Garcia poked home after just three minutes and Adria Pedrosa doubled the lead in the 26th. Espanyol pressed in the second half and Raul Fernandez struck in the 54th, but Rayo held on for a vital win. ■

Italian jets destroyed a drone over Lithuania in the first such shootdown in the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:17:13 UTC
19:17:13 KST

NATO fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania shortly after midnight on 15 September, the first time alliance aircraft have destroyed one over that country, LRT reported. The aircraft crossed in from Belarus and came down near a village in the center of the country, where military police sealed the site. Its type and operator have not been established.
What happened over Lithuania
Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center issued a yellow air alert after midnight, first for the capital and the districts around it, then for the Kaunas region further west. Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons flying NATO's Baltic air policing mission from Šiauliai Air Base destroyed the drone with missile armament, Lithuania's Defense Ministry confirmed, and the army published the first images from the crash site.
The drone was over Lithuanian territory for about half an hour, crisis center head Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT radio. He said there is a high probability it carried an explosive charge, though the wreckage does not yet show whether it was a combat drone. Lithuania chose a yellow alert rather than red because red is used when a strike or a fall is unavoidable, he explained, and the drone was destroyed within seconds of the air defense crews reacting, over farmland with no homes nearby.
Military and civilian police are working at the site under the Shield security plan, and the area has been fenced off and guarded. President Gitanas Nausėda thanked the allied personnel for their swift response, saying that with Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine such readiness is vital for the region.
Whose drone it was
Nothing has been established beyond the direction it came from. The army has not commented on the drone's possible origin while the wreckage is still being collected, and the launch point also remains unreleased. Vilnius airport suspended operations during the alert, and flights from Türkiye and Iceland were delayed.
The same night as this incursion, Poland scrambled fighter jets and raised air defense readiness over Russian drone strikes on western Ukraine, and Romania did the same, with neither country recording a violation of its airspace. The day before, the Polish military recovered a drone from the Baltic Sea that its defense minister said preliminary inspection indicated was Russian and military.

Volker: Ukraine knows how to shoot down drones cheaply, NATO must adopt this experience
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:16:26 EEST
19:16:26 KST

Former U.S. Special Representative for Ukraine (2017–19) and Kyiv Security Forum (KSF) Security Council member Kurt Volker has expressed the conviction that NATO should cooperate with Ukraine to create an integrated air picture in order to counter the infiltration of drones and missiles.
Volker noted during a special meeting of the KSF Security Council in Kyiv that he would like NATO to start cooperating with Ukraine on establishing an integrated air picture and setting up a no-fly zone around NATO airspace together with Ukraine to eliminate the problem of drones, missiles, and other objects penetrating the Alliance's territory, adding that this is one of the ways to support Ukraine.
He specified that this involves closing the airspace around the Alliance's territory at a certain distance, emphasizing that they must support Ukraine's efforts to close the airspace around NATO territory, perhaps at a distance of 150 kilometers.
Separately, the ambassador stressed that NATO countries should adopt Ukrainian experience in countering air threats, adding that they must learn from Ukrainians how to shoot down missiles and drones in a cost-effective manner, something NATO countries have not yet undertaken to do.
He also named three key elements of Ukraine's strategy that he believes the West must strengthen: striking Russian finances, pressuring the war economy, and exhausting the Russian military. Volker emphasized that it is necessary to do everything possible to strike the Kremlin's finances, noting that Russia primarily receives money from oil and gas sales and must be deprived of this source of revenue, and that Russians are feeling the consequences of the war, seeing them in the form of fires, smoke, and fuel lines, with this overall impact on the Russian economy creating pressure on Putin domestically.
Volker stressed that the West must strengthen these areas, in particular through secondary sanctions, stating that they must target the Kremlin's finances and adopt Senator Lindsey Graham's bill, with special attention paid to secondary sanctions against financial institutions that process payments in favor of Russia.
The special meeting of the KSF Security Council was dedicated to the challenges awaiting Ukraine this winter. Its participants, in addition to Volker, included KSF Chairman and former Prime Minister (2014–16) Arseniy Yatsenyuk and former U.S. Central Command Commander (2008–10) and former CIA Director (2011–12) David Petraeus.

Putin's foreign minister blames US for extra year of war in Ukraine, says Russia could have been at peace

Unknown Publisher

Putin's foreign minister blames US for extra year of war in Ukraine, says Russia could have been at peace
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused the U.S. on Sept. 15 of prolonging Moscow's war against Ukraine by a year by withdrawing from what he described as the "Anchorage agreements" reached between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Moscow has repeatedly referred to alleged agreements from Trump's 2025 meeting with Putin in Alaska, although U.S. officials have denied that such agreements existed.
Lavrov claimed that Washington's withdrawal from the purported agreements, allegedly under pressure from Europe, prevented the war from ending.
"If the Americans hadn't backed away from the Anchorage agreements" and Europe hadn't "pulled" the U.S. away from them, "we would have been living without war for a year now," Lavrov said.
His comments came as U.S.-led efforts to broker a broader peace deal remain stalled over Russia's territorial demands. The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv cede the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine.
Moscow is effectively demanding that Ukraine surrender territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily. Kyiv has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line and stressed the need for security guarantees to deter future Russian aggression.
President Volodymyr Zelensky plans to discuss possible limited ceasefires with Trump during a potential meeting in New York next week. Zelensky said Sept. 14 that he wants to discuss halting Russian and Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea.
The meeting could take place on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly between Sept. 21-23 if the presidents' schedules align. Lavrov said he also plans to meet U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month in an attempt to break the deadlock in peace talks. The Kyiv visit was the envoys' first since the latest push to revive negotiations.
The most tangible outcome of their trip was an agreement between Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia to resume trilateral negotiations. Previous rounds produced little political progress but led to major humanitarian initiatives, including prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Lavrov said Moscow remains open to resuming the talks.
"We have never refused to negotiate, and all the talks that have taken place were interrupted not at our initiative. If our colleagues are ready, it is entirely possible to resume them," he said.

====================================================================================================

in 2000, hussein chalayan hid an entire collection inside a living room
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:15:11 UTC
19:15:11 KST

In London in February 2000, Hussein Chalayan staged a small living room at the end of his runway. Four chairs sat beneath gray slipcovers around a low coffee table, and a television sat beyond. Before the models appeared, a family entered and settled into it. It was a strangely familiar setting, as it suggested a domestic space temporarily transplanted into a theater. For the audience, the furniture was background scenery, and it sat there long enough that it was almost forgotten.
The garments passing through the space offered a few clues. Pockets expanded to hold objects taken from the room, and seams traced shapes around the body with architectural precision. Still, the living room remained a living room. Viewers watched the collection move past it, unaware that some garments had been sitting in front of them from the beginning.
Toward the end of After Words, four models approached the chairs and began removing their gray covers. The fabric came away from the furniture and wrapped around their bodies as dresses. The chairs themselves were then folded down and carried away like luggage. Designer Hussein Chalayan later said this sequence, when the models first began stripping the chairs, interested him even more than the coffee table transformation that would become the show’s most famous image.
The audience, with this climactic reveal, is forced to reconsider something it’s been looking at all along. A chair cover becomes clothing — however, the more interesting transformation takes place in the viewer’s head. The set had been part of the collection from the start. Chalayan just withheld that information. For a few seconds, everyone in the theater has to mentally replay the room they thought they understood.
After Words, Hussein Chalayan, Fall/Winter 2000
taking the room with you
After Words grew from Chalayan’s thinking around wartime displacement and his own family history in Cyprus. His mother had been forced from her home as a teenager during the violence that preceded the island’s division in 1974. Chalayan began thinking about the compressed decisions that come with evacuation — a person may have only minutes to decide what can leave the house with them. In the collection, possessions disappear into clothes and furniture gains a second function built around escape.
Seen through that context, the finale changes once more. A model approaches the circular wooden coffee table and removes its center before stepping inside and lifting it toward her waist to create a rigid wooden skirt. She walks away wearing part of the room. By the end, the furniture has been dismantled and carried off to leave the living room empty.
After Words, Hussein Chalayan, Fall/Winter 2000
clothes that only make sense in motion
Chalayan returned to this kind of transformation throughout his work. In Before Minus Now, shown just before After Words, a fiberglass dress used remote-controlled panels that opened across the body like parts of an aircraft.
Several years later, the 2007 show One Hundred and Eleven used concealed mechanics to move garments through historical silhouettes while the models stood onstage. Even while the technology changes, the recurring idea is remains to be that the garment reaches its full meaning through an event.
Even while a still photograph can preserve Chalayan’s table skirt, it will miss the most important part. The strangeness of After Words is seeing one identity become another and realizing that both existed at the same time.
Chalayan designed the clothes as well as the audience’s delay in understanding them. For much of the show, everyone thinks they are looking at a living room. By the end, every object in it has become something that could leave with the body.
Before Minus Now, Hussein Chalayan, Spring/Summer 2000
One Hundred and Eleven, Hussein Chalayan, Spring/Summer 2007

====================================================================================================

The Census Bureau Is Overrun With Staffers From a MAGA Think Tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Multiple staffers at a Trump-aligned policy think tank have burrowed their way into the US Census Bureau, where they have access to sensitive data and have contributed to a public report that bolsters conspiracy theories undermining trust in elections ahead of the midterms.
In August, the Census Bureau published an anonymously authored report titled “Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis,” claiming to show that thousands of noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. A WIRED investigation revealed that the report appeared to employ faulty methodology, casting its conclusions into doubt, and that two of its authors work for the America First Policy Institute, a right-wing think tank with deep ties to the Trump administration. Now WIRED has found that the two authors are part of a larger team, made up almost entirely of AFPI members, who have been detailed to the Census Bureau and given access to its data.
The Census Bureau is home to vast troves of sensitive data on nearly every person living in the country, which is used for apportioning and drawing congressional districts as well as allocating federal funding based on population sizes. Experts and Census employees who spoke to WIRED worry that the noncitizen voting report is the first salvo in Census data possibly being used to undermine the results of the upcoming midterms or the 2028 presidential election.
A Census employee who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity says that there has historically been “nothing close” to what AFPI is doing at the bureau. “Frankly, it's disrespectful to the institution,” they say.
The Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to cast doubt on the accuracy of Census data in order to reshape elections. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that the Department of Commerce, which oversees the bureau, was circulating a rule change that would eliminate noncitizens from being counted in the Census, a move that could drastically reshape how Congressional districts are drawn. Republicans also took aim at a little-known statistical method called differential privacy that is used to protect the privacy of individual respondents, alleging that it makes the Census count inaccurate in ways that favor Democrats in congressional apportionment.
AFPI, meanwhile, has been integral to shaping the Trump administration’s policies and makeup. Brooke Rollins, who served as the group’s first CEO, is now the secretary of agriculture, and Linda McMahon, now the secretary of education, used to sit on the organization’s board. Former AFPI staffers have found their way to some of the highest ranks of the Trump administration, including former attorney general Pam Bondi, secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins, secretary of Housing and Urban Development Scott Turner, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin, US permanent representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, deputy director of White House Domestic Policy Council Heidi Overton, and National Economic Council of the United States director Kevin Hassett.
In addition to Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea, the two AFPI members previously identified by WIRED, at least five other AFPI members have been or are currently staffed at the Census Bureau, according to sources and documents reviewed by WIRED. Sources who spoke to WIRED confirmed that all the AFPI members are detailed to the agency through the Intergovernmental Personnel Act (IPA), which allows people with specialized skills from certain institutions, like nonprofits and universities, to work for the government for up to two years on a temporary appointment.
The Census Bureau and AFPI did not respond to requests for comment.
John Abowd, former associate director for research and methodology and chief scientist at the Census Bureau, says that having so many people from a single organization would be “unusual.”
Among the names viewed by WIRED are Max Kossek, a researcher at AFPI’s Office for Fiscal and Regulatory Analysis, and Ryan Montgomery, who the website lists as a program assistant with the same AFPI office. Montgomery’s LinkedIn profile, however, says that he is now a “research engineer” at AFPI.
AFPI’s director for secure elections policy, Thomas Lane, is also listed as one of the employees that has been detailed to the Census Bureau. Lane, a former Trump campaign staffer and election denier, was subpoenaed by the Department of Justice in 2022 as part of its investigation into the president’s attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. (Lane was not charged by law enforcement.) In a 2020 video posted by the Arizona Republican Party, where a group of fake electors attempted to deliver the state’s electoral votes to Donald Trump, Politico identified a man wearing a jacket with the name “Lane” on it passing out the documents for the electors to sign making them “duly elected” and “qualified.” In 2024, CNN reported that Lane was prepared to serve as a backup elector for that same group.
Earlier this year, Democracy Docket reported that Lane helped write part of an early version of the Save America Act, the law that would require voter ID to register to vote, while working for the Republican majority House Committee on House Administration. Parts of the Save Act have also been included in the separate Save America Act, which, if passed, would require proof of citizenship in order to vote, a move that experts say could disenfranchise more than 20 million people.
Kossek, Montgomery, and Lane did not respond to requests for comment.
David Peterson, who AFPI lists as a research engineer with expertise in “computing, machine learning, and advanced software architecture,” and Jackson Mejia, an AFPI fellow who is an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin with a PhD in economics from MIT focusing on tax policy, also appear to be detailed to the Census Bureau. Peterson and Mejia did not respond to requests for comment.
Another person, listed as an IPA from AFPI, Michael Corey, is also listed among the group at the bureau. AFPI does not list Corey as a staff member on its website, but an AFPI email with Corey’s name does appear to exist. AFPI did not confirm whether Corey was currently associated with the think tank.
Danah Boyd, a professor at Cornell University who studies the census, says that there are vehicles like the American Association for the Advancement of Science through which agencies like the Census Bureau might bring in multiple IPAs. But AFPI, Boyd says, “is not an institution that is set up to bring all the scientists in the world together or that has built this long-standing infrastructure of doing independent statistical research. This is a partisan group with an agenda,” she claims.
All of the AFPI members are listed under the same project, focused on “ad hoc data analyses” to answer questions from senior leaders at Census and the Department of Commerce, according to documentation viewed by WIRED. The project appears to be led by Michael Lachanski, the bureau’s recently appointed deputy director for data, policy, and science, and a former fellow at the Claremont Institute, a conservative think tank that also has connections to the Trump administration. Lachanski is a political appointee. All of the AFPI detailees appear to have the “special sworn status” necessary to access sensitive Census data.
Recent reporting from Talking Points Memo found that the Census Bureau’s Data Stewardship Executive Policy charter had been updated in July to remove stipulations that prevented political appointees from interfering with the bureau’s data.
Another Census employee, who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press, says that access to Census data is only allowed through approved “projects,” where employees and researchers have to explain how they're going to use the data and what they're going to produce. The employee says that it’s not unheard of to have multiple people from the same outside institution on the same project, but there appears to be a lack of civil servants involved in this one. The project’s “explicit reference to answering questions of interest to political appointees” is concerning, the employee says.
Boyd says this kind of work is a clear departure from the bureau’s mandate, which does not include providing data to political appointees. “These are all part of culture norms and practices of how you make certain you run a transparent agency to ensure that you are doing good by the American people,” she says.
There is precedent for political pressure at the Census Bureau: In 2021, less than two weeks after the January 6 insurrection at the end of Trump’s first term, then US Census Bureau director Steven Dillingham announced his resignation after a letter from the Office of the Inspector General revealed that whistleblowers had come forward to allege Census workers had been pressured by political appointees to create a report showing the citizenship status of every US resident.

How Belarus helps Russia and its drone arsenal target Ukraine and threaten NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:14:53 UTC
19:14:53 KST

Belarus appears to have resumed providing infrastructure to support Russian drone attacks on Ukraine and is now also emerging as a threat to NATO after a drone flying from Belarus was shot down over Lithuania. Here's what we know.
The drone shot down by NATO over Lithuania overnight on Tuesday had entered the country’s airspace from neighbouring Belarus, Vilnius said.
The drone flew over Lentvaris close to the Lithuanian capital before being brought down near the village of Pratkūnai, according to Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre.
It was the first time a drone was shot down over Lithuanian territory.
The incident puts Minsk back in focus not only for helping Russia carry out drone attacks against Ukraine, but now also as a source of drone threats to NATO territory.
The incursion came just a day after Ukrainian officials said Russia was using Belarusian mobile networks and signal repeaters to support Shahed-type drones during attacks on western Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said the flight paths of Russian drones during a mass attack on Saturday suggested they were making use of mobile networks across the border.
“If we look at the movement of jet-powered and conventional ‘Shaheds,’ they stay close to the border with Belarus," Beskrestnov said.
Beskrestnov said he believed the drones probably had access to Belarusian commercial LTE networks.
On Monday Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service separately said recent Russian attacks on the western regions of Rivne, Volyn and Lviv had been supported by communications infrastructure located inside Belarus.
“The air assets launched by Russia were fed with a signal through repeaters that were also located precisely on the territory of this country,” border guard spokesperson Andrii Demchenko said.
The claims suggest Russia is again making use of communications infrastructure inside Belarus to support its drone campaign against Ukraine, months after Kyiv demanded that the equipment be shut down.
Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said last week that Kyiv had identified six repeater stations in Belarus used by Russian forces to relay video streams from strike drones, and that some of the equipment had resumed operating.
The equipment has been a source of tension between Kyiv and Minsk since June, when Zelenskyy gave Belarus a week to dismantle or switch off the Russian-installed repeaters, warning that Ukraine would otherwise act itself.
Days later, Zelenskyy said the repeaters had stopped operating on 22 June, although it remained unclear whether they had actually been removed.
The shutdown did not last long. By the end of June Ukrainian military officials said the equipment had not been dismantled and that at least one repeater had been switched back on.
Their apparent return gives Russia another means of maintaining communications with strike drones operating close to Ukraine’s northern and western borders, including areas close to NATO territory.
Russia has increasingly used a mixture of mobile networks and radio technology to maintain links with its long-range strike drones and overcome Ukrainian electronic warfare.

Hunting down Kalibr missile carriers: how Ukraine has lured Russian frigates into a trap and is gradually taking them out
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:13:00 EEST
19:13:00 KST

Hunting down Kalibr missile carriers: how Ukraine has lured Russian frigates into a trap and is gradually taking them out
It was a few years ago that Ukraine's defence forces forced the Russian Navy to flee occupied Sevastopol for the safer port of Novorossiysk. Yet Russian warships have found no sanctuary there either: Ukrainian drones, missiles and uncrewed surface vessels continue to strike terror into the Russian fleet.
On the night of 8-9 September, the defence forces launched another strike on Novorossiysk using drones and domestically-produced Neptune missiles. It is there that the Russian frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov are based, along with a number of other warships that launch Kalibr missiles on Ukrainian cities.
This remarkable operation is just one part of a major naval campaign Ukraine launched in 2026, bringing together forces from several key security agencies. The goal is to destroy what remains of the Black Sea Fleet and leave it incapable of launching cruise missiles.
Analysts from the Plitka Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) community have examined the recent strikes on Russian frigates exclusively for Ukrainska Pravda, detailing how Ukraine's defence forces are gradually disarming the Russian Black Sea Fleet in Novorossiysk.
The retreat from Sevastopol
Sevastopol is a strategically important base for Russia's Black Sea Fleet. The Kremlin once cited the need to control Sevastopol, which it described as the "key to control of the Black Sea", as a justification for its occupation of Crimea. Ironically, just a year and a half into the full-scale war, the city began to rapidly lose that strategic importance.
On 13 September 2023, Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the Sevmorzavod shipyard in Sevastopol. The strike damaged the dock, and the resulting fire destroyed the large landing ship Minsk and the submarine Rostov-on-Don. Nine days later, another strike hit the Black Sea Fleet headquarters.
Satellite imagery from early October showed that Russia's main surface ships armed with cruise missiles had been moved to Novorossiysk, farther away from Ukraine's reach. The frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov were the most significant examples, as they are two of the Black Sea Fleet's most important warships. The Admiral Makarov has served as the fleet's flagship since the cruiser Moskva was sunk.
The logic behind the redeployment was simple: to move the ships out of range of Ukrainian weapons. Novorossiysk lies more than 300 km from the front line, has a naval base in the Geoport area and is protected by coastal air defence systems.
Geography, however, puts these warships at a disadvantage. Sevastopol Bay is narrow, with an entrance that can easily be blocked by booms. Novorossiysk Bay, by contrast, is wider, and Ukrainian aerial and naval weapons can reach its military harbour and the oil terminal's jetties.
The Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov are two of the few Black Sea Fleet ships capable of firing Kalibr cruise missiles. Each is equipped with an eight-cell universal vertical launcher.
Ukraine's defence forces were not going to leave them untouched. In 2026, things took a truly petrifying turn for the two ships.
How Ukraine has attacked Novorossiysk in 2026
In March, the Ukrainian military carried out its first combined strike, sending up to 200 drones into the attack alongside missiles. The Admiral Essen was hit in the middle of the superstructure, and the resulting fire raged for around 18 hours.
Satellite imagery analysis showed that the section housing the ship's defensive and threat-detection systems had been burnt out. The damage affected the PK-10 launchers for passive countermeasures, the TK-25 electronic warfare system, the Fregat-M2M detection radar and the MP-90 Orekh target illumination stations. Without the Orekh stations, the ship's air defence system cannot guide missiles against incoming targets. Ukraine's General Staff officially confirmed that both frigates, the Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov, had been damaged.
In April, attack drones from Ukraine's 1st Separate Drone Centre struck the Sheshkharis oil terminal in an operation supported by long-range strike capabilities. The Russian frigates were also hit during the strikes.
Satellite analysis by the OSINT community CyberBoroshno showed that the Essen had taken a hit to the bow that night, around the A-190 100mm gun mount, directly above the MGK-335M Platina hull-mounted sonar system. Its distinctive white radar domes made it possible to identify the ship in satellite images. The Makarov, meanwhile, was recorded as having been hit near its berth and vertical launch systems.
In late May, Novorossiysk came under a two-day raid by the 1st Separate Drone Centre, led by Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces. This time, the drones came for the Essen from the side rather than from above, skimming in at the waterline despite the ship's air defences.
In August, a major joint operation brought together Defence Intelligence of Ukraine's Department of Active Operations and Department of Unmanned Systems, the Security Service of Ukraine, the Navy and the State Border Guard Service, working in coordination with the General Staff. The forces deployed Palianytsia long-range jet-powered drones, Neptune cruise missiles, uncrewed surface vessels and other assets.
By the end of the night, four vessels had been confirmed hit: both frigates, a Project 21631 Buyan-M-class small missile ship and a Vasily Bykov-class patrol vessel. The strikes also hit a 30N6E radar station belonging to an S-300 air-defence system, the Grushovaya oil depot and an oil-loading jetty.
The August attack appears to have left the frigates critically damaged.
A through-hole is visible on the satellite image of the Makarov, directly over the eight-cell 3S14 universal launcher that fires Kalibr missiles. Because the missile warheads are not normally kept on board in port, the strike did not trigger a detonation. The launcher silo itself, however, was destroyed. Further damage can be seen on the stern superstructure, where the dome of the Kentavr-NM1 secure satellite communications station has been destroyed, and the nearby antenna mast of the Positiv-M1.2 3D radar system has been damaged.
The Essen has taken a different kind of beating. Multiple fires have left the deck around the missile silos blackened with soot, and the PK-10 passive countermeasure launchers and the TK-25 electronic warfare station have been rendered inoperable. The ship remains afloat, and its main weaponry is most likely intact. Four consecutive strikes have nevertheless compromised its close-in defences and detection systems.
The image shows the extent of the damage, but not how deep it goes. A hole in the deck around the launch system is clearly visible. Satellite imagery cannot reveal whether the launch system module beneath the Makarov's deck has been destroyed or whether the damage is limited to the structures above it. The same uncertainty applies to the Essen's superstructure: it is impossible to tell how extensively its interior has been burnt out. Neither the Russian side nor the Ukrainian authorities has released a detailed damage assessment.
That said, the damaged launch tubes could seriously affect the ships' ability to launch Kalibr missiles on Ukraine. The 3S14 is not a standalone structure that can simply be removed and replaced. It is a module integrated into the hull. On Project 11356R frigates such as the Makarov and the Essen, it is recessed into the bow, between the 100mm A-190 gun mount and the superstructure.
The size of the module gives an idea of just how difficult it could be to repair. The Russian export brochure for the 3S-14E launcher lists its height at 9,580 mm – almost ten metres down into the hull – its length at 3,760 mm, and its width at 1,970 mm. The module weighs 14,000 kg and has eight missile launch positions. In other words, this is not a unit that can simply be lifted out by crane from any quay.
In theory, the module is repairable. The deck above it would first have to be opened up so that the launch system could be accessed from above and the upper-deck structures could be cut through. The module would then have to be removed and replaced using cranes capable of handling its weight. All systems linked to the launch mechanisms would also have to be rebuilt.
It sounds like a complex operation, but one that the Russians are capable of carrying out. The Black Sea Fleet has historically relied on the shipyards of Sevastopol for major repairs. However the port has become too dangerous, which forced the frigates to flee several years ago. Novorossiysk was built as a home port, not a repair centre, and has very limited facilities for dockyard work of this scale. As a result, even a partially damaged ship can be effectively out of action for the long term: there is simply nowhere to carry out the necessary repairs.
Interestingly, the August attack hit more than just the two frigates. The Essen and the Makarov stole the headlines, but a comprehensive analysis of the imagery by the Exilenova+ community shows that the damage in the harbour was far more widespread. Traces of damage were also found on five other vessels, each playing a specific role at the base:
- A minesweeper that ensures safe passage out of the bay and provides mine protection for the navigation channels
- The Priazovye, a medium-sized intelligence-gathering vessel responsible for signals intelligence and air surveillance for the Black Sea Fleet
- A Vasily Bykov-class patrol vessel equipped with a Tor-M2KM containerised air-defence system
- The Viktor Cherokov, a naval arms transport vessel used to carry munitions
- A dry cargo vessel near the outer harbour wall; its type is difficult to determine from the photograph.
The Exilenova+ analysis also pinpoints the home port of the 4th Submarine Brigade, which operates the Varshavyanka-class submarines that carry most of the Black Sea Fleet's Kalibr missiles. There are no visible signs of damage to the submarines in the images. Even so, the fact that the area was targeted suggests that the strike zone encompasses the entire base rather than being limited to individual berths.
The strikes have not stopped – the latest came only a few days ago. On the night of 8–9 September, Ukrainian forces struck the Novorossiysk naval base again. Defence Intelligence of Ukraine said operators from its Department of Active Operations took part in a joint deep-strike operation that targeted the base's infrastructure and the frigate Admiral Essen. A fire broke out on the ship's superstructure. An analysis by Ukrainian military outlet Defense Express found that the strike hit the forward part of the superstructure, destroying the bridge and several control stations for the ship's weapons and equipment.
On the same day, the Ukrainian Navy said the weapon used in the attack was a domestically produced Neptune missile. The following day, it clarified that the missile was the extended-range version, known as the Long Neptune.
The Navy stated: "Satellite imagery confirms that the ship's upper superstructure was hit. The damage sustained prevents the ship from carrying out combat missions. The missile carrier will require lengthy and costly repairs."
Why stay in the line of fire?
The obvious question is: if the ships are attacked so frequently, why not take them out into the open sea? The answer is that leaving the harbour would expose them to Ukrainian unmanned surface vessels and anti-ship missiles.
This was how the Russian Navy lost the cruiser Moskva, the large amphibious assault ship Tsezar Kunikov and several other vessels between 2022 and 2024. While in port, the ships at least had the protection of coastal air defences and access to a nearby repair base. In 2026, however, even the ports have become dangerous: the harbour is fully exposed to Ukrainian strikes.
Russians even captured Kalibr launches directly from the harbour on video. The roofline of a distinctive high-rise building and a lower landmark visible in the footage were identified on a satellite image. Their lines of sight intersect at 44.7072, 37.7798, revealing the filming location on the eastern shore of Tsemeskaya Bay. The military harbour lies directly across the water.
In other words, the Russian missile carriers are firing from berths inside the city harbour, under the cover of residential neighbourhoods, rather than moving out to firing positions in the open sea.
Conclusions
A flagship without a strike capability. The Admiral Makarov has become the de facto flagship of the Black Sea Fleet since the Moskva cruiser was sunk in April 2022. Damage to its 3S14 launch system and the destruction of its satellite communications station have stripped it of both capabilities: it can no longer launch Kalibr missiles or coordinate operations. Restoring these capabilities will require a factory-level repair.
The redeployment to Novorossiysk has failed to provide the safety the Russians were seeking. The ships were moved from Sevastopol to put them beyond the reach of Ukrainian strikes. Yet in 2026, combined attacks have repeatedly reached them at their berths, more than 300 km from the front line – five times in just six months. There is nowhere else for them to retreat to in the Black Sea. It is a closed basin.
The missile carriers have turned into floating batteries. Ships built to operate at sea are now firing from the harbour walls because venturing out is more dangerous than staying moored. This works as long as the harbour remains operational. The Black Sea Fleet's strike capability has become tied to a single point on the map – and that point is already under fire.

Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
- Published
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.
The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".
Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making "dangerous manoeuvres" near Russian warships.
It came on the same day that Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."
Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.
The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
In a statement, Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Moscow would "thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the incident" but accused the Danish helicopter of carrying out "provocative actions".
Barbin said this was "not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships".
He said he had complained about a similar incident last year, adding that the latest event showed that "communication problems lie not with the Russian Navy's vessels, but with the Danish side".
Russia's behaviour was "reckless and dangerous," the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said in a post on social media.
This incident – together with the drone over Lithuania – was "part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe", she added.
Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no attempt to make contact with helicopters had been made by the frigate's crew.
Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
The origins of the drone have yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.
President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.
Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".
Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

The questions science may never answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:12:44 UTC
19:12:44 KST

Science, at its best, is a striving toward truth. It is not, although we often think of it as such, the search for absolute truth. It’s more a process of systematically gathering and interpreting data about the universe to understand its past and present and predict its future. What results is the best approximation we can access at any given time with the information, methods and instruments we have.
And what counts as the best approximation of truth often changes. Isaac Newton began to devise his apple-falling theory of gravity in 1666. It worked well for everyone’s purposes in the 17th century. Then about 250 years later Albert Einstein stepped in with a better approximation: the general theory of relativity. Today some scientists are working to find ways to unite relativity with quantum mechanics, seeking a new approximation of the “truth” of gravity.
Not all questions will find answers. Some will likely remain beyond scientific grasp, even with methodological and interdisciplinary advances.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But are there some questions science can never fully answer? There are certainly questions scientists can’t answer yet. There are also queries scientists once thought impossible to resolve that weren’t. In 1835, for instance, philosopher Auguste Comte asserted that humans could never know what stars are made of. Then came spectroscopy, which allowed astronomers to parse stellar light for fingerprints of different chemicals.
Most things that seem forever unknowable eventually fall out of that porous basket. New ways of thinking or measuring expand the boundaries of science. This idea is the thesis of scholar Alexander Krauss’s most recent book, The Engine of Scientific Discovery. Until radio antennas existed, for instance, astronomers didn’t know the universe emitted radio waves, so they didn’t wonder what powered the gigantic jets shooting at nearly light speed from the centers of galaxies. Before microscopes, biologists didn’t know about animalcules, as microbes were first called, so they didn’t know they might someday study how the microbiome impacts mental health. “When scientists invent novel instruments and new computational and experimental techniques, they effectively expand the sensory and cognitive reach of science itself,” Krauss says.
Still, not all questions will find answers. Some will likely remain beyond scientific grasp, even with methodological and interdisciplinary advances. Some will be so beyond our imagination that they will remain unknown unknowns forever. That’s frustrating: science aims to understand the universe by observing, experimenting, interpreting, iterating. But that enterprise hits walls when there is nothing to observe or experiment on, when something lies past a fundamental barrier, or when observing or experimenting changes what is being observed or experimented on.
So how do we make sense of, and make peace with, necessary gaps in our knowledge? Perhaps by accepting that science isn’t about finding the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. We’ll just have a set of evolving best shots and, ideally, shots that keep leading—like a non-Brownian walk—to the next destination.
