Column: China's resilience premium -- policies, industrial depth, new geography of global supply chains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:59:03 CST
18:59:03 KST

by Shan Saeed
The global economy is entering an era in which resilience may command a premium comparable to efficiency.
Geopolitical fragmentation, tariff escalation, technological rivalry, energy insecurity and recurring disruption across strategic trade corridors are rewriting the architecture of global commerce. Corporate strategy is consequently shifting from just-in-time toward just-in-case: efficiency remains important, but redundancy, optionality, inventory security and supply-chain sovereignty increasingly carry measurable economic value.
Against this fractured backdrop, China possesses an asset that is extraordinarily difficult to replicate: industrial depth at continental scale.
China is no longer simply the factory of the world. Increasingly, it is becoming the factory to the factories of the world -- supplying the machinery, electronic components, intermediate inputs, batteries and capital equipment that enable production elsewhere.
Supply chains may geographically diversify away from final assembly in China while remaining deeply connected to Chinese upstream industrial capability. Diversification, therefore, does not automatically mean decoupling. That is the deeper meaning of China's resilience.
China's economic strategy has increasingly been organized around technological self-reliance, industrial modernization, domestic economic resilience, infrastructure connectivity and deeper commercial engagement with emerging markets.
The objective has been broader than headline gross domestic product growth. It has been to strengthen China's ability to absorb external shocks while progressively moving higher along global value chains.
China's emphasis on technological capability and strategic manufacturing has consequently become central to China's economic positioning. In an era of export controls, tariffs and strategic rivalry, economies possessing deep domestic industrial ecosystems enjoy greater capacity to withstand external shocks than those dependent on narrow segments of global production.
China's next economic chapter will increasingly be defined by artificial intelligence, robotics, electric vehicles, batteries, renewable technologies, advanced machinery and digital infrastructure.
China has constructed an industrial ecosystem of unusual breadth: manufacturing scale, supplier density, leadership in several clean-energy technologies, rapidly expanding technological capability, sophisticated infrastructure and increasingly diversified trade relationships.
That is China's resilience premium. And in an age defined increasingly by fragmentation rather than frictionless globalization, industrial depth may prove to be one of the most valuable forms of economic power.
Editor's note: Shan Saeed is global chief economist at Juwai IQI, a global proptech company, and has more than 25 years of experience in global financial markets.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

Across China: Century-old buildings emerge as key assets in urban development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:58:52 CST
18:58:52 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 7, 2026 shows an exterior view of the renovated former residence of renowned modern Chinese diplomat Wellington Koo in north China's Tianjin Municipality. (Xinhua)
TIANJIN, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- As visitors push open the vermilion gate at 267 Hebei Road in the Heping District of north China's Tianjin Municipality, the former residence of renowned modern Chinese diplomat Wellington Koo comes into view through the trees.
Inside, the first-floor reception room traces Koo's diplomatic career. On the second floor, qipao, jewelry and period-costume photography recreate scenes from the life of Koo's wife. Upstairs, a study recreates a period office setting.
The aroma of coffee wafts up from below, mingling with visitors' footsteps and tour guides' voices inside the century-old Western-style building.
Just over a year ago, the house stood almost empty.
Built in 1921, Koo's former residence is part of the modern architectural complex in Tianjin's Wudadao historical urban area, or the Five Great Avenues, which was included in the seventh batch of China's national key cultural relic protection units.
The building was later used as office space for many years. On an architecture-themed tourist route released by Tianjin's culture and tourism authorities in 2025, Koo's former residence was still marked as "exterior viewing only."
"When we first took over, the place was basically empty," recalled Jin Qianwen, curator of Koo's former residence. From planning and positioning the exhibition to sorting through historical stories, attracting businesses, and setting up facilities, the team gradually filled the space.
Revitalizing the building did not simply mean moving commercial ventures into an old house. The team reorganized the space around Koo and his family's stories. His wife's fondness for qipao and jewelry, for example, inspired the introduction of clothing and jewelry offerings, as well as period-costume photography experiences.
Jin said that by weaving the stories of historical figures into products and creating distinctive offerings, businesses can add narrative appeal and value while fostering a healthier commercial cycle.
The team has also continued to explore new ways to enrich the visitor experience. In April this year, nearly 100 students from primary schools, middle schools and universities visited the residence, recreating scenes from the 1919 Paris Peace Conference through dramatized performances, where Koo fought to uphold national sovereignty.
During the May Day holiday, interactive performances at the residence drew more than 300 visits in a single day. In June, the protection and utilization of Koo's former residence in the Wudadao modern architectural complex was named one of Tianjin's outstanding cases of cultural heritage building protection and utilization for 2026.
A tourist surnamed Ma from Beijing recalled that during previous visits to the Five Great Avenues, some Western-style buildings could only be viewed from outside.
"This time, I found that quite a few former residences of notable figures are open to visitors. You can also have coffee, dress up in period costumes and take photos. The experience feels much richer," she said.
Leaving Hebei Road and walking along the neighborhood lanes toward Anshan Road, visitors come upon an old building with exposed brick walls and a red-tiled roof. Built in 1915, it is Zhangyuan, or Zhang's Garden.
Today, the century-old building has become a stage in its own right. Guides dress in period costumes and lead visitors from room to room, blending historical narration, character dialogue and live performance.
In 2023, Zhangyuan was selected for the first batch of China's national pilot projects under an "immersive city storytelling" program launched by the national public culture development center at the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. Its immersive show has been staged more than 2,000 times.
"Every Western-style building has its own cultural story. We hope to make Tianjin's Western-style buildings 'speak,'" said Guo Hongbin, who runs the Zhangyuan.
Farther along, on Tai'an Road, stands the former Kailuan Mining Bureau Building. Beyond a broad flight of steps, more than 10 tall columns support an imposing colonnade, while the interior retains the solemn character of classical architecture.
Completed in 1921, the building now welcomes not only visitors but also employees of financial institutions and business clients. Following two years of revitalization, it opened in 2024 as Tianjin's financial exhibition center and financial institution service center.
Rich in historical and cultural resources, Tianjin is home to 16 historical and cultural blocks, 877 historic buildings and more than 1,000 protected buildings of various types. In recent years, the city has drawn up a conservation plan for its historical and cultural heritage, established committees and expert advisory bodies to protect historic buildings, and encouraged social capital to participate in the protection and use of historic buildings and blocks.
According to the Tianjin Housing and Urban-Rural Construction Commission, the city has revitalized more than 100 Western-style buildings in recent years. This year, Tianjin has moved to a "one building, one plan" approach, targeting the revitalization of 21 such buildings.
Tianjin's efforts offer a glimpse of China's broader push to advance urban renewal while strengthening the protection and inheritance of historical and cultural heritage.
China has proposed to broaden historical and cultural heritage protection from single-building repairs to block renewal, and from preserving physical structures to introducing suitable new functions, integrating it ever more deeply into urban development.
"We will continue to tap the potential of historical and cultural resources, explore more approaches to adaptive reuse suited to the architectural features of these buildings, breathe new life into old buildings, and carry the city's cultural legacy forward in contemporary life," said Peng Peng, director of the Culture and Tourism Bureau of Heping District in Tianjin. ■
This photo taken on Aug. 7, 2026 shows an interior view of the renovated former residence of renowned modern Chinese diplomat Wellington Koo in north China's Tianjin Municipality. (Xinhua)
Visitors watch an immersive performance at Zhangyuan, or Zhang's Garden, in north China's Tianjin Municipality on May 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo)

In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and 12 were injured as Russian forces attacked settlements in the region 32 times over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed, and one was injured by Russian attacks, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Regional Defense Council, said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and the surrounding regions, killing one person and injuring 16 others, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region killed one person and injured 11 others, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed one person and injured nine people over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported, according to the reports published on Sept. 14 and Sept. 15.
In southern Odesa Oblast, Russia launched "a mass attack on civilian infrastructure", Governor Oleh Kiper said. He added that residential buildings, logistics facilities, and port and transport infrastructure were targeted. No casualties were reported.

About 20% of industrial egg production lost at start of war – Poultry Union
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:54:21 EEST
18:54:21 KST

Ukraine lost about 20% of its industrial egg production capacity at the start of the full-scale war due to the loss of production facilities in regions where fighting took place or is still taking place, Serhiy Karpenko, executive director of the Ukrainian Poultry Union, told Interfax-Ukraine.
He said industry enterprises continue to lose production and other assets due to shelling and the subsequent occupation of territories, particularly in Chernihiv, Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
At the same time, the industry has managed to restore its production potential through the relocation of some producers, the expansion of existing capacity, and the emergence of new market players.
Karpenko also said the damage to and destruction of warehouse facilities has affected the supply of poultry meat and eggs to retail chains. Before the war, logistics mainly involved delivering products to distribution centers, from which retail chains would then distribute them to stores.
Following the damage to or destruction of warehouse facilities, retail chains have offered to restructure logistics and have products delivered directly from production facilities to supermarkets.
The war has also affected export logistics. A significant share of poultry products was previously exported in containers from Ukraine's Black Sea ports, and exporters are now forced to revert to the 2022 logistics model. Products are transported by road to ports in Romania, Poland and the Baltic states, from where further export shipments are carried out to destination markets.

Yemen: Renewed fighting puts pressure on the health system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:53:46 UTC
18:53:46 KST

Aden — The recent escalation of fighting in Yemen has led to growing numbers of wounded people, adding pressure to a health system already stretched thin, and forcing thousands of families to flee their homes.
Since 10 September, over 60 injured patients from the west coast have been admitted to Al-Gamhouria hospital in Aden. Many of them require urgent operations, blood transfusions, close monitoring, and long periods of care. This has put significant pressure on the hospital’s emergency room, operating theatres, wards, blood bank, medical stock, and staff.
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has expanded our support to the emergency room in response. Our team is helping hospital staff assess the condition of incoming patients quickly, so the most critical are treated first. They are also supplying the emergency room, operating theatres, and wards with emergency medicines and materials. In coordination with health authorities, MSF has also supported hospitals in Hodeidah with medicines and materials to treat people wounded in the fighting. We have also provided trauma kits to Taiz, Al-Bayda and Al-Jawf hospitals.
Needs are likely to grow as the situation develops. Hospitals need the capacity to absorb sudden increases of wounded patients, while continuing the everyday care that people in Yemen depend on. More than 90,000 people have been newly displaced, according to the International Organization for Migration. Families who have been displaced have little access to food, clean water, shelter, sanitation services, and medical care.
This escalation risks pushing Yemen’s health system past the point of recovery. Years of funding cuts have already left health facilities with little capacity to absorb a new wave of conflict. Sustained and flexible funding for Yemen remains essential, so women, children and the communities already bearing the heaviest burden are not left without care.
MSF has supported the orthopaedic department at Al-Gamhouria hospital in Aden since June 2026. The support covers training nurses, infection prevention and control, microbiology laboratory testing, and the safe use of antibiotics, and a plan for responding when large numbers of wounded people arrive at the same time.
This followed our handover of the Aden trauma centre in 2025, which ended 12 years of treating and rehabilitating thousands of people severely injured by the war in Yemen.
Meanwhile, in Mocha, on the west coast, a small MSF team is still supporting the continuity of essential care in the maternity and paediatric units of the General hospital, despite the severe shortage of health professionals remaining in the city. We are working to identify solutions to reinforce the team and secure supplies of essential medicines and anaesthetics, while also seeking assurances that the medical mission will be respected and that we will be able to operate fully in accordance with our principles of action.
As of Sunday, 13 September, 23 patients were still receiving care in this facility, including 10 babies in the neonatal intensive care unit.

WTO says global trade system at critical juncture, urges reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:52:08 UTC
18:52:08 KST

WTO says global trade system at critical juncture, urges reform
- The WTO warns global trade rules need urgent reform to avoid fragmentation, which could lower global GDP by up to 6.9% and exports by nearly 27% by 2050, hitting poorer countries hardest.
- Four key challenges strain the trade system: shifting economic power, rising state intervention, digital trade changes, and increased political tensions among major powers.
- While regional and plurilateral trade deals may help, they risk undermining multilateral cooperation, leading to trade diversion and higher barriers without a strong WTO framework.
AI generated
GENEVA – The World Trade Organization (WTO) on Sept 15 urged its members to reform global trade rules or risk a slide into fragmentation that could significantly reduce economic output and hit poorer countries hardest.
In its annual report, the Geneva-based global trade body said existing rules have struggled to keep pace with shifts in economic power, the rise of industrial policy, digital trade and escalating political tensions between major powers.
The warning comes after the WTO’s 166 members failed to reach agreement on a reform package at a ministerial meeting in Yaounde, Cameroon, in March, before relaunching talks in Geneva on issues including decision-making, dispute settlement and the challenges posed by subsidies and state intervention.
The WTO has struggled to find agreement on reforms among all members in the consensus-based organisation as members are at different stages of economic development and with often conflicting interests.
WTO economists modelled a scenario in which the world fragments into competing geopolitical blocs and found that global GDP would be 5.1 per cent lower and exports 18.6 per cent lower by 2050 than otherwise. In a more severe scenario, in which multilateral cooperation collapses and is replaced by a patchwork of free trade agreements, global GDP would fall 6.9 per cent and exports, nearly 27 per cent.
By contrast, enhanced multilateral cooperation could raise global GDP by 2.9 per cent and boost exports by almost 18 per cent, according to the report. Least-developed countries would stand to gain the most from stronger cooperation, but could also suffer the largest losses from fragmentation.
Trade at a crossroads
WTO chief economist Rob Staiger told Reuters the trading system was at a “critical juncture”, citing four major challenges identified in the report: a broader distribution of economic power, growing state intervention in economies, changes in the nature of trade driven by digitalisation and global value chains, and rising political friction.
“The rules are under strain, and they really are having an impact. And if things fall apart at the global multilateral level, our scenarios are saying these would be the costs, and those costs would be quite large,” Staiger said.
The findings come as countries increasingly pursue regional and sector-specific trade arrangements amid rising trade tensions and sweeping US tariffs.
In March, a group of WTO members agreed to move ahead with the organisation’s first baseline digital trade rules through a plurilateral agreement, bypassing opposition from some members.
Staiger said regional trade agreements and plurilateral initiatives could strengthen the multilateral system, but warned that they could also undermine it if they evolved into competing blocs.
Without a strong WTO framework, such arrangements risk diverting trade towards preferred partners rather than the most efficient producers, and encouraging blocs to raise barriers against outsiders, Staiger said. WTO rules help limit discrimination against non-members and constrain how free trade agreements are structured, he added.
The WTO said trade policy uncertainty had reached unprecedented levels in recent years as governments increasingly deploy tariffs, subsidies, export controls and industrial policies.
Although about 72 per cent of global merchandise trade still takes place under WTO most-favoured-nation tariff terms, down from roughly 80 per cent in 2022, Staiger called the decline a “worrisome trend” that underscored the risk of a gradual erosion of the multilateral trading system. REUTERS

UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:51:56 UTC
18:51:56 KST

UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
GENEVA – The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes, the UN human rights chief said on Sept 15.
Volker Turk said the remains of what appeared to be entire families were being unearthed from sites destroyed during Israeli attacks, adding that many victims were women and children.
“It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed,” he said in a statement.
He said the discoveries revived concerns raised in a 2024 UN report that found Israeli strikes on residential buildings and other civilian sites during the early weeks of the war may have violated international humanitarian law.
The Israeli Prime Minister’s office and Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians and says it acted in accordance with international law while fighting Hamas militants in Gaza.
Israel's assault on Gaza – launched after Hamas’ deadly raid into Israel in October 2023 – has generated around 61 million tonnes of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United Nations.
A US-brokered ceasefire brought an end to full-scale fighting in October 2025, but has failed to halt regular Israeli strikes as both sides accuse each other of violating the truce.
Widespread destruction in Gaza
The Palestinian Civil Defence says more than 630 bodies and human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025.
The Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the wreckage.
Turk said he feared the remains recovered so far could be “only the tip of the iceberg”, noting that large parts of Gaza had been flattened by Israeli bombing or later demolition and clearance operations.
He also accused Israel of continuing to level some areas of Gaza where its forces remain deployed, saying bulldozers were operating “with no respect for the dead under the rubble”.
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s military campaign, according to Gaza health authorities.
Israel says it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian casualties and that Hamas uses Gaza’s civilians as human shields in densely populated areas, an accusation Hamas denies.
The UN rights chief called for international investigators to be granted access to all parts of Gaza to help preserve evidence, citing ongoing legal proceedings examining conduct during the war.
Israel has blocked the entry of heavy machinery needed to remove rubble, according to Turk's statement.
Francesca Albanese, the UN expert on the Palestinian territories, has said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified before full clearance starts.
In September, the Palestinian Civil Defence said 96 bodies and human remains had been recovered from a single site in the Zeitoun area of Gaza City, including 58 children and 23 women. REUTERS

Drone-hit Saudi oil pipeline to remain non-operational for weeks – AP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Drone-hit Saudi oil pipeline to remain non-operational for weeks – AP
A key Saudi Arabian oil pipeline hit in a drone strike by Iraqi militias will take up to five weeks to repair, AP has reported, citing informed officials.
The East-West Pipeline, which runs 1,200 km across the country towards the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, will remain mostly out of service during the three- to five-week repair period, the agency said in an article on Tuesday.
One official suggested that parts of the infrastructure could function while segments of the pipeline and a major pumping station are being fixed, but couldn’t say how much oil might get through, according to AP.
Oil prices spiked by more than 3% on Monday, with benchmark Brent crude reaching $109 per barrel, following the decision by the Saudi authorities to shut down the pipeline after it was struck by drones in the Riyadh and Medina areas on Thursday.
The Gulf kingdom blamed Iranian-backed militias in Iraq for the attack, with the government in Baghdad confirming that the UAVs came from Iraqi territory and condemning the aggression.
According to some reports, Iraqi fighters targeted the pipeline in solidarity with Yemen’s Houthis, officially known as the Ansarallah movement, who made major gains along Yemeni Red Sea coast last week, pushing back Saudi-supported forces and seizing the ports of Mocha and Dhubab as well as key islands at the entrance to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping chokepoint.
Saudi Arabia, which is the world’s largest supplier of oil, shifted its exports from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut due to the conflict between the US and Iran.
The Houthis further tightened their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on Monday, capturing the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish without a fight, AP reported, citing officials from the group and Saudi-backed forces.
The Yemeni group said on the same day that it had fired dozens of missiles and drones at the King Khalid Air Base in the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
The attack “was accurate and caused heavy damage” to aircraft hangars, radars, landing strips, and ammunition depots at the facility, Houthi military spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree said.
The strike was “a response to the escalation of tension by the Saudi regime and the implementation of more than 300 airstrikes in the past five days,” Saree stressed.
Saudi military spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki said 13 civilians were wounded during the Houthi raid on Khamis Mushait, but didn’t confirm the attack on the airbase.
Riyadh has asked Britain for military support in stemming the Houthi advance in Yemen and repelling strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure, Bloomberg reported on Monday.
Last week, US President Donald Trump reportedly declined several requests by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to order airstrikes against the Houthis.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has so far only agreed to send military advisers to Saudi Arabia, the agency said. Burnham is hesitant to provide further assistance due to concerns of it being viewed as him backing Trump’s war on Iran, which is deeply unpopular in Britain, Bloomberg said.

Civil aviation as a tool for power projection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:50:29 UTC
18:50:29 KST

The attempted drone attack on Aug. 5 at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport showed once again how crucial the role of the aviation industry is for geopolitical interests. Besides being one of the largest cargo hubs in Europe, the airport hosts NATO's Strategic Airlift Interim Solution (SALIS), the air logistics arm of the alliance. Together with Rzeszow Airport in Poland, it is one of the most crucial nodes through which military supply to Eastern Europe is delivered.
The Leipzig attack attempt
The drone incident targeting a parked AN-124 belonging to Ukraine's Antonov Airlines marks a turning point for Germany. What matters is less the attempt itself than the fact that Western aid was physically targeted on German soil for the first time. The timing falls in a very polarized phase of the country: election campaigns are running in three eastern states, once part of the Soviet occupation zone, which is also where the attack attempt took place. This triggered the debate over aid to Ukraine and over Germany's policy towards Russia. As Russian influence remains considerable in the so-called new states even after reunification, the incident deepened the polarization in the country further.
On Sept. 1, the German government attributed the incident openly to Russia for the first time. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt based this assessment on the fact that the means used in the attack were already known from other hybrid operations carried out by Russia. Berlin then ordered the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. A note of protest was handed to the Russian ambassador, and Germany announced that it would push for additional steps at EU level. With this step, Germany acted on its own outside EU institutions for the first time since Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022.
Russia has been linked to similar infrastructure sabotage before, and Western intelligence services regard these cases as part of a hybrid war. The aim is to make Germany more hesitant in its support for Ukraine and, at the same time, to create anxiety in society and to polarize the public over a critical defense question. If this support decreases, Russia will find itself in a stronger position on the battlefield, as Ukraine's defense capability depends to a large extent on these deliveries.
An old pattern
Civil aviation has been used for state interests for many years. State-owned carriers have treated diplomatic traffic and commercial considerations as parallel priorities, and the same applies to state-linked cargo and charter companies. One of the best-known examples of this is Air America. It was an airline established by the United States to carry weapons and supplies directly into the armed conflicts in Southeast Asia within the framework of covert operations. Whether the same aircraft were also used in the opium trade is still debated to this day.
Another example is St. Lucia Airways, on paper a Caribbean airline, which carried weapons to Angola and later missiles to Iran on behalf of the CIA. The revenue from these sales was transferred to the Contras in Nicaragua.
Belonging to the same line are the "Black Flights" that supported the Bosnian Muslims, backed by Iran and the US. Without them, the genocidal campaign of war criminal Ratko Mladic, who passed away last month, could have taken a different course.
A more recent example is the use of Russian-built Ilyushin aircraft by the United Arab Emirates to deliver weapons to the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan. These shipments, carried out through Chad, paved the way for last year’s massacres in El Fasher. A similar structure was seen in Libya as well, where the UAE backed Khalifa Haftar. Such airlifts, moving in the grey zone under a civilian appearance, shape crises to a large extent and determine which side remains standing.
A sector under pressure
The aviation sector has been under pressure for a long time. The Strait of Hormuz crisis, which flared up in Iran on Feb. 28, has affected airlines heavily on the cost side through fuel supply constraints. The closure of Middle Eastern airspace in the same period and the longer routes that followed have driven the crisis further.
In the northern hemisphere, the closure of Russian airspace to the countries that sanctioned Russia creates a serious competitive disadvantage with respect to other carriers. As a result, airlines based in the EU and the US are falling behind, while Turkish and Gulf carriers, together with Southeast Asian companies, are moving ahead.
A further case in point is Israeli state carrier El Al. Its aircraft, equipped with air defense systems and flown by former air force pilots, give the airline room to operate during conflicts. While most airlines suspended their flights in the region during Iranian attacks, El Al continued in line with national interests. The company moved its fleet to the Greek Cypriot Administration during the conflict with Iran in order to protect it. At the same time, the Israeli state fleet was stationed in Athens until the attacks ended, which also marks a remarkable diplomatic move in terms of the relations between these countries.
Strategic use of civil aviation
In such periods, state carriers therefore carry two functions at once. The sector is both an asset that has to be protected and an instrument that secures the state's freedom of action. The Chicago Convention, which applies to civil aircraft, regulates this field. State aircraft in military, customs and police service are left outside its scope. Aircraft of this kind have to obtain separate permission from each country for every transit. What is decisive, however, is not the aircraft itself or the cargo it carries, but the definition, that is, the purpose of use. And this definition is made by the operating state that owns the aircraft. It is this legal gap in Article 3 that makes operations such as the Air America and Ilyushin flights possible.
Aviation can also become a source of leverage for states, through the ability to influence or cut access. Island states in the Pacific and the Caribbean, for instance, depend on a limited number of air links for their vital supplies. The side that provides or subsidizes these routes gains political influence over those states at low cost. Aviation therefore offers third countries considerable opportunities, both in terms of supply capability and in terms of global political influence over island states.
Takeaways from Leipzig
With the increased security measures after Sept. 11, 2001, hijacking incidents, once a widespread method of political action, have disappeared. Their place has been taken by provocative models such as Leipzig. Even when these targets are located in countries that are not a party to the conflict, such facilities start to become targets, and the risk for those countries of being drawn into the conflict rises considerably.
Understanding this dynamic allows a state to use air capacity to its own benefit, or in the opposite direction, by targeting it in a rival. Due to the current airspace restrictions and fuel costs, Europe's maneuvering room has become considerably tighter. An example of how to deal with such threats independently can be observed in Türkiye, which is in a more advantageous position here.
Türkiye in an advantageous position
With Istanbul Airport, Türkiye has one of the highest-capacity hubs in Europe. Turkish Airlines has recently extended its network to Australia and, after the Air Europa acquisition, also to South America. The fact that the operational hub, the fleet, and the reach are under state backing allows Türkiye to pursue its own interests without depending on foreign capacity and foreign permissions, and makes it a supportive partner for its allies.
The side that holds civil aviation capacity can turn geopolitical tensions to its own advantage. The other side attacks precisely that capacity, as in Leipzig.
In conclusion, historically and today alike, civil aviation determines far more than its place in the tourism and transport sector suggests. The attack at Leipzig-Halle Airport once again highlights this fact, underscoring the strategic importance of civil aviation in terms of security and geopolitical competition.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China Airlines General Manager Chen Han-ming (陳漢銘) said Tuesday that two Boeing 787-9 aircraft would be delivered by the end of this year, followed by 12 more next year.

Chen also said the conflict in the Middle East had benefited China Airlines’ transit passenger traffic, as more travelers chose to transfer in Taiwan en route to North America for safety reasons.
Passenger performance in July and August was strong, while monthly cargo revenue remained between NT$7 billion (US$219.55 million) and NT$8 billion, Chen said. He added that he was cautiously optimistic about the company’s fourth-quarter performance.

Twenty-five years on, Dubai's media bet has become a global platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:48:54 UTC
18:48:54 KST

This year’s Arab Media Summit in Dubai, now in its 25th year, is more than just an event organised by the city, says Mona Ghane l Marri in an OpEd for Euronews. It has evolved into a shared platform for an industry that has become more diverse, more global and more interconnected.
Twenty-five years ago, Dubai made a deliberate bet. It set aside land, built a regulatory framework, and invited the world's media to make the city their regional home. At the time, it was a statement of confidence in the role an open and connected media environment could play in the development of a young economy.
Dubai is home to 25,000 private media companies
A quarter of a century later, the results are measurable. The media sector's contribution to Dubai's GDP rose to 1.42% in 2025, while annual foreign direct investment into the sector grew to US$1.62 billion in 2024, and media exports reached US$25 million in 2025. Dubai is now home to 25,000 private media companies employing 120,000 people, including media professionals and creatives drawn from one of the most international talent pools in the region. What began as an invitation has become an industry.
The Arab Media Summit is where that ambition becomes a conversation. From tomorrow and until 17 September, Dubai hosts the largest media gathering in the region, and this year its largest edition to date. What was once a single conference is now a platform of specialised forums spanning the full spectrum of modern media: an Arab Media Forum, a Government Communication Forum, a youth forum, a Films Forum, a Games Forum, Dubai PodFest and a summit for social media creators and influencers, alongside international forums convened with global partners. The Arab Media Award, meanwhile, reaches its 25th edition.
A deeper shift in the global balance of media
That range is deliberate. Media is no longer a single industry. It stretches from newsrooms and television studios to gaming, podcasting, digital platforms and individual creators whose audiences now rival those of established broadcasters. Having conversations running among these components of the industry is necessary.
It also reflects a deeper shift in the global balance of media. For much of the modern era, influence was concentrated in a small number of long established capitals. That is changing quickly. Broadcasters and digital platforms from the Arabian Gulf, Turkey, Central and Southeast Asia and Africa are now reaching international audiences directly. They are producing in their own languages, setting their own editorial agenda, and investing at scale in production, digital distribution and AI driven newsrooms.
This should not be read as a contest between one media capital and another. It is an expansion of the global conversation. The more societies are able to tell their own stories, explain their own priorities and offer their own perspectives, the richer our collective understanding of the world becomes.
International partnerships matter
That is precisely why international partnerships matter. On 16 September, Dubai will host the Euronews Forum as part of the Arab Media Summit, the first time the Forum has been held outside Europe. Its sessions will examine how regional media organisations are building global audiences, how governments and media engage in a transformed information environment, and how verification and artificial intelligence are reshaping the newsroom.
Europe and the Arab world are close neighbours. Our economic and cultural ties continue to deepen, and our audiences increasingly consume the same stories on the same platforms. Our newsrooms should reflect that reality.
Bringing European and Arab media professionals into the same room is not simply about dialogue. It leads to coproductions, new commercial partnerships, shared professional standards, and relationships that endure long after the Summit closes.
Twenty-Five years ago, Dubai opened its doors to the world's media. Today the relationship has matured. Dubai is no longer only a place from which international media covers the region. It is increasingly a place where the future of media itself is debated, built and tested.
Tomorrow, we will welcome that regional, and global, media community to Dubai. And, after almost twenty-five years, the Arab Media Summit has become more than a gathering hosted by the city. It has become a platform shared by an industry that is more diverse, more global and more interconnected.
The Arab Media Summit 2026, which takes place from 15 to 17 September at the Dubai World Trade Centre, features eight specialist forums and is expected to attract 10,000 attendees. Euronews is a partner of the Arab Media Summit.

Suspected sabotage sparks Dutch rail disruption

New Generation Intercity Train of the Dutch Railways at Rotterdam Central Station
Rail travel in large parts of the Netherlands ground to a standstill on Sept. 15, after what authorities suspect were coordinated acts of sabotage with tubes attached to train tracks in multiple locations.
Transport by train in most of the central and eastern part of the country was virtually impossible after authorities discovered items placed on the tracks.
"Materials were found at multiple locations on the track that were deliberately placed there," said rail operator ProRail in a statement.
"This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved," added the operator.
ProRail said its computer systems interpret an item on the track as meaning that section is occupied, even though there is no train.
The system then turns all lights in that section red, meaning no trains can pass.
One train did hit one of the tubes but there were no injuries, said ProRail spokeswoman Joke van der Cruysen.
"Who is responsible for this and what the motive is is not yet known," said ProRail, adding that a police investigation was underway.
It is not clear when traffic will resume.
There has been a knock-on impact on road travel, as level crossings are also malfunctioning due to the sabotage.

Russian drones killed a man and injured eight in Kyiv, hitting two gas stations
Unknown

2026-09-15
09:46:01 UTC
18:46:01 KST

Russian drones killed one man and injured eight people in Kyiv on the morning of 15 September, hitting two gas stations along with warehouses, a restaurant, and an office building, the National Police reported. The strikes came in a night-long wave of 200 drones that also hit Odesa Oblast in southern Ukraine.
What Russia hit in Kyiv
The first drone came down at a gas station in the Darnytskyi district shortly after 06:00, and more drones hit warehouses in the Obolonskyi district around the same time, the Kyiv Military Administration said. The strike critically wounded a man who was standing near the Darnytskyi station.
The attack resumed after 08:00. A drone struck a non-residential building in the Solomianskyi district, then a second gas station in the Holosiivskyi district, where heavy smoke rose over the site. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko reported the number of injured climbing through the morning, from two to four to eight, with two of them in serious condition. Emergency services put six of the eight in the Solomianskyi district, which took a second hit around 10:00.
The man hurt at the Darnytskyi station died in hospital at about 10:35. Beyond the two stations, police recorded damage to warehouses, a fast-food restaurant, and a business center.
The wave that carried them
Russia launched 200 strike drones from 18:00 on 14 September, the Air Force said: Shahed types including jet-powered ones, Gerberas, and Parodiya decoys, flown from Russia and occupied areas. Air defense downed or suppressed 187 of them by 08:00, with hits recorded at seven locations and debris falling at three more. The attack was still running when that count was published.
Russian forces hit Odesa Oblast at the same time. Russian forces struck residential buildings, logistics sites, and port and transport infrastructure, oblast head Oleh Kiper said, damaging roofs, facades, and windows of private houses along with dozens of garages and cars.
The same night, NATO fighters shot down a drone over Lithuania that had crossed from Belarus, and Ukrainian forces struck the Syzran refinery in Samara Oblast and a warehouse in Taganrog.
Why gas stations
Kyiv's filling stations have been under systematic attack since 10 September, when a drone came down at a station near a shopping mall. On 11 September, jet drones hit two Ukrnafta complexes on opposite banks of the city and returned to strike one of them a second time.
Unlike filling stations in the border oblasts, which Russia hits with cheap short-range drones, the Kyiv stations are being struck with its most expensive ones. Ukrainian stations are mostly struck with the Geran-4 Seeker, the variant fitted with machine-vision targeting, according military observer Oleksandr Kovalenko of Information Resistance.
More than 300 gas stations have been attacked across Ukraine since the current wave began, according to energy ministry data. The strikes have moved gradually from front-line oblasts deeper into the country, and about 80% of damaged stations return to work.

‘No child should be deprived of dignity’: Delhi HC allows 15-year-old rape survivor to terminate pregnancy

Delhi HC allows termination of pregnancy of rape survivor
NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has held that compelling a rape survivor to continue with a pregnancy resulting from sexual assault and forcing motherhood upon her against her will would seriously impair her right to live with dignity.The court made the observation while allowing a plea filed on behalf of a 15-year-old rape survivor seeking termination of her pregnancy, which had crossed 30 weeks of gestation, news agency PTI reported.Justice Madhu Jain said the fact that the pregnancy had crossed the statutory limit under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act could not, by itself, be considered in isolation in cases arising from sexual assault.'15-year-old cannot be reduced to description of mother'Justice Jain said courts exercising jurisdiction under Articles 226 or 32 of the Constitution must give due primacy to the best interests and welfare of the minor, while also taking into account the statutory framework under the MTP Act.
The court described the case as "unfortunate and distressing", noting that the girl was only 15, had already suffered the trauma of an alleged heinous sexual assault and had lost both her parents.
"A child of 15 years cannot, in the eyes of this court, be reduced to the description of a 'mother' merely because she has been forced into pregnancy as a consequence of sexual violence," it said.The court said that while the law could provide remedies and procedures, no judicial order could undo the trauma the child had endured.Allowing the plea, the court directed the medical superintendent of Lady Hardinge Medical College and S K Hospital to arrange for termination of the pregnancy at the earliest and maintain a record of the procedure.The doctors were also directed to preserve the tissue or foetal material for DNA identification and other purposes in connection with the criminal case registered over the rape.

ICC trial of 'Angel of Death' Libya prison boss to start 4 May: court
A notorious Libyan prison boss dubbed the "Angel of Death" will stand trial on charges of murder, rape and torture from 4 May, the court said on Monday.
Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri, 48, faces 17 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed between 2014 and 2020 at the Mitiga prison near Tripoli.
Presiding judge Althea Violet Alexis-Windsor set the date for the trial, which will be the first to stem from a United Nations-mandated investigation into alleged crimes in Libya, which began in 2011.
Alexis-Windsor said she wanted the trial to be conducted "fairly and expeditiously... without undue delay".
She also noted that at least six years had passed since the alleged crimes and also the victims' desire to see the trial start as soon as possible.
The prosecution and the defence had jointly called for the trial to start on June 8.
At a previous ICC session in May, deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said El-Hishri "was widely known as a notorious torturer at the helm of Mitiga prison".
Khan quoted one witness as saying El-Hishri was "amongst the worst instigators of violence" and another saying he was nicknamed "the Angel of Death".
"One of his preferred torture methods, as described by witnesses, was to shoot people, especially in the leg and knee," alleged Khan.
"He would also hang people with their hands bound behind their backs and beat people with a shovel."
The suspect personally raped, murdered and tortured prisoners as an "example" to other guards, alleged the prosecutor.
At the May hearing, El-Hishri's defence lawyer said his client denied the charges and lodged an unsuccessful challenge to the ICC's jurisdiction.
Libya is still grappling with the aftermath of the armed conflict and political chaos which followed the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled long-time dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The oil-rich country remains divided between a UN-recognised government in the west and its eastern rival, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
The ICC tries individuals for the world's worst crimes, including war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The court is also seeking Osama Almasri Najim, head of Libya's judicial police, on charges also relating to alleged crimes at the Mitiga prison.
Najim was arrested in Italy but released and returned to Libya, sparking a major political row in Italy and consternation at the ICC.

Britain flies new turbojet drone engine in seven months
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:43:20 BST
18:43:20 KST

Britain has developed a new family of domestically produced turbojet engines, with one design taken from the drawing board to the air in less than seven months and a smaller engine already entering serial production, the Government has announced.
The programme is being run by the Ministry of Defence’s Strategic Capabilities Office with UK start-up Alloyed, combining government investment with matched funding from the company to establish a sovereign British propulsion capability for future weapons and aircraft.
The family spans engines producing between 30N and 2,000N of thrust, covering potential applications ranging from relatively small uncrewed aircraft to larger systems.
Two engines have already moved beyond the initial development stage. A 300N-class engine has completed flight testing and is now in serial production in the UK, while a larger 1,100N-class design progressed from its initial concept to flight-ready status in less than seven months.
The Government said the work had established the ability to design, manufacture, test and support this class of engine domestically, reducing reliance on overseas propulsion supply chains.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said: “Taking a jet engine from concept to flight-ready in just a matter of months shows how defence and industry can work together to deliver capabilities at the speed required by today’s world.”
He added: “The threats we face demand the ability to produce cutting-edge technology on demand and at scale – this programme delivers that, combining sovereign manufacturing, digital engineering and industrial innovation to ensure our Armed Forces retain an operational advantage, while delivering good jobs for working people here in the UK.”
Digital design and production
The engines have been developed using a digitally led engineering and manufacturing process intended to reduce the time between design, testing and production.
Alongside the engines themselves, the programme has established a UK-based digital design and modelling capability which the Government says can be used to develop new propulsion systems and variants in months rather than years.
The approach combines digital engineering with modular design, allowing elements of an engine to be changed or improved without requiring a complete redesign of the propulsion system.
Alloyed chief executive Michael Holmes said: “Working alongside the Ministry of Defence has enabled Alloyed to bring to bear its world-leading metals technologies to mature and demonstrate advanced propulsion systems at remarkable pace while building a lasting capability in the UK.”
He added: “This programme shows the power of combining defence expertise, digital engineering and industrial innovation.”
The 30N to 2,000N thrust range would allow the underlying technology to be applied across systems of markedly different sizes, while the modular architecture is intended to make later adaptations easier as operational requirements change.
Production expanding in Britain
More than 60 engineering and advanced manufacturing jobs have already been created through the programme, according to the Government, with a further 45 positions expected during the next 12 months as production increases.
The work also involves more than 40 suppliers across the UK, most of them small and medium-sized businesses.
The co-development model differs from a conventional procurement in which Defence specifies a finished system and then purchases it from industry. Instead, the Strategic Capabilities Office and Alloyed have jointly funded and developed the technology, with the aim of shortening development cycles and retaining the resulting industrial capability in Britain.
The Government said the programme supports commitments in the Strategic Defence Review to strengthen the domestic defence industrial base and increase the speed at which new technology can be developed and fielded.
There is also an export ambition, as Ministers said the propulsion technology could eventually be offered to allies seeking domestically supportable or resilient engine solutions, although no export customers or specific overseas programmes have yet been announced.
For now, the most concrete result is the move into production of the 300N-class engine and the rapid development of the larger 1,100N design, giving Britain a new domestically based turbojet development and manufacturing capability spanning a much wider family of future systems.

UN says Ebola epidemic still huge and growing
Unknown

UN sees some progress in DR Congo’s Ebola fight, but too early to call peak
- UN officials see some progress in fighting Ebola in eastern DR Congo but say the epidemic remains massive and will take months to control.
- The country's Health Minister reports a drop in daily new cases from 120 to 80, calling this a positive sign but warns to stay vigilant.
- Ebola cases are rising fast in North Kivu, especially Butembo, with security challenges making control efforts difficult, while some areas like Ituri show improvement.
AI generated
GENEVA – United Nations officials said on Sept 15 that efforts to curb Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo were beginning to show results but stressed that the epidemic remained “massive” and would take months to bring under control.
“It remains a deadly and a massive epidemic. There are some areas of progress, but nonetheless, in other areas, we continue to see growth in cases,” Julien Harneis, the UN special Ebola coordinator, told a Geneva press briefing.
The outbreak is the second most lethal on record, behind one in West Africa that lasted from 2014 to 2016.
Asked about reports that the epidemic had reached a turning point, the World Health Organization’s Olivier le Polain said: “It’s too early to confidently say we have passed a peak.”
He said: “It will take many, many months to get this outbreak under control fully, and it will require significant support.”
DR Congo minister points to ‘positive sign’
On Sept 12, DR Congo Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said there were “encouraging signs” in the fight against Ebola since “the peak reached in mid-August”, and that transmission “has been gradually slowing down”.
He said daily new cases had dropped from about 120 “at the peak of the epidemic” to around 80, and that 10 of the 62 affected health zones had recorded no new cases for more than 22 days.
“To me, these figures are a positive sign. They demonstrate that the efforts deployed on the ground are yielding results and that our response strategy is beginning to bend the transmission curve,” he said.
“However, we must remain fully mobilised. While these results are encouraging, they must not lead us to lower our guard.”
Speaking on Sept 15 in Ituri province, where the first cases were recorded, Jean-Jacques Muyembe, director of DR Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research, said the situation there had improved considerably.
“Here in Ituri, the indicators are turning green, whereas they were previously all red. We are not saying that we have ended the epidemic, but we are saying that the response teams... have the situation under control,” he said, adding that he hoped the epidemic would be “behind us” by the end of 2026.
There have been 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths in seven provinces, according to government figures published on Sept 15.
Situation remains ‘alarming’ in North Kivu
UN officials on Sept 15 said they were seeing progress in parts of Ituri, which remains the most affected province, and that in some areas the outbreak is now “under control”. But they said cases are still rising fast in North Kivu, particularly in the city of Butembo.
“It’s such a vast epidemic that it’s difficult to talk about one epidemic, but there’s rather many different locations,” Harneis said.
“We know from past experience that an epidemic can show early signs of improvement and then pick up again quite quickly,” le Polain, the head of epidemiology and analytics for response at the WHO Health Emergencies Programme, said.
Aid workers say more needs to be done to curb transmission in North Kivu.
"The situation in North Kivu, with its very complex security situation, high population density and mobility, is alarming," said Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to DR Congo with Medecins Sans Frontieres.
North Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 1,269 confirmed cases, including 555 reported in the last 21 days, as at Sept 12. REUTERS

Russian Wildberries Orders 478,000 m² of Mesh Netting to Protect Warehouses From Ukrainian Drones

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Wildberries Orders 478,000 m² of Mesh Netting to Protect Warehouses From Ukrainian Drones
Major Russian online marketplace Wildberries is rushing to secure its logistics infrastructure following sustained aerial strikes, launching a tender for 478,000 square meters of galvanized metal wire mesh across eight regions in Russia, The Bell reports on September 14.
By August 17, damage to the company’s facilities reached approximately 2.4 million square meters, which represents nearly 43% of its total storage space.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Bell, the procurement terms published in early August specify that the wire diameter must not exceed 2.5 mm, with delivery required within seven days. While public tender documentation omits the purpose of the order, an industrial source confirmed that the materials are intended for protection against unmanned aerial vehicles.
The procurement effort comes after targeted long-range strikes began on July 18. Over the following month, at least 22 facilities were hit across multiple regions, including Leningrad, Ryazan, Samara, Penza, Tula, Vladimir, and Tver regions, as well as Yekaterinburg.
One of the largest incidents occurred in Samara region in early August, where a fire destroyed a warehouse measuring approximately 160,000 square meters.
Perimeter metal netting set several meters away from structures is increasingly used across Russia to intercept incoming aerial impacts.
Manufacturers describe these modular steel lattice towers as reaching heights of up to 100 meters, capable of absorbing impacts from units weighing up to 400 kg at speeds of up to 200 km/h.
Similar protective structures are now deployed around oil storage sites, thermal power plants, and electrical substations.
The current Wildberries tender remains under evaluation, with bids submitted for three of the eight available lots. Offered prices range from 154 to 474 rubles ($1.80 to $5.60) per square meter, placing the potential total cost between 73.6 million and 226.5 million rubles ($871,000 to $2.68 million).
The company has also opened a separate tender for silica fabric across 14 sites to act as a fire barrier against operational disruption.
Ukrainian drone attacks on Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, have destroyed around one-third of the company’s total warehouse capacity.
The retailer generates roughly 6 trillion rubles ($74 billion) in annual sales through nearly 100,000 pickup locations.

Ilayda Cakirtekin
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
European Union member states extended talks on Russia sanctions for a week as countries failed to reach a consensus on delisting Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov, EUobserver reported Monday.
EU ambassadors agreed in Brussels on Monday to extend the bloc’s Russia sanctions list, which includes Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov, for just one week, pending another meeting on Sept. 22.
The move reportedly marks an unprecedented step since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022.
The bloc’s existing Russia blacklist, comprising roughly 3,000 individuals and entities, requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU countries for renewal every six months.
The list was due to expire at midnight Tuesday, while Slovakia, followed by France, expressed support for delisting Usmanov. The other 25 EU member states, however, did not support the move.
“It means we agree to disagree, for one week,” said an EU diplomat.
A French diplomatic source, meanwhile, cited "national security" grounds.
“We [France] have a specific national security issue and wish to respond positively to our international partners, who are approaching us regarding Mr. Usmanov," the source told EUobserver on Monday.
The EU imposed a visa ban and asset freeze on Uzbek-born metals tycoon Alisher Usmanov in 2022, citing his “particularly close ties” to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Targets hit
- As a result of strikes in the Velikaya Balka settlement in the Odessa Region, a logistics center for the storage and distribution of military cargo arriving in Ukraine from abroad was struck, the ministry reported.

- No details were provided regarding the type or purpose of the facility.
- Power outages have been reported in two regions of Ukraine due to infrastructure damage, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy’s Telegram channel.
- According to the ministry, some residents of the Volyn and Kharkov Regions are without electricity.

Russian convoy resupplies Syria coastal facilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:38:28 UTC
18:38:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Russian convoy resupplies Syria coastal facilities for first time since Moscow-Damascus deal
A convoy of Russian naval and cargo vessels delivered supplies last week to Syria's coastal facilities long used by Moscow’s military, two sources familiar with the operation said, in the first such mission since Damascus and Moscow agreed last month on the future of Russia’s military presence in the country.
The operation offers an early indication that Moscow is continuing to resupply facilities at Tartous port and the Hmeimim airbase under the new deal, which provides for civilian facilities used by Russia to be transferred to Syrian control and military sites to be turned into joint training centres.
Russian forces are to remain at the bases under the agreement. Russia has used Hmeimim and Tartous to project power across the Mediterranean, Middle East and Africa. Tartous provides Moscow with its only naval repair and replenishment facility in the Mediterranean.
Moscow has supplied both sites in recent months but last week's was the first since the 9 August agreement was announced.
The four-vessel convoy arrived at the Mediterranean port of Tartous on 7 September, according to movements tracked by Reuters and maritime intelligence firm SynMax.
Satellite imagery verified by Reuters showed the Russian Ro-Ro cargo ship Sparta and navy replenishment oiler Akademik Pashin docked on September 8 in Tartous at piers 3 and 4, respectively.
A Reuters reporter saw the two vessels docked there on September 9, while Russian tanker General Skobelev remained offshore. A surveillance balloon was seen flying over the port during the unloading operation.
A Syrian military source and a Russian-Syrian businessman familiar with the operation said Sparta unloaded supplies including ammunition destined for Hmeimim and Tartous. Reuters could not independently confirm the contents of the shipment or their intended recipients.
SynMax identified the fourth vessel in the convoy as Admiral Levchenko, a Russian Udaloy-class destroyer.
Syria’s General Authority of Ports and Customs and Russia's embassy in Damascus did not respond to requests for comment.
The vessels stopped transmitting their signal shortly after crossing Strait of Gibraltar towards the Mediterranean. Reuters tracked the group via satellite imagery as it continued east and ultimately reached the Syrian coast.
Sparta has long been used in Russian military logistics in Syria and is under US sanctions. General Skobelev is also under Western sanctions over transporting Russian oil.
Damascus and Moscow reached the agreement over Hmeimim and Tartous after 18 months of negotiations following the December 2024 overthrow of former President Bashar al-Assad, a close Russian ally, who is now reportedly living in the Russian capital.

Ukraine launches offensive push in north of Donetsk region, senior commander says
KYIV, Sept 15 - Ukrainian forces have launched an offensive operation in the north of the eastern Donetsk region, the focal point of intense battles during more than four years of the war, a senior military commander said on Tuesday.
The third army corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 sq km, said Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi, who has commanded Ukraine's defence in the vicinity since last month.
Biletskyi said that the area was in the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called "fortress belt" of cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the capture of which would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire region.
"The third army corps has started offensive operation at this direction. The operation is called 'Vivaldi'," Biletskyi said in a video uploaded on the Telegram app.
Biletskyi said that his troops disrupted Russian military logistics, cleared three villages and an area around a fourth. A village called Serednie was fully under Ukrainian control.
The Donetsk region has seen most of the fiercest battles of the war. Russia wants to control all of it, Moscow's main territorial demand at negotiations that have so far stalled but which the U.S. wants to restart, with envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visiting Moscow and Kyiv this month.
Russia's total advances had slowed this year but its forces have been bearing down on the cities from the south and infiltrating deeper into the eastern city of Kostiantynivka.
Reuters was not able to verify Biletskyi's assertions. Independently determining lines of territorial control in Ukraine is difficult because of drone warfare that has created a wide no-man's land "kill zone" along the front.
The reported gains in the Donetsk region would add to Ukraine's push earlier this year in the southeast, where Kyiv said it clawed back more than 700 sq km of territory during a months-long counterattack. REUTERS

China urges US to stop expanding its military buildup in outer space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:36:25 UTC
18:36:25 KST

China on Tuesday urged the US to stop expanding its military buildup in outer space after Washington publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has deployed operational weapons in Earth's orbit.
"China has long been committed to the peaceful use of outer space and safeguarding the security in space. We oppose any arms race in outer space or any attempts to weaponise it or turn it into a war zone," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
"We urge the US to stop expanding military buildup in outer space and safeguard global strategic stability with concrete actions," Guo said.
His remarks came after US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said on Monday that the Space Force has operational weapons in orbit capable of responding to threats from adversaries.
"We continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist," Meink said at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference.
"This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action," he added.
Meink, whose department oversees both the US Air Force and Space Force, declined to disclose when the weapons became operational, their capabilities or whether they rely on kinetic impactors, directed energy, electronic warfare or cyber capabilities.
He later told reporters that the public acknowledgement was deliberate and that the terminology had been "very well thought out" to reinforce military deterrence.
"Talking about the details of what we're doing would actually not benefit that deterrence," Meink said.
"We're not going to talk about the specifics of what we're doing, whether we've tested, not tested, or anything else. I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the US can operate freely there."
"It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space," he added.
"So, we've had to take steps to make sure that when we're threatened, we can take care of that."
‘Weaponising’ the space
The disclosure comes amid growing military competition in space involving the US, China and Russia, all of which have developed counter-space capabilities.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not explicitly ban conventional weapons in space.
Security experts have warned that publicly confirming the deployment of orbital weapons could encourage rival powers to expand their own capabilities, accelerating an arms race in a domain increasingly vital to communications, navigation, intelligence gathering and military operations.

Intel Reveals 19 Russian Missile, Drone Firms Still Outside International Sanctions

2026-09-15
09:35:06 UTC
18:35:06 KST

Nineteen Russian companies involved in producing components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft remain untouched by sanctions from any country in the international sanctions coalition, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said on Monday.
The companies are among 54 enterprises belonging to or managed by KRET, Russia’s largest radio-electronics holding, and part of the state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec, according to data published by HUR, on its War&Sanctions portal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The agency said the KRET companies develop and manufacture electronic warfare systems, friend-or-foe identification technology, and onboard electronics for Russian fighter jets and helicopters. Their products also include electric motors, drone navigation and control systems, counterdrone equipment, and remotely operated machine-gun platforms.
The intelligence agency identified several KRET enterprises that it said contribute directly to Russia’s ballistic and hypersonic missile programs.
The Stavropol Signal Plant produces compact S200A1 jamming stations for Russia’s 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles. HUR said the Kaluga Scientific Research Radio Engineering Institute supplies components for the 3B228 electronic protection system used in Russia’s 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles.
KRET’s parent organization also covers funding shortages under Russian state defense contracts carried out by companies within the holding, the agency said.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Refinery, Aircraft Plant and Ozon Facility in Massive Overnight Attack
Ukraine has repeatedly called on its partners to impose sanctions not only on major Russian weapons manufacturers, but also on the network of factories producing navigation equipment, electronics, and other specialized components used in Russian weapons.
Among the 19 companies that HUR said remain unsanctioned is Inertial Technologies of Technocomplex, which produces inertial navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion drones.
Another company, the Tambov Elektropribor plant, supplies gyroscopes used in 9M727 cruise missiles launched by the Iskander system, according to the agency.
The Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association manufactures aircraft automation components, radio navigation equipment, and electric motors for drones, HUR said.
KRET is the 10th Rostec holding whose corporate network Ukraine has published through the War&Sanctions database. The portal now contains information on 764 Rostec-linked enterprises, including identifying details, their functions within Russia’s defense-industrial structure, corporate relationships, and existing sanctions.
HUR called for the remaining companies to be added to international sanctions lists and for governments to strengthen enforcement of existing restrictions.
The agency said sanctions would be effective only if accompanied by controls preventing companies from obtaining foreign technology through intermediaries and by penalties for those helping Russia circumvent restrictions.

Melting Mount Ağrı glacier threatens eastern Türkiye villages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:34:24 UTC
18:34:24 KST

(DHA Photo)
The ice cap on Mount Ağrı in the eastern province of Ağrı shrank from 15 to 5 square kilometers, triggering warnings of potential mudflows following a deadly glacier collapse near Nepal.
Satellite measurements show the mountain’s glacial valleys retreated to 4,900 meters from 3,600 meters in the early 1900s, Ağrı İbrahim Çeçen University Faculty of Arts and Sciences Geography Department Professor Faruk Kaya said. Kaya linked the local risk to an Aug. 26 ice avalanche on the northern face of Langtang Lirung peak on the Nepal-Tibet border, leaving over 1,000 dead and nearly 5,000 missing people.
Mount Ağrı experienced a similar event in 1840 when a mudflow destroyed Ahura village in the northeast Cehennem Deresi valley, making it the best-known glacier-sourced disaster in Türkiye’s history, Kaya said. A 2019 Geomorphology journal study debated the event’s mechanics, with theories ranging from a 21-kilometer rock-ice avalanche down the valley to rapid snow-ice melt triggered by an earthquake and possible volcanic activity.
Historical sources report the death toll varied between 1,300 and 1,700 people, Kaya said. The disaster completely destroyed Ahura, a settlement dating back to the 8th century, though locals quickly rebuilt it as Yenidoğan.
Recent ethnographic research shows that the ancient village, traditionally believed to be where Noah and his children spread across the world, reflects a cultural memory of locals living alongside frequent natural disasters, Kaya said.
The same valley saw a glacial mudslide in June 2021 and mud floods triggered by melting ice on July 30, 2026. Sudden glacier-melt flows turned into a recurring pattern in valleys surrounding Mount Ağrı during summer months, Kaya said.
Short-term events in 1921 and 1926 prove that the peak’s ice mass carries risks requiring close observation, Kaya said. He called for systematic satellite monitoring and periodic field studies of Türkiye’s glaciated mountains, including Cilo, Süphan and Kaçkar, to evaluate slope deformation and evacuate settlements near stream beds.
Mount Ağrı stands as Türkiye’s highest peak at 5,137 meters. While experts do not expect Himalaya-scale glacial lake outbursts in the country, climate change accelerates local ice retreat and rock avalanche risks. This continuous risk mirrors international events like the 2021 Chamoli disaster in India, altering hazard profiles for vulnerable mountain communities across the region.

Sunny warmth of up to +26°C will persist in Ukraine through September 20. Rain and a drop in temperatures to +10…+17°C are expected from September 21.
Warm and sunny weather will persist in Ukraine over the next few days, but a sharp cooling is expected as early as September 21. Air temperatures will drop to +10…+17°, and rain will become more frequent in many regions. Forecaster Natalka Didenko reported this, UNN writes.
Details
As Didenko noted, on Wednesday, September 16, a "comfortable weather situation" is expected in Ukraine.
There will be plenty of sunshine and warmth. The highest air temperatures may be recorded in the western regions — up to +22...+26°С.-
Meanwhile, daytime temperatures of +20...+23°С are expected in most regions of Ukraine.
The coolest weather will be in the eastern part of our country — around +17...+20°С.
Wonderful weather is expected in Kyiv tomorrow. It will be dry, sunny, and warm, with temperatures reaching + 23 ° during the day.
We will enjoy a classic Indian summer practically throughout the entire week
However, starting next Monday, September 21, a cooling period will begin in Ukraine.
Air temperatures will drop significantly, reaching + 10 + 17 ° during the day. There will be more rain, - the statement says.
Atmospheric fronts will pass through Ukraine, bringing moderate and heavy precipitation.
At the same time, Didenko noted that "this forecast will still need to be уточнений".
