How a 100-year-old population estimate may have got Australia wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:12:05 UTC
18:12:05 KST

In brief
- Estimates of Australia's pre-colonisation population may have missed the mark by millions, new research suggests.
- Its authors say the findings illustrate the magnitude of colonisation's devastating impacts on the Indigenous population.
How many people lived in Australia before colonisation? For nearly a century, many answers to that question have been influenced by a figure developed by anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown, who estimated the population at 250,000.
But new research from a national team of academics suggests there could have been about 2.2 million Indigenous Australians living on the continent before the British colonisation in 1788.
Based on the revised population figure and comparisons with early Census records, researchers estimate the Indigenous population declined by more than two million people between 1788 and 1861.
Corey Bradshaw, a professor of global ecology at Flinders University who co-led the research, told SBS News the findings illustrate the magnitude of the demographic collapse experienced by Indigenous Australians.
Researchers believe the decline was likely driven by a combination of introduced diseases, frontier violence, malnutrition, dispossession and other impacts of colonisation.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We're now starting to look at things like the massacres and try to de-bias a lot of that as well, because of course that's only the tip of the iceberg in terms of what was recorded," Bradshaw said.
The team relied on three independent approaches — archaeological, genetic and environmental modelling — rather than relying primarily on historical accounts.
Bradshaw said the approach is less vulnerable to the biases and gaps in historical records, and each of the three methods produced a relatively congruent set of estimates.
The 1930 estimate of roughly 250,000, Bradshaw said, was developed at a time when researchers lacked access to modern tools.
He said its creator acknowledged it was likely an underestimate, but the figure became widely accepted despite its limitations.
Other historical estimates suggested the population of Indigenous Australians may have been up to one million people, still under half of what the new research suggests.
'It's something we have to acknowledge'
Bradshaw said understanding the size of Indigenous populations before colonisation was essential to truth-telling and reconciliation.
"It's something that we have to acknowledge in our history and not sweep under the carpet," he said.
"It's part of understanding why the gap still exists in many aspects of society, and how to address it, and how long we might expect things to take to realign. I mean, these are huge demographic catastrophes that affected people for generations and generations."
The Indigenous population in Australia has grown since the 1950s, and represented 3.2 per cent of the overall population at the time of the 2021 Census at just under 813,000 people.
At current growth rates, the study estimates the Indigenous population will not return to its estimated pre-colonial size until around 2047.
Lynette Russell is a professor of Indigenous studies at Monash University's Indigenous Studies Centre and a co-author of the report.
She said the findings bring a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma that can inform future policy that helps Indigenous people.
"In addition to recognising this intergenerational trauma and disadvantage, it is also time to recognise intergenerational privilege," she said.
Bradshaw said the work also illustrates the resilience of Indigenous communities.
"It is remarkable that we have the variation and diversity of Indigenous cultures and languages and approaches to managing country that survived that catastrophe," he said.
More than 100 First Nations languages are still spoken across Australia, though some are in serious danger of being lost.
"We should celebrate the fact that these people were very resilient, and in face of all of that persecution, managed to persist."

Trump announced the purported agreement on Truth Social, writing: “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”

The White House did not provide further information about the terms, duration, or enforcement of the purported truce.

A person familiar with Moscow’s position confirmed that Russia and Ukraine had resumed discussions. However, no formal agreement or credible Russian guarantees had been secured when Trump made his announcement.
Moscow keeps winter pressure option

‘VOICES. An Evening of Premieres’: Kyiv Camerata to Present Music of Memory, Hope and Victory

The loss from the Gulf was therefore approximately 2.2 times greater than the reduction in Russian supplies, the institute said.
Ukraine says its refinery campaign is intended to weaken Russia’s ability to finance and sustain its full-scale invasion, while Moscow continues targeting Ukraine’s energy system and civilian infrastructure.

Seizures follow earlier Israel-bound shipment
The latest detentions came less than two weeks after Malaysian authorities detained another container at Tanjung Pelepas on August 7 over suspected exports to Israel.

Malaysia has prohibited Israeli ships and vessels carrying cargo to Israel from using its ports since December 2023, according to Anwar.
Malaysia tightens oversight of Israel-bound trade
The latest detentions point to broader scrutiny of cargo moving through Tanjung Pelepas, a major regional transshipment hub.
Bloomberg reported that shipping-tracking data showed the three containers carrying the electric bicycle parts were still at the port nearly a month after their detention.
Malaysia does not have diplomatic relations with Israel and has repeatedly tightened restrictions on trade and shipping involving the country.

====================================================================================================

German firm’s new mini drone dock passes final tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:05:49 UTC
18:05:49 KST

- CiS completed validation testing of its ORKA Dock Mini, a compact drone launch and recovery system, ahead of its first delivery to a naval customer.
- The system measures 80 by 80 centimeters and can launch and recover CiS's ORKA drone from small vessels, ground vehicles, and pickup trucks.
German drone developer CiS has finished validation testing on a new compact launch and recovery system called the ORKA Dock Mini, the company announced Sept. 15, 2026 from Rostock, Germany.
The final flight tests took place at night, ahead of the first unit’s delivery to an undisclosed naval customer. The Dock Mini is built to launch and recover CiS’s ORKA drone from small platforms where space is tight, including uncrewed surface vessels, uncrewed ground vehicles, and even pickup trucks. Its footprint measures just 80 by 80 centimeters (about 31 by 31 inches), small enough to fit on vessels and vehicles that couldn’t accommodate CiS’s earlier, larger dock. The system can launch and recover the drone whether its host platform is sitting still or moving, including underway at sea.
During validation, CiS also tested ORKA flying on a tether connected to the Dock Mini’s external power supply. That setup removes the normal limit on flight time, letting the drone hold station over a target for as long as needed instead of having to land and recharge. In its standard, untethered configuration, ORKA has an endurance of up to 75 minutes and a top speed of 100 km/h (62 mph).
“ORKA Dock Mini takes many of the features found in our fully enclosed, but larger, ORKA Dock and repackages them into a much smaller form factor,” said Tom Kaufmann, founder and CEO of CiS. “Dock Mini can be installed on small USVs and land platforms or carried by a conventional pickup truck, giving operators greater freedom over where and how they deploy an airborne capability.”
“The successful completion of these tests is an important milestone ahead of delivery to our naval customer,” Kaufmann said. “It demonstrates that a compact system can still deliver the endurance, flexibility and operator-free performance required for demanding surveillance and security missions.”
CiS designed the Dock Mini to run day or night, in any weather, and in sea states up to 5, a scale that covers waves up to roughly 2.5 meters (8 feet). The company lists intended uses including persistent surveillance and reconnaissance, force protection, perimeter monitoring, convoy overwatch, harbor security, and guarding vessels or critical infrastructure.
The Mini follows CiS’s original ORKA Dock, a larger enclosed version the company unveiled in May 2026 at the Combined Naval Event in Farnborough, England. That system was validated the previous month during SeaSEC 2026, a naval security exercise in Rostock, where it completed automatic launch and recovery cycles from a moving FLANQ Q-RECON 24 uncrewed surface vessel. CiS has said demand for the larger Dock from NATO navies picked up quickly after that unveiling.

41 food executives face detention over price manipulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:04:23 UTC
18:04:23 KST

(DHA Photo)
Turkish prosecutors have launched an investigation into major food distributors supplying fruit and vegetable wholesale markets, with detention warrants issued for 41 company executives over alleged price manipulation and related financial crimes.
The investigation, led by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, examines the pricing chain from farmers to consumers. Authorities reviewed data from the Wholesale Market Registration System and the Farmer Registration System, while the Tax Inspection Board under the Treasury and Finance Ministry prepared a comprehensive report.
Investigators also took statements from over 1,000 farmers to determine the prices at which produce left farms and the conditions under which it was sold to suppliers.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said the investigation found that some major suppliers had allegedly exploited their dominant position in the market by understating the supply of produce and overstating costs.
“Findings indicate that they issued fake producer receipts to create fictitious costs and, through these methods, manipulated prices upward in the fresh fruit and vegetable market to obtain illicit profits,” Gürlek said.
Following the findings and reports, prosecutors ordered the detention of 41 executives. Simultaneous searches were conducted at 109 workplaces and residences across 22 provinces as part of the operation.
Teams from the Istanbul Police Department’s Financial Crimes Unit detained 33 suspects in the raids.
The suspects face charges including manipulating market prices, violating the Tax Procedure Law, document forgery and laundering assets derived from crime.
Gürlek stressed that authorities would not allow any stage of the supply chain “from the field to the table” to become a means of illicit profit at the expense of farmers’ labor and consumers’ household budgets.

Feature: Chinese e-motorcycles ride through Vietnam's green transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:04:04 CST
18:04:04 KST

HANOI, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese electric motorcycle brands are becoming an increasingly common sight on the streets of Vietnam's major cities, as the country accelerates its shift toward greener urban transport.
From July 1 this year, Hanoi began piloting low-emission zones as part of a roadmap to limit gasoline-powered motorcycles from next year. Meanwhile, southern hub Ho Chi Minh City also plans to pilot low-emission zones from July 2027.
More Vietnamese residents are turning to electric motorcycles, with Chinese brands emerging as popular choices thanks to their competitive prices, diverse models and growing presence in the Vietnamese market.
At a Yadea store in Hanoi, the change is already visible.
"Sales have increased by 20 to 30 percent since Hanoi announced its roadmap to phase out gasoline-powered motorcycles," said Le Thu Ha, a sales representative at the store.
Rising demand has even left some models temporarily out of stock, with customers in some cases having to place orders weeks in advance, another Yadea sales representative told Xinhua.
According to Motorcycles Data, a website that tracks motorcycle sales, Chinese electric motorcycle brands recorded impressive growth in the first seven months of this year in the Vietnamese market, with sales of Yadea and TAILG rising 57.2 percent and 43.6 percent, respectively, from the same period last year.
For some buyers, the decision is not only about changing their daily commute but also preparing for a future in which gasoline motorcycles may no longer be an option.
Vi Thi Mai, a Yadea customer in Hanoi, bought an electric motorcycle for her daughter to ride to school.
"In the next five to seven years, Hanoi plans to ban gasoline-powered motorcycles. I want to prepare in advance for my daughter. I see this as an investment in the future," Mai said.
For others, the appeal is more immediate, with lower running costs making electric motorcycles a cheaper way to get around the city.
Nguyen Phi Long, who owns a TAILG electric motorcycle, said a friend's recommendation prompted him to try the brand.
"I feel that riding an electric motorcycle is more environmentally friendly, and the operating costs are lower than those of a gasoline-powered bike," he said.
Beyond cost and environmental considerations, design is becoming another factor attracting young consumers to electric motorcycles.
Nguyen Thanh Thuy, who visited a Yadea store in Hanoi to learn more about its models, said she found the brand's designs particularly suitable for Vietnamese and Asian consumers.
"They offer a wide variety of models. Specifically for women, the vehicles are very compact, lightweight, easy to maneuver and easy to ride," she told Xinhua.
As consumer preferences shift, Chinese electric motorcycle makers are also seeing opportunities to expand their presence in Vietnam.
Chinese brand Aima currently has more than 100 stores in Vietnam, with annual sales exceeding 30,000 units and plans to further expand in Southeast Asia.
For Yadea, Vietnam is emerging as a potential springboard for its overseas expansion.
"The successful experience accumulated in the Vietnamese market is expected to be replicated in other overseas markets, with Vietnam serving as a pivot for further expanding our overseas business," said Liu Jia, general manager of Yadea Vietnam Company.
Tran Van Mieu, vice chairman of the Vietnam Association for Conservation of Nature and Environment, said Chinese technology has been well received by Vietnamese consumers.
He expects the shift toward greener transportation to create a more dynamic market in Vietnam, which could in turn become an important destination for Chinese green-transportation products seeking to expand into overseas markets. ■

China Focus: China propels robots onto industrial frontlines with real-world applications
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:03:58 CST
18:03:58 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- High above the ground, a boxy, wall-climbing robot clings securely to the towering steel exterior of a petrochemical storage tank. Navigating the dizzying heights with expert precision, it autonomously maps its route and systematically executes a seamless sequence of rust removal, inspection, and spraying.
These "mechanical spidermen," developed by a Tianjin-based robotics firm, are already hard at work in the shipbuilding and petroleum sectors, redefining how heavy industry tackles extreme environments.
Zhang Minglu, chairman of BingooRobot, said hazardous tasks like welding and spraying are notoriously difficult for staff. "Robots are now critical to solving this chronic labor shortage," he said.
Traditionally, robots have been largely confined to entertainment and display roles, with very limited use in industrial operations. But in China, that dynamic is beginning to change.
Meng Yang, general manager of a robot innovation center in Zhongguancun, Beijing, said the goal is to delegate high-risk and highly repetitive tasks to robots, allowing humans to focus on more creative and value-driven work. "The true vitality of the robotics industry lies in tangible, real-world applications," he said.
That momentum is increasingly visible across China's vast industrial landscape. In Tianjin, quadruped robots have been deployed to conduct hydrological inspections along the Haihe River basin. They autonomously navigate to the riverbank, collect water samples, and return, enabling real-time data uploading and early warning analysis for water quality.
In the desert near the Fengcheng Oilfield in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, explosion-proof inspection robots equipped with high-precision infrared sensors and LiDAR now patrol flammable and explosive refining facilities around the clock. Powered by large language models, these machines can understand voice commands and use sensor fusion to assess hazards, mastering safety protocols in just three minutes, a process that would typically take a human worker about three months to learn.
Beyond hazardous environments, as domestic application scenarios continue to expand, China's industrial robots are accelerating their entry into thousands of industries.
To date, domestically branded industrial robots have expanded into 253 sub-categories of the national economy. From automotive welding to warehouse logistics, their role in empowering diverse industries continues to strengthen.
To facilitate this transition, China is vigorously promoting the "Robot Plus" application initiative, encouraging robots to iterate their technology in real-world settings and form application loops based on genuine needs.
The momentum is reflected in the data. According to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, China produced 538,000 industrial robots in the first half of 2026, a year-on-year increase of 28 percent. Revenue for large-scale enterprises in the robotics sector reached 165.5 billion yuan (about 24.4 billion U.S. dollars) in the same period, up 24.5 percent, as a batch of competitive emerging companies continues to grow.
Buoyed by this robust domestic momentum, Chinese robotics are rapidly expanding their global footprint. In the first half of 2026, robots were exported to 141 countries and regions, with the total value reaching 6.29 billion yuan, an 18.6 percent increase.
"As Chinese industrial robots penetrate diverse sectors, the shift from standardization to scenario-based applications marks their transition from niche high-end equipment to universal productivity tools," said Zhao Mingguo, an automation researcher at Tsinghua University. "This will empower domestic industries and fuel industrial transformation overseas." ■

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The recent meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi produced important consensus and marked the two leaders' reaffirmation of the growth of China-India ties after they guided the bilateral relations from starting afresh to making further improvements since 2024.
The most important consensus reached during the meeting on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi is that China and India should be partners. It was the third meeting between the two leaders in three years.
As Xi noted during their talks, to promote the steady and sustained development of China-India relations, both sides need to calibrate the direction with an objective and rational strategic perception, help each other succeed in the spirit of win-win cooperation, remove irritants with the political wisdom of mutual respect and mutual understanding, and contribute to a better world with open and inclusive multilateral coordination.

Over the centuries, the peoples of the two neighboring countries have developed precious bonds via exchanges and mutual learning. In modern times, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence -- specified by the Chinese leadership in their entirety for the first time -- were included in the China-India and China-Myanmar joint statements that called for making them basic norms for state-to-state relations, which is an outstanding contribution to the international system.
The two countries should treasure and carry forward the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, and pursue parallel progress in developing bilateral ties and solving border issues with the two tracks reinforcing each other, to maintain peace and tranquility in border areas and advance long-term development of bilateral relations.
China and India are the world's two most populous countries. The essence of their relationship lies in how two major developing countries with a population of over 1.4 billion each can get along with each other.
The two countries offer each other development opportunities, not threats. This strategic judgment is based on the development stages of the two countries and the international environment, and serves the common interests of both countries and their peoples.
Both countries are in a critical period of their respective national modernization drives, and development is the biggest common denominator. The two countries are partners for cooperation, not rivals. Both sides should draw on each other's strengths and develop together.
As major members of the Global South, China and India shoulder the international responsibility of setting an example in seeking strength through unity for developing countries, and contributing to advancing world multipolarity and the democratization of international relations. Both countries should work together to advance high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation and provide more positive energy for global peace, stability, development and prosperity.
It is expected that China and India will maintain the right direction in the development of their relationship, advance exchanges and cooperation in various fields, promote the steady and sustained development of bilateral ties, and make due contributions to the cause of human progress. ■

The market lost steam again in the afternoon as investors moved to the sidelines ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy meeting, due to begin later in the day, with the Bank of Japan's policy meeting also scheduled for later in the week. ■

China Focus: China reallocates educational resources to match changing school-age population
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:03:27 CST
18:03:27 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- As the new fall semester begins, some primary school teachers in China are being reassigned to middle schools, following their students as they move up the educational ladder.
This innovative staffing measure is currently being piloted in Shanghai and several other locations in provinces such as Fujian, Anhui, Hubei, and Jiangxi.
The move comes as the country's education system adjusts to a demographic shift that is reshaping demand for teachers: primary schools are seeing declining enrollment and a surplus of teachers, while secondary schools are facing growing teacher shortages.
According to the Ministry of Education, China is experiencing a "wave-like" shift in its school-age population. Primary school enrollment peaked in 2023, middle school enrollment is expected to peak in 2026, and high school enrollment in 2029.
It noted a serious mismatch between faculty supply and demand across different educational stages, adding that the challenge also presents a historic opportunity to proactively adjust and optimize the country's basic education.
China is home to the world's largest basic education system, with around 430,000 primary and secondary schools and kindergartens serving 220 million students.
In March, Education Minister Huai Jinpeng said China's basic education coverage and key indicators had surpassed the average levels of upper-middle-income countries, with preschool and compulsory education reaching the averages of high-income countries.
In China, the enrollment rate of children in preschool programs reached 92.9 percent in 2025, and the net enrollment rates for primary and secondary schools have remained around 100 percent for years, official statistics showed.
China's two performance indicators surpassed those of high-income countries. In 2025, the enrollment rate of school-age children living with disabilities at the nine-year compulsory education stage stayed above 97 percent, and that of girls above 99 percent.
"Transferring primary school teachers to secondary classrooms can optimize the allocation of teaching resources within the education system," said Ding Changfa, an associate professor of economics at Xiamen University.
But moving teachers from lower grades to higher grades is not simply about shifting the numbers around. It also raises the question of how to improve the quality of the teaching workforce, according to Li Tingzhou, a researcher at Shanghai Normal University.
"China's teaching workforce has reached a critical juncture," Li said. "The question used to be whether we had 'enough teachers.' Now, it is whether we have 'good teachers.'"
Still, some have raised concerns about whether teachers transferred to a higher educational stage are competent enough.
"It depends," said Tang Zhisong, a professor of education at Southwest University. "If a primary school teacher has been trained and has acquired the certificate for teaching at a higher educational stage, they are qualified after further training."
In practice, qualifications, such as a corresponding teaching certificate and experience, are usually specified in recruitment announcements.
In July, Longyan City in Fujian Province and Tianchang in Anhui Province issued recruitment notices for qualified primary school teachers to take up middle school positions, with the required teaching certificates and experience clearly specified.
Shanghai's Jing'an district took the move a step further: after selecting 10 kindergarten teachers and 27 primary ones for new positions at a higher learning level, local education authorities in June launched a special one-year-long training program to prepare them for their new roles.
"With the lectures, seminars and practice teaching provided by the program, I could quickly move from the role of a primary school teacher to that of a middle school teacher," said Xie Nan, a participant in the Shanghai training program.
Apart from training, a performance evaluation system should be in place, said Tang Zhisong.
The reallocation of educational resources is not limited to teachers. As the number of school-age children declines, some localities are also finding new uses for idle school buildings, giving them a new lease on life while saving fiscal expenditure.
Take Nanping in Fujian Province as an example. The city had logged 601 idle school buildings as of the fall semester in 2025. Currently, 20 of them have been refurbished into nursing homes, welfare centers or canteens, while 17 have been converted into factories, including facilities processing local specialty tea, and four into cultural tourism sites.
In Yongren County in southwest China's Yunnan Province, 100 out of 118 idle school buildings have taken a new lease of life, saving 91.6 million yuan (about 13.5 million U.S. dollars) in fiscal expenditure. ■

Xi Story: Making canals channels for connectivity, prosperity, better life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:03:20 CST
18:03:20 KST

NANNING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Sitting in a glass case at a museum in south China's Qinzhou, a glazed porcelain bowl etched with a floral pattern offers a tantalizing clue to this coastal city's maritime-trade past. Despite being centuries old, the bowl bears scarcely any signs of use.
Experts believe that the bowl, instead of being made for use in local households, was likely among the merchandise stockpiled for trade during the Song Dynasty (960-1279), when sugar and ceramics were shipped from Qinzhou to Southeast Asian countries along the Maritime Silk Road.
A historic port city on the coast of the Beibu Gulf in the South China Sea, Qinzhou, located in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is gaining fresh momentum as a maritime hub with the opening of the Pinglu Canal, a major river-to-sea canal project set to become operational on Wednesday.
The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets.
During an inspection tour of Guangxi in December 2023, Chinese President Xi Jinping was briefed on the construction progress of the canal in front of a sand-table model.
Guangxi's future growth potential lies in connecting its waterways to the sea and realizing integrated river-sea transport, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said during that trip.
He added that Guangxi should strengthen itself via maritime development, noting that the region has both a strong need and great potential to further expand opening up, both internally and externally.
Running from north to south, the Pinglu Canal links the Xijiang River shipping route with the Beibu Gulf. It is expected to shorten the shipping distance between China's southwestern hinterland and ASEAN, China's largest trading partner, by 560 km and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent, according to Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi.
China's natural river systems generally run from west to east toward the sea, making it difficult to rely on existing rivers and lakes to connect the country's north and south.
China has a long history of building canals. The best-known is the more than 2,500-year-old Grand Canal, the world's oldest and longest artificial waterway system, and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2014.
Xi has attached great importance to the protection and revitalization of the Grand Canal. He once stressed that the Grand Canal is a "precious heritage passed down to us by our ancestors."
In 2006, when he was secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee, he took a "water bus" along a section of the Grand Canal in the provincial capital Hangzhou to inspect cleanup and revitalization of the canal. The "water bus" passenger service, launched in 2004, was the first of its kind along an urban Grand Canal network.
Along the way, Xi asked in detail about everything from waterway network protection and shipping operations to the development of scenic areas along the canal. He encouraged Hangzhou officials to turn the canal into "a canal for the people" and "a canal for visitors," stressing that the people should be the ultimate beneficiaries.
His attention to the Grand Canal has remained unchanged over the years. In November 2020, as China's top leader, Xi visited the eastern city of Yangzhou, where some of the waterway system's oldest sections are located. "For centuries, the canal has nourished the cities and people along its banks, bringing prosperity and well-being to them," he said.
"I hope everyone will work together to protect the Grand Canal and ensure that it continues to benefit the people for generations to come," he told local officials and residents.
Yangzhou, described by Xi as a "wonderful place built along the water, thriving on it and made beautiful by it," is a vivid example of how the Grand Canal has nourished a city and shaped its fortunes.
Just like Yangzhou, Qinzhou today is poised to reap the benefits of greater connectivity -- this time, connectivity from river to sea, thanks to the Pinglu Canal.
The Pinglu Canal is bringing to life the historical tradition of the Grand Canal in a new era, a tradition of fostering prosperity through waterways, said Xie Zhujun, a researcher with the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences. Ultimately, the purpose of a canal is to improve people's livelihoods and deliver broader economic and social benefits, he noted.
For Ning Qiongri, a Qinzhou native and a vlogger who has posted some 1,600 videos chronicling the construction of the Pinglu Canal, the project promises not only greater prosperity, but also a better life for local people.
"Many people find jobs thanks to the canal's construction. I've also seen brand-new villages and schools built along its banks, as well as supermarkets and restaurants that are eager to name themselves after the canal," Ning revealed. ■

China Focus: Digital technologies bring new way of farming to China's fields
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
17:03:20 CST
18:03:20 KST

CHANGCHUN, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- As the Jiuyuefeng Family Farm in northeast China's Jilin Province prepares for harvest season this autumn, farm manager Xiao Jianbo no longer needs to walk into its 267 hectares of rice fields to check on growth.
In his office, a smart agriculture management system continuously updates data on the farm's soil conditions, weather and crop growth. On his mobile phone, he can view live images from high-definition cameras in the fields in Yongji County's Yilaxi Township, as well as readings from soil sensors. When an on-site inspection is needed, he can dispatch drones to survey the fields.
These changes, now taking place across Jilin, are part of China's broader push to modernize agriculture with digital technologies.
"Satellite remote sensing technology sends data on rice growth of each plot to the system in real time," Xiao said. "Green means the rice is growing normally. Yellow or red may indicate pests or diseases, and we can then promptly check and take action."
The technology has proved useful in this year's flood season. Heavy rainfall triggered alerts when paddy fields were inundated by rainwater backflow.
"In the past, if we failed to discover a problem in time, it could have caused losses. But field management efficiency now has improved significantly," Xiao said.
For farmers like Xiao, satellite remote sensing, drones and the Internet of Things are becoming increasingly important new farming tools, alongside traditional ones.
Jilin, part of one of the world's three major black soil regions and a major grain-producing area, has leveraged its satellite technology hub status to modernize agriculture.
In recent years, Chang Guang Satellite Technology Co., Ltd., headquartered in Changchun, capital of Jilin Province, has launched 161 satellites for its "Jilin-1" satellite constellation.
Liu Huimin, an engineer at the company, said the constellation integrates agricultural information, including weather, farmland conditions and agricultural mechanization data.
Satellite remote sensing is being applied throughout the agricultural production cycle, from plowing and sowing to field management and harvesting, Liu said.
With high-resolution imagery, fast response and broad coverage, the technology can help agricultural authorities assess disasters, monitor farmland protection, and track crop distribution and acreage, Liu said.
This summer, severe convective weather, including strong winds and hail, affected crops in some counties and districts in Jilin.
"We immediately contacted the satellite technology service provider and obtained information on the distribution and severity of the affected farmland," said Wang Hao, an official with the Jilin Provincial Department of Agriculture and Rural Affairs.
The information provided an important reference for post-disaster recovery and verification of crop damage statistics, Wang said.
Digital agriculture is also changing how agricultural products are marketed and sold.
In Yongji County, a visual agriculture livestreaming system allows overseas buyers to see the production and harvesting process, helping build consumer trust. This year, it has helped win customers from the Republic of Korea, Japan, Australia and Southeast Asia.
Over the past few years, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs has issued a series of policies to promote smart agriculture.
China has also built innovation platforms to support smart agriculture. So far, 34 national smart agriculture innovation centers and sub-centers, along with 30 ministry-level key laboratories for agricultural information technology, have been established.
"Watch from the sky, calculate in the cloud and manage from the palm of your hand," Xiao said, referring to the farming revolution. "Farming used to be a laborious and demanding job. Now it is gradually becoming easier and more efficient." ■

Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:02:47 BST
18:02:47 KST

Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
- Published
Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, were hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks on Tuesday morning, the country's railway infrastructure operator said.
ProRail said pipes and cables were laid on tracks at multiple locations in the country's centre and north in more than 35 incidents.
It added the acts appeared to be intentional, causing widespread cancellations and delays, with new disruptions occurring in some places after objects had initially been removed.
No suspects or motives have yet been identified. Police said a criminal investigation had been launched.
The operator said the pipes and cables caused its computer systems to believe trains were on the tracks, meaning traffic control was unable to clear the railway.
"Placing materials on the tracks is extremely dangerous and unacceptable, and fortunately, it did not lead to any accidents today," it said.
Speaking earlier, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the incidents as "disruptive and life-threatening".
In one case early on Monday, a train "struck metal" on the track near Steenwijk, in the country's east. ProRail said there was no further damage because the train was not travelling at full speed.
The national public prosecutor's office and the Netherlands' intelligence agency AIVD are investigating the incident alongside police.
Routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, Eindhoven and Utrecht were among those affected on Tuesday. The closure of some level crossings also caused some disruption to roads.
As of about 17:00 CEST (16:00 GMT), it said no new blockages had been reported since 13:00, with current ones now resolved. Train operator Nederlandse Spoorwegen (NS) still showed disruptions to two lines on Tuesday evening.
Its interim CEO Mirjam van Velthuizen said the events had highlighted the Netherlands' dependence on the railway and called for investment in contingency planning.
"In a world where uncertainties are increasing, we must ensure that the railway can absorb disruptions, that the impact remains limited as much as possible, and that we can recover as quickly as possible," she said.
NS earlier said that disruption was so extensive it was "not possible" to provide a bus replacement service.
Netherlands Police said units from across the country were investigating Tuesday's events.
Tuesday is Prinsjesdag in the Netherlands - the day the government presents its budget.
Hay bales were lit on fire along various roads across the Netherlands in the afternoon, after Farmers Defence Force (FDF) - a group aimed at defending the interests of Dutch farmers and farm workers - said protests would take place.
The group is opposing government plans asking them to reduce nitrogen emissions.
Authorities have not established a link between the protests and the disruption on the rail network.
The FDF said it was not responsible for the railway sabotage, but said it could not rule out the involvement of individual farmers.
Disruption in the Netherlands came after separate reports in French media suggested a derailment in Normandy on Friday could have been an act of sabotage.
According to prosecutors, a section of rail found on the track may have caused the crash. But France's interior minister Laurent Nunez has urged caution while an investigation is ongoing, saying that authorities are pursuing all leads.

US judge blocks Trump rule shortening length of visas for international students, academics, journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:01:55 UTC
18:01:55 KST

Darren Lyn
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
A US judge on Monday blocked a Trump administration rule that would have shortened the validity period of visas for international students, academics and foreign journalists.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued the rule on July 17, which capped all student and academic visas at four years, "regardless of the anticipated or likely length of educational program or research." For journalists, the cap was significantly reduced to 240 days.
In a Massachusetts federal court, Judge F. Dennis Saylor blocked the rule, stating that the Trump administration’s reasons for limiting the length of stay were "exceptionally weak."
Three organizations representing colleges, universities and educators as well as four labor organizations -- including one for journalists -- filed the lawsuit to block the DHS ruling, which would have affected 1.6 million people with F visas pursuing undergraduate and postgraduate degrees and 500,000 people with J visas who require sponsorship to live in the United States.
Foreign journalists would have had to apply for an extension through DHS, and if their applications were denied, they would have had no recourse against the decision and would not have been allowed to appeal.
Saylor ruled that the Trump administration's reasoning for implementing the policy was so arbitrary that the measure itself was unlawful.
"The weakness and the connection between the rule and its purported rationales raises legitimate questions as to whether its real purpose is not to safeguard national security and protect our borders, but to achieve other, undisclosed goals -- such as, for example, asserting greater government control over academic institutions and the press," Saylor stated in his ruling.
The DHS did not say whether it would appeal the ruling, but said in a statement: "If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President (Donald) Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege."
The judge wrote in his ruling that there is no evidence of widespread fraud by immigrants posing as students and said that Trump officials based their reasoning for the rule "almost entirely on a small handful of anecdotes, each of which involved incidents that the new rule would do nothing to prevent or even mitigate."
He also said that the rule would be detrimental to the US.
"The damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be catastrophic," said Saylor. "The government has acknowledged that compliance costs alone will likely total more than $250 million in the first year."
In addition, the judge cited the plaintiffs' argument against the rule that the "change will have the unavoidable effect of making the United States a less attractive destination for the world's top students."
"Many American colleges and universities -- already struggling with declining enrollment based on demographic changes -- will likewise suffer huge economic impacts," said Saylor, adding that the Trump administration's reasons for implementing the rule did not make sense.
"The government's contention that the rule is necessary to safeguard national security borders on the absurd," he said, ruling in favor of the plaintiffs.
"Plaintiffs have demonstrated a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of their claims," wrote Saylor, adding that "immediate irreparable harm will ensue if this Final Rule is not enjoined; and that the balance of the equities and the public interest favor issuance of a preliminary injunction."

Parents and carers in Great Britain spent 12.5% less on school uniform in the run-up to the start of this academic year, turning to promotions and secondhand items to keep expenses down as families struggled with the cost of living crisis.
The average spend on school uniform was £54.53 in the four weeks to 6 September, down an eighth from £62.29 in the same period last year, according to the market research company Worldpanel by Numerator. Overall grocery inflation picked up to 2.3% from 2.1%.
Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at the company, said “value is the watchword for parents this back-to-school season” as they try to balance stretched household budgets.
Almost half of households (44%) prioritised keeping costs low above all else when it comes to buying uniform, even if that means compromising on quality, while a third (33%) aimed to strike a balance between the two, according to a back-to-school survey conducted by Worldpanel in August.
“It’s a clear sign that, for many families, the return to school is landing at a difficult time financially, and retailers who can offer reassurance on price without compromising on quality stand will stand in good stead,” McKevitt said.
Grocery sales rose 2% year on year over the period, the monthly Worldpanel figures showed. August brought more warm weather and the end of a summer of sport. But with the return to school and work looming for many, shopping habits began to shift. Shoppers made 18m fewer trips to supermarkets compared with a peak of 497m in July.
“The end of the summer holidays typically brings a cooling in trip frequency and a pivot towards priority purchases, and this year is no exception,” McKevitt said. “While grocery inflation ticked up modestly last month, it remains significantly lower than the levels we saw earlier in the year, giving households some welcome breathing room.”
Sandwiches featured in more than half of all kids’ lunchboxes, with more than half a million more households that include children buying loaves of bread in the seven days to 6 September compared with the previous week. The number buying satsumas (+29%) and cucumbers (+21%) also rose in the final week before the return to school.
Sales at Asda rose by 0.1% over the 12 weeks to 6 September, as the grocer returned to growth for the first time since March 2024. However, the Leeds-based retailer’s market share dipped to 11.5%.
The online supermarket Ocado, with sales up by 13.3%, remained the fastest-growing grocer overall, with a slightly higher market share of 2.2%. Lidl moved up to 8.7% of the market.
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons maintained their previous market share of 15.2% and 8.4%, respectively. The UK’s largest supermarket, Tesco, dipped to 27.8% from 28.1%. The German discounter Aldi took a 10.6% share.

U.S. Air Force stacks its next nuclear missile for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:01:26 UTC
18:01:26 KST

- The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman vertically assembled a fully integrated inert Sentinel ICBM at Vandenberg Space Force Base on Sept. 14, 2026.
- The milestone and a completed Critical Design Review confirm the missile's design maturity ahead of a planned 2027 flight test.
The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman have fully assembled an inert version of the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the company announced Sept. 14, 2026. The vertical assembly is a step toward flight testing the missile in 2027.
Engineers stacked all of the missile’s stages, propulsion elements, and its protective shroud into a single configuration on the test pad, according to Northrop Grumman. The operation was designed to prove that the process for safely assembling a complete Sentinel missile actually works in practice, not just on paper.
Getting the inert missile onto the pad took a four-month effort. Northrop Grumman moved missile components from facilities around the country to Vandenberg, then used specialized transport equipment and mobile cranes to stack the sections and later take them apart again. The company said the exercise, including verification of how each section’s interfaces connect, showed the team is ready to move toward an actual flight test.
Alongside the assembly, Northrop Grumman and the U.S. Air Force’s 719th Test Squadron completed the program’s first flight test Critical Design Review. The review confirmed that Sentinel’s design and hardware testing meet the Air Force’s requirements for performance, safety, and schedule ahead of the planned 2027 flight test.
“This vertical assembly demonstrates the momentum toward test launching Sentinel in 2027 and having missiles on alert by the early 2030s, ensuring the United States’ ground-based nuclear capabilities remain strong and reliable for decades to come,” said Amanda Davis, vice president and general manager of strategic deterrent systems at Northrop Grumman.
Sentinel, formally designated the LGM-35A, is meant to replace the Minuteman III missiles that have formed the ground-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad since the early 1970s. The Air Force’s plan calls for fielding 659 missiles and modernizing 450 launch silos and associated facilities, a scope that goes well beyond simply swapping out the missile itself.
Northrop Grumman won the original engineering and manufacturing contract in 2020, valued at $13.3 billion. By January 2024, cost growth on the program had triggered a critical breach under the Nunn-McCurdy Act, the law that requires the Pentagon to report major acquisition cost overruns to Congress.
A Pentagon review that July found the overrun had grown to 81 percent above the original baseline, pushing the total program cost estimate to roughly $140.9 billion. Defense officials certified the program to continue but ordered it restructured and pushed the expected fielding timeline back by at least three years.
Sept. 14’s assembly and design review mark the program’s most concrete hardware milestone since that restructuring. Northrop Grumman has not said how many additional assembly cycles or test events are planned between now and the 2027 flight test, and the Air Force has not released an updated cost or schedule baseline beyond the 2024 figures.

Abdi stressed that the Asian Games represent more than just a sporting competition.
“We are not here only for football and sport,” he added. “Sport can bring nations closer together. It teaches us to respect one another, to be good people and to work towards building a better world. In my opinion, respect and humanity are the most important values in sport.”
Abdi also addressed the absence of five players for the opening match, with the fixture falling outside the FIFA international window.
“The schedule means that the first match is being played outside the FIFA window,” Abdi explained. “Unfortunately, this is a problem that we cannot do anything about at the moment. We have to accept the situation. This is the squad we have available for the first match. If we don’t have any injuries, we will face the UAE with 15 outfield players and three goalkeepers.
“That is football. These kinds of challenges exist, and we have to accept the circumstances. We will give everything we have and do our best to put in a good performance against a strong UAE team.”

I’m a psychoanalyst. Social media is damaging children’s inner lives in ways we don’t fully understand | Robin Kirman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

During the landmark social media addiction trial that led to Meta’s recent $17.1bn settlement, a therapist testified that she had once asked the plaintiff – a young woman named Kaley, who had been using social media since she was six – what her miracle day would look like: what she wished to come true, if anything were possible. Kaley replied that she would be prettier.
As a psychoanalyst, I find that exchange devastating in a particular way. A miracle day is an invitation to engage with the full range of human desire: with what one might accomplish or experience, whom one might encounter or love. Kaley’s answer contracted the world and all its possibility into a single preoccupation with her own image.
Kaley’s testimony echoes what I hear from many of my younger patients: teens who are often out of touch with what they want from life, not temporarily undecided, but fundamentally unable to locate a sense of what matters to them. Most also feel consumed by a preoccupation with how they appear – with their bodies, their standing in others’ eyes – that is brutal and unrelenting. These struggles are often accompanied by a cluster of symptoms that have come to define the youth mental health crisis: anxiety, depression, eating disorders, addiction, self-harm, social withdrawal.
Researchers and clinicians have linked these symptoms to heavy social media use, but the discussion has been largely confined to documented behavioral outcomes. What the public conversation has not sufficiently addressed is what social media addiction does to young people’s inner lives, and specifically, the damage done to their emerging desires and identities.
The philosopher Harry Frankfurt argued that what you genuinely care about is, in some fundamental sense, what you are. DW Winnicott, a British pediatrician turned psychoanalyst, arrived at a similar insight through the study of childhood development: desire and identity are inseparable. For Winnicott, the capacity for genuine desire is not innate but developed, and it develops only when a child is free to follow impulses that arise from within. Winnicott was writing about early childhood, but his account, I’d argue, also applies to the years that follow. The child who climbs a fence to see what’s on the other side, who starts a game in the street and finds others drawn in, who keeps pulling books off the shelf until she finds one that addresses her latest curiosity – she is learning that her desires matter, that they can direct her and shape her experience of the world. She discovers not only what she wants, but who she is: her true self, in Winnicott’s terms.
Social media systematically undermines that process. The trial’s expert witnesses explained how these platforms function at the neurological level: they hijack the brain’s dopamine reward system, holding it in a state of chronic activation. The work of the neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, who identified and named the brain’s primary motivational circuit, adds a crucial refinement: what social media exploits is not the pleasure system but the Seeking system, the forward-reaching drive toward wanting itself, the engine of curiosity. What addiction does is fix this system on a compulsive object, stripping desire of its natural range and spontaneity. The platform exploits the Seeking system’s sensitivity to novelty to capture attention and keep it. The result is a distorted relationship to desire: wanting that has been severed from its natural objects in the world and fixed on the feed.
The psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan gave a name to this kind of distortion: jouissance, a corrupted form of desire severed from what genuinely matters and fixed on substitutes that keep it running without resolution. Such desire – the kind social media addiction produces – no longer orients; it dysregulates, becoming out of control. For some, the response is a relationship to desire built around suppression: of appetite, as in eating disorders, or of sexual and romantic desire – its decline increasingly documented among young people today. For others, desire gets channeled into substitute circuits: compulsive shopping, video game playing, online betting – each carrying the felt sense that something is at stake, while pulling desire back into the circuit rather than outward toward the world.
The harm of social media goes beyond its hold on attention, though. The platform also subjects the child to an ever-present observer: making every impulse potentially public and subject to others’ assessment. For Winnicott, the capacity for genuine desire develops only where a child is free from an evaluative gaze and can follow impulses that arise from her own center. Social media destroys that freedom. What forms in its absence is what Winnicott called the “false self” – a performing self, shaped by the reactions of others. When the emptiness beneath that performance can no longer be ignored, what surfaces is the anxiety of unreality: the distress of someone who has been going through the motions of a life without ever really inhabiting it.
At eight, Kaley posted a video of herself playing an online game as an otter character, singing in a put-on British accent: an act of pure play, entirely her own. Within a few years, a video shows her crying tears of joy at reaching 100 YouTube subscribers – and then, in the same breath, saying she looked fat. A decade later, she had given up her hobbies and old interests, stopped making friends, withdrawn from her family. She developed depression, anxiety, body dysmorphia. She began cutting herself. She had suicidal thoughts.
What I find most striking, reading Kaley’s testimony, is the totality of her collapse. In the space of a decade, a child playing freely became a teenager who wanted to stop living. The trial documented her decline, each symptom linked to social media use. But the standard account, which explains her suffering through social comparison and addiction, cannot explain what connects these symptoms and lies at their root. What I read in her story is the loss of something more fundamental: not just her self-regard, but her sense of herself as a desiring subject, whose curiosities and ambitions might have given her an identity beyond how she appears. Genuine desire requires a kind of self-forgetting: what Heidegger, Winnicott, and others have understood as the condition of authentic being – absorption in what one genuinely pursues. The platform made that impossible, and without that absorption, Kaley’s attention turned inward, and against herself.
Kaley is one of thousands of plaintiffs in this litigation, her story a window into a generation’s suffering. The young people I treat want to stop hurting themselves, starving themselves, measuring themselves against ideals that leave them feeling worthless. They want to feel less empty. But what lies beyond that pain – what might make them happy, what kind of life might be worth pursuing – has become, sadly, out of reach.
Last month’s settlement holds Meta accountable for deliberately addicting children to its platforms. This is a sign we are beginning to take that harm seriously. Still, helping these young people heal will require more than the sort of symptom management mostly on offer. It will involve understanding what has been lost, and the slow, patient work of creating the conditions in which genuine desire might, at last, come alive. That work has barely begun.

Australia’s Indigenous population estimated at 2.2m before ‘demographic catastrophe’ of colonisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:00:31 UTC
18:00:31 KST

The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed.
Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 million, compared with early estimates of 250,000 people.
The research, by the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), has been published in the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour.
The authors wrote that, historically, population estimates have been poor “due to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses” and that it’s “invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation” to try to rectify that.
They warn readers that the content of the study is confronting and possibly distressing.
The modelling showed there had to be millions of excess deaths from smallpox and other diseases, massacres, and the other results of colonisation such as dispossession and malnutrition, according to co-author Prof Corey Bradshaw, a global ecology professor at Flinders University.
His previous research found that an 1789 smallpox outbreak alone killed as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people. There were also other smallpox epidemics, as well as outbreaks of measles, influenza, tuberculosis, typhoid and other diseases.
Bradshaw said he would bet his career that massacre databases were underestimated by an “order of magnitude”.
“If you’re a frontier farmer, a colonialist that came out to a new area, and you were trying to remove people from ‘your’ land, you’re not going to write extensively about how many people you killed to do that,” he said.
“There’s another component here that’s essentially greed and racism – the entire concept of terra nullius was based on not many people being here. If there’s a systematic desire to take land [fewer people means a] better justification for imperialism.”
Australia was colonised on the basis of terra nullius, that it belonged to no one. That concept was overthrown with the high court’s Mabo decision, when it was recognised that First Nations people had been here for tens of thousands of years.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were not properly counted in the census until 1971, after the 1967 referendum. At that point, 115,953 people identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander.
In 2021, 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census, a figure revised upwards to 983,257 with post-census recounts.
The estimate of 2.2 million, as well as a new estimate of 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861, means the population was reduced to about 7% of its original size.
“We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story,” distinguished professor Larissa Behrendt said. A Euahleyai/Gamillaroi woman, she is also the chair of the CIEHF’s advisory committee.
Early on after colonisation, various people estimated how many Aboriginal people were in their region. For example, governor Arthur Phillip estimated Gadigal people of the Eora nation came to about 1,500.
The first continent-wide estimate by social anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown put the number between 250,000 and 300,000, but mainly used observations from after the impacts of colonisation had been felt.
Radcliffe-Brown was aware that it was an underestimate, but many researchers since have relied on that count as a baseline. Again, they often recognised it would be an undercount because of historical reasons and changes in who identified or was identified as Aboriginal.
In 1983, economic historian Noel Butlin estimated the population at about 900,000. Later he increased that to between 1.1 million and 1.3 million. In 1987, archaeologists John Mulvaney and J Peter White argued it was more likely 750,000.
There have been many and varied estimates since, usually based on historical and ethnographic information.
The Australian team used different approaches to model the population. They looked at archaeological items to reconstruct how many people would have been there at a particular time, reconstructed the climate and the productivity of the land to infer how many people it could sustain and looked at genetic data to work back in time based on known DNA mutation rates.
They also reviewed, but did not rely on, ethnographic estimates.
“The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonisation, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people,” said co-author and distinguished professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.
The authors wrote that Australia must prioritise reconciliation, engagement and policymaking with Indigenous people who still suffer intergenerational trauma and that the broader community should embrace the rich culture that survived these events.
The lead author, James Cook University associate professor Alan Williams, said the “devastating findings” highlighted the impacts of invasion. However, they also demonstrated the “remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people”.
Behrendt said the research “tells us something extraordinary”.
“Our survival is one of Australian history’s most remarkable stories,” she said.

What to watch as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testifies before Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:00:01 UTC
18:00:01 KST

With the midterm election just weeks away, Democrats laced into Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a combative House hearing Tuesday. They sought to paint him as covering for President Donald Trump in the face of high energy prices and rising interest costs on consumer debt.
"You go on television and you say Trump's economic agenda is a great comeback," said Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., at the hearing held by the House Financial Services Committee. "That makes me question not only your integrity, but if you're operating in the same reality as the people whom you are accountable to," she said.
Bessent presented a spirited defense of Trump's economic record in his testimony, which was formally scheduled as part of International Monetary Fund oversight but rapidly devolved into a free-for-all about partisan views of the economy. Bessent was frequently interrupted not by just Democrats, who insisted he answer yes or no questions on a range of issues, but also by a group of protestors who objected to U.S. sanctions on Iran and Cuba.
The 10-year Treasury note traded at 5% midday Tuesday. It briefly reached a level not seen since 2007. That has raised consumer borrowing costs. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate average topped 7% last week.
"Despite your feeble efforts, there continues to be a sell-off of U.S. Treasuries," Rep. Maxine Waters, the ranking Democrat on the committee, told Bessent.
Bessent attempted to respond at length, but Waters, of California, held up her hand and said she was reclaiming her time.
Bessent defended his management of the U.S. Treasury market during questioning by other lawmakers. The Treasury Department increased its purchases of certain long-dated Treasury bonds that it sees as mispriced. Democrats suggested those buybacks weren't successful because yields on long-dated bonds have continued to rise.
Bessent disagreed, saying bond yields would be yet higher had the department not intervened.
"There was the counterfactual of what it would have done," he said. "And then we proceeded to have two of most successful bond Treasury auctions that we've had in 20 years."
Bessent said he is working on deficit-reduction plans, which would ease Treasury yields.
"I believe that the 10-year yield reflects many things, but the need to address the deficit is one of those," Bessent said.
Yields have risen alongside the price of oil. A barrel of oil is trading above $100 a barrel as the Iran war has heated up again recently. That has pushed the price of gas in the U.S. to an average of $4.32 a gallon as of Monday, up $1.14 from a year ago, according to AAA. Diesel costs $6.23, up $2.54 over the past year.
Bessent has been a full-throated supporter of the war. His department has ratcheted up sanctions on Iran and banks that facilitate its business.
Another thread of testimony focused on artificial intelligence. Washington has been consumed by questions on AI policy after several leading AI executives said they are concerned about potential for AI to advance beyond their ability to control the technology.
Bessent on Tuesday suggested Chinese companies are a greater threat than U.S. firms. Anthropic, creator of Claude, said earlier this month that a Chinese AI model had routed some of its users' queries to Anthropic.
"Kimi had a breach and sent Chinese weapons plans back to Anthropic," Bessent said Tuesday, speaking about the first known example of a Chinese AI model being involved in a breach.
Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Bessent's remarks.
Bessent declined to specify any particular draft regulations or bills he believed would improve AI safety, but he indicated he supported arguments made by critics of large AI labs such as Anthropic.
Former Trump administration AI czar David Sacks and other detractors have attacked Anthropic in recent days. He has said the company is trying to push regulation would that slow down open-source AI models in favor of its own technology, while also easing potential liability issues that may arise if its AI tools are used to compromise other institutions' security.
"I can tell you what we shouldn't do on safety is give these labs a liability exemption, which is what they're asking for," Bessent said.
"We need to develop more open source models in the U.S. We can't let these large labs capture — have regulatory capture," Bessent added.
Bessent and House Republicans emphasized positive aspects of the Trump economy. Stocks have been volatile lately but remain near highs. The S&P 500 is up about 27% since Trump took office for his second term.
The economy has also continued to produce jobs, while the administration slows immigration. Unemployment is low at 4.1%.
Bessent said wages for the bottom 25% of earners have risen faster than the top group of earners. More than 64 million tax returns have claimed one of the tax cuts passed last year, he said.
As the hearing came to a close, Bessent acknowledged the tough nature of the appearance. "It started off great," he said with a shrug.
— Karen James Sloan and Matt Peterson contributed to this report.

System 76 Pangolin Pro Review (2026): Powerhouse Linux Laptop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

I have similar feelings about the very large glass trackpad. For things like photo editing, the trackpad's size is great, but I found my palms occasionally clicked the buttons at the bottom of the trackpad when I took a break from typing. It didn't happen often, but I learned to be careful about where I put my palms.
The 2-MP 1080p webcam is fine for casual use, chatting with family and friends, but if you do a lot of Zoom meetings in a professional context, you may want an external webcam. Also, open-source purists should note that Coreboot still does not support AMD Ryzen chips (or AMD does not support Coreboot, depending on how you want to look at it), so the Pangolin Pro does not use open firmware.
Finally, the Pangolin Pro is easy to open up to replace or repair components. There are nine screws on the bottom of the chassis, and none of them are hidden under the rubber feet or other shenanigans. Unscrew them all, and the bottom lifts off, giving you access to the SSD slots, RAM, WiFi card, and the rest of the internals. You'll have no trouble upgrading components down the road if you decide to, say, upgrade your memory when RAM prices come back down. (Is that actually going to happen? Who knows.)
Pop!_OS Linux Integration
System76's Pop!_OS Linux has long provided what I consider one of the best Linux experiences out there. The Cosmic Desktop and the custom apps System76 ships with it provide that "just works" stability you need to use Linux daily without even noticing you're using Linux.
As a long-time Linux user, I'm probably biased, but I find Linux to offer a better user experience than MacOS or Windows. I never feel like I'm fighting the operating system to get things the way I want them. I mainly run a terminal for writing, email, reading RSS feeds, etc, and a web browser. When I need to edit photos, I open Darktable; videos in DaVinci Resolve. None of that should require much from an operating system, but for some reason it's all easier for me in Linux.
Pop!_OS is particularly good in this regard, as it manages to feel familiar enough for Linux newcomers to find their way around, while still offering a good amount of power-user features. For instance, if you don't know what tiling windows are, you never need to be bothered about them, but if you want them, you can enable them with a toggle switch in the settings app. There are loads of (customizable) keyboard shortcuts for developers who eschew the mouse, and there are plenty of trackpad gestures to control workspaces, window focus, and more.
Should You Buy It?
At the beginning, I said the Pangolin Pro is overkill for most peoples needs, which is true. Although the Pangolin is actually cheaper than the smaller System76 Lemur Pro (review coming soon), the more portable Lemur Pro might be a better fit for many. However, if you're doing highly intensive things with your laptop, building local AI models or training custom agents, compiling software, or just want a powerful, future-proof machine, Pangolin is one of the best Linux laptops I've tested.
If you're a Linux user looking for a 16-inch laptop with all the bells and whistles, and one that isn't crazy expensive or crazy heavy, this is the machine I would get.

A major outage disrupted parts of the Dutch rail network early Tuesday and the company that maintains the infrastructure said it was treating the cause as possible sabotage.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers use the train network each day. The stoppages on Tuesday affected thousands of passengers mainly in the central and eastern areas of the Netherlands, but the problem also affected some services in the busiest western regions of the country.
Joke van der Cruysen, a spokesperson for infrastructure company Prorail, told The Associated Press that there were disruptions at 24 locations.
"Material has been found at several locations. It appears that this material was deliberately placed on the tracks. We suspect sabotage," she said in a telephone interview. "The police are currently involved and are actively investigating the cause and the reasons behind this."
There was no immediate indication of who was suspected of being behind the apparent sabotage.
Van der Cruysen said Prorail was working to clear all rails and handling material taken off rails carefully so as not to compromise potential evidence.
"We wear gloves so that the police can eventually check for fingerprints and the like," she said. "And, of course, we try to get train traffic up and running again as soon as possible."
Police spokeswoman Marloes Wesselink confirmed that an investigation was underway, but declined to give further details. She said that she wasn't aware of any claim of responsibility.
National railway company NS said that train services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort were hit hard around the morning rush hour.
"It is not yet clear how long it will take for train services to return to normal," NS said in an message to travelers.
The disruption happened on the day that the Dutch government is presenting its annual budget to parliament, an event that draws thousands of people to The Hague to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages.

China's retail sales slow again as Beijing struggles to revive consumer spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:56:53 UTC
17:56:53 KST

Retail sales in China grew just 0.4% in August, the slowest pace since growth resumed and the second consecutive monthly slowdown, underlining how little progress Beijing has made in reviving consumer spending even as factory output accelerates.
Chinese shoppers are barely spending more than they were a year ago, and the gap between what the country makes and what it buys is widening.
Figures published by China's National Bureau of Statistics on Tuesday showed year-on-year retail sales growth of just 0.4%, falling short of the 0.8% economists had forecast and slowing from 0.6% in July and 1% in June.
However, the number is at least positive.
Retail sales shrank 0.6% in May, so August represents an improvement on the low point, but it leaves consumption close to flat at a time when the Chinese government has made reviving it a priority.
Domestic spending has been sluggish since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, dragging on economic growth even as exports have boomed.
Factories up, investment down
The rest of the data pulls in opposite directions.
Industrial production expanded 5.2% in August, a jump from July's 4.5% and comfortably ahead of the 4.8% forecast. Fixed-asset investment, by contrast, contracted 7.2% year on year in the first eight months of 2026, in line with forecasts.
The statistics bureau said the economy "operated steadily" last month while conceding that "adverse external factors are intensifying."
It went further in describing the underlying problem by stating that "the domestic imbalance between strong supply and weak demand remains pronounced, some firms face operational difficulties, and the foundation for steady economic improvement requires consolidation."
Analysts read the same split.
"China's economy continues to show diverging signals, as consumption and investment remain weak while industrial production maintains the momentum," wrote Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.
Beijing is targeting economic growth of between 4.5% and 5.0% for this year, its lowest goal in decades.
Money already committed
The figures land days after Beijing moved to shore up its financial system.
Announced the previous Sunday, the finance ministry is leading a 360 billion yuan (€46.1bn) capital injection into eight state-owned banks and insurers, with around 290 billion yuan (€37.2bn) going to banks specifically to preserve their capacity to keep lending as the government presses them to support and stimulate economic activity.
Whether that filters through to household spending remains a question.
Zhang expects continued weakness in the near term precisely because fiscal support takes time to reach the economy.
"The economy faces downside risk in [the third quarter] as the fiscal support takes time to be implemented and transmitted to the economy," he wrote.
That leaves Beijing leaning on the one part of the economy still performing, with industrial output expanding and exports remaining strong.
The next move is diplomatic.
Xi Jinping is expected to travel to Washington on 24 September and is reportedly preparing to bring a large delegation of Chinese business executives — a departure for a leader who rarely travels with corporate figures and has not done so on this scale since 2015.
Many of those executives lost standing during the regulatory crackdowns on technology, education and property that began in 2020.
Bringing them to meet US President Donald Trump would signal a willingness to invest and trade, though expectations for the summit remain modest, with the two sides still divided over which products should count as non-sensitive under existing trade arrangements.
