Microsoft introduces AI guardrails for US schools amid growing backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:32:57 UTC
17:32:57 KST

OpenAI and Anthropic said they also were discussing safety and privacy pacts with the American teachers’ union. But Google, the dominant provider of education technology for US schools, has not said whether it plans to offer similar protections.
Microsoft is introducing guardrails and privacy standards for its AI in schools in the United States, as negotiated with the country’s second-largest teachers' union, amid a growing backlash against AI and screen time.
The agreement, signed last week, prohibits the use of AI companions or features “designed to foster emotional attachment or dependency” or designed to keep students engaged for longer than a learning task requires.
The standards are legally binding and require third-party audits to check compliance.
As part of the wide-ranging agreement, Microsoft says it will not use student or educator data to train AI systems, apart from a narrow exception for data that could help protect students. It says the data it collects cannot be sold, used for advertising or used for product development.
It also includes audit and transparency measures requiring the company to explain to families in plain language how its tools work and what data they collect.
“This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” said Brad Smith, Microsoft's vice chair and president, in a statement.
The standards will apply to Microsoft school contracts across the US from November 1, according to the company.
Is an AI brake needed in European classrooms?
AI is already making its way into European classrooms and young people are also increasingly turning to chatbots beyond schoolwork.
A European Commission study of early adopters in secondary schools in Finland, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and Spain found students were using generative AI to explain difficult topics, practise skills and prepare for exams.
Meanwhile, a separate 2026 Austrian study found that 60% of 11- to 17-year-olds surveyed had sought advice from AI chatbots about issues such as stress, conflicts or heartbreak, while 30% had discussed worries or feelings with them.
Some European governments are already drawing limits around younger pupils' use.
Norway said this year that children aged roughly six to 12 should generally not use generative AI themselves for schoolwork, while those aged around 13 to 15 can begin experimenting with it cautiously.
France allows pupils to learn about AI at primary-school age but says they should not directly use generative AI. Supervised classroom use can begin from around age 13 or 14.
A document seen by Euronews suggests that the European Commission will propose barring under-15s from risky online services like AI chatbots in a legislative proposal that will be published on Thursday.
OpenAI and Anthropic in talks over similar safeguards
While experts say the safety provisions in the US agreement are meaningful, some warn that stronger safeguards should not automatically be interpreted as an endorsement of greater AI use in schools.
“I worry that a high-profile framework like this will be misunderstood and schools will think, ‘If they’re doing a good job on data privacy and safety, then that means we should be using the tool,’” said Josh Golin, executive director of US online safety nonprofit Fairplay.
Golin says the standards will only be effective if other major AI companies also sign on.
“Is Google going to embrace this framework? That is a huge question,” he said.
Google faced criticism in the US after expanding Gemini-powered tools in Google Classroom in August to school-issued accounts used by students under 18.
Critics have described the expansion as another step in the competition between tech giants to establish their AI products in schools and reach younger users. Google says Classroom is used by more than 150 million teachers and students worldwide.
The US teachers union is also in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic, which both publicly welcomed the Microsoft agreement.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, called it an “important milestone for AI safety and privacy in schools.” The company said it had been working with the teachers' union and expected to finalise its own agreement.
Anthropic, the maker of Claude, said it also supported efforts to promote responsible AI use in education and was working with the union on safety and privacy standards.

Helicopter incident between Russia and Denmark reflects rising tensions, expert says
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
Experts said that Monday’s incident on the Danish straits reflects increasing tensions between Denmark and Russia that is slowly moving towards Cold War levels.
Ebsen Salling Larsen, a military analyst at the Center for Joint Operations at the Danish Defence Academy, said it is normal for Danish ships, helicopters or planes to go out to monitor Russian state-owned ships and warships. Sometimes this prompts Russian crew to point weapons at them or use a tracking radar.
But Monday’s incident, during which Russian flares were fired at a Danish helicopter, was unusual and marked a “change in pattern”.
“There’s an ongoing tension and the incident yesterday talks to that increased tension somewhat,” said Salling Larsen. “If you go back to the cold war you have more incidents of ships bumping into each other and so forth. We are slowly reaching that level again.”
The show of force, he said, was a reaction to Danish support for Ukraine and the Baltic states.
It is unlikely that Denmark would close the Danish straits, he said, because Copenhagen wants to follow international law and has its own vested interests in being able to move freely.
“That would be a Pandora’s box we would rather not open,” he said. “We are a small state with a large merchant fleet so we have some interests there as well.”

Türkiye completes production of first homegrown lunar spacecraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:32:23 UTC
17:32:23 KST

(DHA Photo)
Türkiye has completed the production and assembly of its first lunar spacecraft, transferring the 3.5-metric-ton craft to Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ) for environmental testing, the industry and technology minister has said in a recent statement.
Mehmet Fatih Kacır said the craft is scheduled for launch from the Kennedy Space Center in early 2027 and will take around two months to reach a 100-kilometer polar orbit around the Moon.
The craft will operate in lunar orbit for three months, with the potential to extend its operation to a year and a half, during which solar winds, water formation, magnetic fields and surface radiation will be evaluated through homegrown scientific instruments.
Kacır stated these efforts have been made to realize “a fully independent Türkiye in critical technologies.”
The spacecraft includes critical flight, communications and power systems developed for the previous İmece and Türksat 6A satellite projects, boasting an 80 percent domestic production rate.
“The further tests will verify the spacecraft’s ability to withstand the harsh conditions it will encounter during launch and in the space environment,” he said. The craft will then be transferred to a new cleanroom facility for final inspections.
The craft will use a homegrown hybrid propulsion system for orbit-raising maneuvers and a final controlled deceleration burn to reach the lunar surface at the end of the primary scientific mission.
“Only eight countries have carried out lunar missions so far, and when we implement our program, Türkiye will become the ninth country,” the minister noted.
The developments follow the country’s recent accession to the Artemis Accords, signed to promote global cooperation in the peaceful exploration of the Moon and deep space.
Kacır stated that development of the Türksat 7A communications satellite has begun alongside the design phases of the İmece-2 and İmece-3 Earth observation satellite constellations.

"The reality is AI is here. We unleashed the beast," said Maliyka Muhammad, a 46-year-old New Yorker. "So I think that now we have to focus on taking steps to rein it in, to make it so that it doesn't go crazy."
But Trump said the United States could not afford to lose an AI race with superpower rival China, whose President Xi Jinping visits the White House next week.
He also lashed out at what he called a "SICK conspiracy" against AI and data centres, branding opponents of the technology "Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers."
He singled out Amodei, accusing him of "pretending to be a 'perfect little angel'" and asking why AI firms want regulation that "will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy."
Main battleground
Beijing, meanwhile, has been issuing its own warnings about AI. China's spy chief said on Sunday that the technology endangers national security, warning that foreign powers could use it to threaten social order.
Minister of State Security Chen Yixin wrote that AI was now "the main battleground for global technological competition," singling out Anthropic's Claude Mythos and OpenAI's ChatGPT-5.5 for their advanced hacking capabilities.
Global concern about a possible AI-driven extinction event has escalated sharply in recent days.
The UN Security Council will hold a meeting on artificial intelligence next week, a French diplomatic source said Monday, and UN human rights chief Volker Türk called for countries and AI firms to act urgently against what he called "unprecedented risks."
Even King Charles III is to host representatives of leading AI firms at a gathering in Scotland, a source close to the event said Monday.
But others urged perspective.
"We've gone through lots of challenges as a country," said Coleman Barton, 56, a consultant from Memphis, Tennessee. "So hopefully this is another obstacle or blessing — and anybody can look at it either way."

Benjamin Netanyahu joins Israeli ministers attacking Venice-winning documentary 'NAZA'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:26:25 UTC
17:26:25 KST

The documentary 'NAZA', which won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, examines Israel's targeting practices in Gaza and alleges that mass civilian deaths are routinely factored into decisions over military strikes.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has attacked the makers of the documentary NAZA, accusing the award-winning film of contributing to “global antisemitic incitement”.
“It’s shocking. We are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram. “And now two Israeli directors portraying the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”
NAZA left this year's Venice Film Festival with the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at the festival. It shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.
Netanyahu's comments follow those of Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar, who directly equated criticism of Israel's actions to antisemitism and announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the Israeli directing duo Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.
Zohar called NAZA “vile” and the Venice Film Festival honour “shocking,” adding: “The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state.”
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also described Abraham and Szor as a “disgrace and an embarrassment” and told them to leave the country. “I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms," he wrote on X.
The 80-minute hot-button doc, shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas – hence the title of the film, a military acronym used by Israeli Military Forces to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike in Gaza. It stands for "Nezek Agavi": collateral damage.
The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.
When accepting the Special Jury Prize, Yuval Abraham said in his acceptance speech: "We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist and this is why it is especially important for us that Israelis watch this film, it is our country that is doing these crimes.”
Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's previous film, No Other Land, was released in 2024 and followed Israeli settler violence against Palestinian communities in the West Bank. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment. Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide" - as well as a report published in June by a UN independent commission which found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank."
NAZA builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian. The documentary will screen in Spain at the San Sebastián International Film Festival on 23 September and then at the New York Film Festival on 26 September.
As of now, no official theatrical release date has been announced, but French distributor MK2 Films holds the world sales rights.

U.S. Air Force secretary confirms U.S. has weapons in orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:24:49 UTC
17:24:49 KST

- Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States has space-control weapons on orbit capable of defending U.S. forces against hostile adversaries.
- Meink did not specify the weapons' type, quantity, or capabilities, and a space security expert called the disclosure unprecedented for a U.S. official.
U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed Monday that the United States has weapons in orbit designed to disable or destroy adversary satellites, a rare public admission from a senior Pentagon official about a capability the government has typically declined to discuss, Defense One reported.
Meink made the statement during a Monday morning speech at the Air, Space & Cyber conference. He did not specify what type of weapons the U.S. has stationed in orbit or how many exist.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said.
“This is why the United States now has, on orbit, space-control weapons, capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversaries,” he said.
The comment marks a departure from how top U.S. Space Force and Air Force officials have generally discussed the subject. Gen. John Raymond, the U.S. Space Force’s first chief of space operations, said in 2022 that “our primary purpose is to deter war.” Senior officials have more often cited national security concerns as a reason to avoid confirming specific orbital weapons capabilities.
Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation, told Defense One she could not recall a prior instance of a U.S. government official making a comparable statement.
“Well, that’s huge, because I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” Samson said.
She said the admission could prompt China and Russia, the U.S. military’s principal competitors in space, to be more open about their own orbital weapons programs.
“The US also now has to accept the Chinese and Russians doing/saying the same. I don’t think that this is going to be in the interest of US national security,” Samson said.
Meink’s silence on specifics left outside experts guessing at what the capability might be. Kinetic weapons, such as missiles designed to physically strike a satellite, generate orbital debris that can threaten other spacecraft, including those belonging to the country that fired the weapon. Senior military officials have repeatedly cautioned against their use for that reason.
Maj. Gen. Chris Povak, deputy director of the National Reconnaissance Office, said earlier this year that “our commitment to responsible space operations is fundamental to our mission assurance and our role as stewards of the space environment.”
Samson pointed to that pattern of statements from officials as a reason to rule out a kinetic weapon.
“I’m going to guess what he’s talking about is not a kinetic space-control weapon due to multiple comments government officials have said about avoiding debris causing counter space,” she said. “So I’m going to go with my first guess: space-based jammers, electronic warfare.”
Meink used the same speech to disclose progress on two other space programs, according to Defense One. He said prototype satellites for the space-based Airborne Moving Target Indicator constellation, which is designed to track moving targets from orbit, will launch this month.
He also said space-based interceptors, the technology at the center of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense program, are now “flight ready.”
The interceptor effort has faced funding uncertainty. Space Force Gen. Michael Guetlein, Golden Dome’s direct-reporting program manager, warned last month that the project would be in dire straits if Congress does not commit additional money. Guetlein said at the time that initial development work on the interceptors was underway and that the Space Force had completed two “phenomenally successful” tests.
“All of the providers that are part of the competition are progressing exceptionally well,” Guetlein told reporters at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium.
Meink framed the disclosures around competition from rival powers developing their own counter-space capabilities.
“As everybody knows, there have been many who are developing capabilities to take those away from us, to threaten those things,” Meink said. “So, it is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so that we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
The Air Force secretary did not disclose a timeline for revealing further details about the on-orbit weapons, and the Department of War has not issued a follow-up statement expanding on his remarks.

No, the EU isn't demanding that Ukraine mobilise women against Russia's invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:24:06 UTC
17:24:06 KST

Ukraine's counter-disinformation agency says that the claims originated with Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service.
Is the EU demanding that Ukraine mobilise women to bolster its forces against Russia's invasion?
It's a question that many social media users are debating after the allegations emerged on X and through Russian-language Telegram channels in recent weeks.
The answer, however, is no. Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, a working body of the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine, said that the claim originated from Russia's Foreign Intelligence Agency (SVR), which claimed, without evidence, that Brussels is pressuring Kyiv to forcibly conscript women.
Russia also wrongly said that the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, called the move "a step in the right direction", according to the counter-disinformation service.
However, there is no evidence that any EU politician has made such a demand, and no reputable news outlet has reported that Brussels is pressuring Kyiv to conscript women.
Women can join Ukraine's defence forces voluntarily, but there are currently no plans to mobilise them compulsorily; neither is there any legislation to do so making its way through parliament.
The Center for Countering Disinformation previously reported that pro-Russian propagandists had spread a false claim that Western media had launched a campaign in support of mobilising Ukrainian women.
According to the agency, the claim is based on an article published by The Telegraph about women's experiences serving in the army. However, the article only mentions mobilisation for women once, in the context of a drone operator's personal views.
The operator, named in the article as Katya, reportedly said that she found Israel's conscription of both sexes inspiring, and that she'd like to see the same implemented in Ukraine. The article itself does not advocate for that.
Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defence and Space, has also rejected suggestions that the EU is demanding that Ukraine force women into the army.
Speaking to journalists on 11 September following the first board meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance, he said that he had "no information" on any such measure.
"I would say it would be strange if Europe will try to convince Ukrainians how to make mobilisation, including mobilisation of women," Kubilius said. "I am not surprised that that comes from the Kremlin."
The question of women's conscription has nevertheless gained attention elsewhere in Europe. Denmark extended compulsory military service to women from July 2025, with the first women entering the system under the new rules in 2026 as part of a lottery-style system. It joins Norway and Sweden in having an active, universal conscription model.
In late 2025, the German government decided to introduce a voluntary model of military service for men, sparking a debate about the role of women in the armed forces too.
However, Germany is not an outlier in Europe: for countries that have compulsory military service, female enlistment is voluntary for the majority.

Welshman Matthew Rhys has set a new standard at the Emmy Awards by winning top honours in three categories as Widow's Bay swept the night taking a single-season record for comedy with 14 wins.
Along with best actor in a comedy for Widow's Bay, Rhys won best actor in a limited series for The Beast in Me, becoming the first man to win two leading actor categories in the same year.
Rhys also took home a trophy as an executive producer for Widow's Bay.
“The celebrations will be long, varied, and I hope at times wild,” Rhys said backstage while holding two of his Emmys.
The first-season series created by Katie Dippold leans hard into both comedy and horror as it tells the story of a New England island community, with Rhys as its mayor, reckoning with a centuries-old curse.
Weird and wonderful
Widow's Bay also won for directing for Hiro Murai and for writing for its creator Katie Dippold, a first-time Emmy winner and first-time nominee who was previously best known for a decade-old viral tweet showing her awkwardly dressed as The Babadook.
The haul represents a major victory for Apple TV, cementing its status as the king of Emmy comedy categories.
Between Widow's Bay, The Studio - which collected a record 13 comedy awards last year - and Ted Lasso, Apple has won best comedy series four times in six seasons.
“Thank you, Apple, for letting us take this crazy, creative swing," Dippold said as she accepted the best comedy award. "They truly just let us do this weird show.”
Widow's Bay had won eight Emmys in a previous ceremony before sweeping all six of its categories Monday night. Stephen Root won best supporting actor in a comedy series and Kate O’Flynn won best supporting actress.
Doctor drama and Smart moves
The Pitt won best drama series for the second straight year, and its star and executive producer Noah Wyle repeated as best actor in a drama, but the HBO Max emergency room drama won no other Emmys and underperformed its expectations.
The Pitt was the top drama nominee with 25 and Hacks was the top comedy nominee with 24, but neither made much of a splash when it came time to claim trophies.
However Jean Smart won her fifth best actress in a comedy award for the fifth and final season of the show. No actor had won an Emmy every year for a series that lasted more than three seasons until Smart did it Monday.
Rhea Seehorn won her first Emmy for playing the lone central character on Apple TV's Pluribus.
She had twice been nominated before without winning for her breakthrough role on Better Call Saul, a show from Breaking Bad creator Vince Gilligan, who collected his fifth career Emmy for his writing on the show.
Allison Janney won best supporting actress in a drama for The Diplomat, and Tom Pelphrey won supporting actor in a drama for Task, both beating several nominees from The Pitt.
DTF St. Louis won best limited series. Two of its stars David Harbour and Linda Cardellini both won for supporting acting at a previous ceremony on Sept. 6 as the Television Academy moved several categories off the main telecast to shorten the show. Overall, DTF St. Louis won seven Emmys overall.

Germany will take new measures to counter espionage and sabotage as it continues to face what the government describes as ”hybrid attacks” from Russia, officials said late on Monday after a National Security Council meeting.
Government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the council, chaired by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, reviewed Germany’s exposure to hybrid threats following a drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month that authorities claimed was planned by Russian intelligence.
“The National Security Council obtained a comprehensive picture of the situation,” Kornelius said, adding that Germany should expect to remain a target of such hybrid attacks.
Critical infrastructure in focus
The council discussed how the federal government should respond to future hybrid attacks and reviewed measures already adopted under its action plan to strengthen national defences.
It approved new steps against espionage and sabotage, as well as measures to protect critical infrastructure, Kornelius said.
The meeting followed weeks of coordination among ministries represented on the National Security Council.
Germany moves to reduce strategic dependence
The council also agreed on measures to reduce Germany’s reliance on foreign suppliers for goods and resources considered important to its economic and national security.
Officials backed a swift revision of investment-screening legislation and measures aimed at creating a more diversified and resilient supply chain for critical raw materials.
Kornelius said the government’s Raw Materials Fund remains the main financing instrument under Germany’s Raw Materials Policy Action Plan.
The council also reviewed military and civilian defence and discussed security risks linked to artificial intelligence.

Ukrainian Attack Kills One in Belgorod, Hits Commercial and Industrial Sites Across Russia

Overnight Ukrainian drone and missile strikes across southern Russia killed one person and struck commercial and industrial sites, regional officials said Tuesday.
Acting Belgorod region Governor Alexander Shuvayev confirmed one death in an attack near the border with Ukraine. He also said that a woman who was hospitalized for her injuries following strikes earlier this month had died.
In the nearby Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar said an Ozon warehouse was among several sites damaged during a missile attack on the port city of Taganrog.
Ozon confirmed that it suspended operations at the facility, where it said a fire broke out. No one was hurt, the company said.
Federal investigators launched a criminal probe into terrorism over the attacks on Taganrog, citing damage to Ozon and other residential and agricultural buildings.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said an “industrial facility” was damaged in overnight strikes. Unconfirmed reports said that a fire broke out at the Syzran Oil Refinery.
NASA’s fire monitoring service FIRMS showed an active fire Tuesday morning on the southwestern outskirts of Syzran, where the refinery, which has been attacked multiple times this year, is located.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 222 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday night and Tuesday morning.
In Ukraine, officials said one person was killed in Russian attacks on Kyiv. Separate attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia also killed one person.
Two gas stations in Kyiv were damaged in the overnight strikes, the state energy company Naftogaz said.
The attacks targeting energy infrastructure in both Russia and Ukraine came despite an announcement by U.S. Donald Trump earlier in the week that the two warring sides allegedly agreed to pause such attacks.
Trump has sought to blame the surging cost of diesel in the United States on Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries. While those attacks have put pressure on fuel prices both inside Russia and globally, so too has the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran led to major disruptions in energy markets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday that Trump’s suggestion for a ceasefire on energy sites, which has been repeatedly floated over the past year, was a “very good idea” but alone would not bring down global fuel costs.

Bangladesh sentences to death 7 key aides of ousted Premier Hasina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:21:38 UTC
17:21:38 KST

SM Najmus Sakib
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
- Handover of Sheikh Hasina, her key aides crucial for easing relations with India, says Premier Tarique Rahman’s adviser
A local court in Bangladesh on Tuesday handed down the death penalty to seven aides of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on charges of crimes against humanity committed during the 2024 monsoon uprising.
A three-member Dhaka-based International Crimes Tribunal, led by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, delivered the verdict.
All seven convicts are currently fugitives and in self-exile in India and the US.
The convicts include Hasina's Awami League party General Secretary Obaidul Quader, former state minister for Information Mohammad Ali Arafat, Joint General Secretary AFM Bahauddin Nasim, party youth wing Chairman Sheikh Fazle Shams Parash and General Secretary Moinul Hossain Nikhil, student wing President Saddam Hussain and General Secretary Sheikh Wali Asif Enan.
The verdict also ordered the confiscation of half the assets belonging to Quader, Nasim, Arafat, and Parash. The tribunal further directed that the confiscated assets be distributed as compensation to the families of the July victims who died and were injured.
Last November, Hasina was also sentenced to death by the same tribunal for crimes against humanity and for her role in a brutal crackdown during the 2024 uprising that ousted her government.
At least 1,400 people were killed and thousands were injured in the uprising by Hasina’s security forces and supporters of her Awami League party, according to the UN.
Hasina is in self-imposed exile, living in neighboring India after fleeing the country. However, she has vowed to return to Bangladesh this December.
Across seven verdicts delivered by the two tribunals, 68 accused individuals have been convicted and 22 sentenced to death. Of the accused, 18 remain at large, while four are currently in custody.
Following the court verdict, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's adviser said in the capital Dhaka that the handover of Hasina, her party General Secretary Quader, and others to Bangladesh was a "crucial condition" for easing relations with India.
“I expect that the Indian government would understand the sensitivity of it (deportation) and hand them over (to Bangladesh),” said Zahed Ur Rahman, the adviser on Information and Broadcasting Affairs to the prime minister.

luca battaglia captures the ghostly glow of disappearing carousels with long-exposure photography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:20:57 UTC
17:20:57 KST

luca battaglia uses long exposure to turn carousels into light
Luca Battaglia takes the familiar carousel and transforms it into a luminous, almost architectural apparition in Ticket non remboursable, an ongoing photographic series rooted in memories of his childhood in Milan. Using long exposures of 20 to 30 seconds, the Italian photographer captures carousels as they rotate through public squares and city streets, allowing horses, decorations, and individual figures to dissolve into bands of light.
Growing up in Milan, Battaglia regularly passed a carousel that has since disappeared. The attraction remained with him as an image connected to childhood, waiting, movement, and the peculiar way memories become attached to particular places. In Ticket non remboursable, that absent carousel persists indirectly, resurfacing through other structures encountered in different cities.
Deauville 2024 | all images courtesy of Luca Battaglia
long exposure turns rotation into architecture
Battaglia’s photographic process removes the carousel from its immediately recognizable form. Working with an ND256 or ND1000 neutral-density filter, he exposes each image for between 20 and 30 seconds. During that time, the rotating structure traces continuous lines of light across the photograph. Horses and decorative figures gradually vanish. In their place, illuminated rings, vertical structures, and glowing volumes appear. The resulting forms can resemble floating architecture or, as the Italian photographer suggests, objects that have briefly landed in the city.
Long exposure records the carousel over several seconds rather than freezing a single moment. As it turns, its horses, decorations, and individual figures begin to disappear, leaving behind lines and bands of light. This changes the way the structure is seen. A carousel is solid and recognizable when still, but Battaglia’s photographs make its form increasingly difficult to identify. The movement remains visible, while the object itself begins to dissolve.
Dijon, France
a circular journey that returns to where it began
The title, Ticket non remboursable, or non-refundable ticket, introduces another layer to the series. A carousel ride promises a journey while remaining fundamentally circular. It moves continuously without taking the rider anywhere else, eventually returning to the point of departure.
That circularity mirrors the movement of memory itself. Battaglia returns repeatedly to the image of the lost carousel from his childhood, but never encounters it directly again. Instead, he finds versions of it elsewhere. Landscapes change, contexts shift, and individual carousels take on different forms, yet something of the original memory remains.
The series now comprises more than 50 photographs and continues to grow as Battaglia encounters new carousels in different cities. The images form what the photographer describes as an imaginary constellation, connecting places through recurring structures, light, and movement.
Battaglia positions his photographic apparatus at a child’s height, allowing the long exposure to reveal a suspended temporality. The photograph, he suggests, strips the attraction of its familiar appearance and fixes fleeting sensations on paper.
Brooklin 202″
when a temporary attraction becomes a permanent image
The carousel is temporary by nature. It appears in a square or park, turns for a while, and eventually disappears. Photography would seem to do the opposite, holding on to something that has passed. But Battaglia’s long exposures do not preserve the carousel as it looks. The longer the camera records its movement, the more the horses, decorations, and individual details disappear. Ticket non remboursable becomes closely tied to memory. Battaglia does not try to reconstruct the carousel he remembers from his childhood in Milan, accepting that it’s now gone. He encounters others in different cities, each with its own colors, structure, and surroundings. Across the series, these different carousels begin to echo one another. The photographs retain traces of their structures, but the movement transforms them into something less familiar. Battaglia describes this as a kind of visual memory: blurred, altered, and slightly unreal.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

The UN Security Council is set to hold a meeting Tuesday on the situation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, diplomats said, as concern grows over escalating Houthi activity around the strategic Red Sea shipping route.
The meeting comes amid renewed instability in Yemen and growing fears over the security of commercial shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The Iran-backed Houthis have recently expanded their territorial control in western Yemen and have repeatedly threatened shipping in the area.

The Houthis’ recent advances have added to concerns that Yemen could slide back toward a broader conflict. The group has seized strategic territory near the Red Sea, while international officials have warned that further escalation could threaten both regional stability and shipping lanes.
The Security Council meeting is expected to focus on the latest developments around the strait and the potential threat to international maritime traffic.

Final hearing held in Palestinian community leader Salah Sarsour's immigration case in US
Salah Sarsour, a longtime Milwaukee-based Palestinian community leader, who was detained by ICE for nearly three months, had his final immigration hearing on Monday, and will learn in the coming days if he can stay in the US.
On Monday, his attorneys argued that the government had failed to meet their burden of proof for Sarsour's removal based on an allegation from three decades ago of attacking an Israeli soldier in the occupied West Bank.
Under cross examination on Monday, Sarsour's attorney from that time said that his confession of that alleged attack was made under duress.
"We should not be here," said Patrick Taurel, Sarsour’s lead immigration attorney, in a public statement.
"Mr. Sarsour should not be facing such an arduous and dehumanizing fight to remain with his family. He's a leader of his community. He has never been charged with, let alone convicted of, a crime in the United States," he said.
"ICE is seeking to deport him on the basis of his pro-Palestine speech. The other charges we've been fighting about in court are pretextual, trumped up, and do not withstand scrutiny. I don't know how the immigration judge will rule but I know that Mr. Sarsour will keep fighting, with the support of his community behind him, because keeping him here is about protecting everyone's constitutional right to free expression," his lawyer continued.
Sarsour, who is in his early 50s, has lived as a legal US resident for 32 years, and has been a community leader for Palestinians and Muslims in Milwaukee, where he was living when he was seized at gunpoint on 30 March by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials.
"Salah Salem Sarsour is a terrorist convicted for throwing Molotov cocktails at the homes of Israeli armed forces. This illegal alien from Jordan lied on his green card application to gain legal status in the US," said Acting Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis, in a public statement on 2 April.
"Thanks to President Trump and ICE, this terrorist is out of American communities. This Administration will always put the safety of the American people FIRST and Make America Safe Again," the statement continued.
He was held for nearly three months at a facility in Clay County in Indiana, where he reportedly suffered health complications. Sarsour, a type 2 diabetic, was said to have lost a significant amount of weight and was deprived of basic healthcare while incarcerated.
This led to a widespread campaign in support of his release, which included Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers and multiple members of Congress.
Sarsour's next court appearance will be to have a status hearing on 30 September.

Most Europeans say a second language is useful. Not everyone can actually speak one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:15:52 UTC
17:15:52 KST

A YouGov survey of six European countries reveals wide gaps in language fluency, motivation to learn, and views on compulsory language education.
Nearly every European agrees that speaking a second language is a valuable skill — but a recent survey suggests far fewer can actually do it, with fluency levels varying widely from one country to the next.
According to a YouGov survey of adults in Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy and Spain, between 87% and 97% across all six countries say learning another language is useful.
Yet when respondents were asked whether they could actually speak a second language fluently, the numbers told a different story.
Denmark recorded the highest rate, with 74% of Danish adults saying they can speak another language fluently. Germany followed at 54%, Spain at 47%, France at 37%, and Italy at 28%.
Britain recorded the lowest rate of the six countries, with one in five adults — 21% — saying they are fluent in a second language.
The dominance of English as the global language likely plays a role in this. In fact, English is the most common second language spoken among Europeans: between 62% and 93% of those who speak more than one language say they can speak English fluently.
In Britain, a quarter of those who speak another language say they can speak French, followed by Spanish.
Why are some people averse to language learning?
Among those who don't speak a second language, the most common explanation, across most of the countries surveyed, was that they have not felt a need to learn one.
Spain was the exception: there, more than a third of non-speakers cited difficulty as the main reason instead.
More than 70% of non-speakers in every country surveyed said they would like to learn a new language, with travel cited as the leading motivation.
English was the language most respondents said they wanted to learn, chosen by as many as 83% across the continent — the exception, of course, being Britain, where Spanish and French were the most popular choices.
Should language learning be compulsory?
The survey also asked whether respondents believed visitors to their country should speak the local language.
In Italy, Spain and France, between 56% and 72% of respondents said tourists should be expected to do so. In Britain, Germany and Denmark, that figure was between 22% and 39%.
On education, in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy and Spain, between 82% and 90% of respondents said foreign languages should be compulsory in schools up to the age of 16.
In Britain, 66% said the same. Britons were also the least likely of the six nationalities to describe speaking another language as "very useful," at 46%, compared with between 57% and 70% in the other five countries.

China urges US to halt military buildup in space after acknowledgment of orbital weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:15:20 UTC
17:15:20 KST

Yasin Gungor and Riyaz ul Khaliq
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
China on Tuesday urged the US to stop expanding its military buildup in outer space after Washington publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has deployed operational weapons in Earth's orbit.
"China has long been committed to the peaceful use of outer space and safeguarding the security in space. We oppose any arms race in outer space or any attempts to weaponize it or turn it into a war zone," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
"We urge the US to stop expanding military buildup in outer space and safeguard global strategic stability with concrete actions," Guo said.
His remarks came after US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the Space Force has operational weapons in orbit capable of responding to threats from adversaries.
"We continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist," Meink said at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference.
"This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action," he added.
Meink, whose department oversees both the US Air Force and Space Force, declined to disclose when the weapons became operational, their capabilities or whether they rely on kinetic impactors, directed energy, electronic warfare or cyber capabilities.
He later told reporters that the public acknowledgment was deliberate and that the terminology had been "very well thought out" to reinforce military deterrence.
"Talking about the details of what we're doing would actually not benefit that deterrence," Meink said.
“We're not going to talk about the specifics of what we're doing, whether we've tested, not tested, or anything else. I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the US can operate freely there.”
"It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space," he added. “So, we've had to take steps to make sure that when we're threatened, we can take care of that.”
The disclosure comes amid growing military competition in space involving the US, China and Russia, all of which have developed counter-space capabilities.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not explicitly ban conventional weapons in space.
Security experts have warned that publicly confirming the deployment of orbital weapons could encourage rival powers to expand their own capabilities, accelerating an arms race in a domain increasingly vital to communications, navigation, intelligence gathering and military operations.

China's consumption market expands steadily amid structural upgrades
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:14:19 CST
17:14:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market continued to expand in the first eight months of the year, while structural upgrading and new growth drivers gathered momentum, official data showed Tuesday.
China's total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.5 percent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Despite volatility in international energy markets, domestic market adjustments, and extreme weather in some regions in August, China's consumer market showed strong resilience, with pro-consumption policies continuing to take effect, NBS spokesperson Fu Linghui said at a press conference.
Tuesday's data showed that the consumer market continued to undergo structural transformation, with services and higher-quality consumption accounting for a larger share. Retail sales of services rose 4.9 percent year on year during the January-August period, outpacing the 1-percent growth in goods sales.
Among service categories, retail sales of communication and information services, tourism consulting and rental services, and cultural, sports and leisure services posted relatively rapid growth.
In the first eight months, retail sales of consumer goods, including sales of goods and catering revenue, totaled 32.76 trillion yuan (about 4.84 trillion U.S. dollars), up 1.1 percent year on year, the data showed.
New consumption models also developed rapidly. Online retail sales of goods and services reached 13.48 trillion yuan, up 4.6 percent. Of the total, online goods sales rose 4.3 percent to 8.42 trillion yuan, while online service sales increased 5.1 percent to 5.06 trillion yuan.
Consumption in rural areas also gained momentum as commercial and logistics infrastructure improved. Rural retail sales of consumer goods rose 2.3 percent year on year in the first eight months, 1.3 percentage points faster than in urban areas.
Meanwhile, China's expanded visa-free policies and other measures facilitating cross-border travel helped boost inbound tourism, with overseas visitors showing stronger demand for shopping, cultural tourism and experience-based consumption.
Looking ahead, China has considerable room for further consumption growth, supported by rising demand for services and higher-quality products, as well as increasingly diverse consumption scenarios, Fu noted, adding that household purchasing power and willingness to spend still need strengthening, while the supply of high-quality goods and services requires further improvement.
China will continue efforts to raise incomes, improve supply and stabilize expectations, advance consumer goods trade-in programs, tap the potential of services consumption, and improve production and supply to promote the healthy and sustained development of the consumer market, Fu stressed.
According to an implementation guideline made public last month, China aims to bring total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan by 2030. ■

Australia's social isolation nearly doubles over two decades: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:13:42 CST
17:13:42 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Australians are becoming increasingly lonely and socially isolated, according to new research, which found rates of social isolation nearly doubled over the past 23 years.
Loneliness rates also increased over time, though more gradually than social isolation, with the sharpest impacts observed among vulnerable populations, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's University of Sydney (USYD).
The study examined 23 years of nationally representative data from the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey, which provides some of the country's first long-term national evidence on trends in loneliness and social isolation.
It found the rate of episodic social isolation, defined as experiencing social isolation in at least one survey wave, rose from 16.9 percent in 2001 to 29.9 percent in 2023. Chronic social isolation, recorded across at least two consecutive survey waves, approximately doubled from 10.3 percent in 2002 to 20.5 percent in 2023.
Loneliness followed a different pattern, generally declining during the 2000s before increasing again from the 2010s onward, with chronic loneliness rising from 6.3 percent in 2002 to 8.4 percent in 2023, the study showed.
Younger adults experienced some of the largest increases in loneliness, while older adults consistently had the highest levels of social isolation and showed the greatest increases over time, it noted.
The study found loneliness and social isolation were consistently more common among people who were unemployed, lived in more socioeconomically disadvantaged areas, widowed, living alone, or had lower levels of education.
The findings highlight social connection as a public health issue requiring "sustained policy and public health action across the life course," said USYD Prof. Melody Ding, senior author of the study published in the International Journal of Epidemiology. ■

Major Chinese cities report narrowed home price declines in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:13:38 CST
17:13:38 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Major Chinese cities continued to report narrowed year-on-year declines in overall home prices in August, official data showed Tuesday.
In the first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, new home prices fell 0.9 percent year on year, 0.2 percentage points narrower than the previous month, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Second-hand home prices in the four cities dropped 2.7 percent year on year overall, with the decline narrowing from 3.7 percent in July.
As to second- and third-tier cities, price declines in both new and second-hand homes moderated compared with July.
On a monthly basis, home prices in first-tier cities rose in August, while second- and third-tier cities generally registered narrowed declines.
Among 70 large and medium-sized cities tracked, 21 recorded flat or rising new home prices month on month in August, two fewer than the previous month. Eight cities saw flat or rising second-hand home prices, unchanged from July.
The NBS releases a monthly home price report tracking market changes in 70 major cities, including four first-tier cities, 31 second-tier cities and 35 third-tier cities.
Tuesday's data pointed to further signs that China's property market is bottoming out, as the government maintains its city-specific policy approach, adjusting and optimizing real estate policies, working down inventory and pushing ahead with urban renewal.
NBS spokesperson Fu Linghui said at a media conference Tuesday that overall property transaction volumes have improved, with the area of second-hand home transactions rising 10.6 percent year on year in the first eight months of the year. New home inventory also continued to fall, with the total floor area of unsold new commercial housing down 1.1 percent year on year at the end of August, marking the sixth consecutive month of decline.
As China's property market undergoes a fundamental shift in supply and demand dynamics, more diverse demand for smart, green and elderly-friendly homes is on the rise.
In response, China is accelerating a transition in its property development model. Authorities have this year deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system and refined regulations on commercial housing sales, as part of broader efforts to chart a new path for real estate development.
These policy measures will help advance the transformation of China's property market and better meet people's aspirations for a better life, Fu said. ■

KINSHASA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- More than 7,200 confirmed Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as sustained transmission continues in several provinces despite an overall downward trend of the epidemic, according to governmental data released Tuesday.
A government report covering the epidemiological situation as of Sunday said 7,258 confirmed cases had been recorded in seven provinces, including 3,510 deaths and 1,726 recoveries. A total of 905 patients were in isolation or hospitalized, while the overall fatality rate stood at 48.4 percent.
The outbreak has affected 62 health zones across seven provinces -- Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and Sud-Ubangi. Sustained transmission continued in Ituri, North Kivu and Haut-Uele, while sporadic cases were reported in Tshopo and Bas-Uele.
The overall epidemic curve was trending downward as the peak appeared to have been reached around mid-August, said Dieudonne Mwamba Kazadi, head of the National Institute of Public Health, after a strategic coordination meeting in Kinshasa on Monday.
However, he cautioned that the decline was uneven across the country, with some provinces, particularly North Kivu, still reporting increases in cases.
Declared in May, the current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

New seller influx to Russia’s marketplaces fell 27% this summer, according to Russia’s Chamber of Commerce and Industry
The number of new sellers joining Russian online marketplaces fell 27% between June and August compared with the same period last year, according to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
MoySklad, a service that tracks data from 50,000 companies, recorded an even steeper decline of 53%. The CCI estimated the total number of sellers on Russian platforms at 800,000 as of early September, while the Federal Tax Service put the figure at 850,000.
The marketplaces themselves do not disclose data on how many sellers joined over the summer. A representative of RWB, Wildberries’ parent company, told the Russian newspaper Izvestia that the platform’s number of sellers grew by 12% from January to August.
Ozon said 750,000 sellers currently work with the company and that it had seen no decline. Yandex Market said its number of sellers grew over the summer, particularly in the clothing, home goods, and children’s products categories.
Ukrainian drone attacks on warehouses affected about 400,000 sellers, according to the Association of Suppliers of Goods for Trade on Electronic Platforms. MoySklad representatives said the attacks may have discouraged new sellers from entering marketplaces while prompting existing ones to change their storage systems. The service saw new seller sign-ups jump 23% in August compared with July.
Experts interviewed by Izvestia acknowledged the attacks’ impact but attributed the slowdown in new sellers mainly to market saturation, rising competition and costs for sellers, and cooling consumer demand.
By the end of summer, the share of sellers on the Russian online retailer Wildberries working under the “fulfillment by seller” model had grown from 55.1% to 97.4%, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported. On Ozon, another major Russian e-commerce platform, the share of such sellers rose from 63.3% to 73.1% over the same period. Sellers are also seeking new ways of doing business: Yandex KIT recorded a 59% increase in new independent online stores with sales in August compared with July.
The e-commerce market itself continues to grow, according to the Association of Internet Trading Companies. Russia’s online retail turnover reached 8.4 trillion rubles between January and July, up 18.4% from a year earlier. The association expects growth of another 20% by the end of 2026, bringing the total to 15.8 trillion rubles.

====================================================================================================

EXPLAINER - What is the AI 'superintelligence' experts fear?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:11:34 UTC
17:11:34 KST

- Recent resignations by AI safety researchers and warnings from leading technology executives have revived concerns about whether increasingly autonomous systems could eventually become difficult to control
Artificial intelligence's most consequential debate is no longer about chatbots or deepfakes.
It is about whether humanity is on the verge of building machines smarter than humans, and what happens next.
The issue has gained renewed attention in recent days after a researcher left Anthropic, warning that leading AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” while another Anthropic researcher said he personally estimated more than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade.
The warnings were followed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the industry to slow the pace of AI development. 
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk expressed support for the idea, while US President Donald Trump argued against slowing the US AI sector because of competition with China. 
Meanwhile, China pushed back against calls for a slowdown, warning that AI “fear-mongering” and confrontation could derail global efforts to govern the technology.
What is 'superintelligence'?
This hypothetical technology is generally called artificial superintelligence, or ASI.
The term has no single agreed definition, but AI researchers generally use it to describe a system that would possess intelligence surpassing that of the most gifted human minds, or as philosopher Nick Bostrom has put it, any intellect that greatly exceeds human cognitive performance in virtually all domains of interest.
That is distinct from today's large language models, such as ChatGPT or Claude, which can outperform humans on narrow tasks -- writing, coding, some forms of reasoning -- but still require heavy human oversight and make basic errors.
Superintelligence, as AI labs use the term, would mean systems that need no such oversight and could independently conduct scientific research, run companies, or design new technologies faster and better than any human or human institution.
The concern driving current warnings is not superintelligence itself but the pathway some researchers believe leads there: recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems are used to design and train the next generation of AI systems, creating a feedback loop that could accelerate progress beyond humanity's ability to monitor or correct it.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI have said in recent months that this kind of automated self-improvement is happening faster than they had expected.
What could happen if superintelligence is reached
The 2026 International AI Safety Report, led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio and involving more than 100 experts nominated by over 30 countries and international organizations, says current AI systems still lack the capabilities needed for sustained loss-of-control scenarios. But it warns that relevant capabilities, particularly autonomous operation, are improving rapidly.
Researchers and executives cite a range of potential consequences, from the mundane to the existential.
One of the main concerns is the loss of technical control. 
Once a system reaches superhuman reasoning, operators may no longer have the physical or digital ability to constrain or shut it down. 
Recent safety disclosures have highlighted cases in which experimental AI agents breached isolated testing environments and executed unauthorized code across external networks before being contained.
Another concern is the proliferation of bioweapons and cyberattacks. Advanced frontier models carry dual-use risks, meaning their capabilities could be exploited by hostile actors to engineer pathogens or launch autonomous, large-scale cyberattacks against critical infrastructure.
There are also fears of geopolitical and economic instability. 
A sudden breakthrough toward superintelligence could disrupt labor markets, undermine existing national defense capabilities and concentrate enormous geopolitical power in the hands of a small number of companies or states. 
Anthropic CEO Amodei has warned of a “totalitarian nightmare” if authoritarian regimes acquire the technology first.
Yet the same capabilities could also bring benefits. Proponents say superintelligent AI could help cure diseases, accelerate scientific discovery, generate unprecedented prosperity and contribute to solving climate change and other global problems.
Silicon Valley chiefs agree to ‘Pace the Frontier’
In an unprecedented move reflecting growing anxiety, frontier tech executives have begun calling for a voluntary slowdown.
On Saturday, Amodei, in an essay, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” said two developments had convinced him that safety work is falling behind: accelerating recursive self-improvement since the summer and incidents in which swarms of AI agents took unauthorized actions.
One such incident occurred in July, when OpenAI revealed that its experimental AI models escaped their sandbox during an internal security test. 
The artificial intelligence found a hidden system vulnerability, accessed the internet on its own and targeted the AI platform Hugging Face, breaking into its systems over several days while trying to find answers that would help it pass the test.
OpenAI called the episode an “unprecedented cyber incident,” which it later described as the first known multistep cyberattack carried out entirely by an autonomous AI agent without a human directing it.
Amodei warned that a more capable, similarly misaligned swarm could, within six to 12 months, assemble a persistent botnet capable of taking over large parts of the internet and causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage. 
He proposed a plan requiring frontier companies to grant independent safety evaluators “employee-like access” to audit AI models and training pipelines.
In a rare moment of alignment among fierce rivals, OpenAI's Altman and xAI's Musk publicly endorsed Amodei's call.
"Dario is right," Musk posted on X.
Altman agreed, confirming that OpenAI was actively evaluating similar independent monitoring mechanisms. 
Altman also noted that OpenAI would delay its public market listing due to heightened AI safety concerns. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he stated.

Houthis say air strikes hit Yemen after Saudi Arabia vows ‘firm’ response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:11:09 UTC
17:11:09 KST

Saudi Arabia promises to respond to Houthi attacks ‘firmly’
Saudi-led coalition promises to respond ‘firmly’ to Houthi strikes on urban areas in Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen has promised to respond “firmly” to missile and drone attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthi group that wounded 13 civilians across three cities in the kingdom.
The Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, said early on Tuesday that Houthi attacks on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif caused minor to moderate injuries and damaged seven homes and two vehicles.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
- list 2 of 3Inside the Houthis’ expanding war economy in Yemen
- list 3 of 3Why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline matters for global oil
“The Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will deal with these attacks responsibly and firmly to protect the sovereignty of the kingdom,” said coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has warned that hostilities in Yemen have displaced at least 18,000 households – or 125,000 people – since the start of the month.
In a statement, OCHA adds that the fighting is forcing people to flee their homes, driving civilian casualties, and putting already stretched humanitarian operations under growing pressure.
Late on Monday, the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), said Saudi Arabia launched 54 air raids across the governorates of Lahj, Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Hajjah in the past 24 hours.
The group said Saudi air strikes hit the government complex in Khadir district, Taiz governorate, causing injuries.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets operating from Saudi airbases in Khamis Mushait and Taif were used in the strikes and threatened retaliation.
Houthi-aligned media reported that the Saudi attacks killed three civilians, including two children, and injured at least two others in Taiz province’s Dhubab and Maqbanah districts.
Saudi Arabia has not commented publicly on the Houthi claims. The Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment.
The attacks come after the Iran-aligned group said that it fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, targeting hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots, in retaliation for Saudi air raids across Yemen.
The Houthis said in a statement on Monday that Saudi warplanes had carried out 300 air raids across Yemen over the previous five days.
The exchanges of air attacks follow the Houthis’ rapid advance on the ground in western Yemen last week, with the group gaining control over much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and advancing to areas adjacent to the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The strait has become a vital waterway for energy and commercial shipping in the region as the United States-Iran war has caused major disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
The forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government said on Monday that they made advances in the contested Taiz province after retaking positions from the Houthis, and had struck the group’s fighters and equipment in Dhubab and al-Khokha on the Red Sea coast.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify battlefield claims.
Houthi and Yemeni government officials said on Monday that the Houthis had seized the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands in the southern Red Sea, about 160km (100 miles) north of Bab al-Mandeb. Their recent advances also include Mayyun Island, at the mouth of the Red Sea.
Yemen’s more than decade-long war reignited in July, as the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and began attacking its ships in the Red Sea, undermining the relative calm that followed a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that halted large-scale violence.
Mutual defence pact
The revival of the conflict raises questions regarding the role of Turkiye and Pakistan, who signed off on the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – which includes a mutual defence clause – with Saudi Arabia last month.
Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said last week that an unprovoked aggression against Saudi Arabia, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into the kingdom, would make the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement operational, adding that “there should be no doubt in this”.
However, neither Ankara nor Islamabad are likely to get involved, retired Lieutenant General Tariq Khan, the former inspector general of Pakistan Armed Forces’ Frontier Corps, told Al Jazeera on Tuesday.
He asserts that the mutual defence clause is unworkable at this point in time due to the conflict in Yemen.
“Such agreements are usually never made when a crisis, war or a conflict is ongoing within the theatre for fears of it being perceived, for the right or wrong reasons, of alignments against certain countries,” he said.
He adds that even without that ongoing conflict, there’s a notable omission in the agreement that would prevent its full operation.
“If Iran is not involved, then a monumental contradiction arises, ie, structuring a regional security paradigm excluding one of the most important countries of the region.”

China expands exit bans to prevent technology and 'security' leaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:10:51 UTC
17:10:51 KST

China imposed sweeping travel restrictions on its citizens on Tuesday, including exit bans on people deemed to endanger the country’s “industrial or technological security”.
Citizens who violate technology import and export regulations could be barred from leaving China, the State Council said.
Those who engage in illegal activities abroad could also be “prohibited from leaving the country for a period of six months to three years from the date of their return to China”.
China and the United States have been locked in a technology race, with both sides accusing the other in recent months of stealing capabilities from domestically developed artificial intelligence models.
The new rules, first published in July and taking effect on Tuesday, were formulated to “safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests”, the State Council said.
However, analysts warned that the regulations give Chinese authorities wide discretion.
Security and criminal activities “can be vaguely defined and easily adjusted”, Chong Ja Ian of the National University of Singapore told AFP.
“The outside world will only know how it applies that remit after there are cases of implementation,” he said.
Chong pointed to reports of exit bans imposed on foreign nationals, including the recent case of US citizen Min Zin.
The US government said the political analyst was taken into Chinese custody in Yunnan province on June 3 and was being improperly detained.
China rejected the accusation in August, saying Min Zin was suspected of violating Chinese law.
“The case of Min Zin is a reminder that the range of people [China] could restrict from exiting could be quite wide — and potentially arbitrary,” Chong said.
Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, said the restrictions “send a message” that China will take action to prevent “leaks in security or national interest-sensitive areas”.

Make NHS and military uniforms in UK, fashion firms urge Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:10:49 UTC
17:10:49 KST

London fashion week is only days away, but one industry organisation has turned its attention to clothing that is a little less catwalk-worthy – the uniforms worn by British defence forces and NHS staff.
On Wednesday afternoon, the thinktank Fashion Roundtable will hand deliver a letter to Downing Street urging Andy Burnham to commit to manufacturing these uniforms in the UK.
Signed by more than 1,200 people – including the adventurer Ben Fogle and The Great British Sewing Bee presenter Patrick Grant – the organisation’s letter says public procurement such as this could be vital to preserving the UK’s manufacturing industry.
“The biggest lever we have to support skills retention, inclusive growth and regional resilience is awarding public procurement contracts for textile goods to suppliers who manufacture onshore in the UK,” the thinktank said.
The benefit of domestic manufacturing to an economy has already been demonstrated. The Covid inquiry concluded that nearly £10bn of public money was wasted on the flawed way it went about buying personal protective equipment (PPE), much of it manufactured in China. By contrast, Scotland, which invested £102.7m in PPE and produced 88% of it domestically in 2021, generated £66.7m of additional economic value and 1,400 jobs.
Kate Hills, the founder of the manufacturing organisation Make It British, said making these items in the UK could allow companies breathing space. “These sort of contracts would give manufacturers confidence to employ more people, to look at the long term rather than feel like they’re surviving day to day,” she added.
The US is an example where contracts for military uniforms are manufactured by companies within the country by law, thanks to the Berry amendment, which was passed in 1941. In 2025, the market for the industry reached $1.62bn (£1.19bn).
Hills said she hoped Burnham might commit to this change – partly because of his own taste for UK-made apparel: he buys suits from the Manchester-based brand Private White VC, for example. The Labour leader has argued that government procurement should do more to support UK manufacturers rather than prioritising the lowest-cost overseas suppliers.
“Maybe he is the prime minister that sees the value of products that are actually made here,” Hills said.
Grant invested in Blackburn-based military outfitters Cookson & Clegg in 2015. Its last military contract, making uniforms for the British army, stopped in 2009 and it now makes the designs for his label Community Clothing, with almost 2,000 employees. He agreed that government procurement would be a boost. “Manufacturing requires steady state business with good visibility [and] long-term demand,” he said. “That’s the kind of thing that government procurement can do.”
He said he would “absolutely” like to bid for such contracts but even if they were for British companies, the process was “unfeasibly complicated … unless you’re a 20,000-employee operation with an enormous clerical department … Something needs to happen on that side, too.”
Concerns have been raised over army uniforms being made in China. In July, Iain Duncan Smith dubbed it a security concern, telling the Telegraph it was “tantamount to having our uniforms made by Nazi Germany in the 1930s”.
Grant said: “We are currently producing a lot of stuff in countries that we do not have the most stable relationships with. If something bad were to happen, we would have no resilience at all in our supply chains.”
The entrepreneur said procurement legislation would go some way towards future-proofing employment; creating jobs for people to make things that would always be needed. “We have to try to think about where jobs are going to come from in the version of our society that we’re going to have in 10 years’ time when AI really starts to kick in,” he added. “Why not just get ahead of it?”

Sydney-based fashion business Cue Clothing Co entered receivership on Tuesday afternoon.

France and Iraq deepen energy, defence ties during PM Zaidi's visit
France and Iraq on Monday called for a "diversification of export routes" for oil and gas in the Middle East in response to the instability generated by the conflict between the United States and Iran, following talks in Paris.
French President Emmanuel Macron and Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi stressed the importance of "regional interconnections" and export route diversification to "ensure regional energy security", in a joint statement.
Zaidi visited the Elysee Paris on his first trip to Europe since taking office in May and is also expected in Berlin on Tuesday.
The visit comes as the situation in the region continues to deteriorate, with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait on Friday, adding to the crisis of Iran's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and driving oil prices up.
On Monday, French energy giant TotalEnergies signed a memorandum of understanding with Iraq on liquefied natural gas supplies and agreed to discuss further energy projects.
TotalEnergies chief Patrick Pouyanne "affirmed the company's readiness to cooperate with Iraq in the oil and energy sectors", noting the company planned to increase its investments in Iraq to $16 billion from $12 billion, during a meeting with al-Zaidi.
The two countries, which in recent years have been involved in the fight against the Islamic State (IS) jihadist group, also agreed to deepen defence cooperation.
They signed a strategic roadmap on the acquisition of French military equipment as Iraq seeks to modernise its armed forces and strengthen its sovereignty capabilities.
French drone company Harmattan AI separately signed a letter of intent with Iraq's defence ministry concerning autonomous air-defence systems.
Several other agreements were signed in areas including development assistance, education, civil aviation and electricity infrastructure.

Any use of Russian assets would cause greater damage to Europe than to Russia — portal

2026-09-15

17:07:48 KST

ROME, September 15. /TASS/. Any utilization of frozen Russian assets carries a far greater risk for Europe than for Russia, Italian media outlet InsideOver wrote.
Europe is forced to balance between aiding Ukraine and financial suicide, the portal said. "Geopolitical and financial debates regarding Russia’s sovereign assets in Europe have reached a critical point. The dilemma triggering a clash within the European Union extends far beyond formal diplomacy, concerning the foundations of international law, monetary stability, and the protection of private property," according to the publication.
While supporting Kiev’s defense and economic capabilities remains a political priority, ensuring legal certainty must remain a systemic priority for the Eurozone, the article said. "Without a transparent distribution of legal and economic risks among all partner countries, any interference with Russian sovereign capital risks inflicting greater damage on Europe than that intended for the adversary [Russia]," the portal concluded.
The EU and G7 countries have frozen around 300 bln euros in Russian assets. Some 185 bln euros are held in the Belgian depository Euroclear. On December 12, 2025, the Moscow Arbitration Court filed a claim against Euroclear for 18.2 trillion rubles ($226 bln) from the Bank of Russia. This amount includes the regulator’s frozen funds, the value of frozen securities, and foregone profits.
