Zohar called the film “vile” and accused its makers of “treason”.
Gaza: a week of attacks amid a health system nearing collapse
Visiting Ireland this week, US President Trump insisted “there’s very little happening right now in Gaza”. Every day this week told a different story: attacks on Palestinians added to the Strip’s ever-increasing death toll and its already widespread destruction, as humanitarian conditions worsened unabated.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said on September 12 that if European countries took in 20,000 to 30,000 Gaza residents each, “this entire issue would be over”. With no such mass ‘emigration’ materialising yet, airstrikes on Gaza continued on a daily basis.
Following two days of multiple air raids on Gaza wounding women and children, on September 10, Israeli warplanes killed a family of four – father, mother and their two daughters – in the Beit Lahia housing project. Israel alleged the father was involved in attacks. This was followed the next day with a drone strike near the Sumoud camp in Khan Younis, killing Jihad Ismail, 33, and wounding 12 others.
On September 12, a pregnant woman, Iman Shalouf, 27, died from wounds sustained days earlier by Israeli gunfire south of Khan Younis. The next day, an air strike on a vehicle in Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood killed two Palestinians and wounded 13. On September 14, a Palestinian was killed by Israeli gunfire in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah. On the same day, Gaza’s Ministry of Health put the cumulative toll since October 2023 at 73,786 killed and 174,771 wounded, with 1,372 killed since last October’s “ceasefire”.
Meanwhile, Gaza’s health and transport systems edged closer to collapse. Al-Ahli Arab Hospital said its main generator failed because of a lack of oil and spare parts. That suspended its imaging department – including the only functioning CT scanner in northern Gaza. On September 13, Gaza’s public bus operators’ union said it would suspend transport for doctors and nurses beginning on September 16 due to the lack of replacement parts and fuel; the Health Ministry called it “a death sentence” for patient care.
The latest data from the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) found that since March, only 13,445 litres of engine oil have been approved by Israel for entry in Gaza against nearly 93,000 pending – oil needed to keep water, sanitation and hospital generators running.
‘De facto annexation’
The diplomatic rupture over settlements was matched this week by a convergence of reports from NGOs and international bodies reaching similar conclusions about conditions in the West Bank.
Israeli rights groups Yesh Din, Bimkom and HaMoked concluded in a joint report that land seizures, settler violence and movement restrictions “form a continuous process” amounting to “de facto annexation.” The B’Tselem report describes “the growing role of settler militias operating in coordination and cooperation with official forces”, working towards the same end even when not literally acting together. This week’s daily incidents put those dynamics on display.
On September 12, in Faqua, near Jenin, a soldier was filmed shooting Qassem Hussam in the leg during a settler incursion onto Palestinian land – an incident Israeli army radio itself said was carried out “contrary to orders” against a man who “posed no threat”, as the ongoing pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank continued.
A similar pattern played out on September 11, when Palestinian field activists reported that settlers beat five men with metal pipes on the Ramallah-Jericho road, fracturing one man’s knee; no soldiers intervened, though the road runs through an area with a heavy army presence.
Elsewhere, it was Israeli forces carrying out the violence. On September 13, Israeli forces shot and wounded two Palestinian labourers in Beit Jala, according to WAFA. On September 14, forces wounded a young man in Beit Ula, near Hebron, while setting his vehicle on fire, and separately arrested men in Beit Ummar and Dura, according to WAFA.

Oil price could surge to $US150 as war engulfs major Middle East supply routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:51:37 UTC
15:51:37 KST

Oil price could surge to $US150 as war engulfs major Middle East supply routes, analysts say
The Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and inland Saudi Arabia are now active war zones.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military air base in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia overnight.
This latest escalation follows an attack on Thursday, which knocked out the Saudis' East-West pipeline.
The pipeline played a crucial role in easing the world's concerns about an impending global oil shortage.
For months, it had allowed oil tankers to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, a critical supply route for roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil supply.
Loading...
That was a major reason why oil prices were lower than they otherwise would be in the past few months.
The Houthis have also advanced rapidly in Yemen, capturing territory including Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea — a development which pushed oil prices above $US100 per barrel late last week.
And the British maritime security agency, UKMTO, reported on Sunday that another vessel had been struck by a projectile in the strait, forcing the crew to be evacuated as the ship caught on fire.
US in Middle East quagmire
The fighting between the Saudis and Houthis creates another problem for US President Donald Trump and other authorities trying to minimise the disruption to global oil supply.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015, but the conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in the past few years.
The fragile truce collapsed in July as Houthi strikes hit Abha Airport and the Houthis declared a naval blockade targeting Saudi-linked shipping.
Reuters reported that Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support.
More pain at the pump
All those worrying developments have pushed the global benchmark, Brent crude, above $US107 per barrel today.
US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude also jumped to $US103 per barrel.
Tapis, which is Australia's regional benchmark crude price, is now trading at $US110 per barrel, up 46 per cent since July.
The price of Tapis effects the wholesale petrol price, or what service stations pay for fuel.
But the motoring group NRMA has told the ABC that the difference between the wholesale and retail price is currently non-existent.
This means the price of fuel at the bowser is likely to increase in coming weeks.
The average price of unleaded petrol, according to NRMA, has risen to $2.19 per litre, while the national average for diesel has lifted to $2.68.
"Unfortunately, the trajectory [for motorists] for the petrol price is up," NRMA spokesperson Peter Khoury said.
Mr Khoury, however, expects the price at the bowser to fall quickly if the Middle East conflict were to de-escalate.
But the message today from oil analysts is not encouraging on that front.
"The closure of the East‑West pipeline in Saudi Arabia following multiple attacks has materially altered the state of the oil market," Commonwealth Bank's lead mining and energy commodities strategist, Vivek Dhar wrote in a note.
"[It] means that instead of 40‑45 per cent of prewar flows through the Strait of Hormuz needed to keep global oil and refined product inventories unchanged, 65‑70 per cent of prewar flows are now required.
"The sizable shift almost single-handedly reflects the closure of the East‑West pipeline."
World running out of oil
Analysts now say the world is weeks away from returning to critically low levels of oil supply.
"Our low estimate that global markets had five to 11 weeks of global oil and refined product stockpiles is growing in likelihood," Mr Dhar said.
"This compares with our base case of 15‑20 weeks — where flows through the Strait of Hormuz were 30 per cent of prewar levels and global oil markets had the benefit of pipeline bypasses, subdued Chinese imports and rising non‑OPEC+ supply outside the Middle East."
He wrote that: "If inventory depletion is reached, we estimate that Brent oil futures may need to rise to [around] $US150 per barrel to force uncontrolled demand destruction (i.e. where high prices force lower demand) for emerging Asian economies."
That oil price would be even higher than what it was at the height of the global financial crisis.
In July 2008, Brent crude surged as high as $US147 per barrel.
"This price level is derived from the last time that emerging Asian economies saw uncontrolled demand destruction in 2008.
"With nonlinear rises in both oil and refined products now a real possibility, Iran has maximised its leverage against the US."
This will likely make it harder for Mr Trump to extract the United States out of its war with Iran, in a way that does not sound like defeat or capitulation.
Until then, the rest of the world is bearing the brunt of more expensive oil prices and higher cost of living.

Nvidia and Palantir announced on Thursday that they will incorporate an artificial intelligence model into the control of their critical supply chains, giving the automated system decision-making power.
"Nvidia has arguably the most valuable, intricate, and complex supply chain in the world. Our sovereign stack, powered by Nemotron models and Ontology, is delivering capabilities that exceed the frontier while providing alpha protection qualities unavailable otherwise,” said Alex Karp, cofounder and CEO of Palantir Technologies.
The deployment, according to the companies, will allow for "unprecedented supply chain visibility, identify constraints, continuously codify operational expertise and guide decisions at machine speed."
The system will be first implemented in Nvidia's supply chain, which spans millions of parts, thousands of suppliers, and a global network of manufacturing partners, with the objective of unifying every team worldwide into one operating system that improves their efficiency.
"Supply chains are the operating system of the physical economy, and AI factories are among the most complex systems ever built,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia. “From wafers and components to manufacturing, systems and customer delivery, hundreds of companies and trillions of dollars of global economic activity come together to deliver AI infrastructure. NVIDIA and Palantir are transforming this vast operational graph into sovereign intelligence."
The human side is still key for the system
Even if Nvidia reported that planners improved their numbers when using the new model, it also said human employees still provided key insights that weren't possible to get using only an AI system.
According to the company, emails exchanged with partners that week, severe weather in the forecast for a key region, an ongoing geopolitical event, or understanding the transcript from the last supplier debrief call were factors the AI struggled to incorporate when working across the entire supply chain.
The company explained that those inputs were better implemented by human instinct created by years of work rather than by the mathematical algorithm that guided the system, while the AI had an important role in working around the repetitive and predictable tasks.
The company concluded that the best implementation would help workers spend less time reconstructing routine decisions so they could focus on unpredictable situations.
Additionally, the Nvidia explained that the model was only going to train according to insights provided by the workers, with no changes made during production while managing a supply chain.

“In the morning, a dolphin was seen after washing ashore in the city of Tel Aviv-Jaffa (Jerusalem Beach), and was returned to the water by well-intentioned civilians,” the authority said in an update.

Israel releases turtles back to the wild

The turtles spent recent months at the National Sea Turtle Rescue Center receiving veterinary care after arriving with limb injuries caused by entanglement in plastic bags. Their rehabilitation is now complete, and staff released the turtles near the shoreline to help them reach the water quickly.
Dolphins sighted in Israel after more than a year
Dolphins were sighted near Israel in March of 2025, when Shlomi and Hawks, who previously visited the coast of Israel in 2024, were spotted eight kilometers off the coast of Rishon LeZion. The sighting comes amidst reports of a declining apex predator population in the Mediterranean region.
“During an inspection cruise by the Marine Unit inspectors 2.5 miles off the coast of Rishon LeZion following a trawler, three dolphins were suddenly spotted,” reported Guy Levian, the director of the Marine Unit area at the Nature and Parks Authority. “The three played in the waves for several minutes and continued on their way.”
Two of the individuals were later identified as Shlomi and Hawks, a pair of common bottlenose dolphins sighted in November 2024 during a collaborative survey by the Delfis Association and the Morris Kahn Research Station, the Nature and Parks Authority reported.
Researchers identified the two through images of their dorsal fins, which are “excellent means of identification, just like a human fingerprint,” said Kim Kobo, a researcher at the Morris Kahn Marine Research Center.

European Parliament to screen 'The Bibi Files' ahead of Israel's 2026 Knesset election

The documentary film The Bibi Files, one of the most widely discussed works made in recent years about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, will be screened inside the European Parliament in Brussels on September 29, exactly four weeks before Israel's elections.
The film is based in part on footage from Netanyahu's police interrogations, whose publication has previously been the subject of a legal battle by Netanyahu and requires court approval for visual and audio release in Israel. At the Brussels screening, members of the European Parliament and their assistants will view the material during the Israeli election campaign.
According to an invitation circulated ahead of the event, the screening will begin at 6 p.m., followed by a discussion featuring the film's director, Alexis Bloom, and Italian journalist Giulia Innocenzi, who is involved in distributing the film in Italy. Attendance is subject to available seating. Organizers clarified that advance registration does not guarantee entry and that they will send participation confirmations separately.
M5S Europa, the European Parliament delegation of Italy's Five Star Movement, initiated the event. The screening is not an official European Parliament event and does not represent the Parliament or the European Union.
What are the film's claims against Netanyahu?
The Bibi Files, released in 2024, was directed by Bloom and produced, among others, by Oscar winner Alex Gibney and Israeli journalist Raviv Drucker. The original filming for the documentary was carried out by Avner Shahaf, and a significant portion of the film is based on footage recorded by police during investigations into the Netanyahu cases between 2016 and 2018.
According to the film's creators, Gibney received a database containing more than 1,000 hours of interrogation materials in 2023 from an anonymous source through the Signal application. The identity of the leaker has not been revealed.
The materials include footage from the interrogations of Benjamin Netanyahu, his wife Sara, his son Yair, and other individuals questioned in the cases. Bloom said she worked for an extended period with a Hebrew-speaking editor to sort, synchronize, and decipher the materials.
The film shows Netanyahu in the interrogation room being questioned, among other issues, about receiving gifts from businessmen, including cigars and champagne, as well as his relationships with wealthy individuals and media organizations.
Alongside the police footage, the documentary includes interviews with people closely familiar with Netanyahu and the system around him, including former aide and state witness Nir Hefetz, former Shin Bet director Ami Ayalon, former prime minister Ehud Olmert, Drucker, and others.
The film is explicitly critical of Netanyahu and uses the leaked interrogation materials to present a sharp political interpretation of his years in power.
Bloom and Gibney expand the discussion beyond the corruption cases known as Case 1000, Case 2000 and Case 4000, linking Netanyahu's struggle over his legal and political future to a series of major developments in Israel in recent years, including the political alliances he formed, the judicial reform effort and the conduct of his governments during wartime.
Notably, the documentary is the filmmakers' opinions on the situation and has not been established as a finding in the ongoing legal proceedings against Netanyahu.
The prime minister denies the charges against him and has repeatedly argued that the cases against him are the result of political persecution and selective enforcement.

US officials prepare for chaos amid concerns Trump will try use federal power to swing midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:48:19 UTC
15:48:19 KST

Two months before Americans vote in midterm elections that could reshape the balance of power in Washington, local and state officials across the country are rehearsing for a crisis that once seemed unthinkable:
What if the US president tries to use the power of the federal government to tilt the vote his way?
In California, officials have gamed out what would happen if US President Donald Trump dispatches federal agents to polling places, intimidating voters and suppressing turnout.
In Michigan, state officials are advising local clerks how to respond if the federal government demands access to voting machines.
And coast to coast, election officials are bracing for legal battles over everything from ballot seizures to voter-fraud investigations.
Reuters interviewed more than 50 state and local election officials from both political parties, including a dozen secretaries of state, the top election officials in their states. Nearly all said they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyber attacks and even threats of violence ahead of the midterms. Their efforts span jurisdictions large and small, in areas controlled by Trump’s Republican Party as well as the opposition Democratic Party.
White House dismisses concerns of federal interference in midterms
The preparations reflect growing alarm among state and local officials that the biggest threat to November's elections might come not from foreign meddling or technical failures, but from the Trump administration itself, as the president seeks to expand the federal government's role in elections, an area long overseen by states and localities.
The White House has dismissed concerns that federal actions could disrupt the midterms, arguing that the administration is enforcing election laws and safeguarding confidence in voting. It blamed Democrats for what it described as widespread voting by noncitizens, despite scant evidence to support those claims. A Reuters investigation published in July and independent studies have found that voting by noncitizens is extraordinarily rare and unlikely to affect election outcomes.
“The distrust in our elections is caused by extreme Democrats,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis. The Trump administration has good reason for pursuing allegations of voter fraud “despite the media and Democrats denying it for decades,” she added.
Yet Trump has openly portrayed many of his election-related initiatives as ways to help Republicans win.
Under the US Constitution, elections are administered by states and localities, not the president. However, Trump has urged Republicans to "nationalize" voting in at least 15 places, directed federal law enforcement to pursue debunked voter-fraud claims and sought to restrict mail-in balloting. His administration has also launched probes of election officials and offices in Wisconsin, Georgia and elsewhere.
His push to redraw congressional maps before the midterms sparked a nationwide redistricting battle that’s expected to give Republicans a net advantage in House races. He has sued states that refused to provide federal agencies with confidential voter data, including birthdates, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers, and gutted programs designed to thwart cyber attacks and foreign interference. At the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas last week, he urged supporters to “cheat like hell” and vote whether they’re “registered or not” in the upcoming midterms.
“Election officials are concerned about the role the federal government is going to play,” said Bill Gates, a Republican lawyer and former official in Maricopa County, Arizona, who now advises and trains election officials around the country. The mood, he said, is one of “apprehension,” rather than the close cooperation that once characterized election cycles.
More than a dozen local and state election officials said they are hiring outside lawyers or seeking legal training for themselves and their staff to prepare for potential demands by the administration for access to sensitive voting records or election equipment.
Nearly twice that many said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation, including the false claims made by Trump and Republican allies that voting machines are unreliable and mail-in voting is inherently corrupt.
And most said they are scrambling to fill gaps left by the Trump administration’s cuts to programs that help safeguard elections from cyber attacks and physical security threats. That includes ongoing work to fortify election offices with camera systems and bulletproof glass – a trend that began after Trump disputed his loss to Joe Biden in the 2020 election, igniting waves of violent threats by Trump supporters against election workers.
The administration’s election rhetoric could prove to be mere bluster, said David Becker, a former voting-rights lawyer for the US Justice Department who now runs the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a group that works to build confidence in elections. Courts have repeatedly rejected the administration’s efforts to change mail-in ballot rules and obtain confidential voter rolls from states that refused its demands. Other actions, such as sending armed agents to polling sites, would likely be illegal and risk political backlash, Becker added.
But with control of Congress potentially hinging on a small number of races, many election officials say they cannot assume such guardrails will hold. The stakes are enormous: A Republican loss of one or both chambers would end the governing trifecta that has enabled much of Trump's agenda, opening the door to aggressive Democratic oversight of him and new obstacles to his legislative and judicial priorities.
Subpoenas, warrants, private attorneys
Election officials are planning for a wide range of scenarios, particularly in battleground states and Democratic strongholds targeted by Trump's false election-fraud claims. Any disputed result, they say, could trigger federal investigations, courtroom battles, and even civil unrest.
Wisconsin offers insight into those preparations.
In Dane County, home to Wisconsin’s capital, county attorneys have begun drafting court filings to fight any attempt by the Trump administration to seize voting equipment or election records, and they are preparing for the possibility that federal immigration agents could appear at polling places, said the Democratic county clerk, Scott McDonell.
“It’s going to be a matter of speed,” McDonell said of any legal response. The county is also preparing for possible protests over disputed results.
He said January’s FBI raid on election operations in Georgia’s Fulton County was a wake-up call, convincing him that the Trump administration could try to intervene.
Dana Barrett, a Fulton County commissioner, told Reuters the raid exposed a vulnerability few local governments had anticipated. After federal agents seized about 650 boxes of 2020 election records as part of an investigation into voter-fraud allegations previously rejected by courts and audits, the county rushed to hire outside counsel and sued to recover the records. “The only thing that would have been nice is if we had already had those people on board,” said Barrett, a Democrat. “But how could you know?”
The county, Georgia's most populous and a Democratic stronghold, lost that legal fight in May, when a federal judge ruled prosecutors could retain the records while their investigation continues.
Wisconsin faces similar pressure. In May, FBI agents sought to question at least eight current and former Milwaukee city and county employees about the 2020 election. Trump’s loss in the state had spurred him and his allies to sue the state’s two largest Democratic-leaning counties, Milwaukee and Dane, in unsuccessful cases alleging voter fraud. Almost immediately after the FBI visits - some of them to people’s homes - Milwaukee city and county leaders moved to secure legal representation.
The FBI declined to comment on its election-related work.
Milwaukee County retained the Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal nonprofit that has battled the Trump administration in Fulton County and a number of other places. The city separately hired two firms, the Washington Litigation Group and the Public Rights Project, to represent current and former city employees.
Legal groups are providing their services free of charge in the city and county of Milwaukee and in states including California, New Mexico and Pennsylvania. In some jurisdictions, including Fulton County, election offices and individual officials have hired private lawyers at their own expense.
In Michigan, a pivotal state in the fight for control of the US Senate, the Democratic secretary of state’s office has consulted private attorneys about defending local election officials against potential federal scrutiny. The Trump administration has threatened to investigate at least one Democratic-led county in the state over alleged voter fraud in the 2024 election, despite producing no evidence of significant irregularities.
“We’re prepared,” Michigan Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie told Reuters. He said his office has advised local election officials on how to respond if federal authorities seek access to voting records or equipment. “We do have counsel on standby for any local election official that needs it.”
Some are seeking training on how a federal investigation might play out.
In March, nearly two dozen election officials and local attorneys gathered at a Miami Beach hotel for training by two former senior Justice Department officials - one appointed during a Republican administration, the other during a Democratic one. The training explained the mechanics of federal investigations, including how to distinguish different types of warrants and subpoenas - and how to challenge them in court.
According to six participants, they reviewed a redacted copy of the search warrant used in the Trump administration's January raid in Fulton County to better understand what agents could seize and how they could be challenged.
"Most of us aren't even familiar with this stuff," said Chris Walker, clerk of Jackson County, Oregon, a jurisdiction of 220,000 residents that voted for Democrat Barack Obama in 2008 but backed Trump in the last three presidential elections. A federal raid like the one in Georgia would be a "nightmare scenario," she said after attending the training.
Natalie Adona, who runs elections in Marin County, California, a heavily Democratic county north of San Francisco, said the seizure of 650,000 ballots by a far-right, pro-Trump California sheriff this year convinced her to prepare for the worst. The seizure remains tied up in court. State officials and voting-rights groups say the sheriff, Chad Bianco of Riverside County, lacked authority to take the ballots and was pursuing unfounded fraud allegations. In a statement, Bianco said the seizure was lawful.
Adona’s office hosted training on search warrants, subpoenas and questioning by federal agents. She and her team also participated in a drill on how to respond if US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents appeared at a polling place. "I'm just trying to do my job," said Adona, who is not registered with any political party.
In May, Trump refused to rule out sending ICE agents or the military to polling places. Such a move would likely trigger legal challenges under a federal law that generally prohibits armed federal deployments at election sites. At his March confirmation hearing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed concerns that immigration agents could intimidate naturalized citizens and other legal voters.
“There shouldn't be illegals at the polling spot,” he said, and any officers sent to polling places would be there to combat potential threats, “not for intimidation.”
In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” but noted that the agency could make arrests at polling places if an active public-safety threat emerges.
The Supreme Court blocked Trump’s mail voting plan on Monday from taking effect before November’s elections. But the legal battle still forced election officials to prepare for disruptions that could have affected millions of voters.
Trump and his allies have spent years portraying mail voting as vulnerable to fraud despite a lack of evidence of widespread abuse. Trump himself has voted by mail in recent elections in his home state of Florida.
Under the plan, states would have been required to provide the US Postal Service with lists of mail-ballot recipients and use USPS-approved ballot envelopes, allowing the Postal Service to reject ballots that do not meet the new requirements. Before the Supreme Court blocked the plan, a Postal Service whistleblower warned Congress it could wrongly delay or reject thousands of legal ballots.
The USPS has said it will follow court rulings regarding the plan.
In Philadelphia, officials had contingency plans in place in case the plan went ahead, including satellite election offices where voters can pick up ballots, said Seth Bluestein, a Republican on the Philadelphia Board of Elections. "We've worked with our city solicitor to have a plan in place for how to respond."
Panic buttons and a handgun
Election officials say years of false election-fraud claims have raised the threat of harassment and violence, prompting a wave of security upgrades across the country.
Derek Bowens is elections director in Durham County, North Carolina, a heavily Democratic area in a state with a pivotal US Senate race. He said he is acquiring his first firearm to protect himself and his family.
“My perspective has changed,” said Bowens, who was appointed to the nonpartisan role in 2017. "I'm very conscious now of my surroundings. I tend to go home immediately after work. I don't spend a lot of time outside of the house."
Since moving into a new building before the 2024 presidential election, his office has added ballistic doors, bulletproof glass, panic buttons and armed guards. The mailroom has a dedicated exhaust system to remove hazardous fumes from contaminated packages. It’s also stocked with Narcan, a nasal spray used to reverse opioid overdoses in the event of accidental exposure to tainted mail.
The chief election coordinator at each of Durham County's 68 polling places will carry a tracker-equipped badge that can summon law enforcement to their precise location with the press of a button. The county adopted the badges after the 2024 primary election, when a man entered a polling place after voting had ended and threatened to “vote with a bullet” if he couldn’t cast a ballot.
Durham County is among at least a dozen jurisdictions where election officials told Reuters they’re fortifying their offices. The measures include shatter-resistant window film, barriers to prevent vehicles from ramming buildings, surveillance systems and motion sensors to monitor voting equipment and ballot storage areas. Several jurisdictions have arranged security escorts for late-working staff.
In Detroit, a predominantly Black Democratic stronghold, City Clerk Janice Winfrey now has around-the-clock police protection after receiving death threats following Trump's false fraud claims in 2020. The city’s 36 absentee-ballot drop boxes are monitored by police through a network of surveillance cameras. And every window in election headquarters has been replaced with bulletproof glass.
“I long for the days when elections were just boring,” said Winfrey. “It absolutely makes me sad that this is what democracy has come to.”
It isn’t just Democratic locales that are preparing. In Irwin County, Georgia, a Republican area that voted overwhelmingly for Trump in 2024, Election Supervisor Ethan Compton is giving two poll workers at each precinct panic buttons. The devices can transmit a photo and GPS coordinates to election headquarters, the sheriff's office and 911 emergency-call centers. Many poll workers are elderly, Compton said, like “somebody’s grandmother,” and the devices “give them peace of mind.”
Getting the word out: AI has made lies cheaper, easier to create
Election officials say one of the biggest threats may be a battle over reality itself.
Falsehoods about rigged elections, compromised voting machines and voter fraud can ricochet online long before officials can respond, fueled by social media, partisan influencers and increasingly sophisticated AI tools.
The scenarios they fear are multiplying: a convincing video appears to show an election worker destroying ballots; AI chatbots amplify fabricated news stories; or text messages falsely tell voters that polling places have moved or voting machines have been compromised.
AI has made falsehoods cheaper to create, harder to spot and easier to spread. Election officials increasingly view combating misinformation as a defining challenge of the midterms. The falsehoods can come from either party, though it was Trump's debunked claims of rigged voting machines and widespread voter fraud that spread widely online during the last election cycle.
When Bobbie Gross became clerk of Mesa County, Colorado, in 2023, she inherited a crisis of public trust. Her predecessor, Tina Peters, had allowed pro-Trump election-fraud conspiracy theorists to access county voting equipment after the 2020 election and was later convicted on felony charges after sensitive machine data was posted online.
At sentencing, a state judge said Peters had caused “immeasurable damage” to confidence in elections. Peters was released by Colorado’s Democratic governor in June. Peters has argued she was preserving election records and should not have been prosecuted.
Gross, a Republican, responded to the crisis with an aggressive campaign. She invited skeptics, activist groups and students to observe elections in person, used social media to explain every stage of the voting process and hired a technology firm to post ballot images online so voters could inspect them for themselves.
Confidence in local elections has "gotten significantly better," she said, though some voters remain convinced the system is rigged.
Cybersecurity holes
For years, election officials relied on Washington for help defending elections from foreign governments. Now many say that support is fading.
Election officials remain concerned about influence operations linked to Russia, China and Iran. Election-security researchers say those countries have sought to meddle in past US elections, though all three governments deny doing so. Here, too, many officials say Trump is making matters worse.
One of their most important partners was the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA. The agency, set up by Trump during his first term, tracked foreign influence campaigns, shared intelligence on emerging cyber threats and warned state and local officials when false information or malicious cyber activity appeared designed to undermine an election.
But CISA angered Trump in 2020 when its director declared that year's presidential election secure. Within weeks of Trump's return to office in 2025, his administration dismantled much of CISA’s infrastructure. CISA cut nearly 1,000 workers, about 30% of its total staff, and stopped funding a platform that shared real-time intelligence and analysis on election cyber threats with states.
The impact was almost immediate.
In a February 2025 email, CISA's regional director told New England secretaries of state that staff assigned to election security had been placed on administrative leave pending a review of the agency's mission. Those employees included some who ran efforts to counter disinformation and foreign influence operations. Reuters received the email through a public-records request.
Election officials from both parties said they were losing a critical source of expertise. In a March 2025 letter to the homeland security secretary, Pennsylvania’s Republican Secretary of State Al Schmidt warned of “serious consequences” from scaling back CISA's election-security work. He cited a 2024 case in which federal agencies quickly debunked a fabricated video falsely depicting an election worker destroying ballots. Counties would struggle to replicate that kind of forensic analysis on their own, Schmidt said.
In a statement, a CISA spokesperson said the agency “remains fully equipped and prepared to address any national security cyber threats that face our nation” and “is stronger than ever.”
Some election officials, however, are now building their own defenses.
In Maine, another state with a crucial US Senate race, Democratic Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said states are forging new partnerships with one another, nonprofits and private-sector cybersecurity groups to compensate for cuts in federal support. After CISA funding dried up last year, Maine expanded its reliance on private cybersecurity specialists, she said.
But the loss of federal cybersecurity support leaves many local offices exposed to threats they cannot handle alone, said Joseph Kirk, the election supervisor in heavily Republican Bartow County, Georgia.
"My IT director's great," Kirk said. "But he can't fight a nation-state. It takes a nation-state to fight a nation-state."

Bill Gates: Anti-vaccine attitudes in rich countries makes herd immunity for measles impossible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:48:16 UTC
15:48:16 KST

Vaccine hesitancy in rich countries means ending measles as a global public health threat is not currently possible, Bill Gates told Reuters in an interview.
The Microsoft co-founder turned billionaire philanthropist said wiping out the killer childhood disease had previously been a potential goal for his eponymous foundation, which focuses on global health and the world’s poorest people.
But it was now off the table due to increased vaccine hesitancy in wealthier nations, part of a wave of skepticism championed for decades by the now health secretary in the United States under President Donald Trump, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
“At one point, the foundation wanted to eradicate measles, but the vaccine hesitancy in rich countries has meant that’s not on our list of goals,” Gates said. “I think that’s kind of tragic.”
Measles cases rise internationally
Measles, among the world’s most contagious diseases, causes a high fever, a cough and a tell-tale rash.
The virus killed around 2 million children every year before the introduction of a vaccine in the 1960s. Nowadays, around 100,000 children die annually, largely in countries where conflict or logistics make immunization difficult. The WHO says vaccination rates need to be above 95% to prevent outbreaks.
But recent years have also seen a surge in cases in countries where the disease was almost forgotten, including in the US and Europe, as vaccination rates have fallen.
Gates said that vaccine hesitancy had at least not spread to lower-income countries, where measles can be much deadlier than in richer countries due to malnutrition and healthcare gaps.
“There’s always that concern that if you have doubters in the US, that becomes a global thing,” he said. “But we haven’t seen an increase in vaccine hesitancy in the countries the foundation works in.”
Aid cuts led by Trump administration
Gates was speaking ahead of the foundation’s annual Goalkeepers event, which looks at progress towards the United Nations global development goals set for 2030, including on improving health.
In last year's report, Gates warned of the impact of aid cuts led by Trump’s administration, and followed by other wealthy countries like the UK and Germany, on the health of the world’s poorest.
This year, he said the cuts had likely caused many deaths, but the restoration of some money had prevented the worst-case scenario. Efforts from impacted countries and other health groups also held off disaster, as Reuters has reported.
“The most dire predictions, which went above 10 million deaths, we don’t see that taking place,” Gates said, adding that he continued to urge governments to restore aid or at least not cut it further. “It’s still a very tragic situation.”

Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:47:25 UTC
15:47:25 KST

Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.
A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".
Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.
"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.
"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.
"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.
"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."
The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.
In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.
Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.
Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.
"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.
"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.
"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."
Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.
"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.
Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.
"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.
CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

NATO 'committed and ready' after shooting down drone over Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:47:12 UTC
15:47:12 KST

From the Baltics to Poland, Europe's eastern edge is monitoring Russia's war to prevent it spilling over its own borders.
NATO stands "vigilant, committed, and ready," Lithuania's foreign minister said Tuesday, after an allied fighter jet destroyed a drone that crossed into the country's airspace from Belarus — the latest in a string of aerial incursions testing the alliance's eastern border with Russia.
Kestutis Budrys credited the interception to the strength of collective defence, thanking the allies whose air presence, he said, protects Baltic skies and reinforces regional security.
But the message lands beyond Vilnius: as Russia's war on Ukraine grinds on, the alliance's eastern members are increasingly treating airspace violations — deliberate or not — as tests of NATO's resolve, and Tuesday's response was framed as proof the system works.
President Gitanas Nauseda confirmed the incident on social media, saying the drone had been destroyed.
"A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets," Gitanas Nauseda wrote in a post on X.
"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region," he added.
Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre said the drone had crossed from Belarus, moved through the Lentvaris and Trakai areas heading west, and came down in a rural area near the village of Pratkūnai, in Kaunas county — the first time a drone has been shot down over Lithuanian territory.
Moscow has not commented on the incident.
The episode was not isolated. Hours later, Poland announced it had launched its own "aviation operations," citing Russian jet-powered drones striking Ukrainian territory near its borders.
Warsaw described the measures as preventive, intended to secure airspace in regions adjacent to the conflict — a sign that vigilance is spreading well beyond the Baltic states.
Testing fragile energy site truce
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have reported repeated drone incursions since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, but interceptions by NATO aircraft remain rare enough to draw attention.
The alliance's air-policing mission shot down a Ukrainian drone that strayed into Estonian airspace in May — its first such interception since the war started.
European officials have also pointed to Russia diverting Ukrainian drones aimed at industrial and oil facilities near St Petersburg, on the Gulf of Finland.
The incursion comes at a delicate diplomatic moment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv is ready to take "de-escalatory steps" if Moscow reciprocates, after US President Donald Trump announced the two sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.
Even so, fighting continued overnight: Ukrainian forces struck Russian military targets in Krasnodar Krai, while Russia launched 102 drones at Ukraine.
The incident also lands against a longer-running shift in Lithuanian policy. Since Nauseda said in July he wanted the country involved in Western nuclear deterrence against Moscow, Lithuania has begun the process of lifting its constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons — a move likely to draw fresh attention across European capitals as the debate over the continent's own deterrence intensifies.

The UK unemployment rate reached 4.9% in the period of May to July 2026, marking an increase of 0.2 percentage points from the same period last year, official data shows Tuesday.

The estimated UK employment rate dropped by 0.1 percentage points over the year to 75.1% in the latest quarter.

Ayhan Simsek
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) has reached 30% support in a nationwide poll for the first time and now leads Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives by 10 percentage points, according to a GMS survey published Monday.
Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, dropped to 20% -- the lowest level recorded by pollster GMS for the conservatives.
Together with the Social Democrats at 11%, the chancellor’s coalition would not have enough support to form a majority in parliament if elections were held this week.
GMS last surveyed the same question in late July.
Since then the AfD, which campaigns against immigration, has gained 2 points and Merz’s CDU/CSU has lost 3.
The Greens rose 1 point to 14%. The Left Party also gained 1 point to 11%. The liberal Free Democrats slipped to 4% and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance stood at 3%, both below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.
The figures mark a sharp shift from the Feb. 23, 2025, federal election, when Chancellor Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance won 28.5% and the AfD 20.8%.
The poll comes ahead of regional elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin on Sunday.
Those votes are also seen as a test of Chancellor Merz’s political future after the conservatives’ heavy defeat to the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, where the right-wing party won 43.8% on Sept. 6.
Speculation has grown for weeks in the media about a possible change of chancellor, with North Rhine-Westphalia Premier Hendrik Wuest (CDU) named as a potential successor.
A leadership fight in the Christian Democrats after the state elections would not, by itself, dissolve the Bundestag or trigger a snap election. If party pressure forces Merz out, parliament could elect a new chancellor without a national vote.

Building at Scale: How Long-Span Steel Expands Architectural Possibilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

What happens when architecture is asked to create a room without boundaries? Convention halls, stadiums, factories, and logistics centers all begin with the same architectural challenge: creating large, uninterrupted interiors that can accommodate movement, visibility, and changing uses. The larger the span, the greater the structural demands, and the greater the architectural possibilities.
Long-span architecture is not a recent ambition. For centuries, architects have sought ways to enclose large public spaces, from the monumental dome of the Pantheon to the iron-and-glass halls of London's Crystal Palace. Each breakthrough expanded the possibilities of architecture, replacing thicker walls and denser structural systems with lighter, more efficient ways of spanning distance. Today, steel continues that evolution, making it possible to span distances that would be difficult to achieve with conventional structural systems while keeping large public spaces open, flexible, and adaptable. Steel's high strength-to-weight ratio makes longer spans possible with fewer columns and lighter structural systems, while prefabricated components simplify construction and reduce on-site work.
CIDB Convention Centre Sarawak in Kuching / Arkiskape Sdn Bhd
Across Southeast Asia, these structural possibilities are reflected in a growing number of civic, industrial, and commercial projects recognized through the Steel Architectural Awards ASEAN. The awards highlight innovative applications of BlueScope steel across the region, showcasing how steel systems support architecture that responds to climate, scale, and complex building programs.
A contemporary example is the CIDB Convention Centre Sarawak in Kuching, Malaysia, designed by Arkiskape Sdn Bhd. Developed as part of the CIDB Sarawak Complex, the building demonstrates how long-span steel can reinterpret Sarawak's vernacular architecture at the scale of a contemporary civic building. Its design draws inspiration from the Rumah Orang Ulu, the circular Bidayuh Baruk house, and the shaded verandas of Sarawak Malay houses, adapting these vernacular principles into a contemporary building.
The convention center includes a 900-seat main hall, conference rooms, gathering spaces, and supporting facilities beneath a long-span elliptical roof that creates expansive, column-free interiors for conferences, exhibitions, and community events. BlueScope's COLORBOND® steel and COLORBOND® ULTRA steel were selected for the roofing system because their lightweight coated steel construction supports curved and complex roof forms while reducing the overall roof load carried by the long-span steel structure. The pre-painted steel finish also contributes to the roof's architectural expression through a consistent color and finish, while providing long-term durability and corrosion resistance in Sarawak's humid tropical climate.
Louvered facades, semi-open corridors, and openings that draw cooler air across an existing pond reduce dependence on mechanical cooling while bringing daylight and cross-ventilation into the building. These passive strategies contribute to an estimated 30 percent reduction in electricity and air-conditioning demand compared to a conventional convention center of a similar size, while the elliptical roof geometry also helps manage heavy rainfall and prevailing winds.
Beyond its architectural expression, the CIDB Convention Centre reflects a broader shift in how complex buildings are delivered. The project achieved an Industrialized Building System (IBS) score above 70 percent through prefabricated building components and close coordination between architects, engineers, and contractors. Its twisting elliptical roof required repeated surveying and recalibration during construction, demonstrating how steel can support complex geometries while maintaining construction efficiency and budget control.
Industrial Foundry for Marine Vessels in Samut Prakan / Naksit Wisetmora
While convention centers make the spatial qualities of long spans highly visible, the same structural logic underpins industrial buildings. Designed by Naksit Wisetmora, the Industrial Foundry for Marine Vessels was built to produce bronze propellers for naval vessels. Manufacturing requires uninterrupted floor space for heavy machinery, cranes, and production lines, making long spans a practical necessity.
The project uses BlueScope pre-painted steel systems for its roof and facade cladding, creating a lightweight building envelope that could be assembled efficiently on site while offering corrosion resistance suited to its coastal location. Skylights, triangular openings, and continuous ventilation improve daylight distribution and dissipate heat generated by industrial furnaces, reducing glare and supporting naturally ventilated working environments.
Mayora Head Office Canteen in Jakarta / Lex and Architects
Long-span steel also shapes spaces designed for gathering outside industrial settings. The Mayora Head Office Canteen, designed by Lex and Architects, accommodates more than 800 employees beneath a circular roof inspired by the form of a turtle shell.
Designed as both a daily dining hall and an event venue, the building relies on a column-free interior that allows the program to shift between informal meals, company gatherings, and larger functions. Lightweight steel framing and BlueScope roofing systems made it possible to taper and curve the roof while maintaining an open, naturally lit communal space surrounded by landscape. The coated steel roof reinforces the building's smooth, continuous form while providing a durable exterior finish.
Jakarta International Stadium / PDW Architects
At a much larger scale, Jakarta International Stadium demonstrates another defining quality of long-span architecture: preserving uninterrupted sightlines. The stadium's long-span roof creates uninterrupted views across the seating bowl, while COLORBOND® steel forms part of the roofing system, providing a durable exterior envelope for one of Indonesia's largest public venues.
Malaysian Academy of Han Studies in Melaka / Studio 505
A quieter interpretation appears at the Malaysian Academy of Han Studies (MAHS) in Melaka, designed by Studio 505. Inspired by the circular Tulou settlements of southern China, the academy reinterprets vernacular architecture through a complex curving roof assembled from more than 25,000 radial steel profiles.
The roof was realized using LYSAGHT® 360 SEAM®, a BlueScope roofing system selected for its ability to curve and taper across the building's drum-shaped geometry. Finished in COLORBOND® XPD PEARLESCENT steel in Copper Penny, the roof's metallic finish adds depth and color to the building's interpretation of the traditional Tulou, while the coated steel surface provides weather resistance, dirt resistance, and long-term color and gloss retention.
Across these projects, long-span steel serves very different architectural programs, yet recurring patterns begin to emerge. The first is spatial flexibility. Fewer columns create interiors that can accommodate changing uses, from exhibition layouts and manufacturing equipment to sporting events and public ceremonies. The second is construction efficiency. Prefabricated steel components reduce on-site fabrication and allow structural work to progress alongside foundations, helping manage the scale and complexity of large projects. The third is formal freedom. Long-span steel structures paired with lightweight coated steel roofing systems make curved, tapered, and expansive roof forms possible without adding unnecessary structural weight. Alongside durability and weather resistance, coated steel roofing also introduces color, finish, and material character as part of the architectural design, allowing the roof to become an integral element of each building's identity.

Iran issues passive defense plan for 3 scenarios, including full-scale war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:44:23 UTC
15:44:23 KST

Sahin Demir
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff has issued a nationwide passive defense directive outlining preparations for three possible scenarios: the end of war, a ceasefire, and full-scale war.
Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of the Iranian Armed Forces and chairman of the country’s Permanent Passive Defense Committee, issued the 10-article directive for Iran’s 2026 Passive Defense Commemoration programs, according to Fars News Agency on Tuesday.
Under the full-scale war scenario, large public gatherings and in-person events would be suspended, with activities instead focusing on operational preparedness, continuity of essential services, resource management, public assistance and coordination among relevant agencies.
In the event of a ceasefire without a definitive end to hostilities, the directive prioritizes public preparedness, vigilance against hybrid warfare and information security, while the end-of-war scenario provides for the full implementation of planned exercises, training and public programs.
The directive also calls for operational plans to be updated based on experiences from what it describes as Iran’s “second and third imposed wars.”
Iran has issued similar directives for its annual Passive Defense Commemoration in previous years, including 10-article instructions in 2024 and 2025 focusing on public preparedness and protecting critical infrastructure. The latest directive, however, comes amid the ongoing war with the US and explicitly sets out measures for three different conflict scenarios.
The US and Israel launched large-scale attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, targeting government buildings, military sites, missile infrastructure, and air defenses. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks against Israel and US bases across the region.
The conflict has since expanded across the region, while diplomatic efforts have sought to end the hostilities.
Before the current conflict, Iran and Israel had also fought a 12-day war in June 2025, which ended with a US-sponsored ceasefire.

Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:39:40 UTC
15:39:40 KST

Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies.
Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity.
Trump dismissed the anxieties on Monday, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy” and insisting on social media: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”
But the 80-year-old president, who has sidelined Congress on numerous issues during his second term, looks increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late.
Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia, said: “History will look very poorly on that tweet. He’s not paying attention – or he’s paying attention to the wrong people. He’s being really foolish: not the first time he’s been really foolish but perhaps catastrophically foolish in this case.”
Recent surveys by the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation found 85% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want a new federal agency to monitor and regulate AI; and 82% of Democrats and 78% of Republicans favour government safety tests for AI making critical decisions.
While many politicians agree on the need to act, they are divided on what government intervention should look like and how far it should go. Some fear a pause on AI development could allow China to take the lead in the AI race and undermine national security.
Beyer called for Congress to stay in session instead of breaking for the midterm elections to work on AI legislation that has already been introduced. “The first thing that I’m very certain of is that the industry shouldn’t be allowed to regulate themselves; history doesn’t support that at all,” he said.
“Especially when they’re making so much money, there will be absolutely no incentive to regulate themselves at a less profit. If we look at medicines or childcare workers or automobile emissions and safety, all throughout our economy, we have regulatory bodies that keep us safe and promote the common good and allow businesses to be profitable. We need something like that.”
The flurry of debate follows warnings last week from three Anthropic researchers that AI could destroy humanity within the next decade. Recent disclosures from several AI companies that their models hacked into outside organizations during botched safety tests have also raised alarm about potential cybersecurity risks, with Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, claiming in an essay that in six to 12 months a “swarm” of AI agents could attack the entire internet and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
While AI executives have issued their own warnings about the risks from their products, public backlash against the industry and pressure on lawmakers to rein in AI firms have also been mounting throughout the year. The rapid build-out of data centers has generated nationwide protests and become a prominent midterm elections issue, while the tech lobby has spent millions in an attempt to influence political campaigns and shape proposed legislation.
The viral panic over AI’s potential existential threat this past week has intensified the longstanding debate over the technology, which so far has resulted in much political handwringing but only a patchwork of attempts at regulation. Many AI experts, regardless of whether they agree on the merits of the Anthropic researchers’ warnings, see this moment as a unique opportunity.
Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission, said: “You never waste a crisis is an old and well-worn adage in policy land. We’re looking at a really important policy opportunity and a policy window.”
AI industry leaders have also suggested that they are open to increased oversight and the formation of some kind of standards body, while Amodei’s letter advocated for international cooperation with states like China akin to cold war-era arms limitation treaties. Many AI regulation advocates are skeptical of industry proposals, however, arguing that AI companies are attempting to undercut strict government oversight and set their own terms.
In a rare intervention on Monday night, former president Barack Obama welcomed the current debate but warned that “at the end of the day, voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough”.
Writing on X, Obama added: “We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread.”
Members of Congress are holding a series of meetings this week with AI researchers and safety advocates as Congress tries to address the growing alarm. The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, urged the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to senators on AI and work with members of Congress and industry leaders to implement guardrails and block China from accessing the US’s advanced AI chips.
Bernie Sanders, who announced a bill last week aimed at banning “artificial superintelligence,” is holding a private briefing this week for other senators. The briefing will include co-founder of the Future of Life Institute co-founder Max Tegmark, whose organization has become one of the most well-funded and politically connected voices in warning about AI’s alleged existential risks.
Tegmark said: “Every other industry in the US used to be unregulated. There used to be soothing syrup fed to infants with opioids in it. Then the FDA was created, now stuff like that doesn’t reach the market. Eventually safety standards came in. That hasn’t happened with AI companies.”
Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat who will speak with Sanders at the Future of Life Institute’s “Pro-Human Assembly” on Tuesday, dismissed the notion that big tech companies should be responsible for AI safety. “That’s like saying it should be bank robbers that are responsible for bank safety,” he said. “The American people are waking up to the dangers of unregulated artificial intelligence.
“You have these AI CEOs coming to take away people’s jobs, to surveil people and attack our freedoms, and now you have all of these whistleblowers talking about potential mass casualty events. So Congress should be cracking down on these big tech companies and on these AI CEOs, not like what Republican Speaker Mike Johnson and Donald Trump go and do. They go to these AI CEOs and ask for Super Pac checks for their candidates.”
Republicans broke from Trump in acknowledging the potential perils of AI but came up with a variety of different fixes for the problem. Congressman Jay Obernolte of California, the lead Republican negotiating a bipartisan bill to govern AI, said: “We need to avoid overregulation, so we need to achieve these two conflicting goals … of protecting Americans against very real risks of AI in the hands of malicious human actors, while at the same time balancing the need to have a light-touch regulatory environment that allows the positive benefits of AI to improve our economy and our society. So that’s that’s the difficult part is getting that balance right.”
John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, said he would propose a bill on Wednesday to require all AI companies build a kill switch into their models. “It’s not going to put the federal government in charge of the kill switch. They would be in charge of their own kill switch, but they all have to have a kill switch, and I’m going to put that on the floor.”
But despite the growing urgency and public pressure, some members suspect that the bitterly polarised Congress will not be able to meet the moment.
Congressman Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat from Florida, was sceptical about the possibility of passing an AI regulation bill. “I think Congress has already shown they don’t have the capacity,” he said. “The speaker has said, ‘we’re not going to do anything’. In fact, he has said ‘we don’t know enough to do it’. I think that’s not what the American people are looking for. The American people are looking for leadership.”
Rick Scott, a Republican senator for Florida, added: “Did we balance the budget? Oh, did we pass a budget? See, what have we gotten done? So you think we’re going to get AI done?
“By the way, these companies that create a product that they think can destroy mankind – they have a responsibility to do it themselves. They shouldn’t be relying on us. I mean, it’s disgusting. I saw this as governor. People come, ‘go regulate me’. Yeah, we know what they want is they don’t want to be responsible for their actions.”

Leak: EU Commission to pitch social media restrictions for under-15s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:36:48 UTC
15:36:48 KST

The European Commission will propose barring under-15s from social media without parental consent, plus safety-by-design rules for risky online services like AI chatbots and video games in a legislative proposal that will be published on Thursday, according to a document obtained by Euronews.
The European Commission is set to unveil an EU Kids Act proposal restricting minors' access to platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, alongside new safety requirements for online services including video games and AI chatbots.
Minors under 15 would be barred from creating accounts on social media and video-sharing platforms without parental approval, while tech companies would be required to make their digital services safe by design, according to a confidential document obtained by Euronews.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to preview the legislative proposal during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament, meeting in plenary session. The bill itself is due to be published on Thursday.
France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands are all considering or advancing national legislation on social media bans, piling pressure on Brussels to present an EU-wide measure and avoid fragmentation.
In July, a group of experts convened by the EU executive released a series of recommendations on improving child safety online, many of which are reflected in the upcoming draft law.
"Technology companies bear the primary responsibility for making their products safe. Parents, not algorithms, should raise Europe's children," the document reads.
Scope
The scope is broader than originally anticipated: the bill will also cover other online services deemed potentially harmful to minors, notably video games and AI companions – a move Spain and the Netherlands requested only last week.
The draft EU Kids Act covers social media, video-sharing platforms and online games, considered to pose "specific design risks for minors," as well as AI-powered chatbots and companions, described as "virtual tools that can give mental health and personal development advice to minors."
Services designed and operated for education or by public authorities, as well as AI systems intended for office or industrial use, are excluded from the scope.
Age limitations
The proposal combines safety-by-design requirements for all the digital services concerned with a minimum age requirement that applies only to social media platforms like TikTok and video-sharing platforms like YouTube.
The age restrictions apply to all minors under 15, following a graduated approach. Children under three are barred entirely from social media and other high-risk services.
From three to 13, children can access child-friendly services under adult supervision. Those aged 13 to 15 would get restricted access to social media and video-sharing platforms, with limited features and under parental control.
Safety-by-design rules remain in place for minors aged 15 to 18, even though teenagers in this age group could access the platforms without parental consent.
Companies like Meta and Google will have to verify users' age when they open a new account, using an EU-wide age-verification app or other national solutions that check only whether the user is above a certain age.
Proportionate verification is required for existing accounts, based for instance on how long the user has subscribed to the service.
Safety by design
The draft EU Kids Act includes a list of dos and don'ts that tech companies will have to follow to ensure their digital services provide a safe, age-appropriate experience.
In particular, the bill bans design features such as infinite scrolling, artificial notifications and certain reward mechanisms.
Recommender systems, the algorithms that choose which content to display, should be designed to avoid so-called "rabbit holes" and other recommendations driven purely by engagement-based signals.
Risky settings should be disabled by default, while minors' account content would have to be set to private, with unknown users unable to contact them. Reporting harmful content should be made easy.
The bill also envisages offering parents age-appropriate parental control tools.
"These rules and principles will be complemented by tailored commitments for online games, AI chatbots and companions, offering a co-regulatory approach based on industry-led self-regulation," the document reads.
Enforcement
Brussels has often been criticised for being too soft in enforcing its digital rules, as the online environment tends to move too fast for public authorities to keep up.
As a result, the Commission is proposing to shift the burden onto tech companies to prove they are complying with child-safety rules.
Online services already subject to the Digital Services Act's stricter regime, because they are deemed to pose a systemic risk to society, will have to seek authorisation from the Commission before rolling out any new features that could affect children.
Tech companies would be charged a supervisory fee to finance enforcement.

Wholesale prices in Germany increased by 6.8% in August on a yearly basis, largely driven by surging energy and raw material costs stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.

Month-on-month, German wholesale prices grew by 0.9% in August.
