BJP effect: Beef is vanishing from India’s Bengal, forcing diet changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:15:43 UTC
15:15:43 KST

‘More dangerous than drugs’: BJP’s war on beef in India’s West Bengal
Since Prime Minister Modi’s BJP came to power in West Bengal, beef is vanishing from menus as supplies become harder.
Kolkata, India – It’s 12pm on a weekday, and the lane in the city’s Tangra neighbourhood facing the sole bovine slaughterhouse in Kolkata is empty. Run by the city’s municipal corporation, the colonial-era building in the capital of the eastern Indian state of West Bengal looks like a fortress, with its giant iron gates locked from the inside.
A peek through a gap between the gates reveals schoolboys running around and playing in the vast empty campus. “Those boys scale the walls and enter the slaughterhouse ever since it got shut down in May,” says Mehmood Alam, manager of a roadside eatery opposite the facility that mostly caters to daily wage labourers, as well as taxi and autorickshaw drivers. He is still getting used to the desolation, Alam says.
“I don’t think this government will let this reopen any time soon.”
On May 13, the West Bengal government issued a notice on bovine slaughter in the state, only four days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was declared the winner in the state legislature elections that saw the end of the 15-year rule of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress (TMC) party.
The document mentions strict compliance with the West Bengal Animal Slaughter Control Act, 1950, stating that cows, bulls, bullocks, calves and specified buffaloes cannot be slaughtered without a certificate declaring the animal fit for slaughter.
Such a certificate can be issued only if the animal is more than 14 years old, unfit for work or breeding, or has become permanently incapacitated because of age, injury, deformity, or an incurable disease. The notice also states that certified animals may be slaughtered only in a municipal or locally designated slaughterhouse and prohibits slaughter in open public places.
Sales down, beef stew gone
The notification was issued just as Eid approached in May, and the impact was immediate, with restaurants and markets across the city and state reporting an acute shortage of beef. But the effects have outlasted Eid. More than three months later, beef remains in short supply in a state where the meat was widely relished.
That is because the certificate that traders and suppliers need to show, establishing that a specific animal meets the conditions for slaughter, is not the only bottleneck holding up beef trade in Kolkata.
All meat suppliers also need licences authorising them to practise their trade. And the renewal of these licences has been in limbo since the dissolution of the city’s municipal corporation in June, after Firhad Hakim resigned as mayor. Kolkata’s next civic elections are scheduled for December.
Alam’s friend Mushtaq, sitting next to him, is among the affected meat traders. His licence is due for its annual renewal.
He laughs cynically and says none of the six generations before him, all natives of Kolkata who made a living by supplying beef, had to suffer this fate – not under any of the past governments.
“It [the renewal of licence] was halted because of the elections, but they’ve not said anything to us about when they will be renewed. I haven’t made a single penny for more than three months now,” says Mushtaq.
There’s a giant wok of beef bhuna cooking near the entrance of the eatery, and in a smaller one right outside it, pieces of fish rest in a bubbling curry. During “better” days, both woks would have beef cooking. “We only sell the bhuna now,” he says. “Earlier, we’d make a chaap, a stew, but for those, you need better quality beef, not the kind you have been getting in these last few months.”
Prices, however, have risen as supply has dried out. A plate of bhuna now sells for 120 rupees ($1.25), up from 100 rupees ($1.04) before the restrictions came into effect, while buying 1kg (2.2lb) in Kolkata costs anywhere between 350 and 500 rupees ($3.66-$5.22), as opposed to the 200-250 rupee range before May.
“But sales have gone down by a good 50 percent,” says Alam. That’s because he doesn’t have as much beef to sell and he cannot trust the quality as much as he used to – and because many customers are now scared of being seen eating beef in public, under a BJP government, he suggests.
He says he misses a group of young men – mostly Hindus – who would visit his establishment regularly for a plate of beef stew. “And we’ve almost entirely stopped having beef at home, too,” his voice dips further. “Maybe once a week, down from nearly five to six times before. We’re just having vegetables and cheap fish now. Maybe chicken. We can’t afford mutton.”
Bengal’s beef history
West Bengal has historically been among India’s major beef-consuming states. According to government data, 10.4 percent of rural households and 7.9 percent of urban homes in the state reported consuming beef or buffalo meat. In an Indian context, where the cow is held sacred by many Hindus, that’s among the highest beef consumption rates in the country – alongside the neighbouring state of Assam and Kerala in the south.
Among Muslims in West Bengal, two-thirds consume beef, according to government data. Christians, sections of Dalit communities, and some Indigenous communities in West Bengal also eat beef as part of their regular diets.
The law laying down conditions that an animal must meet before it can be slaughtered is not new, but its enforcement has become stringent only now after the BJP came to power in the state.
Officially, the Tangra slaughterhouse is not shut, either. An official, refusing to disclose his identity, opens the small green door along the campus boundary wall and cranes his neck out to see who knocked. “Come back later; the head officer isn’t in today,” he says.
Asked what he does in the office these days, he says: “We just come, spend a few hours and go home.” There is no clarity on when business might return to normal, or whether it will at all, he says.
Some, like Alfaz Laiq, a Kolkata-based businessman, say they saw this crisis coming. In April, as the state held the elections that saw the BJP come to power, Laiq shut down his dairy business in the district of Burdwan in central West Bengal. He sold his retired cows to butchers and meat suppliers at discounted rates.
“If I’d bought a cow for 100 bucks, I sold it for 30 bucks, which is far below the rate at which it would usually go for,” Laiq says. “That’s still better than dealing with the headache” of the harassment that the BJP government has subjected cattle traders to since coming into office, he adds.
Laiq fears that it is only a matter of time before beef becomes a relic of the past in West Bengal’s diet.
In the past, BJP governments have introduced or brought into force strict restrictions on beef consumption in several states. Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Haryana, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka have laws restricting cattle slaughter.
Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana and Uttarakhand also expressly prohibit the sale of beef or beef products. Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh prohibit the possession of beef obtained through illegal slaughter of cattle. Maharashtra prohibits slaughter of cows, bulls and bullocks and possession of their flesh, while Karnataka primarily prohibits slaughter and the sale or transport of cattle for slaughter.
But those legal restrictions have also been accompanied by vigilante justice, with so-called cow-protection gangs attacking and lynching Muslims and Dalits they accuse of either cattle trading or carrying beef. In most cases, law enforcement agencies have subsequently prosecuted survivors of attacks or families of lynching victims, rather than the attackers who carried out the murders.
“I am someone who used to have beef for breakfast but have completely stopped bringing beef,” Laiq says. “Carrying beef has become more dangerous than carrying drugs in Bengal now.”
Laiq has now moved on to buying and selling goats, farming and earning money by leasing out his farmland in the state.
Menus without beef
In the Muslim-majority neighbourhood of Park Circus, a row of beef shop owners refuse to speak about their business except to regular customers. Owners and managers of five such shops selling beef say their businesses have incurred losses of 30-40 percent since May. “All of these shops in this row were shuttered for the first two months. We have only been able to reopen them in the last month-and-a-half,” says one of the shop managers.
“Supply has been erratic, prices have gone up, so sales haven’t been great either. And frankly, the quality of meat has changed as well. It’s not a good time at all,” says another shopkeeper.
Amid tightening regulations on cattle slaughter and declining quality of supplies, at least a dozen restaurants in Kolkata have reported discontinuing their beef dishes in the past three months.
Among them is the iconic Zam Zam Restaurant. The restaurant chain’s director, Shadman Faize, says they could not compromise on quality, so they had to remove beef dishes from their menus at all three branches in the city. “Yes, we have lost customers and are continuing to incur about 40 percent losses. We have even had to lay off staff, but it is what it is,” Faize says. “Hopefully, people will love our other dishes just as much.”
Only a stone’s throw away in the commercial district of Park Street, Olypub – an institution of the city that dates back to 1947 – has for decades been famous for its beef steak. Now, though, it no longer offers that all the time.
“We haven’t taken it off our menu; we just don’t have a regular supply of beef any more, so it’s available only when beef is available,” a member of its management, who requested anonymity, says. “There has never been a situation like this in Kolkata before.”
When Al Jazeera asked Smita Pandey, the commissioner and administrative head of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), when the Tangra slaughterhouse would resume operations and when licence renewals for beef traders would be issued, she said: “The issue is related to the Animal Resources Development Department (ARDD).”
But Nikhil Kumar Shit, director of animal husbandry and veterinary services under the ARDD, said the KMC – under Pandey – was the authority in charge of the slaughterhouse and licences.
“I am not aware of the fact that the Tangra slaughterhouse has not been operational for a while now,” he said. “Usually, the fitness certificates are issued by the KMC and a veterinary officer working with the KMC. I am not really aware of anything beyond this.”
The uncertainty over the future of beef in West Bengal hangs over other parts of the state, too.
In the city of Baruipur, in the district of South 24 Parganas, just beyond the limits of Kolkata, the local market has been running out of beef by 11am since May. “Some days, there is no beef at all,” says Sayed Saifulla, a resident of Baruipur who works as a hairdresser at a salon in Kolkata.
Until May, he says, beef was the one meat whose price did not fluctuate much, even if the cost of fish and mutton rose. Now that has changed. Beef prices have soared, too.
“We had beef almost every day for all our lives,” he says of his family. “Now it’s come down to once or twice a week.” Even with that compromise, the family’s weekly spending on food has gone up 20 percent – from 5,000 rupees before May to 7,000 rupees. “Our earnings aren’t going up the same way, are they?” he asks, rhetorically.
In Malda, a northwestern district where more than half the population is Muslim, a resident requesting anonymity says beef is now only being sold through secret networks. “If you know someone who has a cow, you can ask them to give you some beef,” he says. “So they slaughter the cow in the dead of the night and come and deliver the beef to your doorstep.”
According to him, the fear of being caught dealing with beef is palpable in Malda. “But it’s not easy for the poor Muslim to give up on this meat,” he continues. “So now, they’re risking their safety and their lives to keep eating it.”

Ukraine, Britain wage information war against Russia, GFCN chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:15:25 UTC
15:15:25 KST

MOSCOW, September 15. /TASS/. Ukraine and Britain are waging an aggressive information war against Russia, using specialized institutions and manipulative tactics to influence public perception, President of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) Vladimir Tabak said in an interview with TASS ahead of the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum.
"Ukraine leads the way here, but there is a fairly simple explanation for that. We are in a military conflict, and today the information war is part of the broader war," he said in response to a question about which countries launch the most information attacks against Russia. "At the same time, we understand that several countries also act quite aggressively and use specialized institutions to operate against us. Britain is the primary example. It is a state that acts quite aggressively in the information sphere."
Tabak specified that Kiev has a specialized Center for Information and Psychological Operations, which "is part of the regular armed forces and falls under military units," while London most often relies on "media outlets and platforms that it supports through various grant programs and direct funding."
Britain also uses "AI, work with specific segments of the population, starting with simple narratives in which certain stories are introduced into the information space and extending to more complex operations" to conduct anti-Russian propaganda, the GFCN chief said.
Human psychology as challenge for fact-checking
"But despite the fact that we are in an intense phase of information warfare, we should not overlook ordinary people who often spread false information without malicious intent. This brings us back to the issue of cognitive awareness," he noted. "Our task is to stop constantly saying that everything we see is somehow a product of our adversary. That is not the case. In fact, fake news is nothing new."
People are naturally "inclined, especially when they feel uncertain or do not know the answers to questions that concern them, to come up with rather strange answers themselves, so to speak, or to look for them in completely unverified sources," Tabak emphasized. "That is why we need to work with a broad audience so that people learn to verify information," he concluded.
The GFCN chief therefore concluded that more effective efforts to combat unreliable information at both the professional and everyday level require "broad-based public education and outreach."
About Global Fact-Checking Network
The Global Fact-Checking Network brings together experts and fact-checking organizations worldwide. The association was founded by the TASS news agency, the nonprofit organization Dialogue Regions and the New Media Workshop to combat disinformation. More than 125 journalists from 55 countries already collaborate with GFCN on fact-checking.
The international Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum will take place on September 22 at the Russia National Center in Moscow. TASS is the event’s strategic partner.

The war that changed everything. On historical mistakes, the role of progress and the new world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:13:00 EEST
15:13:00 KST

The war that changed everything. On historical mistakes, the role of progress and the new world
The Russian-Ukrainian war has become the first major war on the territory of Europe, that has no analogues since the Second World War, and it is already part of human history. This is a history not only of events, facts, and the number of victims. This is also the story of the people who stood behind it, people who do not yet realize that they have already entered history. A history that is ruthless toward human feelings because it operates with facts.
However, today this history is only being written. It will be reread and studied much later, in 50 years, when the last witnesses of those events have themselves passed into history, allowing others, people with a cool mind and honesty, to draw conclusions and never repeat the mistakes. To step into history, not get mired in a mess. It was precisely the mistakes that led to this war that prevented it from being brought to a timely end and most importantly failed to predict its consequences.
It is not just a war that has changed so much. In fact, it has changed the most important thing – the world order amidst the applause of absurdity and eccentricity. The world order that our grandfathers built with their own blood over eighty years ago and which we, the generation that still read books, lacked the strength to preserve.
This is a war that, like the Second World War, began due to the cowardice of those who were not being killed at that particular moment. They believed the best course of action was not to disturb the beast.
This is a war that could have ended with far fewer casualties, yet the very people who feared the beast would not sate its appetite and would attack them next simply pretended that these were not their red lines. Because the main thing is to avoid nuclear war.
A war that ultimately became a theater of sympathy for the daily killing of an entire nation choking on its own corruption.
And above all, this is a war that has surrendered itself to marketers and wheeler-dealers – people who, driven by a lack of understanding and strategy, merely stoke the flames of this in pursuit of quick profits, all while increasingly flaunting the rapid pace of technological progress.
A war that came as a surprise, because progress exists not to shape the contours of its conclusion, but precisely to prolong it. For some, it is the conviction that the matter does not concern them, while for others, it is a way of life and a means of earning a living.
A war where strategy and global decisions were left to history while the conflict was still at its peak. And yes, history will not forgive this, because it is people, not machines, who stand behind it all.
This is what the current war means for human history.
However, when speaking specifically about progress as a path to victory and the end of the war, it is necessary to remember: military affairs have their own science, historically developed and still based on established principles, regardless of what content fills TikTok. It is a pity that, due to that very same progress, an understanding of this is increasingly becoming accessible only to a narrow circle of people, and we cannot reach those whose strategy consists solely of social media views and the latest sensational headline.
It was the end of the Second World War that determined two important things that will also characterize the conclusion of this war, which is steadily gaining momentum. The end of the Second World War determined the place and time for the start of the next war, as well as the forms and methods by which that war would begin. And while the first is merely a repetition of mistakes by politicians and their voters, the second undeniably belongs to progress, which will inevitably use these mistakes.
It was precisely this development that lost its intensity with the end of that war and could not lead to anything fundamental. Thus, both the start of the expansion and the restoration of the Russian Empire began as a war in many respects similar to the major conflicts of the 20th century, drawing specifically on the experience of the Second World War. There is nothing surprising or unnatural about this, except for the fact that it was possible to prepare for it at least to avoid it, even if only for a short while.
Then, in the summer of 2023, as military operations within Ukraine intensified and required to survive on the battlefield, the wheel of progress started turning after standing still for nearly 80 years.
My initial thoughts on this in the autumn of 2023 sparked political objections within Ukraine itself and met with absolute incomprehension from representatives of the world's former leading armies.
In Ukraine today, it is politically and financially advantageous to move away from trading in curtains and become a representative for technologies. Those who, just three years ago, formulated their grievances against me now insist that technology is the only right choice for them.
Today, every arms exhibition resembles a scene from science fiction movies and a museum of past wars all at once. Back then, however, everyone thought otherwise. Apart from the progress that was gathering momentum and awaiting the emergence of a new empire to tame it. However, unfortunately, things turned out differently. Progress has become available to our enemies as well, just as it did nearly a century ago, from Verdun and the Somme to Robotyne and Bakhmut. There is nothing wrong with drawing this analogy.
Having gone static, the front brought to life not industrial horrors, but technological ones. And once again, nothing surprising occurred in the evolution of the art of war. The only surprising thing remains that, just as in 2023, using these patterns is still politically disadvantageous here and financially impossible for the world's former leading armies.
This was once the case with cavalry and the famous red trousers worn by the soldiers of one army before the First World War, which were supposed to help against repeating rifles, machine guns, long-range artillery, and the use of smokeless powder, which had been invented there as well, and later against tanks and aircraft. My generation knows how it ended.
And today, the current illusions of collective security, much like that soldier more than a hundred years ago in his dark-blue greatcoat and red trousers, despite being an obvious target on the battlefield, are, regrettably, perceived almost as a symbol of national identity and a source of national pride.
This war has, of course, changed the forms and methods of its conduct, yet it has left its essence unchanged. It is an act of violence, but now violence against the entire country. Violence that, just as in the Second World War, placed on the same level the infantryman physically unable to leave his trench and a newborn baby in another part of the country. Because both of them are constantly in the crosshairs of someone who wants to kill them both. Today's technology of warfare is precisely that it turns an entire country into a vast wasteland, sparing no one – neither those in the trenches nor those in supposedly peaceful places, such as a supermarket. Everything remains the same, yet the bombing process itself has changed, becoming more effective and, consequently, excessively cruel. Do those moving tanks and artillery closer to the crisis zone understand this? Apparently not. The red trousers taught them nothing.
This is no longer a drone war. Someone is about three years behind the times when it comes to drones. They simply no longer exist on their own. They evolved into weapon types more familiar to us, while reducing costs and increasing accessibility and effectiveness.
It is correct to consider that 2026 is a time of war of technologies, and not only technologies. It is also a war of strategies and doctrines that are constantly evolving under the pressure of progress. Therefore, it is a major mistake to focus on individual technologies and their promotion merely as weapons that complement the Soviet strategy and, of course, require specifically Soviet-style executors. Weapons that need to be produced and sold profitably in time and, better yet, used to de-occupy some territory in the process.
It was precisely the desire to liberate the territories and hold them using Soviet methods and strategies, only now with new weapons, that drove mobilisation into a dead end. Mobilization offered only one chance, and fewer and fewer people were willing to take it. But we are not capable of enduring a war of machines against a vast Soviet country, where people are effectively turned into machines and sent to fight against real machines. Damn marketing that kills.
Recognizing technology as a new weapon, it is essential to consider the patterns of the evolution of the art of war and, based on this, invariably shape new forms and methods of its employment. Only then should organizational changes be implemented within the structure of the Armed Forces that employ this new weaponry using new forms and methods of application. This is precisely where mobilisation fits into the new strategy, based on new weapons and specifically on new, rather than Soviet, forms and methods of their employment. Only in this way can we approach the improvement of mobilization and most importantly create systemic pressure and an advantage over the enemy. Of course, this takes time.
These changes are absolutely irreversible and affect the conduct of war at all levels – tactical, operational, and strategic, as well as the development of the military-industrial complex. Logically, all of this inevitably leads to the emergence of a word that some today find rather strange – doctrine. It is doctrine that provides the foundation for systematically influencing the adversary and shapes a strategic vision focused solely on future victory. In whom we observe this systemic influence, and who is closer to victory today – that question remains politically correctly open. However, assessing this in Ukraine through the scale and systematic nature of the strikes and the duration of air-raid alerts is quite straightforward. And a static front certainly cannot reassure those who see it only within the boundaries of operational zones.
It is a pity that many still do not realize or perhaps do not want to realize the scale of these changes. However, this cannot in any way stop scientific and technological progress or the evolution of the art of war.
The old rules no longer apply. The Russian-Ukrainian war demonstrates this daily, and any new major conflicts erupting amidst the reshaping of the old world order will inevitably demonstrate it as well.
The challenges of adapting to new conditions, such as the increased capability and availability of strike assets, the deployment of robotic systems and artificial intelligence, the protection of logistics and ports, effective and uninterrupted communications, space technologies, the digital dimension of security, and the adjustment of personnel training to meet the demands and challenges of modern warfare are challenges that no longer face national armies today, because they should already be prepared for them a priori. These are challenges for governments and alliances, which must unite around technologies that defend their own future.
Modern warfare requires new doctrines. To focus on rapid scientific and technological progress while failing to formulate these doctrines is so shortsighted that it is unlikely to allow us to cast off those same red trousers and see the future. Some still believe it is possible to formulate a truly effective doctrine for the use of drones and robots, while others think it is impossible.
Meanwhile, a war of technologies is already underway, and Ukraine is experiencing systemic pressure resulting from the implementation not only of technologies but also of a new doctrinal approach to their application, including production and research, as an integral part of the strategy. It is precisely this that gives Russia the right to issue us ultimatums through well-known intermediaries. This is precisely what is being targeted, and it could lead to a whole series of crises. Even though some people in a country at war still find it funny, the majority do not need to have it explained to them exactly which crises are involved. Let me remind that a war of attrition involves not only battles but also societal upheavals. The key is who triggers them first.
And if this is obvious, then why do the laws of war once again give way to forecasts, and strategy to marketing? Because capturing general trends for rough forecasts is precisely what curtain marketing requires. Quickly and in large quantities. However, whether this creates systemic pressure on Russia, or increases Russia's systemic pressure on us, remains an unanswered question, even though the ways to understand it are more than obvious.
Thus, to find a way out of this entirely predictable situation, it is necessary to understand the need to seek and implement a systemic response to Russia's systemic pressure. This systemic response must be based on a strategy in which the joint production and implementation of new technological solutions become part of systemic measures both to defend and to impact on Russia's ability to continue the war. For this, of course, the search for resource and technological alliances capable of ensuring this production, including to meet their own defence needs, remains relevant. This production must be doctrinally incorporated into the strategy for victory, where what is produced is not some magic weapon, but the entire new arsenal required, including for civilian purposes, in accordance with the conditions of technological progress.
Ukraine and Russia have turned into real-time testing grounds. Therefore, analyzing and understanding this new logic of war should help not only to shape new doctrines, tactics, and strategies but also, above all, to provide a vision of how peace and people's security can be preserved while we, Ukrainians, are paying for it with our blood.
Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021-2024)

Oil supply squeeze drives up energy bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:09:50 UTC
15:09:50 KST

Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz are raising energy costs worldwide as the war with Iran reaches its 200th day on Sept. 15, putting pressure on importers.
Brent crude rose about 2.8 percent to above $107 a barrel on Sept. 14 as attacks on shipping and the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline increased concerns over supplies.
The pipeline, closed following a drone attack, carries crude to export terminals on the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz. A prolonged outage could threaten up to 4 percent of global oil supplies.
Before the war, Hormuz was a major route for both oil and gas shipments. In 2024, it carried roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption and a similar share of international liquefied natural gas trade, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab estimates that American consumers had incurred more than $100 billion in additional gasoline and diesel costs by Sept. 7.
Its calculations compare actual retail prices with an estimate of what consumers would have paid without the war. The additional spending averaged more than $750 per U.S. household.
Türkiye also remains exposed to higher prices through its dependence on imported fuels. The International Energy Agency identified that reliance and vulnerability to global price fluctuations as continuing challenges in its 2026 review of the country’s energy sector.

That demand was helping to partly offset the effects of conflict in the Middle East and continued uncertainty surrounding trade policies, it added.

Iran war exposes US munitions shortfall, industrial bottlenecks, Pentagon report says
The US military faces shortages of key munitions due to the Iran war and industrial "bottlenecks" to rebuild stockpiles, a Pentagon watchdog warned in a report published on Monday, contradicting US President Donald Trump's assurances that ammunition supplies are "virtually unlimited".
The US Defense Department's inspector general revealed Monday that the United States is facing a shortfall in ammunition as a result of its costly war in Iran.
In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector said that between February 28 and June 30, Operation Epic Fury (OEF) had an estimated cost of $33.4 billion, with $22.3 billion of that spent on expended munitions alone.
The report noted "the munitions expenditure on OEF has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply".
It also lists losses to the American fleet, including four F-15s destroyed, one F-35 damaged, seven KC-135 tanker aircraft damaged and up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly brushed off concerns of depleted weapons stores during the six months of war in the Middle East, saying the US has "virtually unlimited" ammo just a couple weeks ago.
On Monday Trump posted to his Truth Social platform saying again the US is producing "more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History".
CNN previously reported that shortages of long-range guided missiles and air-defence interceptors had affected Trump's strategy in the conflict with Iran, with the US military having "nearly exhausted 80%" of its stock of THAAD interceptors.
Read moreUS military faces ‘beyond critical’ shortage of Patriot missiles in Europe
During the first 24 hours of war against Iran, the United States struck more than 1,000 targets, US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said, and has not returned to such large scale attacks in recent months.
The report notes that "Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict", but does not include those costs in the cost estimates, saying it's not yet clear if all the bases will be built, or who will foot the bill.

The best new hotels around the world

Following the move of the US Embassy in London to its new location in Nine Elms in 2018, 24-31 Grosvenor Square has re-emerged as The Chancery Rosewood.
The Grade II-listed landmark, restored by British architect Sir David Chipperfield, is now an all-suite property.
With more than 700 pieces of art inside, the hotel boasts the largest collection of artwork in a European property.
Another hotel known for its dining options, guests can eat at the first European outpost of Carbone, try Southern Mediterranean cooking at SERRA, discover Masayoshi ‘Masa’ Takayama’s creations at TOBI MASA, or enjoy tea and dessert from executive pastry chef Marius Dufay at JACQUELINE.

Ukraine races to counter Russia's jet-powered drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:06:52 UTC
15:06:52 KST

Ukraine races to counter Russia's jet-powered drone attacks
KYIV/LONDON, Sept 15 - In early July, Ukraine's military invited a large group of producers to test a new generation of interceptors developed to counter the jet-powered attack drones Russia has used to devastating effect in recent months.
According to two sources familiar with the exercise, it did not go to plan.
Many of the interceptor drones proved difficult to control at speeds sometimes exceeding 400 kilometres per hour. Some crashed into nearby fields and forests, the sources said.
The exercise underscored the challenge Ukraine faces heading into another winter without enough Western air defences to counter Russian ballistic missiles and with no clear answer to Moscow's faster, more powerful drones.
Russia increased its use of jet-powered drones roughly sixfold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data seen by Reuters.
Much can change in two months in a conflict marked by rapid technological innovation. But on Friday, a senior commander openly complained that in the key area of jet-powered drones, Kyiv was lagging.
"With the jet drones, we completely screwed up the initiative again, that's a fact," said Maksym Zhorin, deputy commander of the 3rd Army Corps on the Telegram messaging app.
"The Russians have set up mass production and use of jet Shaheds, and we don't even know what to do about them."
Yuriy Cherevashenko, a deputy commander of Ukraine's air force, acknowledged the difficulties of developing faster interceptor drones but said Ukraine was close to fielding a range of mass-produced, low-cost solutions.
"I'm confident that soon we could fully have a class of weapons that will be effective at countering jet-powered UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles)," he told Reuters.
JET DRONES SWARM SKIES OVER KYIV
Russia's rapid expansion of jet drone production has allowed it to bombard Ukraine, particularly Kyiv, with overwhelming numbers of weapons whose speed makes them far harder to shoot down than their piston-powered predecessors.
After Russia began launching thousands of cheap, propeller-driven Shahed drones at Ukraine in 2022, Kyiv developed increasingly effective ways to destroy them, pushing interception rates to around 90%.
Moscow responded by making its drones faster, the latest step in a technological race that has shaped the battlefield throughout nearly five years of war.
The shift comes as Russia continues its relentless use of far more powerful ballistic missiles, while Ukraine struggles with shortages of advanced interceptors needed to counter them.
Russia already produces about 3,000 jet-powered drones a month, Ukraine's defence intelligence estimates. Some resemble the triangular-winged Shaheds, while others have tubular bodies and small wings more akin to cruise missiles.
Russia launched around 450 drones with a speed of between 240 and 500 kilometres per hour in June, a figure that rose to about 2,850 in August, the data showed. A typical Shahed-type drone — a cheap, piston-powered attack drone based on an Iranian design — flies at less than 200 km/h.
The capital Kyiv and its surrounding region were most heavily targeted, accounting for nearly a fifth of all drones launched, the data showed.
Cherevashenko said areas in and around Kyiv and the Black Sea port city of Odesa, a main hub for Ukraine's seaborne exports, had borne the brunt of the attacks.
"Going forward, the overall number of such drones in strikes will increase," Cherevashenko said.
In some attacks, he said the percentage of jet-powered drones is already over 70%.
'SWORD AGAINST SHIELD'
In recent weeks, jet-powered drones have been slamming into targets in central Kyiv.
"The main danger of these drones is that they're guided: meaning they can change their flight route and altitude, through an operator's command," Cherevashenko said.
The drone that struck the headquarters of the SBU security agency last week, hitting the office of its chief with pinpoint accuracy, is thought by officials and military analysts to have been manually guided.
Samuel Bendett, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, said the war in Ukraine was a constant "sword vs. shield" struggle, with each new capability and innovation quickly countered by the adversary.
"The current Russian advantage will eventually be eroded by Ukrainian counter capabilities in the form of fast and cheap interceptors capable of going after (jet powered drones)," he said.
INTERCEPTOR DRONES ALMOST INEFFECTIVE
To counter the thousands of Shahed-type UAVs fired every month last year, Ukraine developed interceptor drones that typically cost less than $2,000 and were able to down a high percentage of incoming drones.
However, these weapons cannot keep up with jet drones.
Borys Dolyna, a commander of an interceptor drone company, said it was sometimes possible to hit certain models of the jet-powered UAVs when they slowed to manoeuvre. But he warned that Russia was already deploying and refining onboard systems that detect approaching objects and automatically accelerate.
Ukraine already has over a thousand trained interceptor drone crews. Companies are rushing to make faster interceptors, some powered by jets themselves, but as the July test failure showed, progress is patchy.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said that more than 60 Ukrainian companies are working on intercepting jet-powered drones, though only a handful have demonstrated results.
One Ukrainian drone industry source said that some prototypes can be too large and slow to deploy in combat, where opportunities to engage fast-moving targets are brief.
NEW SOLUTIONS
One of the most promising solutions, officials and experts say, is a new generation of cheap guided missiles. Ukraine's stocks of expensive Western-supplied air-defence missiles are limited and were never designed to counter massed attacks by jet drones.
Cherevashenko said some of the new rockets were already undergoing testing, and would be significantly cheaper than the drones they are designed to down.
Ukraine was previously able to divert some Russian drones by feeding them false GPS data, but the drone industry source said many jet drones were operating on advanced 16-channel antennae, making them highly resistant to jamming and signal disruption.
Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi, director of development at Fly Group Ukraine, a defence company, told Reuters that individual systems would no longer be enough and that the answer lay in a networked approach, with multiple devices operating as a single "organism" to confuse enemy navigation systems.
"The drone continues to think it is flying toward its target, but its own autopilot, relying on the false coordinates, gradually changes course on its own and steers the craft away from cities into safe areas."
The drone industry source said today's interceptor drones, despite being slower than their targets, could be adapted to attack head-on rather than chase from behind. That would require AI-driven targeting systems capable of precisely calculating an incoming drone's flight path.
Cherevashenko said there had already been successful head-on interceptions using both automated guidance software and manually piloted drones. While the technology still required further development before large-scale deployment, he said it represented the future of air defence.
For now, however, much of the burden falls on military aircraft, which are fast enough to keep pace with jet-powered drones. Dwindling supplies of air-to-air missiles are increasingly forcing pilots to rely on cannons, a hazardous tactic that risks collision with a drone's debris. REUTERS

What to know about Russia's upcoming parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15

15:06:47 KST

What to know about Russia's upcoming parliamentary election
MOSCOW, Sept 15 - Russia holds a parliamentary election on September 18 to 20, the first since it launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022.
The political system is tightly controlled and the ruling United Russia party, backed by President Vladimir Putin, is widely expected to retain its dominance of the 450-seat State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
Here's what to look out for:
WHO IS BEING ELECTED?
• Voters will elect all 450 members of the Duma to five-year terms. Half of the seats are allocated through a nationwide party-list vote. The other 225 are decided by voting in single-seat constituencies.
• A survey by state pollster VTsIOM at the end of August showed United Russia far in the lead of other parties with 37% support among respondents, followed by the Communist Party with 11.6%.
• The margin of United Russia's expected win will be in focus. It currently has 310 seats in the Duma and needs to win at least 300 to keep its supermajority and ability to push through constitutional changes without other parties' support.
LIMITED REAL OPPOSITION
• The four other parties expected to re-enter the Duma, including the Communist Party and the ultra-nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, broadly support the war and tend to vote with United Russia on key issues.
• The Supreme Court has barred the liberal Yabloko party from taking part in the party-list ballot, sidelining the only registered political party to oppose Russia's war in Ukraine. Some Yabloko candidates are still running as the ruling does not apply to single-seat constituencies, but they appear unlikely to win any seats.
• A number of other opposition politicians have been barred from participating after being designated as "foreign agents."
WHAT DO OBSERVERS SAY?
• The only independent nationwide election watchdog, Golos, which sharply criticised the conduct of past elections, closed down in 2025 following years of pressure from the authorities.
• Moscow has not invited international monitors from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe to observe the upcoming vote, which the OSCE said reflected a pattern of Russian government disregard for transparency, democratic accountability and the rule of law.
• The OSCE says Russia's political system has become more restrictive since the last parliamentary vote in 2021 with the exclusion of candidates labelled "foreign agents," further limits on campaign financing and other measures.
• Russian authorities have rejected criticism of the electoral process, saying voting is conducted in accordance with the law, and they have said that Russia's Western enemies are trying to undermine and disrupt the election.
VOTING IN RUSSIAN-CONTROLLED UKRAINE
• The election is also being held in Crimea, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, and in Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine's Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.
• Voting started early in some areas due to security reasons, according to the authorities. REUTERS

The US, facing competition from China, has made a concerted effort in recent years to expand its role in building subsea cables, which carry nearly all international internet traffic.

Battle for Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:01:00 UTC
15:01:00 KST

Belarus is perched atop Ukraine, and the two countries are ethnically and historically entwined. Their people are East Slavic, as are Russians, but they were part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for centuries, which made them distinct. Both countries were also part of the USSR until it collapsed in December 1991 following Ukraine’s departure.
Then in 2014, the feisty Ukrainians staged a revolution against their pro-Russian president, and Moscow invaded, taking 7% of their territory, including Crimea. In 2022, Russian President Putin tried to take over all of Ukraine and, after five years, has bankrupted his economy, shattered his armed forces, and occupies only 19% of the country.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
By contrast, Belarusians staged a pro-democracy revolution in 2020, but it was crushed after Russia got involved and used extreme violence. Ever since, however, its President, Alexander Lukashenko, has fended off a total Russian takeover and, since 2022, has gotten away with refusing Putin’s demand to join his invasion of Ukraine.
Belarus is geopolitically important for many reasons. It is key to Russia’s War against Europe. Putin wants the Belarusian army involved with his forces to open a second, northern front against Ukraine and to hold several NATO nations (the Baltics and Poland) hostage along a lengthy stretch of border.
Putin has had military bases in Belarus for years with only 2,000 troops, but recently installed dozens of tactical nuclear warheads and other powerful missile systems there. Russia also has drone stations along the Belarus-Ukraine border that guide its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine.
Zelensky Seeks Reciprocity as US Urges Halt to Strikes on Russian Energy
But on June 19, President Volodymyr Zelensky demanded that Belarus dismantle these stations and gave Lukashenko a week to do so. “I think a week will be enough for him to do it. If he doesn’t do it, we will,” said Zelensky in a press conference. By June 22, the stations were offline.
Putin’s brutal five-year war has placed Belarus and its leader between a rock and a hard place. So far, he has adeptly finessed his way through the political hazards by staying out of the war. Lukashenko’s carefully choreographed “neutrality” has also helped Ukraine and its allies.
He has done so, despite being economically dependent on Russia, by refusing to order the Belarusian army to support the war. However, Russian military bases in Belarus have helped launch a few invasions and attacks against Ukraine. But now a frustrated Putin wants more assistance, and Lukashenko has impeded that with some impressive diplomatic gymnastics.
On June 26, Lukashenko caved in to Ukraine’s demands to shut down Russian drone stations. Then he was immediately summoned to closed-door meetings with Putin in remote Russia, where he was pressured to join Russia’s war against Ukraine.
But on June 29, he flew to Beijing for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and the two declared their unity, according to a Chinese government press release: “President Xi Jinping stressed that China and Belarus should maintain strategic communication and further promote the high-level bilateral relationship to bring more benefits to the two peoples. China supports Belarus in safeguarding its national sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, and in pursuing a development path befitting its national conditions. China will continue to provide support for the development of Belarus to the best of its capability.”
The statement was extraordinary.
This is because China has had its own assets and ambitions in the region for some time.
After the two met in Beijing, Lukashenko returned to Minsk on July 6 and bluntly and publicly stated that his troops would not be sent to fight in Ukraine. At a military college, he said: “I stress once again, dear comrades, that nobody is going to send you into this bloodbath. We don’t need war; it’s bad that war is going on in Ukraine. We are supporters of solving matters peacefully.”
Lukashenko enlisted China’s help because for 13 years, Beijing has invested heavily in Belarus, building rail and road infrastructure designed to connect China to European markets. It was the Belt and Road Initiative that established a strong bilateral trade and investment relationship. For Belarus, this link with China has been important to reduce its dependence on Russia and also to obtain Chinese trade and technology to overcome Western sanctions. But now their partnership represents his lifeline against Russian demands to fight Ukraine.
Lukashenko’s strategy was also politically cunning because 97% of Belarusians oppose any direct involvement in the Ukraine war. If he balked at that, he would likely have another revolution or street protests on his hands. Estimates are that, since 2022, tens of thousands of Belarusians have secretly helped Ukraine or served in its armed forces. They also resent Russia’s military presence and the de facto occupation of their nation.
Zelensky also addressed the danger to Belarusians if they joined the war: “When Lukashenko says he does not want to be involved in the war, he should be honest, at least with his own people,” Zelensky said. “It is not only he who could be drawn into the war: his entire country could be dragged into it by Russia.”
It was a message that resonates because Ukraine and Belarus suffered some of the highest human casualties and physical destruction of any regions in the world during World War II. Both were completely occupied by Nazi Germany and mostly destroyed because they were the primary battlegrounds of the Eastern Front. More than 10 million died, and the rest were subjugated by the Soviet Union for decades.
Now, once again, the two nation-states find themselves enmeshed in another brutal European war. Ukraine has been ravaged for five years but holds the line for Europe and NATO against all odds. Next in line is Belarus, which is compromised but not yet fully annexed by Moscow.
Thus far, Lukashenko, who is half Ukrainian, juggles his difficult situation, which is not easy considering the circumstances. Belarus gets discounted oil and natural gas from Moscow and has also borrowed huge amounts from Russia, leaving the country without economic independence. It is virtually a full-fledged Russian satellite state and clearly in Putin’s sights as his next territorial acquisition.
China’s involvement is very significant. Beijing obviously believes that Russia’s war will wane and that both Ukraine and Belarus will be economic powerhouses and potential trading partners.
But to Ukrainians, Lukashenko is a sell-out to Moscow. “He had made an all-or-nothing gamble, like someone betting everything on a single number in a casino. He bet that Russia would destroy Ukraine,” said Zelensky. “He walked into the casino on the wrong day. He was certain he’d hit the jackpot. He hit nothing.
The good news is how he differs from Putin, which is that, I think, he fully understands all the risks. If you know the war isn’t won, and you suddenly get pulled in further as an ally in this war – well, he has enough sense to understand that he shouldn’t get dragged into that.”
As for the future, Zelensky stated that good-neighborly relations between Ukraine and Belarus are possible, but only if both nations are genuinely independent from Moscow.

Help-to-buy scheme delivered ‘very high value for money,’ review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:00:29 UTC
15:00:29 KST

George Osborne’s scheme to reduce costs for first-time buyers represented “very high value for money”, according to a government review, bolstering the case of senior government figures who have been arguing to resurrect the idea.
An official audit of the help-to-buy programme has calculated it provided £25bn of social value to the UK in the last financial year, despite criticisms it was overly expensive and only served to inflate house prices.
The findings will boost the case of those, including the housing minister Matthew Pennycook, who have been pushing behind the scenes for Labour to create its own version in a bid to boost home ownership among young voters.
Sources say Pennycook and the former housing secretary Steve Reed advocated strongly for such a move but were ultimately overridden by the chancellor, Rachel Reeves, who wanted to focus more on boosting housing supply.
The report found: “The help-to-buy scheme supported expanded home ownership, particularly in already affordable areas.
“For some people, it helped them on to the housing ladder sooner or enabled them to buy when they might not otherwise have been able to afford to do so.
“For others, it supported people to skip a rung on the housing ladder and buy a larger or more expensive home. On this basis, the help-to-buy scheme delivered its core aim of supporting home ownership.”
The report did not take into account the effect on house prices, but it does rebut a central Treasury argument that it was an expensive way to boost home ownership and expand the supply of new houses.
It added that more than 387,000 people bought their own home through the scheme, more than 328,000 of whom were first-time buyers. Nearly half of customers said they could not have bought a home without the scheme.
A government spokesperson said: “There are no current plans to introduce a new help-to-buy scheme.
“But it’s important to learn what went well and what went wrong with the previous scheme, which is why we undertook a robust evaluation, as is normal for all major programmes.”
Both the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and his predecessor Keir Starmer have prioritised new housebuilding as they seek to tackle the country’s housing crisis.
Starmer promised to oversee 1.5m new homes over the course of this parliament, although the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, admitted this weekend that would prove difficult to meet.
So far ministers have focused on stimulating supply, pledging £39bn for new social and affordable homes and undertaking significant planning reform in an effort to encourage housebuilders to start new projects.
Labour has not, however, followed the Conservatives and introduced a scheme to subsidise first-time buyers.
In 2013, Osborne announced the first iteration of help to buy, offering taxpayer-backed loans to reduce the deposit buyers would need. Later that year, he launched a second version, which covered part of any losses that lenders made on mortgages with a high loan-to-value ratio.
Both applied to homes worth up to £600,000, and by 2014-15, they supported about a fifth of first-time buyer purchases.
The schemes proved popular, but were criticised by some as helping those who would have got on the housing ladder anyway and contributing to soaring house prices.
Earlier this year the Institute for Fiscal Studies found much of the benefit went to higher earners who would eventually have been able to buy a home anyway – particularly those living outside London and south-east England.
Despite these criticisms, multiple sources have told the Guardian that ministers and officials in the housing department were pushing to recreate a version of the scheme as soon as this year’s budget.
Reed wanted to create a scheme that focused on those who would not otherwise be able to afford to buy a home, especially where the housing market has recently cooled.
The former housing secretary is understood to have spoken to housebuilders before he left office about how such a scheme might be structured.
The Home Builders Federation, for example, has proposed a programme whereby developers would pay a fee to allow first-time buyers to buy their properties with the help of a government-backed 20% equity loan.
Sources familiar with previous discussions say such ideas were rebutted by Reeves, who wanted to focus on attempts to free up planning laws to encourage development instead.
A spokesperson for John Healey, however, refused to comment on the new chancellor’s view.

Sky gave my father the hard sell even though he has dementia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:00:29 UTC
15:00:29 KST

I was helping my father, who has dementia and Parkinson’s disease, reduce his £113.50 Sky TV bill.
We explained to the Sky call centre agent that, as his eyesight and attention span have deteriorated, he wanted the cheapest available TV package to free up money for his care.
The agent insisted on offering Sky Cinema, two new televisions, another 24-month Sky Q package and broadband, despite us repeatedly stating that we did not want any further offers. We asked to cancel.
Eventually, we were offered £18-a-month Sky Essential TV. However, we were then asked to authorise a £77 monthly direct debit because Sports and Cinema had been automatically added.
The adviser told us to disregard the amount and trust him to remove the unwanted packages after activation. We refused and asked to cancel instead.
What happened next was extraordinary. We asked six times to cancel, and each time the adviser continued trying to persuade us to stay. They finally allowed the cancellation.
I’m appalled at how persistent the sales pressure was once Sky knew Dad had dementia.
EH, Kent
The fact that customers who wish to cancel, or downgrade, a contract are passed to a “customer loyalty team” suggests what lies in store. That team regards loyalty as non-negotiable, judging by the transcript of your call to the company.
When, after a blizzard of unsuitable deals, you asked to cancel, the loyalty team told you that you would have to discuss the request with the “retention team”. This team, it admitted, would strive to retain your custom. Which, with ruthless tenacity, it did.
It is extremely concerning that you were pressured to sign up to a £77-a-month subscription after being quoted £18 a month.
Over and over again, the retention team adviser claimed he would remove the unwanted Sports and Cinema elements that had inflated the price once you had signed up. Repeatedly he implored you to trust him, and ignored your six requests to cancel.
This would be bad enough for a healthy customer. For an elderly man with dementia, it is deplorable. Telecoms firms have a duty to treat vulnerable customers fairly.
I reported Sky’s behaviour to the regulator Ofcom. It says: “The conditions, or procedures, that providers have in place, must not act as a disincentive for vulnerable customers who wish to cancel their contract.
“Where we see themes emerging, or evidence of widespread harm, we’ve shown we’ll take action where appropriate.”
Sky tells me that it does have procedures for supporting vulnerable customers and that these were not followed in your father’s case. Instead, it says, the agent followed “standard process”.
That suggests that customers who are not vulnerable are routinely exposed to this oppressive hard sell before they can escape.
The company admits that the unwanted Sports and Cinema elements should have been removed from the package before you were asked to sign, and claims that the agent did not have the system access to do so.
“We are very sorry for how the customer’s request was handled,” it adds. “His experience was not in line with the standards of care and support we expect customers with additional needs to receive, and our established process was not followed on this occasion.”
Your father is finally free of the company, albeit minus his favourite TV channels. Other customers who feel they have been mis-sold or misled can complain to the Communication & Internet Services Adjudication Scheme, CISAS.

Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions.

One in five black, Asian and minority ethnic NHS managers in England plan to quit amid racism, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

The NHS in England is facing an exodus of minority ethnic managers who have suffered racism, exclusion and discrimination during their working lives, a report has found.
Almost four-fifths of managers from black, Asian and minority ethnic (BAME) backgrounds have experienced racism, exclusion and obstacles to progressing in their careers, according to a survey carried out by the NHS Alliance.
The problem is so widespread that one in five say they will quit the NHS in the next three years, amid renewed concern the service is doing too little to eradicate ingrained racism.
The NHS Alliance, which surveyed 950 BAME managers, said the findings are “further evidence of the corrosive and demoralising impact of racism in the NHS”. They risk a “haemorrhaging” of managers and senior leaders from BAME backgrounds, it warned.
Sir Ciarán Devane, the NHS Alliance’s chief executive, said “political and cultural polarisation” meant the diversity of the NHS’s leadership is more important than ever.
“Yet we now face a very real risk of senior minority ethnic colleagues walking away, discouraged, disheartened and disillusioned. This also represents a huge loss of talent from the NHS,” Devane added.
Survey participants described a lack of diversity in the senior leadership teams where they worked, being excluded from informal networks and “progression disparities” – not getting a fair chance to advance their careers compared with white colleagues. There is a worrying gap between BAME managers’ desire to rise through the ranks and their belief they will be able to do so.
“I am the only brown face at 99% of my meetings at strategic and policy level,” a black senior manager said. An Asian manager said: “There is a culture of nepotism. Although I believe I have the experiences, knowledge and ability to be promoted, the culture is too strong.”
A third manager, of African heritage, said: “There is a clear lack of diversity at senior levels and this absence makes it difficult to feel seen, supported or inspired to progress.”
The NHS’s leadership is more diverse than before. For example, the proportion of BAME members of NHS boards has risen from 7.1% in 2016 to 17.3% in 2025.
However, enduring institutional and structural racism means a series of initiatives it has undertaken to tackle discrimination have produced little meaningful change, a new report by the alliance said.
Too many BAME managers, including some who occupy very senior roles, face “continuing racism, exclusion and inequity in their everyday working lives” as well as “isolation and covert discrimination”, the alliance found.
In an upcoming episode of the NHS Alliance’s podcast, Health on the Line, Victor Adebowale, its chair, said: “The fact is the NHS is institutionally racist.”
In a plea to NHS bosses to do more, Lord Adebowale said: “If you are a competent leader, then you should be leading everyone everywhere all the time. In order to do that, you need to understand who you are employing; who they are. You need to raise the issue of race and racism not as a special thing, but as part of business as usual. This is what we do.”
The NHS Race and Health Observatory said it had seen a growing number of inquiries from BAME NHS staff who had experienced racism in their workplaces.
“These findings are alarming, but not surprising,” said Prof Habib Naqvi, its chief executive, responding to the NHS Alliance’s report.
“They expose a stark reality: too many black, Asian and minority ethnic NHS staff are still facing racism at work, with serious consequences for their mental and physical wellbeing, careers and willingness to stay in the service.
“Racism has become too normalised in parts of the system and NHS leaders must confront it with urgency, accountability and sustained action.”
An NHS England spokesperson said: “Racism and discrimination have no place in the NHS and it is completely unacceptable for any member of staff to experience them at work.
“While there has been progress in increasing minority ethnic representation in senior roles, we know there is much more to do to ensure equal representation and equal opportunities for all staff to progress and be treated fairly and with respect.
“That is why the new NHS staff standards require trusts to take sustained action to tackle racism, with clear board-level accountability and action to ensure equity in recruitment and career progression, with progress measured through the NHS oversight framework.”

Why unwanted fridges are piling up at recycling centres across England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

‘In Oxfordshire, recycling centres are filling almost three articulated lorries with discarded fridges every week,” says Simon Perry of W&S Waste Management, which runs a recycling centre in Ardley.
Together, those fridges would cover an area just under half the size of a football pitch. But the space to store them – in Oxfordshire and beyond – has become a growing problem after the Local Government Association (LGA) warned that a mountain of broken fridges was rising in waste centres across England and Wales, as this year’s heatwaves push more white goods to breaking point, and a trend for second/backup refrigeration products keeps growing.
Councils say there are now not enough facilities to recycle fridges after a major centre at Newport Docks went into liquidation last year, leaving more than 80,000 fridges and freezers stranded, overwhelming local storage capacity. Two other centres have shut in recent years.
Councils from Bradford to Gloucestershire, Durham and Nottinghamshire are among 26 to have suspended fridge collections this month, and the backlog is adding to financial pressures on local authorities.
At the centre in Ardley, four fridges sit waiting to be taken away – two small, two large, several looking barely worn. The council has managed capacity this year by asking people to book slots before bringing in fridges, but is having to tighten those restrictions further. Fridge and freezer drop-offs are temporarily limited to Oxfordshire residents only, and booking slots – limited to the week ahead – cannot be made for new appointments until 28 September, though existing district bulky waste collections will still be honoured.
Laura Gordon, an Oxfordshire county councillor, fears that unless the issue is resolved, for Oxfordshire and other councils the situation will get worse. “There’s a window of opportunity now to fix the problem,” she says. “The cost of not doing that – both financially and environmentally – will start to mount up really quickly if that window isn’t taken.” The Newport site could be brought back online, but otherwise the only option is a new facility opening in January, she says, which will take time to reach full capacity.
Part of the problem is that fridges are hard to recycle. Every fridge contains refrigerant gas that must be safely drained before the unit can be processed. Perry points to a small box fitted to the back of one fridge: the compressor, which holds the refrigerant and has to come out first. Even the foam insulation inside the walls is a hazard, meaning fridges cannot go through a standard metal recycling line – they need specialist plants equipped to degas them safely. That means sites holding fridges need an environmental permit or registered exemption, since they are classed as hazardous waste.
Purchasing patterns suggest the wave of fridges in recycling centres is not due to a sudden increase in new fridge purchases or replacements. Stefan Hay, the chief executive of the UK Home Appliance Association (AMDEA), said the market for fridges over the last five years had been “pretty flat”. He said: “Sales in the first half of 2026 were actually down slightly, as were WEEE (waste electrical and electronic equipment) collections against target.” The trend towards larger American-style fridges is also not contributing.
There has, however, been growth in additional refrigeration. Hildreth said: “In recent years there has been a growth in second/backup refrigeration products, driven initially by Covid but a trend that has continued and potentially because of the more recent advice from government to ‘stock up’ in preparation for El Niño. We expect extreme weather will drive it further.”
Jon Hubbard, the chair of the LGA’s neighbourhoods committee, said the situation was a “system failure”. With three facilities out of action, he said, there was not enough spare capacity and councils were facing complaints as some residents were told not to bring fridges in at all.
Under the “polluter pays” principle behind the WEEE recycling system, it should be manufacturers and retailers, not councils, who fund the collection, treatment and storage of old fridges, through producer compliance schemes. But because the treatment capacity is squeezed, those schemes have been unable to keep clearing council sites, leaving some local authorities footing the storage bill themselves. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs has said future compliance-fee rules could take the shortage into account, but any change is not expected to be decided until early 2027.
“We do not want the cost of a failure elsewhere in the system to be passed on to residents,” Hubbard said. “The recycling scheme is already funded by producers. If councils are being asked to step in and provide temporary solutions, the additional costs should be funded too.” Ultimately, he said, councils need confidence that the system works: “We cannot find ourselves putting out the same warnings about mountains of unwanted fridges every summer.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “Delays to collection or being unable to dispose of your fridge or freezer is frustrating, and we are pushing producers to fix this fast and keep disruption to a minimum. We appreciate the challenges facing local authorities, and are working closely with them, the Environment Agency and industry to manage the impact of capacity shortages, including allowing temporary storage sites.”

====================================================================================================

Sweden’s far right is down, but not yet out. Left and centre leaders must seize this opportunity | Cas Mudde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:00:27 UTC
15:00:27 KST

After the previous Swedish general election, in 2022, the leaders of the two biggest Swedish parties made a risky decision. Jimmie Åkesson, the leader of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), chose to support the rightwing minority government of the Moderate party prime minister Ulf Kristersson, while Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats’ leader, decided to copy the “Danish model” in an attempt to regain power. In both cases, the strategy led to electoral loss but political success.
After the general election in the country on Sunday, the Social Democrats (often referred to as S or Sap), in common with its Danish counterparts, will probably lead the new government despite an electoral defeat, losing roughly 2%, its worst result since 1908. The party’s return to power is purely a result of Swedish bloc politics and the victories of its likely coalition partners: the Left party (V), the Green party and the Center party (C), which all increased their support by 1.5%, 1.7% and 0.4% respectively. Together, this left bloc has a majority of just three seats in the new parliament. So while Andersson will probably return to power, she is also in a very vulnerable position.
While the three leftwing parties agree on a lot of socioeconomic issues, particularly undoing some of the worst rightwing policies of the past years and investing more in the public sector, they hold very different views on issues like crime and immigration. Should Andersson continue to demand strict immigration rules and link crime to immigration, this could lead to significant tensions in her coalition, similar to those that her Danish counterpart, Mette Frederiksen, faced in her first government.
At the same time the small Center party, the least leftwing of the left bloc, has ruled out a (formal) coalition with the “radical” Left party, and will want to protect the market from too much state intervention. This will create further tensions within the left bloc in a probable minority government. Given that format and the inevitable internal tensions, a majority of just three seats would require almost unrealistic levels of discipline for the minority government to sit out a full term.
On the other side of the political spectrum, the Sweden Democrats had their first loss in a national parliamentary election. Still, there is little reason to assume that Åkesson will face a backlash. First, he was the only leader who had any significance to a majority of his party’s electorate. Second, his support strategy worked: the Sweden Democrats is now completely normalised within the right bloc, as the leader of the Moderate party (or M), Kristersson, had already announced before the election that the Sweden Democrats would be part of a next rightwing government. Third, the party’s nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.
We should also not forget that the 2022 election campaign offered the perfect political context for the Sweden Democrats, given that it was dominated by two themes: immigration and the acceptance of the Sweden Democrats. As we know from other elections (such as in the Netherlands in 2023), when opposition to immigration and the acceptance of the far right dominate the political agenda, the far right wins big. This time round, those topics were still there, but they did not dominate the campaign – in fact, no single issue did. On top of that, the Sweden Democrats were linked to some scandals close to the election, which might have further decreased support for the party. Still, it held on to 78% of its 2022 electorate, more than the centre-right Moderates (59%) and centre-left Social Democrats (73%).
While Andersson may try to convince her party, and herself, that the “Danish model” has worked, she should take a better look at her small neighbour to the west. The Danish Social Democratic party has hit historical lows in national and local elections (notably in the capital, Copenhagen). And although Frederiksen in Denmark is such a convincing nativist that even far-right leaders in other countries hail her as an example, the far right is barely less popular than before – just more divided.
Interestingly, while Andersson thanked the youth and student branches for their great work in her election night speech, the Social Democrats scored significantly lower among first-time voters than among the electorate as a whole (21% and 28%, respectively). In contrast, the Left and the Greens did significantly better among the youth. This reflects a development we see across Europe, namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties. The Social Democrats were the most popular among Swedes with non-European roots, however, gaining no less than 38% of support within this growing part of the electorate. No doubt this group is also not looking for more nativist policies and rhetoric.
In short, even if the Social Democrats have regained power because of the “Danish model”, which is in itself debatable, this same strategy will be a risk for the new coalition and for the electoral future of the party. Rather than continuing to be a “moderate” or “sensible” alternative to the Moderates, Andersson should fully commit to a progressive political agenda, both on socioeconomic and socio-cultural policies. That way she not only has a better chance of holding her coalition together, but also might make her party attractive to new and younger voters again.
- 
  Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author of The Far Right Today
