It has also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter, pushing oil prices above the $100 threshold.

The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed on Tuesday that there had been missile and drone attacks the previous day on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, reporting 13 wounded.
Riyadh responded with more than 50 strikes, as it had the day before, according to the Houthis.
The coalition said it would deal with the attacks "firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom" and would take "all necessary operational measures to deter this... hostile and extremist approach".
Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis' politburo said the "Yemeni response will continue and escalate as long as they (Saudi Arabia) persist in their aggression against our people".

"The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage - The concept of which we are open to," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was expected to hold talks with Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el Sisi on Tuesday, Cairo announced.
Yemeni government forces on Sunday said they had recaptured positions in the southwestern province of Taiz from Houthis and carried out air strikes, telling the official Saba news agency they killed at least 10 gunmen.
The Saudi crown prince received US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday to discuss "the latest developments in the region", according to Saudi news agency SPA.
The admiral travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination meetings, according to US news site Axios.
The Houthis seized Yemen's capital Sanaa in 2014 at the outset of the civil war, driving the government to Aden in the south.
The following year, Saudi Arabia led a coalition to intervene on the side of the government, launching wave after wave of air strikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.

On the International Day of Democracy: Encounter, Equity and the Symbolic Power of Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

On the International Day of Democracy, this year the United Nations revisits a traditional idea within the concept: broad citizen participation in government decision-making. On this occasion, the international body invites reflection on how participation and the inclusion of diverse voices in government decision-making can help build a more equitable society. From a spatial perspective, reflection on democracy can move beyond this vertical framing and instead understand it through encounter. What does it mean for a space to be democratic? How can architecture contribute to achieving the principles historically associated with democracy? In the current context of crisis in political organization systems worldwide, this day serves as a platform to question individualization and authoritarianism through the socio-spatial tools available to us.
Broad as it is, the concept of democracy is neither neutral nor objective. Historically, democracy has also been used as grounds for processes of colonization, the validation of abusive power structures, and the protection of private property. However, the concept is largely understood as a channel toward shared values such as justice, equity, and social security. In the words of the United Nations, "as much a process as a goal." How can we pursue these values through the design of the built environment and the study of territory? From the angle of freedom of expression, we can understand public space as a platform for encounters between strangers, capable of fostering dialogue and tolerance. From the angle of territorial justice, we have design and private-property regulation tools available to confront the climate crisis and issues of representation and access to housing. At the scale of the building, we can recognize both construction as a political activity and buildings as bearers of social symbols.
Below, we present a selection of articles on four themes: public spaces for participation, climate resilience and property in the territory, public policies for fair access to housing, and symbolism in the design of our buildings. The aim is to open up reflection on the relationship between architecture and democracy from a global, open, and civic perspective.

'Tareekh Pe Tareekh': 100% complete, still no keys - Inside RERA’s extension loop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:29:39 UTC
14:29:39 KST

A housing project misses its promised completion date. The developer asks for more time. The regulator grants it. There is nothing extraordinary about that sequence. Construction can be held up for many reasons, some of them outside a developer's control. Sometimes a few more months are exactly what a project needs to get buyers their homes. The difficulty begins when the wait becomes tareekh pe tareekh.The question is simple. When a delayed project is given more time, how often does that extra time actually result in completion? There is no national public number that answers it.TOI tried to get closer to one by examining Maharashtra, one of the country's largest RERA (Real Estate Regulatory Authority) markets. It analysed 4,237 registrations appearing on MahaRERA's list of projects kept in abeyance after their completion dates had lapsed, as the list stood on Sept 10, 2026. A public reconstruction of MahaRERA filings by ReraGenie was used to identify projects with recorded extension histories. TOI then checked all 110 that the reconstruction showed with at least three recorded extension-history events against MahaRERA's own records.
The reconstruction identified 1,154 of the 4,237, or 27.2%, with at least one recorded extension-history event. There were 392 with two or more and 110 with three or more. The 27.2% is not a failure rate. These projects were already on a lapse-related abeyance list, and abeyance is an administrative status. MahaRERA says projects on its lapse-related abeyance list have their bank accounts frozen, while promoters are prohibited from executing agreements for sale or sale deeds until the required compliances are fulfilled.Not every extension-history event represents a new deadline either. More than one filing can relate to the same revised date. What the exercise does establish is how often the completion clock can keep running long after the original date has passed.Abhay Upadhyay, president of the Forum for People's Collective Efforts (FPCE), a homebuyers' body that has examined the use of extensions across several states, argues that the statute is not where the problem lies. He says, "RERA is watertight, what has gone wrong is the practice built around it." The force majeure route under Section 6, in his view, has come to be treated almost as a given, with promoters approaching the regulator confident that an extension will follow.
When the percentage does not tell the whole story
Often numbers can flatter to deceive. Take Indraprasthanagari Phase 1 in Pune. MahaRERA was told in one extension filing that the project was 98% complete. In another it was 95%. In a later filing it was back to 98%, while the revised completion date moved from December 2022 to May 2023 and then June 2024. An engineer's certificate in January 2023 put the project cost at ₹16.62 crore, with ₹1.66 crore still to be spent. An architect's certificate from the same period put key finishing and services work at 80% in Building A and 90% in Buildings B and C; the same figures appeared a year later.The same gap between a headline completion number and the documents underneath it appears in FPCE's 192-page report on project extensions. The report describes its cases as samples, not a census.In one Karnataka project, an April 2024 regulatory order recorded the project as 94% complete. A later order cited completion at 76%, relying on progress information that was more than two years old.Upadhyay's objection is to the sequence. "As soon as a promoter wants an extension, they should be asked the hard question, in the first instance only," he says. In Uttar Pradesh, he says, the report found instances where UPRERA granted extensions and carried out site visits afterwards.
The project that was 97% complete in 2020
Gajanan Plaza in Mumbai's Borivali shows how long the gap between "almost complete" and delivery can stretch. In January 2020, its promoter told MahaRERA that 97% of the project had been completed onsite. Some buyers had been promised possession as far back as 2012.They had originally booked residential flats before the project was converted to commercial use. By July 2024, 11 complainants across seven units, who had paid a combined ₹1.67 crore, were still before MahaRERA seeking enforcement of orders in their favour.In one proceeding, the regulator recorded "intentional default" in complying with its earlier directions. Gajanan Plaza had originally been registered to finish on Dec 31, 2018. At a February 2025 hearing, the promoter sought time until December 2027, saying Phase 1 was almost complete but financially dependent on a proposed Phase 2.MahaRERA's live project page, as of September 2026, carries a revised completion date of April 30, 2028. The page states that the date includes the four-month extension granted under MahaRERA Order 66/2026, a blanket force majeure extension applied automatically to eligible projects across the state.
The Main Issues
Extensions are a large part of the system
MahaRERA's own annual figures give a sense of how much of its work is now extension work. In 2025-26, the regulator reported 4,204 fresh registrations, 2,488 corrections and 3,687 timeline extensions. That works out to nearly 88 extensions for every 100 fresh registrations. Extensions made up 35.5% of those three categories. That does not mean 88% of new projects were delayed. An extension granted in 2025-26 can relate to a project registered several years earlier.But the figures do indicate how much regulatory activity now involves projects whose original timelines have already changed. Keeping a registration alive can also matter commercially. In four of the 110 projects examined by TOI, promoters explicitly stated that an extension or extension number was needed to continue selling unsold flats.
When 100% still isn't possession
Among the 110 projects, TOI found at least 12 where a promoter filing described the project or overall construction as at least 95% complete while seeking more time. At least five explicitly claimed 100% completion. At least four made a 95%-plus claim in more than one filing.Shiv Sparsh Phase II is a case in point. Its promoter described the project as 100% complete in three extension filings while also stating that fire and lift NOCs were awaited. The revised deadlines eventually ran through July 2024. A March 2025 architect's certificate again put the main building-work categories at 100%. Its separate common-area entry for "Fire Protection & Fire Safety requirements" carried no completion percentage. At other projects, even the basic progress update may be missing. In May 2026, MahaRERA issued show-cause notices to 8,212 of 33,029 registered housing projects after they failed to file mandatory quarterly progress reports for the January-March quarter by the April 20 deadline.
What happens when another deadline is needed?
TOI also examined 10 MahaRERA orders issued in 2025 under Section 7(3), which allows the authority, instead of revoking a project's registration, to let it continue subject to conditions. All 10 recorded that the promoter had failed to obtain the 51% majority allottee consent referred to in MahaRERA's procedure. All 10 nevertheless granted further time. That is not, in itself, improper. Across the orders, though, the argument is substantially the same: refusing continuation could stop the project and harm buyers, and the "balance of convenience" therefore favours allowing it to proceed subject to conditions.Upadhyay says the pattern is not confined to Maharashtra. Extensions granted despite the absence of the 51% consent also turn up in FPCE's examination of orders across states.
The law allows more than one route
The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act was passed in 2016 and came fully into force on May 1, 2017, after years of demands for a law to discipline a sector in which buyers had little recourse against delay. It is a central statute administered locally: each state and union territory frames its own rules and appoints its own authority. MahaRERA, which began work in 2017, is among the oldest and busiest.RERA does not contain a simple one-extension rule. Section 6 limits extensions granted under it to one year in aggregate. Section 7(3), separately, allows a regulator, instead of revoking registration, to keep it in force subject to conditions. MahaRERA has used this route in post-lapse continuation proceedings.In its 2017 Neelkamal Realtors judgment, the Bombay High Court held that continuation beyond the ordinary extension framework could be considered case by case in exceptional, compelling circumstances. For buyers, another clock runs alongside the regulatory one. Under Section 18, an allottee who stays in a delayed project is entitled to interest for every month of delay until possession. A buyer who withdraws can seek a refund with interest. Upadhyay points to Supreme Court rulings affirming that entitlement and says very little has changed on the ground.
The database which is needed
Even official estimates put the scale of housing stress high. A government-appointed committee headed by Amitabh Kant cited Indian Banks' Association estimates of around 4.12 lakh stressed dwelling units involving ₹4.08 lakh crore in legacy stalled projects. FPCE reaches a much larger figure: ₹12.44 lakh crore affecting around 27.6 lakh families, by its estimate. The figure is modelled, not a project-by-project count.India does have a count of registered RERA projects. When the Centre launched its Unified RERA Portal in September 2025, 1,51,113 projects had been registered nationally. At the same meeting, however, the government said a nationwide project database should still be prepared.
FPCE view
And in March 2026, the housing ministry told Parliament that detailed state-level information sought by MPs was "not centrally maintained". However a publicly accessible national record linking the complete journey of a project is currently missing. Upadhyay says the gap is not for want of asking. The issue has been raised in central forums and instructions to furnish the data have been issued, he says, but the data has not followed.
Section 8, which allows a project to be taken out of a promoter's hands, should be used far more often, Upadhyay argues, on the reasoning that the prospect of losing the project is what makes a developer move. By the time a project has lost its financial viability, action against the promoter achieves little. "What a RERA registration ought to carry is a definitive guarantee to the ordinary buyer," Upadhyay says.Ten years after RERA came into force, the unresolved question is no longer whether delayed projects sometimes need more time. It is how regulators decide when more time is still a solution, and when it has simply become another deadline.

Taiwan warns of growing black bear encounters as range expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:28:58 UTC
14:28:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency warned Monday that the expanding range of Formosan black bears was increasing the likelihood of encounters with humans.
The agency released footage showing two bears moving close to areas of human activity following their release into the wild. Long-term monitoring has found bears entering farmland, work sheds, and other areas frequented by people, per a press release.
The agency warned that bears could become accustomed to human food and return to inhabited or frequently visited areas. It urged people in mountainous areas to take their garbage with them and properly manage food waste and other potential food sources.
The agency’s Hualien Branch has installed bear-resistant trash cans in black bear hotspots in Zhuoxi Township, Hualien County. It has also introduced AI image-recognition and early-warning systems at high-risk locations, including the Jiaming Lake and Xiangyang mountain huts and Daxueshan National Forest Recreation Area.
The agency also issued new guidelines for responding to bear encounters. It advised people who encounter bears to remain calm and retreat slowly.
The public can report sightings online or through a 24-hour toll-free hotline at 0800-000-930. Reports will be used for risk assessments, incident response, and conservation management.
Agency Director-General Lin Hwa-ching (林華慶) urged mountain visitors to follow the principles of “no feeding, no disturbance, and proper management of food and garbage.” Preventing bears from gaining access to human food is essential to coexistence, the agency said, per CNA.
Officials also released data showing that one bear remained secluded in a cave for up to 70 days over the winter following its release into the wild. The agency said the finding provided valuable information about the winter behavior of Formosan black bears. Another monitored bear did not display the same behavior.
Lin Liang-gong (林良恭), a professor at Tunghai University’s Center for Ecology and Environmental Research, said research in Japan also indicated that food was a primary cause of human-bear conflict. Although Taiwan’s problem was not as severe as Japan’s, the Formosan black bear population was expected to continue growing, making greater preventive efforts necessary.

Government documents reveal AI can train on data without paying creators

AI companies could use creators' work without paying them under leaked government copyright proposal
AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying its creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders, under one copyright reform plan put forward in government documents seen by the ABC.
The attorney-general's department made the proposal as part of consultations with rights-holders' groups earlier this month, which would make inclusion in AI training opt-out by default.
The revelation comes as the Albanese government tries to break a months-long gridlock over reforms to copyright law.
AI models are typically trained on enormous amounts of data scraped from the internet, including copyrighted materials taken without their owners' permissions, to the chagrin of creative groups.
Uncertainty about the legality of training models this way has been a sticking point for the government's efforts to attract AI companies to make the major investments in Australia that would come with AI training efforts.
ACT independent senator David Pocock pressed the government about its previously unrevealed plans in the Senate today.
"This would be huge and mean that our legal system would protect AI companies first and Australians second. The burden should not fall on Australians to defend the rights over content they hold, create and invest in," he said.
Senator Don Farrell said that he would need to consult with Attorney-General Michelle Rowland on the topic, but reiterated the government's stance against watering down copyright.
"The government has taken a deep interest in artificial intelligence with a view to maximising the benefits that come from this new technology, but on the other hand making sure […] we get the best possible results for the Australian community," he said.
A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the government was continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation.
OpenAI confirmed that it had been part of consultations about proposals.
"We are committed to engaging constructively throughout this process with the government, creators and industry on an approach that is practical, sustainable and right for Australia," a spokesperson said.
Two proposals to pave way for AI training in Australia
Slides of the confidential consultation, titled "AI on Australian Terms", seen by the ABC, revealed two options presented to rights-holder groups earlier this month.
Both options would give copyright owners an opt-out if they wanted to keep their online material out of AI training without a licence.
The first proposal sets out two possible ways to pay copyright owners, in addition to voluntary deals with AI companies.
One would give AI companies legal permission to use "unprotected" — meaning content whose owners had not opted-out — online material for training as long as they had made payments to a central body and met other conditions. This body would distribute the money to registered copyright owners.
This first proposal would give the option for AI companies to get a license for training by directly doing deals with Australian collecting groups that represent copyright owners.
This would clear the way for companies to train on content from industries such as music or writing, including content that belongs to people who are not members of the groups who received payments.
The alternative proposal put forward by the Attorney-General's Department would instead require AI companies to strike deals with a minimum number of companies for a minimum period before receiving legal permission to train on unprotected material online.
These deals would be negotiated between the AI companies and the rights-holder companies, the slides say: "No additional $ would be payable to creators or rights holders beyond deals negotiated to achieve quota."
The slides also say the proposals include other protections, including penalties for ignoring opt-outs, "protections for Indigenous Cultural and intellectual Property", as well as transparency and audit requirements.
It would also require AI companies to make "best efforts" to ensure they were not training on pirated material.
Material without those protections could be used even if it was covered by copyright.
The slides say the options would address AI companies' concerns about the "long tail": openly available online material for which striking voluntary deals is unrealistic or impossible.
These options would "improve legal certainty for AI companies and bring advantage of AI training home for Australians" while also "upholding Prime Minister's commitment to a strong and vibrant Australian creative and media sector", the slides say.
Major AI companies say copyright is a hurdle to Australian investment
OpenAI's vice president of global policy Ann O'Leary told The Australian that copyright settings were preventing the company from building an AI training centre in Australia.
"We will not be able to build a … training centre here if the copyright law is as it exists," she said while on a trip to Australia.
An OpenAI spokesperson told the ABC it had been taking part in consultation on the copyright reforms.
"Australia has enormous potential to benefit from AI, and we want to work for and with Australia to help realise Australia's AI ambitions. This is truly a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Australia's economy and it's crucial the country gets this right," they said.
Anthropic had made similar advances to the federal government as early as April, according to a Treasury Freedom of Information (FOI) showing that it was preparing for discussion with the AI company that would say their investment was "contingent" on "clarity" on copyright law.
That briefing said Anthropic could negotiate with larger copyright owners, but argued the "long tail" of smaller owners made identifying and buying licences difficult.
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles hosed down claims that OpenAI had delivered an ultimatum about copyright.
"It's a historic opportunity for our nation, but we need to be doing it in a way which protects rights holders," Mr Marles told News24 earlier today.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

What Malaysia’s Recent State Election Results Say About the Country’s Political Direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:11:00 UTC
14:11:00 KST

The Malaysian states Johor and Negeri Sembilan recently held state elections that produced disappointing results for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition.
During the July 11 polls in Johor, an economically important state at the tip of peninsular Malaysia, Barisan Nasional (BN), secured a commanding victory, winning 48 of 56 state assembly seats, up from 40 at the last election in 2022. Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition won the remaining eight seats, down from 12 previously.
This result was largely replicated in Negeri Sembilan on August 1. Here BN won 18 of the 36 seats in the state’s legislative assembly and was set to form government with the pan-Malay Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which won seven seats. PH, which had ruled the state in coalition with BN prior to the election, saw its share of seats drop from 17 to 11.
In both contests, the losses were particularly marked for the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key member of the PH coalition that is traditionally associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese community. In Negeri Sembilan, the election was also marked by close cooperation between the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and the Islamist party PAS, the primary components of the BN and PN coalitions, respectively. This has raised suggestions that a new “Malay wave” could be set to wash away Anwar’s coalition at the next general election.
The twist is that BN and PH remain in coalition at the federal level, following the close-run general election of 2022. The growing competition between the two nominal partners has even raised the possibility that Anwar may choose to call a snap election.
Dr. Oh Ei Sun, a senior fellow at the Singapore Institute of International Affairs, spoke to The Diplomat’s Southeast Asia Editor Sebastian Strangio recently about what the results might mean for Anwar’s leadership and federal politics as Malaysia moves toward its next general election.
Let’s start with the most obvious question: How do you interpret the collapse of PH’s position in Johor and Negeri Sembilan?
I think there are similarities and differences in some of the major factors that led to PH’s collapse in these two states. The similarities lie primarily in the voters’ seeming conflation of PH’s perceived performance (or non-performance) at the federal level with their political solicitation at the state level.
To be more specific, we may look closer into PKR [the People’s Justice Party] and DAP – PH’s two largest component parties – respectively but also relatedly. PKR’s core supporters are those seeking social and political reforms, ranging from those advocating revamp of parliamentary and electoral systems to those who are fervently against corruption and power abuses. Many of them have become increasingly impatient with what they perceived as PKR’s feet-dragging since coming to federal power at fulfilling its reform promises that were loudly proclaimed during its opposition years. Worse still, some of them saw regressive measures that were unashamedly touted, such as those controlling freedom of expression online, that were reminiscent of pre-2018 BN days.
At the same time, PKR at the government’s driver seat was also perceived to be at best lackluster in its microeconomic performance, with many members of lower- and even middle-income groups finding it hard to carry on with livelihood, a scenario that was perceived to be worse than the BN days. So these core PKR supporters carried this rather disgruntled attitude toward PKR from the federal to the state level, and did not come out in droves to support PKR. Yet PKR, with its same, reformist image, remained inept in competing with UMNO and PAS in attracting an increasingly conservative Malay voters cohort to make up or surpass the difference.
DAP shared many of these misgivings and thus non-votes by its core supporters as PKR, plus disillusion from its non-Malay core supporters who had even higher expectations of DAP championing their long-held dream of attaining political and social equality. When they perceived DAP as having been non-enthusiastic in advancing this dear cause of theirs since coming to federal power, and furthermore remained silent when their rights were perceived to have been trampled upon, they wanted to “punish” DAP by not voting for it.
But these conflated or “transferred” disfavors against PH aside, there were also respective distinct factors that favor BN in these two states. The Johor chief minister, Onn Hafiz, turned out to be both charismatic and pragmatic, having brought in large amounts of foreign investment into the state that were transforming the state’s economic outlook. So the voters were comfortable with his helmsmanship and would like to see him continue in his leading role. In Negeri Sembilan, UMNO and PAS non-contest arrangements prevented vote splitting and handed easy wins to UMNO and participation by PAS for the first time in the state administration. This was a win-win situation for both parties. How long the state ruling coalition could hold is quite another question, if past disastrous collaboration history between UMNO and PAS provides any lesson.
Do you anticipate a similar result in Melaka, the next state to hold an election?
The conflated or “transferred” disfavors against PH by its core supporters would most likely remain quite intact in Melaka, as nothing much is likely to take place within a space of at most a few months to dissuade them otherwise. On the other hand, the Onn Hafiz favorite-son factor is certainly missing in Melaka, which saw at best average socioeconomic performance over the last half decade. And it would appear that BN and the PAS-led PN could still not reach a no-contest agreement in Melaka. As such, PH could aspire to holding on to its present state seats in Melaka. Anything more would be a distinct bonus.
The Negeri Sembilan election in particular was marked by close cooperation between BN and PN (particularly between UMNO and PAS), which have recently been at loggerheads. This has prompted some to suggest that a “Malay wave” could wash away Anwar and PH at the next general election. Do you think this is likely, and if so, why?
I think a Malay-Muslim wave that would be swept to power remains a very viable political scenario, as it almost did in the last general election. This is due not so much to PAS’ or UMNO’s revitalized political or electoral prowess. Rather, it is an electoral manifestation of an increasingly vibrant Malay-Muslim desire to attain a much more conservative and religiously oriented social and political outlook for the country. This is in line with yet another wave of religious revivalism that is sweeping across many Muslim-majority countries, ranging from Turkey to Indonesia. So the majority of Malay voters see PAS as a most conducive political vehicle for the soonest realization of this earnest desire, with UMNO as perhaps second best in realizing so. Therefore, a PAS-UMNO electoral alliance is likely to trump PH hands down.
But ironically, Anwar may remain prime minister after the next general election. This is due to the power struggles that are taking place within UMNO and PAS, which are usually more intense than their confrontations with PH. UMNO’s internecine fights are mainly factional in nature, with different warlords and their power bases rallying against one another. So Zahid the party president may ultimately not be touted as a viable prime ministerial candidate, with his many unresolved legal cases as the pretext. The fights in PAS, on the other hand, are usually ideological in nature, pitching the conservative ulamas against the more moderate professionals. The ulamas would loath to see a moderate such as the much-mentioned Terengganu chief minister Shamsuri to become prime minister. So Anwar, with his sizable religious and communal credentials in the past, may actually emerge as a compromise figurehead prime minister with PAS and to a lesser extent UMNO pulling the string behind the scene.
PH and BN insist their federal partnership can co-exist with rivalries at the state level, but how sustainable is the current situation? Do you anticipate Anwar calling a GE any time soon?
Malaysia has entered a very fragmented political landscape, with perhaps no single party being able to command an outright parliamentary majority, thus necessitating the forming of ruling coalitions. So the main calculation for alliance or split is not so much an ideological one as a politically convenient one. Therefore, the answer to the sustainability of any political coalitions really depends on the electoral viability and the thirst for power of its potential component parties.
It really does not matter when Anwar would call for a general election. The Malay-Muslim wave will sweep aside a large portion of its PH, but he may remain politically useful as prime minister.
How do you interpret the collapse of the DAP vote in the two recent elections, and also the state election in Sabah in November? What does this say about the dynamics of ethnic Chinese politics in peninsular Malaysia? If the party decides to leave the PH coalition, what impact could that have on Anwar’s political chances at the next GE?
See particularly the answer to the first question above. But there is a bit of a nuance to DAP in Sabah. DAP was trounced in Sabah mainly because it aligned itself too closely to the state ruling coalition there that was evidently disfavored by DAP’s core Sabah supporters, who decided to pitch their tent with Warisan instead, which they thought would come back to power. Nationally, the non-Malays continue to aspire to a fairer and more equal Malaysia. DAP’s decision to remain in cabinet is likely to come back to haunt it in the general election, as it would have to continue to collectively shoulder the kind of decisions which non-Malays may perceive to be unfair and unequal.

Governments worldwide are way behind on AI, says Bill Gates

Governments worldwide are way behind on AI, says Bill Gates
- Bill Gates warns that no government is prepared for the societal changes AI will bring, highlighting risks to jobs, security, and addiction.
- His foundation plans to spend over US$1 billion to expand AI access in education, healthcare, and agriculture, aiming to help the poorest.
- Gates urges global cooperation on AI regulation, comparing AI's arrival to an urgent disaster scenario requiring unified action.
AI generated
LONDON - No government in the world is ready for the changes artificial intelligence will bring to society, Bill Gates said in an interview with Reuters, as he warned of the risks ahead.
The Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist had until recently been optimistic about AI, but has changed his position, warning of the threats to jobs, concerns about attacks and the dangers of addiction to AI companions.
“I don’t think any government is nearly as deep on this as they have to be,” he said.
However, he added that the technology has great potential to help the world’s poorest if managed properly and accessed equally – and his namesake foundation said on Sept 15 that it plans to spend at least US$1 billion (S$1.27 billion) in the next two years on expanding access to AI.
Gates said he has been talking to world leaders about his concerns, including President Donald Trump and his team in the US, and said he aims to meet China’s President Xi Jinping later in 2026.
“Governments are way behind on this one,” he added.
But despite his concerns, Gates and his foundation hope AI can help narrow gaps between the richest and poorest, rather than widening them.
The foundation’s US$1 billion spending plan, part of its previously announced plans to spend US$9 billion annually, will go to partners working in education, healthcare and agriculture, the foundation said.
It also aims to help build the data foundations AI is built on, such as ensuring that large language models work in every language people speak.
“For health it’s hard to overstate what the potential is,” Gates said, from supporting frontline health care workers to discovering new drugs and vaccines.
But he said governments must work together to avoid problems, likening the arrival of AI to a disaster movie.
“There’s all sorts of movies where some aliens are coming, and magically the US and China and everybody comes together to solve the problem,” he said. “AI is kind of like this alien intelligence. It’s here, and we better do like it shows in those movies.”
Reputational hit?
In June, Gates appeared in front of Congress to testify about his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Gates, who is not accused of any crimes, has repeatedly said he regrets his association with Epstein, who he hoped would donate to global health causes.
Instead, the financier attempted to blackmail Gates over his extramarital affairs.
However, despite prompting an external review at his foundation, which found no payments to Epstein or participation in criminal activities, Gates said the links had not caused him or the foundation a significant reputational hit.
“In terms of having access to government leaders, or you know, journalists being willing to interview me, I don’t see any diminishment,” he said, adding that the desire to draw on the foundation’s expertise to cut child deaths and end malaria had also not reduced “even one iota”. REUTERS

Want a comfortable retirement? Here's the new super figure Australians need
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:05:57 UTC
14:05:57 KST

IN BRIEF
- Goods and services that retirees spend most on rise faster than inflation, a peak body says.
- A comfortable retirement is becoming more expensive as a result.
Australians now need a little bit more in their super to retire comfortably, with the rising cost of living driving up the latest retirement standard.
A couple who own their home and are seeking a comfortable retirement will need $78,998 a year, or $1,513 a week. A single homeowner will need $56,166 a year, or $1,076 a week.
Those figures were released on Tuesday by the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), the peak body for the super industry.
It showed for homeowners aged 65 to 84, the budget for a comfortable retirement rose 0.5 per cent for couples and 0.4 per cent for singles in the June quarter.
For a modest retirement, their budget rose 0.4 per cent for couples and 0.3 per cent for singles, to $52,690 and $36,548 a year respectively.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
For retirees aged 85 and over, a comfortable retirement will cost $74,484 per year for couples and $53,964 per year for singles. For retirees who rent privately, a modest budget is now $69,376 per year for a couple and $51,418 per year for a single.
ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty says retirees are being affected by the soaring cost of living more than others because the things they buy are rising quicker than the inflation rate of 3.8 per cent.
These include electricity, which the group said rose 22.4 per cent after federal and state rebates ended (22 per cent), car costs (6.5 per cent), medical services (5 per cent), insurance (almost 5 per cent) and meals out (4 per cent).
"Retirees are among the groups hit hardest by the cost of living crisis because their budgets are weighted towards the things going up in price the most," Delahunty said.
What's a comfortable retirement compared to a modest one?
AFSA defines a comfortable retirement as being able to afford quality private health insurance, eat out most weeks, and go on a yearly holiday in Australia or overseas every few years.
A modest retirement includes basic health cover, such as a hospital-only plan, domestic-only holidays, and occasional eating out.
On the age pension alone, it's a much slimmer budget with limited lifestyle and basic living spending.
"Most of these things drop out of your budget entirely," ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty said.
She said while the age pension goes up with inflation, it doesn't allow for spending on other things like private health and holidays, which are increasing in price, and leaving retirees more reliant on their super to make those payments.
"Super is the difference between watching every dollar and having a sense of financial security in retirement," Delahunty said.
Superannuation as an election issue
As Australia nears a federal election, superannuation has become a major political campaign line as the parties try to win voters amid a cost of living crisis.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers signalled super could become a political issue at the next federal election, and accused his political opponents of trying to "end compulsory superannuation as we know it".
His calls came after Liberal senator Andrew Bragg declared superannuation an "illiberal experiment".
One Nation has proposed allowing workers paying rent or a mortgage to divert 3 per cent of their super payments straight to their wallet for up to three years — investing only 9 per cent instead of the current compulsory rate of 12 per cent.
The policy has come under criticism from super firms and the government, with some estimates that people opting into the scheme could lose $25,000 from their retirement fund.
ASFA calculates a similar loss, saying a 30-year-old on average full-time earnings who takes three years of super as cash under the One Nation proposal would receive around $54 a week now and retire with $23,900 less in today's dollars.
"The cost of living and housing crises need their own solutions. Forcing Australians to solve them by robbing from their own future selves is not a helping hand. It is a worse deal than previous generations had," Delahunty said.

Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
06:01:46 BST
14:01:46 KST

Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
- Published
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."
Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.
As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.
That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.
Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in
If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."
Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.
She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.
One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."
Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"
But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.
She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."
The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.
For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.
Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

They’re the sopranos of the forest, so what’s silencing the gibbons’ morning chorus?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

Dawn has broken, and the air is cool and still. It’s at about this time that gibbons usually erupt into song, wa-oo-ing and wa-ing from the highest branches and filling the tree tops with rich melodies. But in this corner of Malaysian forest, bordered by housing and roads, the resident white-handed gibbons are quiet. All that can be heard is the hum of traffic from a nearby highway.
This isn’t a rare occurrence for this group of gibbons, according to research, which found these particular gibbons, named Mambang and Walinong, appeared to be producing far fewer morning songs than others that are not exposed to the same level of traffic noise.
White-handed gibbons, arboreal animals whose calls can travel more than half a mile through dense forest canopies, are known for their complex songs and vocal techniques that have been likened to those of soprano singers. But as their habitats are increasingly fragmented by roads, industry and urban development, researchers say there is a growing need to understand how human-generated noise is affecting when and how they sing.
“Their songs are not just background noise or a way of announcing their presence. They play an important role in communication between groups, territorial interactions and social relationships,” says Nadine Ruppert, associate professor at Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and a supervisor of the research. “So when we introduce persistent human-generated noise into their habitat, we are potentially interfering with a very important part of their lives,” she says.
In 2023 and 2024, for a week in both wet and dry seasons, Benjamin Galea, a final-year PhD student at Universiti Sains Malaysia, and the author of the study, recorded and analysed the morning calls of white-handed gibbons living in three different locations that had varying levels of background noise. They included the spot near the highway, which had the highest level of continual noise pollution, a popular hiking trail, and a secluded beachfront location that was the furthest from human activity.
Galea’s research, which is yet to be peer reviewed, found that the greater the background noise, the less likely gibbons were to call. The group living close to the highway called in 36% of recordings – far less than the seaside group (71.4%), and the hiking trail group (84.6%).
Within sites, the estimated odds of calling also decreased as background sound increased.
Galea found that the hiking trail group sang in more recordings than the gibbons located at the beach, a quieter spot. Various possible reasons exist for this, including the hiking trail gibbons’ proximity to another gibbon group, which may have prompted them to sing more to demarcate their territory. The hiking trail group was also located towards the forest interior, so noise posed less of a problem, he says. “They seem to have been able to sing despite the acute noise from humans, but we found that they increase their bandwidth when vehicle noise becomes significant,” says Galea.
It is possible that the highway group avoided singing because the traffic was too loud, or that they were singing at an earlier time – before the study’s monitoring devices began recording, from 6am until 1pm, says Galea. On some days, the gibbons were already midway through their songs when the recordings started at 6am.
Singing earlier could help individuals overcome the problem of noisy cars, but it might introduce other problems, and potentially interfere “with resting, foraging, coordination between partners, or communication with neighbouring groups that are not active at the same time”, he says.
If background noise is driving gibbons to avoid singing, this could affect their ability to maintain their territory, attract mates or warn of predators – though further research is needed to understand if this would ultimately affect an individual’s ability to reproduce or survive.
Notably, when the highway gibbons did sing, most of their “phrases” (93.3%) occurred in the context of a solo song, but it is not clear if this reflects normal differences between the groups. “We can only guess,” says Galea. “It’s possible that traffic noise may have made it harder for the pair to hear and coordinate with each other.”
The study adds to a growing body of research that is exploring how human-generated noise is disrupting animals’ routines. Noise pollution has been found to reduce the ability of mammals to hear their prey, with species such as the the greater mouse-eared bat less able to forage effectively when exposed to background noise.
Noise pollution has also been shown to have various effects on birds. One paper found that it reduced the survival of passerine birds by masking parent-offspring communication, while another study in Brazil found it reduced the diversity of bird species in urban parks.
Determining the exact effects of noise on gibbons requires further study. “One important question that we have to ask is how much calling is necessary for successful communication,” says Ulrich H Reichard, professor of anthropology at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, who was not involved in the Malaysia research.
“Even with sustained noise, do they have to call every day? Do they have to call every other day? Do they have to call for 20 minutes or 10 minutes or in order to achieve their goal?” Reichard says.
If gibbons were to issue fewer alarm calls, this might not necessarily put them at high risk of predation, given their ability to swing rapidly through the tree tops, Reichard says. Though it may be bad news for birds and squirrels, which appear to recognise and respond to gibbons’ warnings.
“If you have interspecies communication, even if one species shifts their common behaviour, then that will impact the others,” says Reichard.
Such questions are likely to become increasingly important as forests are more exposed to greater human development. The white-handed gibbon is listed as endangered by the IUCN, which warns that its population is believed to have declined more than 50% over the past 45 years, driven by habitat destruction, and the threat of hunting and capture for the pet and photo-prop trade.
In Malaysia there is no recent population estimate, though the number of white-handed gibbons is believed to have declined over recent decades. Unusually, gibbons remain in isolated plots of land in urban centres, including the capital, Kuala Lumpur.
“In Malaysia, for example, a forest fragment can still look like perfectly good gibbon habitat from a purely physical perspective, that is, it may contain trees, food and sleeping sites – but it may also be surrounded by roads, housing, industry or other sources of chronic noise,” Ruppert says.
As we increasingly recognise the conservation value of urban and peri-urban forests, we need to start thinking about habitat quality in a broader way, adds Ruppert. “It is not only about how much forest is left, but also about what the animals experience within that forest.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

Rukmiini Iyer’s recipe for mozzarella in carozza – and the leftover crusts | Cook once, eat twice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

For an exceptionally luxe snack or kids’ tea, mozzarella in carrozza is your girl. It’s the love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread – instead of toasting it, you dip the cheese sandwich in egg and fry it. In other words, it’s mozzarella in a fancy carriage. I like to use a combination of mozzarella and mature cheddar for flavour, and while it’s best eaten piping hot from the pan, it’s a good (and filling) lunchbox option for children, too.
Mozzarella in carrozza
You will need a very large shallow bowl (or medium roasting tin) for the egg dip.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 10 min
 Serves 1-2
30g mature cheddar, grated
2 very large slices white sourdough, crusts removed (but hang on to them)
60g mozzarella, sliced
1 egg, lightly beaten
2 tbsp olive oil
  Flaky sea salt
Pat down the cheddar evenly on one slice of bread, leaving a 1cm border, then top with the mozzarella. Brush a little beaten egg around the edges of the bread, then top with the second slice of sourdough and gently squash the edges together to seal.
Pour the remaining egg into a large, shallow container, then carefully dip both sides of the sandwich in the egg wash – the bread should absorb all of the egg. (Any excess can be poured on once the sandwich is in the pan.)
Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, then carefully lift the sandwich into the pan and fry for two minutes on each side, until golden brown. Use your biggest fish slice (or two) to transfer the mozzarella in carrozza on to a plate lined with kitchen paper, then serve immediately, scattered with a little sea salt.
For a more balanced meal, serve with a green salad (dressing: one tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, one scant teaspoon dijon mustard and salt, to taste) or a cherry tomato salad (one big handful of cherry tomatoes, halved and dressed with extra-virgin olive oil, salt and fresh basil). Alternatively, if feeding children, serve with cucumber sticks and some fruit.
Eat twice
It was thinking about (and constantly making) children’s lunches that put me on the next-day dish ideas for this week’s column: what do you do with three days’ worth of cut-off sandwich crusts? I can’t bear to waste them, so they get stashed in a plastic container in the fridge. You could take them down the bread-and-butter pudding route: chop or blitz the crusts in a food processor, pack into a small baking dish, then pour over a chocolate custard (three egg yolks, 350ml whole milk or single cream, or a mix of both, 50g sugar, 100g 70% dark chocolate, melted) and bake for 20 minutes or so. Lovely by itself, or for breakfast with Greek yoghurt and just-ripe or baked pears.
My favourite savoury option, though, is this: whisk a couple of eggs and a good splash of milk with a handful of grated cheese, then stir this through the chopped or blitzed sandwich crusts. Bake in a shallow dish at 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 for 10-12 minutes, until just set. Once cool (you can refrigerate it overnight, if you wish), cut into squares, then fry in a little olive oil until golden brown and crisp. I billed these as “bread rosti” to the family, and topped them with cream cheese for the children and sriracha for my husband. They were a hit – not bad for half a week’s worth of sandwich leftovers.

Canada is eyeing a ‘unique alliance’ with the EU. How far can Brussels go?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

President Trump’s tariff war and territorial threats have made Ottawa pivot towards Europe. Brussels now wants to seize the political moment and draw Canada deeper into its orbit.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has seized Europe’s political spotlight this week with his clearest overtures yet towards the European Union (EU), days before he is set to join senior EU officials at a European Parliament plenary in Strasbourg.
Carney said overnight that he’s seeking a “unique alliance” between Canada and the European Union but not full membership of the bloc, after the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that Ottawa was seeking formal talks with Brussels on “associate” EU membership.
The reports come just ahead of Carney’s visit to Strasbourg, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to flesh out the EU’s vision for a deeper relationship with Canada during her annual State of the Union speech on Wednesday, according to EU officials.
It’s the latest in a series of public signs of rapprochement. Carney became the first non-European leader to attend a European Political Community (EPC) summit in May, and Canadian ministers have recently stepped up their participation in EU ministerial meetings.
The shift comes as Canada faces growing economic and political pressure from its southern neighbour. US President Donald Trump’s tariff war has hit $20 billion worth of Canadian products with 50% tariffs, while his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st US state have prompted Ottawa to rethink its security and defence alliances.
European nations have emerged as natural partners as Carney seeks to build what he describes as a coalition of “middle powers” that can spearhead a new rules-based order.
With Carney ruling out full EU membership — despite polling showing broad support for the idea among Canadians — Brussels sees an opportunity to seize on a rare political opening. But what exactly a special EU-Canada “alliance” could look like remains unclear, with no obvious legal or political precedent for such an arrangement.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed on Monday that the EU’s level of ambition for its strategic partnership with Canada is “even higher” this year ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal in October, describing Canada as a “strategically important partner” and “close friend”.
The head of the European Parliament’s Liberal group has meanwhile called on the Commission to “match Canada’s ambition” by further strengthening trade, economic and security ties.
A ‘symbolic’ upgrade
“This is more about symbolism than anything else,” Dr. Steven Blockmans, deputy director at the International Centre for Defence and Security, told Euronews.
He expects Brussels to dismiss talk of “associate membership” and instead “spin it as an agenda which sees even closer trans-Atlantic cooperation with Canada”.
Reports of Ottawa seeking “associate membership” echo a similar plan floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for Ukraine in May, which was quickly dismissed by most EU countries and Ukraine as a non-starter.
It pitched a seat for Ukraine at the table in summits and ministerial meetings without voting rights, coverage under the bloc's mutual assistance clause, and eligibility for funding under EU programmes.
Ideas of “levels” of EU membership in a pre-accession phase have been gaining traction, but associate membership for a country that is not seeking to become a full member is not likely to gain traction.
“This is a notion that makes no legal sense,” Blockmans explained, but added that it is still possible for Canada to “strengthen its trade relations with the EU in different domains”.
Trade and economics drive rapprochement
Greater access to the EU’s €18 trillion single market is considered a major driver of Ottawa’s agenda, and potentially the biggest prize Brussels could offer Canada in the age of Trump’s tariff war.
Talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down last month, with Trump vowing to impose 50% tariffs on cars and steel from 2027, in a move that has dented hopes of an easing of tensions.
The EU-Canada trade deal, known as CETA, was signed over a decade ago but is yet to be fully ratified across the EU. More privileged access to the single market — potentially moving Canada closer to arrangements enjoyed by countries such as Norway or Switzerland — could help Ottawa diversify away from its traditional reliance on the US.
But Blockmans says it is almost inconceivable that the EU would contemplate such privileged access for a country that has no membership aspirations and follows a “completely different rulebook” in areas such as food and agricultural policy.
“An arrangement such as that of Norway and Switzerland is definitely off the books,” he said, adding that upgrading the current trade deal, known as CETA, is also difficult given the fierce protests the agreement sparked in several parts of Europe.
“This is almost a return to the Brexit situation,” Nicolai von Ondarza, a political scientist and senior fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said, recalling the famous "Barnier staircase" used by the EU’s former chief Brexit negotiator, Michel Barnier, to show the trade-offs facing the UK during post-Brexit negotiations.
“If you want to upgrade the trading relations, you get into territory of a European Economic Area (EEA) arrangement,” von Ondarza explained, referring to the model that gives Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein access to the single market in return for alignment with EU rules.
That level of access would come at a political price for Ottawa. The EU has traditionally demanded close alignment with its laws and judicial framework in exchange for deep participation in its market, conditions that Canada has resisted in its relationship with the US, von Ondarza said, raising questions over whether Ottawa would accept them from Brussels.
“The question is: how prepared is Canada to accept EU rules?”
Interests converge
Experts do see scope to deepen trade ties in areas where Canadian and European interests already converge, including critical raw materials. Talks are ongoing on offering the EU greater access to Canada’s rare metals and minerals, as Brussels seeks to diversify its supply chains and reduce reliance on China.
Canada is also seeking access to the bloc’s “Made in Europe” scheme, designed to shield strategic sectors such as clean energy from unfair competition, mostly from China, by restricting foreign companies’ access to public procurement.
Brussels is open to including partners beyond its member states if they offer reciprocal access to their subsidy programmes.
While Canada and European allies work together on their common security and defence within the NATO alliance, a renewed alliance could also see both sides deepen their defence industry partnerships and work closer together to bolster Ukraine as US support wanes.
Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence procurement programme, and is currently negotiating a contribution to the EU’s €90 billion loan for Ukraine, according to the Financial Times.
But Ottawa could also demand greater political courage from Brussels when geopolitical disputes threaten to fracture Western unity, Nicolai von Ondarza told Euronews.
He pointed to what he described as an imbalance in the relationship: Canada openly backed its European allies when Trump threatened to seize Greenland, while the EU hesitated to side with Ottawa in its trade confrontation with Washington, explaining that Canada “could ask the EU to address this imbalance” in future talks.

Revealed: The world's best destinations for a last-minute holiday – with plenty in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

Not one for planning months ahead? New research has revealed where travellers are most likely to book accommodation within a week of arrival, with four European countries making the global top 10.
Many Type A travellers plan their trips months in advance, but there’s a more laid-back type of tripper who prefers to leave it until the very last minute to book a holiday.
A new study has revealed the most popular destinations for last-minute vacations – that’s trips booked within just seven days before arriving.
Hotel management system company Sirvoy looked at its customer base of independent hotels, B&Bs, guesthouses, hostels and holiday rentals to reveal where the most last-minute accommodation bookings take place worldwide.
It then examined the proportion of accommodation booked within a week of check-in and the percentage of bookings made on the same or next day as check-in to create a ranking.
Among the top 10 are four destinations in Europe – Norway, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden.
It was countries far further away that took the top spots, though, with Thailand, the Philippines and Australia making up the top three.
“Travellers are embracing spontaneity when booking their next vacation, with every destination in the top 10 seeing more than half of its accommodation bookings made within seven days of check-in,” Nichlas Linderborg, Chief Customer Officer of Sirvoy, said.
Here’s what the ranking revealed.
Asia reigns supreme for last-minute bookings
With summer drawing to a close, many of us are craving that peak season heat, so it’s little surprise that Thailand is the most popular last-minute holiday destination.
The Asian nation saw 74.8% of accommodation bookings made within seven days of check-in and 56.8% on the next or same day.
If you’re keen to head to Thailand any time soon, be warned that it’s currently monsoon season, so the hot weather and low prices may well be accompanied by plenty of rainfall.
That’s the same case in the Philippines too, which takes second place in the ranking.
Last-minute bookings here account for 71.7% of all accommodation reservations, although it’s likely to be rainy until at least October.
In Australia, it may only be early spring, but temperatures in Sydney alone are already well into the 20s. That suggests that the 61.2% of those booking accommodation last minute will be able to enjoy the culture, swimming and surfing in very pleasant weather.
Mexico, which boasts rich history and pristine beaches, is fourth in the ranking, with 59.7% of bookings made within seven days of check-in, while New Zealand comes in fifth place.
Australia’s neighbour has 58.3% of accommodation bookings made within seven days ahead of arrival and is a year-round destination, thanks to its stunning natural beauty.
For sixth place, it’s back to Asia with Indonesia, where 55.8% of bookings were found to be made last-minute.
The rest of the top 10 is rounded out by European nations, all known for their vast amount of outdoor activities, if not clement weather.
Norway is in seventh place, with 53.8% of bookings less than a week out, and 39.1% made the day before or on the day of travel.
That’s 53.3% and 31.8% for Finland, which ranks eighth.
Next up is the Netherlands in ninth, with 52.3% of week-ahead bookings and 33.9% of absolutely last-minute trips booked.
Rounding out the top 10 is Sweden, where last-minute bookings account for 51.9% of all trips, and 30.9% of travellers book the day before arrival or on the day itself.

Cambodia, Thailand Begin Compulsory Conciliation in Maritime Boundary Dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:57:00 UTC
13:57:00 KST

Cambodia and Thailand began compulsory conciliation proceedings in Singapore yesterday, aimed at resolving a long-running maritime dispute.
The three-day session marks the opening of a process conducted under Article 298 and Annex V of the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which is intended to resolve the two nations’ overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand.
After a closed-door session yesterday that was chaired by Katrina Cooper, the head of the Conciliation Commission, a public session took place today in which the Cambodian and Thai foreign ministers delivered opening statements laying out their governments’ respective positions.
Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn told the Commission that his government’s objective was “to achieve a resolution that serves the peoples of both nations and contributes to peace, cooperation and shared prosperity in the region.”
“A peaceful resolution is in the shared interests of both countries and will contribute to peace and stability in the region,” he said. “It will protect sovereignty, strengthen confidence, unlock energy resources, support development, and create new job opportunities not only for now, but also for the future generations of the Cambodian and Thai peoples.”
In his statement, Thailand’s Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkaew said that Thailand “enters this conciliation in good faith, fully mindful of the provisions of UNCLOS.” He added that his government “stands ready to engage in this process constructively, with the aim of achieving, with the Commission’s assistance, a negotiated and equitable solution.”
The maritime dispute between Cambodia and Thailand relates to a 26,000-square-kilometer area in the Gulf of Thailand, known as the Overlapping Claims Area (OCA). The OCA is estimated to hold abundant reserves of oil and natural gas, the exploitation of which has become more pressing due to the current global oil supply crisis.
Maritime tensions between Phnom Penh and Bangkok have increased in parallel with the intensification of the dispute over the Thailand-Cambodia land border, which flared into conflict twice last year – for five days in July and then for nearly three weeks in December – killing nearly 150 people and displacing around a million on both sides of the border.
Cambodia initiated the UNCLOS process in June, shortly after Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s government unilaterally cancelled a 2001 agreement with Cambodia that governed joint offshore energy exploration and the demarcation of maritime boundaries in the OCA. Anutin denied that the cancelation had anything to do with the tensions over the land border, instead citing the lack of progress made under the agreement.
In his statement yesterday, Prak Sokhonn said that after the cancelation of the MoU, Cambodia chose to initiate compulsory conciliation in order to “find a peaceful pathway forward in accordance with international law.” He added that Phnom Penh “sees this conciliation process as a means to rebuild trust, not as a form of escalation.”
Sihasak was in general more combative, accusing Cambodia of taking refuge behind international law, while “repeatedly vilif[ying] Thailand through false narratives, distortion of facts, and unfounded accusations.” He added that Thailand had chosen to cancel the 2001 MoU because it “had produced no concrete progress” and that the government “chose to give negotiations a fresh start.” Sihasak also claimed that Thailand had offered direct bilateral talks over the maritime boundary, and expressed disappointment that Cambodia chose to initiate compulsory conciliation. “Thailand has consistently believed that differences between neighbors should be addressed through dialogue,” he said.
The Thai foreign minister also stated that the conciliation proceedings concerned “only maritime boundary delimitation between Thailand and Cambodia in the Gulf of Thailand” and would not address the island of Koh Kut, part of which was claimed by Cambodia in a continental shelf claim submitted in 1972.
Thai nationalist fears over Koh Kut derailed attempts by a previous Thai government to negotiate with Cambodia a resolution of the OCA in late 2024 and early 2025. This created tensions that quickly snowballed into armed clashes on the land border. The potential loss of Koh Kut is also why Thai nationalist lobby groups have long pushed for the cancellation of the 2001 MoU.
According to Annex V of UNCLOS, compulsory conciliation is a process in which a panel of independent experts – known as conciliators – examines a dispute and helps states parties reach an amicable settlement. Its findings are not legally binding on either party, but the process offers a way of discussing complex and sensitive disputes away from the domestic political hothouse.
The mechanism has only ever been invoked once before, in 2016, when Timor-Leste opted to refer its maritime dispute with Australia to compulsory conciliation. In that instance, Australia accepted conciliation and the five conciliators were able to offer a compromise that was ultimately accepted by both parties.
It is too soon to determine whether the UNCLOS process will allow Cambodia and Thailand to reach a similarly felicitous arrangement. The maritime dispute stems from divergent interpretations of a land border treaty signed between Siam and French Indochina in 1907. This did not delineate the maritime border but provided a point on land from which both countries have charted their claims.
In principle, the maritime dispute should be a lot easier to resolve than the disagreements over the land border. The latter involves more intricate questions of demarcation undertaken by French colonial cartographers, as well as the presence of Angkorian temple ruins that are charged with cultural and political significance, particularly for the Cambodian side.
However, as the tone of Sihasak’s address suggests, last year’s armed clashes have poisoned relations between Bangkok and Phnom Penh to such an extent that any agreement between the two sides, even one that opens the way to mutual exploitation of rich undersea resources, will be challenging.
The UNCLOS process probably offers the best means of reaching a resolution, but any recommendations handed down by the Conciliation Commission will still need to be “sold” to publics that are touchy about sovereignty and liable to pounce at the merest hint of compromise. This is particularly the case in Thailand. Indeed, Thai nationalist agitation is the primary reason that the two nations made so little progress in negotiating maritime border issues under the 2001 MoU.

RIYADH, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Thirteen civilians were injured in Houthi attacks on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government said Tuesday.
The Houthis launched attacks on civilian targets in the southwestern Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif on Monday using ballistic missiles and drones, said Turki Al-Malki, spokesperson for the coalition.
The attacks left 13 civilians with minor to moderate injuries and damaged seven houses and two vehicles, Al-Malki said in a post on X.
The coalition's Joint Forces Command would respond to the attacks "responsibly and firmly" to protect Saudi sovereignty, civilians and civilian objects, Al-Malki said, adding that necessary operational measures would be taken to deter the Houthis and counter what he described as their "hostile and extremist approach."
The attacks came amid a sharp escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. Earlier Monday, the Houthis said they had launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia, describing the attack as retaliation for more than 300 Saudi airstrikes that they said had targeted Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen in recent days. ■
