New Zealand house prices steady as sales activity slows
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:55:59 CST
13:55:59 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's national median house price fell 1.3 percent year on year to 750,000 NZ dollars (431,543 U.S. dollars) in August, while sales activity slowed significantly, according to data released on Tuesday.
The number of homes sold fell 13 percent from a year earlier to 5,430, the sixth lowest August total in 35 years of the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ) records, according to a REINZ property market overview.
Properties took a median of 51 days to sell, three days longer than in August 2025, it said, noting the REINZ house price index fell 0.9 percent year on year, indicating relative stability in national property values despite weaker transactions.
Regional performance varied considerably, with a clear difference between the North and South Islands, according to REINZ.
National inventory rose 9.7 percent year on year to 32,908 properties, while new listings fell by 5.1 percent to 8,326 in August 2026, it said.
REINZ CEO Lizzy Ryley said in a statement that members generally expect market conditions to remain broadly steady in the coming months, although borrowing costs, job security, the November general election and local stock levels would influence activity. ■

More than 19,000 housing pockets have rooftop solar systems, benefits 9 lakh households
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:49:39 UTC
13:49:39 KST

More than 19,000 housing pockets have rooftop solar systems, benefits 9 lakh households
NEW DELHI: More than 19,000 residential areas have set up community rooftop solar systems under PM Surya Ghar Yojana to power common utilities, benefiting over 9 lakh households.Officials said the clean energy generated is used for operating lifts, common-area lighting, water pumps, security systems and sewage treatment plants. Govt has released Rs 422 crore as central financial assistance to resident welfare associations (RWAs) to help them install the systems.“With common-area electricity bills forming a significant component of monthly maintenance expenses in many large housing complexes, govt support helps them reduce recurring costs while transitioning to cleaner energy,” an official said. The cumulative rooftop solar capacity of over 278 MW has been installed for these communities.Gujarat leads in total installations, with more than 9,000 housing societies setting up solar capacity, followed by Maharashtra, where over 7,500 residential areas have opted for the facility. Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka are also steadily expanding the adoption of community solar, said another official.
Ahmedabad, Pune, Vadodara, Nashik and Surat are among the top five cities with the highest number of rooftop solar installations for housing societies.To make community-scale rooftop solar financially viable, govt provides central financial assistance of Rs 18,000 per kW for eligible RWA and group housing society projects. Housing societies in special category states and Union territories, including the North-Eastern states, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep, are eligible for a higher central financial assistance (CFA) of Rs 19,800 per kW, the official added.
Launched in Feb 2024, PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSGMBY) aims to bring rooftop solar to one crore Indian homes by March 2027. The total number of rooftop solar installations, including individual households, has reached 47.8 lakh with total installed capacity of 16.8 GW, benefitting nearly 56.9 lakh families. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has so far disbursed over Rs 31,515 crore as central financial assistance, while several states are also running separate subsidy schemes to promote the installation of rooftop solar systems.

Emmy winners 2026: ‘Widow’s Bay’ and ‘The Pitt’ dominate
Jean Smart earns fifth Emmy for “Hacks,” becoming the first to win lead comedy actress for every show season.
Emergency room drama “The Pitt” and comedy-horror “Widow’s Bay” have won television’s highest honours, the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards, presented in Los Angeles.
Set in a cursed New England town, “Widow’s Bay” won the best comedy series prize on Monday, overcoming last season’s winner, “Hacks”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Artists speak out for Palestine at Emmy Awards
- list 2 of 3Al Jazeera journalist’s emotional speech after winning Emmy
- list 3 of 3Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, dies at age 80
Matthew Rhys, starring in “Widow’s Bay”, made history by becoming the first person to win two lead acting honours at the same ceremony. Fellow actor in the TV series, Stephen Root, won best supporting actor in a comedy, beating favourite Harrison Ford of “Shrinking”.
“Thank you, sir, for all your many years of great, great, great acting,” Root told Ford during his acceptance speech.
“Hacks” actress Jean Smart won her fifth Emmy for portraying stand-up comic Deborah Vance, making her the first actress to win the award for best lead comedy actress for every season of a show’s run. Smart has won eight Emmys overall in her acting career.
“What a ride this has been,” Smart said after receiving a standing ovation.
Actress Julia Louis-Dreyfus is the only performer to come close to Smart’s comedy lead actress sweep, having won the award for six of the seven seasons of the political satire “Veep”.
Noah Wyle, who starred as Dr “Robby” Robinavitch on “The Pitt”, told the Emmy audience it felt overwhelming to win his second straight Emmy for best lead drama actor.
“The Pitt”, set in a Pittsburgh emergency department, won its second consecutive Emmy award for best drama series, beating fellow nominees including “Pluribus”, “Paradise” and “The Diplomat”.
“This is the only club I’ve ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me,” Wyle said while accepting the award.
Rhea Seehorn won best actress in a drama for playing the lone character on “Pluribus”, after being nominated twice without receiving any honours for her breakthrough role on “Better Call Saul”.
Vince Gilligan, who created “Breaking Bad” and its spin-off “Better Call Saul”, won best drama writing for “Pluribus”.
“The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” won for best variety series, concluding its farewell season with six total Emmys after CBS cancelled the programme, citing financial pressures.
Colbert rejected that explanation, accusing network executives of succumbing to pressure from President Donald Trump over his frequent mockery of the administration.

In the United States, a House committee approved a bill on sanctions against Russia with tariffs of up to 500%
Kyiv • UNN
The bill provides for tariffs of up to 500% on goods from Russia and its energy partners. The measure could be brought to a vote as early as this week.
The U.S. House Rules Committee approved a bipartisan bill to strengthen sanctions against Russia over its war against Ukraine, clearing the way for consideration by the full House. The bill provides, among other things, for the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 500% on goods from Russia and countries that continue to trade in Russian energy resources, The Hill reports, writes UNN.
Details
The bill would give U.S. President Donald Trump the authority to impose sanctions on individuals acting on behalf of the Russian authorities to disrupt peace negotiations with Ukraine, violate a possible peace agreement, or undermine the Ukrainian government.
The document would also allow visa restrictions to be imposed and the assets of putin, individual Russian military commanders, and foreign persons who knowingly supply defense products to the armed forces of the russian federation to be blocked.
Tariffs could reach 500%
A separate section of the bill provides for the possibility of raising tariffs to 500% on goods from Russia, as well as from states that knowingly conduct transactions involving Russian uranium and petroleum products.
Last month, the U.S. Senate had already supported the bill by a vote of 86 to 11. Now, following its passage through the Rules Committee, the document could be brought to a House vote as early as this week.
Putin's war machine continues to kill Ukrainian civilians, and this bill hits the Kremlin's coffers hard. Now is exactly the time to pass it and force Putin to sit down at the negotiating table
House Speaker Mike Johnson also allowed for expedited consideration of the document. In that case, its passage would require the support of at least two-thirds of the members of the House of Representatives.
Consideration of the bill is taking place ahead of a scheduled seven-week recess of the House of Representatives, which is set to begin after work concludes on Thursday.

Wiping out measles impossible due to vaccine hesitancy in rich countries, says Bill Gates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

Wiping out measles impossible due to vaccine hesitancy in rich countries, says Bill Gates
- Bill Gates says vaccine hesitancy in rich countries makes eradicating measles impossible, calling it a tragic setback for global health efforts.
- Measles still kills about 100,000 children yearly, mainly in conflict zones with low immunisation and poor healthcare.
- Gates warns aid cuts by wealthy nations have worsened health outcomes but some funding restoration has prevented a major crisis.
AI generated
LONDON - Vaccine hesitancy in rich countries means ending measles as a global public health threat is not currently possible, Bill Gates told Reuters in an interview.
The Microsoft co-founder turned billionaire philanthropist said wiping out the killer childhood disease had previously been a potential goal for his eponymous foundation, which focuses on global health and the world’s poorest people.
But it was now off the table due to increased vaccine hesitancy in wealthier nations, part of a wave of scepticism championed for decades by the now health secretary in the United States under President Donald Trump, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
“At one point, the foundation wanted to eradicate measles, but the vaccine hesitancy in rich countries has meant that’s not on our list of goals,” Gates said. “I think that’s kind of tragic.”
Measles, among the world’s most contagious diseases, causes a high fever, a cough and a tell-tale rash.
The virus killed around 2 million children every year before the introduction of a vaccine in the 1960s.
Nowadays, around 100,000 children die annually, largely in countries where conflict or logistics make immunisation difficult.
The WHO says vaccination rates need to be above 95 per cent to prevent outbreaks.
But recent years have also seen a surge in cases in countries where the disease was almost forgotten, including in the United States and Europe, as vaccination rates have fallen.
Gates said that vaccine hesitancy had at least not spread to lower-income countries, where measles can be much deadlier than in richer countries due to malnutrition and healthcare gaps.
“There’s always that concern that if you have doubters in the US, that becomes a global thing,” he said. “But we haven’t seen an increase in vaccine hesitancy in the countries the foundation works in.”
Aid cuts
Gates was speaking ahead of the foundation’s annual Goalkeepers event, which looks at progress towards the United Nations global development goals set for 2030, including on improving health.
In 2025’s report, Gates warned of the impact of aid cuts led by Trump’s administration, and followed by other wealthy countries like Britain and Germany, on the health of the world’s poorest.
For 2026, he said the cuts had likely caused many deaths, but the restoration of some money had prevented the worst-case scenario.
Efforts from impacted countries and other health groups also held off disaster, as Reuters has reported.
“The most dire predictions, which went above 10 million deaths, we don’t see that taking place,” Gates said, adding that he continued to urge governments to restore aid or at least not cut it further. “It’s still a very tragic situation.” REUTERS

Russia to hold tightly controlled vote in fifth year of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:37:00 KST

Russia to hold tightly controlled vote in fifth year of war
- Russia will hold tightly controlled parliamentary elections from Sept 18-20, seen by the Kremlin as a measure of public opinion on the ongoing war with Ukraine.
- Only pro-Putin parties are allowed to participate, with no real opposition, ensuring a guaranteed majority for United Russia amid heavy censorship and repression.
- The vote also raises fears of a possible new military mobilisation, although experts doubt this will happen, viewing the election mainly as a legitimacy boost for Putin's leadership and war effort.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russia will this week hold a tightly controlled election in a vote seen by the Kremlin as a barometer of public opinion on the war with Ukraine, which is dragging into its fifth year.
Some Russians have grown weary of economic stagnation and intensifying Ukrainian retaliatory attacks, and there are fears in some quarters that Russian President Vladimir Putin could order a mass call-up of new soldiers after the election.
The parliamentary vote – held from Sept 18 to 20 – will be the first since Russia launched its offensive in February 2022, and only the second nationwide poll since then, after a presidential contest that re-elected Putin in 2024.
Voting is also due to take place in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia’s army.
The war has killed hundreds of thousands, brought widespread censorship at home, devastated eastern Ukraine and seen Moscow hit with unprecedented Western sanctions.
With Moscow having banned criticism of the war, no real opposition parties will be on the ballot, and Putin’s ruling United Russia party is assured of scooping a majority of seats in the State Duma.
A European diplomat told AFP that while the election was “quite a sham”, it was a “ritual the Kremlin considers essential”, and that it would be striving to “ensure a high turnout”.
Even if the results are “predefined”, voting still matters, exiled Russian political scientist Nikolai Petrov said.
“Just like at the time of the Soviet Union, elections should demonstrate (the) loyalty of citizens.”
For Putin – who has been in power for 26 years – it is important to “demonstrate to elites that he is still supported, still trusted by ordinary people”, Petrov said.
Half of the 450 seats up for grabs will be decided by a nationwide vote for party blocs, with the other half allocated to single-member districts across the country.
Only parties that support Putin and the war have been permitted to stand on the national ballot: the ruling United Russia party, the Communist Party, A Just Russia, the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, and New People.
Russia’s sole anti-war party still active inside the country, Yabloko, was barred from standing.
“It’s a choice without a choice,” said 18-year-old Yevdokia. She had planned to vote for Yabloko, which has called for an end to fighting in Ukraine, but will now vote for New People.
The authorities have used the backdrop of the war to ramp up repression to levels unseen since days of the Soviet Union.
All of Putin’s top opponents are in jail, in exile or dead – like his main challenger Alexei Navalny, who died in a Russian prison in 2024.
While Russia’s Parliament has seen its powers hugely reduced under Putin, legislative elections have previously been sources of tension. In 2011, widespread fraud and the return of Putin to the Kremlin from the role of prime minister led to Russia’s largest protests since the end of the USSR.
In Moscow, there are few signs that an election will even take place in 2026. Campaign posters are few and far between, save for generic ones from the authorities urging people to participate – featuring the slogan, “Your voice is Russia’s strength”.
Mobilisation fears
The vote will serve as a barometer of feelings on a war that has killed hundreds of thousands and undermined the daily lives of Russians, even those living thousands of kilometres from the front.
In recent months, Kyiv has stepped up its long-range strikes on Russia – cast as fair retribution for Moscow’s own barrages – causing fuel shortages and billions of roubles in damage and killing civilians.
Amid persistent rumours, Putin himself has been forced to deny that Moscow plans a new round of mobilisation – similar to the unpopular 2022 call-up of 300,000 reservists – after the vote.
Kremlin critics, Kyiv and some Western countries have accused him of planning just that.
Russia expert Tatiana Stanovaya – of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, which Moscow banned – believes a call-up is unlikely.
“They made so much effort to convince Russians not (to) worry about it... I would be very, very surprised if it happens.”
With his inevitable victory, Putin would instead see “confirmation of his legitimacy”, she said – “legitimacy of his war”. AFP

Lawmakers push for Iran's withdrawal from NPT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:36:51 UTC
13:36:51 KST

The statement, said the NPT is based on a reciprocal balance of "commitment to non-proliferation" and "guaranteeing members' rights and security," but recent years and especially recent developments have proven that international structures based on the treaty have become completely ineffective, structurally discriminatory and incapable of securing Iran's minimum legal rights.
The lawmakers listed four reasons for the necessity and urgency of Iran's withdrawal from the NPT and the defining new scientific, technical and legal cooperation with aligned countries.
First, they said the treaty has been ineffective in securing the safety of nuclear facilities. Peaceful facilities under supervision should enjoy the highest level of international protection and immunity from any threat or military attack, but responsible bodies have taken no deterrent action against open threats and attacks on Iran's nuclear centres, effectively endorsing the aggression through silence and passivity.
Second, they cited enemy attacks on infrastructure and the assassination of scientists, including direct attacks, organised sabotage, two recent imposed wars, the assassination of nuclear scientists and repeated threats by U.S. and Israeli officials to launch nuclear strikes against Iran. These, they said, are undeniable evidence that accepting maximum supervision has brought Iran no security and has become a tool for identifying and targeting the country's power components.
Third, they said Iran has been completely deprived of the NPT's legal benefits. Despite fully implementing its obligations and accepting unprecedented supervision, Iran has always been denied its rights under Article 4 of the treaty, especially non-discriminatory access to peaceful technology and international cooperation, and has instead faced the harshest unjust and illegal sanctions.
Fourth, they said the IAEA's inspections have become a cover for industrial and security espionage and continuous political pressure rather than a tool for verification, the latest example being the unjustified referral of Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council.
The statement cited Article 10 of the NPT, which gives any member the right to withdraw from the treaty if it decides that extraordinary events related to the subject matter of the treaty have jeopardised its supreme interests, with three months' notice to all members and the UN Security Council.
The lawmakers said that with continued existential threats, open aggression against Iran's territory and facilities, and the absolute ineffectiveness of international guarantees, Iran's supreme interests and national security are in serious jeopardy and an extraordinary situation.
They called on the parliament's presiding board to activate the legal process for Iran's full withdrawal from the NPT and defining new international cooperation with Iran's friends as quickly as possible, in accordance with parliament's internal regulations.

Taiwan bars athletes from representing China in international competitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:36:26 UTC
13:36:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Sports has revised regulations governing sports exchanges with China to explicitly prohibit Taiwanese citizens from serving as athletes on Chinese national teams in international competitions.
The ministry announced the revision Thursday, saying it was intended to provide clearer guidance for sports organizations and local governments conducting sports exchanges with China. The amendment was the fifth revision of regulations first introduced in 1998 and took effect immediately.
The main change adds Article 7, which explicitly states that Taiwanese citizens may not serve as athletes on China's national team in international competitions, per TTV. The ministry said representing China involves national identity and falls under restrictions established by Article 33 of the Act Governing Relations between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area.
The article prohibits Taiwanese from holding positions in the Chinese Communist Party, military, administrative, or political organizations and requires permission for certain other positions. The ministry said the new provision incorporates the legal intent of the cross-strait law and establishes a clear policy boundary for sports exchanges.
The ministry reiterated that public and private organizations and individuals conducting sports exchanges with China should follow the principles of equality, dignity, and mutual respect and maintain exchanges within the professional scope of sports. The ministry also said it will work with the Mainland Affairs Council to promote relevant cross-strait laws, regulations, and policies to sports organizations and schools, per LTN.
Furthermore, the ministry specifically warned organizations invited to China to assess potential risks and carefully review the background of organizers, itineraries, and promotional materials. It advised organizations to avoid participating in national-level events hosted by China or events that could have united front objectives.

Taiwan airport MRT to add evening train from Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:36:23 UTC
13:36:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taoyuan Airport MRT will add a weekday evening train from Taipei Main Station starting Sept. 21 to ease congestion during the evening rush.
Taoyuan Metro said the additional local train will depart Taipei Main Station at 6:04 p.m., stop at every station, and arrive at Airport Terminal 2 at 6:50 p.m. The service will reduce the average interval between trains from Taipei Main Station to the airport to 5.5 minutes between 6 and 7 p.m.
The airport MRT has seen record ridership this year, averaging 130,681 passengers per day through August. The operator identified concentrated evening peak demand among commuters and students traveling from Taipei toward the Xinzhuang, Linkou, and Guishan areas.
The company has added 17 services since 2023 as part of efforts to increase capacity and encourage ridership. It said the latest service will help spread out passengers during the evening peak.
Passengers traveling to Taoyuan HSR Station or Zhongli should get off at Airport Terminal 2, where the 6:04 p.m. service terminates, and transfer to a local train on the same platform.
Taoyuan Metro said it will continue monitoring ridership and passenger loads on key sections of the line and adjust services accordingly. Passengers can check updated schedules on the Taoyuan Metro website or the Taoyuan Airport MRT app.

Taiwan cleanroom engineering firms hit record revenue on chip investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:35:59 UTC
13:35:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s major cleanroom engineering firms reported strong revenue growth in August as semiconductor companies accelerate capacity expansion across manufacturing and downstream facilities.
L&K Engineering Co. posted revenue of NT$11 billion (US$346.8 million) in August, up 41.7% from the same month a year earlier. Revenue for the first eight months reached NT$67.9 billion, a 63.4% year-over-year increase and a record high for the period, according to UDN.
L&K secured NT$303.7 billion in new orders in the first half of this year. Its backlog of signed but unrecognized orders also reached a record NT$440.1 billion, with the orders expected to be recognized over the next three years.
United Integrated Services Co. reported August revenue of NT$9.4 billion, up 59.1% year-over-year and marking a record high for the month. Revenue for the first eight months totaled NT$65.7 billion, an increase of 71.6% from a year earlier and also a record for the period.
UIS secured NT$67.4 billion in new contracts in the first five months of the year. As of the end of May, the company had a record NT$193.9 billion in signed contracts that had yet to be recognized as revenue. UIS expects to benefit from continued investment in the global semiconductor industry.
Yankey Engineering Co. reported August revenue of NT$5.3 billion, up 213.7% from a year earlier and a record monthly high. Revenue for the first eight months reached NT$28.2 billion, rising 112.8% year-over-year and setting a record for the period.
The company said August revenue was mainly driven by the accelerated recognition of a NT$20 billion project at Micron Technology’s Nanke facility in Tainan. The project is expected to be completed by the end of this year or early next year, according to MoneyDJ.
Yankey also expects an ASML project to be substantially completed by the end of this year, with final completion scheduled for early next year. The two projects are expected to support revenue in the coming months.
The strong results reflect a broader wave of investment in semiconductor production facilities. Cleanrooms are critical to the manufacturing process, with forced-air circulation and multiple layers of precision filters used to remove gaseous and particulate contaminants from the air, according to LTN.
They also regulate temperature, humidity, electromagnetic conditions, static electricity, and micro-vibrations to keep sensitive production environments stable. Such controls are especially important in semiconductor manufacturing, where small environmental changes can affect production and product quality.

Taiwan real wages post strongest seven-month growth in 11 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:35:54 UTC
13:35:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said Monday that inflation-adjusted total wages rose 2.33% in the first seven months of 2026, the strongest growth for the period in 11 years,
CNA reported that inflation-adjusted regular wages increased 1.12% during the same period, the strongest seven-month growth in six years. Both figures rose because wages increased faster than consumer prices.
In July, average regular wages increased 3.32% from a year earlier, while average total wages, including bonuses and overtime pay, rose 8.25%. The median regular wage increased 3.47%, a figure less affected by unusually high salaries.
The statistics agency said consumer prices rose an average of 1.8% during the first seven months of the year. Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said wages were growing faster than inflation, allowing workers’ purchasing power to improve, per Economic Daily News.
However, inflation has accelerated in recent months, with annual consumer price growth exceeding 2%. Tan said faster price increases could slow real wage growth in the coming months.

However, inflation has accelerated in recent months, with annual consumer price growth exceeding 2%. Tan said faster price increases could slow real wage growth in the coming months.

Country diary: Goldfinches and grasses, together in an explosion of movement | Mark Cocker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:30:25 UTC
13:30:25 KST

Stands of tufted hair-grass, some over a metre tall, burned beige by the summer heat, were churned by strong autumn westerlies. Over and through the vegetation’s swaying lather roved a flock of about 200 goldfinches, most of them this year’s young. They were intent on the hanks of thistle and knapweed seed which lay below the hair-grass “canopy”.
These immature finches lack any of the red and black bands of the adult’s head. Instead of the smooth mocha buff on their parents’ underparts, the youngsters were dull and streaky. What they had to perfection were the semi-circular disks of yellow across each black wing, while every feather through that full fan was tipped with white.
As they moved from place to place, working through the grasses, so the birds created double bands of brightness that shone in intermittent sunlight. The whole scene – the frothing plant stems and the shifting birds – produced exquisite countervailing patterns of movement.
An old name for goldfinch is “tailorbird”. It’s said to refer to the white eye-holes inserted into their tail- and wing-tips. As the birds worked away, winnowing thistle floss from seed, letting hanks float off on the breeze, it occurred to me that these prolonged ecological relationships with cottony material could also explain the “tailor” name. It may further account for the birds’ love of spiders’ silk and wool and other fibres as nest material: they are surely tailorbirds in name and nature.
As they showered up and descended again in patterns of yellow flecking, it also came to me that the visual impact and the sounds of the flock are more than mere analogues. They seem party to some greater creative whole. Goldfinch calls are soft, tinkling, fragmented, but also somehow molten and blended one to another like melting flakes of gold – no, not gold, but something rarer, something more meaningful than mere metal. Let’s say the dust from some exploded star in a far galaxy that wandered and settled hereabouts 5 billion years ago, only to be infused with something rarest of all: soiled, earthy and – here at Priestcliffe today – called “life”.

Hanson apologises if she caused offence by Indigenous Australian remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:27:50 UTC
13:27:50 KST

Pauline Hanson offers qualified apologies to Indigenous Australians and Anthony Albanese
In short:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has offered two qualified apologies, including to Indigenous Australians who she labelled "the most primitive race on Earth".
Senator Hanson says she apologises if she has offended people by using the term "primitive".
She also addressed criticising the amount of time that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's mother Maryanne lived in public housing, arguing the remarks were not "derogatory".
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has offered qualified apologies for labelling Indigenous Australians "the most primitive race on Earth" and criticising the prime minister's late mother.
Senator Hanson faced widespread condemnation on Monday after the remarks from conservative-leaning Jamie J podcast came to light, where she criticised the amount of focus on Indigenous history in the school curriculum.
"Sorry they're the most primitive race on Earth and we're supposed to be holding them up and saying what they've achieved. They've achieved nothing," she said last September.
Politicians from across the divide swiftly rebuked the comments, among them Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy, who said they were "derogatory" and "completely racist" and urged her to apologise.
In her first public remarks since, Senator Hanson said she did not mean to cause offence by the comments.
"If I've offended people by using that, yes, I will apologise for that," she told reporters.
"I've always advocated, we are Australians all together and should be all treated equally on a needs basis, not about race. And until we actually do that, we're not going to move over what's happened in the past."
On Monday, several Indigenous leaders expressed their "disappointment" over the "primitive" label, calling Senator Hanson's claims not only "false" but demonstrating ignorance.
Indigenous author and human rights activist Thomas Mayo was among them, arguing that Senator Hanson's view is not shared by Australians.
"Many Australians have learnt that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples built sophisticated systems of law, governance, culture, trade, and land management over tens of thousands of years," he said.
"We have survived invasion, dispossession and every attempt to erase us. We are still here and will always remain in the rich tapestry of Australian identity."
Speaking to News24 earlier today, Senator Hanson claimed "[I] put my foot in my mouth" and that the comments about First Nations people were referring to the past, when Australia was colonised.
"If we go back at the time of settlement in Australia, they were primitive compared to what the settlers that came out here from England, that type of thing. But I'm not talking those terms now. It's not about now," Senator Hanson said.
"I regret saying that because I don't want to upset people. That's not my intention. That wasn't my intention to hurt people."
Calls for Hanson to apologise to PM
Senator Hanson was also asked if she regretted saying it was "not on" for Anthony Albanese's mother Maryanne, who suffered from severe rheumatoid arthritis, to have spent much of her life in housing commission.
"I don't think my comments were derogatory towards his mother at all. I was referring to house commission at that time. So if he's taken offence to it, well, I'm sorry for that," she said.
The criticism of Mr Albanese's late mother, who died in 2002, prompted calls from several politicians for Senator Hanson to apologise to the prime minister.
Mr Albanese has been open about his upbringing in public housing in Sydney's inner west, with repeated references that Senator Hanson labelled "pathetic" on a podcast with Karl Stefanovic earlier this year.
"I actually grew up in a street where we had housing commission houses there. It was a helping hand to those people, but they had jobs. And they worked," she told Stefanovic.
"Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years] — and he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years."
In a fierce defence of his mother on Sunday morning, Mr Albanese said he was "stunned" by the attack, recalling a woman of "great character".
"If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine, but my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league, way out of it," he said.
Hanson's apology 'gaslighting'
Senior government minister Madeleine King has questioned whether Senator Hanson's apology was "genuine".
"Sorry if I caused offence is not really an apology," she told the ABC.
"She says outrageous things about Indigenous Australians, disgusting things, and then walks back into this building and says she didn't say it at all. Now, that is gaslighting.
"What she said about the prime minister's much-beloved mother is beyond the pale, and a pseudo apology is just pathetic on her behalf."
Liberal MP Andrew Bragg welcomed the retraction but said it was not unusual for One Nation to attack sections of the Australian community.
"It was a silly thing to do, but it's all part of the business model, where you tee off on minority interests; it's the business model One Nation has had for years," he said.
"There are no winners from that sort of attack."
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie was pleased to see Senator Hanson apologise for language he "unequivocally" repudiates.
"I just can't see how you justify that comment, which is why I'm glad she's apologised for it," he told the ABC.
"I believe that every single person, human being, has innate worth and dignity."

2026-09-15

13:27:18 KST

Charged with a single count of money laundering tied to an alleged conspiracy to create fake companies and falsify shipping records, Saab is scheduled to appear before Judge in Miami on Tuesday for a change of plea hearing, according to court records.
Alex Saab, a close ally of deposed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, is scheduled to enter a guilty plea on Tuesday in a court prosecution alleging that he bribed officials to secure lucrative contracts to import food during a period of widespread hardship in the South American nation.
Deported in May by Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez in response to pressure from the US, which has been targeting the Colombian-born businessman for more than a decade, Saab is charged with a single count of money laundering tied to an alleged conspiracy to create fake companies, falsify shipping records and skim from government contracts to import food from Colombia and Mexico.
He is scheduled to appear before Judge Kathleen Williams in Miami on Tuesday for a change of plea hearing, according to court records.
The details of the plea were not immediately made public, and Saab’s attorney, Neil Schuster, declined to comment, but prosecutors allege Saab and others allegedly expanded their corrupt influence deep inside the Maduro government, accessing billions of dollars in oil sales from state-run oil company PDVSA.
The new indictment accuses Saab and others of setting up a web of companies to bribe top Venezuelan officials controlling contracts for the so-called CLAP programme set up by Maduro to provide staples — rice, corn flour, and cooking oil — to poor Venezuelans at a time of rampant hyperinflation and a crumbling currency.
The 54-year-old was previously charged during the first Trump administration in 2019 and then arrested during a refuelling stop in Cape Verde on what the Venezuelan government described as a high-level humanitarian mission to Iran.
But President Joe Biden pardoned him in 2023 in exchange for the release of several imprisoned Americans in Venezuela. The deal, part of a failed effort by the Biden White House to lure Maduro into holding a free presidential election, was harshly criticised by Republicans and federal law enforcement officials, who immediately began investigating Saab for other alleged crimes not covered by the narrowly tailored pardon.
US officials have long described Saab as Maduro’s “bag man” and could ask him to serve as a character witness against the former president, who is awaiting trial on drug charges in Manhattan after being captured in a raid by the US military in January.
Saab's prosecution comes amid new US-Venezuela relations
Saab was little known even in Venezuela until after his first arrest, in 2020, when Maduro’s government invested huge resources rallying public support for his release.
Rodríguez, then serving as Maduro’s vice president, helped mount an international campaign in which she referred to Saab as an “innocent Venezuelan diplomat” who had been illegally “kidnapped” by Washington.
But following Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez distanced herself from Saab, firing him from her cabinet and stripping him of his role as the main conduit for foreign companies looking to invest in Venezuela.
His prosecution now comes as the Trump administration overhauls relations with Venezuela, focusing its attention on tapping into Venezuela’s vast oil reserves.
Earlier this month, Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in history” with Venezuela, a partnership with Venezuelan oil entrepreneur Alejandro Betancourt in which Washington will gain a stake and access to at-cost crude shipments from oil fields with a potential to produce 65 billion barrels.
Saab amassed a fortune through Venezuelan government contracts but became even more valuable to Maduro as US sanctions forced Venezuela to conduct much of its oil sales and foreign trade outside of Western financial institutions.

Houthis seize strategic Red Sea islands as analysts warn of impending oil crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:22:16 UTC
13:22:16 KST

Yemen’s Houthi militants have seized two strategic islands in the Red Sea, reinforcing the Iran-backed group’s ability to control a key shipping route, as concerns mount that the world is facing a new oil supply crisis.
The seizure of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish is the latest in the militant group’s swift advance across Yemen’s Red Sea coast, after the capture of the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
The islands lie 160km north of the strait which is a chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the open ocean and Saudi Arabia’s key Asian markets.
The speed of the Houthis’ advance has left Yemen’s Saudi-backed government trying to claw back territory captured by the militants in recent days, while Riyadh grapples with attacks on a critical oil pipeline by Iran-allied militants in Iraq.
Threats from Houthis have left Saudi Arabia on high alert, with air alerts flashing across the country daily, while a series of attacks carried out by the militant group using ballistic missiles and drones wounded 13 civilians on Monday.
Nearly 94,000 people in Yemen have fled their homes since fighting between the Houthis and government forces escalated this month, the International Organization for Migration said on Monday. About 200 schools have been converted to shelters in south-western Yemen to absorb an influx of families, the International Rescue Committee said.
More than 2,000 people have reportedly fled across the sea into Djibouti. The Houthi advance puts them just 32km from a US military base in the tiny country on the Horn of Africa, on the other side of the Bab al-Mandab strait.
On Monday, experts warned that the closure of Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which has been vital for Riyadh to move oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will further pile pressure on its shipments and global oil supplies. Officials have estimated it could take weeks to fully repair it.
“The big question for traders right now is the duration of the east-west outage. Any prolonged disruption and the associated supply loss could easily push prices to the next level higher,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.
Research company Rystad Energy said on Monday that since late August, an average 2.6m to 4m barrels of oil a day moved through the pipeline and out of the port of Yanbu – a volume it said was now at risk of “disappearing from the market”.
Janiv Shah, vice-president of oil markets for Rystad Energy, noted the recent jump in Brent prices proved the market was already responding to “a significant loss of supply”. Saudi inventories could sustain exports in the coming days, but that could “change quickly,” Shah added.
On Tuesday morning, Brent crude oil rose 1.17% to $106.92 a barrel. The average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, as the Iran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, squeezed supply.
The Houthi leadership has said it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked ships. Supplies from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of oil, are vital to economies in Africa and Asia, which rely on oil imports from the Middle East and have been hit hardest by the disruption in trade.
Experts say the stock buffers that existed in the system earlier this year, shielding the world from the worst effects of an oil shock by limiting price increases, have now largely disappeared.
Since the war began in February, countries have released some crude stockpiles to the market, and the US also lifted restrictions on oil stored on ships floating at sea from countries under sanctions. Those buffers have now been “played out”, Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said on Friday.
“It’s harder to envision a scenario where prices soften and quickly,” he said. “I think the risks remain to the upside over the next few months.“

The Russian enterprise "Metafrax Chemicals" in the Perm Krai allegedly completely halted operations after a drone attack on September 11. This was reported by the Exilenova+ Telegram channel, UNN writes.
Details
According to the channel, around 10 UAVs hit the enterprise's facilities. The formalin, pentaerythritol, urea and hexamine production units, the nitrogen-oxygen station, and the main step-down substation were allegedly damaged.

The enterprise produces critical raw materials for explosives

Pentaerythritol, which is also produced by the enterprise, is used to obtain pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN)—an explosive substance used in detonators and other munitions components.
Formalin, meanwhile, is a raw material for the further production of hexamine and pentaerythritol. Thus, damage to several technological links at once may affect the enterprise's entire production cycle.

One of the main drama awards went to Rhea Seehorn, who was named Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for "Pluribus." The supporting acting awards in a drama went to Allison Janney for "The Diplomat" and Tom Pelphrey for "Task."
The best limited series was named "DTF St. Louis." Sally Field won in the category of Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for "Remarkably Bright Creatures," while Matthew Rhys earned another acting award—for his leading role in "The Beast in Me."
The film "Remarkably Bright Creatures" itself received the Emmy for Outstanding Television Movie.
"The Traitors" was named Outstanding Reality Competition Program, while "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" received the award in the category of Outstanding Variety Series.
A separate highlight of the evening was the presentation of the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award to Michael J. Fox. The ceremony in Los Angeles was hosted by "Law & Order" star Mariska Hargitay.
Thus, the main winners of the 2026 Emmys were "Widow's Bay" in the comedy segment and "The Pitt" among dramas, while Jean Smart achieved a historic feat with her fifth consecutive win for "Hacks."

====================================================================================================

The Emmys Squandered Beloved First-Time Host Mariska Hargitay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:12:52 UTC
13:12:52 KST

A day before Monday’s 78th Primetime Emmys, giddy headlines proclaimed that reigning king of basketball Jalen Brunson would be joining host Mariska Hargitay for a pre-taped intro bit. Well, it happened. We got a few seconds of the real-life pals steaming work outfits together, of all things. Then, suddenly, Hargitay was leading an “I Love Rock ‘n’ Roll” production number that had her singing about Guy Fieri on an airplane and cuddling up with Jean Smart in a hotel bed, in what felt uncomfortably like an ad for Marriott and United Airlines, whose logos were prominently placed. And then she was onstage at LA’s Peacock Theater, delivering a notably brief monologue. Spanning just eight minutes, the opening segment proved to be an accurate preview of a mediocre NBC and Peacock telecast that was by turns hasty, random, heavily reliant on big-name cameos, and not much of a showcase for Hargitay at all.
It was a shame, not least because Hargitay was touted as the Emmys’ first female host since Jane Lynch in 2011. For many years after the Glee standout’s stint, the awards relied on a rotating cast of SNL and talk-show guys. Recently, however, with late night in decline, they’ve cast a wider net, and results have been all over the map. Following Anthony Anderson’s forgettable performance, we got an effortlessly charming turn from Eugene and Dan Levy—and then last year’s tedious, gimmick-freighted telecast, led by standup superstar Nate Bargatze.
It wasn’t just gender that set Hargitay apart from those predecessors, though. She was also the Emmys’ first emcee not known primarily for her comedy work since 2008, when the five first-ever nominees in a new reality-TV-hosting category, including Ryan Seacrest and Heidi Klum, delivered what critics agreed was one of the worst ceremonies in history. Hargitay is, of course, synonymous with Olivia Benson, the heroic sex-crimes investigator she has portrayed in NBC’s Law & Order: SVU since its 1999 premiere. What casual fans might not have known is that she trained with legendary improv troupe the Groundlings and appeared in sitcoms like Seinfeld; “all I wanted to be was you,” she told Amy Poehler on the latter’s podcast, Good Hang. Hargitay also went into the gig with lots of goodwill from audiences inside the Peacock Theater and at home. Not only is she an advocate for survivors of sexual violence, on screen and off; she’s also in the midst of a pop-culture renaissance, having won two Emmys for the documentary she directed about her famous mom, Jayne Mansfield, conquered the one-woman play Every Brilliant Thing on Broadway, and endeared herself to Knicks fans as a stalwart supporter on the sidelines of this year’s NBA Finals. In light of all this, Variety dubbed her “a national best friend.”
Maybe that explains why Hargitay was just kinda there with us throughout the ceremony, more an affable companion than a genuine ringmaster. In a monologue that was practically over before it started, she quipped about how many of the stars in the room she’d “arrested” in their guest appearances as SVU’s twisted perp of the week. There was a sendup of Nicole Kidman’s five-year-old viral AMC Theatres commercial, featuring an interjection (“That’s my line”) from Kidman herself. It wasn’t the only joke of the night that felt stale (see: Hargitay griping that the Game of Thrones furs she donned to introduce two of the franchise’s stars were “hot as balls”). Minutes after Hargitay joked that male hosts had dominated the Emmys for so long because “for 15 straight years, Amy and Tina said no,” Poehler presented an award with a joke about the night’s losers outnumbering its winners that surpassed anything in the monologue.
Mariska Hargitay and Nicole Kidman Parody Viral AMC Theatres Ad in Emmys Opening Monologue
She was only the first scene stealer in a program full of them—and I’m not even talking about the many deserving winners, to whom the Emmys do rightly belong. (It does seem worth noting that Writing for a Drama Series winner Vince Gilligan made the strongest political statement of a telecast whose scripted portions steered conspicuously clear of controversy, urging Americans to show each other respect and “stop listening to a relative few who tell us that that is for suckers and who get their power from dividing us.”) Presenting the award for Lead Actor in a Drama Series, frequent awards-show MVP John Mulaney eclipsed the monologue in both humor and stage time with a tongue-in-cheek celebration of men that ultimately had him reading from A Guy’s Guide to Being a Man’s Man by Frank Vincent. Andrew Rannells swooped in with a burst of musical theater energy to save Hargitay’s shaky song about canceled series. The host didn’t even get to own the obligatory pre-taped SVU parody, whose mock-investigation into whether Taylor Swift would attend the Emmys landed as a flimsy excuse to get the most famous entertainer on Earth (who is also famously an SVU superfan and Hargitay pal) on screen.
All told, it was neither an excruciating Emmys nor a great one. There were certainly some lovely moments. The Catherine O’Hara tribute from her on-screen children Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy, and Dan Levy stood out as moving in its genuine warmth and specificity. More often, opportunities to honor a beloved person or show were squandered; was Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz presenting an award together really the exciting 30th anniversary Buffy the Vampire Slayer reunion fans were anticipating? Similarly, Hargitay didn’t embarrass herself. Many of the flaws in her performance should be blamed on lackluster writing, from a non sequitur segue after her self-deprecating Ghoulies flashback to that unforgivable “Hannah Mammogramma” pun. She may have failed to match the Levys’ energy or belatedly prove herself as a great comic talent, but at least she avoided a Bargatze- or Seacrest-level disaster and came out with her likability intact. Regardless of whether she gets invited back, here’s to the Emmys giving women more chances to be wonderful, awful, and even just-OK Emmys hosts.

US has weapons deployed in orbit, Space Force says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:10:00 UTC
13:10:00 KST

US has weapons deployed in orbit, Space Force says
WASHINGTON – The United States has weapons deployed in space, the US Space Force said on Sept 14, confirming the presence of such capabilities in orbit for the first time.
“The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” a US Space Force spokesperson said in a statement that did not provide specifics on the weapons.
“Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities,” the statement said, adding that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”.
Both Russia and China – the two main geopolitical rivals of the United States – pose potential threats to US interests in space.
China “develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy”, while Russia “views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts”, according to the US Space Force.
The militarisation of space is as old as the space race itself – as soon as Sputnik was launched into orbit in 1957, Washington and Moscow began exploring ways to both arm and destroy satellites.
The biggest worry was once about nuclear weapons in space, but the superpowers and other countries signed the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, banning weapons of mass destruction in orbit.
Since then, Russia, the United States, China and India have explored ways to fight in space outside of that treaty, including by targeting rivals’ satellites, which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation. AFP

‘Serious lapse’: Air India CEO summoned after 3 foreigners 'skip' immigration check
Unknown

13:07:48 KST

NEW DELHI: Centre has summoned Air India CEO after three foreign nationals departed India without undergoing mandatory departure immigration clearance, news agency ANI reported, citing sources.Sources told ANI that the ministry of civil aviation has sought an explanation from the airline after the incident, terming it a "serious security and immigration-related lapse."This comes after the civil aviation ministry issued a show-cause notice to the airline over alleged procedural lapses that allowed three Italian passengers to board a connecting flight from Delhi without completing immigration formalities earlier this month.
What happened
Three Italian nationals fly into Delhi from Amritsar on September 4 and then, within an hour, depart for Munich on a codeshare Lufthansa flight from Delhi airport without the mandatory immigration check.According to the ministry, the incident occurred during Air India's hub-and-spoke operation and involved a violation of the prescribed Standard Operating Procedure.Amritsar airport is among the airports where Air India operates flights under its ‘Hub-and-Spoke’ model.
Under this arrangement, passengers complete immigration formalities at the airport of origin and can then travel to an overseas destination through a designated hub. At the hub airport, where the international flight departs, passengers are required only to undergo security checks before boarding.
If a person is travelling from Amritsar via Delhi to a foreign destination, then Amritsar is the spoke and Delhi is the hub.In this case, the sources told PTI that the Italian nationals were issued boarding passes at Amritsar airport for Delhi as well as the Lufthansa flight to Munich.Meanwhile, home secretary Govind Mohan is expected to chair a meeting to discuss the incident on Tuesday. Secretary and additional secretary at the civil aviation ministry, director of Intelligence Bureau, additional secretary (UT and Foreigners) at the home ministry, Bureau of Immigration (BoI) commissioner, and Delhi airport CEO will attend the meeting, they added.The aviation ministry is also expected to make a presentation on ways to plug the gaps at the meeting.

When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:27 UTC
13:00:27 KST

When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.
However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.
After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.
Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.
Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.
Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.
Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.
The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.
On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.
“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.
It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.
While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.
“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”
Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.
Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.
The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.
They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.
Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.
The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”
In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.
“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”

I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship | Carolin Würfel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:27 UTC
13:00:27 KST

The fear that a fascist, far-right movement would rise to power again in Germany has been with me since my youth. On 6 September, the far-right, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) won a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the biggest party in the state parliament, with a shocking 44% of the vote, on a record turnout. If it finds a way to power it will be the first far-right party to govern a German state since the Nazi era.
The night before the vote, I sent a message to a friend, who, like myself, has an East German background. Was she as worried, scared even, about the vote as I was, I asked. I’d fallen into a loop for days, scrolling videos, reels, reports, interviews done on the ground. And I knew these AfD voters. They could have been relatives, friends of my parents, old teachers, former schoolmates. Why were they saying such incoherent stuff?
I did not grow up in Saxony-Anhalt, but in Saxony – a sibling eastern German state, not entirely the same but similar in many core aspects. When I went to high school in Leipzig in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the presence of rightwing extremists was part of my coming-of-age experience. Every Friday night, you felt the fear that neo-Nazis would be waiting outside the clubs, the bars, the tram stops, fists clenched or baseball bats in hand. Every 1 May was a flashpoint when neo-Nazis were allowed to march through the city-centre. And still, Saxony’s first prime minister after reunification, Kurt Biedenkopf – a West German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician and a close ally of Helmut Kohl – promised, stoically, throughout his 12 years in office: “Saxony is immune to rightwing extremism.”
By 2004, a year before I graduated, the far-right National Democratic party (NPD) had entered the Saxon state parliament for the first time, with 9.2% of the vote. In 2005, I left Saxony and moved to Berlin. One reason was the unbearable, dangerous presence of neo-Nazis and rightwing extremists. Many peers did the same, because it was clear that the blooming landscapes that Kohl, the German chancellor in charge of reunification, had confidently promised in 1990 weren’t going to materialise.
Instead, rightwing extremism has grown steadily in eastern Germany ever since. Only the names have changed – from NPD, to Pegida (the anti-migrant protest movement launched in 2014), to AfD. I am terrified, if not surprised. Because fascist structures, left unchecked, will always keep going.
But this result is also a function of the deeply troubled relationship between the former East and West Germany.
A couple of weeks ago, Magnus Brechtken, deputy director of the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in Munich – Germany’s leading institute for contemporary history – gave an interview to the FAZ newspaper. It went viral. The headline: “Many west Germans have had enough now.”
The interview was framed as a reminder to angry east Germans – meaning, specifically, those tempted to vote AfD out of spite towards the west – of some historical facts. Brechtken argued that the differences east Germans have been complaining about for 36 years are, by now, emotional rather than rational – the product, he suggested, of a lack of honest self-examination. He went further: the German west, he said, has spent the past 75 years proving it understands democracy and knows how to handle extremism, that it is better equipped to counter radical movements and prevent parties like the AfD from rising in the first place – while east Germans, he implied, have always had an inherited longing for authoritarian solutions.
You couldn’t help but wonder how much of it was history, and how much was personal opinion. But I do think Brechtken was right about one thing. This supposed east German anger, the AfD’s popularity, the result in Saxony-Anhalt and – in all likelihood – the party’s performance in two upcoming state elections on 20 September should be used as a reminder of some actual historical facts, and of follow-up questions Brechtken apparently decided not to ask.
The AfD was founded in west Germany. A large share of its leadership was born and raised in western states such as Rheinland-Pfalz and Nordrhein-Westfalen. The question shouldn’t only be what draws the east of Germany towards the AfD. It’s just as much: what draws a certain kind of west German towards building a party like this one, pushing it, and choosing the east as the place to make it grow?
I believe the west German states – which officially claimed to have carried out denazification after 1945, and prided themselves on the culture of remembrance, or “coming to terms” with the Nazi past – need to look, just as urgently as the east German states, at why this fascination with fascism keeps recurring. And why, by now, are there no working structures against the rise of right-extremist movements, parties and agendas – but somehow still a system that lets them flourish?
It’s also worth asking whether a party like the AfD went east only because east Germans are more susceptible – or because the visible inequalities there are excellent material to organise around.
In 1989, a lot of east Germans had hoped for something between socialism and capitalism. Reunification wasn’t necessarily the preferred option. What followed felt, to many, badly mishandled – too fast, laws and decisions imposed rather than negotiated. And then there was the Treuhand – the agency put in charge of privatising the former GDR’s entire state-owned economy. In the process of reunification, 94% of East German companies were taken over by West German or international investors. Six per cent stayed with the people of East Germany. Six per cent. Approximately two million jobs were eliminated in the east.
In the autumn and winter of 1990-91, people took to the streets again – not against their own government’s repression this time, but against the perceived occupier: West Germany. They demanded new elections, a renegotiation of the agreements that had left millions empty-handed and jobless, as unemployment in the east skyrocketed. Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand and the key figure in overhauling the former East Germany, was asked in an interview back then by a TV host: “If it doesn’t get better, aren’t you afraid there might be another revolution in East Germany?”
In those years, the former East Germany was treated like a child that had to follow the laws and orders of its wiser western counterpart – a parent. Now, that child is all grown. But it remembers the experience – and quite possibly holds on to it too tightly. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s man in Saxony-Anhalt, was born the same year as reunification.
One of his main promises is to take back control. Maybe you could say that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt went beyond a question of control and was driven by the desire for a sort of revenge. The east, finally, daring to say to the overpowering west: enough. Or as Siegmund at his first victory press conference said, the result showed that the people of Saxony-Anhalt wouldn’t be “patronised” any longer. With this he was tapping into something almost visceral. The remark also clarified for me something about the motives of the countless potential AfD voters I had listened to over the past weeks and months. Most of them don’t actually read or know what’s in the AfD’s programme. And they don’t seem to care. What won people over was simpler: I hear you. I see you. Yes, you have every right to be unhappy.
Throughout the campaign, Siegmund travelled the entire state and threw parties: free sausages, free beer, dancing, music and maybe for some, it felt like the return of community. Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.
What many have not realised yet is that the AfD won’t improve life in east Germany. But that was never the point. It gave people attention in exchange for a vote.
And for now, that was what counted most.
Because the AfD is bigger than east versus west. It was built by west Germans, carried by east Germans, and now it strives for power across the country. Its programme runs on ideas Germany once needed a war and total defeat to bury: racism, the belief in superiority and a hierarchy of who really belongs, contempt for who doesn’t, a hunger for enemies dressed up as pride. That’s not a regional problem. It’s a national one, and it should frighten every single German citizen.
A vote for the AfD is a vote for that same set of beliefs. Whatever anger, disappointment, or legitimate demand to finally be seen or heard got bundled in alongside it.
In April 1932, the Nazi party became the strongest party in the state election in the region that now makes up Saxony-Anhalt, with 40.7% of the vote, and formed, with coalition partners, the first Nazi-led state government in Germany. Whatever happens next, it will be hard to say we didn’t know.
- 
  Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalist
